title: What Stops Recursive Self-Improvement in Robotics? Lessons from 123 Rounds of Agentic Skill Discovery
summary: Can a robot improve itself the way coding agents now improve software? We built an agentic system to find out. It watches a robot fail, works out which capability is missing, writes new skills or finds and installs external models, tests every change in simulation, and repeats, with no human writing robot code. We ran it for 123 improvement rounds on household manipulation tasks. This report describes what we learned. The good news is that the agent can discover capabilities on its own: noticing that its targets were out of view, it asked for an active-viewing model, debugged it, and deployed a working search skill. The bad news is that its improvements did not add up. Changes kept passing their tests, yet the target task, putting condiments on the top shelf of a fridge, never succeeded. We found that the agent was rarely the bottleneck. Three things around it were. First, chained perception modules do not understand relations. Segmenters such as SAM 3 find shelves but not "the top shelf", so the agent filled the gap with ever more geometric rules that never converged, when what it needed was a different kind of model. Second, skill chains lock learning onto the first step. Long tasks mostly fail early, so evidence and fixes pile up there, and later skills are rarely reached, tested, or improved. Third, what the agent learns is decided by the harness. The agent optimized exactly what the evaluator measured, including where it was wrong, and weak tests and misleading memory turned activity into a standstill. We distill these lessons into concrete recommendations for building robot systems that improve themselves, each paired with an experiment that could prove it wrong.

AI.tldr: An agentic system self-improved a robot over 123 rounds of household manipulation tasks; it autonomously discovered and deployed new skills, but its improvements never compounded—the target task (placing condiments on the top fridge shelf) never succeeded. The real bottlenecks were three elements surrounding the agent: relational blindness of chained perception modules, early-step lock-in in skill chains, and an evaluator/harness that dictated and misdirected learning. The authors distill these into concrete recommendations, each paired with a falsifying experiment.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a robot can improve itself the way coding agents now improve software. It aims to test an end-to-end agentic loop—failure detection, capability gap identification, skill writing or external model installation, simulation testing, and iteration—with no human-written robot code, and to understand why such self-improvement may fail to accumulate.
AI.method: Build an agentic system that watches a robot fail, diagnoses the missing capability, writes new skills or finds and installs external models, tests every change in simulation, and repeats. Run it for 123 improvement rounds on household manipulation tasks, with the target task of putting condiments on the top shelf of a fridge. Analyze the failures to identify bottlenecks.
AI.result: The agent could discover capabilities on its own: noticing targets were out of view, it requested an active-viewing model, debugged it, and deployed a working search skill. However, improvements did not add up; changes kept passing their tests while the target task never succeeded. The agent was rarely the bottleneck; three surrounding factors were: (1) chained perception modules do not understand relations—segmenters such as SAM 3 find shelves but not "the top shelf", so the agent filled the gap with geometric rules that never converged; (2) skill chains lock learning onto the first step—long tasks fail early, so evidence and fixes pile up there and later skills are rarely reached, tested, or improved; (3) the harness decides what the agent learns—the agent optimized exactly what the evaluator measured, including where it was wrong, and weak tests and misleading memory turned activity into standstill.
AI.conclusion: Self-improving robot systems require addressing the environment around the agent, not just the agent itself. The paper distills lessons into concrete recommendations for building robot systems that improve themselves, each paired with an experiment that could prove it wrong.

title: Robot Manipulation with GPT-6-Astra: Body Knowledge, Experience Reuse, Emergent Skills, and Sim2Real Transfer
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables. Code, data, prompts, and skills: https://github.com/hesd10/astra-robot-sim2real
summary: General-purpose multimodal agents can write robot-control programs, but repeated exploration and model-mediated action selection can make execution slow. We study how external body knowledge, successful experience, and executable skills improve an XLeRobot controlled by GPT-6-Astra in a simulated and a physical elevator-button task. In 30 fixed-start simulation trials, complete robot geometry and camera information reduce mean completion time by 57.4% relative to a baseline with only the common control interface and no prior experience; images with synchronized action and state records reduce it by 68.6% without additional body assets. In nine paired comparisons (18 trials) at starts displaced by 10-100 cm, experience recorded at the original start reduces mean time by 58-63% relative to no experience, demonstrating generalization to the tested new starting positions. During experience experiments, GPT-6-Astra spontaneously generates a short visual-feedback program. Researcher-refactored versions reduce mean local-task time by 29-31% in 27 simulation trials. Finally, 12 real-robot trials using operator-confirmed button contact demonstrate sim2real reuse: at a shared nominal start, simulation XML assets and simulation experience reduce mean time by 53.0% and 49.9%, respectively; real experience also transfers to two new starts. These results suggest a practical way to build general-purpose manipulation experiments around GPT-6-Astra: supply machine-readable body descriptions and synchronized demonstrations, and turn useful agent-generated feedback routines into reusable skills, while the agent adapts actions from current images. We release all task prompts, trial-level experimental data, and acquired skill implementations at https://github.com/hesd10/astra-robot-sim2real.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how body knowledge, recorded experience, and executable skills speed up an XLeRobot controlled by GPT-6-Astra on an elevator-button task, showing large completion-time reductions in both simulation and real-robot trials.
AI.motivation: General-purpose multimodal agents can write robot-control programs, but repeated exploration and model-mediated action selection make execution slow. The paper asks how external body knowledge, successful experience, and executable skills can improve efficiency.
AI.method: The XLeRobot, controlled by GPT-6-Astra, is evaluated on a simulated and a physical elevator-button task. The authors compare a baseline (common control interface only) against complete robot geometry and camera information, synchronized images with action and state records, experience recorded at original and displaced starts, agent-generated visual-feedback programs, researcher-refactored reusable skills, and sim2real reuse of XML assets and experience.
AI.result: In 30 fixed-start simulation trials, full geometry and camera information cut mean completion time by 57.4%; synchronized images with action/state records cut it by 68.6%. In nine paired comparisons (18 trials) at starts displaced 10-100 cm, original-start experience reduced mean time by 58-63%. Researcher-refactored skills reduced mean local-task time by 29-31% across 27 simulation trials. In 12 real-robot trials, simulation XML assets and simulation experience reduced mean time by 53.0% and 49.9% at a shared nominal start, and real experience transferred to two new starts.
AI.conclusion: A practical recipe for building general-purpose manipulation experiments around GPT-6-Astra is to supply machine-readable body descriptions and synchronized demonstrations, convert useful agent-generated feedback routines into reusable skills, and let the agent adapt actions from current images. Prompts, trial-level data, and skill implementations are released.

title: Reduced Cartesian Kinetostatics for Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots: Residual-Stabilized Full-Shape Propagation
summary: Many planning and control tasks for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) require the complete Cartesian backbone geometry. We present a reduced Cartesian framework for planar, axially compressible TDCRs that propagates equilibrium configurations along prescribed tendon-force and tendon-displacement trajectories. The backbone is represented by two global position fields. Following exact variation, a Taylor-Galerkin reduction condenses prescribed spatial properties and distributed loads into offline moment vectors, yielding analytic reduced residuals and Jacobians without online spatial quadrature or numerical differentiation. Analytical differentiation and residual correction yield first-order rate systems requiring one fixed-dimensional linear solve per rate evaluation after initial equilibrium alignment on a regular branch. Across four simulated cases covering variable tendon routing, nonuniform geometry, axial compression, and their combined effects, the propagated Cartesian shapes and distributed strains closely match pointwise geometrically variable-strain (GVS) equilibrium solutions. Residual correction suppresses propagation drift across the tested step sizes while adding only about 0.98% to the mean update time of uncorrected Euler. The proposed method requires 0.508 ms per update on average, approximately 11 times faster than pointwise GVS solves. Displacement-driven experiments yield a maximum normalized mean backbone position error of 1.02% and a maximum end-effector position error of 0.28%. These results support efficient and accurate Cartesian full-shape prediction along prescribed actuation paths.

AI.tldr: A reduced Cartesian framework propagates complete backbone geometry of planar, axially compressible tendon-driven continuum robots along prescribed actuation trajectories, achieving ~11x speedup over pointwise GVS solves with ~1% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Planning and control tasks for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) require the complete Cartesian backbone geometry, but obtaining full-shape solutions along actuation trajectories is computationally expensive.
AI.method: The backbone is represented by two global position fields for planar, axially compressible TDCRs. Exact variation followed by a Taylor-Galerkin reduction condenses prescribed spatial properties and distributed loads into offline moment vectors, giving analytic reduced residuals and Jacobians without online spatial quadrature or numerical differentiation. Analytical differentiation and residual correction produce first-order rate systems needing one fixed-dimensional linear solve per rate evaluation after initial equilibrium alignment on a regular branch.
AI.result: Across four simulated cases (variable tendon routing, nonuniform geometry, axial compression, and combined effects), propagated Cartesian shapes and distributed strains closely match pointwise GVS equilibrium solutions. Residual correction suppresses propagation drift across tested step sizes, adding only ~0.98% to mean update time of uncorrected Euler. Average update time is 0.508 ms, ~11x faster than pointwise GVS solves. Displacement-driven experiments show max normalized mean backbone position error of 1.02% and max end-effector position error of 0.28%.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables efficient and accurate Cartesian full-shape prediction along prescribed actuation paths, supporting planning and control of tendon-driven continuum robots.

title: Timed Rule-Based Supervision of an End-to-End Autonomous Parking Policy
summary: We study whether a manually specified runtime supervisor can correct recurring failures of an existing end-to-end parking policy in a fixed CARLA parking lot. The vision-based Transformer architecture is inherited from Yang et al.; our contribution is a timed, rule-based Parametric Safety Shield (PSS) applied to its control outputs. The PSS uses hand-calibrated speed, position, and duration thresholds to intervene in observed failure modes, including boundary exits, delayed braking, and stalled or oscillatory control. In the reported closed-loop evaluation, 16 held-out target slots and six initial poses are each evaluated in four rounds (384 attempts per configuration). Target success increases from 327/384 (85.16%) for the retrained policy to 375/384 (97.66%) with the PSS; mean position and orientation errors among successful attempts are 0.21m and 0.33 degrees. These results show an improvement within this simulator setup. The repeated attempts share one map, vehicle, and sensor configuration, and the PSS uses simulator world coordinates; thus the results do not establish generalization to other lots or real vehicles, or a formal safety guarantee.

AI.tldr: A timed, rule-based Parametric Safety Shield (PSS) is added on top of an end-to-end vision-based Transformer parking policy in a fixed CARLA parking lot, raising target success rate from 85.16% to 97.66%.
AI.motivation: An existing end-to-end parking policy exhibits recurring failure modes (boundary exits, delayed braking, stalled or oscillatory control) in a fixed simulator parking lot, and the authors ask whether a manually specified runtime supervisor can correct these without retraining the underlying policy.
AI.method: The vision-based Transformer architecture is inherited from Yang et al.; the contribution is a timed, rule-based Parametric Safety Shield applied to its control outputs. The PSS uses hand-calibrated speed, position, and duration thresholds to intervene in the observed failure modes. Closed-loop evaluation covers 16 held-out target slots and six initial poses, each run in four rounds (384 attempts per configuration).
AI.result: Target success increases from 327/384 (85.16%) for the retrained policy to 375/384 (97.66%) with the PSS; mean position and orientation errors among successful attempts are 0.21m and 0.33 degrees.
AI.conclusion: The PSS yields an improvement within this simulator setup. However, all repeated attempts share one map, vehicle, and sensor configuration, and the PSS relies on simulator world coordinates; thus the results do not establish generalization to other lots or real vehicles, nor a formal safety guarantee.

title: SMARtCARE: Privacy-Preserving Agentic AI Systems for Bounded-Autonomy Clinical Decision Support
comment: Paper accepted to, and to appear in, the 2026 IEEE HealthCom Conference
summary: Long-context clinical AI systems can miss relevant patient history when prior admissions fall outside the active reasoning context. In ICU monitoring, this can cause early vital-sign drift to appear nonspecific even when it resembles a prior deterioration pattern. SMARtCARE addresses this gap through a four-state clinical decision-support architecture: Stable, Meta-cognitive, Assisted, and Regulated (Revoked). Rather than automatically retrieving prior records, SMARtCARE uses a lossy six-channel fingerprint of the patient's prior trajectory. When current drift matches that fingerprint and the prior record is absent from context, the system raises a Meta-cognitive escalation for clinician review; full retrieval occurs only through clinician action in the Assisted state. A patient-identity guard is designed to enforce correct attribution across data loading, logging, and audit layers. Evaluation combines a synthetic Monte Carlo study that validates the state-transition logic and estimator stability, not clinical performance, with real-data runs on both the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV Clinical Database Demos. On MIMIC-III, one prior-pattern recurrence was identified among 14 two-admission patients; on MIMIC-IV, the same pipeline produced no fingerprint matches among 9 two-admission patients, which illustrates a key limitation of a fixed canonical pattern library. Across both runs all logged decisions were fully traceable and correctly attributed. The results support SMARtCARE as a traceable, privacy-aware mechanism for surfacing middle-context risk; they are not a clinical efficacy claim.

AI.tldr: SMARtCARE is a four-state clinical decision-support architecture (Stable, Meta-cognitive, Assisted, Regulated/Revoked) that uses a lossy six-channel fingerprint of prior patient trajectories to surface middle-context risk when relevant history falls outside the active reasoning context. Validated with a synthetic Monte Carlo study plus MIMIC-III/IV Demo runs, it shows fully traceable, correctly attributed decisions and privacy-aware escalation, though fixed pattern libraries limit match rates.
AI.motivation: Long-context clinical AI systems can fail to retrieve relevant patient history when prior admissions fall outside the active reasoning context. In ICU monitoring this causes early vital-sign drift to appear nonspecific, even when it actually mirrors a prior deterioration pattern. The paper targets this "middle-context" gap while addressing privacy and attribution concerns.
AI.method: A four-state decision-support architecture: Stable, Meta-cognitive, Assisted, and Regulated (Revoked). Instead of automatically retrieving prior records, it uses a lossy six-channel fingerprint of the patient's prior trajectory. When current drift matches the fingerprint and the prior record is absent from context, the system triggers a Meta-cognitive escalation for clinician review; full retrieval only happens through clinician action in the Assisted state. A patient-identity guard enforces correct attribution across data loading, logging, and audit layers. Evaluation combines a synthetic Monte Carlo study (validating state-transition logic and estimator stability, not clinical performance) with real-data runs on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV Clinical Database Demos.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III, one prior-pattern recurrence was identified among 14 two-admission patients. On MIMIC-IV, the same pipeline produced no fingerprint matches among 9 two-admission patients, illustrating a key limitation of a fixed canonical pattern library. Across both runs, all logged decisions were fully traceable and correctly attributed.
AI.conclusion: SMARtCARE supports a traceable, privacy-aware mechanism for surfacing middle-context risk through clinician-gated escalation rather than automatic retrieval. The findings demonstrate traceability and attribution integrity, but do not constitute a clinical efficacy claim; low match rates highlight the limitation of a fixed canonical pattern library.

title: Path Planning with Motion Primitives in Dynamic Environments: SIPP on Lattices
comment: Accepted to International Conference on Interactive Collaborative Robotics (ICR 2026), Vladivostok, Russia
summary: Autonomous navigation in dynamic environments is a critical challenge, particularly when spaces are shared with other mobile agents whose future trajectories are known. While traditional grid-based planners efficiently find collision-free paths, their reliance on stop-and-turn mechanics over $2^k$-connected grids produces piecewise-linear trajectories that are kinodynamically highly sub-optimal for differentially constrained robots. In this paper, we present an adaptation of Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) that operates on state lattices, utilizing precomputed, kinodynamically smooth motion primitives. To efficiently handle dynamic environments, we rasterize the spatiotemporal swept volumes of moving obstacles directly onto the grid, treating grid cells as atomic units of space, whose resolution is typically dictated by inherent localization noise. We perform a comprehensive comparative analysis between our lattice-based approach and $2^k$-connected grid planners across diverse topological environments. Our evaluation considers a broad spectrum of performance metrics, including planning time, path angularity, cumulative heading change (angle-over-length), and bending energy. The results demonstrate that while the expanded state space of lattice-based search increases computational overhead, it yields trajectories with significantly superior kinodynamic properties. Specifically, our method achieves a reachability comparable to highly connected grids while ensuring smooth, continuous, and physically executable paths ready for real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) to state lattices using kinodynamically smooth motion primitives, rasterizing moving-obstacle swept volumes onto the grid, and shows superior trajectory smoothness over 2^k-connected grid planners at higher computational cost.
AI.motivation: Autonomous navigation in dynamic environments shared with other mobile agents whose future trajectories are known is challenging. Traditional grid-based planners find collision-free paths but rely on stop-and-turn mechanics over 2^k-connected grids, producing piecewise-linear trajectories that are kinodynamically sub-optimal for differentially constrained robots.
AI.method: An adaptation of Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) operating on state lattices with precomputed, kinodynamically smooth motion primitives. Spatiotemporal swept volumes of moving obstacles are rasterized directly onto the grid, treating grid cells as atomic spatial units whose resolution is typically dictated by localization noise. A comparative analysis against 2^k-connected grid planners is performed across diverse topological environments.
AI.result: Evaluation uses metrics including planning time, path angularity, cumulative heading change (angle-over-length), and bending energy. The expanded state space of lattice-based search increases computational overhead but yields trajectories with significantly superior kinodynamic properties. The method achieves reachability comparable to highly connected grids while ensuring smooth, continuous, physically executable paths.
AI.conclusion: Lattice-based SIPP sacrifices computational efficiency yet delivers kinodynamically superior, real-world-deployable trajectories, offering a favorable trade-off between planning overhead and trajectory quality for differentially constrained robots in dynamic environments.

title: Witeness Overlap: Directional Provenance Inside Open-Weight Model Families
summary: Open-weight models are often released, fine-tuned, aligned, merged, and re-released, making provenance audits ask not only whether checkpoints are related, but also which checkpoint came first. Many existing model-provenance methods are designed for a base-known audit setting: given a victim or source model, they test whether a suspect model is related to it. Although these audits are framed as source-to-suspect tests, their underlying evidence is often symmetric, relying on representation similarity, weight similarity, behavioral fingerprints, or correlation statistics. Symmetric pairwise comparisons can detect relatedness, but they cannot by themselves orient relationship between checkpoints A and B. We therefore introduce a local geometric comparison: instead of comparing two checkpoints directly, we add a third same-family checkpoint as a witness and compare the geometry around each candidate endpoint. Direction is inferred by asking which candidate behaves more like a branching parent. Motivated by this idea, and by the empirically observed asymmetry between parent-anchored and child-anchored witness-overlap distributions, we propose Witness Overlap, a prompt-free, training-free white-box test for directional provenance. On 176 LLM checkpoints from 16 families, our one-witness test orients 95.3\% of parent-child decisions using Frobenius cosine. We further evaluate root identification, sibling discrimination, generalizations to VLM and diffusion families, and chain-structured ordering. The signal is robust to weight noise and sparse pruning, with a proposed SVD weight reduction variant showing greater robustness than Frobenius cosine.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Witness Overlap, a prompt-free, training-free white-box test using a third same-family checkpoint as a "witness" to infer directional provenance between checkpoints, achieving 95.3% accuracy on parent-child orientation across 176 LLM checkpoints.
AI.motivation: Open-weight models are frequently fine-tuned, aligned, merged, and re-released, so provenance audits must determine not only whether checkpoints are related but which came first. Existing provenance methods rely on symmetric evidence (representation/weight similarity, behavioral fingerprints, correlation statistics), which can detect relatedness but cannot orient the direction of the relationship between checkpoints A and B.
AI.method: The authors propose a local geometric comparison: rather than comparing two checkpoints directly, they add a third same-family checkpoint as a witness and compare the geometry around each candidate endpoint, inferring direction by determining which candidate behaves more like a branching parent. This is motivated by the empirically observed asymmetry between parent-anchored and child-anchored witness-overlap distributions, yielding Witness Overlap—a prompt-free, training-free white-box test for directional provenance.
AI.result: On 176 LLM checkpoints from 16 families, the one-witness test orients 95.3% of parent-child decisions using Frobenius cosine. The authors also evaluate root identification, sibling discrimination, generalization to VLM and diffusion families, and chain-structured ordering. The signal is robust to weight noise and sparse pruning, with an SVD weight reduction variant showing greater robustness than Frobenius cosine.
AI.conclusion: Directional model provenance can be recovered from symmetric pairwise comparisons by introducing a third witness checkpoint and analyzing local geometry. Witness Overlap provides an effective, training-free, prompt-free method for orienting parent-child relationships, with robustness to noise and pruning and applicability across model families and structured provenance chains.

title: Humanoid Badminton: Learning Dynamic Racket Skills from Limited Human Motion Data
summary: High-speed racket sports provide a demanding testbed for humanoid robots, requiring time-critical decisions, precise striking, and dynamic whole-body coordination. In badminton, fast-changing shuttle trajectories require timely contact decisions, while successful returns demand precise racket pose and velocity within a brief contact window and across a broad three-dimensional striking workspace. Human motion data provide valuable priors for such athletic skills, but usable badminton references are limited and imperfect. Direct tracking provides insufficient executable variation for diverse shuttle conditions, while purely task-driven optimization may produce unnatural motion. To address these challenges, we present a three-stage hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for dynamic humanoid badminton. First, task-randomized motion augmentation expands sparse annotated hitting events into executable target-conditioned stroke variations, forming a continuous latent skill space. Second, a high-level planner outputs continuous latent skill codes to compose these skills online according to the observed shuttle state. Third, a context-conditioned adversarial regularizer encourages more natural planner-level skill usage while preserving return performance. When deployed on a real humanoid robot, our system achieves sustained multi-skill rallies with human players, including forehand, backhand, and highly dynamic jump returns. This is the first real-world humanoid racket-sport system to demonstrate multi-skill human--robot rallies including highly dynamic jump returns.

AI.tldr: A three-stage hierarchical reinforcement learning framework enables a real humanoid robot to perform dynamic badminton rallies with humans, including forehand, backhand, and jump returns.
AI.motivation: High-speed racket sports are a demanding testbed for humanoid robots, requiring time-critical decisions, precise striking, and whole-body coordination. In badminton, fast shuttle trajectories demand timely contact decisions and precise racket pose/velocity within a brief contact window across a 3D workspace. Human motion data offer useful priors, but usable badminton references are limited and imperfect: direct tracking yields insufficient executable variation for diverse shuttle conditions, while purely task-driven optimization can produce unnatural motion.
AI.method: Three-stage hierarchical RL framework: (1) task-randomized motion augmentation expands sparse annotated hitting events into executable target-conditioned stroke variations, forming a continuous latent skill space; (2) a high-level planner outputs continuous latent skill codes to compose skills online from observed shuttle state; (3) a context-conditioned adversarial regularizer promotes natural planner-level skill usage while preserving return performance.
AI.result: Deployed on a real humanoid robot, the system achieves sustained multi-skill rallies with human players, including forehand, backhand, and highly dynamic jump returns.
AI.conclusion: The work presents the first real-world humanoid racket-sport system demonstrating multi-skill human–robot rallies, including highly dynamic jump returns.

title: CP-Agent: A Harness-Engineered Agent for Crystal Plasticity Simulation Workflows
summary: Crystal plasticity (CP) simulations predict the mechanical behavior of polycrystalline metals, yet their routine use is hindered by the manual effort of configuring heterogeneous tools, orchestrating multi-step data pipelines, and calibrating constitutive parameters against experiments. These bottlenecks impede productivity in systematic parameter studies, motivating interest in automated workflows. This study presents CP-Agent, a harness-engineered LLM-based agent that autonomously executes complete CP modeling workflows from natural-language tasks. Operating under the ReAct paradigm, the agent reasons about tool selection and sequencing while delegating numerical search to established optimizers. The harness comprises a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions, a dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop, encoding domain knowledge through tool schemas rather than hard-coded logic. CP-Agent is demonstrated on four case studies: calibrating four slip parameters of additively manufactured stainless steel 316L against tensile data; validating the workflow against published copper benchmarks, reproducing stress-strain and texture evolution; recovering the initial crystallographic texture of copper, where the agent correctly identifies a diffuse initial texture; and reproducing the multi-pass rolling texture evolution of a Mg-Zn-Ca alloy, where the agent chains five deformation passes and recovers the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. In all cases, the agent inferred the correct execution sequence from the task statement, robustly across repeated runs, and delivered physically interpretable results. This work establishes harness engineering as a systematic approach to automating CP modeling workflows while maintaining physical interpretability and auditability through visible reasoning traces.

AI.tldr: CP-Agent is a harness-engineered LLM agent that autonomously runs complete crystal plasticity modeling workflows from natural-language tasks, demonstrated across four case studies spanning parameter calibration, benchmark validation, texture recovery, and multi-pass rolling simulation.
AI.motivation: Crystal plasticity simulations are powerful for predicting polycrystalline metal behavior, but their routine use is limited by manual effort: configuring heterogeneous tools, orchestrating multi-step data pipelines, and calibrating constitutive parameters against experiments. These bottlenecks hamper systematic parameter studies, creating a need for automated, reliable workflows.
AI.method: CP-Agent is a harness-engineered LLM-based agent operating under the ReAct paradigm. It reasons about tool selection and sequencing while delegating numerical search to established optimizers. The harness consists of a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions, a dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop, encoding domain knowledge through tool schemas rather than hard-coded logic.
AI.result: Four case studies were demonstrated: (1) calibrating four slip parameters of additively manufactured stainless steel 316L against tensile data; (2) validating the workflow against published copper benchmarks, reproducing stress-strain and texture evolution; (3) recovering copper's initial crystallographic texture, correctly identifying a diffuse initial texture; and (4) reproducing multi-pass rolling texture evolution of a Mg-Zn-Ca alloy, chaining five deformation passes and recovering the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. In all cases, the agent inferred the correct execution sequence from the task statement, was robust across repeated runs, and delivered physically interpretable results.
AI.conclusion: Harness engineering is established as a systematic approach to automating crystal plasticity modeling workflows, while maintaining physical interpretability and auditability through visible reasoning traces.

title: PHIRL: Aligning Learned Rewards with Task Progress for Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: Human demonstrations provide dense policy-level information but sometimes lack local precision. Human feedback presents accurate local critiques, but offers sparse evaluations rather than direct policy guidance. We propose Progress-Heuristicized Inverse Reinforcement Learning (PHIRL), a data-efficient framework that learns robust reward functions by jointly leveraging demonstrations and feedback. Specifically, we use progress, a feedback modality that describes cumulative task completion. PHIRL iteratively infers a reward function from demonstrations via inverse reinforcement learning, calculates the learned rewards over the progress-annotated demonstrations, and aligns the rewards with progress annotations over four dimensions. We evaluate PHIRL on real and simulated robot tasks, with additional exploration using a fine-tuned vision-language model to provide progress feedback. Results demonstrate that PHIRL significantly outperforms the baselines, achieving substantially higher environmental return rewards and task success with only twenty percent of demonstrations annotated. Analysis of reward-hacking scenarios demonstrates that PHIRL learned reward functions are reliable against exploitation.

AI.tldr: PHIRL jointly leverages demonstrations and progress feedback to learn robust reward functions, outperforming baselines with only 20% of demonstrations annotated.
AI.motivation: Human demonstrations offer dense policy-level information but lack local precision, while human feedback provides accurate local critiques but is sparse rather than direct policy guidance. The paper aims to combine the strengths of both modalities for data-efficient reward learning.
AI.method: PHIRL iteratively infers a reward function from demonstrations via inverse reinforcement learning, computes learned rewards over progress-annotated demonstrations, and aligns those rewards with progress annotations (a cumulative task completion feedback modality) along four dimensions.
AI.result: Evaluated on real and simulated robot tasks, with additional exploration using a fine-tuned vision-language model to supply progress feedback, PHIRL substantially outperforms baselines, achieving higher environmental return rewards and task success with only 20% of demonstrations annotated. Reward-hacking analysis shows the learned reward functions are reliable against exploitation.
AI.conclusion: Jointly leveraging demonstrations and progress feedback yields data-efficient, robust reward functions, and PHIRL's learned rewards resist reward hacking, making it effective for real and simulated robot tasks.

title: ConflictVLA-Bench: Benchmarking Behavioral Responses of Vision-Language-Action Models to Premise Conflicts
summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform strongly on manipulation tasks, their responses to invalid task premises remain underexplored. Existing evaluations of premise conflicts often focus on terminal task outcomes, yet task failure alone cannot distinguish behavioral disengagement from continued pursuit followed by an execution error. We call the latter pattern Failed Persistence. To study this phenomenon, we introduce ConflictVLA-Bench, which pairs conflict rollouts with premise-consistent reference rollouts and evaluates both outcomes and execution processes. Built on LIBERO, the benchmark contains 2,826 prompt-conditioned conflict tasks spanning four conflict families, four structural configurations, and two prompt conditions. Across all eight VLAs, invalid premises reduce original goal completion by at least 17.3 percentage points, with the reduction reaching 56.2 percentage points for OpenVLA. Crucially, even when models succeed on premise-consistent tasks and fail on their matched conflict tasks, they often continue to approach the original targets, retain early trajectory structure, and show limited action magnitude suppression. Failed Persistence therefore recurs across the evaluated models. Explicit premise checking does not consistently produce selective and coordinated behavioral changes. These findings show that terminal failure alone establishes neither behavioral disengagement nor refusal and that outcomes alone are insufficient for VLA evaluation. Experimental data and additional details are available on the project page: https://github.com/EmbodiedAISurvey/ConflictVLA-Bench

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ConflictVLA-Bench to study how Vision-Language-Action models respond to invalid task premises, revealing a recurring "Failed Persistence" pattern where models continue pursuing unachievable original goals rather than disengaging, demonstrating that outcome-based evaluation alone is insufficient.
AI.motivation: While VLA models perform strongly on manipulation tasks, their responses to invalid task premises remain underexplored. Existing evaluations focus on terminal task outcomes, but task failure alone cannot distinguish behavioral disengagement from continued pursuit followed by an execution error. The authors identify this distinction as critical yet unstudied.
AI.method: The authors introduce ConflictVLA-Bench, built on LIBERO, pairing conflict rollouts with premise-consistent reference rollouts and evaluating both outcomes and execution processes. The benchmark contains 2,826 prompt-conditioned conflict tasks spanning four conflict families, four structural configurations, and two prompt conditions. Eight VLAs are evaluated on this benchmark.
AI.result: Across all eight VLAs, invalid premises reduce original goal completion by at least 17.3 percentage points, with reductions reaching 56.2 percentage points for OpenVLA. Even when models succeed on premise-consistent tasks and fail on matched conflict tasks, they often continue to approach original targets, retain early trajectory structure, and show limited action magnitude suppression, confirming recurring Failed Persistence. Explicit premise checking does not consistently produce selective and coordinated behavioral changes.
AI.conclusion: Terminal failure alone establishes neither behavioral disengagement nor refusal, and outcomes alone are insufficient for VLA evaluation. The recurring Failed Persistence pattern demonstrates the need for process-level evaluation of VLA models.

title: Efficient Bezier Velocity Optimization for Free-Floating Space Manipulators
summary: We present FAVOR (Free-floating Arm Velocity Optimization with Recursive Sensitivities), a planner for collision-free reaching, tracking, and prescribed-time pre-grasp interception on an unactuated spacecraft. It optimizes Bezier joint-velocity curves with linear velocity, acceleration, and continuity constraints. Decision dimension is independent of rollout resolution. Analytical recursive sensitivities provide task and clearance gradients through the coupled base-arm motion. Parallel evaluation, caching, and incremental collision discovery reduce computation. With a seven-DoF arm and five simulated spacecraft models, FAVOR achieves 99.8% point-to-point success with 1.779 s mean computation, versus 62.9% and 50.270 s for an IK-initialized position-spline baseline. Means include failures and timeouts. FAVOR completes 30 of 36 tracking cases, versus 15 for single-step QP, and all 36 interception instances, versus 22 for the spline baseline. A controlled ablation shows that finite differences increase mean planning time 4.7-fold.

AI.tldr: FAVOR is a motion planner for a free-floating spacecraft's arm that optimizes Bezier joint-velocity curves with analytical recursive sensitivities, achieving 99.8% success in point-to-point reaching and outperforming IK-initialized spline and single-step QP baselines across tracking and prescribed-time interception tasks.
AI.motivation: Planning collision-free arm motion on an unactuated (free-floating) spacecraft is challenging because the arm's motion perturbs the coupled base, so task and clearance gradients must propagate through combined base-arm dynamics. Prior baselines (IK-initialized position-spline, single-step QP) show low success and high computation, motivating a more efficient, robust planner.
AI.method: FAVOR optimizes Bezier joint-velocity curves subject to linear velocity, acceleration, and continuity constraints, decoupling decision dimension from rollout resolution. Analytical recursive sensitivities yield task and clearance gradients through the coupled base-arm motion. Parallel evaluation, caching, and incremental collision discovery reduce computation.
AI.result: With a seven-DoF arm and five simulated spacecraft models: 99.8% point-to-point success at 1.779 s mean computation vs. 62.9% and 50.270 s for the IK-initialized position-spline baseline (means include failures/timeouts). Tracking: 30/36 vs. 15/36 for single-step QP. Interception: 36/36 vs. 22/36 for the spline baseline. A controlled ablation shows finite differences increase mean planning time 4.7-fold.
AI.conclusion: FAVOR provides an efficient, high-success planner for reaching, tracking, and prescribed-time pre-grasp interception on free-floating spacecraft, with analytical recursive sensitivities and computational optimizations delivering substantial gains over spline and QP baselines; analytical gradients markedly outperform finite differences in planning time.

title: Working with AI: A Design Framework for Human-AI Collaboration
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly GenAI, is becoming an increasingly important part of modern work. In industrial settings, AI can support decision-making, automate routine activities, assist humans, and improve productivity. However, successful AI adoption depends on more than what the technology can do. It also depends on how people experience and work with it. This raises an important question: how should human-AI collaboration be designed so that it works well for both people and organisations? This white paper addresses that question by presenting a practical framework for designing human-AI collaboration. The framework considers the human, the AI system, the task, the organisation, and the wider societal environment. It explains what effective collaboration looks like, what conditions influence it, what requirements should be met, and what design decisions organisations should consider. The report also includes a human-AI collaborative assembly system with cobot use case to demonstrate how the framework can be applied in practice. The use case shows how design requirements can be translated into specific collaboration features and evaluated through a case study. The aim of this white paper is to provide a clear and practical guide for designing human-AI collaboration that is effective, human-centred, and responsible.

AI.tldr: This white paper presents a practical framework for designing human-AI collaboration, structured around the human, AI system, task, organisation, and societal environment, and demonstrates its application via a cobot-based collaborative assembly use case.
AI.motivation: Successful AI adoption in industrial settings depends not only on technological capability but also on how people experience and work with AI. This raises the need to understand how human-AI collaboration should be designed to benefit both people and organisations.
AI.method: The paper develops a practical design framework covering five dimensions: the human, the AI system, the task, the organisation, and the wider societal environment. It specifies what effective collaboration looks like, the conditions influencing it, the requirements to be met, and the design decisions organisations should consider. The framework is applied through a human-AI collaborative assembly system with a cobot use case, translating design requirements into concrete collaboration features evaluated via a case study.
AI.result: The white paper furnishes a clear practical framework for human-AI collaboration design and shows, through the collaborative assembly cobot use case, how design requirements can be operationalised into specific collaboration features and assessed in a case study.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a clear, practical guide for designing human-AI collaboration that is effective, human-centred, and responsible, addressing the human, technological, task, organisational, and societal facets of collaboration.

title: Differentiable Dynamics for Autonomous Micro-Mobility Navigation
summary: Autonomous micro-mobility vehicles (MMVs) such as wheelchairs, scooters, and bicycles have the potential to improve mobility access and support safe low-speed transportation in pedestrian-shared spaces. Achieving MMV autonomy will require realistic, predictable MMV motion. However, many existing autonomous vehicle stacks rely on simplified kinematic models that fail to capture key MMV characteristics such as tire slip, friction, and wheel layouts, limiting realism and gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we explore differentiable formulations of dynamics models for autonomous micro-mobility systems. We first construct DiffKBM, a differentiable version of the kinematic bicycle model (KBM). Then, we introduce DiffGM3, a differentiable formulation of the General Micro-Mobility Model (GM3), a unified tire-based dynamics formulation for micro-mobility vehicles that supports a wide range of MMV configurations. DiffKBM and DiffGM3 enable end-to-end differentiable optimization through MMV dynamics, making them suitable for integration into differentiable autonomy stacks. We evaluate these dynamics models in both open-loop and closed-loop settings: (1) open-loop trajectory matching, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are integrated as a dynamics layer within DiffStack and optimized to reproduce real-world MMV trajectories, and (2) closed-loop autonomous navigation, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are paired with a differentiable MPC controller in CrowdNav pedestrian scenarios. In the open-loop setting, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in reproducing trajectories with improvements in ADE and NLL across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle modes, and reductions in planning loss for bicycle and motorcycle trajectories. We also find that, in closed-loop settings, DiffGM3 improves on DiffKBM's CrowdNav performance by producing 55\% fewer collisions and a 75\% lower discomfort frequency for the bicycle mode.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DiffKBM and DiffGM3, differentiable dynamics models for autonomous micro-mobility vehicles, and shows DiffGM3 better reproduces real trajectories and enables safer, smoother closed-loop navigation.
AI.motivation: Autonomous micro-mobility vehicles (MMVs) like wheelchairs, scooters, and bicycles can improve mobility access and support safe low-speed transport in pedestrian-shared spaces. However, existing autonomous vehicle stacks typically rely on simplified kinematic models that ignore key MMV characteristics such as tire slip, friction, and wheel layouts, which limits realism and gradient-based optimization.
AI.method: The authors construct DiffKBM, a differentiable version of the kinematic bicycle model, and DiffGM3, a differentiable formulation of the General Micro-Mobility Model (GM3), a unified tire-based dynamics formulation supporting diverse MMV configurations. Both enable end-to-end differentiable optimization through MMV dynamics and are evaluated in open-loop trajectory matching (integrated as a dynamics layer in DiffStack) and closed-loop autonomous navigation (paired with a differentiable MPC controller in CrowdNav pedestrian scenarios).
AI.result: In open-loop settings, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in reproducing trajectories, improving ADE and NLL across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle modes, and reducing planning loss for bicycle and motorcycle trajectories. In closed-loop settings, DiffGM3 improves CrowdNav performance over DiffKBM for the bicycle mode, producing 55% fewer collisions and 75% lower discomfort frequency.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable tire-based MMV dynamics, particularly DiffGM3, yield more realistic trajectory reproduction and safer, more comfortable closed-loop navigation than simpler differentiable kinematic models, supporting integration into differentiable autonomy stacks.

title: DriveHierarchy: A Benchmark for Diagnosing VLM Driving Capabilities from Open-Loop Understanding to Closed-Loop Execution
summary: Evaluating VLM-based autonomous driving remains difficult because driving competence is composite, where a capable system must ground traffic participants and hazards, integrate context across views and time, reason about future evolution, and act appropriately under closed-loop interaction. Existing benchmarks usually assess either open-loop understanding or closed-loop driving but provide limited structure for explaining how these abilities are organized, how they relate, and how they may inform model diagnosis and improvement. We present \textsc{DriveHierarchy}, a hierarchical benchmark that organizes VLM-based autonomous driving into four ranks, spanning perceptual grounding, contextual memory, mental reasoning, and closed-loop execution. To instantiate this hierarchy, we integrate multiple open-source autonomous-driving datasets into a unified open-loop benchmark with 76,798 question-answer pairs over 84,279 frames and develop a closed-loop simulation platform with interactive scenario construction on a real-world road network, from which 100 driving scenarios are curated for embodied evaluation. Experiments on 15 VLMs show that \textsc{DriveHierarchy} captures structured but non-redundant capability variation, relates open-loop understanding to closed-loop driving, and provides a practical basis for diagnosis and benchmark-guided optimization. \textsc{DriveHierarchy} therefore serves as a unified framework for evaluating and improving VLM-based autonomous driving systems. An anonymized project has been released on https://github.com/PerfectXu88/DriveHierarchy

AI.tldr: DriveHierarchy is a hierarchical benchmark that organizes VLM-based autonomous driving into four ranks—perceptual grounding, contextual memory, mental reasoning, and closed-loop execution—with 76,798 QA pairs over 84,279 frames plus 100 closed-loop scenarios, enabling structured, non-redundant diagnosis of 15 VLMs.
AI.motivation: Driving competence is composite: a capable system must ground traffic participants and hazards, integrate context across views and time, reason about future evolution, and act under closed-loop interaction. Existing benchmarks assess either open-loop understanding or closed-loop driving, offering limited structure for explaining how these abilities are organized, how they relate, and how they inform model diagnosis and improvement.
AI.method: The authors propose DriveHierarchy, a hierarchical benchmark with four ranks spanning perceptual grounding, contextual memory, mental reasoning, and closed-loop execution. They integrate multiple open-source autonomous-driving datasets into a unified open-loop benchmark comprising 76,798 QA pairs over 84,279 frames, and build a closed-loop simulation platform with interactive scenario construction on a real-world road network, curating 100 driving scenarios for embodied evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on 15 VLMs show that DriveHierarchy captures structured but non-redundant capability variation, relates open-loop understanding to closed-loop driving, and provides a practical basis for diagnosis and benchmark-guided optimization.
AI.conclusion: DriveHierarchy serves as a unified framework for evaluating and improving VLM-based autonomous driving systems, with an anonymized project released at https://github.com/PerfectXu88/DriveHierarchy.

title: Game-Theoretic Control with Constrained Potential Surgery
summary: Constrained general-sum dynamic games are a popular formulation for highly interactive multi-agent planning problems. In recent years, Generalized Nash Equilibrium (GNE) solvers have achieved real-time performance for small dynamic games. However, solution speed still remains a bottleneck, and controlling even a small number of agents (e.g., more than four) in a dynamic task remains elusive. In addition, Newton solvers that focus on the first-order conditions are vulnerable to non-Nash saddle points, limiting the usefulness of the provided solution. In this work, we propose a fast and versatile interior point solver for constrained dynamic games, along with a computationally efficient second-order correction that increases the probability of converging to a local GNE solution in constrained dynamic games. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on numerical benchmarks and a physical experiment involving scaled race cars.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a fast interior point solver for constrained general-sum dynamic games, with an efficient second-order correction that improves convergence to local Generalized Nash Equilibria, validated on benchmarks and a scaled race car experiment.
AI.motivation: Constrained general-sum dynamic games are widely used for highly interactive multi-agent planning. While GNE solvers now achieve real-time performance on small problems, solution speed remains a bottleneck, and controlling more than about four agents in dynamic tasks is still difficult. Additionally, Newton solvers focused on first-order conditions are vulnerable to non-Nash saddle points, which undermines the usefulness of the returned solutions.
AI.method: The authors propose a fast and versatile interior point solver for constrained dynamic games, combined with a computationally efficient second-order correction that increases the likelihood of converging to a local GNE solution in constrained dynamic games.
AI.result: The proposed method's performance is evaluated on numerical benchmarks and a physical experiment involving scaled race cars.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a fast, versatile solver for constrained dynamic games and, via the second-order correction, mitigates saddle-point convergence issues, enabling more reliable GNE solutions and scaling to more agents.

title: LLM Judge Validation Under Sparse Overlap: From Inference to Design
summary: Validating an LLM-as-a-judge requires estimating its agreement with humans, yet annotation budgets rarely allow every item to be multiply labeled. We prove that this \emph{overlap sparsity} is the first-order determinant of wrong deployment decisions: at 5\% pairwise overlap, wrong-decision rates reach 25\% and the probability of selecting the wrong best judge among ten candidates is 65\%. The two actionable levers are overlap \emph{quantity} and \emph{allocation}. For quantity, we derive a minimum-overlap formula showing $ρ\geq 0.25$ suffices for non-borderline judges while borderline cases remain fundamentally hard. For allocation, a zero-cost stratified scheme halves false-rejection rates relative to random sampling when strata are informative. We validate on 10 LLM judges across four evaluation matrices spanning visual assessment, causal reasoning, and summarization.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that overlap sparsity in human annotation is the dominant cause of incorrect LLM-judge deployment decisions, and it derives two remedies: a minimum-overlap formula and a zero-cost stratified allocation scheme.
AI.motivation: Validating an LLM-as-a-judge requires estimating its agreement with humans, but annotation budgets rarely permit multiple labels per item, creating sparse pairwise overlap. The paper argues this overlap sparsity is the first-order determinant of wrong deployment decisions, motivating a principled treatment of both how much overlap and how it is allocated.
AI.method: The authors formalize overlap sparsity and derive a minimum-overlap formula, showing that ρ ≥ 0.25 suffices for non-borderline judges while borderline judges remain fundamentally hard. For allocation, they propose a zero-cost stratified scheme that halves false-rejection rates relative to random sampling when strata are informative. Validation covers 10 LLM judges across four evaluation matrices spanning visual assessment, causal reasoning, and summarization.
AI.result: At 5% pairwise overlap, wrong-decision rates reach 25%, and the probability of selecting the wrong best judge among ten candidates is 65%. The derived minimum-overlap threshold (ρ ≥ 0.25) works for non-borderline judges, and the stratified allocation scheme halves false-rejection rates versus random sampling under informative strata.
AI.conclusion: Overlap sparsity, not merely sample size, drives erroneous LLM-judge deployment decisions. Both overlap quantity and overlap allocation are actionable levers, and a low-cost stratified design can substantially reduce false rejections.

title: GT-VLA: Target-Conditioned Trace Guidance for Generalizable Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on robotic manipulation, but they often struggle to generalize to unseen tasks, configurations, and long-horizon settings. A key challenge is that VLAs overfit to training scenes and fail to follow novel language instructions. Off-the-shelf vision-language models (VLMs) often provide stronger generalization, but cannot directly control robot actions. To combine the common sense of VLMs with VLA control, we propose Guided Trace VLA (GT-VLA), a steerable framework that accepts guidance from an external generalist VLM through trace-conditioned action generation. GT-VLA uses a generalist model to identify semantic guidance for the current skill, converts this guidance into a 2D visual trace, and conditions its action policy on the resulting trace-rendered observation. This design separates semantic target acquisition, trace generation, and low-level action execution, allowing high-level guidance to propagate to robot actions. GT-VLA uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with skill-specific trace and action modules for robust execution. We evaluate GT-VLA on LIBERO and a physical robot platform, showing improved generalization over recent VLA baselines in both settings. The code and additional supplemental materials are available on our project website at https://ivaniz.github.io/gt-vla/.

AI.tldr: GT-VLA is a steerable VLA framework that combines a generalist VLM's common sense with robot control by converting VLM-derived semantic guidance into a 2D visual trace and conditioning action generation on it, using a Mixture-of-Experts design with skill-specific trace and action modules.
AI.motivation: VLA models perform well on robotic manipulation but generalize poorly to unseen tasks, configurations, and long-horizon settings—they overfit training scenes and fail to follow novel language instructions. Off-the-shelf VLMs generalize better but cannot directly control robot actions, so there is a need to combine VLM common sense with VLA control.
AI.method: GT-VLA accepts guidance from an external generalist VLM via trace-conditioned action generation. A generalist model identifies semantic guidance for the current skill, which is converted into a 2D visual trace; the action policy is then conditioned on the trace-rendered observation. This separates semantic target acquisition, trace generation, and low-level action execution. A Mixture-of-Experts architecture with skill-specific trace and action modules enables robust execution.
AI.result: Evaluated on LIBERO and a physical robot platform, GT-VLA shows improved generalization over recent VLA baselines in both settings. Code and supplemental materials are available at https://ivaniz.github.io/gt-vla/.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing control into VLM-based semantic guidance, trace generation, and low-level execution—linked through trace-conditioned observations and a skill-specific Mixture-of-Experts design—effectively propagates high-level VLM guidance to robot actions and improves generalization.

title: Metro-WM: Long-Horizon Latent Planning with Realisable Sub-Goals
summary: Model-predictive control with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provides a strong zero-shot goal-reaching planner, but it is only effective over short planning horizons. Hierarchical extensions attempt to bridge this gap by learning a macro planner to predict intermediate latent sub-goals to guide the micro planner. In this work, we demonstrate that unconstrained latent sub-goal prediction is fundamentally flawed. A rigorous evaluation reveals that a leading state-of-the-art macro planner routinely emits physically unrealisable sub-goals. To resolve this, we introduce Metro-WM, a hierarchical framework that issues sub-goals by retrieving genuine states from prior experience rather than generating ungrounded latent vectors. Specifically, Metro-WM constructs a graph whose vertices are observed frames from offline expert demonstrations or random-action trajectories, allowing frames from different episodes to be connected and stitched into routes to the goal. Planning over the full graph also makes the system highly robust to execution errors: if the micro planner drifts off course, Metro-WM instantly finds a new optimal path from the current state. Our experiments show that Metro-WM achieves superior long-horizon success rates of up to 37.33 percentage points over the next best hierarchical approach while being up to 10.9 times faster, requiring both 13-56 times less offline compute and fewer tuned hyperparameters. Additional analysis reveals that Metro-WM finds shorter paths than the offline demonstrations, outperforms an oracle relying on the query's own demonstration, and maintains robust performance under extremely sparse dataset conditions.

AI.tldr: Metro-WM is a hierarchical planning framework that replaces ungrounded latent sub-goal prediction with retrieval of genuine observed states from a graph of offline trajectories, achieving large gains in long-horizon success rate, speed, and compute efficiency.
AI.motivation: JEPA-based model-predictive control offers strong zero-shot goal-reaching but only over short horizons. Existing hierarchical fixes rely on a macro planner that predicts intermediate latent sub-goals; the authors argue this unconstrained latent sub-goal prediction is fundamentally flawed and show a leading macro planner routinely emits physically unrealisable sub-goals.
AI.method: Metro-WM issues sub-goals by retrieving genuine states from prior experience instead of generating ungrounded latent vectors. It constructs a graph whose vertices are observed frames from offline expert demonstrations or random-action trajectories, connects frames across different episodes, and stitches them into routes to the goal. Planning over the full graph also makes the system robust to execution errors: if the micro planner drifts off course, Metro-WM instantly finds a new optimal path from the current state.
AI.result: Metro-WM achieves superior long-horizon success rates of up to 37.33 percentage points over the next best hierarchical approach while being up to 10.9x faster, requiring 13-56x less offline compute and fewer tuned hyperparameters. Additional analysis shows it finds shorter paths than the offline demonstrations, outperforms an oracle relying on the query's own demonstration, and maintains robust performance under extremely sparse dataset conditions.
AI.conclusion: Grounded, retrieval-based sub-goal selection over a trajectory graph is a more effective and efficient alternative to unconstrained latent sub-goal generation for hierarchical JEPA planning, improving long-horizon goal reaching, robustness, and data efficiency.

title: End-to-end QP-based policies: A unified perspective on robust control and robot learning
summary: We present an end-to-end QP-based policy framework that enables systematic policy construction with minimal domain-specific design, while preserving the transparency and interpretability of model-based control. The proposed policy representation supports both domain-randomized model-based auto-tuning, where policy parameters are optimized over distributions of disturbances and model variations, and black-box policy construction, where the problem is formulated in terms of a (possibly) unknown model without requiring explicit notions of states, inputs, or the underlying system dynamics. We establish connections to existing policy representations and control paradigms, including robust control, multilayer perceptrons, and robot learning, and interpret our end-to-end QP policies as a common abstraction of these approaches. We validate the resulting framework in both simulation and hardware, demonstrating a broad range of applications spanning robustness, automatic policy tuning, and control under unknown system dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an end-to-end quadratic program (QP)-based policy framework that enables systematic, minimal-design policy construction while retaining the transparency and interpretability of model-based control, and validates it across simulation and hardware.
AI.motivation: Policymaking often requires heavy domain-specific engineering, while model-based controllers are interpretable but hard to tune; the paper seeks a unified representation that preserves interpretability while supporting automatic tuning and learning under unknown dynamics.
AI.method: A QP-based policy representation that supports (i) domain-randomized model-based auto-tuning, optimizing policy parameters over distributions of disturbances and model variations, and (ii) black-box policy construction formulated in terms of a possibly unknown model without explicit states, inputs, or dynamics; connections to robust control, MLPs, and robot learning are established as a common abstraction.
AI.result: The framework is validated in simulation and hardware, demonstrating robustness, automatic policy tuning, and control under unknown system dynamics across a broad range of applications.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end QP policies serve as a common abstraction linking robust control, neural policies, and robot learning, offering a systematic, interpretable, and broadly applicable policy construction framework.

title: IndustryLLM: Failure-Driven LLM Training for Industrial Procurement
comment: Technical Report, 56 pages, 6 figures. Model weights and configs available at https://huggingface.co/alibaba-multimodal-industrial-ai/IndustryLLM
summary: Industrial procurement requires language models to bridge informal buyer jargon, sparse marketplace attributes, and authoritative engineering standards under strict safety tolerances. We present IndustryLLM, an open-weight industrial language model trained from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base (35B total parameters with ~3B activated per token, with the vision encoder frozen). Rather than relying on generic text scaling, we introduce a failure-driven adaptation recipe spanning continued pre-training (CPT) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). CPT leverages a curated ~100B-token corpus integrating 5B tokens of national standards (e.g., GB/T) and technical archives, 10B tokens of de-identified real-world industrial transaction and inquiry records, and 60B tokens of general replay. To overcome register mismatch and factual brittleness, we systematically reconstruct an estimated 20B-token domain subset via multi-register rewriting across 10 genres and 8 writing styles, confidence-routed minimal factual editing, and error-targeted QA synthesis (resolving colloquial typos like '42-luo-mu' -> 42CrMo, expanding ambiguous codes like '16674' -> GB/T 16674, and clarifying conflicting dimensional specs). For downstream deployment, we formalize an evidence-gated constraint-evaluation interface enforcing three-valued logic where unverified product evidence remains unknown rather than satisfied. Offline evaluations demonstrate consistent gains on procurement-query structuring (+2.97 percentage points in exact match, 95% CI [2.11, 3.86] in No-Think mode), while randomized online A/B experiments in production yield substantial improvements (+4.25% GMV, +8.3% satisfied inquiries) alongside a latency reduction from 6-7 s to 1.5 s. Model weights and configs are released at https://huggingface.co/alibaba-multimodal-industrial-ai/IndustryLLM.

AI.tldr: IndustryLLM is an open-weight industrial domain language model built from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base using a failure-driven CPT+SFT recipe, achieving offline gains and large online production improvements (GMV, satisfied inquiries, latency).
AI.motivation: Industrial procurement requires language models to bridge informal buyer jargon, sparse marketplace attributes, and authoritative engineering standards under strict safety tolerances, a task poorly served by generic text scaling.
AI.method: Failure-driven adaptation recipe spanning continued pre-training (CPT) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). CPT uses a curated ~100B-token corpus: 5B national standards (GB/T) and technical archives, 10B de-identified industrial transaction/inquiry records, 60B general replay. A reconstructed ~20B-token domain subset via multi-register rewriting (10 genres, 8 styles), confidence-routed minimal factual editing, and error-targeted QA synthesis (typo/dialect mapping, code expansion, dimensional conflict resolution). Deployment uses an evidence-gated constraint-evaluation interface with three-valued logic (unknown vs. satisfied).
AI.result: Offline: +2.97 pp exact match on procurement-query structuring (95% CI [2.11, 3.86], No-Think). Online randomized A/B in production: +4.25% GMV, +8.3% satisfied inquiries, latency reduced from 6-7 s to 1.5 s.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific, failure-driven data construction and evidence-gated evaluation yield consistent quality gains and substantial production impact, with weights and configs publicly released.

title: HapticWorld: an Interactive World Simulator with Real-time Torque Feedback
summary: Contact-rich manipulation depends on force sensing that is hard to infer from visual signals alone, both for collecting demonstrations and for training policies. Force-annotated data, however, remains hard to obtain at scale: real-robot collection ties every demonstration to physical hardware, physics simulators report contact forces that deviate systematically from real measurements, and learned world simulators, though scalable and realistic, are vision-only, so operators feel nothing during data collection and the data carries no force/torque (F/T) labels. We present HapticWorld, an interactive world simulator that predicts joint torque together with observations and renders it back to the operator in real time, closing the haptic loop between a human and a learned world model. Across three contact-rich tasks, torque feedback raises data collection throughput by 1.6 times on average. Policies trained on HapticWorld-generated demonstrations succeed in 54/60 real-world trials, approaching the 56/60 upper bound of real-world data, and far exceeding the 19/60 success rate of the vision-only baseline. Moreover, the success rates measured inside HapticWorld closely match real-world evaluation, demonstrating that HapticWorld can serve as a stand-alone F/T-conditioned policy evaluation platform.

AI.tldr: HapticWorld is an interactive, torque-predicting world simulator that closes the haptic loop with a human operator, boosting contact-rich data collection throughput and enabling policies that transfer to real robots far better than vision-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation relies on force sensing that is hard to infer from vision alone, yet large-scale force-annotated data is difficult to obtain: real-robot collection is hardware-bound, physics simulators misreport contact forces relative to reality, and learned world simulators are vision-only, so operators feel nothing and data lacks F/T labels.
AI.method: HapticWorld is an interactive world simulator that predicts joint torque alongside observations and renders that torque back to the operator in real time, closing a haptic loop between the human and the learned world model, thereby enabling force-labeled demonstration collection and policy training.
AI.result: Across three contact-rich tasks, torque feedback raised data collection throughput by 1.6x on average. Policies trained on HapticWorld demonstrations succeeded in 54/60 real-world trials, near the 56/60 real-data upper bound and far above the 19/60 vision-only baseline. In-simulator success rates closely matched real-world evaluation.
AI.conclusion: HapticWorld provides scalable F/T-annotated demonstration data and can serve as a stand-alone F/T-conditioned policy evaluation platform, with in-simulator metrics that predict real-world performance.

title: COUNTERMEM: World-Model Verified Counter-Factual Memory for Language Agents
summary: Existing agent memory frameworks mainly create memory through an agent's interaction with the factual world, e.g., remembering feedback from actions taken to improve performance on future tasks. However, these frameworks seldom ask the "what if" question during memory construction: what if a different action had been taken, would the feedback have changed, and how could this feedback become useful memory? Obtaining such feedback directly in an active environment can be expensive and can alter the state needed for comparison. In this work, we introduce COUNTERMEM, a reinforcement-learning framework for constructing and using verified counterfactual memory across tasks. After a failed action, COUNTERMEM evaluates local alternatives from a copy or reset of the original state using executable world models, such as tests, proof checkers, and solvers. It stores improvements with the original and corrected actions, checked outcomes, and conditions for reuse. A learned memory-use policy selects a retrieved record or skips memory to balance task success and interaction cost, while the base LLM remains fixed. Both memory and policy are frozen during held-out evaluation. We evaluate COUNTERMEM on 12 benchmark settings across six domains. With gpt-oss-120b, COUNTERMEM improves both ReAct and Reflexion on all 12 benchmarks across six domains, averaging a gain of 12.6 percentage points over their unaugmented versions. In the four-domain comparison across two backbones, task-run tokens decrease by 7.7-42.0%, excluding offline selector-training costs. Further analyses show that removing verification or persistent storage weakens the gains, while applying verified corrections to unsuitable decisions can reverse them. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: COUNTERMEM is an RL framework that constructs and uses verified counterfactual memory across tasks, improving ReAct and Reflexion by an average of 12.6 percentage points on 12 benchmarks while reducing task-run tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing agent memory frameworks build memory mainly from an agent's interaction with the factual world (e.g., remembering action feedback), but rarely ask the "what if" question during memory construction: what if a different action had been taken, would feedback have changed, and how could such feedback become useful memory? Directly obtaining this feedback in an active environment is expensive and can alter the state required for comparison.
AI.method: After a failed action, COUNTERMEM evaluates local alternatives from a copy or reset of the original state using executable world models (e.g., tests, proof checkers, solvers). It stores improvements together with original and corrected actions, checked outcomes, and reuse conditions. A learned memory-use policy selects a retrieved record or skips memory to balance task success against interaction cost, while the base LLM remains fixed. Both memory and policy are frozen during held-out evaluation.
AI.result: Evaluated on 12 benchmark settings across six domains. With gpt-oss-120b, COUNTERMEM improves both ReAct and Reflexion on all 12 benchmarks, averaging a 12.6 percentage-point gain over their unaugmented versions. In the four-domain comparison across two backbones, task-run tokens decrease by 7.7–42.0%, excluding offline selector-training costs. Ablations show that removing verification or persistent storage weakens gains, while applying verified corrections to unsuitable decisions can reverse them.
AI.conclusion: Constructing and using verified counterfactual memory, grounded in safe state-reset evaluation and governed by a learned memory-use policy, yields consistent cross-task gains and reduced interaction cost. Verification and persistent storage are essential, and corrections must be applied selectively. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Inertia-Corrected Newton Method For Generalized Nash Equilibria in Dynamic Games with Optimality Verification
summary:
Newton methods efficiently find Generalized Nash Equilibria (GNE) in dynamic games by solving for the KKT necessary conditions. These methods are fast and can support multi-agent Model Predictive Control (MPC) for highly dynamic robots. However, a small KKT residual alone does not certify that the returned solution satisfies the second-order sufficient conditions for a local GNE.
  In this paper, we propose an efficient numerical method to verify the second-order sufficient conditions (SOSC) for a local GNE. We connect the inertia of the agent KKT matrix with the positive definiteness of the reduced Hessian of the cost function, projected onto the null space of the constraints. Furthermore, we introduce an inertia-corrected update step that improves convergence to local GNEs by destabilizing strict saddle points with weak cross-agent coupling.
  Our main contribution is a fast Newton solver for Constrained Dynamic Games that provides efficient optimality checking. Through numerical benchmarks, we demonstrate the proposed solver's runtime and convergence performance in practical multi-agent planning problems. We also validate the solver's real-time capabilities in physical experiments using a platform of miniature autonomous race cars.
