AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fast Newton solver for constrained dynamic games that verifies second-order sufficient conditions (SOSC) for local GNE by connecting KKT matrix inertia to reduced Hessian positive definiteness, plus an inertia-corrected update that destabilizes strict saddle points.
AI.motivation: Newton methods find GNE in dynamic games by solving KKT conditions and are fast enough for multi-agent MPC of highly dynamic robots. However, a small KKT residual alone does not certify that the returned solution satisfies the second-order sufficient conditions for a local GNE, so a fast optimality check is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop an efficient numerical method to verify SOSC for a local GNE. They link the inertia of the agent KKT matrix to the positive definiteness of the reduced Hessian of the cost projected onto the constraint null space, and introduce an inertia-corrected update step that improves convergence to local GNEs by destabilizing strict saddle points with weak cross-agent coupling.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks show the proposed solver's runtime and convergence performance in practical multi-agent planning problems. Real-time capability is validated in physical experiments on a platform of miniature autonomous race cars.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is a fast Newton solver for constrained dynamic games that provides efficient optimality checking, combining SOSC verification with an inertia-corrected update for improved convergence.

title: Context-dependent agent evaluation with orthogonal equilibrium learning
summary: Many applications require to evaluate agents under contextual information (e.g., a prompt, task, or user group). We study how to perform such context-dependent agent evaluation from offline feedback. Existing score-based models for this purpose (e.g., Bradley-Terry) impose a transitive preference ordering, which fails to reflect collective preferences when human judgements are heterogeneous. Inspired by social choice theory, we frame evaluation as a contextual game between two players, each selecting a distribution over agents as the strategy to receive greater collective preference than the other. Then, the support of the Nash equilibrium defines a context-specific set of winners. However, learning context-specific equilibria from offline logs is difficult because each context reveals human feedback on only a subset of agents, and, hence, a naive plug-in estimator can therefore be biased. To address these challenges, we propose NashEval, a general framework for robust contextual equilibrium learning. NashEval first constructs debiased estimates of the contextual payoff matrix that characterizes the game. NashEval then learns the context-to-equilibrium mapping with a tailored orthogonal loss, which avoids the need to solve a separate game for each context. We show theoretically that errors in estimating the nuisance functions underlying the payoff matrix affect the risk of the learned equilibrium (i.e., exploitability) only through higher-order terms. Across various experiments, NashEval improves robustness of equilibrium learning and consistently identifies the set of top-performing agents across contexts.

AI.tldr: NashEval is a framework for context-dependent agent evaluation that frames evaluation as a contextual two-player game, learning debiased contextual equilibria from offline feedback to identify context-specific winner sets that better reflect heterogeneous human preferences.
AI.motivation: Many applications require evaluating agents under contextual information (prompt, task, or user group). Existing score-based models like Bradley-Terry impose a transitive preference ordering, which fails to capture collective preferences when human judgements are heterogeneous. Additionally, learning context-specific equilibria from offline logs is difficult because each context reveals human feedback on only a subset of agents, making naive plug-in estimators biased.
AI.method: Inspired by social choice theory, the authors frame evaluation as a contextual game between two players, each selecting a distribution over agents as a strategy to obtain greater collective preference. The support of the Nash equilibrium defines a context-specific set of winners. They propose NashEval, which (1) constructs debiased estimates of the contextual payoff matrix characterizing the game, and (2) learns the context-to-equilibrium mapping with a tailored orthogonal loss, avoiding the need to solve a separate game per context.
AI.result: The authors prove theoretically that errors in estimating the nuisance functions underlying the payoff matrix affect the risk of the learned equilibrium (exploitability) only through higher-order terms. Across various experiments, NashEval improves robustness of equilibrium learning and consistently identifies the set of top-performing agents across contexts.
AI.conclusion: NashEval provides a general, robust framework for contextual equilibrium learning from offline feedback, enabling context-dependent agent evaluation that better reflects heterogeneous collective preferences than transitive score-based models, with favorable theoretical guarantees and empirical performance.

title: Low Cost Eye Tracking for Vision Screening
summary: This engineering study assesses gaze-assisted data acquisition during visual screening with a Gaze Quest implementation via webcam and GC308 near infrared camera with an Orlosky eye tracking pipeline. Ten subjects performed under both acquisition conditions. Accuracy of Tumbling E orientation, reported application logMAR value,and response latency were determined from keyboard responses and hence are behavioral outputs as opposed toeye tracker screening results. Frame-to-frame change in theangle between successive normalized gaze vectors (28.2degrees) served as the GC308 eye tracker derived diagnostic with an effective sampling rate of roughly 8 FPS. No screen target calibration or gaze to screen translation was done on the GC308 eye tracker output data for the current analysis and hence, these data represent acquisition stability and not gaze accuracy in relation to the target. The webcam pipeline relied on 25-point screen calibration. Because the display resolution and pixel pitch could not be retained in the records of the study, the reported application logMAR values cannot be viewed as measures of visual acuity in any way.

AI.tldr: An engineering study evaluating gaze-assisted data acquisition for visual screening using Gaze Quest, comparing webcam and GC308 near-infrared eye trackers across behavioral and eye-tracking-derived measures in ten subjects.
AI.motivation: To assess the feasibility of gaze-assisted data acquisition during visual screening, addressing how eye tracking pipelines (webcam vs. GC308 near-infrared) can support or augment screening workflows and provide acquisition metrics.
AI.method: Ten subjects performed under two acquisition conditions (webcam and GC308 near-infrared camera) using an Orlosky eye tracking pipeline. Behavioral outputs (Tumbling E orientation accuracy, reported application logMAR value, response latency) were derived from keyboard responses. The GC308 tracker diagnostic was the frame-to-frame change in angle between successive normalized gaze vectors (28.2 degrees), with an effective sampling rate of roughly 8 FPS. Webcam pipeline used 25-point screen calibration. No screen target calibration or gaze-to-screen translation was applied to GC308 output.
AI.result: GC308-derived diagnostic showed a frame-to-frame gaze vector angle change of 28.2 degrees at about 8 FPS. GC308 data represent acquisition stability rather than gaze accuracy relative to targets. Reported application logMAR values cannot be interpreted as measures of visual acuity due to missing display resolution and pixel pitch records.
AI.conclusion: GC308 eye tracker output, without screen calibration, yields acquisition stability metrics rather than gaze accuracy. The study's reported logMAR values are not valid measures of visual acuity. The engineering assessment highlights methodological constraints and the need for retained display parameters for meaningful acuity-related interpretation.

title: Choir: An Open Protocol for Distributed Multi-Agent Autoformalization
summary: AI agents can now formalize entire textbooks and major theorems in proof assistants such as Lean, but current efforts are typically centralized: a single team runs all agents and bears the full computational cost. We introduce Choir, an open protocol for distributed formalization. Choir decomposes a project into tasks that can be completed by independent contributors, each running their own agent with their own LLM subscription, while coordinating entirely through the project's GitHub repository. To support open participation, every contribution is checked by a deterministic gate before merge. Choir supports Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq, and is open source and modular, allowing projects to replace individual components or extend the protocol.

AI.tldr: Choir is an open protocol for distributed formalization that decomposes projects into independently contributable tasks coordinated via GitHub, with deterministic gating of contributions, targeting Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq.
AI.motivation: Formalizing textbooks and major theorems in proof assistants currently relies on centralized efforts where a single team runs all agents and bears the full computational cost. This limits participation and scalability of formalization projects.
AI.method: Choir decomposes a formalization project into tasks that independent contributors can complete, each using their own agent and LLM subscription, coordinating entirely through the project's GitHub repository. A deterministic gate checks every contribution before merge to support open participation.
AI.result: Choir supports Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq, and is open source and modular, allowing projects to replace individual components or extend the protocol.
AI.conclusion: Choir enables decentralized, cost-distributed formalization through an open, modular protocol with deterministic verification, broadening participation beyond a single centralized team.

title: Grasp2Twist: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Jar Opening by Reinforcement Learning
summary: This paper presents Grasp2Twist, a bimanual dexterous manipulation system that learns to grasp and twist open jar lids using reinforcement learning. Learning this task raises three challenges: learning a unified policy for a multi-stage task, sustaining lid twisting, and sim-to-real transfer. To address the first challenge, we introduce a continuous enclosure measure to guide grasp formation and a binary enclosure indicator to guide the grasp-to-twist transition for unified policy learning. We derive both from the geometric relationship between the object center and the convex hull formed by the hand's palm and fingertips. Kinematic constraints limit how far the hand can rotate the lid with fixed contacts, so sustained twisting requires finger contact reconfiguration. We use a three-stage curriculum to facilitate exploration of these contact changes and also improve robustness for sim-to-real transfer. With our approach, the learned policy demonstrates finger gaiting, reconfiguring hand-object contacts to sustain lid rotation. It transfers zero-shot to the physical system and achieves an 88% task success rate across six household containers, including peanut-butter, vitamin, and instant-coffee jars. Ablations further validate the roles of the geometric enclosure in grasp formation and the curriculum in contact-reconfiguration exploration.

AI.tldr: Grasp2Twist is a bimanual dexterous manipulation system that learns to grasp and twist open jar lids via reinforcement learning, using geometric enclosure measures for unified policy learning and a three-stage curriculum for sustained twisting and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer (88% success across six containers).
AI.motivation: Learning to grasp and twist open jar lids bimanually poses three challenges: (1) learning a unified policy for a multi-stage task, (2) sustaining lid twisting under kinematic constraints, and (3) sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: The authors introduce a continuous enclosure measure to guide grasp formation and a binary enclosure indicator to guide the grasp-to-twist transition, both derived from the geometric relationship between the object center and the convex hull formed by the palm and fingertips. A three-stage curriculum facilitates exploration of finger contact reconfiguration (finger gaiting) needed to sustain lid rotation and improves sim-to-real robustness.
AI.result: The learned policy exhibits finger gaiting, reconfiguring hand-object contacts to sustain lid rotation. It transfers zero-shot to the physical system and achieves an 88% task success rate across six household containers (peanut-butter, vitamin, and instant-coffee jars). Ablations validate the roles of the geometric enclosure in grasp formation and the curriculum in contact-reconfiguration exploration.
AI.conclusion: Geometric enclosure measures enable unified multi-stage policy learning, and a curriculum-driven approach supports contact reconfiguration for sustained twisting, yielding effective zero-shot sim-to-real bimanual jar-opening.

title: EmailBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on Enterprise Email and Productivity Tasks
summary: Enterprise email agents must combine information retrieval, structured state changes, temporal reasoning, and multi-step coordination. Recent agent benchmarks include productivity tasks, but few center on typed email workflows in a self-contained environment. We introduce EmailBench, a benchmark of 206 email and productivity scenarios across 16 task categories. The benchmark couples a typed email API specification with provider-neutral naming, a deterministic synthetic Enron-inspired corpus, and a scenario suite whose topic selection was informed by aggregate task-intent telemetry from an interactive prototype. Its hybrid evaluation protocol combines 258 executable static assertions with 211 LLM rubrics. We evaluate eight LM configurations on a fixed single-user corpus. The best-performing configuration passes only 33.5% of scenarios despite 99.7% of its tool calls completing without an observed API failure, with pass rates varying substantially across task categories. This gap shows that valid tool execution is not equivalent to task completion. EmailBench provides a self-contained environment for end-to-end email-agent evaluation, with broader tool coverage, multi-persona testing, and repeated-run evaluation as future work areas.

AI.tldr: EmailBench is a benchmark of 206 email and productivity scenarios across 16 categories, built on a typed email API, a synthetic Enron-inspired corpus, and a hybrid evaluation combining static assertions and LLM rubrics. On eight LM configurations, the best passes only 33.5% of scenarios despite 99.7% of tool calls succeeding.
AI.motivation: Enterprise email agents must integrate information retrieval, structured state changes, temporal reasoning, and multi-step coordination. Existing agent benchmarks cover productivity tasks but rarely focus on typed email workflows in a self-contained environment, leaving a gap for end-to-end email-agent evaluation.
AI.method: EmailBench comprises 206 email and productivity scenarios spanning 16 task categories. It couples a typed email API specification with provider-neutral naming, a deterministic synthetic Enron-inspired corpus, and a scenario suite whose topic selection was informed by aggregate task-intent telemetry from an interactive prototype. Evaluation uses a hybrid protocol of 258 executable static assertions plus 211 LLM rubrics, tested on eight LM configurations over a fixed single-user corpus.
AI.result: The best-performing configuration passes only 33.5% of scenarios, even though 99.7% of its tool calls complete without an observed API failure; pass rates vary substantially across task categories.
AI.conclusion: Valid tool execution is not equivalent to task completion, exposing a substantial gap between API-level success and end-to-end task success. EmailBench offers a self-contained environment for end-to-end email-agent evaluation, with broader tool coverage, multi-persona testing, and repeated-run evaluation left as future work.

title: Find Something You Can't Do: Agentic Real-World Reinforcement Learning for Self-Improving VLA Models
summary: Vision--language--action (VLA) models provide strong priors for robotic manipulation but are typically deployed as frozen policies, unable to improve from their own failures. Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) offers a path to continued improvement, yet manual environment resets and task-success supervision hinder autonomous learning. We introduce \textbf{FIND}, an agentic real-world RL framework that closes the loop between scene understanding, weakness-aware practice, self-evaluation, and policy improvement in a persistent workspace. FIND reframes autonomous practice as a scene-conditioned, performance-aware task-selection problem: instead of restoring a predefined scene after each rollout, it uses the resulting scene to determine what to practice next. A vision--language agent identifies feasible tasks from a predefined library, prioritizes those with lower recent success rates, and evaluates outcomes using paired pre- and post-execution observations. We instantiate FIND with a frozen $π_{0.5}$ VLA and residual off-policy RL. Across eight real-world manipulation tasks, the independent human-assessed success rate improves from $55\%$ to $71.9\%$. A representative run completes 456 autonomous episodes within 6 hours of interaction, requiring 30 scene-recovery interventions and no human-provided reward labels during online learning. Ablations and systematic evaluations further examine key design choices, agent evaluation accuracy, and human intervention requirements. Our website is made publicly available at: FIND.github.io.

AI.tldr: FIND is an agentic real-world RL framework that enables VLA-based manipulation policies to autonomously improve from their own failures in a persistent workspace, raising success from 55% to 71.9% across eight tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA models provide strong manipulation priors but are deployed as frozen policies that cannot improve from their own failures. Real-world RL could enable continued improvement, yet manual environment resets and reliance on task-success supervision prevent autonomous learning.
AI.method: FIND reframes autonomous practice as scene-conditioned, performance-aware task selection: rather than resetting a predefined scene after each rollout, it uses the resulting scene to decide what to practice next. A vision-language agent identifies feasible tasks from a predefined library, prioritizes those with lower recent success rates, and self-evaluates outcomes via paired pre- and post-execution observations. It is instantiated with a frozen π0.5 VLA plus residual off-policy RL.
AI.result: Across eight real-world manipulation tasks, independent human-assessed success improves from 55% to 71.9%. A representative run completes 456 autonomous episodes in 6 hours with 30 scene-recovery interventions and no human-provided reward labels during online learning. Ablations and systematic evaluations examine design choices, agent evaluation accuracy, and human intervention requirements.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between scene understanding, weakness-aware practice, self-evaluation, and policy improvement in a persistent workspace enables autonomous real-world RL for manipulation, overcoming the need for manual resets and human success labels.

title: Improving Medical Calculation of LLMs with Embedded Coding
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on medical examinations and question-answering benchmarks, but remain unreliable on medical calculation tasks that require exact numerical outputs. These calculations support high-stakes decisions such as medication dosing, organ-function assessment, and prognostic scoring, for which even small errors can have serious clinical consequences. We introduce MedCode, a framework that improves medical calculation by training LLMs to generate embedded executable code. Given a clinical context, the model identifies the relevant calculator, extracts its input variables, and produces a script that delegates arithmetic operations to a deterministic interpreter. Executing the script returns the calculated value together with an explanation and the appropriate unit. We construct supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference datasets from the MedCalc benchmark and additionally curate a dataset for calculation tasks in Intensive Care Unit (ICU) scenarios. We further propose weighted Direct Preference Optimization (wDPO), which adaptively emphasizes preference pairs that are difficult for the model to distinguish. Experiments with LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B show absolute accuracy gains of 20--30 percentage points, demonstrating the effectiveness of embedded code generation for medical calculation.

AI.tldr: MedCode trains LLMs to generate embedded executable code for medical calculations, delegating arithmetic to a deterministic interpreter to improve numerical accuracy. Using SFT and preference data from MedCalc plus a curated ICU dataset, and a new weighted DPO (wDPO), it achieves 20-30 percentage point accuracy gains on LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well on medical exams and QA benchmarks but remain unreliable on medical calculation tasks requiring exact numerical outputs. Such calculations underpin high-stakes decisions like medication dosing, organ-function assessment, and prognostic scoring, where small errors can cause serious clinical consequences.
AI.method: MedCode is a framework that trains LLMs to generate embedded executable code. Given clinical context, the model identifies the relevant calculator, extracts its input variables, and produces a script that delegates arithmetic to a deterministic interpreter; execution returns the value with an explanation and appropriate unit. The authors build SFT and preference datasets from the MedCalc benchmark, curate an ICU calculation dataset, and propose weighted Direct Preference Optimization (wDPO), which adaptively emphasizes preference pairs the model finds difficult to distinguish.
AI.result: Experiments with LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B show absolute accuracy gains of 20-30 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Embedded code generation is effective for medical calculation, substantially improving exact numerical accuracy and offering a reliable approach for high-stakes clinical computations.

title: Fiber-Normalized Manipulability and Determinant Proxies: Intrinsic Redundancy Optimization Across and Within Task Fibers
summary:
This work establishes that determinant-based manipulability is an exact objective for fixed-task redundancy optimization, despite its dependence on task coordinates and the choice of task-space metric used for volume measurement. On every regular task fiber, the determinant proxy, its representation in any task chart, and every metric-completed manipulability differ only by positive constants. They consequently induce the same complete ordering, constrained extrema, gradient directions, critical points, and local optimality classifications.
  For comparisons and trajectory optimization across task fibers, this work introduces fiber-normalized manipulability: the capability attained at an internal state divided by the best capability available on the same fiber. The resulting dimensionless scalar is invariant under coordinate changes on the internal-state and task manifolds and independent of the task-space metric. Its associated loss provides an intrinsic objective for physically admissible cross-fiber trajectories, including problems with prescribed or free task evolution and temporal coupling. Planar-manipulator and redundant aerodynamic-allocation examples demonstrate fixed-fiber equivalence, task-dependent cross-fiber differences, and invariant fiber-normalized trajectory optimization.

AI.tldr: Determinant-based manipulability is shown to be an exact objective for fixed-task redundancy optimization, and a new dimensionless "fiber-normalized manipulability" is introduced for cross-fiber comparisons and trajectory optimization.
AI.motivation: Determinant-based manipulability depends on task coordinates and the chosen task-space metric for volume measurement, raising concerns about whether it is a well-posed optimization objective. The paper aims to resolve this ambiguity and extend manipulability to cross-fiber comparisons.
AI.method: The authors analyze the determinant proxy on regular task fibers, showing it, its representation in any task chart, and every metric-completed manipulability differ only by positive constants within a fiber. They then define fiber-normalized manipulability as the capability at an internal state divided by the best capability on the same fiber, yielding a dimensionless, invariant scalar independent of the task-space metric.
AI.result: Within a fixed fiber, all these manipulability variants induce identical complete orderings, constrained extrema, gradient directions, critical points, and local optimality classifications. Cross-fiber comparisons generally differ by task, but the fiber-normalized quantity is invariant under coordinate changes and metric choice and yields an intrinsic loss for physically admissible cross-fiber trajectory optimization, including prescribed or free task evolution and temporal coupling. Planar-manipulator and redundant aerodynamic-allocation examples validate these claims.
AI.conclusion: Determinant-based manipulability is an exact objective for fixed-task redundancy optimization, and fiber-normalized manipulability provides an intrinsic, metric- and coordinate-invariant objective for cross-fiber comparisons and trajectory optimization.

title: BioDyad: Synchronize Biomedical Discovery and Machine Learning Engineering
summary: Agentic biomedical machine learning (ML) draws on complementary advances in biomedical evidence acquisition and executable program search. Existing systems connect aspects of these capabilities, but coordinating them throughout program search remains challenging. New evidence must guide candidate construction, execution outcomes must inform subsequent discovery and reuse, and validation demands must fit the search budget. We introduce BioDyad, which couples biomedical discovery and ML engineering through two hierarchies within Monte Carlo graph search. Its scientific hierarchy combines prior biomedical guidance with iterative discovery, then links biomedical plans to execution outcomes in memory for reuse across candidates. Its engineering hierarchy moves candidate programs from smoke execution, through train/validation evaluation, to full-data retraining. We evaluate BioDyad on the 76-task BioXArena benchmark under a two-hour per-task budget with three matched LLM backends. It achieves the highest penalized all-task score and task success rate among four agent methods and a one-shot baseline under each backend. These results support coordinating biomedical discovery and ML engineering to integrate external knowledge into executable programs across heterogeneous biomedical tasks.

AI.tldr: BioDyad couples biomedical discovery and ML engineering via two hierarchies in Monte Carlo graph search, achieving top penalized score and success rate on the 76-task BioXArena benchmark within a two-hour per-task budget across three matched LLM backends.
AI.motivation: Agentic biomedical ML combines advances in biomedical evidence acquisition and executable program search, but existing systems only connect aspects of these capabilities. Coordinating them throughout program search is hard: new evidence must guide candidate construction, execution outcomes must inform later discovery and reuse, and validation demands must fit the search budget.
AI.method: BioDyad couples biomedical discovery and ML engineering through two hierarchies within Monte Carlo graph search. The scientific hierarchy combines prior biomedical guidance with iterative discovery, then links biomedical plans to execution outcomes in memory for reuse across candidates. The engineering hierarchy moves candidate programs from smoke execution, through train/validation evaluation, to full-data retraining.
AI.result: On the 76-task BioXArena benchmark with a two-hour per-task budget and three matched LLM backends, BioDyad achieves the highest penalized all-task score and task success rate among four agent methods and a one-shot baseline under each backend.
AI.conclusion: The results support coordinating biomedical discovery and ML engineering to integrate external knowledge into executable programs across heterogeneous biomedical tasks.

title: Active 3D weaves for load-bearing and damage-resilient locomotion
summary: The craft of weaving, where different materials are interlaced, has tremendous potential for creating active and functional systems for use in soft robots, prosthetics, wearables, exoskeletons, and more. These textile-like systems are flexible and safe for human-machine interaction; however, this inherent flexibility limits their ability to carry loads, which is essential for many robotic functions. In this work, we introduce a general framework for integrating active materials into three-dimensional (3D) woven shells to create robotic structures that combine high axial stiffness for load bearing, low bending stiffness for efficient actuation, and system-level resilience for damage tolerance. These woven robots can be modularly assembled from 'woven corners', a fundamental unit of 3D woven structures. We use eigenvalue calculations to identify load bearing and actuation mechanisms of the 3D woven structures, and use that information to make five different robots capable of locomotion. We demonstrate that these 3D woven robots can locomote carrying loads 70 times their self-weight, and can maintain repeatable performance even after being subjected to extreme compression. This work is a pathway toward the design, manufacturing, and simulation of future 3D woven robotic systems where load bearing, high stiffness, active functional deformation, locomotion, and system-level resilience are all needed.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for embedding active materials into 3D woven shells to create modular robots that combine high axial stiffness for load bearing, low bending stiffness for efficient actuation, and damage tolerance. Five locomotion-capable robots were built using eigenvalue analysis, demonstrating load carrying of 70x self-weight and resilient performance after extreme compression.
AI.motivation: Weaving offers great potential for active and functional systems in soft robots, prosthetics, wearables, and exoskeletons, and textile-like systems are flexible and safe for human-machine interaction. However, this inherent flexibility restricts their load-carrying capacity, which is essential for many robotic functions, creating a need for structures that are both flexible for actuation and stiff for load bearing.
AI.method: The authors integrate active materials into three-dimensional woven shells, using 'woven corners' as a fundamental unit for modular assembly of robotic structures. They perform eigenvalue calculations to identify the load bearing and actuation mechanisms of the 3D woven structures, and use these results to design five different robots capable of locomotion.
AI.result: The 3D woven robots can locomote while carrying loads 70 times their self-weight and maintain repeatable performance even after being subjected to extreme compression. Five distinct locomotion-capable robots were successfully designed and demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a pathway toward the design, manufacturing, and simulation of future 3D woven robotic systems that simultaneously require load bearing, high stiffness, active functional deformation, locomotion, and system-level resilience.

title: Symbolic Guidance for LLM Agents in Distributed Multiagent Coordination
comment: A preliminary version of this work was published as an extended abstract in the Proceedings of AAMAS 2026
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in multi-agent systems, yet their ability to reliably execute distributed coordination protocols remains poorly understood. While AgentsNet, a benchmark framework for distributed coordination among LLM agents, enables such coordination, granting full reasoning autonomy often leads to inconsistent or degraded performance in complex domains.
  We hypothesize that coordination can be improved by regulating agent autonomy through symbolic guidance derived from established algorithms. To investigate this, we introduce the \emph{Symbolic Guidance Taxonomy (SGT)}, which characterizes a spectrum of autonomy ranging from open-ended natural language reasoning to fully prescribed algorithmic execution, with intermediate levels providing partial pseudocode guidance. Our results show that intermediate autonomy levels consistently outperform both unguided agents and fully prescriptive specifications. These findings identify autonomy regulation as a key design principle for LLM-based distributed coordination.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how regulating LLM agent autonomy with symbolic guidance affects distributed coordination performance, introducing the Symbolic Guidance Taxonomy (SGT) and showing intermediate autonomy levels outperform both unguided and fully prescribed approaches.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as autonomous agents in multi-agent systems, but their reliability in executing distributed coordination protocols is poorly understood. Granting full reasoning autonomy often causes inconsistent or degraded performance in complex domains, motivating a need to understand how to regulate autonomy.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Symbolic Guidance Taxonomy (SGT), a framework characterizing a spectrum of agent autonomy from open-ended natural language reasoning to fully prescribed algorithmic execution, with intermediate levels offering partial pseudocode guidance. They investigate this within the AgentsNet benchmark framework for distributed coordination among LLM agents.
AI.result: Intermediate autonomy levels consistently outperform both unguided agents (full reasoning autonomy) and fully prescriptive specifications (full algorithmic execution).
AI.conclusion: Autonomy regulation is identified as a key design principle for LLM-based distributed coordination, suggesting that partial symbolic guidance balances flexibility and reliability better than either extreme of the autonomy spectrum.

title: Residual Denoising Enables Sample-Efficient Multi-Agent Coordination on Demand
summary: Pretrained robot policies offer strong manipulation skills but are typically limited to single-agent settings, where a robot acts in isolation. In this work, we study how to adapt pretrained single-agent diffusion policies to multi-agent settings using minimal collaborative data, co-optimizing for two key objectives: high coordination performance and single-agent skill retention. To this end, we introduce ALTER, an adaptation method for coordination on demand: the adapted policy coordinates with other robots when deployed in a team while remaining capable of acting independently when operating alone. Execution is decentralized: each robot acts only on its own visual observations, without explicit inter-agent communication. Our method trains a coordination head that predicts a residual denoiser to transform single-agent behavior into coordinated multi-agent behavior when necessary while also preserving single-agent capabilities. To preserve single-agent capabilities, we augment a small number of collaborative demonstrations with self-distilled data generated by the base policy during training of the residual denoiser. In simulation,ALTER achieves higher coordination success over our baselines while retaining much higher source-skill retention. In our hardware experiments, we find similar trends where ALTER better co-optimizes for coordination success and single-agent skill retention than the baselines

AI.tldr: ALTER adapts pretrained single-agent diffusion policies to decentralized multi-agent coordination using minimal collaborative data, jointly optimizing coordination success and single-agent skill retention.
AI.motivation: Pretrained robot policies possess strong manipulation skills but are confined to single-agent settings. The paper aims to adapt such pretrained single-agent diffusion policies to multi-agent settings under minimal collaborative data, co-optimizing coordination performance and single-agent skill retention.
AI.method: Proposes ALTER, which trains a coordination head predicting a residual denoiser that transforms single-agent behavior into coordinated multi-agent behavior when needed. Execution is decentralized—each robot acts solely on its own visual observations with no explicit inter-agent communication. To preserve single-agent capabilities, a small number of collaborative demonstrations are augmented with self-distilled data generated by the base policy during training of the residual denoiser.
AI.result: In simulation, ALTER achieves higher coordination success over baselines while retaining much higher source-skill retention. Hardware experiments show similar trends, with ALTER better co-optimizing coordination success and single-agent skill retention than baselines.
AI.conclusion: ALTER enables "coordination on demand": the adapted policy coordinates with teammates when deployed in a team yet remains capable of independent action when operating alone, effectively balancing multi-agent coordination and single-agent skill retention under minimal collaborative data.

title: Goal-Persistent Coding Agents as Scientific Performance Engineers: A Fixed-Radius Nearest-Neighbor Case Study
summary: Coding agents can pursue persistent objectives across many tool-use turns, but evidence that general-purpose agents can conduct rigorous scientific performance engineering remains limited. We present a repository-scale case study in which off-the-shelf Codex and Claude Code agents optimize fixed-radius nearest-neighbor (FRNN) search for particle tracking. Starting from a PyTorch-dependent CUDA implementation, the agents follow an executable goal that specifies exact-correctness tests, profiling requirements, and acceptance criteria without prescribing code transformations. In the primary sequential trajectory, they autonomously remove the PyTorch dependency and conduct hypothesis-driven optimization experiments. The resulting standalone C++/CUDA library exactly reproduces the targeted reference result. Its synchronous NumPy interface achieved 1.6-fold speedup over the original GPU-resident PyTorch interface, despite including host transfers. Similar speedups were observed across different GPU architectures and software stacks. An independent optimization rerun followed a different sequence of hypotheses and reached even better performance on the target workload. These results show that goal-persistent coding agents can act as experimental performance engineers, and that executable scientific contracts are needed both to guide and to validate their optimization.

AI.tldr: A repository-scale case study shows off-the-shelf Codex and Claude Code agents can act as experimental performance engineers, autonomously optimizing a PyTorch-based FRNN particle-tracking search into a standalone C++/CUDA library that exactly reproduces reference results while achieving ~1.6x speedup over the original GPU-resident PyTorch interface.
AI.motivation: Coding agents can pursue persistent objectives across many tool-use turns, yet evidence that general-purpose agents can conduct rigorous scientific performance engineering remains limited. This work investigates whether such agents can autonomously perform high-quality optimization under strict correctness and profiling constraints.
AI.method: A repository-scale case study in which off-the-shelf Codex and Claude Code agents optimize fixed-radius nearest-neighbor (FRNN) search for particle tracking. Starting from a PyTorch-dependent CUDA implementation, agents follow an executable goal specifying exact-correctness tests, profiling requirements, and acceptance criteria without prescribing code transformations. In the primary sequential trajectory, agents autonomously remove the PyTorch dependency and run hypothesis-driven optimization experiments, producing a standalone C++/CUDA library with a synchronous NumPy interface.
AI.result: The resulting library exactly reproduces the targeted reference result. Its synchronous NumPy interface achieved 1.6-fold speedup over the original GPU-resident PyTorch interface, even while including host transfers. Similar speedups held across different GPU architectures and software stacks. An independent optimization rerun followed a different hypothesis sequence and reached even better performance on the target workload.
AI.conclusion: Goal-persistent coding agents can function as experimental performance engineers. Executable scientific contracts are needed both to guide and to validate their optimization efforts.

title: GAUGE: Planner-Conditioned Active Calibration of Opaque Quadruped Velocity Interfaces
summary: In this paper, we present a Goal-Aware Uncertainty-Guided Exploration (GAUGE) framework for planner-conditioned active calibration of opaque quadruped velocity interfaces. Commercial quadrupeds commonly expose planar-velocity commands, but the underlying locomotion controller remains inaccessible and can produce systematic discrepancies between commanded and realized motion. A navigation planner typically uses a structured subset of the command envelope. GAUGE maintains a Bayesian command-to-motion model and selects authorized trials according to their expected reduction of posterior epistemic uncertainty under the planner-induced command distribution. The resulting posterior supports validation-based stopping, bounded inverse compensation, and task-relevant recalibration after detected interface shifts. In three controlled response families, GAUGE reaches the joint criterion for task-facing accuracy and uncertainty with fewer trials than passive, D-optimal, and task-agnostic alternatives. Across six held-out Isaac Sim navigation maps, it meets the declared noninferiority margins against dense calibration. Code is available at https://github.com/EurekaZang/CalibAgent.

AI.tldr: GAUGE is a goal-aware, uncertainty-guided framework for actively calibrating opaque quadruped velocity interfaces conditioned on a navigation planner's command distribution, achieving task-facing accuracy with fewer trials than passive, D-optimal, and task-agnostic baselines.
AI.motivation: Commercial quadrupeds expose planar-velocity command interfaces while the underlying locomotion controller stays inaccessible, causing systematic commanded-vs-realized motion discrepancies. Generic calibration ignores that a planner only uses a structured subset of the command envelope, so uniform exploration wastes trials on irrelevant regions and does not target task-facing accuracy.
AI.method: GAUGE maintains a Bayesian command-to-motion model and selects authorized trials by their expected reduction of posterior epistemic uncertainty under the planner-induced command distribution. The resulting posterior drives validation-based stopping, bounded inverse compensation, and task-relevant recalibration after detected interface shifts.
AI.result: In three controlled response families, GAUGE attains the joint criterion for task-facing accuracy and uncertainty with fewer trials than passive, D-optimal, and task-agnostic alternatives. Across six held-out Isaac Sim navigation maps it satisfies the declared noninferiority margins relative to dense calibration.
AI.conclusion: Planner-conditioned, uncertainty-guided active calibration makes opaque quadruped velocity interfaces usable with substantially reduced trial budgets while preserving task-relevant accuracy, and it extends to stopping, inverse compensation, and recalibration under interface shifts.

title: CSI-Agent: LLM-Assisted Few-Shot Adaptation for Cross-Domain Wi-Fi CSI Sensing
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to INFOCOM
summary: Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) has enabled device-free sensing applications such as human activity recognition. However, CSI sensing models remain brittle in cross-domain deployment, where changes in users or environments can produce incorrect predictions. Existing solutions usually treat this problem as an offline model-design problem, by pretraining a stronger representation or applying one fixed adaptation method to the entire target domain. In practice, labeled target data are scarce and different classes may fail in different ways under the same domain shift. To address this, we propose CSI-Agent, an evidence-seeking LLM agent that reformulates cross-domain CSI adaptation as a deployment-time decision-making problem. Rather than processing raw CSI or making sample-level predictions, CSI-Agent summarizes target-domain behavior into sensing-grounded class-level evidence. It establishes a strong target-adaptive default from complementary CSI views and uses an LLM planner to determine whether each class should retain the default or invoke a specialized action. Deterministic verification and bounded execution further reduce unreliable interventions. We evaluate CSI-Agent on four public datasets using five cross-domain splits covering device, user, environment, and compositional shifts. Under 1-shot adaptation, CSI-Agent achieves the best target-domain performance across all splits and improves the average Macro-F1 by about 16\% compared to the strongest baseline method.

AI.tldr: CSI-Agent reformulates cross-domain Wi-Fi CSI adaptation as a deployment-time decision-making problem, using an evidence-seeking LLM agent that summarizes target-domain behavior into class-level evidence and decides per class whether to keep a target-adaptive default or invoke a specialized action.
AI.motivation: CSI-based device-free sensing models are brittle under cross-domain deployment (user/environment changes cause errors). Existing solutions treat this as an offline model-design problem: pretraining stronger representations or applying one fixed adaptation method to the entire target domain. In practice, labeled target data are scarce and different classes may fail differently under the same domain shift.
AI.method: CSI-Agent is an evidence-seeking LLM agent. Instead of processing raw CSI or making sample-level predictions, it summarizes target-domain behavior into sensing-grounded class-level evidence. It builds a strong target-adaptive default from complementary CSI views, then uses an LLM planner to decide for each class whether to retain the default or invoke a specialized action. Deterministic verification and bounded execution are added to reduce unreliable interventions.
AI.result: Evaluated on four public datasets with five cross-domain splits covering device, user, environment, and compositional shifts. Under 1-shot adaptation, CSI-Agent achieves the best target-domain performance on all splits, improving average Macro-F1 by about 16% over the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Framing cross-domain CSI adaptation as deployment-time, class-level decision-making with an LLM agent yields consistent gains over fixed offline adaptation baselines, with verification and bounded execution mitigating risky interventions.

title: RecastVLA: From Past Interaction to Future Control with Adaptive Policy States
summary: Sequential manipulation requires a robot to track what has already happened, even when the current scene no longer reveals it. Policies with explicit history representations make past interactions available as context for current decisions. We ask how action generation itself can form a persistent state for subsequent control. Building on action-side test-time training, RecastVLA maintains an adaptive policy state within a flow-matching vision-language-action policy. The state is represented by shared fast weights and remains fixed throughout action generation. Depth-specific interfaces read the same state, while features across depths and flow evaluations jointly define one update for the next policy call. Subsequent action losses train the initialization, interfaces, and update rule by differentiating through earlier state transitions. At deployment, updates use the policy's own action-generation features without expert action labels. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and twelve real-robot tasks, RecastVLA improves mean success over a matched policy trained without test-time training, including 10.68 percentage points on RoboTwin Clean-to-Clean. In controlled RoboTwin comparisons, retaining state improves success, and the shared design exceeds independently trained layer-local TTT by 2.58 points.

AI.tldr: RecastVLA embeds a persistent, adaptive policy state within a flow-matching vision-language-action policy, where action generation itself forms the state via shared fast weights updated through test-time training.
AI.motivation: Sequential manipulation requires robots to track past interactions even when the current scene no longer reveals them. While explicit history representations provide past context, the paper asks whether action generation itself can form a persistent state for subsequent control.
AI.method: Built on action-side test-time training, RecastVLA maintains an adaptive policy state represented by shared fast weights, fixed throughout action generation. Depth-specific interfaces read the same state, and features across depths and flow evaluations jointly define one update for the next policy call. Subsequent action losses train the initialization, interfaces, and update rule by differentiating through earlier state transitions. At deployment, updates rely on the policy's own action-generation features without expert action labels.
AI.result: Across LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and twelve real-robot tasks, RecastVLA improves mean success over a matched policy trained without test-time training, including +10.68 percentage points on RoboTwin Clean-to-Clean. In controlled RoboTwin comparisons, retaining state improves success, and the shared design exceeds independently trained layer-local TTT by 2.58 points.
AI.conclusion: Action generation can serve as a persistent control state: maintaining and updating shared fast weights through test-time training yields consistent gains across simulation and real-robot benchmarks.

title: SenseAgent: An LLM Agent for Adaptive Cross-Domain IMU Sensing
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Plan to submit to SenSys Phase 2
summary: Deep learning has improved inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensing for mobile and wearable applications. However, an IMU model trained in one domain often becomes unreliable when it is used with a new user, device, or body position. Existing methods usually treat this problem as a static model-design task: they pretrain a stronger representation, add data augmentation, or select one adaptation method before deployment. In practice, the target domain is only gradually observed, labels are scarce, and different domain shifts require different sensing actions. This paper presents SenseAgent, an LLM-guided sensing agent for cross-domain IMU activity recognition. Instead of asking an LLM to classify raw IMU signals, SenseAgent uses the LLM as a runtime planner over sensing tools, source-domain experience memory, online target memory, and verifiers. The agent builds a label-free diagnosis report from the target stream and uses it to decide whether to keep raw inference or invoke specialized tools, including gravity-aware sensing, prototype transfer, and style normalization. Verifiers check source calibration, target-memory reliability, and no-harm criteria before accepting high-risk tool decisions. SenseAgent also supports scarce feedback without retraining the backbone or replacing the label-free route. This design converts cross-domain IMU sensing from a fixed inference pipeline into a closed-loop sensing process that diagnoses target shifts, selects suitable sensing actions, and rejects unsafe adaptations. We evaluate SenseAgent across multiple IMU datasets and deployment shifts. Results show that its verified route selection improves cross-domain sensing, especially under harder placement and compound shifts, and further benefits from limited user feedback.

AI.tldr: SenseAgent is an LLM-guided sensing agent for cross-domain IMU activity recognition that uses the LLM as a runtime planner over sensing tools, memory, and verifiers, converting fixed inference into a closed-loop sensing process that diagnoses target shifts and selects verified sensing actions.
AI.motivation: IMU models trained in one domain become unreliable under new users, devices, or body positions. Existing methods treat cross-domain IMU sensing as a static model-design task (pretraining stronger representations, data augmentation, or selecting one adaptation method before deployment), but in practice the target domain is only gradually observed, labels are scarce, and different domain shifts require different sensing actions.
AI.method: SenseAgent uses an LLM as a runtime planner over sensing tools, source-domain experience memory, online target memory, and verifiers, rather than classifying raw IMU signals. It builds a label-free diagnosis report from the target stream to decide whether to keep raw inference or invoke specialized tools (gravity-aware sensing, prototype transfer, style normalization). Verifiers check source calibration, target-memory reliability, and no-harm criteria before accepting high-risk tool decisions. It also supports scarce feedback without retraining the backbone or replacing the label-free route.
AI.result: Across multiple IMU datasets and deployment shifts, SenseAgent's verified route selection improves cross-domain sensing, especially under harder placement and compound shifts, and further benefits from limited user feedback.
AI.conclusion: SenseAgent converts cross-domain IMU sensing from a fixed inference pipeline into a closed-loop sensing process that diagnoses target shifts, selects suitable sensing actions, and rejects unsafe adaptations, improving robustness under domain shift.

title: AquaBEV-Nav: Learned BEV Occupancy for Underwater Navigation and Exploration
summary: Safe underwater exploration requires a robot to understand where surrounding structures are located and which regions are available for motion. Existing vision-based underwater exploration systems commonly obtain this information indirectly by estimating monocular depth, unprojecting the geometry into 3D space, and accumulating it into a 2D bird's-eye-view occupancy map. This reliance on intermediate depth estimation is particularly problematic underwater, where scattering and wavelength-dependent attenuation degrade visual cues and limit the reliability of monocular depth estimates. We introduce AquaBEV-Nav, an underwater exploration framework that bypasses explicit monocular depth estimation through direct bird's-eye-view occupancy prediction. Built upon the CORAL hierarchical exploration framework, AquaBEV-Nav replaces its depth-based perception front end with AquaBEV. Given a single RGB frame, AquaBEV maps visual features into a learned polar representation, performs causal reasoning along the range dimension, and reconstructs local Cartesian occupancy without relying on intermediate depth prediction. The resulting occupancy map is accumulated into CORAL's persistent spatial memory, providing spatial context for VLM-based high-level planning and collision constraints for dynamics-aware local trajectory generation. Across ten simulated reef environments and six occupancy backbones evaluated under a single protocol, AquaBEV-Nav reaches 37.48 structure IoU and 53.2 target IoU, 88.95% closed-loop coverage with zero collisions.

AI.tldr: AquaBEV-Nav is an underwater exploration framework that replaces monocular depth estimation with direct bird's-eye-view (BEV) occupancy prediction, enabling safer and more reliable autonomous navigation in degraded underwater visual conditions.
AI.motivation: Safe underwater exploration requires understanding surrounding structures and free-space regions. Existing vision-based systems rely on monocular depth estimation, unprojection into 3D, and accumulation into a 2D BEV occupancy map. This intermediate depth step is unreliable underwater due to scattering and wavelength-dependent attenuation, which degrade visual cues and monocular depth accuracy.
AI.method: AquaBEV-Nav builds on the CORAL hierarchical exploration framework and replaces its depth-based perception front end with AquaBEV. From a single RGB frame, AquaBEV maps visual features into a learned polar representation, performs causal reasoning along the range dimension, and reconstructs local Cartesian occupancy without explicit depth prediction. This occupancy is accumulated into CORAL's persistent spatial memory, supplying spatial context for VLM-based high-level planning and collision constraints for dynamics-aware local trajectory generation.
AI.result: Evaluated across ten simulated reef environments and six occupancy backbones under a single protocol, AquaBEV-Nav achieves 37.48 structure IoU and 53.2 target IoU, with 88.95% closed-loop coverage and zero collisions.
AI.conclusion: Bypassing explicit monocular depth estimation in favor of direct BEV occupancy prediction provides a more robust and collision-free perception front end for underwater exploration, improving coverage and occupancy accuracy over depth-dependent pipelines.

title: What Does the Rank Buy? A Spectral and Distributional Analysis of Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: The rank $r$ in LoRA is widely treated as a capacity control: a smaller rank is assumed to yield a simpler model that generalizes better. We show that, under hard per-factor norm budgets---the idealization of the weight decay and norm control used in practice---this intuition breaks down. The reason is structural: under such budgets, the updates LoRA can reach are exactly the matrices of rank at most $r$ inside a nuclear-norm ball, and every complexity and displacement functional we analyze is maximized over this set by a rank-one update---so the rank cap never binds. The consequences follow directly. The linear-readout model class we study is identical for every $r \ge 1$, its Rademacher complexity carries no dependence on $r$, and the distance the adaptation can move the source distribution obeys a rank-independent upper bound that we show is sharp. If rank does not control capacity, where does it act? We identify two places. Statistically, replacing the per-factor budgets with a joint budget on the product restores a data-dependent, rank-sensitive complexity bound---though the gain appears only for well-spread feature distributions, and the worst case remains rank-free. Spectrally, rank sets the price of adaptation: canceling the leading singular directions of the pretrained weight requires both sufficient rank and sufficient budget. We bound the smallest rank achieving a desired source--target alignment, with upper and lower bounds that match under two-sided spectral decay. Together, these results recast rank as governing which updates are reachable and what cancellation costs---not how much capacity the model has.

AI.tldr: Under hard per-factor norm budgets, LoRA's rank r does not control capacity: the reachable updates are exactly rank-≤r matrices in a nuclear-norm ball, and every complexity/displacement functional analyzed is maximized by a rank-one update, so the rank cap never binds. Rank instead governs which updates are reachable and the cost of spectral cancellation.
AI.motivation: The prevailing intuition treats LoRA rank r as a capacity knob—smaller r assumed to give a simpler, better-generalizing model. The paper challenges this assumption under hard per-factor norm budgets, which idealize the weight decay and norm control used in practice.
AI.method: Structural analysis of LoRA's reachable update set under per-factor norm budgets, showing it equals rank-≤r matrices within a nuclear-norm ball. Complexity and displacement functionals (Rademacher complexity, source-distribution displacement) are analyzed over this set. A joint budget on the product is compared against per-factor budgets. Spectral analysis bounds the smallest rank achieving desired source–target alignment via singular-direction cancellation.
AI.result: The linear-readout model class is identical for all r≥1; Rademacher complexity has no r-dependence; and the source-distribution displacement obeys a sharp rank-independent upper bound. Joint product budget restores a data-dependent, rank-sensitive complexity bound—but only for well-spread feature distributions, with worst case remaining rank-free. Canceling leading singular directions of the pretrained weight requires both sufficient rank and sufficient budget; smallest-rank bounds match under two-sided spectral decay.
AI.conclusion: Rank should be recast as governing which updates are reachable and what spectral cancellation costs—not how much capacity the model has. Under per-factor norm budgets, the rank cap never binds for the analyzed functionals.

title: FutureRay: Control-Aligned Future Range for Agile Quadruped Navigation
summary: Moving obstacles can block a previously clear route while a quadruped robot executes a motion command. We investigate whether predicting changing clearance improves navigation when motion selection accounts for the robot footprint and the time needed to react and brake. We present FutureRay, which predicts ranges across viewing directions and future times, together with encounter risk, from depth-derived range history and observable robot motion. Training emphasizes near-term clearance and penalizes errors that overstate available space. A local planner queries the same forecast for candidate headings and combines it with current observations to check clearance around the robot footprint. Model-based reaction--braking limits guide speed selection, and the resulting velocity commands are passed to a fixed locomotion policy. In paired evaluations on 60 static and dynamic simulation scenes, FutureRay achieves 93.3% completion, compared with 75.0% for current-range persistence and 80.0% for Cartesian Kalman rollout, with perception, planning, and locomotion held fixed. FutureRay also records fewer collisions than both baselines. Qualitative trials on a physical quadruped show avoidance initiated while an obstacle is approaching the route, followed by renewed goal progress. These results show that joint range and encounter-risk prediction can improve obstacle avoidance without retraining the locomotion policy.

AI.tldr: FutureRay predicts future ranges and encounter risk across viewing directions to improve quadruped navigation around moving obstacles, achieving 93.3% completion versus 75–80% for baselines.
AI.motivation: Moving obstacles can block a previously clear path while a quadruped executes a motion command. The paper investigates whether anticipating changing clearance, combined with accounting for the robot footprint and reaction/braking time, improves navigation and motion selection.
AI.method: FutureRay forecasts ranges over viewing directions and future time steps plus encounter risk, using depth-derived range history and observable robot motion. Training emphasizes near-term clearance and penalizes errors overstating free space. A local planner queries the forecast across candidate headings and fuses it with current observations to verify clearance around the footprint. Model-based reaction–braking limits set speed, and resulting velocity commands feed a fixed locomotion policy.
AI.result: On 60 paired static and dynamic simulation scenes with perception, planning, and locomotion fixed, FutureRay reaches 93.3% completion versus 75.0% for current-range persistence and 80.0% for Cartesian Kalman rollout, with fewer collisions than both baselines. Physical quadruped trials show avoidance initiated as an obstacle approaches the route, followed by resumed goal progress.
AI.conclusion: Joint prediction of range and encounter risk can improve obstacle avoidance for quadrupeds without retraining the locomotion policy.

title: Decentralized Master-Mind: Joint Action Refinement through Iterative Intent Denoising in Multi-Agent Pathfinding
summary: Decentralized multi-agent path finding (MAPF) with communication requires agents to reach individual goals without collisions under partial observability. Learnable policies trained on expert data provide an effective approach to this problem. However, when several coordinated joint actions are valid in the same context, independently sampling from per-agent distributions can recombine locally valid choices into incompatible joint actions. This failure can arise from the final sampling mechanism even when the per-agent action distributions are learned correctly. DMM (Decentralized Master-Mind) addresses this by replacing one-shot action sampling with discrete, iterative refinement of action intents across communication rounds, inspired by denoising in diffusion models. Agents initialize random action intents and refine them through local communication, coupling their choices before commitment. DMM is pretrained with imitation learning on expert MAPF solutions and further optimized with MICPO, a critic-free group-relative reinforcement-learning method designed for multi-agent, multi-round action refinement. DMM generally achieves higher success rates and lower solution costs than the evaluated learnable baselines. On 1,600 MovingAI tasks, DMM fine-tuned with MICPO solves 1,598, the highest coverage among the evaluated methods, while achieving solution costs close to those of the strongest baselines. DMM also scales to over one million simultaneously acting agents in obstacle-rich environments. These results show that round-level intent refinement can improve joint-action coordination while preserving decentralized execution.

AI.tldr: DMM replaces one-shot per-agent action sampling in decentralized MAPF with iterative, communication-based refinement of discrete action intents, pretrained via imitation learning and fine-tuned with the critic-free MICPO method.
AI.motivation: In decentralized MAPF under partial observability with communication, learnable policies trained on expert data are effective, but when multiple coordinated joint actions are valid in the same context, independently sampling from per-agent distributions can recombine locally valid choices into incompatible joint actions—a failure stemming from the final sampling mechanism even when per-agent distributions are learned correctly.
AI.method: DMM (Decentralized Master-Mind) replaces one-shot action sampling with discrete, iterative refinement of action intents across communication rounds, inspired by denoising in diffusion models. Agents initialize random action intents and refine them through local communication, coupling choices before commitment. DMM is pretrained with imitation learning on expert MAPF solutions and further optimized with MICPO, a critic-free group-relative reinforcement-learning method designed for multi-agent, multi-round action refinement.
AI.result: DMM generally achieves higher success rates and lower solution costs than the evaluated learnable baselines. On 1,600 MovingAI tasks, DMM fine-tuned with MICPO solves 1,598—the highest coverage among evaluated methods—while achieving solution costs close to the strongest baselines. DMM also scales to over one million simultaneously acting agents in obstacle-rich environments.
AI.conclusion: Round-level intent refinement can improve joint-action coordination while preserving decentralized execution.

title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
summary: Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website: https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/.

AI.tldr: RoboFFT is a forward-process reinforcement learning framework that finetunes generative robot policies (diffusion/flow-based) by applying forward noising to sampled actions and using a weighted score/flow matching loss to build a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates, improving performance, stability, and efficiency in simulation and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Generative models (diffusion and flow-based) capture complex, multimodal action distributions for robot policy learning, but imitation-trained policies suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, and improving them usually needs more expert data. Reinforcement learning via environment interaction is a natural fix, yet finetuning generative robot policies is hard because likelihood estimation is intractable.
AI.method: RoboFFT applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score/flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio, enabling PPO-style reinforcement learning updates for generative robot policies.
AI.result: Evaluated with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings, RoboFFT consistently improves performance with better stability and training efficiency. It was further integrated into a real-world RL framework and shown effective on real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: RoboFFT provides an effective and practical forward-process RL method for finetuning generative robot policies, delivering consistent gains in simulation and real-world settings.

title: A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science Topics
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational settings, yet educators lack robust, standards-aligned tools to evaluate their effectiveness in K-12 science contexts. Existing benchmarks predominantly assess general language or advanced scientific reasoning, leaving a critical gap in understanding LLMs' performance on content directly relevant to secondary science curricula. To address this gap, we developed a comprehensive NGSS-aligned benchmark for both middle and high school science using a rigorous synthetic data pipeline, multi-judge validation, and item-level psychometric analysis. Nine open-weight LLMs were systematically evaluated using this benchmark, indicating that several smaller, locally deployable models achieved high accuracy across diverse science domains and question types. Our findings indicate that model size did not consistently predict performance, emphasizing the importance of intentional model selection for educational deployment. We then incorporated a human reviewer into the loop, reviewing the items generated by the LLMs for alignment with NGSS standards. The human review indicated that synthetically generated items were not in perfect alignment with the NGSS standards, indicating the benefits of human-in-the-loop item development, the need to explore the intersection of content and pedagogical knowledge, and the need to extend benchmarks to evaluate LLMs' capacity for interactive, evidence-based feedback in educational scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an NGSS-aligned benchmark for middle and high school science, evaluates nine open-weight LLMs, and finds smaller models can perform well while synthetic items need human review for standards alignment.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in education, but educators lack robust, standards-aligned tools to evaluate their effectiveness in K-12 science. Existing benchmarks focus on general language or advanced scientific reasoning, leaving a gap in assessing LLM performance on content directly tied to secondary science curricula.
AI.method: The authors built a comprehensive NGSS-aligned benchmark for middle and high school science using a rigorous synthetic data pipeline, multi-judge validation, and item-level psychometric analysis. Nine open-weight LLMs were systematically evaluated, and a human reviewer was incorporated into the loop to assess item alignment with NGSS standards.
AI.result: Several smaller, locally deployable models achieved high accuracy across diverse science domains and question types. Model size did not consistently predict performance. Human review revealed that synthetically generated items were not perfectly aligned with NGSS standards.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of intentional model selection for educational deployment, the benefits of human-in-the-loop item development, the need to explore the intersection of content and pedagogical knowledge, and the need to extend benchmarks to evaluate LLMs' capacity for interactive, evidence-based feedback in educational scenarios.

title: Federated Subspace Guided Vision-Language-Action Policy Distillation for Non-IID Multi-Robot Manipulation
summary: Federated learning offers a natural way for multiple robots to jointly improve manipulation policies without requiring centralized access to training demonstrations. However, non-IID task and environment distributions can induce representation drift and mutually incompatible robot-policy updates, making naive parameter aggregation destructive. We present FedDRMan, a federated subspace-guided distillation framework for heterogeneous robot manipulation. At each communication round, the server model provides a frozen teacher for local behavior cloning, while low-rank multimodal subspace and action-distribution distillation preserve globally useful representation geometry and policy behavior. To address heterogeneous aggregation, FedDRMan groups clients by update compatibility and maintains a persistent model for each cluster. The server then spectrally rebalances each compatible aggregate to mitigate attenuation of weaker task-relevant robot-policy update directions. Extensive experiments on LIBERO across diverse non-IID settings, heterogeneity levels, client participation variation, together with ablations and aggregation analyses, show that FedDRMan substantially improves knowledge transfer and consistently outperforms strong federated baselines achieving a peak mean success rate of 80.7%, 11.6 percentage points above the strongest evaluated federated baseline.

AI.tldr: FedDRMan is a federated subspace-guided distillation framework for heterogeneous robot manipulation that combats representation drift and update incompatibility under non-IID distributions, achieving 80.7% peak mean success on LIBERO.
AI.motivation: Federated learning enables multiple robots to jointly improve manipulation policies without centralized access to demonstrations. However, non-IID task and environment distributions cause representation drift and mutually incompatible policy updates, making naive parameter aggregation destructive.
AI.method: At each communication round, the server model serves as a frozen teacher for local behavior cloning, while low-rank multimodal subspace distillation and action-distribution distillation preserve globally useful representation geometry and policy behavior. For heterogeneous aggregation, clients are grouped by update compatibility, each cluster maintains a persistent model, and the server spectrally rebalances each compatible aggregate to mitigate attenuation of weaker task-relevant update directions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on LIBERO across diverse non-IID settings, heterogeneity levels, and client participation variation, with ablations and aggregation analyses, show substantially improved knowledge transfer and consistent outperformance of strong federated baselines, reaching a peak mean success rate of 80.7%, 11.6 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
AI.conclusion: FedDRMan effectively addresses non-IID heterogeneity in federated robot manipulation through subspace-guided distillation and compatibility-based clustering with spectral rebalancing, delivering superior knowledge transfer and policy performance over existing federated baselines.

title: Reasoning Concentrates Errors, and Self-Consistency Never Notices
summary: Self-consistency assumes that independent samples disagree when a model is unsure, so agreement is evidence of correctness. Holding weights fixed and toggling only a reasoning mode, over five benchmarks and 74,944 samples, we show that reasoning concentrates a model's errors: the probability that two independently drawn wrong answers coincide rises in all ten dataset-scale comparisons (p = 0.00098), and in nine of nine after restricting both arms to the problems each gets wrong. Where the answer space is unbounded, reasoning cuts the distinct answers produced to 0.43-0.65 of the non-reasoning count; where it is bounded, both arms hold an identical option set and reasoning concentrates mass on it instead, which no positional prior can explain at fixed weights. The aggregate cost is smaller than the mechanism predicts, because reasoning also shrinks the set of problems where answer diversity can decide anything, in ten of ten cells and by 2.7x; normalized for available headroom, both arms convert a quarter of it in domain. Confidence weighting does not recover what is left. Across 280 method-dataset-model combinations on eight models and five benchmarks, not one beats plain majority voting after correction; weighted voting agrees with it on 98.5% of problem-method pairs and is right 56.3% of the time on the rest; and a signal's direction can invert within fixed weights, with answer log-probability predicting correctness when reasoning is off and error when it is on. A learned six-signal combination gains nothing out of domain. Confidence signals should be evaluated on decisions, not on discrimination.
