AI.tldr: Reasoning does not reduce a fixed-weight model's error but concentrates it: independent wrong answers coincide more often, and no confidence-weighting method beats plain majority voting across 280 combinations.
AI.motivation: Self-consistency treats agreement among independent samples as evidence of correctness, on the assumption that independent samples disagree when a model is unsure. This paper questions that assumption by asking whether a reasoning mode, at fixed weights, actually increases diversity or instead makes errors systematic.
AI.method: Holding weights fixed and toggling only the reasoning mode, the authors compare reasoning vs. non-reasoning arms over five benchmarks and 74,944 samples. They measure coincidence probability of two independently drawn wrong answers, count distinct answers under unbounded answer spaces, test positional priors under bounded option sets, normalize error concentration by available headroom, and evaluate 280 method-dataset-model combinations on eight models and five benchmarks, including majority vs. weighted voting and a learned six-signal combiner for in- vs. out-of-domain behavior.
AI.result: The probability that two independently drawn wrong answers coincide rises in all ten dataset-scale comparisons (p = 0.00098) and in nine of nine after restricting both arms to commonly-wrong problems. Under unbounded answer spaces reasoning cuts distinct answers to 0.43-0.65 of the non-reasoning count; under bounded option sets it concentrates mass on an identical option set that positional priors cannot explain at fixed weights. Aggregate cost is smaller than the mechanism predicts because reasoning shrinks the set of problems where diversity can decide anything in ten of ten cells by 2.7x; normalized for headroom, both arms convert about a quarter. No confidence method beats plain majority voting after correction; weighted voting agrees with it on 98.5% of problem-method pairs and is right 56.3% on the rest. Signal direction can invert within fixed weights (answer log-probability predicts correctness when reasoning is off, error when on), and a learned six-signal combination gains nothing out of domain.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning at fixed weights concentrates errors rather than reducing them, so agreement is weaker evidence of correctness than self-consistency assumes. Confidence signals should be evaluated on decisions rather than on discrimination, since weighted voting offers no reliable gain over plain majority voting.

title: DS-VLA: A Dendritic-inspired Vision-Language-Action Model for Robust Action Control
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance in language-conditioned manipulation, yet success under nominal evaluation does not necessarily translate into robust closed-loop behavior when executed actions are transiently corrupted. We introduce DS-VLA, a dendritic-inspired action architecture that incorporates dendritic spiking dynamics into VLA control to address this limitation. Specifically, to enable modularized feature processing and temporal information integration, DS-VLA equips action neurons with multiple sparsely connected dendritic branches, each featuring heterogeneous, learned decay factors. Furthermore, to suppress unreliable state updates while preserving task-relevant historical information, we introduce a neuron-wise inhibitory gate that adaptively regulates the admission of new multimodal evidence into dendritic states prior to somatic dynamics. We evaluate DS-VLA on all four LIBERO suites under both nominal rollouts and a unified closed-loop action-perturbation protocol. DS-VLA achieves a 91.6\% average nominal success rate and an 87.35\% average perturbed success rate, retaining 95.4\% of its nominal performance. Under the same reported perturbation setting, OpenVLA-OFT, FAST, $π_0$, and GR00T achieve 39.45\%, 23.90\%, 28.55\%, and 30.75\%, respectively. A controlled ablation isolates the contribution of neuron-wise shared inhibition, while analyses of neural dynamics and post-perturbation trajectories associate robust performance with selective evidence suppression and effective behavioral recovery. Together, these results demonstrate that integrating brain-inspired computational mechanisms offers a promising architectural prior for robust embodied intelligence beyond merely scaling vision-language backbones or generative action decoders.

AI.tldr: DS-VLA introduces dendritic spiking dynamics into vision-language-action control, achieving 91.6% nominal and 87.35% perturbed success on LIBERO suites, far surpassing OpenVLA-OFT, FAST, π₀, and GR00T under action perturbation.
AI.motivation: VLA models perform well under nominal evaluation but degrade under closed-loop execution where actions are transiently corrupted, indicating a gap in robust embodied control beyond scaling backbones or decoders.
AI.method: DS-VLA equips action neurons with multiple sparsely connected dendritic branches with heterogeneous learned decay factors for modular processing and temporal integration, plus a neuron-wise inhibitory gate that adaptively regulates admission of new multimodal evidence into dendritic states before somatic dynamics to suppress unreliable updates while preserving task-relevant history.
AI.result: On all four LIBERO suites, DS-VLA achieves 91.6% average nominal success and 87.35% average perturbed success, retaining 95.4% of nominal performance; under the same perturbation setting OpenVLA-OFT, FAST, π₀, and GR00T reach 39.45%, 23.90%, 28.55%, and 30.75%. Ablations isolate the contribution of neuron-wise shared inhibition, and dynamics/trajectory analyses link robustness to selective evidence suppression and behavioral recovery.
AI.conclusion: Integrating brain-inspired computational mechanisms provides a promising architectural prior for robust embodied intelligence, complementing rather than replacing scaling of vision-language backbones or generative action decoders.

title: Receiver-Conditioned Latent Communication gives 94% CacheBack
summary: Multi-agent systems distribute large contexts across agents that communicate to solve a task. Text messages are compact but require decoding and may omit evidence the receiving agent needs. Recent latent communication instead transfers KV caches. This avoids text generation and can improve accuracy and latency. However, a full KV cache grows linearly with both the context an individual agent processes, and the number of agents that coordinate together. This raises memory and context costs, often far exceeding available GPU resources and context window sizes. Our key observation is that agents need only send what the receiving agent requires for its local task -- which we call receiver-conditioned communication. The receiver agent passes the sender a small description of its information needs, which serves to filter and compress the sender agent's KV cache. CacheBack is a simple, robust, training-free instance of receiver conditioning based on the sender's attention weights. On FanOutQA, CacheBack with Qwen 3 removes 75% of the state the agent would otherwise receive, improving accuracy by 14.7 percentage points and reducing median task-completion latency by 3.2x relative to text communication. We show comparable improvements across model families that span dense Transformers, Mamba-attention hybrids, and sliding-window attention.

AI.tldr: CacheBack enables receiver-conditioned latent communication between agents, compressing KV caches by filtering what the receiver needs, cutting state by 75% while improving accuracy and latency.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems distribute large contexts across communicating agents. Text messages are compact but lossy and require decoding. Latent KV cache transfer avoids text generation and improves accuracy/latency, but a full KV cache grows linearly with the individual agent's context and the number of coordinating agents, causing memory and context costs that often exceed available GPU resources and context windows.
AI.method: The authors propose receiver-conditioned communication: the receiver sends the sender a small description of its information needs, which filters and compresses the sender's KV cache. CacheBack is a simple, robust, training-free instance of this idea based on the sender's attention weights, requiring no additional training.
AI.result: On FanOutQA, CacheBack with Qwen 3 removes 75% of the state an agent would otherwise receive, improves accuracy by 14.7 percentage points, and reduces median task-completion latency by 3.2x relative to text communication. Comparable improvements were observed across model families spanning dense Transformers, Mamba-attention hybrids, and sliding-window attention.
AI.conclusion: Receiver-conditioned communication, instantiated as the training-free CacheBack, effectively mitigates the memory and context costs of latent KV cache transfer in multi-agent systems while improving accuracy and latency across diverse architectures.

title: Affordance-Conditioned Decision Making: Bridging the Semantic-Spatial Gap in Zero-Shot Cross-Floor Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-language navigation increasingly relies on general-purpose semantic planners, yet translating correct high-level intent into reliable physical execution remains difficult in spatially constrained transitions. Reaching a staircase, doorway, or narrow passage does not ensure traversal; the agent must identify an executable affordance pose and recover from accumulated action errors. We propose PACE (Preference-refined Affordance-Conditioned Execution), a supervised local execution module that augments frozen zero-shot semantic planners for reliable cross-floor navigation. PACE grounds transition-related semantics into a long-horizon, agent-centric traversable affordance pose and conditions short-horizon action generation on this spatial target, thereby aligning semantic goals with physical execution. We further post-train PACE through failure-aware preference refinement using rollout-derived pairs that contrast normal or recovery behaviors with deviation-amplifying behaviors, thereby improving closed-loop correction. We integrate PACE into six open-source zero-shot VLN navigators and demonstrate consistent improvements on the cross-floor subsets of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, increasing the average success rate from 16.35% to 27.65% and from 4.76% to 12.06%, respectively. Real-world experiments further demonstrate PACE's applicability in unseen environments, highlighting the potential of traversable affordances to bridge semantic intent and reliable embodied behavior.

AI.tldr: PACE is a supervised local execution module that augments frozen zero-shot semantic planners, using traversable affordance poses and failure-aware preference refinement to enable reliable cross-floor navigation, improving success rates across six VLN navigators.
AI.motivation: General-purpose semantic planners in vision-and-language navigation translate high-level intent poorly into reliable physical execution, especially in spatially constrained transitions like staircases, doorways, or narrow passages. Reaching such locations does not ensure traversal; the agent must find an executable affordance pose and recover from accumulated action errors.
AI.method: PACE (Preference-refined Affordance-Conditioned Execution): a supervised local execution module. It grounds transition-related semantics into a long-horizon, agent-centric traversable affordance pose and conditions short-horizon action generation on this spatial target. It is post-trained via failure-aware preference refinement using rollout-derived pairs that contrast normal or recovery behaviors against deviation-amplifying behaviors to improve closed-loop correction.
AI.result: Integrated into six open-source zero-shot VLN navigators, PACE consistently improved cross-floor subsets of R2R-CE (average success rate 16.35% to 27.65%) and RxR-CE (4.76% to 12.06%). Real-world experiments demonstrated applicability in unseen environments.
AI.conclusion: Traversable affordances can bridge semantic intent and reliable embodied behavior, enabling more dependable cross-floor navigation and physical execution.

title: EngramRAG: Dynamic Usage-Weighted Topology and Synaptic Consolidation for Multi-Hop Agentic Memory
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Code and reproduction suite: https://github.com/bpoti001/epigraph
summary: As autonomous LLM agents are deployed across multi-session environments, conventional memory architectures suffer from Associative Blindness (inability to traverse multi-hop relational dependencies), Scaffolding Amnesia (temporal decay evicting core persona invariants), and Static Topology Stagnation (immutable graphs ignoring usage dynamics). Grounded in Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) principles, we propose EngramRAG, an adaptive memory architecture coupling a low-latency Waking State reflex with an asynchronous background Dreaming State consolidation cycle. EngramRAG introduces: (1) Usage-Modulated Personalized PageRank (U-PPR), where transition probabilities adapt via Hebbian plasticity to promote persistent entities into high-centrality Epistemic Macro-Hubs; (2) Consolidation-Activated Topology Decay (CATD), which scales retention half-life by topological load-bearing weight rather than wall-clock recency, protected by a cold-start grace period (N_grace >= 4); (3) Directed SUPERSEDES DAG filtering to suppress obsolete state during fact mutations; and (4) Triple-source hybrid retrieval fusing dense vectors, BM25, and U-PPR via dynamic Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Evaluating on all 1,982 QA pairs across 10 long-term conversations in the LoCoMo benchmark, EngramRAG achieves +38.9% relative improvement in Recall@5 (53.21% vs. 38.29%, p < 0.001) and +43.1% in MRR (0.4203 vs. 0.2937) over dense vector RAG, significantly outperforming Okapi BM25 (48.66%) and isolated static graph retrieval (8.50%). On temporal reasoning, EngramRAG reaches 62.33% Recall@5 (+16.67 points over dense vectors). In controlled mutation tests, SUPERSEDES suppresses split-brain hallucinations from 70.0% to 0.0%, while 90-day simulations show 100.0% scaffolding retention under a 26.21ms interactive retrieval reflex.

AI.tldr: EngramRAG is an adaptive, CLS-inspired memory architecture for LLM agents that couples a low-latency Waking State with an asynchronous Dreaming State consolidation cycle, achieving large gains in Recall@5 and MRR on the LoCoMo benchmark.
AI.motivation: Conventional memory architectures for autonomous LLM agents in multi-session environments suffer from three failures: Associative Blindness (cannot traverse multi-hop relational dependencies), Scaffolding Amnesia (temporal decay evicts core persona invariants), and Static Topology Stagnation (immutable graphs ignore usage dynamics).
AI.method: Grounded in Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) principles, EngramRAG couples a low-latency Waking State reflex with an asynchronous Dreaming State consolidation cycle. It introduces four components: (1) Usage-Modulated Personalized PageRank (U-PPR) with Hebbian-adaptive transition probabilities promoting persistent entities into Epistemic Macro-Hubs; (2) Consolidation-Activated Topology Decay (CATD) scaling retention half-life by topological load-bearing weight rather than wall-clock recency, with a cold-start grace period (N_grace >= 4); (3) Directed SUPERSEDES DAG filtering to suppress obsolete state during fact mutations; and (4) triple-source hybrid retrieval fusing dense vectors, BM25, and U-PPR via dynamic Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
AI.result: On all 1,982 QA pairs across 10 long-term conversations in the LoCoMo benchmark, EngramRAG achieves +38.9% relative improvement in Recall@5 (53.21% vs. 38.29%, p < 0.001) and +43.1% in MRR (0.4203 vs. 0.2937) over dense vector RAG, outperforming Okapi BM25 (48.66%) and isolated static graph retrieval (8.50%). On temporal reasoning it reaches 62.33% Recall@5 (+16.67 points over dense vectors). In mutation tests, SUPERSEDES reduces split-brain hallucinations from 70.0% to 0.0%, and 90-day simulations show 100.0% scaffolding retention at a 26.21ms interactive retrieval reflex.
AI.conclusion: EngramRAG effectively addresses the three identified memory failure modes of LLM agents, delivering substantial gains in retrieval accuracy, temporal reasoning, and long-term persona retention while maintaining low-latency interactive retrieval.

title: MemTransfer: Benchmarking Memory Beyond Matched Experience in Embodied Decision-Making
summary: Memory lets an embodied agent reuse past experience, yet retaining useful information does not ensure that the agent can apply it when conditions change. We present MemTransfer, a benchmark comparing six memory representations, a working-memory baseline and five representations of past experience, under a shared frozen vision-language-model policy. It comprises 100 navigation cases across ten task types in a simulated warehouse, with expert demonstrations supplying the history. Three comparisons vary the starting pose, route availability, and amount and task relevance of history. With one demonstration per task, Full-context and Episodic memory reach 95.3% and 100.0% success at the original demonstration start, but lose 48-49 percentage points at a new test start. Summary changes little between these two test starts, yet with four demonstrations per task it retains a smaller fraction of its unchanged-route success after blocking (39.3%) than Working memory (44.8%) or the two trajectory memories (56-58%). At the new test start, increasing from one to four relevant demonstrations raises Episodic success by 14.3 percentage points, while the other evaluated representations gain no more than 1.3 percentage points. Replacing half of the relevant histories with other-task experience lowers success for both trajectory memories. These results show that robustness to one kind of mismatch does not imply robustness to another, motivating evaluation of both stored information and its use at decision time.

AI.tldr: MemTransfer benchmarks six memory representations under a frozen VLM policy across 100 simulated warehouse navigation cases, revealing that memory retention does not equal robust application when task conditions change.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents benefit from reusing past experience, but storing useful information does not guarantee it can be applied effectively when conditions shift. Existing evaluations rarely disentangle retention of memory from its use at decision time.
AI.method: A benchmark comparing six memory representations—a working-memory baseline plus five representations of past experience—under a shared frozen vision-language-model policy. It includes 100 navigation cases across ten task types in a simulated warehouse, with expert demonstrations as history. Three comparison axes vary starting pose, route availability, and the amount/task relevance of history.
AI.result: With one demonstration per task, Full-context and Episodic memory achieve 95.3% and 100.0% success at the original start, but drop 48-49 percentage points at a new start. Summary is stable across starts yet, with four demonstrations, retains less unchanged-route success after blocking (39.3%) than Working memory (44.8%) or trajectory memories (56-58%). At the new start, scaling from one to four relevant demonstrations improves Episodic success by 14.3 points, while others gain ≤1.3 points. Substituting half the relevant histories with other-task experience lowers both trajectory memories' success.
AI.conclusion: Robustness to one type of mismatch does not imply robustness to another, motivating evaluation of both stored information and its use at decision time.

title: Contract monitoring: governing AI via separation of powers
summary: We propose an AI safety framework that binds worker agents to contracts specifying their permitted actions. We show how these contracts can be enforced and specified by assigning distinct responsibilities to monitor agents and judges, and asymmetric computational resources to monitors and workers. Our framework allows us to empirically measure statistical safety guarantees. The framework applies to a wide range of settings, including code security and escape-the-box scenarios.

AI.tldr: A contract-based AI safety framework binds worker agents to action-permitting contracts, enforced via monitor agents and judges with asymmetric computational resources, enabling empirical measurement of statistical safety guarantees across settings like code security and escape-the-box scenarios.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the need for AI safety mechanisms that can reliably constrain the behavior of worker agents and provide measurable safety guarantees across diverse deployment settings.
AI.method: The proposed framework binds worker agents to contracts specifying their permitted actions. These contracts are enforced and specified by assigning distinct responsibilities to monitor agents and judges, and by allocating asymmetric computational resources between monitors and workers.
AI.result: The framework enables empirical measurement of statistical safety guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The framework applies to a wide range of settings, including code security and escape-the-box scenarios.

title: WSM-Aware HRI: An IoT-Enhanced Framework for Early Detection and Norm-Guided Repair of Failures with LLM Guidance
summary: Human-robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world-state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that reframes HRI failures as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model, using an LLM to surface implicit assumptions and enable proactive mismatch detection during intention formation.
AI.motivation: HRI failures remain a major barrier to real-world robot deployment. Prior work typically treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery. In reality, many breakdowns stem from humans and robots operating under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state, which existing approaches do not explicitly address.
AI.method: The authors introduce WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. An LLM makes implicit assumptions explicit, maps them to a small set of mismatch types, and specifies the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. The framework shifts handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, with interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations.
AI.result: Mismatch identification was evaluated on ten everyday cases covering both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system accurately produced the expected outputs, and ablations showed that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement.
AI.conclusion: Treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world-state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and provides a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human-robot interaction.

title: Toward Interactive Understanding of Code APIs
summary: Empowered by advances in Language Model agents, systems have made substantial strides in code generation and understanding. However, these approaches often rely on read access to the relevant code, an assumption which does not hold when dealing with external APIs. In this work, we introduce the PAU (Python API Understanding) benchmark, where we provide models with black-box, API-level access to code snippets. Models must query the API with exploratory inputs and draw insights from the resulting outputs, with the goal of describing the snippet's true functionality. By treating the code snippets as external tools that must be understood via interaction alone, PAU studies the more general problem of unsupervised tool understanding, specifically for tools implemented as Python methods. Despite recent progress in coding agents, even frontier models struggle to achieve high performance on PAU, with the best model (Claude-4-Opus) failing to understand over 45% of the PAU test set. An investigation into the common error modes reveals that models are overconfident; they often overrate the quality of their current hypothesis, leading to insufficient exploration and premature termination. Finally, we take inspiration from the Asymmetric Actor Critic (AAC) paradigm, frequently used in robot learning, to post-train models for interactive code understanding. Models trained with AAC conduct more active exploration of the APIs, with an AAC-tuned Qwen3-8B model matching the performance of GPT-5-mini.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAU, a benchmark for black-box API understanding where models must infer code snippet functionality through exploratory queries alone, revealing frontier model failures and proposing an AAC-based post-training method to improve interactive understanding.
AI.motivation: Existing code generation and understanding systems assume read access to the relevant code, an assumption that breaks down for external APIs. This motivates studying the more general problem of unsupervised tool understanding, where code snippets function as black boxes that must be understood purely through interaction.
AI.method: The authors introduce the PAU (Python API Understanding) benchmark, providing models with black-box, API-level access to code snippets. Models must probe the API with exploratory inputs and infer the snippet's true functionality from outputs. They also post-train models using the Asymmetric Actor Critic (AAC) paradigm from robot learning for interactive code understanding.
AI.result: Even frontier models perform poorly: the best model (Claude-4-Opus) fails to understand over 45% of the PAU test set. Error analysis shows models are overconfident, overrating their hypotheses, leading to insufficient exploration and premature termination. An AAC-tuned Qwen3-8B model matches GPT-5-mini's performance and exhibits more active API exploration.
AI.conclusion: Interactive black-box API understanding remains a challenging unsolved problem, and overconfidence-driven insufficient exploration is a key failure mode. AAC-based post-training offers a promising direction to improve exploration and understanding in interactive code agents.

title: Human Motion Prediction for Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: This paper compares three human motion prediction methods - GMM-based clustering, TransFusion, and Graph-Mixer - evaluating their effectiveness in human-robot collaboration. These predictions are valuable for improving robot motion planning by anticipating human movements and enhancing safety and efficiency in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks three human motion prediction methods—GMM-based clustering, TransFusion, and Graph-Mixer—for their effectiveness in human-robot collaboration.
AI.motivation: Improving robot motion planning by anticipating human movements, thereby enhancing safety and efficiency in dynamic environments.
AI.method: A comparative evaluation of three human motion prediction methods: GMM-based clustering, TransFusion, and Graph-Mixer.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative outcomes; it states that the three methods are compared in terms of their effectiveness for human-robot collaboration.
AI.conclusion: Human motion prediction is valuable for human-robot collaboration, and the three methods are assessed for this purpose, though the abstract does not specify which method performs best.

title: Memory as Middleware for Self-Improving AI Agents
comment: Conditionally accepted to Middleware 2026. Extended version
summary:
AI agents are stateless across sessions by default and therefore operationally amnesic: each session begins with little durable knowledge of prior failures, repairs, preferences, or successful strategies. As a result, agents repeat the same mistakes and discard hard-won experience. The dominant fix is \emph{bespoke memory}---retrieval, persistence, and learning logic hand-wired into one agent and bound to one storage engine. This creates a fragmented landscape where memory cannot be swapped, shared, isolated, or reasoned about independently of the agent that owns it. We argue that this is a middleware problem: agent memory deserves a first-class, pluggable layer, just as data access, messaging, and persistence each became middleware concerns.
  We develop this vision through six systems challenges: two-sided pluggability, host-native interposition, multi-tenant isolation, write-path consistency, federated sharing with provenance, and lifecycle governance. We present ALTK-Evolve, a reference implementation of memory middleware for self-improving agents, and use it to motivate a broader research agenda for future memory middleware.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that agent memory should be treated as a first-class, pluggable middleware layer rather than bespoke per-agent logic, and proposes six systems challenges plus a reference implementation (ALTK-Evolve) to frame a research agenda.
AI.motivation: AI agents are stateless across sessions by default, making them operationally amnesic: they begin each session with little durable knowledge of prior failures, repairs, preferences, or successful strategies. Consequently, agents repeat the same mistakes and discard hard-won experience. The dominant fix—bespoke memory with retrieval, persistence, and learning logic hand-wired into one agent and bound to one storage engine—creates a fragmented landscape where memory cannot be swapped, shared, isolated, or reasoned about independently of its owning agent.
AI.method: The authors reframe agent memory as a middleware problem, analogous to data access, messaging, and persistence. They develop this vision through six systems challenges: two-sided pluggability, host-native interposition, multi-tenant isolation, write-path consistency, federated sharing with provenance, and lifecycle governance. They present ALTK-Evolve, a reference implementation of memory middleware for self-improving agents, to motivate a broader research agenda.
AI.result: The paper identifies and articulates six key systems challenges for memory middleware and demonstrates a concrete reference implementation (ALTK-Evolve) that operationalizes the middleware vision for self-improving agents.
AI.conclusion: Agent memory should be elevated to a first-class, pluggable middleware layer, decoupled from individual agents and storage engines, to enable swapping, sharing, isolation, and independent reasoning. The proposed challenges and ALTK-Evolve reference implementation aim to catalyze a broader research agenda for future memory middleware.

title: Proactive Motion Planning for Human-Robot Cooperation
summary: This abstract addresses the incorporation of human motion prediction into proactive and dynamic human-aware motion planning, with the goal of enabling safe collaboration between humans and robots. A deep learning, graph-based model is used to forecast human motion and is integrated into a planning framework. This framework employs a static roadmap along with a time-variant A* algorithm to modify the trajectory of a UR5e manipulator. This method greatly improves human-robot interaction and enables proactive collision avoidance by combining precise motion forecasts with adaptive trajectory planning.

AI.tldr: This work integrates a graph-based deep learning human motion predictor into a proactive, human-aware planning framework that uses a static roadmap and a time-variant A* algorithm to adaptively replan a UR5e manipulator's trajectory, enabling proactive collision avoidance in human-robot collaboration.
AI.motivation: Safe human-robot collaboration requires the robot to anticipate human movement rather than react to it. Reactive planners are insufficient for avoiding collisions in shared, dynamic workspaces, so proactive planning driven by accurate motion forecasts is needed.
AI.method: A deep learning, graph-based model forecasts human motion; the predictions are integrated into a planning framework combining a static roadmap with a time-variant A* algorithm that modifies the trajectory of a UR5e manipulator.
AI.result: The approach reportedly greatly improves human-robot interaction and enables proactive collision avoidance by combining precise motion forecasts with adaptive trajectory planning.
AI.conclusion: Coupling learned, graph-based human motion prediction with time-variant roadmap search yields proactive, human-aware motion planning for safe robotic collaboration.

title: GameBoyWorlds: A Testbed for Self-Improvement in Embodied Video Games
summary: Powered by expert guidance, agents can operate in interactive environments; however, it is unclear whether they can learn autonomously from their own experience. To evaluate such self-improvement methods, we introduce GameBoyWorlds, a testbed for agentic self-improvement in video games. GameBoyWorlds-Execution evaluates task execution on a collection of 5 distinct game series. Agents are allowed access to dedicated training games but are provided no demonstrations, documentation, or rewards. Agents must ground themselves in the environment through self-directed exploration and by inferring actionable knowledge from their own experience. At test time, agents must complete short-horizon tasks that evaluate their ability to navigate, interact, and engage with game-specific mechanics in unseen games. Out-of-the-box frontier models complete fewer than 50% of the 500 tasks due to failures in multimodal grounding, establishing that self-improvement methods have room to push performance. We demonstrate that contemporary approaches to self-improvement are lacking, with world modelling and autonomous skill discovery failing, and a novel strategy that uses curiosity-based exploration to write guides achieving only partial success. GameBoyWorlds-Playthrough tests end-to-end game completion in two fan-made Pokémon games. We show that while frontier models have been pre-exposed to official releases such as Pokémon Red, they lack essential information on the games in our testbed. Instead of relying on their parametric knowledge to succeed, agents must learn from their own experience and autonomously improve over the course of the playthrough. We show that a sophisticated agentic pipeline with multimodal memory and hierarchical subgoals fails to reach even the first major milestone in both games, establishing GameBoyWorlds as an ambitious target for self-improving agents.

AI.tldr: GameBoyWorlds is a new testbed for evaluating agentic self-improvement in video games, comprising GameBoyWorlds-Execution (500 short-horizon tasks across 5 game series) and GameBoyWorlds-Playthrough (end-to-end completion of two fan-made Pokémon games). Frontier models and contemporary self-improvement methods, including world modelling, autonomous skill discovery, curiosity-based guide-writing, and a multimodal-memory hierarchical agentic pipeline, all fail substantially, showing self-improvement remains an open challenge.
AI.motivation: Although expert-guided agents can operate in interactive environments, it is unclear whether they can learn autonomously from their own experience. Existing evaluation settings provide demonstrations, documentation, or rewards, which masks the true difficulty of self-improvement. The paper introduces a testbed that removes these crutches to measure how well agents ground themselves and infer actionable knowledge purely from self-directed exploration.
AI.method: The authors build GameBoyWorlds with two tracks. GameBoyWorlds-Execution evaluates short-horizon tasks (navigation, interaction, game-specific mechanics) on 5 distinct game series, giving agents access to dedicated training games but no demonstrations, documentation, or rewards; agents must explore self-directedly and infer actionable knowledge from their own experience, then generalize to unseen games across 500 tasks. GameBoyWorlds-Playthrough tests end-to-end completion of two fan-made Pokémon games, requiring agents to learn from experience and improve throughout a playthrough rather than relying on parametric knowledge. The paper evaluates out-of-the-box frontier models and several self-improvement approaches: world modelling, autonomous skill discovery, curiosity-based exploration that writes guides, and a sophisticated agentic pipeline with multimodal memory and hierarchical subgoals.
AI.result: Out-of-the-box frontier models complete fewer than 50% of the 500 Execution tasks, failing due to multimodal grounding issues. Contemporary self-improvement approaches are lacking: world modelling and autonomous skill discovery fail, and a curiosity-based exploration strategy that writes guides achieves only partial success. In Playthrough, frontier models lack essential information about the fan-made games despite pre-exposure to official releases such as Pokémon Red; the sophisticated agentic pipeline with multimodal memory and hierarchical subgoals fails to reach even the first major milestone in both games.
AI.conclusion: GameBoyWorlds establishes self-improvement as a challenging, unsolved problem for agents. Current methods, including frontier models and dedicated self-improvement pipelines, are far from achieving autonomous learning from experience in interactive environments, positioning GameBoyWorlds as an ambitious target for future self-improving agents.

title: RE-0: Verified Recursive Improvement of Embodied Code-as-Policy Agents through Local On-Policy Distillation
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Corresponding author: Hongzhou Wang (wanghongzhou@jlu.edu.cn)
summary: Code-as-Policy agents accomplish long-horizon embodied tasks by generating and executing code, yet continually improving them with teachers that are stronger but not globally reliable remains a key challenge. Existing distillation methods typically treat the teacher's complete behavior as the supervision target and thus misassign training credit on states where the teacher fails. We propose RE-0, a recursively verified policy improvement framework: rather than assuming that the teacher globally outperforms the student, RE-0 requests local corrections from the teacher on the student's own failure histories and checks in the environment whether each correction is genuinely beneficial; verified corrections yield immediate improvement. Building on this, we propose RE-OPD, which turns verified interventions into supervision for on-policy distillation. Only counterfactually verified teacher interventions provide distribution-level supervision, weighted by their measured local benefit, and the improvement they induce is projected back into the standalone student, so both where supervision is applied and how much credit the teacher receives co-evolve with the student policy. We further prove that the student's per-round gain is lower-bounded by its verified intervention gain up to verification and projection error terms. Experiments across multiple Code-as-Policy embodied tasks show that RE-0 improves both teacher-assisted execution and the standalone student, and generalizes to novel robots and scenes.

AI.tldr: RE-0 is a recursively verified policy improvement framework for Code-as-Policy embodied agents that uses only locally verified teacher corrections rather than treating the teacher's full behavior as supervision, and RE-OPD converts these counterfactually verified interventions into weighted on-policy distillation signals, yielding improvement in both teacher-assisted and standalone student performance.
AI.motivation: Code-as-Policy agents handle long-horizon embodied tasks via generated code, but continual improvement is hampered by teachers that are stronger yet not globally reliable. Existing distillation methods assume the teacher globally outperforms the student and treat its complete behavior as the supervision target, thereby misassigning training credit on states where the teacher fails.
AI.method: RE-0 requests local corrections from the teacher on the student's own failure histories and verifies in the environment whether each correction is genuinely beneficial, so verified corrections yield immediate improvement. RE-OPD then turns these verified interventions into on-policy distillation supervision: only counterfactually verified teacher interventions provide distribution-level supervision, weighted by their measured local benefit, and the induced improvement is projected back into the standalone student, allowing both the application of supervision and the teacher's credit to co-evolve with the student policy.
AI.result: The authors prove that the student's per-round gain is lower-bounded by its verified intervention gain up to verification and projection error terms. Experiments on multiple Code-as-Policy embodied tasks show that RE-0 improves both teacher-assisted execution and the standalone student, and generalizes to novel robots and scenes.
AI.conclusion: Selective, environment-verified teacher interventions with benefit-weighted credit assignment provide a principled and effective route to continual policy improvement for Code-as-Policy embodied agents, avoiding the misassigned credit of full-behavior imitation distillation.

title: Residual Streams Read, Recurrent States Remember: The Global Workspace in Mamba Models
summary: Can the global-workspace account of transformer representations extend to state-space language models? We fit Jacobian lenses to the residual streams and recurrent states of Mamba-1, Mamba-2 and Mamba-3, using the original 1000-prompt recipe. Joint residual--state readouts improve recovery of known intermediate concepts over the residual lens on at least five of six task families in every tested Mamba checkpoint. On Mamba-2, state alone exceeds residual and logit lenses on all six families; a normalised joint readout improves on both components on five. Temporal maps and word-list experiments show earlier content remaining state-readable as residual visibility changes. We also propose sign-guarded steering, which improves target top-five success over coordinate exchange on matched verbal-report trials in five models. Recurrent state alone supports this verbal access. These gains do not extend consistently to relational answers: guarded edits often output the edited concept itself, and Mamba-3's joint edits can disrupt successful state-only redirection. Recurrent state thus provides a complementary carrier of workspace content, whose recovery, persistence and causal uses require separate measurements.

AI.tldr: Jacobian lenses applied to Mamba-1/2/3 show that recurrent states—alone or jointly with residuals—recover known intermediate concepts better than residual-only lenses, and sign-guarded steering improves verbal-report success, though relational-answer access lags.
AI.motivation: The global-workspace account is established for transformer representations, but it is unclear whether it extends to state-space language models. The paper probes whether recurrent states in Mamba models serve as a complementary carrier of workspace content.
AI.method: The authors fit Jacobian lenses to residual streams and recurrent states of Mamba-1, Mamba-2, and Mamba-3 using the original 1000-prompt recipe, comparing residual-only, state-only, logit, and joint readouts. They add temporal-map and word-list experiments, and propose sign-guarded steering, benchmarked against coordinate exchange on matched verbal-report trials.
AI.result: Joint residual–state readouts improve recovery over the residual lens on at least five of six task families in every tested Mamba checkpoint. On Mamba-2, state alone outperforms residual and logit lenses on all six families, and a normalized joint readout improves on both components on five. Sign-guarded steering improves target top-five success in five models. Gains do not extend consistently to relational answers: guarded edits often emit the edited concept itself, and Mamba-3 joint edits can disrupt successful state-only redirection.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent state provides a complementary carrier of workspace content whose recovery, persistence, and causal uses require separate measurement, and the global-workspace account only partially transfers to state-space language models.

title: DRAM: Delta-rule Recurrent Associative Memory for Robot Manipulation Policies
summary: Robotic manipulation is inherently history-dependent, yet most pretrained robotic policies condition on only the current observation or a short temporal window. Equipping such policies with long-term memory remains challenging: existing approaches either feed the backbone multi-frame observation windows, which substantially increase inference cost, or rely on pre-defined semantic features, which limit task generality and may also require the retraining of the backbone to adapt to the memory. We introduce DRAM (Delta-rule Recurrent Associative Memory), a plug-and-play memory module that can be attached to a wide range of pretrained robotic policies, endowing them with long-horizon memory without architectural modification or backbone retraining, requiring only task-specific post-training of the memory module and action expert. DRAM maintains a fixed-size associative memory using gated delta-rule linear attention, with a modified update that incorporates all tokens within each frame in parallel. An architecture-agnostic readout integrates historical context into action prediction across different policy architectures. Experiments show that DRAM consistently improves frozen pretrained policies over short-context baselines and alternative compact memory designs, validating its effectiveness as a fixed-size, post-hoc memory module trained with the backbone frozen.

AI.tldr: DRAM is a plug-and-play associative memory module that gives pretrained robotic policies long-horizon memory without architectural changes or backbone retraining.
AI.motivation: Most pretrained robotic policies condition only on current observation or a short temporal window, but manipulation is history-dependent. Existing memory approaches are costly (multi-frame windows raise inference cost) or restrictive (pre-defined semantic features limit generality and may require backbone retraining).
AI.method: DRAM (Delta-rule Recurrent Associative Memory) uses a fixed-size associative memory with gated delta-rule linear attention, with a modified update incorporating all tokens within each frame in parallel. An architecture-agnostic readout integrates historical context into action prediction across policy architectures. It attaches to pretrained policies, requiring only task-specific post-training of the memory module and action expert while keeping the backbone frozen.
AI.result: DRAM consistently improves frozen pretrained policies over short-context baselines and alternative compact memory designs.
AI.conclusion: DRAM validates its effectiveness as a fixed-size, post-hoc memory module trained with a frozen backbone, enabling long-horizon memory in a plug-and-play manner.

title: Escaping Alignment: A Physical Trap Model of Best-of-N Jailbreaking
summary: Best-of-$N$ jailbreaking (BoN) bypasses safeguards of aligned models by drawing $N$ independent augmentations of an unsafe prompt and sampling $M$ completions of each. Previous works have shown that the attack success rate (ASR) seems to follow a power-law in $N$, which we challenge. The exponent drifts with $N$, with an exponential crossover which is a finite-size artifact of the adversarial dataset. Little work has been done to explore the entire two-budget ($N, M$) attack surface as well as its dependence on the generation temperature $T$. We introduce a simple barrier model where each prompt has a baseline safety level and each augmentation a random thermally activated barrier. Then four numbers, each backed by an interpretable safety mechanism, determine the entire ($N, M$) attack surface. They extrapolate predictions from $N \leq 100$ to $N = 10^4$, collapse five distinct models on the same scaling function and predict ASR at different temperatures from the one they were fitted at.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the claimed power-law scaling of Best-of-N jailbreaking, showing the exponent drifts as a finite-size artifact, and introduces a barrier model where four interpretable numbers fully determine the (N, M, T) attack surface.
AI.motivation: Prior work reported that Best-of-N jailbreak attack success rate follows a power-law in N, but this is questioned as an artifact. The full two-budget (N, M) attack surface and its temperature dependence remain underexplored.
AI.method: A simple barrier model is proposed: each prompt has a baseline safety level, and each augmentation has a random thermally activated barrier. Four parameters, each tied to an interpretable safety mechanism, govern the entire (N, M) attack surface.
AI.result: The model extrapolates from N ≤ 100 to N = 10^4, collapses five distinct models onto a single scaling function, and predicts ASR at temperatures different from the fitted one.
AI.conclusion: The apparent power-law exponent drifts with N due to an exponential crossover that is a finite-size artifact of the adversarial dataset; the barrier framework provides a compact, interpretable, and generalizable description of BoN jailbreaking.

title: GlowTact: Simple and Compact Vision-Based Tactile Sensing with High Sensitivity and Spatial Resolution
summary: Vision-based tactile sensors (VBTS) provide rich contact information for robotic manipulation, but existing designs can be hard to simplify and adapt to the size and constraints of humanoid fingertips. We introduce \textbf{GlowTact}, a pressure-responsive vision-based tactile sensing mechanism that directly visualizes contact pressure. \textbf{GlowTact} requires only single-color, non-directional illumination, and the raw tactile image directly represents the pressure distribution without explicit geometry reconstruction. This simple sensing principle enables compact, customizable tactile sensors while preserving high sensitivity and rich spatial detail. We demonstrate gram-scale contact detection, accurate normal-force estimation, and reconstruction of fine contact geometry, including M1 screw threads. These results establish \textbf{GlowTact} as a practical new sensing technology for compact humanoid fingertips, combining a durable nitrile membrane and simple optical design with sensitive and information-rich tactile perception.

AI.tldr: GlowTact is a pressure-responsive vision-based tactile sensing mechanism that directly visualizes contact pressure using only single-color, non-directional illumination, enabling compact, customizable sensors for humanoid fingertips.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-based tactile sensors (VBTS) provide rich contact information but are difficult to simplify and adapt to the size and constraints of humanoid fingertips. A simpler, more compact sensing principle is needed that preserves high sensitivity and rich spatial detail.
AI.method: GlowTact uses a pressure-responsive visual sensing mechanism that directly visualizes contact pressure. It requires only single-color, non-directional illumination, and the raw tactile image directly represents the pressure distribution without explicit geometry reconstruction. The design combines a durable nitrile membrane with a simple optical setup.
AI.result: The sensor achieves gram-scale contact detection, accurate normal-force estimation, and reconstruction of fine contact geometry, including M1 screw threads.
AI.conclusion: GlowTact establishes a practical new sensing technology for compact humanoid fingertips, combining a durable nitrile membrane and simple optical design with sensitive and information-rich tactile perception.

title: READ-Bench: Benchmarking Historical Instance Retrieval for Time-Series Diagnosis
summary: Time-series diagnostic systems rarely rely on retrieving relevant historical cases, and when they do, retrieval is evaluated only indirectly through downstream prediction. We introduce READ-Bench, a benchmark for historical-case retrieval across 12 diagnostic datasets, centered on multivariate time series, that defines relevance by shared fault or event type rather than signal shape, so visually different traces of the same fault count as relevant while similar-looking traces of different faults do not. Treating retrieval as a base retriever followed by a reranker, we evaluate classical distances, symbolic retrievers, self-supervised and foundation-model embedders, and their fusion, plus label-aware and language-model rerankers, under one protocol that varies supervision, pollution, and corpus scale with significance testing. Under a common channel-independent interface, pretrained representations offer no statistically detectable advantage over strong classical and symbolic baselines for search alone. The decisive factor is a small amount of resolved-case supervision at reranking, namely a Gaussian-process reranker that propagates a few neighbor labels in embedding space, which helps far more than more sophisticated representations or language-model reasoning and holds under pollution and at full corpus scale. Guided by these findings, we fuse a normal-residual-scored embedder with a dynamic time warping leg via reciprocal-rank fusion, then rerank with the Gaussian-process reranker, improving NDCG@10 over its own search stage on all 12 datasets, by +0.11 from reranking and +0.16 over the strongest single base retriever.

AI.tldr: READ-Bench benchmarks historical-case retrieval for multivariate time-series diagnostics, defining relevance by shared fault/event type. Under a unified protocol, pretrained representations show no significant advantage for search alone; a lightweight Gaussian-process reranker with a few resolved-case labels is the decisive factor and, fused with classical and symbolic retrievers, improves NDCG@10 on all 12 datasets.
AI.motivation: Time-series diagnostic systems rarely retrieve relevant historical cases, and when they do, retrieval is evaluated only indirectly via downstream prediction. There is no standardized, directly-evaluated benchmark for historical-case retrieval in diagnostics, and it is unclear whether modern pretrained representations or language-model reasoning actually help relative to classical methods.
AI.method: Introduces READ-Bench, a benchmark for historical-case retrieval across 12 diagnostic datasets on multivariate time series, where relevance is defined by shared fault or event type rather than signal shape (so visually different traces of the same fault are relevant, and similar-looking traces of different faults are not). Retrieval is modeled as a base retriever plus a reranker. The study evaluates classical distances, symbolic retrievers, self-supervised and foundation-model embedders and their fusion, plus label-aware and language-model rerankers, under one protocol varying supervision, pollution, and corpus scale with significance testing, all behind a common channel-independent interface. A Gaussian-process reranker propagates a few neighbor labels in embedding space. The final system fuses a normal-residual-scored embedder with a dynamic time warping leg via reciprocal-rank fusion, then applies the Gaussian-process reranker.
AI.result: Pretrained representations offer no statistically detectable advantage over strong classical and symbolic baselines for search alone. Supervision at reranking is decisive: a Gaussian-process reranker propagating a few neighbor labels helps far more than more sophisticated representations or language-model reasoning, holding under pollution and at full corpus scale. The fused system improves NDCG@10 over its own search stage on all 12 datasets, by +0.11 from reranking and +0.16 over the strongest single base retriever.
AI.conclusion: For time-series diagnostic retrieval, relevance should be defined semantically (by fault/event type), and gains come from a small amount of resolved-case supervision at reranking rather than from more sophisticated representations or language-model reasoning. A simple, well-designed fusion of classical, symbolic, and residual-scored retrieval with a Gaussian-process reranker yields consistent improvements across all datasets.

title: Assisting for Open-Ended Tasks: Goal-Oriented Shared Autonomy as a Particle Filter
summary: A common approach for shared autonomy blends human inputs with autonomous assistance based on the human's likely goal. However, most existing approaches assume that a static set of possible goals is known a priori, which limits the use of such methods in unstructured assistive settings. We instead investigate how to enable shared autonomy with open-ended and dynamically changing goals. We formulate goal-oriented shared autonomy as a particle filter in which particles represent candidate human goals. Unlike conventional approaches with a fixed goal set, our transition model dynamically proposes new candidate goals as the interaction evolves, and human actions update the belief over these goals in real time. We instantiate this framework with foundation models (e.g., vision grounding and large language models) that propose context-relevant semantic goals, generate goal-conditioned assistance from low-level skill primitives, and refine those skills from human corrections. We assess our approach through a user study where 12 participants perform a variety of tabletop manipulation tasks with our method and state-of-the-art shared autonomy baselines. The results show that our particle filter-based approach reduces the amount of time users spend teleoperating the system and improves user satisfaction. User study videos: https://youtu.be/Ii26XuRqm9c

AI.tldr: The paper proposes goal-oriented shared autonomy as a particle filter over open-ended, dynamically emerging human goals, using foundation models to propose semantic goals and generate goal-conditioned assistance via low-level skill primitives.
AI.motivation: Most shared autonomy methods assume a static, known-a-priori goal set, which restricts their applicability in unstructured assistive settings where goals are open-ended and change dynamically.
AI.method: The authors formulate goal-oriented shared autonomy as a particle filter where particles represent candidate human goals. A transition model dynamically proposes new candidate goals as the interaction evolves, while human actions update the belief over goals in real time. The framework is instantiated with foundation models (vision grounding and large language models) that propose context-relevant semantic goals, generate goal-conditioned assistance from low-level skill primitives, and refine skills from human corrections.
AI.result: In a user study with 12 participants performing a variety of tabletop manipulation tasks, the method was compared against state-of-the-art shared autonomy baselines. The particle filter-based approach reduced user teleoperation time and improved user satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: Particle filter-based shared autonomy with dynamically proposed, foundation-model-derived goals enables effective assistance in unstructured settings, cutting teleoperation time and boosting satisfaction relative to fixed-goal-set baselines.

title: PastForward: Faster On-Device GUI Agents via Computational Experience Reuse
summary: Running GUI agents on edge devices can keep sensitive screens and interaction histories local, but the computational cost of inference at every action step makes deployment challenging. Existing GUI agent systems either perform full vision-language model (VLM) inference at each action step or reuse coarse-grained knowledge matched to prior tasks. However, dynamic mobile environments and user tasks make it difficult to fully utilize prior task executions without additional fine-tuning or task-specific offline exploration. To address this challenge, we present PastForward, a system that accelerates GUI agents through validated, fine-grained reuse of computational experience accumulated during ordinary task execution. During decoding, PastForward retrieves prior output sequences as device-adaptive multi-token proposals and verifies them in a single VLM forward pass. Across action steps, it uses prior GUI transitions to begin next-step inference while the device executes the current action, retains the early computation only when the predicted screen matches the observed screen, and carries reusable KV states forward. We evaluate PastForward on AndroidWorld workloads derived from real mobile usage patterns using multiple VLM backbones across server and edge platforms. On device, PastForward achieves action-step latency speedups of 1.63-2.36$\times$ while maintaining task success rates.

AI.tldr: PastForward accelerates on-device GUI agents via validated, fine-grained reuse of computation from ordinary task executions, achieving 1.63-2.36x action-step latency speedups on AndroidWorld without losing task success rates.
AI.motivation: Running GUI agents on edge devices keeps sensitive screens and interaction histories local, but per-action-step VLM inference is computationally expensive. Existing systems either run full VLM inference at each step or reuse only coarse-grained knowledge from prior tasks, which fails to exploit prior executions in dynamic mobile environments without fine-tuning or task-specific offline exploration.
AI.method: PastForward reuses computational experience accumulated during ordinary task execution at two levels. During decoding, it retrieves prior output sequences as device-adaptive multi-token proposals and verifies them in a single VLM forward pass. Across action steps, it uses prior GUI transitions to begin next-step inference while the device executes the current action, retains early computation only when the predicted screen matches the observed screen, and carries reusable KV states forward.
AI.result: Evaluated on AndroidWorld workloads derived from real mobile usage patterns with multiple VLM backbones on server and edge platforms. On device, PastForward achieves 1.63-2.36x action-step latency speedups while maintaining task success rates.
AI.conclusion: Validated, fine-grained reuse of prior computation enables practical on-device GUI agent deployment, delivering significant latency reductions without sacrificing task performance.

title: Think Fast, Plan Selectively: Adaptive Deliberation for Efficient Data-Driven MPC
summary: Data-driven model predictive control (MPC) combines learned world models with online trajectory optimization, achieving strong performance in continuous control. However, the per-step cost of sampling and evaluating hundreds of candidate trajectories restricts deployment to control frequencies well below what real-time robotics demands. Motivated by the dual-process theory of human cognition, which distinguishes between fast, intuitive processing (System 1) and slower, deliberative reasoning (System 2), we ask whether every decision requires the same degree of computational deliberation. We propose Fast-TD-MPC, a lightweight framework that adaptively routes between fast policy execution and test-time planning, reserving costly deliberation for states where it is most needed. Fast-TD-MPC delivers competitive task performance across 103 continuous control tasks while achieving up to ~4x faster inference. Under external disturbances, Fast-TD-MPC selectively falls back to planning, maintaining robustness comparable to the original planner.

AI.tldr: Fast-TD-MPC adaptively routes between fast policy execution and test-time planning, cutting inference cost up to ~4x while preserving task performance and robustness across 103 continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Data-driven MPC achieves strong continuous-control performance but its per-step sampling and evaluation of hundreds of candidate trajectories limits deployment to control frequencies far below real-time robotics requirements. Inspired by dual-process theory (fast System 1 vs. slow System 2), the authors question whether every decision requires equal computational deliberation.
AI.method: The authors propose Fast-TD-MPC, a lightweight framework that adaptively routes between fast policy execution and test-time planning, reserving costly deliberation for states where it is most needed. It selectively falls back to planning under external disturbances.
AI.result: Fast-TD-MPC achieves competitive task performance across 103 continuous control tasks while delivering up to ~4x faster inference, and under external disturbances it maintains robustness comparable to the original planner by selectively falling back to planning.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive routing between reactive policy execution and deliberative test-time planning can substantially reduce inference cost without sacrificing task performance or disturbance robustness, offering a more deployment-friendly alternative to always-on MPC.

title: Noisy Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Code LLMs
comment: This paper has been accepted by EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various code-related tasks. However, unlike carefully curated datasets that are typically high-quality and error-free, real-world user instructions are often vague and error-prone, posing significant challenges to the robustness of code LLMs. Furthermore, robustness-oriented fine-tuning relies on paired clean-noisy samples, which are costly to curate and require sophisticated noisy simulation techniques. To address these challenges, we propose the Noisy Test-time Reinforcement Learning framework (NTRL-Code), which enables robust self-evolution of code LLMs using only unlabeled noisy data during the testing stage. Specifically, NTRL-Code uses conservative self-denoising to obtain a cleaner semantic anchor for target estimation, and employs an abstract-syntax-tree (AST)-based structural aggregation mechanism to estimate a proxy target from multiple candidate programs. The policy is then optimized on the original noisy prompts with a hybrid reward that combines format validity, code similarity, and anti-repetition signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks, each incorporating character-level, word-level, and paragraph-level perturbations, demonstrate that NTRL-Code yields robust and consistent improvements, stabilizing the predictions of various base models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xikai97/NTRL-Code.

AI.tldr: NTRL-Code enables robust self-evolution of code LLMs at test time using only unlabeled noisy data, via conservative self-denoising and AST-based structural aggregation.
AI.motivation: Real-world user instructions for code tasks are often vague and error-prone, unlike curated datasets. Robustness-oriented fine-tuning depends on costly paired clean-noisy samples and requires sophisticated noisy simulation techniques.
AI.method: Proposes Noisy Test-time Reinforcement Learning (NTRL-Code). It uses conservative self-denoising to obtain a cleaner semantic anchor for target estimation, and an AST-based structural aggregation mechanism to estimate a proxy target from multiple candidate programs. The policy is optimized on the original noisy prompts with a hybrid reward combining format validity, code similarity, and anti-repetition signals.
AI.result: Experiments on three benchmarks with character-level, word-level, and paragraph-level perturbations show robust and consistent improvements, stabilizing predictions of various base models.
AI.conclusion: NTRL-Code achieves robust self-evolution of code LLMs using only unlabeled noisy test-time data, avoiding the need for paired clean-noisy samples.

title: RECAST: Recasting Vision-Language Semantics into an Actionable Cost Map for Robot Navigation
summary: Safe and robust robot navigation across diverse environments requires a high-level understanding of complex scenes and the ability to carry it into stable motion. Recent works tackle this with learning-based models trained at scale and with approaches built on vision-language models (VLMs). However, learning-based models break down outside their training distribution, while VLM-based approaches bring that understanding but rarely ground it in the scene or align the action with it. To address these limitations, we present RECAST, a robot navigation framework that combines the reasoning of a VLM with the spatial grounding of vision foundation models to build an Actionable Cost map. Given the robot's front view and the user's instruction, we first decompose the scene with the VLM, judging which surfaces are traversable, which objects pose a risk, which heading to prefer, and which gaps are passable. Vision foundation models then ground these surfaces and objects in the image, and all four judgments are spatially recast into one compact cost map. This map both conditions the trajectory decoders and scores their proposals to select the one to execute. As the VLM's answers trail the live scene, both steps draw on cost maps from two points in time: the pivot frame the VLM judged, which carries all four judgments, and the current frame, whose terrain and collision costs are rebuilt from the current image. RECAST improves success over the strongest prior method by 13.3 points in simulation and 31.4 points on a real quadruped, and reduces the collision rate relative to it by 9.6 and 14.3 points, reaching the lowest collision rate among all methods. The project page is available at https://recast-nav.github.io/

AI.tldr: RECAST is a robot navigation framework that fuses VLM reasoning with vision foundation model spatial grounding into a single Actionable Cost map, improving success rates and lowering collisions in simulation and on a real quadruped.
AI.motivation: Learning-based navigation models fail outside their training distribution, while VLM-based approaches provide high-level scene understanding but rarely ground it spatially or align actions with it. A method is needed that combines robust semantic reasoning with scene-grounded, stable motion.
AI.method: Given the robot's front view and a user instruction, a VLM decomposes the scene into four judgments: traversable surfaces, risky objects, preferred heading, and passable gaps. Vision foundation models ground these surfaces and objects in the image, and all four judgments are spatially recast into one compact Actionable Cost map. This map conditions trajectory decoders and scores their proposals for selection. To handle the VLM's temporal lag, both steps use cost maps from two time points: the pivot frame judged by the VLM and the current frame, whose terrain and collision costs are rebuilt from the current image.
AI.result: RECAST improves success over the strongest prior method by 13.3 points in simulation and 31.4 points on a real quadruped, and reduces collision rate by 9.6 and 14.3 points respectively, achieving the lowest collision rate among all methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining VLM reasoning with vision foundation model grounding into an Actionable Cost map yields safer, more robust robot navigation, outperforming prior methods in both simulation and real-world quadruped deployment.

title: AI Harness: Certification under Proposal-Conditioned Information for Foundation-Model Agents
summary: Foundation-model agents are often modeled as policies over an observed state. In deployed systems, however, a runtime may intervene only after the model has emitted a semantic proposal, making the proposal both an action candidate and a decision-time observation generated by a history-conditioned process. We show that collapsing this structure into a state-only proposal envelope can preserve proposal coverage while destroying certifiability. In a finite robust interface, the viability kernel of the collapsed model is contained in the physical projection of the history-augmented kernel, and the collapse is lossless exactly when every proposal-conditioned collapsed fiber retains a common robust-safe intervention. This gap can be maximal even with constant-size proposal and history alphabets. The same common-action condition yields a dual result: observing the current proposal can restore robust feasibility when it separates latent modes requiring incompatible interventions. We extend these one-step results over time using exact finite beliefs and standard safety and reachability fixed points, separating indefinite operational viability from finite worst-case verified progress. Controlled model-in-the-loop tests reproduce the predicted obstructions when telemetry or effect verification is removed or intervention authority is restricted. Thus, our contribution is not a new fixed-point calculus, but a characterization of when proposal--history correlation at the model--tool boundary is necessary for certification.

AI.tldr: Treating a foundation-model agent's semantic proposal as both an action candidate and a decision-time observation (rather than collapsing it into a state-only envelope) is provably necessary for certifiability: the collapsed viability kernel is a subset of the true history-augmented kernel's physical projection, and the collapse is lossless exactly when every proposal-conditioned fiber admits a common robust-safe intervention—a gap that can be maximal.
AI.motivation: Deployed foundation-model agents typically act after a runtime intervention on a semantic proposal, so the proposal is simultaneously an action candidate and a history-conditioned decision-time observation. Standard state-only policy abstractions erase this proposal–history correlation, and the paper asks whether such collapsing preserves the ability to certify safety.
AI.method: A finite robust interface formalism is used to compare a collapsed state-only proposal envelope against a history-augmented model via viability kernels. The analysis derives a fiber-wise common-action condition for losslessness, extends the one-step results over time using exact finite beliefs and standard safety/reachability fixed points, and validates predictions with controlled model-in-the-loop tests that ablate telemetry, effect verification, and intervention authority.
AI.result: Collapsing to a state-only proposal envelope can preserve proposal coverage yet destroy certifiability: the collapsed viability kernel lies within the physical projection of the history-augmented kernel, and the collapse is lossless exactly when every proposal-conditioned collapsed fiber retains a common robust-safe intervention. This gap can be maximal even with constant-size proposal and history alphabets. Dually, observing the current proposal can restore robust feasibility when it separates latent modes requiring incompatible interventions. Model-in-the-loop tests reproduce the predicted obstructions when telemetry or effect verification is removed or intervention authority is restricted.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a new fixed-point calculus but a characterization of when proposal–history correlation at the model–tool boundary is necessary for certification. It separates indefinite operational viability from finite worst-case verified progress and shows that preserving proposal-conditioned structure is essential for sound runtime certification of foundation-model agents.

title: World SLAM Model: Joint World Modeling for SLAM and Navigation
summary: We introduce World SLAM Model (WSM), a unified framework that brings the SLAM paradigm directly into downstream navigation. Rather than treating SLAM merely as an upstream module that provides poses, maps or tokens, WSM adopts its core mechanisms, including incremental state updates with persistent memory and backend refinement of accumulated errors, to maintain a consistent world state during interaction. Given the current observation and a navigation goal, WSM predicts future visual states and jointly estimates their camera motion and dense geometry, grounding visual prediction in an evolving spatial world state. This spatial state is continuously updated as new observations arrive and provides the basis for action generation and closed-loop navigation. WSM is trained end-to-end with a joint navigation--SLAM objective, enabling downstream navigation to benefit directly from SLAM-style state maintenance and refinement while preserving accurate geometric estimation. Experiments demonstrate improved navigation performance together with strong SLAM accuracy, highlighting the potential of SLAM as an intrinsic mechanism for long-horizon world modeling and embodied interaction.

AI.tldr: WSM integrates SLAM mechanisms (incremental state updates, persistent memory, backend refinement) directly into navigation, predicting future visual states with joint camera motion and dense geometry estimation to support action generation and closed-loop navigation.
AI.motivation: SLAM is typically treated as an upstream module that only supplies poses, maps, or tokens to downstream navigation, limiting its role. The authors argue SLAM's core mechanisms are valuable for maintaining a consistent world state during interaction.
AI.method: WSM adopts SLAM's core mechanisms—incremental state updates with persistent memory and backend refinement of accumulated errors—to maintain a consistent world state. Given current observation and a navigation goal, it predicts future visual states and jointly estimates camera motion and dense geometry, grounding prediction in an evolving spatial world state. The state updates continuously with new observations, providing the basis for action generation and closed-loop navigation. It is trained end-to-end with a joint navigation–SLAM objective.
