AI.result: Experiments show improved navigation performance together with strong SLAM accuracy, demonstrating benefits from SLAM-style state maintenance and refinement while preserving accurate geometric estimation.
AI.conclusion: SLAM can serve as an intrinsic mechanism for long-horizon world modeling and embodied interaction, rather than merely an upstream module.

title: CoMemBench: Benchmarking Collaborative Memory Boundaries across Multi-Agent Workflow Topologies
summary: Multi-agent workflows require task-relevant information to be shared across agents, while irrelevant, stale, unverified, or incompatible information must remain isolated. We call this task-conditioned scope of information a collaborative memory boundary. Workflow topology determines which intermediate artifacts are applicable to which downstream workers and when they cease to be valid, thereby providing a structural stress dimension for sharing and isolation. Existing memory benchmarks primarily evaluate retention and retrieval, whereas multi-agent benchmarks emphasize coordination and end-to-end completion, leaving topology-conditioned memory boundaries largely unmeasured. We introduce CoMemBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for collaborative memory sharing and isolation across multi-agent workflow topologies. It constructs 800 composite workflows across four domains from source-grounded dependency graphs, with node-local specifications, verifiable artifact handoffs, native evaluators, and matched isolation challenges. CoMemBench measures workflow completion, verified node progress, required-handoff reliability, isolation robustness, and token cost. Experiments reveal a sharing-isolation trade-off: broader context improves information availability but can weaken isolation, while system rankings shift across topologies and artifact violations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoMemBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for measuring task-conditioned memory sharing and isolation boundaries in multi-agent workflows across four topologies, revealing a sharing-isolation trade-off.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent workflows need to share task-relevant information while isolating irrelevant, stale, unverified, or incompatible information—a concept termed the collaborative memory boundary. Workflow topology determines artifact applicability and validity, creating a structural stress dimension. Existing memory benchmarks focus on retention/retrieval, and multi-agent benchmarks on coordination and end-to-end completion, so topology-conditioned memory boundaries remain largely unmeasured.
AI.method: The authors build CoMemBench from source-grounded dependency graphs, generating 800 composite workflows spanning four domains. Each includes node-local specifications, verifiable artifact handoffs, native evaluators, and matched isolation challenges. It measures workflow completion, verified node progress, required-handoff reliability, isolation robustness, and token cost.
AI.result: Experiments expose a sharing-isolation trade-off: broader context improves information availability but can weaken isolation. System rankings shift across different topologies and artifact violations.
AI.conclusion: CoMemBench provides an execution-grounded evaluation of collaborative memory boundaries, showing that topology and artifact validity critically affect the balance between information sharing and isolation in multi-agent workflows.

title: PF-RL: Progress Field Reinforcement Learning via Goal-Conditioned Value Geometry for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning~(RFT) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving Vision-Language-Action~(VLA) policies, yet sparse task-level outcomes provide limited credit for intermediate transitions, especially in long-horizon manipulation. A natural approach is to model intermediate task progress and use it as dense feedback for policy improvement. Despite their architectural differences, existing progress-aware methods commonly formulate task progress as an explicit scalar prediction, providing limited structure for modeling how intermediate observations relate to the task goal, which may hinder effective transition-level credit assignment. We introduce Progress Field Reinforcement Learning (PF-RL), which learns a structured goal-conditioned progress representation over pretrained VLA features and converts it into dense credit for policy optimization. A lightweight shared Progress Field head maps current and goal representations into a compact progress space, where geometric distance induces goal-conditioned value, while complementary temporal and goal-structure objectives shape the learned geometry. Transition-level value changes naturally yield dense progress advantages, enabling fine-grained credit assignment for both offline policy improvement and online reinforcement fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin2.0, and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks show that PF-RL consistently improves policy performance over strong supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning, and progress-aware baselines.

AI.tldr: PF-RL learns a structured goal-conditioned progress representation (a "progress field") over pretrained VLA features and converts its geometry into dense transition-level credit, yielding consistent gains over SFT, RFT, and progress-aware baselines on LIBERO, RoboTwin2.0, and real-world bimanual tasks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement fine-tuning of VLA policies relies on sparse task-level rewards, which give weak credit to intermediate transitions—problematic in long-horizon manipulation. Existing progress-aware methods model progress as an explicit scalar prediction, offering limited structure for relating intermediate observations to the goal, thus hindering effective transition-level credit assignment.
AI.method: PF-RL learns a structured goal-conditioned progress representation built on pretrained VLA features. A lightweight shared Progress Field head maps current and goal representations into a compact progress space; geometric distance in this space induces goal-conditioned value, while temporal and goal-structure objectives shape the learned geometry. Transition-level value changes yield dense progress advantages, used for both offline policy improvement and online reinforcement fine-tuning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin2.0, and real-world bimanual manipulation show PF-RL consistently outperforms strong supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning, and progress-aware baselines.
AI.conclusion: Replacing scalar progress prediction with a structured goal-conditioned progress field enables fine-grained, dense credit assignment and consistently improves VLA policy performance in both offline and online fine-tuning settings, including real-world bimanual tasks.

title: Instruct, Not Answer: Using Instruction Privileges in On-Policy Context Distillation
summary: On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD) has recently emerged as a powerful technique for transferring context to student models and for self-improvement. In OPCD, the teacher is conditioned on privileged information, and the goal is to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the privileged teacher and the student, evaluated on student-generated tokens. Many existing studies show that using instance-specific gold answers or gold demonstrations as the default privilege can hurt training performance, especially out-of-distribution (OOD). In this work, we instead design general instructions that target common student mistakes observed on the training samples, and show that such simple instructions can outperform gold as the OPCD privilege. In autoformalization tasks, using a matched formatting instruction as the privilege could outperform gold in OOD accuracy by a large margin. In 7 out of 8 experiments using ProverQA, ProofWriter, and ProntoQA as datasets, and Qwen3-Thinking and Olmo3-Thinking families as models, matched instruction privileges outperform gold in OOD by 4 to 17 points, while remaining on par with gold in-domain. Each instruction is only a few sentences (and thus contains much less information compared to all instance-specific gold) and is applied uniformly to every training sample. These results indicate that a general instruction, which applies equally to source and target domain examples, can be substantially more transferable than instance-specific gold in OPCD while maintaining in-domain performance.

AI.tldr: General instructions targeting common student mistakes outperform instance-specific gold answers as the privileged information in on-policy context distillation, improving OOD accuracy by 4–17 points while matching gold in-domain.
AI.motivation: Gold answers or gold demonstrations are the default privilege in OPCD, but prior work shows they can hurt training performance, especially on out-of-distribution (OOD) data. The authors question whether instance-specific gold is the optimal privilege and seek a more transferable alternative.
AI.method: The authors replace instance-specific gold privileges with short, general instructions that target common student mistakes observed on training samples. These instructions are a few sentences long and applied uniformly to every training sample as the teacher's privilege in OPCD, while training minimizes KL divergence between the privileged teacher and student on student-generated tokens.
AI.result: Across 8 experiments (ProverQA, ProofWriter, ProntoQA datasets; Qwen3-Thinking and Olmo3-Thinking model families), matched instruction privileges outperform gold in OOD by 4–17 points in 7 of 8 cases while remaining on par with gold in-domain. In autoformalization tasks, a matched formatting instruction as privilege substantially outperforms gold in OOD accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A general instruction that applies equally to source and target domain examples can be substantially more transferable than instance-specific gold in OPCD while maintaining in-domain performance, despite containing far less information.

title: SEES: A Self-Evolving Embodied System via Failure-Guided VLA Policy Adaptation
summary: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies demonstrate promising generalization across diverse short-horizon tasks. However, they remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks, partly because the large-scale training data is biased toward single-stage manipulation tasks that are cheaper to demonstrate. A single weak atomic skill can cause failures across multiple multi-stage tasks. To address such failures, existing methods often require experts to identify the bottleneck and provide additional demonstrations, making the improvement costly and potentially impractical after deployment. To this end, we present a Self-Evolving Embodied System (SEES) that learns from failures and improves the VLA policy without additional expert demonstrations. SEES decomposes long-horizon tasks into atomic tasks and routes them to corresponding family policies. Each family consists of related atomic skills that share one VLA adapter. During execution, the system automatically monitors atomic-task outcomes to identify the most frequently failing atomic skills as the current bottlenecks. To overcome these bottlenecks, SEES constructs tailored RL tasks in simulation by restoring previously encountered states and generating task-specific success criteria with an LLM. Online RL updates the shared family adapters to promote positive transfer among related atomic skills and cumulative improvement across evolution rounds. Extensive experiments show that SEES can be integrated with different VLA backbones to progressively improve their long-horizon performance. We also observe continued improvement on unseen tasks, providing evidence of transfer beyond the evolution settings.

AI.tldr: SEES is a self-evolving embodied system that learns from failures to improve VLA policies without expert demonstrations, by decomposing long-horizon tasks into atomic tasks, routing them to family adapters, and applying LLM-guided online RL to fix bottleneck skills.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action policies generalize well on short-horizon tasks but fail on long-horizon tasks, largely because large-scale training data is biased toward cheap single-stage manipulation tasks. A single weak atomic skill can cascade into failures across multiple multi-stage tasks. Existing remedies require experts to diagnose bottlenecks and provide extra demonstrations, which is costly and often impractical post-deployment.
AI.method: SEES decomposes long-horizon tasks into atomic tasks and routes each to a corresponding family policy, where each family groups related atomic skills sharing one VLA adapter. During execution, it monitors atomic-task outcomes to identify the most frequently failing skills as bottlenecks. It then builds tailored RL tasks in simulation by restoring previously encountered states and generating task-specific success criteria via an LLM. Online RL updates the shared family adapters, enabling positive transfer among related skills and cumulative improvement across evolution rounds.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show SEES integrates with different VLA backbones and progressively improves their long-horizon performance. Continued improvement is also observed on unseen tasks, providing evidence of transfer beyond the evolution settings.
AI.conclusion: SEES offers a self-improving, expert-free route to strengthening long-horizon VLA policies: automatic failure monitoring and LLM-driven simulation RL on shared family adapters convert failures into targeted skill improvement, with demonstrated cross-task transfer.

title: Witness: Discovery, Deciphering, and Epiphany in Interactive Puzzle Environments
summary: Automated science needs agents that can work out the rules of an unfamiliar environment by interacting with it. Interactive rule-discovery puzzles offer a controlled setting for studying this ability: an agent infers hidden rules through experimentation and uses what it has inferred to reach a stated goal. We ask what limits current language models on these puzzles and whether reinforcement learning (RL) improves performance on rules held out from training. To study both, we introduce WITNESS, a 2D grid-based puzzle environment with ground-truth ASCII observations and controlled access to rules. An agentic pipeline generates games for WitnessGym, the RL training suite, and WitnessBench, comprising public validation and private test games. The validation set separately tests new compositions of trained rule primitives and primitives absent from training. Under a shared harness, the best of 18 frontier proprietary and open-weight models solves only 24\% of private test level slots, with scores sensitive to the observation interface and agent configuration. Providing ground-truth rules raises Opus-5's validation RHAE-L5 (relative human action efficiency over the first five levels) from 59.9 to 97.8, whereas a 27B open-weight model gains only 2.1 points and remains limited even with the rules provided. RL on WitnessGym raises the 27B model's private test RHAE-L5 from 2.1 to 5.4 and yields a mean gain of 4.1 points on four external discovery benchmarks. Together, these results point to rule acquisition as a major difficulty for frontier models like Opus-5 while smaller models further struggle on rule-based execution, and indicate that RL on hidden-rule puzzles transfers to broader rules and real-world tasks beyond training. Benchmark is available at: https://witnessbench.ai

AI.tldr: WITNESS is a 2D grid puzzle environment with ground-truth ASCII observations and controlled rule access, used to test whether LMs can infer hidden rules and whether RL improves generalization to unseen rules; the best of 18 frontier models solves only 24% of private test slots, and RL on the training suite transfers to external discovery benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Automated science requires agents that can infer the rules of an unfamiliar environment through interaction. Interactive rule-discovery puzzles provide a controlled testbed for this capability, but it is unclear what limits current language models on such puzzles and whether RL improves performance on rules held out from training.
AI.method: The authors introduce WITNESS, a 2D grid-based puzzle environment with ground-truth ASCII observations and controlled access to rules. An agentic pipeline generates games for WitnessGym (RL training suite) and WitnessBench (public validation and private test games). The validation set separately tests new compositions of trained rule primitives and primitives absent from training. Models are evaluated under a shared harness, and a 27B open-weight model is RL-trained on WitnessGym and tested on four external discovery benchmarks.
AI.result: The best of 18 frontier proprietary and open-weight models solves only 24% of private test level slots, with scores sensitive to the observation interface and agent configuration. Providing ground-truth rules raises Opus-5's validation RHAE-L5 from 59.9 to 97.8, while a 27B open-weight model gains only 2.1 points and remains limited even with rules provided. RL on WitnessGym raises the 27B model's private test RHAE-L5 from 2.1 to 5.4 and yields a mean gain of 4.1 points on four external discovery benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Rule acquisition is a major difficulty for frontier models such as Opus-5, while smaller models additionally struggle with rule-based execution. RL on hidden-rule puzzles transfers to broader rules and real-world tasks beyond training, indicating that interactive rule-discovery training is a promising path toward automated science agents.

title: MORPH: Self-Organising Multi-Robot Task Allocation via Neuroplasticity-Inspired Adaptive Topology
comment: Full version of the paper published in The 23rd European Conference on Multi-Agent Systems (EUMAS), 2026.The implementation and experiment scripts are available at https://github.com/Cyber-physical-Systems-Lab/morph_v2
summary: Multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) in dynamic environments faces a fundamental tension: effective coordination requires learned structure, but that structure must adapt when conditions change. Existing methods resolve this by assuming prior task knowledge, a utility function, a cost matrix, or a trained policy making them brittle when deployed without such knowledge or when task distributions shift. We present MORPH(Multi-agent Online Rewiring through Plasticity-guided Hierarchy), a training-free MRTA framework where global allocation quality emerges from 4 local plasticity rules (synaptic, homeostatic, structural, and metaplasticity) applied to a directed pairwise preference matrix updated from runtime co-occurrence and task-completion feedback. MORPH requires no task model, no bid computation, and no offline training; response decisions use learned AGV-to-Picker preferences rather than a fixed proximity rule. Within the Gerkey-Mataric MRTA taxonomy, MORPH is the first method in the single-task, single-robot, instantaneous-assignment class to learn directed pairwise allocation preferences online. Evaluated on the TA-RWARE warehouse benchmark (8-24 agents, 4 maps, 800 steps per episode, 5 seeds), MORPH achieves 110% of all-to-all throughput at N=24 while using only 21% of possible coordination links as an efficiency advantage that grows monotonically with fleet size. Under spatial task distribution shift, MORPH degrades 3x less than proximity-based methods while its learned preferences remain uncorrelated with Manhattan distance. Systematic ablation confirms all four plasticity rules contribute measurably. Two allocation properties emerge without programming: cross-type preference dominance and progressive preference sparsification, mirroring the developmental refinement of biological neural circuits. Learned preferences are driven by task co-occurrence history, not spatial proximity.

AI.tldr: MORPH is a training-free multi-robot task allocation framework where global allocation emerges from four local plasticity rules operating on a directed pairwise preference matrix, achieving full throughput with far fewer coordination links than all-to-all.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot task allocation in dynamic environments faces a tension: effective coordination requires learned structure, yet existing methods assume prior task knowledge, utility functions, cost matrices, or trained policies, making them brittle under missing knowledge or distribution shift.
AI.method: MORPH applies four local plasticity rules (synaptic, homeostatic, structural, metaplasticity) to a directed pairwise preference matrix updated from runtime co-occurrence and task-completion feedback. It requires no task model, no bid computation, and no offline training; response decisions use learned AGV-to-Picker preferences rather than fixed proximity.
AI.result: On TA-RWARE (8-24 agents, 4 maps, 800 steps, 5 seeds), MORPH reaches 110% of all-to-all throughput at N=24 using only 21% of possible coordination links, with efficiency gains growing monotonically with fleet size. Under spatial task distribution shift it degrades 3x less than proximity-based methods, and learned preferences are uncorrelated with Manhattan distance. Ablations confirm all four plasticity rules contribute.
AI.conclusion: MORPH is the first method in the single-task, single-robot, instantaneous-assignment class of the Gerkey-Mataric taxonomy to learn directed pairwise allocation preferences online, yielding emergent cross-type preference dominance and progressive preference sparsification driven by task co-occurrence history rather than spatial proximity.

title: Fracast-0: Fractal Weight Sharing for a Time Series Foundation Model with Only 85K Parameters
summary: Time series foundation models must preserve multi-domain breadth, probabilistic output, and multiple temporal scales, but parameter count grows when each scale receives a separate representation. We introduce Fracast-0, a probabilistic forecasting foundation model that exploits temporal self-similarity to reuse one operator across scales. A parameter-free detector extracts significant seasonal structure. The encoder applies a shared local block along a geometric dilation ladder with scale conditioning, while the decoder combines context-gathered states with an explicit seasonal future state and reuses a second block along another ladder before emitting nine quantiles. Pretraining across six corpora preserves multi-domain breadth within 85,001 parameters. On 97 GIFT-Eval configurations without per-dataset fine-tuning, Fracast-0 is the smallest of 28 evaluated checkpoints and remains non-dominated in the aggregate parameter-accuracy plane with MASE 0.808 and WQL 0.564. It uses 42.0% fewer parameters than TinyCast, whose MASE and WQL are 4.2% and 3.3% lower. These results support cross-scale weight reuse as a practical route to further time series foundation model compression.

AI.tldr: Fracast-0 is a 85,001-parameter probabilistic forecasting foundation model that reuses a single operator across temporal scales via self-similarity, achieving competitive zero-shot accuracy on 97 GIFT-Eval configurations.
AI.motivation: Time series foundation models need to keep multi-domain breadth, probabilistic outputs, and multiple temporal scales, but adding a separate representation per scale inflates parameter count. The authors aim to break this scaling cost by exploiting temporal self-similarity.
AI.method: A parameter-free detector extracts significant seasonal structure. The encoder applies a shared local block along a geometric dilation ladder with scale conditioning; the decoder combines context-gathered states with an explicit seasonal future state and reuses a second block along another ladder before emitting nine quantiles. Pretraining spans six corpora.
AI.result: On 97 GIFT-Eval configurations without per-dataset fine-tuning, Fracast-0 is the smallest of 28 evaluated checkpoints and stays non-dominated in the aggregate parameter-accuracy plane with MASE 0.808 and WQL 0.564. It uses 42.0% fewer parameters than TinyCast, whose MASE and WQL are 4.2% and 3.3% lower.
AI.conclusion: Cross-scale weight reuse is supported as a practical route to further compressing time series foundation models.

title: An Empirical Study on What Matters for Viewpoint-Generalizable Policies in Visual Imitation Learning
summary: Visual imitation learning is a promising approach to training robot manipulation policies capable of completing a wide variety of tasks. However, policies today remain brittle to viewpoint perturbations, making deployment in diverse environments a challenge. We present a controlled empirical study of which design choices allow visuomotor policies to generalize across viewpoints. We find that viewpoint generalization improves when dense visual tokens are retained and the action head participates in geometric reasoning. On a suite of simulated tasks that span a wide range of camera poses, we show that these design choices yield a policy that remains performant across viewpoints. As a practical consequence, a policy trained with these design choices also transfers zero-shot from simulation to the real world under random camera configurations.

AI.tldr: A controlled empirical study identifies two key design choices—retaining dense visual tokens and having the action head participate in geometric reasoning—that make visuomotor policies generalize across viewpoints, including zero-shot sim-to-real transfer under random camera poses.
AI.motivation: Visual imitation learning can train robot manipulation policies for many tasks, but current policies are brittle to viewpoint perturbations, hindering deployment in diverse environments. The paper aims to determine which design choices enable viewpoint generalization.
AI.method: A controlled empirical study comparing design choices for visuomotor policies. The two identified factors are (1) retaining dense visual tokens (rather than compressing/discarding them) and (2) having the action head participate in geometric reasoning. Evaluated on a suite of simulated tasks spanning a wide range of camera poses.
AI.result: The design choices yield a policy that remains performant across viewpoints in simulation. As a practical consequence, the policy trained with these choices also transfers zero-shot from simulation to the real world under random camera configurations.
AI.conclusion: Viewpoint generalization in visuomotor policies is achievable through dense visual token retention and geometry-aware action heads, and this improves robustness enough to enable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer under random camera poses.

title: A bilingual AI audiologist built through rubric-guided playbook induction outperforms human audiologists in a blinded evaluation of simulated cases
comment: 75 pages, including 51 pages of Supplementary Information
summary: Audiology consultation requires structured history-taking, audiometric interpretation and patient-centred communication, yet real-world case material is scarce. We present a bilingual AI audiologist pairing a general-purpose large language model with rubric-guided playbook induction, multimodal audiogram interpretation and retrieval-augmented grounding, without fine-tuning the language-model backbone. Using a 21-item rubric and an AI patient simulator, we induced a 19-rule consultation policy from 73 training cases (43 English, 30 Chinese) and evaluated the system on 58 independent simulated cases (30 Chinese, 28 English) in a pre-specified, source-blinded comparison with 17 practising audiologists. The AI audiologist outperformed human audiologists on every case (58/58; mean paired $Δ$ = +1.35 on a 5-point composite, Cohen's d = 1.84, $P = 4.5 \times 10^{-20}$), on 20 of 21 rubric items and in both languages. Component ablation identified the playbook as the largest contributor, offering a practical route to specialist consultation agents in low-data medical domains.

AI.tldr: A bilingual AI audiologist built on a general-purpose LLM (no fine-tuning) with rubric-guided playbook induction, multimodal audiogram interpretation, and retrieval-augmented grounding outperformed 17 practising audiologists on all 58 independent simulated cases.
AI.motivation: Real-world audiology case material is scarce, yet consultation demands structured history-taking, audiometric interpretation, and patient-centred communication. The work aims to provide a practical route to specialist consultation agents in low-data medical domains.
AI.method: A general-purpose LLM is paired with rubric-guided playbook induction, multimodal audiogram interpretation, and retrieval-augmented grounding, without fine-tuning the backbone. Using a 21-item rubric and an AI patient simulator, a 19-rule consultation policy was induced from 73 training cases (43 English, 30 Chinese); evaluation used 58 independent simulated cases (30 Chinese, 28 English) in a pre-specified, source-blinded comparison with 17 practising audiologists. Component ablation was also performed.
AI.result: The AI audiologist outperformed human audiologists on every case (58/58; mean paired Δ = +1.35 on a 5-point composite, Cohen's d = 1.84, P = 4.5 × 10⁻²⁰), on 20 of 21 rubric items, and in both languages. Ablation identified the playbook as the largest contributing component.
AI.conclusion: Combining playbook induction with multimodal interpretation and retrieval-augmented grounding enables a specialist-level consultation agent without fine-tuning, offering a practical route to specialist consultation agents in low-data medical domains.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Alignment with Pressure for Precise Suction Manipulation
summary: Stacking and palletising demand precise placement: error left in one layer is inherited by the next, and a flat pad offers no feature to funnel a wrong pose into the right one. Top-down suction suits such dense arrangements, and suction has already been brought into vision-language-action (VLA) policies. What that work does not report, however, is a policy conditioned on a measured vacuum signal, or one that uses it to abandon an action already under way. Vision does not settle the question here, because at the moment it matters the cup and the face it holds occlude each other. We present CLAP, which makes the attachment state observable through a pressure module tapped into the vacuum line. The decoded reading replaces the suction command in the policy's proprioception, is fused with the visual features, and terminates the open-loop execution window so that the policy re-infers from a fresh observation. For data, we record goal-state disassembly on the physical robot and reverse the joint-state sequence offline, without a simulation replay. Targeted phase demonstrations, 8.3% of the training frames, cover the suction transitions and the configurations an interrupted grasp leaves behind. On a real Unitree Z1, one multi-task checkpoint reaches 96.67% average success in both colour settings, 16.67 and 10.00 points above the strongest baseline, its monochromatic four-block successes averaging 15.92 mm of error. Four ablation settings fall 5.00 to 13.33 points short. We will release code and trained weights.

AI.tldr: CLAP makes the vacuum attachment state observable via a pressure module in the vacuum line; the decoded reading replaces the suction command in proprioception, is fused with visual features, and terminates the open-loop execution window so the VLA policy re-infers from a fresh observation. On a real Unitree Z1, one multi-task checkpoint reaches 96.67% average success across both colour settings, 16.67 and 10.00 points above the strongest baseline, with 15.92 mm average error on monochromatic four-block tasks.
AI.motivation: Stacking and palletising require precise placement, where error in one layer is inherited by the next and a flat pad provides no feature to funnel a wrong pose into the right one. Top-down suction suits such dense arrangements and has been integrated into vision-language-action (VLA) policies, but prior work does not report a policy conditioned on a measured vacuum signal or one that uses it to abandon an action already under way. Vision alone cannot resolve this because the cup and the face it holds occlude each other at the critical moment.
AI.method: A pressure module is tapped into the vacuum line to make the attachment state observable. The decoded reading replaces the suction command in the policy's proprioception, is fused with visual features, and terminates the open-loop execution window so the policy re-infers from a fresh observation. Data is collected by recording goal-state disassembly on the physical robot and reversing the joint-state sequence offline, without simulation replay. Targeted phase demonstrations (8.3% of training frames) cover suction transitions and configurations left behind by an interrupted grasp.
AI.result: On a real Unitree Z1, one multi-task checkpoint reaches 96.67% average success in both colour settings, 16.67 and 10.00 points above the strongest baseline, with its monochromatic four-block successes averaging 15.92 mm error. Four ablation settings fall 5.00 to 13.33 points short.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning a VLA policy on a measured vacuum signal and using it to terminate an ongoing action substantially improves real-robot stacking and palletising success. Code and trained weights will be released.

title: RAO-Nav: Probing Omni-Language Models for Zero-shot Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation
summary: We explore whether Omni-Language Models (OLMs) can be directly applied to zero-shot Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation (SAVN). Recent work demonstrates that even state-of-the-art specialized models still struggle to achieve generalist multimodal navigation, despite extensive task-specific training. In this paper, we introduce RAO-Nav, short for Reasoning All-in-One OLM, a deployment pipeline for zero-shot SAVN. By leveraging the rich implicit audio-visual knowledge encoded in OLMs, the embodied agent is enabled to ``hear'', ``see'', ``reason'', and ``act'' in the environment. To further elicit the built-in thinking ability of OLMs, we propose a test-time Latent Navigation Reasoning (LNR) module that can be seamlessly integrated into the decoding space. LNR encourages the model to retrieve more target-relevant observations and make effective navigation decisions. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that our framework surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines on public SAVN benchmarks without using any training data. Moreover, we introduce a new \emph{Global Navigation Instruction} setting to further evaluate the ability of OLMs to serve as embodied navigation agents. Code: https://github.com/rikeilong/OmniAV\_Nav.

AI.tldr: RAO-Nav is a zero-shot pipeline that repurposes Omni-Language Models for Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation, adding a test-time Latent Navigation Reasoning module; it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines without training data.
AI.motivation: Specialized models still struggle with generalist multimodal navigation despite heavy task-specific training, so the authors ask whether OLMs can be applied directly to zero-shot SAVN, exploiting their implicit audio-visual knowledge.
AI.method: RAO-Nav, a deployment pipeline letting an embodied agent hear, see, reason, and act via OLMs; a test-time Latent Navigation Reasoning (LNR) module integrated into the decoding space to elicit built-in thinking and retrieve target-relevant observations.
AI.result: The framework surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines on public SAVN benchmarks without any training data; a new Global Navigation Instruction setting is introduced to evaluate OLMs as embodied agents.
AI.conclusion: OLMs can serve as effective zero-shot embodied navigation agents, and test-time latent reasoning further improves their navigation decisions.

title: Copper-Policy: Focus on the Representation for Robust Robot Manipulation
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) acquire behavioral priors by modeling future scene evolution, but predicting detailed futures in pixel or latent space incurs substantial cost. Recent evidence that co-training gains persist without test-time generation raises a question: what must a WAM learn to improve control? We introduce Copper-Policy, which learns a compact World representation with the policy rather than relying on a predefined target space. Through temporal joint-embedding prediction, it predicts future observation embeddings conditioned on task intention without reconstructing pixels. This prediction and action decoding shape the representation jointly, while the policy retains access to current-frame spatial detail for execution. Representation analyses show that the learned features better separate task-driven change from perturbations and provide complementary information for control. Compact prediction targets reduce training tokens per sample, enabling a 2B-parameter model trained in 9.67 hours on 8$\times$ RTX 5090 GPUs and 6$\times$ faster than Fast-WAM on matched A100 GPUs. Copper-Policy outperforms every compared method without embodied pretraining on RoboTwin and several embodied-pretrained VLAs on LIBERO-Plus (80.85%). On three challenging real-robot tasks, it performs comparably to $π_{0.5}$ and attains a higher average score. Together, these results show that Copper-Policy combines strong control performance with efficient training.

AI.tldr: Copper-Policy learns a compact world representation jointly with the policy via temporal joint-embedding prediction, avoiding pixel reconstruction while improving control performance and training efficiency.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) acquire behavioral priors by modeling future scene evolution, but predicting detailed futures in pixel or latent space is costly. Co-training gains persist even without test-time generation, raising the question of what a WAM must actually learn to improve control.
AI.method: Copper-Policy learns a compact World representation jointly with the policy instead of relying on a predefined target space. It uses temporal joint-embedding prediction to predict future observation embeddings conditioned on task intention without reconstructing pixels. The prediction and action decoding jointly shape the representation, while the policy retains access to current-frame spatial detail for execution.
AI.result: Representation analyses show learned features better separate task-driven change from perturbations and provide complementary control information. Compact prediction targets reduce training tokens per sample, enabling a 2B-parameter model trained in 9.67 hours on 8x RTX 5090 GPUs and 6x faster than Fast-WAM on matched A100 GPUs. Copper-Policy outperforms every compared method without embodied pretraining on RoboTwin and several embodied-pretrained VLAs on LIBERO-Plus (80.85%). On three challenging real-robot tasks, it performs comparably to pi_0.5 with a higher average score.
AI.conclusion: Copper-Policy combines strong control performance with efficient training by learning a compact world representation jointly with the policy.

title: Certifying Interventional Agreement Among Observationally Equivalent Causal Models
summary: Observationally equivalent causal models can still disagree about what happens under intervention, because interventions create inputs that never occur in observational data. We introduce Interventional Separation Selection (ISS), which repeatedly queries the true system with an admissible intervention on which the surviving candidate models disagree, discards the candidates the outcome contradicts, and stops once no intervention within a cost bound separates the survivors. If the true system is among the candidates, this stopping condition certifies that every survivor agrees with it on every admissible intervention within the bound, a guarantee that no observational learner can give, however much data it sees. The stopping condition depends only on the survivors, so it can be checked without knowing the truth. For continuous variables the candidates form an infinite version space, and mixed-integer linear programs decide the stopping condition exactly over all of it, with agreement holding up to a tolerance. On a three-digit colored MNIST causal abstraction task in which ink hue tracks digit size, plain convolutional networks trained on examples reach zero held-out error, yet disagree with shape-based labels on 26% of single-digit edits, as often as hue-based labels do. Auditing the causal abstractions of networks observed only on such images, ISS certifies what each network perceives with 13.6 interventions per image on average, and each certificate, checked against every admissible intervention, holds whenever the network's true abstraction is among the candidates. When a network bypasses a unit that every candidate abstraction relies on, certificates covering interventions on that unit can be silently void, and twenty random validation interventions refute 69% of them.

AI.tldr: Interventional Separation Selection (ISS) repeatedly intervenes on a true system to prune observationally equivalent causal models, certifying interventional agreement among survivors without knowing the truth; applied to auditing causal abstractions of CNNs on a hue-vs-shape MNIST task, achieving certificates within 13.6 interventions per image.
AI.motivation: Observationally equivalent causal models can still disagree under intervention, because interventions generate inputs absent from observational data. Consequently, no observational learner can guarantee interventional agreement no matter how much data it sees, motivating a procedure that actively intervenes to distinguish surviving candidate models.
AI.method: ISS repeatedly queries the true system with an admissible intervention on which surviving candidates disagree, discards candidates contradicted by the outcome, and stops when no intervention within a cost bound separates the survivors. The stopping condition depends only on the survivors and is therefore checkable without knowing the truth. For continuous variables the candidate set is an infinite version space, and mixed-integer linear programs decide the stopping condition exactly over all of it, with agreement holding up to a tolerance. Included ablation: bypassed units that every candidate abstraction relies on can render certificates silently void.
AI.result: On a three-digit colored MNIST causal abstraction task where ink hue tracks digit size, plain CNNs reach zero held-out error yet disagree with shape-based labels on 26% of single-digit edits, as often as hue-based labels do. Auditing causal abstractions of networks observed only on such images, ISS certifies what each network perceives with 13.6 interventions per image on average; each certificate, checked against every admissible intervention, holds whenever the network's true abstraction is among the candidates. Twenty random validation interventions refute 69% of certificates that cover interventions on a bypassed unit relied upon by every candidate abstraction.
AI.conclusion: ISS provides a stopping condition that certifies every surviving model agrees with the true system on all admissible interventions within the cost bound—a guarantee unavailable to observational learners—while remaining checkable without access to ground truth. It extends to infinite continuous version spaces via exact MILP decision, and proves effective for auditing causal abstractions in vision models, though certificates can be silently void when networks bypass units all candidate abstractions depend on.

title: CollisionGAT: Controller-Agnostic One-Step Collision Screening for Multi-Agent Motion
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 1 table, 2 algorithms. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)
summary: Before a team of robots moves, each proposed step must be checked for collisions with other robots and with obstacles. We present CollisionGAT, a graph-attention network that reads the current and proposed states of moving agents together with locally relevant stationary obstacles and returns one collision-risk score per moving agent. Any controller can use these scores to accept, repair, replan, or postpone a proposed step. We mount CollisionGAT on a continuous path-following controller and on GATeD, an obstacle-blind D* Lite planner that uses typed vetoes to update its planning graphs. Exact geometric checks supply the training labels and independently audit every executed step.

AI.tldr: CollisionGAT is a graph-attention network that scores collision risk per moving agent from current and proposed states plus local obstacles, enabling controllers to accept, repair, replan, or postpone steps.
AI.motivation: Before a team of robots moves, each proposed step must be checked for collisions with other robots and with obstacles.
AI.method: A graph-attention network reads the current and proposed states of moving agents together with locally relevant stationary obstacles and returns one collision-risk score per moving agent. It is mounted on a continuous path-following controller and on GATeD, an obstacle-blind D* Lite planner that uses typed vetoes to update its planning graphs. Exact geometric checks supply the training labels and independently audit every executed step.
AI.result: The abstract reports the architecture and integration (path-following controller, GATeD planner with typed vetoes) but does not state quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Collision-risk scores from CollisionGAT let any controller accept, repair, replan, or postpone a proposed step, with geometric checks providing labels and auditing executed steps.

title: Why Directly Learning Periodic Trajectories Can Fail
summary: Operator learning of periodic solutions requires deciding how simulation data should be recorded and represented. A natural choice is to integrate long enough for transients to decay and record a window wide enough to contain at least one full period of all trajectories. We find that these conservative choices can make the resulting trajectories difficult to learn, even when the underlying periodic orbits vary regularly with system parameters. Unaligned trajectories generalize poorly even within the training distribution. Phase alignment substantially improves in-distribution generalization, but models trained on a fixed physical-time window still have large errors on trajectories with periods outside the training range. We explain both failures through a common mechanism: frequency differences accumulate over time, so the target phase varies rapidly with the parameters. Predictors that cannot track this variation incur a population MSE floor in both settings; for fixed window prediction, we also derive a per-sample lower bound. We then study one of the simplest representations that escape these floors: learning an aligned, normalized waveform and its period separately. We establish regularity of the decoupled targets under ODE assumptions and show experimentally that this approach avoids both failures in ODE systems and a PDE case study.

AI.tldr: Common data-recording choices for learning periodic solutions (long transients, wide windows) induce a generalization failure caused by frequency differences accumulating over time; decoupling an aligned, normalized waveform from its period escapes the resulting MSE floors.
AI.motivation: Operator learning of periodic solutions needs a decision on how simulation data is recorded and represented. The natural, conservative choice—integrating until transients decay and recording a window containing at least one full period of all trajectories—is shown to make trajectories hard to learn, even when the underlying periodic orbits vary regularly with system parameters.
AI.method: The authors diagnose two failure modes: (i) unaligned trajectories generalize poorly even in-distribution, and (ii) phase alignment fixes in-distribution generalization but models trained on a fixed physical-time window still incur large errors for periods outside the training range. They explain both via a common mechanism—frequency differences accumulate over time, so the target phase varies rapidly with parameters—and derive a population MSE floor for predictors that cannot track this variation, plus a per-sample lower bound for fixed-window prediction. They then study a representation that escapes these floors: learning an aligned, normalized waveform and its period separately, establishing regularity of the decoupled targets under ODE assumptions.
AI.result: Unaligned trajectories generalize poorly within the training distribution; phase alignment substantially improves in-distribution generalization but leaves large errors on out-of-range periods under fixed physical-time windows. The proposed decoupled representation avoids both failures experimentally in ODE systems and in a PDE case study.
AI.conclusion: Conservative data-recording choices can be actively harmful for learning periodic solutions. Frequency-driven phase drift is the shared cause of both observed failures, captured by derived MSE floors. Learning an aligned, normalized waveform separately from its period is a simple representation that escapes these floors, supported by regularity results and experiments on ODE systems and a PDE case study.

title: Towards Kinematic Actionable Infeasibility Detection in Motion Planning
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Motion planning in robotics requires not only computing collision-free paths but also certifying infeasibility when no such path exists. Complete methods are limited to low-dimensional spaces, while sampling-based planners scale efficiently but cannot provide finite-time infeasibility certificates, leaving this problem largely unresolved in high-dimensional spaces. In this letter, we present a geometry-driven framework for certifying infeasibility through an explicit resolution-dependent analysis of configuration space topology. Leveraging signed distance field representations, the proposed method traces separating manifolds induced by obstacle boundaries directly in configuration space, enabling both detection of infeasibility and identification of the specific geometric cause. To address computational challenges, we develop a parallel frontier-expansion algorithm that exploits GPU acceleration for efficient simplicial reconstruction in high-dimensional spaces. We validate the approach on 4-DOF and 5-DOF robot scenarios, certifying infeasibility within seconds for 4-DOF cases and under four minutes for 5-DOF cases. We further discuss avenues for improving scalability to higher-dimensional spaces.

AI.tldr: This letter proposes a geometry-driven framework that certifies motion-planning infeasibility in high-dimensional configuration spaces by tracing separating manifolds induced by obstacle boundaries using signed distance fields and a GPU-accelerated parallel frontier-expansion algorithm.
AI.motivation: Motion planning must both compute collision-free paths and certify infeasibility when none exists. Complete methods handle only low-dimensional spaces, while sampling-based planners scale well but cannot provide finite-time infeasibility certificates, leaving high-dimensional infeasibility certification largely unresolved.
AI.method: The approach performs an explicit resolution-dependent analysis of configuration space topology. Using signed distance field representations, it traces separating manifolds induced by obstacle boundaries directly in configuration space, enabling infeasibility detection and identification of the geometric cause. A parallel frontier-expansion algorithm with GPU acceleration enables efficient simplicial reconstruction in high-dimensional spaces.
AI.result: Validated on 4-DOF and 5-DOF robot scenarios, the method certifies infeasibility within seconds for 4-DOF cases and under four minutes for 5-DOF cases.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides finite-time, geometry-based infeasibility certificates in high-dimensional spaces and opens avenues for improving scalability to higher-dimensional spaces.

title: Clarify the User or Verify the World? Uncertainty Routing for Proactive Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents must decide not only whether additional information is needed, but also which source can resolve the uncertainty. Existing proactive approaches often specialize in either user clarification or environment verification, without explicitly determining the appropriate information source for each decision. We formulate this problem as uncertainty routing among ACT, CLARIFY, and VERIFY, and propose PROUR, a proactive uncertainty routing framework. PROUR decomposes action uncertainty into disagreement across plausible user-goal interpretations, which signals user-side ambiguity, and the entropy remaining within each interpretation, which signals missing world-side evidence. To acquire information from the routed source, a query generator is trained with a mode-conditioned information-gain reward, targeting user-goal identification under CLARIFY and next-action identification under VERIFY. On $τ$-bench, PROUR achieves 28.17% average success rate across retail and airline, outperforming the strongest prior method by 4.57% while using 2.17 fewer interaction steps. The learned policy further generalizes to stronger task agents and transactional domains of $τ^3$-bench without retraining, demonstrating the benefit of source-aligned uncertainty resolution for proactive agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PROUR, a proactive uncertainty routing framework for tool-using LLM agents that routes decisions among ACT, CLARIFY, and VERIFY by decomposing action uncertainty into user-side ambiguity and world-side evidence gaps.
AI.motivation: Existing proactive approaches typically specialize in either user clarification or environment verification, without explicitly determining which information source is appropriate for each decision. Tool-using LLM agents need to decide not only whether more information is needed, but also which source can resolve the uncertainty.
AI.method: PROUR formulates the task as uncertainty routing among ACT, CLARIFY, and VERIFY. It decomposes action uncertainty into disagreement across plausible user-goal interpretations (signaling user-side ambiguity) and the entropy remaining within each interpretation (signaling missing world-side evidence). A query generator is trained with a mode-conditioned information-gain reward: user-goal identification under CLARIFY, and next-action identification under VERIFY.
AI.result: On τ-bench, PROUR achieves 28.17% average success rate across retail and airline, surpassing the strongest prior method by 4.57% while using 2.17 fewer interaction steps. The learned policy also generalizes to stronger task agents and transactional domains of τ³-bench without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly routing uncertainty to the appropriate source—user versus world—yields more effective and efficient proactive agents, and the resulting policy transfers across agents and domains without retraining.

title: Scanning While Imagining: A Scene-Graph World Model for Robotic Ultrasound Navigation
summary: Ultrasound (US) acquisition depends on the operator's ability to interpret anatomy and anticipate how the view will change with probe motion. Many robotic US navigation methods select actions without explicitly predicting these anatomical changes. We propose SonoGraph-WM, an action- and goal-conditioned world model for anticipatory probe navigation. The model represents anatomy as scene graphs (SGs), capturing visible structures, their geometry, and spatial relationships without synthesizing US images. Given a history of SGs and probe poses, a unified Transformer jointly predicts future SGs and poses. A receding-horizon planner recursively imagines candidate trajectories, selects the shortest predicted path reaching a goal graph, and follows it over a short execution horizon before replanning from new observations. To reduce reliance on tracked and anatomically annotated US sequences, we generate aligned SG--pose training data from computed tomography (CT) label maps along surface-constrained probe trajectories. On four held-out CT cases, spatial relation F1 remains above 93% over 20 prediction steps, and closed-loop navigation achieves 77.50% and 75.00% success for the gallbladder and pancreas, respectively, using annotation-derived SGs. In robot--phantom navigation experiments with label-map-derived SGs, the planner reached the target view in 73.7% of trials. These findings support CT-supervised anatomical world modeling for probe planning and highlight the importance of frequent observation updates for reliable navigation. Project Page: https://noseefood.github.io/us-sonograph-wm/

AI.tldr: SonoGraph-WM is an action- and goal-conditioned world model for robotic ultrasound probe navigation that represents anatomy as scene graphs and uses a unified Transformer to jointly predict future scene graphs and probe poses, enabling anticipatory planning without synthesizing ultrasound images.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound acquisition relies heavily on the operator's ability to interpret anatomy and anticipate view changes from probe motion. Existing robotic ultrasound navigation methods select actions without explicitly predicting anatomical changes, limiting anticipatory, goal-directed navigation.
AI.method: The model encodes anatomy as scene graphs capturing visible structures, geometry, and spatial relations, avoiding ultrasound image synthesis. A unified Transformer, conditioned on action and goal, jointly predicts future scene graphs and probe poses from a history of scene graphs and poses. A receding-horizon planner recursively imagines candidate trajectories, selects the shortest predicted path to a goal graph, and executes it over a short horizon before replanning. To reduce reliance on tracked and anatomically annotated US sequences, aligned scene-graph/pose training data are generated from CT label maps along surface-constrained probe trajectories.
AI.result: On four held-out CT cases, spatial relation F1 stays above 93% over 20 prediction steps. Closed-loop navigation achieves 77.50% (gallbladder) and 75.00% (pancreas) success using annotation-derived scene graphs. In robot-phantom experiments with label-map-derived scene graphs, the planner reached the target view in 73.7% of trials.
AI.conclusion: The results support CT-supervised anatomical world modeling for probe planning and underscore the importance of frequent observation updates for reliable navigation.

title: LAM: Efficient Lossy Agent Memory Framework With A Retrieval-Score Error Bound
summary: Agent memory grows as agents read inputs, reason, and call tools. Longer histories increase inference cost and eventually exceed the context window. LLM-based summarization reduces this history but adds latency and provides no explicit bound on information loss. We propose LAM, a Lossy Agent Memory system with three components: a deterministic deduplication rule with a substitution bound on retrieval scores - a bound on score perturbation, not a certificate of unchanged ranking; a memory manager that preserves the cached prefix and overlaps compaction with inference; and a performance model that estimates compaction costs before deployment. On 600 agent trajectories, LAM removes 22.47% of observation tokens while retaining 99.984% of the measured gold-patch evidence. At a fixed deletion set, the performance model predicts a 71.4x-91.6x end-to-end speedup from removing records before prefill instead of deleting them from a prefilled context. That benefit comes from the schedule rather than the rule and applies to any prefix-preserving test.

AI.tldr: LAM is a Lossy Agent Memory system that reduces agent history via deterministic deduplication with a substitution bound, a prefix-preserving memory manager overlapping compaction with inference, and a pre-deployment performance model, removing 22.47% of observation tokens at minimal evidence loss.
AI.motivation: Agent memory grows with inputs, reasoning, and tool calls, raising inference cost and eventually exceeding the context window. LLM-based summarization mitigates this but adds latency and gives no explicit bound on information loss, so a memory reduction method with bounded loss and predictable cost is needed.
AI.method: LAM comprises three components: (1) a deterministic deduplication rule with a substitution bound on retrieval scores, bounding score perturbation (not certifying unchanged ranking); (2) a memory manager that preserves the cached prefix and overlaps compaction with inference; and (3) a performance model estimating compaction costs before deployment.
AI.result: On 600 agent trajectories, LAM removes 22.47% of observation tokens while retaining 99.984% of measured gold-patch evidence. At a fixed deletion set, the performance model predicts a 71.4x-91.6x end-to-end speedup from removing records before prefill rather than deleting them from a prefilled context.
AI.conclusion: The speedup benefit derives from the schedule, not the rule, and applies to any prefix-preserving test, indicating the scheduling strategy generalizes beyond LAM's specific deduplication.

title: FINE: Future-Informed Navigation Encoding for Data-Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Adapting vision-language navigation (VLN) policies to new environments is expensive because every additional route and instruction requires an embodied demonstration. Yet standard observation-to-action training uses only a small fraction of the information already contained in each trajectory. In particular, future observations reveal the instruction-relevant landmarks that the agent will encounter, including what they look like and how they are arranged in 3D. We introduce FINE, a Future-Informed Navigation Encoding framework that extracts this latent supervision from existing demonstrations. FINE equips a VLN backbone with two complementary auxiliary representations. First, explicit landmark tokens follow the ordered landmarks specified by the instruction and are trained to predict future landmark regions in both semantic 2D patch-feature space and viewpoint-dependent 3D geometric feature space. Second, an implicit future token learns to distinguish the landmark state that is actually reached from plausible same-scene counterfactual futures generated by a video world model. On R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen, FINE improves InternVLA-N1 by 2.6 and 4.5 success-rate points, respectively, at full training data. More importantly, as demonstrations become limited, the benefit grows: at a 70% demonstration budget, FINE improves success rate by 6.8 points, recovering roughly one-third of the performance lost by reducing the training demonstrations. Project page is available at https://finevln.github.io/.

AI.tldr: FINE is a Future-Informed Navigation Encoding framework that extracts latent supervision from future observations in existing VLN demonstrations via explicit landmark tokens and an implicit future token, improving navigation success while being especially beneficial under limited demonstration budgets.
AI.motivation: Adapting vision-language navigation (VLN) policies to new environments is costly because each added route and instruction requires an embodied demonstration. Standard observation-to-action training underuses the information available in each trajectory: future observations implicitly encode instruction-relevant landmarks, including their appearance and 3D arrangement, which could serve as free supervision.
AI.method: FINE augments a VLN backbone with two auxiliary representations. (1) Explicit landmark tokens follow the ordered landmarks specified by the instruction and are trained to predict future landmark regions in both semantic 2D patch-feature space and viewpoint-dependent 3D geometric feature space. (2) An implicit future token learns to distinguish the actually reached landmark state from plausible same-scene counterfactual futures generated by a video world model.
AI.result: On R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen, FINE improves InternVLA-N1 by 2.6 and 4.5 success-rate points at full training data. The gains grow as demonstrations become limited: at a 70% demonstration budget, FINE improves success rate by 6.8 points, recovering roughly one-third of the performance lost from reducing demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Future observations in existing VLN demonstrations provide valuable latent supervision. FINE exploits this signal to boost navigation performance, with benefits that increase under scarce data, mitigating the high cost of collecting embodied demonstrations.

title: Prefill-Free Cross-Family KV Cache Transfer for Heterogeneous Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: Recent multi-agent LLM systems increasingly combine heterogeneous models for specialized agent roles. However, text-based communication requires each receiver to prefill shared context already processed by the sender. Reusing the sender's key-value (KV) cache avoids this redundancy, but prefill-free transfer across model families must handle differences in tokenization, model depth, and KV representations. To address these issues, we propose \textit{HeteroFold}, a prefill-free cross-family KV cache transfer method that keeps both the sender and receiver frozen. HeteroFold aligns model structures, maps the sender cache into the receiver space, and calibrates it to preserve receiver behavior. Across six transfer directions, HeteroFold achieves the best cache-transfer performance on all four long-context benchmarks and most short-context settings. It also matches text-based communication on the multi-agent benchmark. At 32K context length, Llama-3.1-8B$\rightarrow$Ministral-3-14B transfer is $10.7\times$ faster than Native Prefill and $1.18$--$1.47\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art prefill-free baselines, Dense Latent and KV Ridge. These results show that HeteroFold enables efficient cross-family KV reuse without receiver prefill.

AI.tldr: HeteroFold enables prefill-free cross-family KV cache transfer between heterogeneous LLM agents by aligning structures, mapping caches, and calibrating behavior, achieving up to 10.7x speedup over native prefill.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly use heterogeneous models per role, but text-based communication forces each receiver to redundantly prefill shared context already processed by the sender. Reusing the sender's KV cache could remove this redundancy, yet prefill-free transfer across model families must overcome mismatches in tokenization, model depth, and KV representations.
AI.method: HeteroFold is a prefill-free cross-family KV cache transfer method that keeps both sender and receiver frozen. It (1) aligns model structures, (2) maps the sender cache into the receiver space, and (3) calibrates the mapped cache to preserve receiver behavior.
AI.result: Across six transfer directions, HeteroFold attains the best cache-transfer performance on all four long-context benchmarks and most short-context settings, and matches text-based communication on the multi-agent benchmark. At 32K context, Llama-3.1-8B→Ministral-3-14B transfer is 10.7x faster than Native Prefill and 1.18-1.47x faster than the SOTA prefill-free baselines Dense Latent and KV Ridge.
AI.conclusion: HeteroFold enables efficient cross-family KV reuse without receiver prefill, offering a practical path to eliminate redundant context processing in heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems.

title: RoboFoundry: System-as-Policy Evolution for Self-Learning Embodied Agents
summary: A foundation model should not act in isolation as an embodied agent. Yet, existing methods often optimize individual components of the agent stack, such as memory, context, skills, or action interfaces, rather than treating the supporting system itself as a unified policy. Moreover, interaction alone does not yield self-improvement unless execution experience is converted into persistent, validated system changes. We therefore propose RoboFoundry, the first embodied agentic framework that formulates this process as Self-Evolving System-as-Policy. RoboFoundry diagnoses capability gaps in decision-making and memory management, converts execution traces into validated task-specific system updates, and promotes recurring improvements to the general system. Evolution operates over two complementary surfaces: a context system that manages active internal context and persistent file-system memory, and a hierarchical skill system that organizes atomic skills, reusable compositions, and failure-conditioned recovery. A shared semantic interface separates embodiment-invariant decisions from embodiment-specific execution, allowing evolved system capabilities to transfer across heterogeneous robots. On EmbodiedBench, RoboFoundry achieves state-of-the-art performance, notably improving GPT-5.5 by 27.8%. It also brings Qwen3.7-Plus to near parity with GPT-5.5 (70.3% vs. 72.7%), showing consistent gains from system-as-policy evolution across foundation models. For long-horizon memory, RoboFoundry outperforms all baselines on RoboMemArena by at least 39.0%, even against methods assisted by external foundation models. On LIBERO-PRO, it further outperforms Cap-Agent0 by 243.8%-679.7% across all perturbation types. In real-world deployments, RoboFoundry demonstrates zero-shot transfer and online evolution across robots and tasks, highlighting its potential for fully autonomous embodied agents.

AI.tldr: RoboFoundry is the first embodied agentic framework framing agent improvement as Self-Evolving System-as-Policy, evolving context/memory and hierarchical skill systems via validated updates, achieving SOTA across benchmarks and real-world transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied agents optimize isolated components (memory, context, skills, action interfaces) rather than treating the supporting system as a unified policy; also, raw interaction does not produce self-improvement unless execution experience is converted into persistent, validated system changes.
AI.method: Formulates the process as Self-Evolving System-as-Policy: diagnoses capability gaps in decision-making and memory management, converts execution traces into validated task-specific system updates, and promotes recurring improvements to the general system. Evolution spans two surfaces—a context system (active internal context + persistent file-system memory) and a hierarchical skill system (atomic skills, reusable compositions, failure-conditioned recovery). A shared semantic interface separates embodiment-invariant decisions from embodiment-specific execution, enabling transfer across heterogeneous robots.
AI.result: State-of-the-art on EmbodiedBench, improving GPT-5.5 by 27.8%; brings Qwen3.7-Plus to near parity with GPT-5.5 (70.3% vs 72.7%). On RoboMemArena, outperforms all baselines by at least 39.0%, even vs. methods assisted by external foundation models. On LIBERO-PRO, beats Cap-Agent0 by 243.8%–679.7% across all perturbation types. Real-world deployments show zero-shot transfer and online evolution across robots and tasks.
AI.conclusion: RoboFoundry demonstrates that system-as-policy evolution yields consistent gains across foundation models and benchmarks, highlighting its potential for fully autonomous embodied agents.

title: When Does a Skill Add Value? Task-Conditional Gain Prediction for Selective Skill Use
summary: Agent skills are expected to improve task performance. Yet we find that they often provide no benefit, and can even hurt performance while incurring additional token costs. Can we predict whether a skill will help before the agent acts? We introduce SkillDelta, a framework for predicting task-conditional skill gains from paired executions of the same agent with and without the skill. A local predictor transfers these historical gains to new tasks without retraining the agent. Under explicit transfer assumptions, our analysis links support coverage, representation mismatch, and execution noise to prediction error and decision regret. Across five benchmarks and three target agents, paired history improves observed-gain ranking over skill-assisted outcomes alone in 12 of 15 settings. At matched expected skill-use rates, SkillDelta improves success over random activation in all 15 settings, with an average absolute gain of 4.3%. Most of this advantage comes from allocation across task groups. Evidence for additional within-group selection value is strongest on ToolQA and weaker elsewhere. Code is available at https://github.com/TankTechnology/skilldelta.

AI.tldr: SkillDelta predicts whether a skill will help an agent on a given task by transferring paired with/without-skill execution history to new tasks, improving success over random skill activation by 4.3% on average across 15 settings.
AI.motivation: Agent skills are assumed to improve task performance, but the authors find they often yield no benefit and can even degrade performance while adding token costs. The paper addresses the question of whether a skill's usefulness can be predicted before the agent acts, motivating a task-conditional, pre-execution decision mechanism.
AI.method: SkillDelta is a framework for predicting task-conditional skill gains from paired executions of the same agent with and without the skill. A local predictor transfers these historical gains to new tasks without retraining the agent. Under explicit transfer assumptions, the analysis relates support coverage, representation mismatch, and execution noise to prediction error and decision regret.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and three target agents, paired history improves observed-gain ranking over skill-assisted outcomes alone in 12 of 15 settings. At matched expected skill-use rates, SkillDelta improves success over random activation in all 15 settings, with an average absolute gain of 4.3%. Most of this advantage stems from allocation across task groups; evidence for additional within-group selection value is strongest on ToolQA and weaker elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: Predicting task-conditional skill gains from paired execution history is feasible and beneficial, reliably outperforming random skill activation, with gains driven mainly by cross-group allocation rather than within-group selection.

title: Communication-Aware Heterogeneous Graph Learning for Decentralized Multi-Human Multi-Robot Task Allocation
summary: Multi-human multi-robot (MH-MR) teams combine robotic autonomy with human expertise, but effective task allocation requires coordinating scarce, dynamically available human support with distributed robot execution. Limited robot-robot and human-robot communication further complicates this coupling by delaying information exchange and supervisory intervention. We introduce CommHG, a communication-aware heterogeneous graph learning framework for decentralized MH-MR task allocation. CommHG represents coupled human-robot-task interactions through local graphs conditioned on information availability and age. Learned communication actions enable robots to decide when and which operator to query, and when to share information with peers. Allocation and communication are jointly optimized through cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, allowing the team to acquire useful information while managing limited communication and supervisory resources. We also introduce a benchmark integrating heterogeneous humans and robots, dynamic tasks and operational states, and constrained robot-robot and bidirectional human-robot links. Experiments across heterogeneous teams with up to 16 robots, 6 humans, and 112 tasks show that CommHG improves timely weighted mission completion as coordination scale increases, outperforming the strongest baseline in the Large scenario.

AI.tldr: CommHG is a communication-aware heterogeneous graph learning framework for decentralized multi-human multi-robot task allocation, jointly optimizing allocation and communication via cooperative MARL.
AI.motivation: MH-MR teams require coordinating scarce, dynamically available human support with distributed robot execution. Limited robot-robot and human-robot communication delays information exchange and supervisory intervention, complicating this coupling.
AI.method: CommHG models coupled human-robot-task interactions using local graphs conditioned on information availability and age. Learned communication actions let robots decide when and which operator to query and when to share with peers. Allocation and communication are jointly optimized via cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, enabling the team to acquire useful information under limited communication and supervisory resources.
AI.result: A benchmark is introduced integrating heterogeneous humans and robots, dynamic tasks and operational states, and constrained robot-robot and bidirectional human-robot links. Experiments with up to 16 robots, 6 humans, and 112 tasks show CommHG improves timely weighted mission completion as coordination scale increases, outperforming the strongest baseline in the Large scenario.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning task allocation and communication decisions through a communication-aware heterogeneous graph representation scales effectively for decentralized MH-MR coordination under constrained communication.

title: GLIDE: Generalized Layer-wise Intrinsic Distributional Evaluation for Heterogeneous LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents require reliable step-level evaluation to compare candidate branches and allocate computation effectively. However, lightweight evaluation remains challenging. External verifiers introduce additional inference cost, while agent-produced confidence or self-evaluation scores can be miscalibrated, especially when candidates are generated by heterogeneous agents. We propose \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{L}ayer-wise \textbf{I}ntrinsic \textbf{D}istributional \textbf{E}valuation (\textbf{GLIDE}) for LLM agents. \textsc{GLIDE} derives intrinsic step evidence from layer-wise residual coherence, which measures whether local residual updates consistently support the global residual change induced by a candidate step. It calibrates this evidence against the recent score distribution of the generating agent and converts it into a pessimistic reward that jointly accounts for absolute residual evidence and agent-relative standing. The reward provides a cross-agent value signal for MCTS branch selection, while normalized predictive uncertainty guides adaptive branching. Experiments on multi-hop reasoning, sequential decision making, and symbolic logic show that \textsc{GLIDE} improves task performance, step-level ranking quality, and computational efficiency without external verifiers or task-specific supervision.

AI.tldr: GLIDE is a training-free, intrinsic step-level evaluation method for LLM agents that derives reward signals from layer-wise residual coherence, calibrated against each agent's recent score distribution, enabling cross-agent MCTS branch selection and adaptive branching without external verifiers.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need reliable step-level evaluation to compare candidate branches and allocate computation. Existing options are costly or unreliable: external verifiers add inference cost, while agent-produced confidence or self-evaluation scores are often miscalibrated, particularly when candidates come from heterogeneous agents.
