Post-training Qwen3.5-4B through unmodified harnesses and memory systems yielded reading 6.8x fewer file lines with a 16.7-point higher SWE-bench Verified pass rate, richer memory records, and up to 11.8 points higher held-out MetaClaw accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SCLATE removes the need for custom per-pair scheduling loops, enables reproducible head-to-head comparison of harnesses and memory systems, and serves as a rollout engine for post-training agents to better use their harness and memory.

title: Beyond Tasks: A Vision for Reproducing an Animal-like Behavioral Substrate Using Modern Robot Learning Techniques
summary: Recent advances in robot learning have produced increasingly capable embodied agents. Yet comparatively less attention has been given to a more basic form of competence that animals exhibit continuously: the ability to remain situated, responsive, and behaviorally coherent as physical, environmental, and social demands change over time. We propose the ethological behavioral substrate as a conceptual lens for studying this form of competence in artificial agents. Rather than treating these behaviors that animals exhibit as a set of isolated skills, we argue that their continual coordination under competing demands constitutes an important and underexplored target for modern robot learning. We further propose robotic animal companions as a useful research setting for studying sustained interaction and adaptation in human-centered environments. Such systems provide an opportunity to investigate how social behavior, memory, and continual learning develop over long periods of interaction. This perspective motivates further investigation of how such persistent behavioral competence may complement higher-level capabilities in embodied agents.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper proposes the "ethological behavioral substrate" as a conceptual lens for studying sustained behavioral competence in embodied agents, and advocates robotic animal companions as a research setting for studying long-term interaction and adaptation.
AI.motivation: Robot learning has produced increasingly capable embodied agents, but comparatively little attention has been paid to a more basic competence that animals exhibit continuously: remaining situated, responsive, and behaviorally coherent as physical, environmental, and social demands change over time. This gap motivates the paper.
AI.method: Conceptual/position paper. It reframes animal behaviors not as isolated skills but as a continually coordinated repertoire under competing demands, introducing the "ethological behavioral substrate" as an analytical lens. It further proposes robotic animal companions as an experimental setting for studying sustained interaction, adaptation, social behavior, memory, and continual learning over long periods.
AI.result: As a perspective piece, it reports no empirical results; instead it identifies sustained behavioral competence as an important and underexplored target for modern robot learning and argues that robotic animal companions offer a productive venue for investigating it.
AI.conclusion: Persistent behavioral competence may complement higher-level capabilities in embodied agents, motivating further investigation of how such competence develops and is maintained over long-term interaction.

title: Beyond Scripted Search: Sample-Efficient Reward Discovery via Agentic Black-box Optimization
summary: Designing dense reward functions for low-level reinforcement learning (RL) control remains difficult. Recent work uses large language models (LLMs) to iteratively generate and refine reward functions using policy-training feedback within scripted search algorithms. However, evaluating each candidate requires a full RL training run, making sample efficiency a central challenge for reward search on complex control tasks. To address this limitation, we propose an Agentic Reward Black-box Optimization (ARBO) framework, in which an LLM agent builds the search strategy at run time from an evaluation history maintained as its persistent workspace. The evaluation history comprises two components: observations maintained by the evaluation oracle, including candidate scores, per-term training curves, and error tracebacks; and an agent-maintained belief that records diagnoses and intended next steps. The agent queries both with tools and generates the next batch of reward candidates, rather than generating them in a single pass from a fixed prompt. Across four control domains, ARBO achieves gains of 29.9% in manipulation success rate and 192.8% in power-grid score over baseline means under a shared evaluation budget. Ablations examine each component's contribution and sensitivity to backbone choice.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ARBO, an agentic framework where an LLM agent dynamically builds a reward-function search strategy at run time using an evaluation history (oracle observations + agent belief) as persistent workspace, improving sample efficiency over scripted search baselines.
AI.motivation: Designing dense reward functions for low-level RL control is difficult. LLM-based approaches generate and refine rewards via policy-training feedback, but each candidate needs a full RL training run, making sample efficiency a central challenge for reward search on complex control tasks.
AI.method: ARBO (Agentic Reward Black-box Optimization): an LLM agent constructs its search strategy at run time from an evaluation history serving as persistent workspace. The history has two parts: oracle-maintained observations (candidate scores, per-term training curves, error tracebacks) and an agent-maintained belief (diagnoses, intended next steps). The agent queries both via tools and generates the next batch of reward candidates rather than a single-pass generation from a fixed prompt.
AI.result: Across four control domains under a shared evaluation budget, ARBO achieves 29.9% gains in manipulation success rate and 192.8% in power-grid score over baseline means. Ablations assess each component's contribution and sensitivity to backbone choice.
AI.conclusion: Framing reward search as agentic black-box optimization with a persistent, dual-component evaluation history improves sample efficiency and performance over scripted LLM reward-search baselines.

title: Dynamic Manipulation with World-Action Models via Counterfactual Planning
comment: 48 pages, including appendices. Project page: https://methoder00.github.io/DPP/
summary:
World-Action models (WAMs) trained on static demonstrations often fail to manipulate moving targets even when they possess the required manipulation skills. We attribute this failure to target-response collapse: as execution advances, the policy becomes increasingly biased toward the learned continuation of its ongoing behavior and less responsive to target relocation.
  To bridge the gap between what the model has learned and what it can generate from the current context, we formulate dynamic manipulation as counterfactual planning by decoupling the context used for plan generation from the physical state used for execution. Our framework, Dynamic Predictive Planning (DPP), first uses the WAM's predictive rollout to estimate when an interaction is expected to occur, and combines this timing estimate with observed target motion to predict the target's future interaction position. DPP then constructs a counterfactual observation that places this predicted target position in a familiar robot context, allowing the model to invoke an existing manipulation skill rather than generate a recovery behavior from an unfamiliar robot-target configuration. The resulting plan is connected to the robot's actual state during execution.
  DPP enables real-time dynamic manipulation on a single consumer GPU without additional training on dynamic data. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse target motions, with simulation performance surpassing all evaluated baselines, including methods additionally trained on dynamic data.
  Project page: https://methoder00.github.io/DPP/

AI.tldr: DPP reframes dynamic manipulation as counterfactual planning: it decouples the context used to generate a plan from the physical state used to execute it, enabling a static-trained World-Action Model to manipulate moving targets in real time without dynamic-data training.
AI.motivation: World-Action Models (WAMs) trained on static demonstrations fail to manipulate moving targets even when they already possess the necessary manipulation skills. The authors attribute this to target-response collapse: as execution progresses, the policy becomes increasingly biased toward continuing its ongoing learned behavior and less responsive to target relocation. This creates a gap between what the model has learned and what it can generate from the current context.
AI.method: The authors formulate dynamic manipulation as counterfactual planning, decoupling the context used for plan generation from the physical state used for execution. Their framework, Dynamic Predictive Planning (DPP), (1) uses the WAM's predictive rollout to estimate when an interaction is expected to occur, (2) combines this timing estimate with observed target motion to predict the target's future interaction position, (3) constructs a counterfactual observation placing this predicted target position in a familiar robot context, so the model invokes an existing manipulation skill instead of generating a recovery behavior from an unfamiliar robot-target configuration, and (4) connects the resulting plan to the robot's actual state during execution.
AI.result: DPP enables real-time dynamic manipulation on a single consumer GPU without additional training on dynamic data. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse target motions, with simulation performance surpassing all evaluated baselines, including methods additionally trained on dynamic data.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling plan-generation context from execution state via counterfactual planning effectively mitigates target-response collapse, allowing static-trained WAMs to perform dynamic manipulation without dynamic-data training, on commodity hardware.

title: Memory as a cache: Exact context reuse and deletion by construction
summary: The KV cache of a transformer entangles every token's representation with its entire prefix: a passage encoded once cannot be reused under a different prefix or removed without recomputing everything after it, so exact cache reuse is limited to shared prefixes. We present SMem, an architecture whose context representation is a cache by construction. A block-local encoder maps each block to memory rows independently of other blocks, and a reader conditions generation on their union through cross-attention. For every parameter setting, memory composes exactly at fixed block indices, deleting a block is an exact $O(b)$ update for $b$-token blocks, and the memory state is independent of the edit path. At $4\times$ the training context, under the shared recipe, SMem retrieves planted needles beyond any trained-length window (exact match 0.14-0.28 at distances of 31 and 63 blocks), where learned-position, RoPE, and Block-Attention-style transformers all score at most 0.02. A fully cached context is served by computing one block alone at a near-constant 3.1-6.2 ms, whereas cold prefill grows with context; batched decode stores 34-38% fewer KV rows and runs 1.4-1.7$\times$ faster when bandwidth-bound; and deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5$\times$ at 512 blocks and 452$\times$ at 4096 blocks (32-256$\times$ the trained length, probing the cost model rather than a served regime). The cost is a perplexity gap of -4.7% to +2.8% (negative favors SMem) against a parameter-matched transformer with the same positional scheme, at 160M-1.5B on FineWeb-Edu across two recipes and a learning-rate search. SMem also composes with RoPE: at 160M and 410M the composite matches or leads the matched transformer and closes 29-59% of SMem's gap to a RoPE transformer. Dropping prefix entanglement thus keeps perplexity comparable while making the cache exactly composable and editable.

AI.tldr: SMem is a transformer architecture whose context representation is a cache by construction: a block-local encoder maps each block to memory rows independently, and a reader cross-attends to their union, enabling exact block composition, O(b) deletion, and edit-path independence, with matched perplexity and large memory/reuse gains over prefix-entangled KV caches.
AI.motivation: Standard KV caches entangle each token with its entire prefix, so a cached passage cannot be reused under a different prefix or deleted without recomputing everything after it; exact reuse is restricted to shared prefixes, which limits caching and editing flexibility.
AI.method: SMem replaces prefix-entangled attention with a block-local encoder that maps each b-token block to memory rows independently of other blocks, plus a reader that conditions generation on the union of these rows via cross-attention. Memory composes exactly at fixed block indices, block deletion is an exact O(b) update, and the memory state is independent of the edit path. It also composes with RoPE.
AI.result: At 4x the training context, SMem retrieves planted needles beyond any trained-length window (exact match 0.14-0.28 at 31 and 63 blocks), where learned-position, RoPE, and Block-Attention-style transformers score at most 0.02. Fully cached context is served by computing one block alone at 3.1-6.2 ms near-constant, while cold prefill grows with context. Batched decode stores 34-38% fewer KV rows and runs 1.4-1.7x faster when bandwidth-bound. Deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5x at 512 blocks and 452x at 4096 blocks (32-256x trained length). Perplexity gap is -4.7% to +2.8% (negative favors SMem) versus a parameter-matched transformer with the same positional scheme at 160M-1.5B on FineWeb-Edu. With RoPE, at 160M and 410M the composite matches or leads the matched transformer and closes 29-59% of SMem's gap to a RoPE transformer.
AI.conclusion: Dropping prefix entanglement keeps perplexity comparable while making the cache exactly composable and editable, yielding strong advantages in long-context retrieval, near-constant cached prefill, reduced decode KV storage and faster bandwidth-bound decode, and much cheaper block deletion.

title: Multi-Terrain Mastery: A Comprehensive Controller for Bipedal Locomotion
summary: Advancing bipedal robots to navigate diverse terrains remains a significant challenge in robotics. Traditional locomotion controllers excel on specific surfaces but struggle across varied environments, limiting their practical applications. Given the unpredictable nature of real-world environments, a single controller capable of handling multiple terrains is ideal, eliminating the need for multiple specialized controllers. We propose a multi-terrain controller to enhance the versatility and robustness of bipedal locomotion. Building on previous work with a stance ankle motor for stability on inclined and rough surfaces, this paper extends capabilities to steep wet uneven grassy slopes, and compliant terrains such as sand, gravel, rocks, and constrained terrains like staircases. To address the unique demands of these terrains, we introduce a new impact map that is essential for maintaining performance and robustness against unseen terrains. We also discuss in detail the control structure for real-time deployment on the robot. We validate our controller on the 20 degree-of-freedom Cassie bipedal robot.

AI.tldr: A multi-terrain bipedal locomotion controller extending prior stance-ankle work to steep wet grassy slopes, compliant terrains (sand, gravel, rocks), and stairs, using a new impact map and real-time control structure, validated on the 20-DOF Cassie robot.
AI.motivation: Bipedal robots struggle to navigate diverse terrains. Traditional locomotion controllers perform well on specific surfaces but fail across varied environments, limiting practical deployment. Since real-world environments are unpredictable, a single unified controller handling multiple terrains is preferable to multiple specialized controllers.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-terrain controller that builds on prior work using a stance ankle motor for stability on inclined and rough surfaces. A new impact map is introduced to maintain performance and robustness against unseen terrains. The paper also details the control structure for real-time deployment on the robot.
AI.result: The controller extends capabilities to steep wet uneven grassy slopes, compliant terrains such as sand, gravel, and rocks, and constrained terrains like staircases. It is validated on the 20 degree-of-freedom Cassie bipedal robot, demonstrating enhanced versatility and robustness.
AI.conclusion: A single multi-terrain controller can enhance bipedal locomotion versatility and robustness, addressing the need for unified control across unpredictable real-world environments without relying on multiple specialized controllers.

title: Function Over Form: Distributional Orthogonalization in Mixture-of-Experts with Replica Expert Mechanism
summary: The scaling of LLMs increasingly relies on MoE architectures to decouple active computation from total parameter count. However, the efficacy of MoE is often constrained by expert collapse and representation redundancy, both leading to underutilization of model capacity. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Distributional Orthogonalization Loss (DO-loss), an auxiliary regularization that shifts the focus from static weight diversity to dynamic routing behavior. By representing each expert's token assignment history as a high-dimensional binary load signature, DO-loss penalizes signature overlap to prevent expert collapse while encouraging functional specialization. To align this algorithmic design with system efficiency, we further introduce the Replica Expert Mechanism (REM), which improves load balancing through a two-tiered strategy: adjusting replica expert placement at the global-batch level and performing real-time token dispatching at the micro-batch level. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method outperforms the evaluated routing algorithms on downstream tasks for both 4.8BA0.5B and 30BA3B MoE models, while maintaining comparable training efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DO-loss, a distributional orthogonalization regularizer based on expert load signatures to combat expert collapse and representation redundancy in MoE LLMs, paired with a Replica Expert Mechanism (REM) for two-tier load balancing, achieving gains on downstream tasks without hurting training efficiency.
AI.motivation: MoE architectures decouple active computation from total parameter count for LLM scaling, but expert collapse and representation redundancy cause underutilization of model capacity. Existing approaches emphasize static weight diversity rather than actual routing dynamics.
AI.method: DO-loss encodes each expert's token assignment history as a high-dimensional binary load signature and penalizes signature overlap, thereby preventing expert collapse while promoting functional specialization. REM complements this with a two-tier load-balancing strategy: global-batch-level replica expert placement adjustment and micro-batch-level real-time token dispatching.
AI.result: On downstream tasks, the method outperforms the evaluated routing algorithms for both 4.8B-A0.5B and 30B-A3B MoE models while maintaining comparable training efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Shifting regularization from static weight diversity to dynamic routing behavior, combined with a replica-based load-balancing mechanism, improves MoE capacity utilization and downstream performance at comparable training cost.

title: DeltaWAM: Change-Centric Visual Foresight via Delta Tokens for an Efficient World-Action Model
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) offer visual foresight for robotic manipulation, but pixel-space models repeatedly reconstruct entire future scenes, incurring high computational cost and spatio-temporal redundancy. In physical manipulation, consecutive frames often share most of their visual context; the changes between them are what an action policy needs to anticipate. We introduce DeltaWAM, a change-centric WAM that makes a compact delta token the unit of future prediction. Each token is a single vector encoding changes between consecutive dense DINO feature maps. DeltaWAM builds on DeltaWorld, a latent world model pretrained on large-scale videos, to autoregressively predict one delta token per future frame. A flow-matching action expert then conditions on the predicted transitions and current DINO features, which serve as spatial anchors, to generate action chunks. Trained for 256 GPU hours on two H100 GPUs, DeltaWAM has 0.725B parameters and achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO. It also shows robust generalization under procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro. Inference takes 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory.

AI.tldr: DeltaWAM is a change-centric world-action model that predicts compact "delta tokens" (vectors of changes between consecutive DINO feature maps) instead of reconstructing full pixel-space futures, then uses a flow-matching action expert for action generation, achieving 92.8% success on LIBERO with 0.725B parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing pixel-space World-Action Models reconstruct entire future scenes, causing high computational cost and spatio-temporal redundancy. In manipulation, consecutive frames largely share visual context, so only the changes between frames are relevant for action anticipation.
AI.method: DeltaWAM makes a compact delta token the unit of prediction. Each token is a single vector encoding changes between consecutive dense DINO feature maps. It builds on DeltaWorld, a latent world model pretrained on large-scale videos, to autoregressively predict one delta token per future frame. A flow-matching action expert then conditions on the predicted transitions and current DINO features (spatial anchors) to generate action chunks.
AI.result: Trained for 256 GPU hours on two H100 GPUs with 0.725B parameters. Achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO and robust generalization under procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro. Inference takes 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory.
AI.conclusion: A change-centric, delta-token formulation provides an efficient and effective alternative to pixel-space world-action models, delivering strong manipulation performance and generalization with modest compute and memory.

title: Opening LLM Judges: Recovering Preference Signals Beyond the Final Verdict
summary: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate model outputs, but their verdicts can be unreliable: a judge may favor the worse answer for its position, length, or other surface features. When a judge is wrong, is the information needed to judge correctly absent from the model, or present in its internal representations but not reflected in the output? We study this across 64 open-weight evaluators and 14 datasets, including causal interventions on 41 judges (editing activations mid-run to see whether the verdict changes). On LLMBar, built so the superficially better answer is the worse one, the verdicts of 50 judges agree with human labels only 0.456 of the time, even after averaging both answer orders. Yet a small probe on the same judges' activations, with no weight updates, reaches 0.846, and 0.686 once surface features such as length and position are residualized out (0.507 with shuffled labels). The gap holds across eight benchmarks and model families, but is not universal: a score of how well surface features alone predict the human label, computed before any probe is trained, predicts the size of the gain (Spearman rho = 0.90). On rubric tasks that score one answer at a time, leaving no surface cue to exploit, reading the internals gives no advantage. The interventions also show that editing activations mid-network already changes the verdict, before it can be read off directly, and locate the pathways carrying position and length bias. At the same label budget, the recovered signal lets a judge flag cases where it is likely wrong and yields better labels for preference learning. A wrong verdict, then, does not mean the judge lacks the information, and a simple diagnostic shows when it is worth recovering.

AI.tldr: Across 64 open-weight evaluators and 14 datasets, LLM judges often give wrong verdicts on surface-cue tasks, yet their internal activations contain the correct signal: a trained probe recovers it without weight updates, and a pre-computed surface-predictability score forecasts when recovery helps.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate model outputs, but their verdicts can be unreliable because judges may favor a worse answer for its position, length, or other surface features. The key question is whether a wrong judge verdict reflects missing information or information that is present in internal representations but not reflected in the output.
AI.method: The authors study 64 open-weight evaluators and 14 datasets, including causal interventions on 41 judges by editing activations mid-run to test whether verdicts change. They train small probes on judge activations with no weight updates, and residualize out surface features such as length and position. They also run rubric tasks scoring one answer at a time, and compute a score of how well surface features alone predict the human label before any probe is trained.
AI.result: On LLMBar, where the superficially better answer is worse, the verdicts of 50 judges agree with human labels only 0.456 of the time even after averaging both answer orders, while a small probe on the same judges' activations reaches 0.846, and 0.686 once surface features such as length and position are residualized out (0.507 with shuffled labels). The gap holds across eight benchmarks and model families, and the surface-predictability score predicts the size of the gain (Spearman rho = 0.90). On rubric tasks with one answer at a time, reading internals gives no advantage. Interventions show that editing activations mid-network already changes the verdict and locate pathways carrying position and length bias.
AI.conclusion: A wrong verdict does not mean the judge lacks the information. At the same label budget, the recovered signal lets a judge flag likely-wrong cases and yields better labels for preference learning, and a simple diagnostic shows when recovery is worthwhile.

title: TAO-DA: Towards Autonomous Operation--A Dual-Arm Vision-Language-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for grounding high-level semantic information into low-level robot actions, enabling scalable robotic manipulation across diverse tasks. However, existing VLA models lack explicit mechanisms to disentangle the states and intents of the two arms, leading to unintended cross-arm interference that degrades task execution success. To address this issue, we propose a symmetric Dual-Arm Expert (DAE) architecture built upon a shared Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone with decoupled, arm-specific expert towers. Expert selection is carried out through a two-stage dual-arm intent routing scheme, in which experts are routed either by explicit language instructions in the first stage or by implicit visual semantics in the second stage. Moreover, we introduce a lightweight task progress prediction module that leverages cross-attention between the pre-chunk temporal features and semantic representations of proprioceptive and visual observations to accurately estimate frame-wise task completion progress. This module facilitates task progress synchronization to support coordinated scheduling for collaborative multi-robot tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in dual-arm intent routing and the disentanglement of cross-arm interference, and further provide preliminary evidence of emergent skill generalization from single- to dual-arm tasks (as well as the reverse), together with cross-arm motion-domain skill transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symmetric Dual-Arm Expert (DAE) VLA architecture with decoupled arm-specific expert towers, a two-stage dual-arm intent routing scheme, and a task progress prediction module to mitigate cross-arm interference and enable coordinated dual-arm manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models lack explicit mechanisms to disentangle the states and intents of the two arms, causing unintended cross-arm interference that degrades task execution success.
AI.method: A symmetric Dual-Arm Expert architecture built on a shared VLM backbone with decoupled, arm-specific expert towers. Expert selection uses a two-stage dual-arm intent routing scheme: stage one routes by explicit language instructions, stage two by implicit visual semantics. A lightweight task progress prediction module applies cross-attention between pre-chunk temporal features and semantic representations of proprioceptive and visual observations to estimate frame-wise task completion progress, supporting task progress synchronization for collaborative multi-robot scheduling.
AI.result: Experiments show effectiveness in dual-arm intent routing and disentanglement of cross-arm interference, provide preliminary evidence of emergent skill generalization from single- to dual-arm tasks (and the reverse), and demonstrate cross-arm motion-domain skill transfer.
AI.conclusion: The symmetric DAE architecture with decoupled experts, two-stage intent routing, and progress prediction improves dual-arm manipulation by reducing cross-arm interference and enabling coordination, with evidence of skill generalization and transfer.

title: Carnator: Fast Text-to-Video Generation with Generation-Native Compatibility-Guided Cross-Request Reuse
summary: Video diffusion transformers produce high-quality videos, yet iterative denoising incurs substantial inference latency, limiting interactive and large-scale serving. Most existing acceleration methods focus on individual requests, thereby restricting efficiency gains to redundancy within a single generation trajectory. Recent cross-request reuse offers an additional source of savings, but existing approaches often infer reusability from coarse semantic similarity. This conflates semantic relatedness with generation-level computational compatibility, so aggressive reuse may accept incompatible historical computation while conservative reuse leaves substantial acceleration unrealized. We present \emph{Carnator}, a cross-request acceleration framework that addresses this challenge by extracting and using generation-native compatibility evidence directly from the model's evolving internal states. Specifically, \emph{Carnator} performs a lightweight early probe to construct an Early Signature from internal diffusion states, assessing reuse validity through risk-aware compatibility decisions. The same evidence characterizes reuse scope by localizing target-specific computation and guiding joint reuse of historical latent trajectories and sparse attention connectivity. Across three text-to-video backbones, Carnator consistently achieves higher cache-hit end-to-end acceleration than the evaluated cross-request baselines despite more selective cache acceptance, reaching up to 2.17$\times$ speedup while maintaining competitive generation quality.

AI.tldr: Carnator is a cross-request acceleration framework for video diffusion transformers that extracts generation-native compatibility evidence from the model's internal diffusion states, enabling risk-aware reuse of historical computation across requests.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion transformers suffer from high inference latency due to iterative denoising, and most acceleration methods only exploit redundancy within a single trajectory. Existing cross-request reuse approaches infer reusability from coarse semantic similarity, conflating semantic relatedness with generation-level computational compatibility, leading to either incompatible reuse or unrealized acceleration.
AI.method: Carnator performs a lightweight early probe to construct an Early Signature from internal diffusion states, assessing reuse validity through risk-aware compatibility decisions. The same evidence localizes target-specific computation and guides joint reuse of historical latent trajectories and sparse attention connectivity.
AI.result: Across three text-to-video backbones, Carnator consistently achieves higher cache-hit end-to-end acceleration than evaluated cross-request baselines despite more selective cache acceptance, reaching up to 2.17x speedup while maintaining competitive generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Using generation-native compatibility evidence from internal states enables more effective and selective cross-request reuse, delivering substantial acceleration in video diffusion inference without sacrificing generation quality.

title: Learning with Object-centric Representations of Tactile Interactive Perception for Robot Manipulation
summary: Implicit object properties that are difficult to directly infer from vision, such as material, container contents, or softness, can be revealed through tactile sensing and exploratory interactions. However, because tactile signals are transient and sparse, extracting informative tactile events and effectively incorporating them into robotic manipulation remains a challenge. In this work, we present an object-centric context-aware manipulation framework that learns task-agnostic object representations through tactile exploration. A token learner autonomously selects representative tactile segments from long-horizon exploration, while contrastive alignment with descriptive text embeddings enables a latent space that captures multiple physical object properties. These learned representations are then used as semantic context to guide object-centric manipulation policies and adapt strategies based on object properties. Experiments show that the learned representations achieve 93% and 84% property estimation accuracy on seen and unseen objects. Evaluated on three tasks involving visually ambiguous objects, i.e. multi-object rearrangement, pouring, and box opening, the proposed framework improves both target selection and property-dependent manipulation adaptation, raising task success, aggregated over all evaluation trials, from 41% to 92% on seen objects and from 19% to 67% on unseen objects over baseline policies without object-context conditioning. Videos and additional results are available at https://xinyiyxyx.github.io/tactile-object-centric/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an object-centric, context-aware manipulation framework that learns task-agnostic object representations from tactile exploration, using a token learner to select representative tactile segments and contrastive alignment with text to encode physical properties, then uses these as semantic context to guide manipulation policies.
AI.motivation: Implicit object properties such as material, container contents, or softness cannot be reliably inferred from vision alone and require tactile sensing and exploratory interaction. However, tactile signals are transient and sparse, making it hard to extract informative tactile events and effectively integrate them into robotic manipulation.
AI.method: A token learner autonomously selects representative tactile segments from long-horizon exploration. Contrastive alignment with descriptive text embeddings yields a latent space capturing multiple physical object properties. The learned representations serve as semantic context to condition object-centric manipulation policies, enabling property-dependent strategy adaptation.
AI.result: Property estimation accuracy reaches 93% on seen objects and 84% on unseen objects. Across three tasks with visually ambiguous objects (multi-object rearrangement, pouring, box opening), the framework improves target selection and manipulation adaptation, raising aggregate task success from 41% to 92% on seen objects and from 19% to 67% on unseen objects versus baselines without object-context conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Learning task-agnostic object representations through tactile exploration and grounding them in text provides effective semantic context that substantially improves object-centric manipulation, particularly for visually ambiguous objects and generalization to unseen objects.

title: MergeHEIR: Mitigating Multimodal Hallucinations as the Tax of Model Merging
summary: Model merging consolidates task-specialized experts into a single deployable model. However, we show that such capability consolidation incurs a merging tax of increased hallucination: across 8 model-merging methods, every merged checkpoint exhibits a higher hallucination rate than the average of its constituent experts. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing hallucination-mitigation methods to the post-merge model, yet this unconstrained adaptation disrupts inherited capabilities, creating a tension between hallucination mitigation and expertise retention. To tackle this challenge, we introduce MergeHEIR, a post-merge adaptation framework designed to reduce this merging tax while preserving expertise inherited from initial experts. Using small expert-task calibration sets, MergeHEIR constructs layer-wise null-space projectors via SVD from task-specific activations collected from the merged checkpoint, and periodically projects the accumulated post-merge displacement onto the resulting null spaces to preserve inherited expertise. Theoretically, we establish minimum-distortion and maximum-dimensionality guarantees, characterize the threshold-controlled adaptation-retention trade-off, and extend perturbation guarantees beyond finite calibration data. Across 24 paired comparisons spanning three MLLM configurations and 8 model-merging methods, MergeHEIR consistently mitigates hallucination while largely preserving inherited expertise, demonstrating a more favorable hallucination-retention trade-off.

AI.tldr: Model merging introduces a "merging tax": all merged checkpoints hallucinate more than the average of their experts, and naive mitigation harms retained expertise. MergeHEIR uses layer-wise null-space projectors from SVD to mitigate hallucination post-merge while preserving inherited expertise, with theoretical guarantees and consistent empirical gains.
AI.motivation: Model merging consolidates task-specialized experts into one deployable model, but the authors show this capability consolidation incurs a merging tax of increased hallucination: across 8 merging methods, every merged checkpoint hallucinates more than the average of its constituent experts. Naively applying existing hallucination-mitigation methods post-merge disrupts inherited capabilities, creating a tension between hallucination mitigation and expertise retention. This motivates a post-merge adaptation framework that reduces hallucination without sacrificing inherited expertise.
AI.method: MergeHEIR is a post-merge adaptation framework. Using small expert-task calibration sets, it constructs layer-wise null-space projectors via SVD from task-specific activations collected at the merged checkpoint, then periodically projects the accumulated post-merge displacement onto these null spaces to preserve inherited expertise while reducing hallucination. Theoretically, the authors establish minimum-distortion and maximum-dimensionality guarantees, characterize the threshold-controlled adaptation-retention trade-off, and extend perturbation guarantees beyond finite calibration data.
AI.result: Across 24 paired comparisons spanning three MLLM configurations and 8 model-merging methods, MergeHEIR consistently mitigates hallucination while largely preserving inherited expertise, achieving a more favorable hallucination-retention trade-off than unconstrained adaptation baselines.
AI.conclusion: The merging tax of increased hallucination is real and universal across merging methods, and it can be addressed via null-space projection-based post-merge adaptation. MergeHEIR reduces hallucination while retaining expert capabilities, offering a better trade-off supported by both theory and extensive empirical validation.

title: SurgFlow: 3D Object-Centric Contact Flow for Surgical Robot Manipulation
summary: Paired video-action demonstrations enable autonomous surgical behavior, but such data is scarce: robots perform roughly 1% of surgeries, while video-only data is abundant. Learning 3D object flow offers an embodiment-agnostic way to utilize video data, but flow alone specifies how an object should move, not where and when the tool should engage it, a distinction that is critical in surgery. We introduce SurgFlow, a framework that learns 3D Object-Centric Contact Flow from stereo surgical video without action labels. For each object point, it predicts a future 3D trajectory and contact scores. We extract targets via 3D tracking and tool-object proximity, train a flow matching generator to predict them, and use predicted contact to trigger grasp and release while optimizing end effector motion from flow. On the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK), SurgFlow succeeds in 37 of 39 stage evaluations across tissue retraction, bimanual reveal, needle pickup, and handover, outperforming baselines trained on equal data with or without action labels. Zero-shot transfer to a humanoid-based laparoscopic robot achieves 85% and 70% average success under similar and novel camera viewpoints, respectively.

AI.tldr: SurgFlow learns 3D Object-Centric Contact Flow from stereo surgical video without action labels, predicting per-point future 3D trajectories plus contact scores, to enable autonomous surgical manipulation.
AI.motivation: Paired video-action demonstrations for autonomous surgery are scarce (robots perform only ~1% of surgeries), while video-only data is abundant. Prior flow-based, embodiment-agnostic learning specifies how an object should move but not where or when the tool should engage it—a critical distinction in surgery.
AI.method: SurgFlow predicts, for each object point, a future 3D trajectory and contact scores. Targets are extracted via 3D tracking and tool-object proximity; a flow matching generator is trained to predict them. Predicted contact triggers grasp and release, while end effector motion is optimized from the flow. Trained on stereo surgical video without action labels.
AI.result: On the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK), SurgFlow succeeds in 37 of 39 stage evaluations across tissue retraction, bimanual reveal, needle pickup, and handover, outperforming baselines trained on equal data with or without action labels. Zero-shot transfer to a humanoid-based laparoscopic robot reaches 85% and 70% average success under similar and novel camera viewpoints.
AI.conclusion: Contact-aware 3D object-centric flow learned from unlabeled stereo surgical video enables label-free, embodiment-agnostic autonomous surgical manipulation with strong real-robot and zero-shot cross-platform transfer performance.

title: PluginRSI: Recursive Improvement of Agent Harnesses with Reusable Plugins
summary: The harness surrounding a language model is a central determinant of agent performance. Recent methods optimize harnesses by searching over complete programs, where individual mechanisms are difficult to isolate and reuse. We introduce PluginRSI, which represents a harness as a composition of atomized plugins and organizes harness evolution around these plugins. Individual plugins are improved independently and accumulated in a shared library, then recombined into new harnesses at each iteration. PluginRSI improves over existing harness optimization methods across software engineering, command-line interaction, and question-answering tasks. The resulting harnesses retain their advantage when transferred to other solver models without further optimization. The evolved plugin library accelerates subsequent optimization from the initial harness, which helps faster and higher convergence on unseen tasks. These results show that accumulating reusable mechanisms provides an effective basis for continued harness improvement.

AI.tldr: PluginRSI represents a language model harness as a composition of atomized plugins, enabling independent improvement and reuse of individual mechanisms. It outperforms existing harness optimization methods across software engineering, command-line interaction, and QA tasks, transfers well to other solver models, and accelerates convergence on unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: The harness surrounding a language model strongly determines agent performance, yet current harness optimization methods search over complete programs, making individual mechanisms hard to isolate and reuse. This limits accumulation of reusable improvements.
AI.method: PluginRSI decomposes the harness into a composition of atomized plugins and organizes harness evolution around them. Individual plugins are improved independently and accumulated in a shared library, then recombined into new harnesses at each iteration.
AI.result: PluginRSI improves over existing harness optimization methods on software engineering, command-line interaction, and question-answering tasks. Evolved harnesses retain their advantage when transferred to other solver models without further optimization, and the plugin library accelerates subsequent optimization, yielding faster and higher convergence on unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: Accumulating reusable mechanisms provides an effective basis for continued harness improvement.

title: ActionGround: Training-Free Runtime Refinement of Frozen VLA Policies
summary:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions, but they do not explicitly represent the phase structure of manipulation tasks or the rigid-body dynamics governing execution. We present ActionGround, a neuro-symbolic, training-free runtime layer that wraps a frozen VLA policy without retraining, fine-tuning, or weight access, adding less than 1 ms of overhead per control step. A symbolic phase-aware finite-state machine identifies the manipulation phase (approach, grasp, transport, or place) and applies a phase-specific rule-based correction. In parallel, an always-on, inertia-weighted Euler-Lagrange term incorporates the robot's equations of motion into each control step, while its dynamics residual is logged as a consistency diagnostic rather than used as a gate.
  We evaluate ActionGround across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, Force-VLA, and Generalist-VLA on ten LIBERO-Spatial pick-and-place tasks using a 7-DoF Franka Panda. With fixed parameters across tasks and backbones, ActionGround improves success rate by up to 6 percentage points and stability by up to 19.3 percentage points, while improving trajectory efficiency by up to 15%. In a separate Robosuite noise sweep, ActionGround provides approximately a 10x improvement in trajectory-jerk robustness under injected action noise. In a matched-seed Robosuite simulation companion to a real Agilex Piper trial, simulated baseline success increases from 35% to 95%. The physical-hardware experiment is presented as a qualitative deployment demonstration; quantitative per-trial success on the real arm is left for future work. Our evaluation is limited to rigid-object pick-and-place manipulation.

AI.tldr: ActionGround is a training-free, neuro-symbolic runtime wrapper for frozen VLA policies that injects phase-aware symbolic corrections and Euler-Lagrange dynamics terms, improving success, stability, and robustness across multiple backbones on LIBERO-Spatial pick-and-place.
AI.motivation: VLA models map vision and language directly to actions but lack explicit representations of manipulation phase structure and rigid-body dynamics, which limits execution reliability.
AI.method: A training-free runtime layer wraps a frozen VLA policy without retraining, fine-tuning, or weight access, adding under 1 ms per control step. A symbolic phase-aware finite-state machine identifies manipulation phases (approach, grasp, transport, place) and applies phase-specific rule-based corrections. In parallel, an always-on, inertia-weighted Euler-Lagrange term embeds the robot's equations of motion into each control step; its dynamics residual is logged as a consistency diagnostic, not used as a gate.
AI.result: Evaluated on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, Force-VLA, and Generalist-VLA across ten LIBERO-Spatial pick-and-place tasks with a 7-DoF Franka Panda: up to +6 pp success, +19.3 pp stability, +15% trajectory efficiency with fixed parameters. Robosuite noise sweep showed ~10x improvement in trajectory-jerk robustness. In a matched-seed Robosuite companion to a real Agilex Piper trial, simulated baseline success rose from 35% to 95%. Physical-hardware results are only a qualitative deployment demonstration.
AI.conclusion: ActionGround improves VLA execution via phase-aware symbolic correction and dynamics regularization without retraining, but evaluation is limited to rigid-object pick-and-place, and quantitative per-trial real-arm success is left for future work.

title: Authorization Closure Graph: Minimal Repair for LLM Agents with Evolving User Instructions
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Preprint under review
summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform state-changing actions that require user authorization. Yet existing approaches do not provide a principled mechanism for selectively updating prior authorization when only part of an instruction changes. To this end, we propose an Authorization-Closure-Graph (ACG)-based framework that represents authorization and its dependencies as an evolving, versioned state. ACG selectively invalidates authority affected by a revision while preserving unaffected portions of the authorization state, and computes a minimal repair that identifies only the missing evidence or authority required for execution. This enables agents to adapt to revised instructions while avoiding stale authority and unnecessary authorization requests. We evaluate ACG across three advanced LLMs in two natural tasks, and ACG consistently improves action safety rate and task success rate. Code is available at https://github.com/weiliang822/ACG.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Authorization-Closure-Graph (ACG) framework that models authorization and its dependencies as an evolving, versioned state, enabling selective invalidation and minimal repair of authority when instructions are revised. Evaluated on three LLMs across two tasks, ACG improves both action safety and task success rates.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly perform state-changing actions requiring user authorization, but existing approaches lack a principled mechanism to selectively update prior authorization when only part of an instruction changes. This leads to either stale authority or unnecessary re-authorization requests.
AI.method: An Authorization-Closure-Graph (ACG)-based framework that represents authorization and its dependencies as an evolving, versioned state. ACG selectively invalidates authority affected by a revision while preserving unaffected authorization state, and computes a minimal repair identifying only the missing evidence or authority required for execution.
AI.result: Evaluated across three advanced LLMs on two natural tasks, ACG consistently improves both action safety rate and task success rate.
AI.conclusion: ACG enables agents to adapt to revised instructions while avoiding stale authority and unnecessary authorization requests, with code released on GitHub.

title: PORTER: Edge-Cloud Residency for Persistent 3D Scene Graph Memory
summary: Recent task-driven and just-in-time 3D Scene Graph (3DSG) methods reduce per-task representations by constructing or activating only task-relevant information. Yet sparse per-task working sets do not bound onboard memory usage over a robot's lifetime: as tasks change, payloads accumulated for earlier tasks may become irrelevant to the current task but can be useful again in future tasks. Over repeated task switches and expanding environments, retaining such reusable payloads causes local memory to grow, whereas discarding them entirely can lead to costly repeated construction of the same payloads later. We introduce PORTER, which decouples persistence from residency: lightweight anchors remain in the limited memory of the edge robot while heavy object payloads migrate between the edge and the cloud. Relevance alone is insufficient for deciding residency because multiple relevant payloads may provide redundant information. We therefore decompose each task into functional requirements and introduce Irreplaceable Support Erasure (ISE), which measures the loss in requirement coverage caused by offloading. ISE discounts replaceable support and penalizes losses more strongly when the remaining coverage of a requirement is weak. PORTER constructs a budget-aware local working set by repeatedly offloading the payload with the smallest marginal ISE per byte. Experiments on JITOMA-Bench evaluate PORTER across four 3DSG builders. Under progressive compression, pooled relative mR@3 remains at 100% through 91% payload-byte offloading.

AI.tldr: PORTER decouples persistence from residency in edge-cloud 3D Scene Graphs, migrating heavy object payloads off-board via an Irreplaceable Support Erasure (ISE) metric that accounts for redundancy, keeping pooled relative mR@3 at 100% while offloading 91% of payload bytes.
AI.motivation: Task-driven and just-in-time 3DSG methods limit per-task representations but do not bound onboard memory over a robot's lifetime: payloads from earlier tasks may be irrelevant now yet useful later, so retaining them grows local memory while discarding them forces costly repeated construction. Relevance alone cannot decide residency, because multiple relevant payloads may be redundant.
AI.method: PORTER keeps lightweight anchors resident on the edge robot and migrates heavy object payloads between edge and cloud. Each task is decomposed into functional requirements, and Irreplaceable Support Erasure (ISE) quantifies the loss in requirement coverage caused by offloading—discounting replaceable support and penalizing losses more heavily when residual coverage is weak. A budget-aware local working set is built by repeatedly offloading the payload with the smallest marginal ISE per byte.
AI.result: Evaluated on JITOMA-Bench across four 3DSG builders. Under progressive compression, pooled relative mR@3 remains at 100% through 91% payload-byte offloading.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling persistence from residency with a redundancy-aware, coverage-sensitive erasure metric enables substantial edge-memory reduction with no measurable loss in task-relevant retrieval performance.

title: PrismQuant: Optimal Null-Space Rotations for Grouped Quantizers
comment: The paper is currently under review. Code, checkpoints, and implementation details are available at: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PrismQuant
summary: Smaller activation outliers do not necessarily imply better low-bit quantization: their alignment with the quantizer matters. We introduce PrismQuant, a quantizer-aware rotation framework that aligns the leading activation eigenspace with the constant group subspace of asymmetric grouped INT4. The affine offsets represent the energy in this subspace without widening the range within the group. We formulate rotation design as a Ky Fan trace maximization and derive a closed-form solution that is provably optimal for this alignment objective. Compact Householder transformations and their compact-WY representation enable gradient-free construction and efficient application at both foldable and online sites. A predictive range law further connects unaligned activation energy and group size to quantization-relevant variation. Experiments on Llama, Qwen, and Mistral span dense models up to 70B parameters and a 30B mixture-of-experts model. Under W4A4KV4, PrismQuant sets the state of the art on Llama-3.2-3B among the compared methods in both perplexity and accuracy. On Llama-3.1-70B, it attains 3.85 perplexity and 72.46% average zero-shot accuracy, only 0.22 percentage points below full precision. In the deployment study on Llama-3.1-8B, our optimized implementation achieves 1.51x prefill and 1.22x CUDA Graph decode speedups over matched FP16 baselines, with 56.34% lower decode peak memory and only 2.35% additional Graph decode latency over Hadamard. Code is available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PrismQuant.

AI.tldr: PrismQuant is a quantizer-aware rotation framework that aligns the leading activation eigenspace with the constant group subspace of asymmetric grouped INT4, improving low-bit quantization via a closed-form, provably optimal rotation and efficient Householder/WY implementation.
AI.motivation: Smaller activation outliers do not necessarily imply better low-bit quantization; what matters is how well those outliers align with the quantizer. Existing rotation-based quantization methods overlook this alignment between activation energy and the quantizer's constant group subspace, limiting W4A4KV4 performance.
AI.method: The paper formulates rotation design as Ky Fan trace maximization to align the leading activation eigenspace with the constant group subspace of asymmetric grouped INT4, where affine offsets absorb subspace energy without widening the in-group range. It derives a closed-form, provably optimal solution and uses compact Householder transformations with compact-WY representation for gradient-free construction and efficient foldable/online application. A predictive range law links unaligned activation energy and group size to quantization-relevant variation.
AI.result: Experiments span Llama, Qwen, and Mistral, including dense models up to 70B and a 30B MoE model. Under W4A4KV4, PrismQuant achieves state-of-the-art perplexity and accuracy on Llama-3.2-3B. On Llama-3.1-70B it reaches 3.85 perplexity and 72.46% average zero-shot accuracy (only 0.22 points below full precision). On Llama-3.1-8B deployment, it delivers 1.51x prefill and 1.22x CUDA Graph decode speedups over FP16, 56.34% lower decode peak memory, and only 2.35% additional Graph decode latency over Hadamard.
AI.conclusion: Alignment between activation energy and the quantizer's constant subspace, rather than merely reducing outlier magnitude, is key to low-bit quantization quality. PrismQuant operationalizes this insight with an optimal, efficient rotation framework, achieving strong accuracy and deployment speedups across diverse model scales.

title: Q-WAM: 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models with Action-Subspace Protection
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate video and robot actions through iterative diffusion and perform strongly in robotic manipulation. However, their prohibitive compute and memory costs pose substantial deployment challenges. Post-training quantization (PTQ) can reduce these costs, but existing PTQ methods such as smoothing and rotation are insufficient to maintain the precision of action generation. To overcome this limitation, we propose Q-WAM, a new 4-bit weight-activation quantization for WAMs that preserves the actions the model generates. Specifically, we introduce the \textit{Action Observability Gramian (AOG)}, which measures how much rounding errors in each weighted combination of a layer's input channels change the final action through all denoising steps. We also develop Action-Subspace Protection (ASP), which keeps the few most action-sensitive channel combinations in a tiny 16-bit low-rank branch and quantizes the complementary weights and activations to 4 bits, both as dense matrix multiplications that run efficiently on GPUs. Finally, to preserve action quality with minimal overhead, we identify the experts that matter most for the generated action by aggregating the AOG-derived action mass across the layers of each expert and apply ASP only to those experts. We evaluate Q-WAM on three WAMs, both in simulation and in real-world deployment. On the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, it reaches 89.6--93.0\% average success rate, within 1.1 percentage points of the 16-bit models, while reducing the memory of the quantized blocks by 3.1--3.4$\times$. Our method outperforms the strongest baseline, SVDQuant, by 2.5--8.7 percentage points. On a Unitree G1 humanoid and a bimanual UR3 robot, it improves success over SVDQuant by 12.8-17.6 percentage points.

AI.tldr: Q-WAM introduces a 4-bit weight-activation post-training quantization method for World Action Models that preserves action generation quality via the Action Observability Gramian and Action-Subspace Protection, achieving near-16-bit success rates with large memory savings.
AI.motivation: World Action Models generate video and robot actions via iterative diffusion but have prohibitive compute and memory costs, hindering deployment. Existing PTQ methods like smoothing and rotation fail to maintain action generation precision.
AI.method: The paper proposes Q-WAM, a 4-bit weight-activation quantization for WAMs. It introduces the Action Observability Gramian (AOG) to measure how rounding errors in each weighted combination of input channels affect the final action across denoising steps, and Action-Subspace Protection (ASP) that retains the most action-sensitive channel combinations in a 16-bit low-rank branch while quantizing complementary weights/activations to 4 bits as dense GPU-efficient matmuls. It selectively applies ASP to the most action-relevant experts by aggregating AOG-derived action mass.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0, Q-WAM achieves 89.6–93.0% average success rate, within 1.1 percentage points of 16-bit models, while cutting quantized block memory by 3.1–3.4×. It outperforms SVDQuant by 2.5–8.7 points. On a Unitree G1 humanoid and bimanual UR3 robot, it improves success over SVDQuant by 12.8–17.6 points.
AI.conclusion: Q-WAM enables efficient 4-bit quantization of WAMs while preserving action generation quality, validated across three WAMs in simulation and real-world deployment.

title: Multi-Agent System Search via Active Substructure-aware Policy Optimization
summary: LLMs enable multi-agent systems (MAS) to tackle complex tasks, but manually designing agent roles, prompts, and communication structures requires substantial expertise and effort. This motivates learning policies that construct query-specific MAS from execution reward. Existing approaches typically train these policies by repeatedly traversing a fixed set of training queries and assigning rewards at the workflow level. However, this overlooks differences in queries' evolving learning potential and obscures which substructures improve solution quality. In this paper, we propose Active Substructure-aware Policy Optimization (ASPO), a RL framework for query-level MAS search. ASPO introduces an Adaptive Query-Selection Mechanism (AQSM) that focuses training on queries at the policy's competence boundary: those it can solve but not yet reliably. A complementary discovery mechanism widens architectural exploration for hard queries, helping distinguish insufficient exploration from operator capability limits. Beyond query selection, ASPO introduces substructure-level rewards that measure output-quality gains within each action's descendant subgraph. These rewards guide proximal policy optimization to reinforce useful architectural refinements and discourage redundant or harmful computation. Together, these mechanisms prioritize learnable queries and provide fine-grained feedback for learning effective MASs. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, general question answering, and code generation, ASPO ranks first on every benchmark against twelve baselines.

AI.tldr: ASPO is an RL framework for query-level multi-agent system (MAS) search that combines an adaptive query-selection mechanism targeting queries at the policy's competence boundary with substructure-level rewards measuring output-quality gains within each action's descendant subgraph, achieving first place on all six benchmarks against twelve baselines.
AI.motivation: Manually designing agent roles, prompts, and communication structures in LLM-based multi-agent systems requires substantial expertise and effort, motivating learned policies that construct query-specific MAS from execution reward. Existing training approaches repeatedly traverse a fixed set of training queries and assign workflow-level rewards, which overlooks differences in queries' evolving learning potential and obscures which substructures improve solution quality.
AI.method: ASPO introduces three mechanisms: (1) an Adaptive Query-Selection Mechanism (AQSM) that focuses training on queries at the policy's competence boundary—those it can solve but not yet reliably; (2) a complementary discovery mechanism that widens architectural exploration for hard queries, helping distinguish insufficient exploration from operator capability limits; and (3) substructure-level rewards that measure output-quality gains within each action's descendant subgraph, guiding proximal policy optimization to reinforce useful architectural refinements and discourage redundant or harmful computation.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, general question answering, and code generation, ASPO ranks first on every benchmark against twelve baselines.
AI.conclusion: By prioritizing learnable queries and providing fine-grained substructure-level feedback, ASPO enables effective learning of query-specific MAS architectures, outperforming all evaluated baselines across diverse task domains.

title: AquaWAM: A Dynamics-aware World Action Model for Underwater Embodied Agents
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) are becoming increasingly important and useful for embodied intelligence, as they enable robots to anticipate the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with the physical environment. However, underwater robots are usually subject to passive dynamics, such as inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift, which can continue to affect the vehicle even after an action is completed. Existing WAMs, which primarily predict action-conditioned visual observations, are not explicitly designed to capture such passive motion dynamics. In this paper, we present AquaWAM, the first World Action Model designed for underwater embodied agents. Instead of predicting future images, AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including the thruster dead band, the inertial glide that outlasts each command, and ambient currents. Specifically, it senses through the DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for understanding goals and target pose. By modeling compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations, AquaWAM substantially reduces the model size and computational cost compared with conventional WAMs. Experimentally, AquaWAM achieves a 72.6% task success rate across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods while making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Our model also remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable. For example, without DVL velocity measurements, our method still achieves a 61.6% success rate, compared with 39.4% for U0.

AI.tldr: AquaWAM is the first World Action Model for underwater embodied agents that models passive physical dynamics (thruster dead band, inertial glide, ambient currents) using compact navigation states instead of visual observations, achieving 72.6% success on 20 USIM tasks with 2.7x faster decisions.
AI.motivation: Underwater robots experience passive dynamics like inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift that continue affecting motion after actions end. Existing World Action Models predict action-conditioned visual observations and are not designed to capture these passive motion dynamics.
AI.method: AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including thruster dead band, inertial glide outlasting each command, and ambient currents. It senses via DVL, IMU, pressure sensor, and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for goal understanding and target pose. It models compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations.
AI.result: AquaWAM achieves 72.6% task success across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods and making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Without DVL velocity measurements, it still achieves 61.6% success versus 39.4% for U0.
AI.conclusion: Modeling compact navigation states instead of visual observations substantially reduces model size and computational cost versus conventional WAMs, and the approach remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable.

title: From Latents to Wires: Surgical Post-Editing on Large Language Models
summary: Given a large language model (LLM), can whoever holds the weights name a semantic target (e.g., the model's identity), locate the model components that produce it, and edit them so that the target no longer appears while other capability is preserved? We call such an edit on a trained model a post-edit. We present L2W (latents to wires), a framework that performs surgical post-edits for named semantic targets. For localization, L2W uses Jacobian lens (J-lens) attribution to score components against the semantic target. For surgical removal, because LLM mechanisms are redundant (i.e., a semantic target may have multiple components producing it), L2W runs Counterexample-Guided Causal Cut (CGCC) until the target no longer appears. CGCC first cumulatively closes model components, treating each surviving expression of the target as a counterexample that exposes the next components to close, and then reopens some of them to preserve capability. In a controlled experiment with an implanted behavioural watermark, L2W removes the watermark, and its localization lands on the model region the implant changed. Across three model configurations, L2W removes model-metadata (e.g., identity) self-claims in all nine runs, and adult-content refusal in all three, with no held-out target residual. L2W further composes two post-edits on a text-to-image model: one removes the refusal of requested nudity, and a second removes the nude rendering the first exposes. The results support post-editing as a complement to post-training: post-training installs preferred behaviours, and post-editing removes named unwanted ones.

AI.tldr: L2W is a framework for surgical "post-edits" of trained LLMs: it localizes components producing a named semantic target via Jacobian-lens attribution and removes the target using Counterexample-Guided Causal Cut, preserving other capabilities.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether, given a large language model's weights, one can name a semantic target (e.g., the model's identity), locate the components producing it, and edit them so the target disappears while other capabilities are preserved. It frames this as "post-editing" — a complement to post-training, which installs preferred behaviors rather than removing named unwanted ones.
AI.method: L2W (latents to wires) performs surgical post-edits for named semantic targets. For localization, it uses Jacobian lens (J-lens) attribution to score components against the semantic target. For surgical removal, recognizing that LLM mechanisms are redundant (a target may have multiple producing components), it runs Counterexample-Guided Causal Cut (CGCC) until the target no longer appears: CGCC cumulatively closes components, treating each surviving expression of the target as a counterexample that exposes the next components to close, then reopens some to preserve capability.
AI.result: In a controlled experiment with an implanted behavioral watermark, L2W removes the watermark, and its localization lands on the model region the implant changed. Across three model configurations, L2W removes model-metadata (e.g., identity) self-claims in all nine runs and adult-content refusal in all three, with no held-out target residual. L2W also composes two post-edits on a text-to-image model: one removes refusal of requested nudity, and a second removes the nude rendering the first exposes.
AI.conclusion: The results support post-editing as a complement to post-training: post-training installs preferred behaviors, whereas post-editing removes named unwanted ones.

title: CompliantWBC: Whole-Body Compliance for Heavy Humanoids via Force Latent Estimation and Residual Impedance Targets
summary: Whole-body compliant control is essential for deploying heavy humanoids under high payload in human-centric environments. Most prior force-aware learning-based pipelines focus on end-effector resistance, per-link upper-body springs, or end-effector stiffness modulation, leaving arbitrary-site perturbations on heavy platforms with lower-body engagement largely unaddressed. We close this gap with CompliantWBC comprising: (1) A base policy trained with RL to maximize compliance-fidelity reward, guided by a multi-site whole-body impedance reference controller, extending classical Cartesian impedance to any controlled link; (2) A bounded residual policy that edits the per-link impedance equilibrium over a frozen base, correcting the coarse but structured wrench estimate supplied by a force encoder co-trained behind a gradient barrier; (3) A Phong-weighted force-origin sampler with an axis-decoupled pelvis anchor induces lower-body-inclusive compliance curriculum training via two interpretable parameters. We evaluate CompliantWBC in simulation against both compliant and stiff baselines, achieving best compliant fidelity of 2.58cm deviation from analytical solutions, and demonstrate it on a real heavy humanoid across static/dynamic force reaction, board wiping, squat under payload, and cooperative payload transport. Project website: https://dotandung.github.io/compliantwbc/

AI.tldr: CompliantWBC enables whole-body compliant control for heavy humanoids under high payloads, achieving 2.58cm deviation from analytical solutions in simulation and validated on a real heavy humanoid across multiple force-reaction and payload tasks.
AI.motivation: Deploying heavy humanoids under high payload in human-centric environments requires whole-body compliance. Prior force-aware learning pipelines only address end-effector resistance, per-link upper-body springs, or end-effector stiffness modulation, leaving arbitrary-site perturbations on heavy platforms with lower-body engagement unaddressed.
AI.method: CompliantWBC comprises: (1) a base policy trained with RL to maximize a compliance-fidelity reward, guided by a multi-site whole-body impedance reference controller extending classical Cartesian impedance to any controlled link; (2) a bounded residual policy editing per-link impedance equilibrium over a frozen base, correcting a coarse wrench estimate from a force encoder co-trained behind a gradient barrier; (3) a Phong-weighted force-origin sampler with an axis-decoupled pelvis anchor for lower-body-inclusive compliance curriculum training via two interpretable parameters.
AI.result: In simulation, CompliantWBC achieves best compliant fidelity with 2.58cm deviation from analytical solutions versus compliant and stiff baselines. On a real heavy humanoid, it is demonstrated across static/dynamic force reaction, board wiping, squat under payload, and cooperative payload transport.
AI.conclusion: CompliantWBC closes the gap in arbitrary-site whole-body compliance for heavy humanoid platforms with lower-body engagement, showing strong simulation fidelity and real-world deployment across diverse force-interaction and payload tasks.

title: Controllable GNN Explanations via Multi-Metric Preference Selection
summary: Mechanisms for generating GNN explanations are crucial for building trust and mitigating biases in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), especially in high-stakes scenarios. Most current methods optimize only for fidelity under the sparsity constraint. However, this discounts the need for interpretable explanations (those that consist of familiar motif patterns) and stable explanations (those that remain unchanged under structural perturbations). We propose a novel approach that optimizes GNN explanations across these metrics, exposing their relative weighing as a control. Experiments on various real-world datasets, including MUTAG, BA-2Motif, BAMultiShapes, and PROTEINS, suggest that our method produces higher-fidelity explanations than a state-of-the-art baseline on MUTAG and PROTEINS across all evaluated budgets, and on BA-2Motif at larger budgets, while being faster in the regime of small explanation budgets. We also explore how, given an input motif library containing standard motifs for the corresponding domain, the method can be used to determine the relative importance of those motifs in generating the explanations, and how this information can be used to further improve the quality of the output explanations. We also examine the relationship between different metrics through their induced tradeoff surface, and explore its dependence on the nature of the motif library.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel GNN explanation generation approach that jointly optimizes fidelity, interpretability (motif familiarity), and stability under structural perturbations, exposing their relative weighting as a controllable tradeoff, and shows improved faithfulness across several real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Generating explanations for Graph Neural Networks is important for building trust and mitigating biases in high-stakes scenarios. Most existing methods optimize only fidelity under a sparsity constraint, neglecting the need for interpretable explanations (composed of familiar motif patterns) and stable explanations (invariant under structural perturbations).
AI.method: The authors propose an approach that optimizes GNN explanations across multiple metrics: fidelity, interpretability (motif-based), and stability, treating their relative weighting as a controllable parameter. Additionally, they leverage an input motif library of standard domain motifs to determine the relative importance of those motifs in generating explanations and use this to further enhance explanation quality, while also analyzing tradeoff surfaces between metrics.
AI.result: On real-world datasets including MUTAG, BA-2Motif, BAMultiShapes, and PROTEINS, the method produces higher-fidelity explanations than a state-of-the-art baseline on MUTAG and PROTEINS across all evaluated budgets, and on BA-2Motif at larger budgets, while being faster under small explanation budgets. The method also reveals motif importance from a motif library and improves explanation quality, with metric tradeoffs dependent on the motif library's nature.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing explanations across fidelity, interpretability, and stability with controllable weighting yields more useful GNN explanations, and motif-library-guided importance estimation can further improve output quality, with metric relationships governed by induced tradeoff surfaces.
