title: SocialHumanoid: Towards Expressive Humanoid Behavior via One-Step Co-Speech Motion Generation
summary: Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to serve as embodied social agents that communicate naturally with humans through face-to-face interaction. During such communication, humanoid robots require body behaviors that are synchronized with speech, affectively expressive, and suitable for real-time execution. However, existing co-speech methods are primarily developed for digital humans and lack joint support for affective control and low-latency continuous generation on physical embodiments. To bridge this gap, we present SocialHumanoid, a system for expressive humanoid behavior via one-step co-speech motion generation. Given response speech and a specified affective condition, SocialHumanoid generates each full-body motion window in a single forward pass and connects successive windows through motion-history conditioning. The generated human motion is further converted online into embodiment-compatible robot references and tracked by a whole-body controller for physical execution. To provide explicit supervision for affective body expression, we further introduce AffectMoCap, a 4-hour dataset captured from two professional actors, containing synchronized speech, body motion, fine-grained hand motion, and emotion annotations. On BEAT2, SocialHumanoid achieves the best FGD among the compared generation methods, competitive speech-motion synchrony, and approximately $6\times$ faster inference than GestureLSM under the same protocol. Perceptual evaluations further show that training with AffectMoCap improves affect recognition from generated body motion, while real-robot experiments demonstrate continuous affect-conditioned behavior and stable long-horizon execution. Our project page is https://rex0191.github.io/SocialHumanoid/.

AI.tldr: SocialHumanoid is a one-step co-speech motion generation system that produces affectively expressive, real-time whole-body behavior for humanoid robots, supported by a new 4-hour affective mocap dataset (AffectMoCap).
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to act as embodied social agents communicating face-to-face, requiring body behaviors synchronized with speech, affectively expressive, and executable in real time. Existing co-speech methods target digital humans and lack joint support for affective control and low-latency continuous generation on physical embodiments.
AI.method: Given response speech and a specified affective condition, SocialHumanoid generates each full-body motion window in a single forward pass (one-step generation) and connects successive windows via motion-history conditioning. Generated human motion is converted online into embodiment-compatible robot references and tracked by a whole-body controller for physical execution. To supervise affective body expression, the authors introduce AffectMoCap, a 4-hour dataset from two professional actors with synchronized speech, body motion, fine-grained hand motion, and emotion annotations.
AI.result: On BEAT2, SocialHumanoid achieves the best FGD among compared generation methods, competitive speech-motion synchrony, and roughly 6x faster inference than GestureLSM under the same protocol. Perceptual evaluations show training with AffectMoCap improves affect recognition from generated body motion. Real-robot experiments demonstrate continuous affect-conditioned behavior and stable long-horizon execution.
AI.conclusion: SocialHumanoid bridges the gap between co-speech motion generation for digital humans and affective, low-latency physical humanoid behavior, with a new affective mocap dataset and validated real-robot performance.

title: ForkLeft: Entropy-First Rollouts for Prefix-Aligned Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Distillation
summary: Autoregressive Next-Token Prediction (NTP) has enabled strong reasoning capabilities in language models, while Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer flexible token orders and parallel generation. We ask whether DLMs can acquire NTP-style reasoning through distillation without giving up their native generation process. Direct distillation, however, faces a fundamental mismatch: an autoregressive teacher predicts from a left prefix, whereas a DLM can condition on tokens on both sides. We introduce ForkLeft, a distillation framework that resolves this mismatch by separating the student's rollout from teacher supervision. During training, the student first performs entropy-first rollouts that commit uncertain positions and expose potential forks. We then fix the resulting student prefix and distill an NTP teacher under the same context, with answer correctness determining the supervision source. At inference, the student returns to its native confidence-first parallel decoding. With Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, ForkLeft improves Efficient-DLM-4B on all ten benchmarks, raising MATH500 from 72.60% to 79.60% and consistently outperforming three alternative designs. The gains scale with teacher strength and generalize to SDAR-4B with only $500$ updates. At matched scale, the distilled 4B and 8B students exceed the published SDAR-Chat and OPDLM models on seven benchmarks, showing that DLMs can learn NTP-style reasoning without sacrificing native parallel generation. Code and datasets will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: ForkLeft is a distillation framework that lets Diffusion Language Models acquire NTP-style reasoning from an autoregressive teacher without abandoning their native parallel decoding, by decoupling student rollouts from teacher supervision.
AI.motivation: DLMs offer flexible token orders and parallel generation but lack the strong reasoning of autoregressive NTP models. A key question is whether DLMs can inherit NTP-style reasoning via distillation without giving up native generation. Direct distillation fails due to a fundamental mismatch: the AR teacher predicts from a left prefix, while a DLM can condition on tokens on both sides.
AI.method: ForkLeft separates the student's rollout from teacher supervision. During training, the student performs entropy-first rollouts that commit uncertain positions and expose potential forks; the resulting student prefix is then fixed and an NTP teacher is distilled under the same context, with answer correctness selecting the supervision source. At inference, the student reverts to its native confidence-first parallel decoding.
AI.result: Using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base as teacher, ForkLeft improves Efficient-DLM-4B on all ten benchmarks, raising MATH500 from 72.60% to 79.60%, and consistently outperforms three alternative designs. Gains scale with teacher strength and transfer to SDAR-4B with only 500 updates. At matched scale, distilled 4B and 8B students surpass published SDAR-Chat and OPDLM on seven benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DLMs can learn NTP-style reasoning through distillation while retaining native parallel generation, resolving the AR-prefix vs. bidirectional-context mismatch and yielding consistent, scalable improvements.

title: Traceable Human-to-Humanoid Sign Language Benchmarking
summary: Sign data collection is costly, and teleoperation scales poorly, motivating reuse of large video corpora. Humanoid signing requires converting video-derived human motion into robot trajectories while preserving linguistic motion cues. Errors from fitting, human-motion repair, retargeting, robot geometry repair, and control are hard to separate from the final trajectory alone. We introduce HumanoidCSL-20K, a dataset and benchmark of 20,648 sentence-level Chinese Sign Language sequences, each with four aligned versions: the source, the repaired human motion, the direct robot reference, and the geometry-repaired robot reference. Observation-supported local human-motion repair, full-robot geometry repair, and cross-representation provenance make each transformation traceable. Paired evaluations measure human-motion continuity and content preservation, robot-reference feasibility, and physical execution. A sign-specific kinematic-reference protocol scores handshape, location, palm orientation, and inter-hand relation over the full planned motion. Full-corpus results show fewer abnormal arm / hand steps and less inter-hand and hand-body penetration after repair. Control experiments separate reference learnability from curriculum effects, while component scores expose remaining execution errors.

AI.tldr: HumanoidCSL-20K is introduced as a dataset and benchmark of 20,648 sentence-level Chinese Sign Language sequences, each with four aligned versions (source, repaired human motion, direct robot reference, geometry-repaired robot reference) to trace and evaluate the video-to-humanoid pipeline.
AI.motivation: Sign data collection is costly and teleoperation scales poorly, motivating reuse of large video corpora. Converting video-derived human motion into humanoid robot trajectories must preserve linguistic motion cues, but errors from fitting, human-motion repair, retargeting, robot geometry repair, and control are hard to disentangle from the final trajectory alone.
AI.method: The work builds a four-stage aligned representation with observation-supported local human-motion repair, full-robot geometry repair, and cross-representation provenance for traceability. Paired evaluations assess human-motion continuity and content preservation, robot-reference feasibility, and physical execution. A sign-specific kinematic-reference protocol scores handshape, location, palm orientation, and inter-hand relation across the full planned motion, plus control experiments separating reference learnability from curriculum effects.
AI.result: Full-corpus results show fewer abnormal arm/hand steps and reduced inter-hand and hand-body penetration after repair. Component scores expose remaining execution errors.
AI.conclusion: HumanoidCSL-20K enables traceable, stage-wise benchmarking of the video-to-humanoid signing pipeline, separating error sources and providing sign-specific kinematic evaluation for physical execution.

title: PULSE: Identifying Demonstration-Utility Features with Sparse Autoencoders
summary: In-context learning is highly sensitive to demonstration choice, yet most methods select demonstrations using external query-demonstration similarity. Such criteria can miss model-specific signals: Similar demonstrations may activate different internal features and downstream behaviors. We introduce PULSE (Paired Utility Localization over Sparse Encodings), an SAE-based framework for identifying model-internal features associated with demonstration utility and using them for demonstration selection. Using a small labeled discovery set, PULSE samples candidate demonstration sets, measures their zero-shot-relative utility under the target model, and scores SAE features by how their activation differences align with utility differences. The top positive and negative coordinates form a sparse utility-localization vector. We use this vector in two complementary ways: as a signed score for controlled complete-set ranking, and as PULSE-Retriever, which converts its magnitude into a feature-relevance mask for scalable pool-scale retrieval. Across classification, generation, and reasoning benchmarks, PULSE-Retriever improves over the strongest baseline by 2-3 accuracy points, 0.6-0.9 BLEU-4, and 3.2 exact-match points, respectively, while controlled ranking validates the identified features encode a predictive set-level utility signal. Feature inspection and cross-dataset experiments suggest that the identified features capture task-relevant, dataset-conditioned patterns, yet retain utility signals that partially transfer across datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/aohenuo/PULSE.

AI.tldr: PULSE is an SAE-based framework that identifies model-internal features aligned with in-context demonstration utility and uses them for demonstration selection, outperforming baselines across classification, generation, and reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Most demonstration selection methods for in-context learning rely on external query-demonstration similarity, which can miss model-specific signals: similar demonstrations may activate different internal features and downstream behaviors.
AI.method: PULSE (Paired Utility Localization over Sparse Encodings) uses a small labeled discovery set to sample candidate demonstration sets, measures their zero-shot-relative utility under the target model, and scores SAE features by alignment of activation differences with utility differences. Top positive and negative coordinates form a sparse utility-localization vector, used both as a signed score for controlled complete-set ranking and as PULSE-Retriever, which converts magnitude into a feature-relevance mask for scalable pool-scale retrieval.
AI.result: PULSE-Retriever improves over the strongest baseline by 2-3 accuracy points (classification), 0.6-0.9 BLEU-4 (generation), and 3.2 exact-match points (reasoning). Controlled ranking validates that identified features encode a predictive set-level utility signal. Feature inspection and cross-dataset experiments suggest identified features capture task-relevant, dataset-conditioned patterns while retaining partially transferable utility signals.
AI.conclusion: Model-internal, SAE-derived utility features provide an effective alternative to external similarity for demonstration selection, delivering consistent gains and revealing partially transferable, dataset-conditioned utility signals.

title: Recursive Harness Distillation across Agents for Robot Manipulation
summary: A central goal in robotics is to enable manipulation across changing tasks and environments. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide broad manipulation capabilities but can struggle when execution requires diagnosing failures and adapting behavior. Strong agents can discover effective interventions through interaction with these policies. We propose Recursive Harness Distillation to accumulate this experience as reusable guidance across agents. A strong agent distills its experience into a playbook for a light agent, then recursively refines the playbook using the light agent's execution feedback. The resulting playbook enables agents to reuse accumulated intervention knowledge in new task instances without updating model parameters. In real-world manipulation, the harness improves success from 37.3% to 64.0%. On SimplerEnv Bridge, the light agent with the playbook achieves 66.7% success, compared with 41.7% for the GR00T-only baseline, and outperforms the strong agent without a playbook. The same playbook also benefits the strong agent, which reaches 79.2% success. These results demonstrate the feasibility of harness distillation for robotics: intervention experience can be accumulated, refined through execution, and reused across agents to improve manipulation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Recursive Harness Distillation, where a strong agent distills its failure-diagnosis and intervention experience into a reusable "playbook" for a light agent, then recursively refines it using the light agent's execution feedback—improving real-world manipulation success from 37.3% to 64.0% and SimplerEnv Bridge success from 41.7% to 66.7%.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer broad manipulation capabilities but struggle when tasks require diagnosing execution failures and adapting behavior. The goal is to enable effective manipulation across changing tasks and environments without updating model parameters.
AI.method: Recursive Harness Distillation: a strong agent distills its intervention experience into a playbook for a light agent, which is then recursively refined using the light agent's execution feedback. The resulting playbook lets agents reuse accumulated intervention knowledge on new task instances without parameter updates.
AI.result: Real-world manipulation success improved from 37.3% to 64.0%. On SimplerEnv Bridge, the light agent with the playbook reached 66.7% success vs. 41.7% for the GR00T-only baseline, outperforming even the strong agent without a playbook. The same playbook also benefits the strong agent, reaching 79.2% success.
AI.conclusion: Harness distillation is feasible for robotics: intervention experience can be accumulated, refined through execution, and reused across agents to improve manipulation performance.

title: VPEvolve: A Self-Evolving Virtual Process Engineer for Computational Lithography
summary: Optical proximity correction (OPC) recipes grow as engineers add local rules to repair newly discovered lithography hotspots. Each correction can interact with existing rules, while lessons from commercial-tool trials remain scattered across code and logs. \system combines a Virtual Process Engineer (VPE) harness with a Skill Bank of measured engineering experience. The harness equips a frozen language model with process manuals, layout analysis, recipe editing, and commercial-tool evaluation. The actor proposes changes to the global parameters, local targeted rules, or diagnostic trials. After each evaluation, an LLM reflector and curator turn the measured response into evidence-linked judgments. The actor retrieves them before its next trial. Feasible improvements update the retained recipe; every measured trial informs the Skill Bank that guides the next edit. The model weights remain fixed. On a FreePDK45-derived benchmark with ten commercial-tool evaluations per case, \system reduces the mean per-case maximum edge placement error from 18.294 to 5.361 nm on Poly and from 22.052 to 15.692 nm on Metal1. Every final recipe satisfies the predefined quality constraints and improves the maximum error by at least 0.1 nm.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a system combining a Virtual Process Engineer harness with a Skill Bank of measured engineering experience to iteratively improve OPC recipes for lithography using a frozen language model, achieving significant error reductions on a FreePDK45-derived benchmark.
AI.motivation: OPC recipes grow increasingly complex as engineers add local rules to fix newly discovered lithography hotspots. Each new correction can interact with existing rules, and lessons learned from commercial-tool trials remain scattered across code and logs, making systematic recipe improvement difficult.
AI.method: The system combines a Virtual Process Engineer (VPE) harness with a Skill Bank of measured engineering experience. The harness equips a frozen language model with process manuals, layout analysis, recipe editing, and commercial-tool evaluation. The actor proposes changes to global parameters, local targeted rules, or diagnostic trials. After each evaluation, an LLM reflector and curator convert the measured response into evidence-linked judgments, which the actor retrieves before its next trial. Feasible improvements update the retained recipe, and every measured trial informs the Skill Bank guiding the next edit, while model weights remain fixed.
AI.result: On a FreePDK45-derived benchmark with ten commercial-tool evaluations per case, the system reduces the mean per-case maximum edge placement error from 18.294 to 5.361 nm on Poly and from 22.052 to 15.692 nm on Metal1. Every final recipe satisfies predefined quality constraints and improves the maximum error by at least 0.1 nm.
AI.conclusion: The proposed experience-driven, frozen-model approach effectively optimizes OPC recipes, delivering substantial edge placement error reductions while consistently meeting quality constraints on the evaluated benchmark.

title: Large Language Models for Model-Based Robot Design
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can contribute useful engineering knowledge to robot design, but directly generated designs may rely on implicit assumptions and provide no guarantees of feasibility or optimality. These assumptions are critical because different reasonable modeling choices can materially change which designs are predicted to be feasible or optimal. We therefore present a framework that uses LLMs to construct explicit engineering models containing physical relationships, compatibility constraints, and objectives, allowing these modeling choices to be inspected and revised before formal optimization. The model can then be updated with additional engineering, manufacturer, or system-specific information before formal multi-objective optimization provides feasibility and Pareto-optimality guarantees with respect to the finalized model and specified design space. We evaluate the framework on quadcopter and line-following robot component-selection problems. Across 30 direct LLM design trials, none could be verified as feasible under the corresponding finalized model. Comparisons with an independently developed expert model and successive stages of model refinement further showed that changes in modeling assumptions substantially altered the predicted feasible and Pareto-optimal design sets. Together, these results show that using LLMs to construct explicit engineering models makes the underlying design choices available for inspection and revision before those assumptions determine the optimized designs. Explicit modeling therefore provides an interface for combining LLM-generated engineering knowledge, system-specific information, and formal design optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework where LLMs construct explicit engineering models (physics, compatibility constraints, objectives) that can be inspected and revised, then solved via multi-objective optimization to guarantee feasibility and Pareto-optimality; validation on quadcopter and line-following robot design shows direct LLM designs failed verification and modeling assumptions strongly affected optimized design sets.
AI.motivation: Directly LLM-generated robot designs rely on implicit assumptions and offer no feasibility or optimality guarantees; because different reasonable modeling choices materially change which designs appear feasible or optimal, these hidden assumptions must be made explicit before optimization.
AI.method: A framework in which LLMs build explicit engineering models capturing physical relationships, compatibility constraints, and objectives; these models are inspectable and revisable, can be augmented with engineering, manufacturer, or system-specific information, and are then solved by formal multi-objective optimization to yield feasibility and Pareto-optimality guarantees relative to the finalized model and specified design space.
AI.result: Evaluated on quadcopter and line-following robot component-selection problems: across 30 direct LLM design trials, none was verifiable as feasible under the finalized model; comparison with an independently developed expert model and successive refinement stages showed modeling-assumption changes substantially altered predicted feasible and Pareto-optimal design sets.
AI.conclusion: Using LLMs to construct explicit engineering models exposes underlying design choices for inspection and revision before assumptions determine optimized designs, providing an interface that combines LLM-generated engineering knowledge, system-specific information, and formal design optimization.

title: From Outcomes to Strategies: Learning Strategy Utility for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has substantially improved mathematical reasoning. However, terminal correctness alone provides limited insight into the quality of high-level strategies, such as theorem selection and subgoal decomposition, when considered separately from their subsequent execution. This paper studies strategy utility, which is defined as the likelihood that a strategy supports a correct downstream solution under a given executor. We introduce SURE, a framework for learning and leveraging relative strategy utility. In this framework, high-level strategies are separated from their detailed reasoning. Based on the pairwise preferences constructed from strategy-conditioned rollouts and teacher-generated contrasts, a Strategy Reward Model is learned to estimate relative strategy utility. During reinforcement learning, the frozen reward model reads only the extracted strategy, whose score is combined with the correctness and format rewards in a sequence-level GRPO objective. Compared with outcome-and-format GRPO baselines, experiments show that SURE improves average pass@1 by 1.87%, 2.64%, and 2.93% across three policy backbones. Our method also achieves competitive or better accuracy than stronger reward baselines while requiring substantially lower GRPO-stage compute.

AI.tldr: SURE learns a Strategy Reward Model from pairwise preferences to estimate relative strategy utility, then uses it as an additional reward in sequence-level GRPO, improving pass@1 by 1.87–2.93% across three backbones with lower compute than stronger reward baselines.
AI.motivation: RL with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning, but terminal correctness alone cannot assess high-level strategy quality (theorem selection, subgoal decomposition) separately from execution. The paper therefore targets strategy utility, the likelihood a strategy supports a correct downstream solution under a given executor.
AI.method: High-level strategies are extracted and separated from detailed reasoning. Pairwise preferences are built from strategy-conditioned rollouts and teacher-generated contrasts, and a Strategy Reward Model is trained to estimate relative strategy utility. During RL, the frozen reward model scores only the extracted strategy; this score is combined with correctness and format rewards in a sequence-level GRPO objective.
AI.result: Average pass@1 improves by 1.87%, 2.64%, and 2.93% over outcome-and-format GRPO baselines across three policy backbones. SURE also matches or exceeds stronger reward baselines while requiring substantially lower GRPO-stage compute.
AI.conclusion: Rewarding relative strategy utility, decoupled from execution, is an effective and compute-efficient complement to outcome-based verifiable rewards for mathematical reasoning.

title: VIDEAS: Distilling Explicit Action Semantics from Demonstration Videos for World Models via Prior-Guided Simulation
summary: World models learn internal representations of environment dynamics to predict future states, enabling agents to optimize action plans without physical interactions. However, developing world models that genuinely internalize underlying causal physical laws to explicitly reason about action preconditions and subsequent state transitions remains an open challenge. In this paper, we propose VIDEAS, a data distillation framework that transforms continuous physical dynamics from operational videos into explicit action semantics for foundation models. Specifically, it deconstructs visual demonstrations into discrete action trajectories and utilizes advanced vision-language models (VLMs) to extract structured knowledge encapsulating action preconditions and effects. To ensure physical consistency, we introduce a prior-guided trajectory simulation mechanism grounded within a text-based environment to rigorously validate the extracted knowledge. Notably, we incorporate negative trajectories to enrich knowledge completeness and enhance data diversity to mitigate cognitive bias. Furthermore, we present VIDEAS-WM, an 8B/9B-parameter suite of language-based world models trained on 34K high-quality samples derived from AgiBot-World dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VIDEAS-WM establishes state-of-the-art performance in high-level embodied action semantic reasoning, exhibiting profound physical understanding and robust generalization across unseen scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VIDEAS, a data distillation framework that converts continuous physical dynamics from operational videos into explicit action semantics (preconditions and effects) for foundation models, and trains VIDEAS-WM, an 8B/9B language-based world model suite achieving SOTA in embodied action semantic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing world models predict future states but often fail to genuinely internalize underlying causal physical laws, i.e., they cannot explicitly reason about action preconditions and subsequent state transitions. Building such causally-grounded world models remains an open challenge.
AI.method: VIDEAS deconstructs visual demonstrations into discrete action trajectories and uses advanced VLMs to extract structured knowledge encoding action preconditions and effects. A prior-guided trajectory simulation mechanism in a text-based environment validates physical consistency. Negative trajectories are incorporated to enrich knowledge completeness, and data diversity is enhanced to mitigate cognitive bias. The distilled data trains VIDEAS-WM, an 8B/9B-parameter language-based world model suite, on 34K high-quality samples from the AgiBot-World dataset.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show VIDEAS-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in high-level embodied action semantic reasoning, with profound physical understanding and robust generalization to unseen scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Distilling explicit action semantics from videos via a validation-grounded data pipeline yields language-based world models with strong causal physical reasoning and generalization, offering a scalable path toward embodied world models that reason about preconditions and state transitions.

title: Separating Diagnosis from Disease Representation: Dual-View EEG Learning with Neural-Dynamics-Guided Deformation
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based closed-loop neuromodulation calls for a subject-specific structured state, as opposed to a single disease probability, specifying which brain regions are deviant, at which frequencies, and at which lags. Sensor-space models keep the strongest diagnostic evidence without anatomy, source-space models give anatomy at a loss of predictive signal, and post-hoc attributions stay outside the prediction. We separate the two instead of forcing them into one representation, and propose DMD-EEG (Dual-view Multiscale Deformation for EEG), which keeps a fixed scalp spectral expert for diagnosis and models the source-space disease-related representation as a low-rank, sparse, iterative deformation of a healthy neural-dynamics prior in a $46$-region-of-interest (ROI) $\times$ $5$-frequency $\times$ $4$-lag (autocorrelation-timescale) space. The two experts meet only at a fixed decision level, so the source state is architecturally separate from the scalp expert. Across major depressive disorder (MDD), first-episode psychosis (FEP), and Parkinson's disease (PD), decision-level fusion matches the strongest single expert on MDD and FEP and exceeds the source branch on PD. On FEP the source expert is the strongest branch, the task where the deformation contributes most. The source state is an explicit ROI-frequency-lag attribution defined in a shared source coordinate system across montages, which we treat as an anatomically-coordinated predictive representation whose coordinates are directly readable and hypothesis-generating. The highest-saliency coordinates align with established disease circuitry (fronto-limbic-temporal regions in MDD, motor-cortex beta in PD), and the MDD state transfers by rank to an unseen cohort recorded with a different montage.

AI.tldr: DMD-EEG is a dual-view, decision-level-fusion framework that pairs a fixed scalp spectral diagnostic expert with a distinct source-space expert modeling disease-related neural dynamics as a low-rank, sparse, iterative deformation of a healthy prior over a 46-ROI x 5-frequency x 4-lag space, yielding an explicit, anatomically readable attribution.
AI.motivation: EEG-based closed-loop neuromodulation needs a subject-specific structured state rather than a single disease probability, specifying deviant brain regions, frequencies, and lags. However, existing approaches force an unfit compromise: sensor-space models retain predictive signal but lack anatomy, source-space models provide anatomy but lose predictive signal, and post-hoc attributions remain outside the prediction.
AI.method: The authors separate rather than merge the two representations and propose DMD-EEG (Dual-view Multiscale Deformation for EEG). It keeps a fixed scalp spectral expert for diagnosis and models the source-space disease-related representation as a low-rank, sparse, iterative deformation of a healthy neural-dynamics prior in a 46-ROI x 5-frequency x 4-lag (autocorrelation-timescale) space. The two experts meet only at a fixed decision level, keeping the source state architecturally separate from the scalp expert.
AI.result: Across MDD, FEP, and PD, decision-level fusion matches the strongest single expert on MDD and FEP and exceeds the source branch on PD. On FEP the source expert is the strongest branch, the task where deformation contributes most. The source state is an explicit ROI-frequency-lag attribution in a shared source coordinate system across montages. Highest-saliency coordinates align with established disease circuitry (fronto-limbic-temporal regions in MDD, motor-cortex beta in PD), and the MDD state transfers by rank to an unseen cohort recorded with a different montage.
AI.conclusion: DMD-EEG treats the source state as an anatomically-coordinated predictive representation whose coordinates are directly readable and hypothesis-generating, offering a structured, subject-specific disease state rather than a single probability while preserving diagnostic performance.

title: AMBIT: Anticipatory Multimodal Body Recruitment for Bimanual Tracking on a Humanoid
summary: A humanoid with 5-DoF arms cannot track generic bimanual end-effector trajectories with its arms alone; pelvis and waist motion must be recruited, but which motion, and when, is not uniquely determined. On a Unitree R1 in fixed double support, the set of dynamically valid recruitment strategies (pelvis pose and waist trajectories) for a task is a diverse continuous manifold, and a deterministic regressor trained on it mode-averages into strategies valid only 35% of the time, against 52% for a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) and 82% for the best of 16 CVAE samples. We introduce AMBIT: the CVAE proposes strategies from a preview of the commanded trajectory, a non-learned selector filters, ranks and verifies them, and a receding-horizon loop commits to one with hysteresis. The committed strategy is the reference of the same whole-body differential-IK QP a reactive tracker runs, which keeps authority over residual error. On 160 held-out episodes that admit a valid strategy, in full MuJoCo dynamics under a torque controller, AMBIT reaches 85% success at a 3 cm/15 deg tolerance against 74% for the tracker (disjoint confidence intervals) and recruits the body before the arms saturate in 48% of episodes against 35%. Because diversity is preserved, constraints unknown at training time are enforced by selection alone: under five zero-shot shifts AMBIT beats the warm-started tracker on every shift and matches a test-time re-optimisation baseline 17x more expensive. On a Unitree G1, with hyperparameters unchanged, the protocol reproduces the structure of the valid set and widens the gap over the tracker to 0.85 against 0.53. Five selected strategies execute on the externally supported physical R1, distinct in pelvis excursion and tracking the planned end-effector motion to a median of 11 mm by encoder forward kinematics, which establishes kinematic realisability, not balance.

AI.tldr: AMBIT uses a CVAE to propose diverse dynamically valid pelvis/waist recruitment strategies for bimanual trajectory tracking on 5-DoF-arm humanoids, with a non-learned selector and receding-horizon commitment feeding a whole-body differential-IK QP, achieving 85% success on R1 versus 74% for a reactive tracker.
AI.motivation: Humanoids with 5-DoF arms cannot track generic bimanual end-effector trajectories using arms alone, so pelvis and waist motion must be recruited, but which motion and when is not uniquely determined. On a Unitree R1 in fixed double support, the set of dynamically valid recruitment strategies forms a diverse continuous manifold, and deterministic regressors trained on it mode-average into strategies valid only 35% of the time, motivating a generative approach that preserves diversity.
AI.method: AMBIT: a CVAE proposes recruitment strategies from a preview of the commanded trajectory; a non-learned selector filters, ranks, and verifies them; a receding-horizon loop commits to one strategy with hysteresis. The committed strategy serves as the reference for the same whole-body differential-IK QP that a reactive tracker runs, which retains authority over residual error.
AI.result: On 160 held-out episodes admitting a valid strategy, in full MuJoCo dynamics under a torque controller, AMBIT reaches 85% success at 3 cm/15 deg tolerance versus 74% for the tracker (disjoint confidence intervals), and recruits the body before arm saturation in 48% of episodes versus 35%. Under five zero-shot shifts AMBIT beats the warm-started tracker on every shift and matches a test-time re-optimisation baseline 17x more expensive. On a Unitree G1 with unchanged hyperparameters, the protocol reproduces the valid-set structure and widens the gap to 0.85 versus 0.53. Five selected strategies execute on the externally supported physical R1, distinct in pelvis excursion and tracking planned end-effector motion to a median of 11 mm by encoder forward kinematics.
AI.conclusion: Preserving strategy diversity lets constraints unknown at training time be enforced by selection alone, yielding robust zero-shot generalisation and reduced reliance on expensive test-time re-optimisation. Physical R1 results establish kinematic realisability of the selected strategies, though not balance.

title: Towards Scalable Data Diversification for Language Model Pretraining via Leverage Score Sampling
summary: Data selection for language model pretraining faces a fundamental tension between quality and diversity. While quality filtering is empirically effective, it often induces diversity collapse: by favoring texts similar to high-quality reference corpora (e.g., educational or QA-style data), it systematically excludes valuable data from underrepresented domains. In contrast, diversified selection preserves domain balance and encourages robust downstream performance, yet existing methods either focus on coverage-oriented objectives that indirectly enhance diversity, or directly optimize for diversity via costly covariance matrix recomputation that limits scalability. To address these issues, we introduce \textbf{Leverage Score Sampling (Lev)}, which iteratively selects samples that maximally expand the determinantal volume of the embedded data via leverage scores, a computationally efficient criterion that eliminates matrix recomputation and enables scalable selection. Empirically, Lev delivers up to $72\times$ speedup and improves dataset diversity, measured by the Vendi score, by $9.2\%$ over the strong diversification baseline \textbf{DiSF}. On CommonCrawl (CC) web data selection, Lev improves accuracy across seven downstream tasks by up to $1.31\%$ over existing baselines. For domains where robust quality criteria are inherently difficult to define (e.g., code), Lev serves as an effective unsupervised curation alternative: on StarCoderData, the selected subset reduces bits-per-byte by $3.08\%$ over DiSF. Notably, we uncover a cross-domain collapse of quality filtering: CC data filtered by DCLM-fastText fail to retain sufficient code-related content, yielding inferior code performance relative to Lev-selected data. These findings advocate for integrating diversity-aware practices into quality filtering for more effective data curation in language model pretraining.

AI.tldr: Lev is a scalable data selection method using leverage score sampling that expands the determinantal volume of embedded data, achieving up to 72x speedup, 9.2% higher Vendi diversity over DiSF, and improved downstream accuracy and code BPB by selecting diverse, high-value pretraining data.
AI.motivation: Quality filtering in language model pretraining improves data quality but causes diversity collapse by biasing toward high-quality reference corpora and excluding underrepresented domains. Existing diversification methods either only indirectly enhance diversity through coverage objectives or are unscalable due to costly covariance matrix recomputation.
AI.method: The authors propose Leverage Score Sampling (Lev), which iteratively selects samples that maximally expand the determinantal volume of the embedded data using leverage scores. This criterion is computationally efficient, avoids matrix recomputation, and enables scalable diversity-aware selection.
AI.result: Lev achieves up to 72x speedup and improves Vendi score diversity by 9.2% over DiSF. On CommonCrawl, it improves accuracy across seven downstream tasks by up to 1.31%. On StarCoderData, it reduces bits-per-byte by 3.08% versus DiSF. DCLM-fastText-filtered CC data fails to retain sufficient code content, yielding inferior code performance versus Lev.
AI.conclusion: Diversity-aware selection via Lev is efficient, scalable, and effective, and can serve as an unsupervised curation alternative where quality criteria are hard to define. The cross-domain collapse of quality filtering shows that diversity-aware practices should be integrated into quality filtering for better pretraining data curation.

title: AI-Driven Collaborative Assembly Line Inspection: System Integration and Deployment Challenges
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the 22nd International Conference on Mobile Web and Intelligent Information Systems (MobiWIS 2026)
summary: Manual visual inspection on assembly lines is a persistent manufacturing bottleneck: operator fatigue over extended shifts lowers defect-detection rates. This paper presents the design, integration, and field deployment of an AI-assisted collaborative inspection cell at the Silverline kitchen-appliance factory, developed within the AI-PRISM project. The cell couples a Universal Robots UR 10e cobot carrying a machine-vision defect-detection pipeline with a Comau Racer-5 cobot for functional tests, coordinated through ROS 2 Humble on an Ubuntu 22.04 LTS server. Multi-modal data (Basler camera imagery, TIA microphone acoustics, and SPS electrical-safety measurements) are logged locally and visualised in real time with Grafana. We report the practical deployment challenges (close-proximity safety, AI robustness under glare and reflections, ROS 2 namespace collisions across two cobots, and operating-system and dependency issues) together with the engineering solutions adopted, and structure the integration through a four-level Human-Robot Interaction analysis. The deployed cell cuts per-unit quality-check time from 82 s to 61 s (about 25%), raises final-control resource efficiency from 0.75 to 0.88, reduces operator visual-inspection viewing time by 82%, and significantly lowers operator mental demand (p = 0.005, NASA-TLX).

AI.tldr: This paper presents the design, integration, and field deployment of an AI-assisted collaborative inspection cell at the Silverline kitchen-appliance factory within the AI-PRISM project, pairing a UR 10e cobot with a machine-vision defect-detection pipeline and a Comau Racer-5 cobot for functional tests, coordinated via ROS 2 Humble, and reports both deployment challenges and quantitative performance gains.
AI.motivation: Manual visual inspection on assembly lines is a persistent manufacturing bottleneck: operator fatigue over extended shifts lowers defect-detection rates, motivating an AI-assisted collaborative solution to improve quality-check throughput and reduce operator burden.
AI.method: The cell couples a Universal Robots UR 10e cobot carrying a machine-vision defect-detection pipeline with a Comau Racer-5 cobot for functional tests, coordinated through ROS 2 Humble on an Ubuntu 22.04 LTS server. Multi-modal data (Basler camera imagery, TIA microphone acoustics, and SPS electrical-safety measurements) are logged locally and visualised in real time with Grafana. The integration is structured through a four-level Human-Robot Interaction analysis.
AI.result: The deployed cell cuts per-unit quality-check time from 82 s to 61 s (about 25%), raises final-control resource efficiency from 0.75 to 0.88, reduces operator visual-inspection viewing time by 82%, and significantly lowers operator mental demand (p = 0.005, NASA-TLX).
AI.conclusion: The paper reports practical deployment challenges (close-proximity safety, AI robustness under glare and reflections, ROS 2 namespace collisions across two cobots, and operating-system and dependency issues) together with the engineering solutions adopted, demonstrating that the AI-assisted collaborative inspection cell delivers measurable efficiency and ergonomic benefits in a real factory setting.

title: When Helpful Text Hurts: Option-Redirecting Bias in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026 (ACM MM 2026). 25 pages, 16 figures. This arXiv version includes supplementary material
summary: In tri-modal visual question answering (VQA), auxiliary text is commonly used to complement visual and textual inputs, yet its reliability is often uncontrolled. While prior work studies modality conflicts in general, it remains unclear how different types of unreliable auxiliary text affect answer selection under fixed image-question-option contexts. In this work, we show that the most harmful auxiliary text is not necessarily the most factually incorrect, but the one that aligns with the question while contradicting the image and favoring a specific distractor, leading to systematic redirection of model predictions. To isolate this effect, we introduce the Textual Reliability Ladder, a controlled diagnostic protocol that decomposes auxiliary text along three axes: image consistency, question relevance, and option support. Across multiple datasets (ScienceQA, VCR, A-OKVQA, Causal-VidQA) and recent VLMs, we find that such distractor-supporting text induces the largest accuracy drops (up to 53.1%) and concentrates errors on specific incorrect options. To mitigate this failure mode, we propose a training-free inference-time intervention that explicitly counteracts this redirection effect via noise-stability steering and dynamic grounding, reducing redirected errors while largely preserving performance under faithful text. Our results highlight that auxiliary-text reliability must be understood at the decision level, rather than solely through factual correctness, and provide a practical pathway toward more robust tri-modal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the most harmful unreliable auxiliary text in tri-modal VQA is not the most factually incorrect one, but text that supports a distractor while aligning with the question and contradicting the image. It introduces the Textual Reliability Ladder diagnostic protocol to isolate this effect and proposes a training-free inference-time intervention to mitigate it.
AI.motivation: In tri-modal VQA, auxiliary text is commonly used to complement visual and textual inputs, but its reliability is often uncontrolled. While prior work studies modality conflicts in general, it remains unclear how different types of unreliable auxiliary text affect answer selection under fixed image-question-option contexts.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Textual Reliability Ladder, a controlled diagnostic protocol that decomposes auxiliary text along three axes: image consistency, question relevance, and option support. They evaluate across multiple datasets (ScienceQA, VCR, A-OKVQA, Causal-VidQA) and recent VLMs. To mitigate the identified failure mode, they propose a training-free inference-time intervention that counteracts the redirection effect via noise-stability steering and dynamic grounding.
AI.result: Distractor-supporting text induces the largest accuracy drops (up to 53.1%) and concentrates errors on specific incorrect options. The proposed training-free intervention reduces redirected errors while largely preserving performance under faithful text.
AI.conclusion: Auxiliary-text reliability must be understood at the decision level rather than solely through factual correctness. The work provides a practical pathway toward more robust tri-modal reasoning.

title: A Disk-Shaped Magnetoelastic Torque Sensor for Robotic Joints Using Permanent Magnetization
summary: Direct torque sensing is a growing need in the robotics community to enable precise control and interactions where torque estimation from motor current is not sufficient. This paper presents a novel disk-shaped magnetoelastic torque sensor with a compact axial envelope of about 1 cm, suitable for integration in robotic joints. A four-magnetometer architecture is used to measure the field modulated by the stress affecting a narrow magnetized region while rejecting the effects of parasitic cross forces. A custom-designed magnetic shield enhances the torque sensitivity while reducing the external stray fields by a factor 7x. The device measures the torque with an accuracy of 1.34 %FS relative to the 50 Nm full scale (FS). The paper details the development of the sensor through the mechanical design, the magnetization procedure, and the experimental validation. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed sensor for robotic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compact disk-shaped magnetoelastic torque sensor (~1 cm axial envelope) for robotic joints, using a four-magnetometer architecture and a custom magnetic shield to reject cross forces and stray fields, achieving 1.34 %FS accuracy over a 50 Nm range.
AI.motivation: The robotics community increasingly requires direct torque sensing for precise control and interaction, because torque estimation from motor current is often insufficient.
AI.method: A disk-shaped magnetoelastic torque sensor with a compact axial envelope of about 1 cm was developed. A four-magnetometer architecture measures the field modulated by stress in a narrow magnetized region while rejecting parasitic cross forces. A custom-designed magnetic shield enhances torque sensitivity and reduces external stray fields by a factor of 7. The development covers mechanical design, magnetization procedure, and experimental validation.
AI.result: The device measures torque with an accuracy of 1.34 %FS relative to a 50 Nm full scale. The magnetic shield improves sensitivity and attenuates external stray fields by 7x.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed magnetoelastic torque sensor for robotic applications.

title: RepoMAS: Solving Progressively Specified Tasks with Issue-Driven Multi-Agent Systems
summary:
LLM-based multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown strong potential for solving complex tasks, but most assume that task requirements are sufficiently specified before execution. In practice, user requests are often incomplete, and additional requirements may only become clear during reasoning, tool use, or execution. We refer to such problems as progressively specified tasks.
  To systematically study this setting, we introduce ProgSpec, a benchmark that evaluates final outputs against requirements explicitly stated in the initial request and additional requirements supported by the available task evidence. We further propose RepoMAS, an issue-driven multi-agent framework inspired by open-source project management. RepoMAS records newly discovered requirements, conflicts, and failures as structured Issues and uses them to revise the task specification and execution structure during problem solving.
  Across ProgSpec and five existing benchmarks, RepoMAS achieves the best performance. Further analyses show that its issue-driven revision and repository maintenance mechanisms consistently contribute to performance. These results highlight the importance of allowing MASs to revise not only how a task is solved, but also revise their explicit representation of task requirements during execution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ProgSpec, a benchmark for "progressively specified tasks" where user requirements emerge during execution, and RepoMAS, an issue-driven multi-agent framework that records discovered requirements, conflicts, and failures as structured Issues to revise task specifications and execution structure during problem solving.
AI.motivation: Most LLM-based multi-agent systems assume task requirements are sufficiently specified before execution. In reality, user requests are often incomplete, and additional requirements only become clear during reasoning, tool use, or execution. This mismatch between static specifications and dynamic requirement discovery is the gap the paper addresses.
AI.method: The authors introduce ProgSpec, a benchmark evaluating final outputs against both explicitly stated initial requirements and additional requirements supported by available task evidence. They also propose RepoMAS, an issue-driven multi-agent framework inspired by open-source project management: newly discovered requirements, conflicts, and failures are recorded as structured Issues, which are then used to revise the task specification and execution structure during problem solving.
AI.result: RepoMAS achieves the best performance on ProgSpec as well as on five existing benchmarks. Further analyses show that its issue-driven revision and repository maintenance mechanisms consistently contribute to performance gains.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of enabling multi-agent systems to revise not only how a task is solved, but also their explicit representation of task requirements during execution.

title: Steer2Grasp: Inference-Time Embodiment-Aware Steering for Diverse Physically Feasible Grasp Diffusion
summary: Current grasp diffusion models provide rich priors for generation, yet their object-centric approach can violate the kinematic and collision constraints imposed by the embodiment and the environment. Existing embodiment-aware methods primarily perform local corrections around generated grasps through gradient guidance or optimization, making it difficult to recover from fundamentally infeasible modes. We present Steer2Grasp, a training-free, embodiment-agnostic framework for inference-time grasp steering that adapts a frozen Cartesian grasp diffusion model using deployment-specific rewards. Through Feynman-Kac (FK) inspired particle reweighting and resampling, the method reallocates population mass from infeasible to high-reward grasp modes, enabling population-level mode transitions without modifying the pretrained diffusion model or requiring differentiable constraints. The framework enables a unified treatment for single and dual arm grasping through reachability and collision aware rewards, followed by gradient free gripper level local refinement. Across diverse objects, robot embodiments, and constrained environments, our method substantially improves feasible grasp generation while maintaining proximity to the underlying grasp prior.

AI.tldr: Steer2Grasp is a training-free, embodiment-agnostic inference-time framework that adapts a frozen Cartesian grasp diffusion model using deployment-specific rewards via Feynman-Kac particle reweighting and resampling.
AI.motivation: Object-centric grasp diffusion models generate rich priors but can violate kinematic and collision constraints imposed by the embodiment and environment. Existing embodiment-aware methods perform only local corrections around generated grasps via gradient guidance or optimization, making it difficult to recover from fundamentally infeasible modes.
AI.method: The framework performs inference-time grasp steering on a frozen Cartesian grasp diffusion model without training. It uses Feynman-Kac (FK) inspired particle reweighting and resampling to reallocate population mass from infeasible to high-reward grasp modes, enabling population-level mode transitions without modifying the pretrained model or requiring differentiable constraints. A unified reachability- and collision-aware reward handles single and dual arm grasping, followed by gradient-free gripper-level local refinement.
AI.result: Across diverse objects, robot embodiments, and constrained environments, the method substantially improves feasible grasp generation while maintaining proximity to the underlying grasp prior.
AI.conclusion: Steer2Grasp provides a training-free, embodiment-agnostic solution for inference-time grasp steering, achieving population-level mode transitions and improved feasible grasp generation without retraining or differentiable constraints.

title: Beyond Prompt or Skill? Attribution-Guided Optimization of Modular LLM Programs
summary: Large language models can solve increasingly diverse reasoning tasks, yet their performance remains highly sensitive to task prompts, intermediate instructions, and the way reusable problem-solving knowledge is incorporated. Existing optimization methods usually focus on only one part of this design space: they either optimize a monolithic prompt, or separately induce and refine skills from model traces. As a result, they lack a principled mechanism for deciding which component should be updated when failures occur, and they rarely optimize prompts, skills, and skill-use policies in a unified framework. We propose SPARO (Skill, Prompt, And Routing Optimization), a framework that jointly optimizes task instructions, reusable skill blocks, and routing rules. It performs controlled counterfactual evaluations, converts examples' effects into a probabilistic responsibility distribution over prompt, skill, and routing components, samples one component from that distribution, and applies the corresponding targeted mutation. This design moves language-program optimization beyond global prompt rewriting toward structured, reusable, and selectively activated task knowledge. Across five benchmarks and five worker models, SPARO consistently outperforms both prompt-centered and skill-centered optimization baselines. These results suggest that effective language-program optimization depends not only on discovering useful task knowledge, but also on deciding where that knowledge should be stored and when it should be activated.

AI.tldr: SPARO jointly optimizes task instructions, reusable skill blocks, and routing rules via counterfactual evaluation and responsibility-based component selection, outperforming prompt- and skill-centered baselines across five benchmarks and five models.
AI.motivation: LLM performance is highly sensitive to prompts, intermediate instructions, and how reusable knowledge is incorporated. Existing methods optimize only one part of this design space—either a monolithic prompt or separately induced skills—lacking a principled mechanism for deciding which component to update on failure and never optimizing prompts, skills, and skill-use policies in a unified framework.
AI.method: SPARO performs controlled counterfactual evaluations to convert each example's effect into a probabilistic responsibility distribution over prompt, skill, and routing components; it samples one component from this distribution and applies a targeted mutation to it.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and five worker models, SPARO consistently outperforms both prompt-centered and skill-centered optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: Effective language-program optimization depends not only on discovering useful task knowledge, but also on deciding where that knowledge should be stored and when it should be activated—advancing beyond global prompt rewriting toward structured, reusable, selectively activated task knowledge.

title: FoLD: Force-Informed Learning for Dexterous Articulated Object Manipulation
summary: Transferring human demonstrations to dexterous robots remains challenging because differences in hand morphology and contact dynamics often cause retargeted motions to fail at producing the intended object behavior. We present \textbf{FoLD}, a framework for learning dexterous manipulation of articulated objects through explicit force guidance. FoLD compute compensatory force fields from human demonstrations together with the robot's current interaction state, yielding a force prior that promotes the demonstrated object motion. This force prior informs a residual policy that adapts retargeted hand motions to the contact requirements of the task. We evaluate FoLD on a public benchmark for articulated object manipulation, where it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across tasks and embodiments. We further validate FoLD on real dexterous robot platforms, demonstrating successful transfer of human manipulation skills to robot execution. Here is the link of our project page: https://gghgghgghgg.github.io/FoLD-project-page/.

AI.tldr: FoLD learns dexterous manipulation of articulated objects by deriving compensatory force fields from human demonstrations and robot interaction state, using them as a force prior to guide a residual policy that adapts retargeted hand motions to task contact requirements.
AI.motivation: Transferring human demonstrations to dexterous robots is difficult because mismatches in hand morphology and contact dynamics cause retargeted motions to fail at producing the intended object behavior.
AI.method: FoLD computes compensatory force fields from human demonstrations combined with the robot's current interaction state, producing a force prior that promotes the demonstrated object motion. This prior informs a residual policy that adapts retargeted hand motions to the contact requirements of the task.
AI.result: On a public benchmark for articulated object manipulation, FoLD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across tasks and embodiments. It is further validated on real dexterous robot platforms, demonstrating successful transfer of human manipulation skills to robot execution.
AI.conclusion: Explicit force guidance enables effective transfer of human demonstrations to dexterous robots for articulated object manipulation, improving both benchmark performance and real-world skill transfer.

title: DAAF: From Failure Localization to Editable System Assets in LLM Agents
summary: Deployed LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent, versioned system assets such as routing rules, knowledge segments, prompt instructions, and reusable skills. Failure-localization methods can identify where an error manifests in an agent or execution trace, but repair requires a different decision: which editable system asset should be changed, and is that change expected to improve the task outcome? We study this gap through component-attribute failure attribution, where diagnosis targets versioned, addressable items rather than execution locations. We propose the Detection-Aware Attribution Framework (DAAF), which learns the effects of valid attribute replacements and amortizes this intervention evidence into deployment-time diagnosis. DAAF combines sparse and noisy failure signals to decide whether intervention is warranted, learns component-type-conditioned replacement effects from controlled replays evaluated by executable task outcomes, and shares supervision across requests with compatible intervention responses. At diagnosis time, DAAF uses only the observed execution, registered candidates, and available failure signals; it requires neither counterfactual replay nor task reward and returns no_change, a repair target, or an unresolved decision when evidence is insufficient. On held-out tau^2-bench Telecom tasks, DAAF achieves 80.72% attribute Hit@1, recovers 62.65% of failed executions while limiting clean-task regression to 3.23%, and reaches 71.93% overall task success. These results show that intervention-grounded attribute attribution can connect failure localization to executable system repair.

AI.tldr: DAAF attributes LLM agent failures to editable, versioned system assets (not execution locations) by learning intervention effects, achieving 80.72% attribute Hit@1 and 71.93% overall task success on tau^2-bench Telecom.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLM agents depend on persistent, versioned assets (routing rules, knowledge segments, prompt instructions, skills). Existing failure-localization methods identify where an error manifests, but repair needs a different decision: which editable asset to change and whether the change will improve the outcome. This component-attribute failure-attribution gap is unaddressed.
AI.method: DAAF (Detection-Aware Attribution Framework) learns the effects of valid attribute replacements and amortizes intervention evidence into deployment-time diagnosis. It combines sparse and noisy failure signals to decide whether intervention is warranted, learns component-type-conditioned replacement effects from controlled replays evaluated by executable task outcomes, and shares supervision across requests with compatible intervention responses. At diagnosis time it uses only the observed execution, registered candidates, and failure signals, requiring no counterfactual replay or task reward, and returns no_change, a repair target, or unresolved.
AI.result: On held-out tau^2-bench Telecom tasks: 80.72% attribute Hit@1, 62.65% of failed executions recovered, clean-task regression limited to 3.23%, and 71.93% overall task success.
AI.conclusion: Intervention-grounded attribute attribution connects failure localization to executable system repair, enabling practical diagnosis of versioned agent assets without counterfactual replay at deployment.

title: SLIP-VLA: Single-Step Latent Imagination for Policy Learning in Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Project page and demonstration videos: https://haoxuanxu1024.github.io/SLIP_VLA/
summary: Vision-Language-Action models are increasingly effective for robotic manipulation, yet most predict actions directly from current observations without explicitly modeling future scene evolution. Recent methods introduce future prediction to improve action generation, but dense future modeling often requires expensive iterative denoising, while one-step alternatives can underperform their multi-step counterparts. To reconcile efficient future modeling with strong action performance, we present SLIP-VLA, a policy learning framework that equips VLA models with a Single-Step Latent Imagination for future-aware action prediction. SLIP-VLA obtains temporally dense future latent representations with a single denoising update, and we improve the perceptual sufficiency of these representations by aligning intermediate latents with future geometric and semantic features. We further improve their control sufficiency through action-conditioned latent world modeling and inverse dynamics modeling, explicitly coupling latent transitions with robot actions. SLIP-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, while its single-step latent imagination takes only 12 ms.

AI.tldr: SLIP-VLA is a policy learning framework that equips Vision-Language-Action models with single-step latent imagination for efficient, future-aware action prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results with only 12 ms inference.
AI.motivation: Most VLA models predict actions directly from current observations without explicitly modeling future scene evolution. Existing future-prediction methods face a trade-off: dense future modeling requires expensive iterative denoising, while one-step alternatives underperform multi-step counterparts. The goal is to reconcile efficient future modeling with strong action performance.
AI.method: SLIP-VLA obtains temporally dense future latent representations with a single denoising update. It improves perceptual sufficiency by aligning intermediate latents with future geometric and semantic features, and improves control sufficiency through action-conditioned latent world modeling and inverse dynamics modeling, explicitly coupling latent transitions with robot actions.
AI.result: SLIP-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, with its single-step latent imagination taking only 12 ms.
AI.conclusion: Single-step latent imagination can deliver efficient, future-aware VLA policies that match or exceed stronger multi-step future-modeling approaches, enabling practical real-world robotic manipulation.

title: TreeRef-BFN: Equivariance-Free De Novo Molecule Generation based on 2D Topology and Internal 3D Geometry
summary: De novo 3D molecular generation jointly models molecular size, topology, and geometry. Most methods pre-sample molecular size and generate Cartesian coordinates, limiting variable-size conditional tasks such as fragment completion and scaffold decoration while often relying on equivariant architectures. Internal-coordinate methods avoid rigid-body redundancy but typically require a known molecular graph or autoregressive construction, which may accumulate errors. We propose TreeRef, a tree-based molecular representation that assigns molecular topology and topology-dependent local 3D geometry to a naturally variable-size tree. RingRef nodes encode ring closures while preserving the tree structure, while Null nodes allow molecular size to emerge directly from node occupancy. Based on TreeRef, we develop TreeRef-BFN, a Bayesian Flow Network with a standard Transformer backbone that globally couples these locally defined variables and jointly generates discrete molecular variables and continuous local geometry. A single pretrained TreeRef-BFN supports unconditional generation and variable-size structure-conditioned 3D generation through masking alone, without retraining. Empirical studies demonstrate strong chemical validity, molecular stability, and diversity, accurate local geometric distributions, fast sampling, and competitive property-conditioned generation, establishing TreeRef-BFN as an efficient and flexible framework for 3D molecular generation.

AI.tldr: TreeRef represents molecules as trees encoding topology and local 3D geometry with ring-closure (RingRef) and Null nodes, enabling variable-size generation; TreeRef-BFN, a Transformer-based Bayesian Flow Network, jointly generates discrete and continuous variables, supporting unconditional and structure-conditioned 3D generation via masking without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing de novo 3D molecular generation methods pre-sample molecular size and generate Cartesian coordinates, which limits variable-size conditional tasks like fragment completion and scaffold decoration and often necessitates equivariant architectures. Internal-coordinate alternatives avoid rigid-body redundancy but require a known graph or autoregressive construction, incurring error accumulation.
AI.method: The authors introduce TreeRef, a tree-based molecular representation assigning topology and topology-dependent local 3D geometry to a naturally variable-size tree. RingRef nodes encode ring closures while preserving tree structure, and Null nodes let molecular size emerge from node occupancy. Built on TreeRef, TreeRef-BFN is a Bayesian Flow Network with a standard Transformer backbone that globally couples locally defined variables and jointly generates discrete molecular variables and continuous local geometry.
AI.result: Empirical studies show strong chemical validity, molecular stability, and diversity, accurate local geometric distributions, fast sampling, and competitive property-conditioned generation. A single pretrained TreeRef-BFN supports both unconditional and variable-size structure-conditioned 3D generation via masking alone, without retraining.
AI.conclusion: TreeRef-BFN establishes an efficient and flexible framework for 3D molecular generation, offering variable-size conditional capability and avoiding equivariant architectures while mitigating autoregressive error accumulation.

title: Beyond One-Step Accuracy: State-Affine Latent Transition for Reliable Visual Planning
summary: Joint-embedding world models enable visual planning by learning action-conditioned dynamics in latent space. Yet they are commonly trained for one-step prediction on encoded states, while planning recursively applies the learned transition to its own predictions. One-step accuracy therefore does not capture how prediction errors propagate under recursive rollout. We decompose multi-step rollout error into the errors introduced at individual steps and their propagation through subsequent transitions. We show that state-affine dynamics are precisely the differentiable transitions with state-independent Jacobians, eliminating the nonlinear propagation residual and making the error propagation operators depend only on the action sequence. Guided by this result, we introduce SALT (State-Affine Latent Transition), an action-conditioned state-affine dynamics model in which the action modulates both the state transformation and the additive update. We train SALT through recursive multi-step rollout supervision, feeding each predicted latent state back into the transition so that training matches how the model is used during planning. Across four visual planning environments, SALT exhibits $1.48$--$2.19\times$ higher one-step prediction error than the matched LeWM baseline, yet improves closed-loop success in every environment by $10.0$ percentage points on average. On OGBench-Cube, the fraction of episodes that fail with a sharp rise in model-predicted cost after execution decreases from $23.3%$ to $2.0%$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes multi-step rollout error propagation in joint-embedding world models, shows state-affine dynamics eliminate nonlinear propagation residual, and proposes SALT, a state-affine latent transition model trained with recursive rollout supervision that improves closed-loop planning success despite worse one-step accuracy.
AI.motivation: Joint-embedding world models are commonly trained for one-step prediction, but planning recursively applies the learned transition to its own predictions. One-step accuracy thus fails to capture how errors propagate under recursive rollout. The paper aims to address this mismatch between training objective and planning-time usage.
AI.method: The authors decompose multi-step rollout error into per-step error introduction and its propagation through subsequent transitions. They prove that state-affine dynamics correspond exactly to differentiable transitions with state-independent Jacobians, removing the nonlinear propagation residual and making error propagation operators action-sequence-dependent only. Based on this, they propose SALT, an action-conditioned state-affine dynamics model where the action modulates both the state transformation and the additive update, trained via recursive multi-step rollout supervision that feeds predicted latents back into the transition.
AI.result: Across four visual planning environments, SALT shows 1.48-2.19x higher one-step prediction error than the matched LeWM baseline, yet improves closed-loop success by 10.0 percentage points on average in every environment. On OGBench-Cube, episodes failing with a sharp post-execution rise in model-predicted cost drop from 23.3% to 2.0%.
AI.conclusion: One-step prediction accuracy is a poor proxy for planning performance. State-affine dynamics with recursive rollout supervision improve closed-loop planning, showing that aligning training with recursive usage matters more than minimizing one-step error.

title: Learning from Others, Acting for You: Cross-User Memory Sharing for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents serving different users often solve related tasks, yet separate user histories can leave reusable experience inaccessible to other agents. Pooling memories expands access but risks transferring preferences that conflict with the receiving user's requirements. We introduce ShareMem, a memory architecture that shares reusable experience while grounding its application in the receiving user's own preferences. Shared experiences indicate how to act and which preferences to consult; the receiving user's memory supplies their concrete values. Two-stage consolidation refines experience locally before integrating accepted edits into a shared pool. During execution, scope-first retrieval jointly selects local and shared experiences under a common entry budget, while a user-bound channel supports initial and agent-initiated preference retrieval. We evaluate ShareMem across web navigation (Mind2Web), online personalized interaction (VitaBench~2.0), and multi-session coding (MemoryCode) with four backbone models. It improves step success, average task success, and dialogue-macro coding scores, respectively, over matched user-local memory across all four models. Ablations favor two-stage consolidation for smaller shared pools, lower induction token usage, and better downstream performance, and support complementarity between experience guidance and active preference retrieval. Further analyses show that sharing helps most when relevant local experience is scarce, while source quality and cross-user preference interference limit useful transfer.

AI.tldr: ShareMem is a memory architecture for LLM agents that shares reusable experience across users while grounding its application in each receiving user's own preferences, via two-stage consolidation and scope-first retrieval, improving task success across web navigation, personalized interaction, and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents serving different users often solve related tasks, but separate user histories make reusable experience inaccessible across agents. Pooling memories improves access yet risks transferring preferences that conflict with the receiving user's requirements, creating a tension between experience reuse and preference fidelity.
AI.method: ShareMem separates shared experiences, which indicate how to act and which preferences to consult, from the receiving user's memory, which supplies concrete preference values. It uses two-stage consolidation that refines experience locally before integrating accepted edits into a shared pool. At execution, scope-first retrieval jointly selects local and shared experiences under a common entry budget, and a user-bound channel supports initial and agent-initiated preference retrieval.
AI.result: Evaluated on Mind2Web (web navigation), VitaBench~2.0 (online personalized interaction), and MemoryCode (multi-session coding) with four backbone models, ShareMem improves step success, average task success, and dialogue-macro coding scores over matched user-local memory across all four models. Ablations favor two-stage consolidation for smaller shared pools, lower induction token usage, and better downstream performance, and support complementarity between experience guidance and active preference retrieval. Sharing helps most when relevant local experience is scarce, while source quality and cross-user preference interference limit useful transfer.
AI.conclusion: ShareMem enables cross-user experience sharing without imposing conflicting preferences, by letting shared experience guide action and preference selection while the receiving user's memory supplies concrete values. Its gains are largest when local experience is scarce, and transfer quality is bounded by source quality and cross-user preference interference.

title: InfraVLA: Extending Vision-Language-Action Navigation with Infrastructure Cameras
