summary: Many indoor environments in which robots operate, such as warehouses, offices, and hospitals, already have cameras installed. They observe parts of the building that the robot cannot see from where it stands, yet navigation policies, including recent vision-language-action (VLA) models, do not use them. We propose InfraVLA, an end-to-end method that adapts a pretrained navigation VLA to such static infrastructure views: a closed-circuit television (CCTV) encoder turns each external view into tokens of the input sequence. Because the views matter only at rare decision points, fine-tuning alone did not make the policy use them in our experiments; we therefore train in two stages, on demonstrations with upsampled counterfactual data and then on recovery data. We evaluate on two simulated warehouse tasks, finding an object named in the instruction and rerouting around blocked aisles, where the deciding information is often visible only to the infrastructure cameras. Tested in distribution, InfraVLA reached a success rate of 100% on both, against 34.0% and 73.6% for a baseline without CCTV input. On out-of-distribution test sets it reached 88.2% and 88.9%. On a real quadruped fine-tuned with under 10 minutes of demonstrations, the policy reached 83.3% against 29.2% for the on-board-only baseline.

AI.tldr: InfraVLA adapts a pretrained navigation VLA to leverage static infrastructure cameras (e.g., CCTV) via a CCTV encoder and two-stage training, achieving large success-rate gains over camera-free baselines in simulation and on a real quadruped.
AI.motivation: Robots in warehouses, offices, and hospitals operate in spaces where cameras are already installed, and these cameras observe building regions that are invisible from the robot's current viewpoint. However, existing navigation policies, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, ignore these infrastructure views, leaving task-critical information (e.g., blocked aisles or named objects visible only externally) unexploited.
AI.method: InfraVLA is an end-to-end method that adapts a pretrained navigation VLA to static infrastructure views. A CCTV encoder converts each external view into tokens appended to the input sequence. Since external views matter only at rare decision points and fine-tuning alone failed to induce their use, training proceeds in two stages: first on demonstrations augmented with upsampled counterfactual data, then on recovery data.
AI.result: Evaluated on two simulated warehouse tasks—finding an object named in the instruction and rerouting around blocked aisles—where decisive information is often visible only to infrastructure cameras, InfraVLA achieved 100% success on both in-distribution, versus 34.0% and 73.6% for a baseline without CCTV input. On out-of-distribution test sets it reached 88.2% and 88.9%. On a real quadruped fine-tuned with under 10 minutes of demonstrations, it reached 83.3% versus 29.2% for the on-board-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Static infrastructure cameras provide task-critical information for robot navigation, and InfraVLA shows that a pretrained navigation VLA can be effectively adapted to use them. The two-stage training with counterfactual and recovery data is crucial for making the policy actually rely on external views, yielding substantial improvements over on-board-only baselines across simulation and real-world deployment.

title: From Anomalies to Failures: Constructing Causal Error Graphs for Agentic Trace Diagnosis
summary: LLM-driven agents are increasingly deployed in complex applications, where long agentic traces make failures difficult to diagnose. Existing trace diagnosis methods often conflate anomalies, errors, and failures, making diagnostic targets ambiguous; they also lack structured modeling of how causally relevant errors propagate and amplify into final task failures, resulting in unreliable failure attribution. To address these problems, we propose CEG-Agent, a tool-augmented agentic framework for causal diagnosis of agentic traces. Specifically, CEG-Agent introduces an explicit taxonomy of anomalies, errors, and failures, and constructs Causal Error Graphs (CEGs), a unified typed representation that links execution events, diagnostic nodes, and failure outcomes through causal relations. To evaluate causal trace diagnosis, we further construct CEG-Bench, a fully agent-annotated benchmark with high-confidence, consensus-derived CEG annotations obtained through an Adversarial Agentic Adjudication Protocol (AAAP). We validate the resulting annotations against an expert-curated human gold set, which shows close agreement with the automatic annotations. Experiments on CEG-Bench demonstrate that CEG-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance under both semantically relaxed and structurally exact evaluation criteria. Our code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: CEG-Agent is a tool-augmented framework for causal diagnosis of LLM agentic traces that introduces an anomaly/error/failure taxonomy and Causal Error Graphs, plus CEG-Bench, a benchmark with agent-annotated causal annotations, achieving state-of-the-art failure attribution.
AI.motivation: Long agentic traces in LLM-driven agents make failures hard to diagnose. Existing trace diagnosis methods conflate anomalies, errors, and failures, making diagnostic targets ambiguous, and they lack structured modeling of how causally relevant errors propagate and amplify into final task failures, leading to unreliable failure attribution.
AI.method: The authors propose CEG-Agent, a tool-augmented agentic framework (1) introducing an explicit taxonomy distinguishing anomalies, errors, and failures, and (2) constructing Causal Error Graphs (CEGs), a unified typed representation linking execution events, diagnostic nodes, and failure outcomes via causal relations. They also build CEG-Bench, a fully agent-annotated benchmark with consensus-derived CEG annotations produced via an Adversarial Agentic Adjudication Protocol (AAAP), validated against an expert-curated human gold set.
AI.result: Automatic CEG annotations show close agreement with the expert-curated human gold set. Experiments on CEG-Bench show CEG-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance under both semantically relaxed and structurally exact evaluation criteria.
AI.conclusion: CEG-Agent provides structured causal diagnosis of agentic traces via Causal Error Graphs and a clear anomaly/error/failure taxonomy, with CEG-Bench enabling evaluation and validation confirming strong performance. Code is publicly available.

title: Demonstration-Free Success-Probability Reward Learning for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables generalist robot policies to improve through trial-and-error interaction, yet its effectiveness is fundamentally constrained by sparse task rewards. Existing general-purpose reward models typically alleviate this issue by learning task progress from expert demonstrations, but introduce a distribution mismatch with the mixed-quality rollouts encountered during policy optimization, making their estimates unreliable on suboptimal and failed behaviors from which the policy must learn. In this work, we introduce a demonstration-free reward learning paradigm where dense reward feedback can be learned directly from sparse task outcomes and policy experience. We theoretically show that terminal task outcomes implicitly define dense success-probability feedback at intermediate timesteps, which can be recursively learned through bootstrapping. Based on this insight, we introduce eVTA$_0$, which learns success probabilities from mixed-quality policy rollouts through temporal-difference-style bootstrapping, without expert demonstrations or intermediate annotations. We further introduce RL with Evolving Rewards (RLER), a closed-loop framework that adapts eVTA$_0$ using newly collected rollouts as the policy evolves. Experiments show that eVTA$_0$ provides more informative rewards than state-of-the-art reward models and achieves the best average policy performance across all LIBERO task suites under the same RL training budget, improving success rates by 5.4%-13.8% over the initial policy. In real-world manipulation, RLER further improves overall success rates by 20%-26%, with 35%-36% gains under out-of-distribution conditions. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of demonstration-free reward learning and adapting rewards as the policy evolves. Project webpage: https://duowuyms.github.io/evta0.

AI.tldr: eVTA0 learns dense success-probability rewards from sparse outcomes and policy rollouts via temporal-difference bootstrapping, without expert demonstrations. Coupled with RL with Evolving Rewards (RLER), it outperforms SOTA reward models on LIBERO and improves real-world manipulation, especially out-of-distribution.
AI.motivation: RL for generalist robot policies is limited by sparse task rewards. Existing reward models learn progress from expert demonstrations, causing a distribution mismatch with mixed-quality rollouts during policy optimization and unreliable estimates on suboptimal/failed behaviors.
AI.method: Introduces a demonstration-free reward learning paradigm. Theoretically shows terminal outcomes implicitly define dense success-probability feedback at intermediate timesteps, recursively learnable via bootstrapping. Proposes eVTA0, which learns success probabilities from mixed-quality rollouts via TD-style bootstrapping without expert demos or intermediate annotations. Adds RLER, a closed-loop framework adapting eVTA0 with newly collected rollouts as the policy evolves.
AI.result: eVTA0 provides more informative rewards than SOTA reward models and achieves best average policy performance across all LIBERO task suites under equal RL budget, improving success rates by 5.4%-13.8% over the initial policy. In real-world manipulation, RLER improves overall success rates by 20%-26%, with 35%-36% gains under out-of-distribution conditions.
AI.conclusion: Demonstration-free reward learning with rewards adapted as the policy evolves is effective, yielding robust policy improvement in simulation and real-world manipulation, including OOD settings.

title: LocalProp: Neuro-Localized Memory-Efficient Backpropagation
summary: The current deep learning training paradigm employs end-to-end backpropagation, regardless of the training stage, i.e. pre-training or fine-tuning. However, backpropagating through the entire model is neither biologically plausible nor memory efficient, since learning inside the brain is highly localized. Therefore, we propose LocalProp, a training procedure that locally updates the weights of a model. Our neuro-localized weight updates follow the "pre-training then fine-tuning" paradigm, where the pre-training is based on I-JEPA. After locally updating the weights, a pruning operation is performed, followed by a short final fine-tuning phase. Pruning helps by sending the learning signal from higher blocks to lower blocks. We perform experiments on several datasets, including large-scale benchmarks such as ImageNet, and empirically show that LocalProp reaches good performance at a fraction of GPU peak memory. By varying the number of jointly optimized blocks, we identify gradient-propagation span as a practical control over the accuracy-memory trade-off.

AI.tldr: LocalProp is a training procedure that updates model weights locally rather than via end-to-end backpropagation, combining I-JEPA-based pre-training, localized weight updates, pruning, and a short fine-tuning phase, achieving good accuracy at a fraction of peak GPU memory.
AI.motivation: Standard end-to-end backpropagation is neither biologically plausible (brain learning is highly localized) nor memory efficient, since gradients must propagate through the entire model regardless of training stage (pre-training or fine-tuning).
AI.method: LocalProp performs neuro-localized weight updates following a "pre-training then fine-tuning" paradigm: pre-training is based on I-JEPA; weights are then updated locally; a pruning operation follows, which sends the learning signal from higher blocks to lower blocks; finally, a short fine-tuning phase is applied. The number of jointly optimized blocks can be varied to control the gradient-propagation span.
AI.result: Experiments on several datasets, including the large-scale ImageNet benchmark, empirically show that LocalProp reaches good performance at a fraction of GPU peak memory. Varying the number of jointly optimized blocks identifies gradient-propagation span as a practical control over the accuracy-memory trade-off.
AI.conclusion: LocalProp provides a biologically plausible and memory-efficient alternative to end-to-end backpropagation, offering a controllable accuracy-memory trade-off via the gradient-propagation span.

title: Observability-Informed Optimal Sensor Placement for Soft Robots
comment: Published in IEEE Robosoft 2026. 8 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables
summary: This paper presents the application and experimental evaluation of a systematic method for optimal sensor placement in soft robots. Existing methods either lack generalizability across different soft robot morphologies or do not account for system dynamics. The applied method uses convex optimization to find the optimal sensor configuration that maximizes an observability Gramian-based metric. The framework is experimentally evaluated using position and strain measurements on a soft continuum arm. Kalman filter state estimates using optimal sensor placements yield lower reconstruction error than a baseline across all sinusoidal input trials, with improvements on the order of millimeters. This case study shows that linear control theory tools can guide optimal sensor placement in soft robots, suggesting an interpretable approach to sensor placement that may extend to other morphologies.

AI.tldr: This paper applies and experimentally evaluates a convex optimization method for optimal sensor placement in soft robots, using an observability Gramian-based metric. Kalman filter estimates with optimal placements outperform a baseline on a soft continuum arm.
AI.motivation: Existing sensor placement methods for soft robots either lack generalizability across different morphologies or fail to account for system dynamics.
AI.method: A systematic method based on convex optimization is applied to find the optimal sensor configuration that maximizes an observability Gramian-based metric. The framework is experimentally evaluated using position and strain measurements on a soft continuum arm.
AI.result: Kalman filter state estimates using optimal sensor placements yield lower reconstruction error than a baseline across all sinusoidal input trials, with improvements on the order of millimeters.
AI.conclusion: This case study demonstrates that linear control theory tools can guide optimal sensor placement in soft robots, suggesting an interpretable approach that may extend to other morphologies.

title: STR: Supervised Transcoder Replacement for Reducing Steering Side Effects
summary: Model steering can strengthen a target behavior while degrading other useful behaviors. We introduce Supervised Transcoder Replacement (STR) to reduce these side effects for existing steering methods, including those fitted without a protection objective. STR learns a replacement for the multilayer perceptron (MLP) computation at the steering layer through supervision for target control, non-target preservation, and fidelity without steering. Selected steering methods then fit directions on the frozen replacement while retaining their own fitting objectives. We evaluate three steering methods across Gemma and Llama models using Corrigibility preferences and four harmful-request safety datasets. SALAD-Bench supplies protection training data and a separate in-distribution evaluation split; HarmBench, AdvBench, and StrongREJECT are reserved for out-of-distribution testing. STR substantially reduces steering side effects on the in-distribution evaluation and extends this protection to the unseen safety datasets while retaining effective target control. For target-only supervised steering vectors, pooled out-of-distribution attack success rate falls from 42.46% to 14.42% on Gemma-3-4B and from 34.97% to 12.91% on Gemma-3-12B. These results show that replacement training can benefit steering methods fitted without protection objectives.

AI.tldr: STR replaces the MLP computation at the steering layer via supervised training (target control, non-target preservation, fidelity) so that existing steering methods fitted without protection objectives can reduce side effects while retaining target control.
AI.motivation: Model steering can strengthen a target behavior but degrades other useful behaviors, and this side effect persists for steering methods fitted without a protection objective.
AI.method: Supervised Transcoder Replacement (STR) learns a replacement for the MLP computation at the steering layer through supervision for target control, non-target preservation, and fidelity without steering; selected steering methods then fit directions on the frozen replacement while keeping their own fitting objectives. Evaluated on Gemma and Llama models with Corrigibility preferences and four harmful-request safety datasets (SALAD-Bench for protection training plus in-distribution split; HarmBench, AdvBench, StrongREJECT for out-of-distribution testing), across three steering methods.
AI.result: STR substantially reduces steering side effects on the in-distribution evaluation and extends protection to unseen safety datasets while retaining effective target control. For target-only supervised steering vectors, pooled out-of-distribution attack success rate drops from 42.46% to 14.42% on Gemma-3-4B and from 34.97% to 12.91% on Gemma-3-12B.
AI.conclusion: Replacement training can benefit steering methods fitted without protection objectives, reducing side effects while preserving target control.

title: MomWorld: Momentum-Aware Latent World Model for Long-Horizon Autonomous Driving
summary: Long-horizon planning enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate scene evolution and potential risks, supporting safe and stable decisions in complex interactions. However, existing methods struggle to propagate motion trends from observed history into the future. Long rollouts based on a single latent state may further attenuate useful dynamics, retain stale motion patterns, and disrupt reliable near-term plans. We introduce MomWorld, a momentum-aware latent world model for long-horizon planning. MomWorld extracts scene motion trends from historical-to-current observations and propagates latent momentum into future horizons, jointly predicting future configuration and momentum states. A learnable momentum persistence mechanism preserves stable trends, scene-conditioned momentum updates adapt future dynamics, and a scene-adaptive reset gate suppresses stale momentum under abrupt changes. We further propose MoFlow, a momentum-conditioned flow-matching module that refines a base trajectory to align with the predicted future scene evolution in only a few integration steps, with a horizon-aware residual fusion that preserves near-term planning stability while permitting stronger long-range corrections. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM, nuScenes and Bench2Drive demonstrate that MomWorld improves long-horizon planning consistency and reduces the average collision rate by 12.2% relative to MomAD over a 6-second planning horizon.

AI.tldr: MomWorld is a momentum-aware latent world model for long-horizon autonomous driving planning that extracts and propagates scene motion trends into the future, coupled with MoFlow for trajectory refinement, reducing collision rate by 12.2% vs. MomAD over a 6-second horizon.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon planning requires anticipating scene evolution and risks for safe decisions, but existing methods fail to propagate motion trends from observed history into the future; long rollouts from a single latent state attenuate useful dynamics, retain stale motion patterns, and destabilize reliable near-term plans.
AI.method: MomWorld extracts scene motion trends from historical-to-current observations and propagates latent momentum into future horizons, jointly predicting future configuration and momentum states. It uses a learnable momentum persistence mechanism for stable trends, scene-conditioned momentum updates for adaptive future dynamics, and a scene-adaptive reset gate to suppress stale momentum under abrupt changes. MoFlow, a momentum-conditioned flow-matching module, refines a base trajectory in few integration steps with horizon-aware residual fusion for near-term stability and long-range corrections.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on NAVSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive show improved long-horizon planning consistency and a 12.2% reduction in average collision rate relative to MomAD over a 6-second planning horizon.
AI.conclusion: Momentum-aware latent world modeling with momentum-conditioned trajectory refinement improves long-horizon planning consistency and safety, validating the momentum propagation paradigm for autonomous driving.

title: MemAgent: Learning to Manage Heterogeneous Memory Providers for LLM Agents
summary: Current agents remain largely stateless across tasks, limiting their ability to continually improve from prior interactions and making memory essential for long-horizon agentic behavior. Existing memory methods seek to reuse past experience, but most rely on a single memory representation (e.g., trajectories, reflections, skills, structured knowledge) whose effectiveness varies across task distributions. Rethinking this design space, we evaluate 13 memory methods and find that no single method generalizes across benchmarks, revealing the potential of managing heterogeneous memory providers. We formulate agent memory as a routing problem in which a memory agent decides which memory provider to retrieve from, whether to inject short-term memory, and which providers should store the resulting experience. Based on this perspective, we propose MemAgent, featuring a content-aware routing architecture and a training-data synthesis pipeline. The routing architecture combines content-aware probing before retrieval, short-term memory gating during execution, and selective multi-provider storage, while the training pipeline synthesizes phase-specific supervision for routing decisions. Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, MemAgent improves average accuracy by 10.0% and outperforms every individual memory method across all three benchmarks. These gains come with less than 0.3% routing overhead and a 12% reduction in average task steps.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MemAgent, which reframes agent memory as a routing problem over heterogeneous memory providers, using a content-aware routing architecture plus a training-data synthesis pipeline, achieving a 10.0% average accuracy gain across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Agents are largely stateless across tasks, limiting continual improvement and long-horizon behavior, making memory essential. Existing memory methods rely on a single memory representation (trajectories, reflections, skills, structured knowledge) whose effectiveness varies across task distributions. An evaluation of 13 memory methods shows none generalizes across benchmarks, motivating the management of heterogeneous memory providers.
AI.method: The authors formulate agent memory as a routing problem where a memory agent decides: which memory provider to retrieve from, whether to inject short-term memory, and which providers should store resulting experience. Based on this, they propose MemAgent with (1) a content-aware routing architecture combining content-aware probing before retrieval, short-term memory gating during execution, and selective multi-provider storage, and (2) a training-data synthesis pipeline producing phase-specific supervision for routing decisions.
AI.result: Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, MemAgent improves average accuracy by 10.0% and outperforms every individual memory method across all three benchmarks, with less than 0.3% routing overhead and a 12% reduction in average task steps.
AI.conclusion: Managing heterogeneous memory providers via routing is more effective than relying on any single memory representation, as no individual method generalizes. MemAgent demonstrates that learned, content-aware routing over multiple providers yields consistent cross-benchmark gains with negligible overhead and improved efficiency in task steps.

title: AnyStep-WAM: Budget-Aligned Distillation and Adaptive Inference for World Action Models
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple predictive visual modeling with action generation, typically relying on iterative denoising with a fixed denoising steps. However, manipulation tasks contain actions chunks with varying sensitivity to generation errors: critical actions require precision, while less sensitive actions allow faster generation with fewer denoising steps. Here we introduce AnyStep World Action Model, a general framework for tunable-budget prediction and scene-dependent computation allocation. Our budget-aligned teacher-trajectory distillation trains interval-conditioned flow maps using explicit frozen-teacher transitions and shared low-rank adapters, supporting action generation from one-step prediction to multi-step refinement. Building on this capability, a lightweight risk-benefit scheduler predicts teacher-curvature-based difficulty and budget-specific student-teacher fidelity from a single one-step preview, selecting the smallest budget predicted to satisfy risk-adaptive fidelity requirements. We evaluate our framework on three widely used WAMs Motus, FastWAM, and LingBotVA using RoboTwin 2.0. Our method reduces average denoising steps by 60.2%, 49.8%, and 85.28%, respectively, while maintaining baseline task success rates. In particular, our AnyStep training substantially improves model performance under a one-step denoising budget, increasing task success rates by 7.07%, 12.08%, and 8.94% on Motus, FastWAM, and LingBotVA, respectively. Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks further validate its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: AnyStep World Action Model enables tunable-budget action generation for world-action models, cutting denoising steps by up to 85% while preserving success rates and boosting one-step performance.
AI.motivation: World-action models typically use fixed denoising steps, ignoring that manipulation action chunks differ in sensitivity to generation errors—critical actions need precision while others tolerate fewer steps. A tunable-budget, scene-adaptive compute allocation is needed.
AI.method: Budget-aligned teacher-trajectory distillation trains interval-conditioned flow maps using explicit frozen-teacher transitions and shared low-rank adapters, supporting one-step to multi-step generation. A lightweight risk-benefit scheduler predicts teacher-curvature-based difficulty and budget-specific student-teacher fidelity from a one-step preview, choosing the smallest budget meeting risk-adaptive fidelity requirements.
AI.result: On three WAMs (Motus, FastWAM, LingBotVA) with RoboTwin 2.0, denoising steps drop 60.2%, 49.8%, 85.28% while maintaining baseline success rates. One-step performance improves by 7.07%, 12.08%, 8.94%. Validated on six real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables efficient, adaptive-budget action generation, delivering major step reductions with maintained success and improved low-step performance, generalizing across WAMs and real-world tasks.

title: Beyond Dyadic Memory: Interaction-Aware Multimodal Memory with Adaptive Agentic Retrieval for Multi-Party Spoken Conversations
summary: Long-term memory enables agents to accumulate information and reason across sessions, yet existing research primarily focuses on dyadic text or image-text conversations, leaving long-term memory for multi-party spoken conversations underexplored. This setting requires preserving conversational content, identifying participants across sessions, and retaining who speaks to whom. To this end, we propose VoxPolyMem, an interaction-aware multimodal memory framework combining incremental speaker identification with a memory hierarchy comprising interaction memory, fact memory, and participant profiles. We formulate retrieval as sequential decision-making, where an agent rewrites queries and selects retrieval tools and memory layers based on accumulated evidence to address information gaps. We further introduce Evidence-Gain GRPO (EG-GRPO), which uses round-wise credit assignment to encourage complementary evidence acquisition. We also construct VoxPolyBench to evaluate memory evolution, personalized answering, memory retrieval and reasoning, and interaction reasoning and attribution in multi-party spoken conversations. VoxPolyMem achieves an overall score of 85.0 on VoxPolyBench, surpassing the strongest evaluated baseline by 23.6 points. On Mem-Gallery and H2HMem-Multi, it scores 89.6 and 74.4, respectively, exceeding the strongest evaluated public memory baselines by over 8 points each. These results highlight its potential for persistent, personalized assistance in multi-party multimodal interactions. Code and datasets are available at https://voxpolymem.github.io/VoxPolyBench/demo/

AI.tldr: VoxPolyMem is an interaction-aware multimodal memory framework for long-term memory in multi-party spoken conversations, featuring incremental speaker identification, a three-layer memory hierarchy, sequential decision-making retrieval, and Evidence-Gain GRPO training; it achieves 85.0 on the new VoxPolyBench and outperforms baselines on Mem-Gallery and H2HMem-Multi.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory research focuses mainly on dyadic text or image-text conversations, leaving multi-party spoken conversations underexplored. This setting is harder because it requires preserving conversational content, identifying participants across sessions, and tracking who speaks to whom.
AI.method: The paper proposes VoxPolyMem, combining incremental speaker identification with a memory hierarchy of interaction memory, fact memory, and participant profiles. Retrieval is formulated as sequential decision-making, where an agent rewrites queries and selects retrieval tools and memory layers based on accumulated evidence. It also introduces Evidence-Gain GRPO (EG-GRPO) with round-wise credit assignment to encourage complementary evidence acquisition.
AI.result: VoxPolyMem scores 85.0 overall on VoxPolyBench, surpassing the strongest evaluated baseline by 23.6 points. It scores 89.6 on Mem-Gallery and 74.4 on H2HMem-Multi, exceeding the strongest evaluated public memory baselines by over 8 points each.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate VoxPolyMem's potential for persistent, personalized assistance in multi-party multimodal interactions. The authors also construct VoxPolyBench to evaluate memory evolution, personalized answering, memory retrieval and reasoning, and interaction reasoning and attribution, with code and datasets publicly available.

title: Principal Steering Subspaces for Online Adaptation of Frozen Generative Robot Policies
summary: Generative robot policies provide expressive behavior priors, but updating a large diffusion or flow-matching model through online interaction is costly. Latent-space reinforcement learning avoids updating the pretrained generator by controlling its initial sampling noise, yet high-dimensional noise can have strongly anisotropic effects on decoded actions. We introduce Principal Steering Subspaces (PSS), a forward-query interface that constructs a fixed low-dimensional control basis from finite-difference decoder responses. Soft Actor-Critic controls the leading response directions, while the orthogonal complement is independently resampled from the Gaussian prior at each query. On three RoboMimic tasks with diffusion and flow-matching policies, response spectra reveal substantial concentration. Across five matched task-generator pairs, the training curves indicate that PSS generally converges faster and exhibits more stable late-training behavior than full-latent control, while achieving stronger final performance overall. Controlled Diffusion-Square ablations further show that leading-response directions outperform random and least-responsive subspaces of equal dimension. We further integrate PSS with a frozen, closed-source 3B-parameter vision-language-action (VLA) policy in a humanoid learning system with synchronous transition collection, reset-time optimization, and latency-aware asynchronous deployment. In an exploratory screwdriver-placement evaluation, success is observed in 2/10 trials for the frozen VLA policy and 6/10 after SAC+PSS adaptation. These results support decoder-response geometry as a practical basis for online adaptation of frozen generative robot policies.

AI.tldr: PSS builds a fixed low-dimensional control basis from decoder response directions, letting SAC steer frozen generative robot policies via sampling noise, converging faster and more stably than full-latent control, and enabling adaptation of a frozen 3B VLA policy (2/10 to 6/10 success).
AI.motivation: Online updating of large diffusion or flow-matching generative policies is costly. Latent-space RL avoids fine-tuning by controlling initial sampling noise, but high-dimensional noise affects decoded actions anisotropically, making full-latent control inefficient and unstable.
AI.method: Principal Steering Subspaces (PSS), a forward-query interface that constructs a fixed low-dimensional control basis from finite-difference decoder responses. SAC controls the leading response directions, while the orthogonal complement is independently resampled from the Gaussian prior at each query. Integrated with a frozen closed-source 3B VLA policy using synchronous transition collection, reset-time optimization, and latency-aware asynchronous deployment.
AI.result: On three RoboMimic tasks with diffusion and flow-matching policies, response spectra show substantial concentration; across five matched task-generator pairs PSS converges faster, is more stable late in training, and achieves stronger final performance than full-latent control. Controlled Diffusion-Square ablations show leading-response directions beat random and least-responsive subspaces of equal dimension. In screwdriver placement, success rises from 2/10 (frozen VLA) to 6/10 (SAC+PSS).
AI.conclusion: Decoder-response geometry provides a practical basis for online adaptation of frozen generative robot policies, enabling efficient latent-space RL and adaptation of large pretrained VLA models without updating their weights.

title: AmbiModBench: Benchmarking Gene Perturbation Prediction Beyond Shared Responses
summary: Predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations helps prioritize experiments in single-cell genomics, where exhaustive measurement is infeasible. While computational models increasingly predict these responses, three evaluation deficiencies obscure what their scores demonstrate. First, absolute metrics cannot separate target-specific predictions from a shared background response. Second, common metrics remain high under gene shuffling, so gene-level accuracy is never verified. Third, a score at one training size says nothing about coverage, which depends on representation-space proximity and response-constraining power. We propose AmbiModBench, a specificity-aware, gene-resolved and coverage-aware benchmark. It pairs every score with a training-mean reference fitted on the same split, screens each readout by gene-coordinate permutation, and links embedding distance to response variation. Across K562, RPE1 and Norman, strong absolute scores largely reflect shared background rather than target-specific learning. Widely used readouts track response magnitude distributions rather than the affected genes. Detectable gain follows representation-space coverage rather than training-set size. Nonetheless, on RPE1 the protocol yields a reproducible target-specific gain across five additional splits and three gene selections, which absolute scores alone cannot distinguish from shared background.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AmbiModBench, a specificity-aware, gene-resolved, and coverage-aware benchmark that exposes three evaluation deficiencies in models predicting single-cell responses to genetic perturbations.
AI.motivation: Computational models predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations are increasingly used to prioritize experiments in single-cell genomics, where exhaustive measurement is infeasible. However, three evaluation deficiencies obscure what model scores actually demonstrate: (1) absolute metrics cannot separate target-specific predictions from a shared background response, (2) common metrics remain high under gene shuffling, so gene-level accuracy is never verified, and (3) a score at one training size says nothing about coverage, which depends on representation-space proximity and response-constraining power.
AI.method: AmbiModBench is proposed as a specificity-aware, gene-resolved, and coverage-aware benchmark. It pairs every score with a training-mean reference fitted on the same split, screens each readout by gene-coordinate permutation, and links embedding distance to response variation.
AI.result: Across K562, RPE1, and Norman datasets, strong absolute scores largely reflect shared background rather than target-specific learning. Widely used readouts track response-magnitude distributions rather than the affected genes. Detectable gain follows representation-space coverage rather than training-set size. Nonetheless, on RPE1 the protocol yields a reproducible target-specific gain across five additional splits and three gene selections, which absolute scores alone cannot distinguish from shared background.
AI.conclusion: Standard absolute metrics are insufficient for evaluating perturbation-response models. A specificity-aware, gene-resolved, and coverage-aware evaluation is needed to verify genuine target-specific learning, as demonstrated by the reproducible target-specific gain identified on RPE1.

title: CodeActionBench: Evaluating Agentic Code-as-Policy for Embodied Manipulation
comment: 28 pages including references and appendices, 10 figures. Project website: https://codeactionbench.org
summary: How well can general-purpose multimodal models turn visual understanding and reasoning into embodied manipulation via executable code? We introduce CodeActionBench, a benchmark of 25 manipulation tasks that evaluates this capability through agentic Code-as-Policy. Without task-specific fine-tuning, demonstrations, external specialist perception or grasp modules, privileged scene state, or predefined task policies, agents should select visual evidence, form task-relevant 3D estimates, construct manipulation targets, and iteratively execute and revise their policies. A shared robot API provides RGB observations, calibrated geometric operations, robot feedback, and bounded motion, leaving task-dependent decisions to the evaluated agent. Fixed task instances, resource budgets, and a hidden physical-outcome verifier support controlled comparisons across models and harness configurations. Extensive evaluations across nine configurations and 675 attempts achieve success rates ranging from 2.7% to 73.3%. The strongest configuration, GPT-6 Astra with Codex CLI, solves 22 of 25 tasks at least once in three attempts, demonstrating the best performance while still leaving substantial room for improvement. Trajectory analyses reveal difficulties in spatial alignment, object retention, and completion judgment, including task failures despite successfully completed motions. CodeActionBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring how general-purpose models translate their capabilities into manipulation behavior and for examining typical failure scenarios in that process.

AI.tldr: CodeActionBench is a 25-task benchmark evaluating general-purpose multimodal models' ability to perform embodied manipulation via agentic Code-as-Policy, without task-specific tuning, demonstrations, or privileged state. Across 675 attempts (9 configs), success ranges 2.7%–73.3%, with the best config (GPT-6 Astra with Codex CLI) solving 22/25 tasks at least once.
AI.motivation: General-purpose multimodal models show strong visual understanding and reasoning, but it remains unclear how well they can convert these capabilities into embodied manipulation through executable code. Existing evaluations often rely on task-specific fine-tuning, demonstrations, specialist perception/grasp modules, privileged scene state, or predefined policies, which conflates model capability with external scaffolding. CodeActionBench aims to isolate and measure this translation capability under controlled, scaffolding-free conditions.
AI.method: A benchmark of 25 manipulation tasks using an agentic Code-as-Policy paradigm. Agents receive no task-specific fine-tuning, demonstrations, external specialist perception or grasp modules, privileged scene state, or predefined policies; they must select visual evidence, form task-relevant 3D estimates, construct targets, and iteratively execute and revise policies. A shared robot API provides RGB observations, calibrated geometric operations, robot feedback, and bounded motion, leaving task-dependent decisions to the agent. Fixed task instances, resource budgets, and a hidden physical-outcome verifier enable controlled comparisons across models and harness configurations.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation across nine configurations and 675 attempts yields success rates from 2.7% to 73.3%. The strongest configuration, GPT-6 Astra with Codex CLI, solves 22 of 25 tasks at least once within three attempts, achieving the best performance while still leaving substantial room for improvement.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory analyses expose recurring difficulties in spatial alignment, object retention, and completion judgment, including failures where motions succeed but tasks fail. CodeActionBench offers a controlled testbed for measuring how general-purpose models translate their capabilities into manipulation behavior and for examining typical failure scenarios in that process.

title: Fail Loudly: An Auditable Runtime for Agentic Data Analysis
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled data-science agents to automate multi-step analyses over heterogeneous files. However, incorrect choices regarding data sources, scope, or statistical definitions often lead to silent errors: computations execute successfully but produce plausible yet incorrect outputs that fail to answer the intended question. To mitigate this, we present RADAR, an auditable runtime that makes an agent's analytical choices inspectable and supports their revision through execution feedback. RADAR operates through three core mechanisms. First, an evidence-preserving exploration module retrieves task-relevant content while retaining source locations and observation coverage. Next, the runtime uses typed operators to record the agent's declared inputs, operation arguments, and resulting observations. Finally, runtime validation checks proposed operations against these observations. When a conflict is detected, the runtime rejects the operation or provides diagnostic feedback, allowing the agent to revise its choices before errors propagate. This design enables agents to fail loudly while leaving semantic interpretation to the LLM. On KramaBench, RADAR achieves overall scores of 0.723 with full source retrieval and 0.747 with gold sources supplied, corresponding to relative gains of 35.9% and 28.8% over the strongest baselines. Beyond KramaBench, RADAR achieves relative performance gains of 14.0% on DA-Code and 59.3% on DABStep, demonstrating its applicability across diverse agentic data-analysis workflows.

AI.tldr: RADAR is an auditable runtime for LLM-based data-science agents that makes analytical choices inspectable and revisable via execution feedback, converting silent errors into loud failures and improving benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: LLM data-science agents automate multi-step analyses over heterogeneous files, but incorrect choices about data sources, scope, or statistical definitions cause silent errors—computation succeeds yet yields plausible but wrong outputs that miss the intended question.
AI.method: RADAR has three mechanisms: (1) an evidence-preserving exploration module that retrieves task-relevant content while retaining source locations and observation coverage; (2) typed operators that record the agent's declared inputs, operation arguments, and resulting observations; and (3) runtime validation that checks proposed operations against these observations, rejecting conflicting operations or providing diagnostic feedback so the agent can revise before errors propagate.
AI.result: On KramaBench, RADAR scores 0.723 with full source retrieval and 0.747 with gold sources, relative gains of 35.9% and 28.8% over the strongest baselines. It also gains 14.0% on DA-Code and 59.3% on DABStep.
AI.conclusion: RADAR enables agents to fail loudly while leaving semantic interpretation to the LLM, and generalizes across diverse agentic data-analysis workflows.

title: Achieve What You Imagined: Learning to Align Actions with Visual Plans
summary: World-action models can jointly predict future visual observations and robot actions. However, discrepancies may exist between their visual predictions and the consequences implied by generated actions. We observe that WAMs can often generate visually plausible task-completion outcomes before producing action sequences that reliably achieve them. Consequently, we treat the WAM-generated visual prediction as a goal-conditioned visual proposal rather than a directly executable plan. We use a frozen action-conditioned world model to predict action-conditioned consequences and construct feedback based on consistency between the two future predictions and alignment with the terminal goal. Leveraging this feedback, we employ Flow Policy Optimization (FPO) to optimize the action head of the WAM. This framework avoids online robot interaction and additional training of task-specific reward models. Across four real-world UR5 manipulation tasks, our method increases the mean success rate from 43.4% to 75.1%, compared with 61.4% for $π_{0.5}$. These results show that cross-model prediction discrepancy can provide useful feedback for improving robot policies under the evaluated manipulation tasks. Website: https://imagine-to-achieve.github.io/

AI.tldr: The paper reframes a World-Action Model's (WAM) visual prediction as a goal-conditioned visual proposal rather than an executable plan, and uses cross-model prediction discrepancy as feedback to optimize the WAM's action head via Flow Policy Optimization (FPO), raising real-world UR5 manipulation success from 43.4% to 75.1%.
AI.motivation: World-action models jointly predict future visual observations and robot actions, but their visual predictions and the consequences implied by generated actions can diverge. The authors observe that WAMs often produce visually plausible task-completion outcomes before generating action sequences that reliably achieve them, so the predicted visuals should not be treated as directly executable plans.
AI.method: The WAM-generated visual prediction is treated as a goal-conditioned visual proposal. A frozen action-conditioned world model predicts action-conditioned consequences, and feedback is constructed from consistency between the two future predictions and their alignment with the terminal goal. This feedback drives Flow Policy Optimization (FPO) to optimize the WAM's action head. The framework requires no online robot interaction and no task-specific reward model training.
AI.result: Across four real-world UR5 manipulation tasks, the method raises the mean success rate from 43.4% to 75.1%, compared to 61.4% for the π_0.5 baseline.
AI.conclusion: Cross-model prediction discrepancy can serve as useful feedback for improving robot policies on the evaluated manipulation tasks. Project website: https://imagine-to-achieve.github.io/

title: LLMAdBench: A Human Preference Benchmark for Advertising in LLM Responses
summary: Inserting advertisements (ads) into consumer-facing LLM output is emerging as a new business model, but there is little shared evidence on how such ad insertion should be evaluated or how it affects user preferences. We introduce LLMAdBench, a human-preference benchmark for studying advertising in LLM-generated content. The benchmark isolates a simple but practically important decision: given a user conversation, an LLM response, and a matched advertisement, where should the ad be placed? Our dataset compares pairs of responses that differ only in ad position while holding all other conditions fixed including the user query, base answer, advertisement, and disclosure condition. Human annotators evaluate each pair based on six criteria from both advertiser's and user's perspectives. The resulting benchmark contains more than 18000 human judgments across two disclosure conditions: explicitly labeling the ad as sponsored and merging it into the response without disclosure. We use LLMAdBench to evaluate eight frontier LLMs as preference judges and find that they are not reliable substitutes for human evaluation. Even the most stable models reverse roughly one quarter of their decisions when the presentation order is swapped, agreement across models is low, and their placement preferences differ systematically from those of human annotators. Moreover, LLMAdBench contains substantial learnable signal. In particular, a Qwen3-8B model fine-tuned on the human preferences improves substantially over its base model and outperforms all zero-shot frontier judges on the held-out prediction task. Beyond model evaluation, LLMAdBench provides quantitative evidence on the advertiser-user trade-off and shows that the sponsorship disclosure systematically changes users' preference over ad placement.

AI.tldr: LLMAdBench is a 18,000-judgment human-preference benchmark for evaluating where ads should be placed in LLM-generated responses, showing that frontier LLMs are unreliable ad-placement judges and that fine-tuning on human preferences substantially improves prediction.
AI.motivation: Inserting ads into consumer-facing LLM output is an emerging business model, yet there is little shared evidence on how ad insertion should be evaluated or how it affects user preferences. The work aims to establish a rigorous, reusable evaluation resource for this practically important decision.
AI.method: The authors build a paired-preference dataset that isolates a single variable: ad placement position. Each pair holds constant the user query, base answer, advertisement, and disclosure condition, differing only in ad position. Human annotators rate each pair on six criteria from both advertiser and user perspectives, yielding 18,000+ judgments across two disclosure conditions (explicit sponsorship labeling vs. undisclosed merging). Eight frontier LLMs are then evaluated as zero-shot preference judges, and a Qwen3-8B model is fine-tuned on the human preferences for the held-out prediction task.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs are unreliable substitutes for human evaluation: the most stable models reverse about one quarter of decisions under presentation-order swaps, inter-model agreement is low, and their placement preferences systematically deviate from human annotators. The benchmark contains substantial learnable signal—a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B substantially outperforms its base model and beats all zero-shot frontier judges on held-out prediction.
AI.conclusion: LLMAdBench provides quantitative evidence on the advertiser-user trade-off and shows that sponsorship disclosure systematically shifts users' preferences over ad placement. It serves as a shared benchmark and demonstrates that human preferences for ad placement are learnable, offering a path toward more reliable ad-placement evaluation.

title: DeltaSeek: Toward Active Perception in Evolving Construction Environments
summary: Construction environments evolve continuously, causing large geometric changes that degrade static mapping and registration performance. This necessitates active perception, where robots deliberately select sensing configurations to resolve the environment's current state. We present DeltaSeek, an initial framework toward active perception in evolving built environments. While our broader objective is a system that reasons about where, how, and when to observe, this paper addresses a critical prerequisite: how a robot's sensing embodiment constrains the observations it can acquire. We formalize an embodiment's permissible observation set and evaluate with a Husky A300 equipped with a UR5e on an IFC-derived benchmark under chassis-mounted and wrist-mounted RGB-D configurations, scoring observations by geometric visibility and effort by drivable distance. In a room-scale scene with eight controlled changes spanning four observability conditions, exhaustive evaluation over 240 permissible base poses and five arm postures shows that two changes admit no chassis viewpoint whatsoever, while the wrist camera resolves both. For changes observed by both embodiments, the median base travel is $6.0$~m for the wrist camera and $15.2$~m for the chassis camera. These results distinguish sensing limitations from acquisition costs, clarifying whether an observation is impossible or simply requires more travel.

AI.tldr: DeltaSeek is an initial framework for active perception in evolving built environments, formalizing how a robot's sensing embodiment constrains the observations it can acquire. Using a Husky A300 with a UR5e in chassis- vs wrist-mounted RGB-D setups, it shows embodiment choice determines whether changes are observable at all and at what travel cost.
AI.motivation: Construction environments evolve continuously, producing large geometric changes that degrade static mapping and registration. This calls for active perception, where robots deliberately select sensing configurations to resolve the environment's current state. Before reasoning about where, how, and when to observe, a prerequisite must be addressed: how a robot's sensing embodiment constrains the observations it can acquire.
AI.method: The paper formalizes an embodiment's permissible observation set and evaluates it on an IFC-derived benchmark with a Husky A300 equipped with a UR5e. Two RGB-D configurations are compared: chassis-mounted and wrist-mounted. Observations are scored by geometric visibility, and effort is measured by drivable distance. The evaluation is exhaustive over 240 permissible base poses and five arm postures in a room-scale scene with eight controlled changes spanning four observability conditions.
AI.result: Two of the eight changes admit no chassis viewpoint whatsoever, while the wrist camera resolves both. For changes observed by both embodiments, the median base travel is 6.0 m for the wrist camera versus 15.2 m for the chassis camera.
AI.conclusion: The results distinguish sensing limitations from acquisition costs, clarifying whether an observation is impossible or simply requires more travel. This supports embodiment-aware reasoning as a prerequisite for active perception in evolving built environments.

title: Interpretable Physics Informed WiFi Indoor Localization: Learning an Effective Access Point Geometry and Using It to Prune
summary:
Deep learning models can achieve high accuracy for indoor localization, but their black-box nature limits interpretability and the reuse of learned information. We propose a hierarchical deep learning framework for WiFi fingerprint-based indoor localization that jointly predicts user location and learns an effective geometry of the surrounding access points (APs). Physics-informed decoders infer this geometry directly from RSSI measurements and labelled user positions, without requiring the true AP coordinates during training. The learned geometry is then used to rank and prune APs.
  On the UJIIndoorLoc dataset, the proposed chained model achieves a mean 3D localization error of 7.07 m, reducing error by 26% to 36% compared with baseline models. Previously published methods evaluated on the same official split report errors 10.6% to 31.0% higher. Pruning 35% or 50% of the APs causes only a small loss in localization accuracy. The inferred geometry also enables Fisher-information-based AP ranking even when fingerprint databases do not contain surveyed AP coordinates. Experiments on the Tampere/TUT and UTSIndoorLoc datasets show that geometry-guided AP selection performs comparably to selectors built directly from labelled data. These results show that physics-informed interpretability can improve indoor localization while also supporting effective feature selection.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical, physics-informed deep learning framework for WiFi fingerprint indoor localization jointly predicts user position and infers AP geometry from RSSI and labels, enabling AP ranking/pruning without surveyed AP coordinates.
AI.motivation: Deep learning achieves high indoor localization accuracy but is a black box, limiting interpretability and reuse of learned information. The authors aim to embed physical structure so the model learns an interpretable AP geometry usable for feature selection.
AI.method: Hierarchical (chained) deep model with physics-informed decoders that infer AP geometry directly from RSSI measurements and labelled user positions, requiring no true AP coordinates during training. Learned geometry ranks/prunes APs; Fisher-information-based AP ranking is derived from it.
AI.result: On UJIIndoorLoc: mean 3D error 7.07 m, a 26-36% reduction vs baselines; prior published methods on the same split report 10.6-31.0% higher errors. Pruning 35-50% of APs yields only small accuracy loss. On Tampere/TUT and UTSIndoorLoc, geometry-guided AP selection is comparable to selectors built from labelled data.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed interpretability improves indoor localization accuracy while supporting effective, coordinate-free AP feature selection, generalizing across datasets.

title: Robot-GST: geometry-aware spatial-temporal robot policy representation and evaluation
summary: Robotic manipulation policies are advancing rapidly with increasing reliance on vision-language models for end-to-end decision making. However, reliable deployment remains challenging because many policies lack explicit mechanisms for predicting task outcomes and evaluating whether generated actions will achieve desired final states, causing execution errors to accumulate during long-horizon manipulation. We present Robot-GST, a geometry-aware spatio-temporal behaviour representation and evaluation framework that constructs a Gaussian-SAM robotic environment for real-to-sim policy verification and improves the reliability of real-world manipulation deployment. Our approach constructs a high-fidelity robotic environment from RGB-D observations using 3D Gaussian Splatting and SAM3D, enabling ``simulation and evaluation before acting''. It integrates visual observations and language instructions with spatio-temporal reasoning for long-horizon task planning using large vision-language models. To bridge high-level planning and real-world execution, we introduce Gaussian-aware final-state estimation through geometric sampling and state-based trajectory planning. Before execution, candidate action sequences are simulated and evaluated in the Gaussian-SAM environment to filter infeasible behaviours. We validate our approach on representative manipulation tasks involving rigid, soft, and deformable objects, including cube placing, toy packing, and duck rearrangement, demonstrating that geometry-aware spatio-temporal reasoning and state-aware execution improve manipulation reliability across different object categories. Our results suggest that combining geometry-aware reconstruction with high-quality rendering and simulation provides a scalable approach for evaluating robotic manipulation behaviours. Website: https://robot-gst.github.io

AI.tldr: Robot-GST is a geometry-aware spatio-temporal behaviour representation and evaluation framework that builds a Gaussian-SAM robotic environment from RGB-D observations for real-to-sim policy verification, enabling simulation and evaluation before real-world execution.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation policies increasingly rely on vision-language models for end-to-end decision making, but reliable deployment remains difficult because many policies lack explicit mechanisms for predicting task outcomes and evaluating whether generated actions will achieve desired final states, causing errors to accumulate during long-horizon manipulation.
AI.method: The framework constructs a high-fidelity robotic environment from RGB-D observations using 3D Gaussian Splatting and SAM3D. It integrates visual observations and language instructions with spatio-temporal reasoning for long-horizon task planning via large vision-language models. To bridge high-level planning and real-world execution, it introduces Gaussian-aware final-state estimation through geometric sampling and state-based trajectory planning; candidate action sequences are simulated and evaluated in the Gaussian-SAM environment to filter infeasible behaviours.
AI.result: Validated on manipulation tasks with rigid, soft, and deformable objects, including cube placing, toy packing, and duck rearrangement, showing that geometry-aware spatio-temporal reasoning and state-aware execution improve manipulation reliability across object categories.
AI.conclusion: Combining geometry-aware reconstruction with high-quality rendering and simulation offers a scalable approach for evaluating robotic manipulation behaviours, improving real-world deployment reliability.

title: Porimon: An LLM-Based Pokémon Battle Agent Enhanced by Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation
summary: In this paper, we use Pokémon Battles as a case study to investigate how to improve the performance of LLM-based agents in tasks that require opponent-aware planning without additional fine-tuning. We propose Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation (LSTKAG), a mechanism that enables LLM-based agents to leverage past states of the current task and retrieve experience summaries from similar previous task instances based on the current state. Based on LSTKAG, we design Porimon, an LLM-based agent structure for Pokémon Battles. For optimization, we introduce an external API for precise damage calculation and more detailed information about the game. We conduct tournament-like evaluation experiments comprising 15,000 battles for hyperparameter optimization, ablation studies, and performance evaluation. The results indicate that Porimon-based players with hyperparameter optimization significantly outperform players based on PokéLLMon, an LLM-based agent structure proposed in previous research, and the rule-based heuristic player. Furthermore, our ablation study shows that Porimon variants outperform the one without extension in game information retrieval, which shows the contribution of that extension. However, the current experiment results are inconclusive regarding the contribution of Long-Term KAG. These results suggest that introducing external resources, information from previous states of the current task, and experience summaries from similar previous task instances could elevate the performance of LLM-based agents designed for tasks requiring opponent-aware planning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation (LSTKAG) and an LLM-based agent structure called Porimon for opponent-aware planning in Pokémon Battles, showing that Porimon with hyperparameter optimization outperforms prior LLM-based and heuristic players.
AI.motivation: Improving LLM-based agents' performance on tasks requiring opponent-aware planning without additional fine-tuning, using Pokémon Battles as a case study.
AI.method: LSTKAG enables agents to use past states of the current task and retrieve experience summaries from similar previous task instances based on current state. Porimon is built on LSTKAG for Pokémon Battles, with an external API for precise damage calculation and detailed game information.
AI.result: In 15,000 tournament-like battles, Porimon with hyperparameter optimization significantly outperformed PokéLLMon and a rule-based heuristic player. Ablation shows Porimon variants outperform those without extended game information retrieval, but results are inconclusive on Long-Term KAG contribution.
AI.conclusion: Introducing external resources, prior-state information, and experience summaries from similar tasks can elevate performance of LLM-based agents for opponent-aware planning tasks.

title: DexTaG: Tactile-as-Guidance in Reinforcement Learning for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Glove-based motion capture is emerging as a scalable approach to collecting dexterous-hand demonstration data. However, due to the kinematic gap between the human and robot hand, the recorded human motions cannot be executed directly on the robot, especially for contact-rich tool-use tasks involving in-hand reorientation. Prior work bridges this gap in simulation through reinforcement learning (RL) or trajectory optimization, but the human contact pattern is hard to preserve under such formulations, often producing unnatural manipulation and unstable functional grasps. These methods also train a separate policy or solve a separate optimization for each reference trajectory, which is inefficient. To solve these problems, we propose DexTaG, a tactile-guided RL framework for dexterous manipulation. During training, tactile signals captured by the glove guide policy search toward the measured human contact pattern, reducing reliance on precise reference geometry for contact supervision. To improve efficiency, we train a single generalizable retargeter jointly on all training trajectories of the same object. The retargeter is further distilled into a tactile-free student controller conditioned on the target object trajectory for real-world deployment. On marker-pen and hammer manipulation tasks, DexTaG learns natural, contact-rich behaviors that baselines with distance-based contact heuristics fail to learn, generalizes to held-out trajectories of the same object and task, and outperforms single-trajectory baselines on OakInk2.

AI.tldr: DexTaG is a tactile-guided RL framework that retargets gloved human hand motion to a robot hand, using glove-recorded tactile signals to steer policy search toward human contact patterns, training one generalizable retargeter per object, and distilling it into a tactile-free student controller for real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Glove-based motion capture enables scalable collection of dexterous-hand demonstrations, but the kinematic gap between human and robot hands prevents direct execution of captured motions on robots, particularly for contact-rich tool-use tasks with in-hand reorientation. Existing RL or trajectory-optimization retargeting in simulation struggles to preserve human contact patterns, yielding unnatural manipulation and unstable functional grasps. Moreover, these methods train a separate policy or solve a separate optimization per reference trajectory, which is inefficient.
AI.method: DexTaG uses tactile signals from the glove to guide policy search toward the measured human contact pattern, reducing dependence on precise reference geometry for contact supervision. To improve efficiency, a single generalizable retargeter is trained jointly on all training trajectories of the same object. This retargeter is then distilled into a tactile-free student controller conditioned on the target object trajectory for real-world deployment.
AI.result: On marker-pen and hammer manipulation tasks, DexTaG learns natural, contact-rich behaviors that distance-based contact heuristic baselines fail to learn. It generalizes to held-out trajectories of the same object and task, and outperforms single-trajectory baselines on OakInk2.
AI.conclusion: Tactile-guided RL with a shared, generalizable retargeter and tactile-free student distillation provides an effective and efficient route for transferring gloved human demonstrations to robot hands, producing natural contact-rich manipulation that generalizes across trajectories of the same object and task.

title: Are Vision-Language-Action Models Robust to One-Step Observation Perturbations?
summary: Understanding the safety risks of vision-language-action (VLA) models is essential for their deployment in the physical world. Existing safety research has mainly considered persistent perturbations that are applied continuously to observations throughout an episode. However, momentary observation corruption, in which observations are severely perturbed only briefly within an episode, remains an underexplored safety threat. To address this gap, this work investigates robustness to one-step perturbations applied at a single time step per episode. Our experiments reveal that these perturbations substantially degrade VLA performance and that their impact depends on the action chunk execution length. Based on them, we propose CARE, which dynamically selects the execution length based on consistency with the previously predicted action chunk. CARE improves robustness with low computational overhead while preserving clean performance by selecting shorter execution lengths only under perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies momentary (one-step) observation corruption as an underexplored safety threat to vision-language-action (VLA) models, shows that such perturbations severely degrade performance and that their impact depends on action chunk execution length, and proposes CARE, a method that dynamically selects execution length based on consistency with the previously predicted action chunk.
AI.motivation: Existing safety research on VLA models focuses mainly on persistent perturbations applied continuously to observations throughout an episode. The threat of momentary observation corruption—severe perturbation applied only briefly within an episode—remains underexplored, despite its relevance to safe deployment of VLA models in the physical world.
AI.method: The authors investigate robustness to one-step perturbations applied at a single time step per episode, and analyze how their impact depends on the action chunk execution length. Building on these findings, they propose CARE, which dynamically selects the execution length based on consistency with the previously predicted action chunk, choosing shorter execution lengths only under perturbations.
AI.result: One-step perturbations at a single time step substantially degrade VLA performance, and their impact is dependent on the action chunk execution length.
AI.conclusion: CARE improves robustness to momentary observation corruption with low computational overhead while preserving clean performance, since shorter execution lengths are selected only under perturbations.

title: Residual Learning-Based Control of Vehicle Platoons with $\ell_2$ Stability Guarantees via Recurrent Equilibrium Networks
comment: Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC)
summary: This paper proposes a residual learning-based control framework for heterogeneous vehicle platoons subject to parametric uncertainty and external disturbances. A nominal controller designed via Linear Matrix Inequalities (LMIs), along with disturbance-observer compensation, is enhanced by a Recurrent Equilibrium Network (REN) trained offline using stored trajectories and nominal-model prediction errors. The REN is constrained to satisfy a prescribed $\ell_2$-gain bound, enabling sufficient small-gain conditions for local closed-loop stability and disturbance string stability. Experiments demonstrate reduced spacing and velocity errors relative to the nominal controller.

AI.tldr: A residual learning framework combines an LMI-based nominal controller with disturbance-observer compensation and a Recurrent Equilibrium Network (REN) to control heterogeneous vehicle platoons under parametric uncertainty and disturbances, achieving improved spacing and velocity tracking.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous vehicle platoons face parametric uncertainty and external disturbances, which degrade spacing and velocity regulation. A purely nominal controller may not fully compensate these effects, motivating a learning-augmented residual approach.
AI.method: A nominal controller is designed via Linear Matrix Inequalities (LMIs) with disturbance-observer compensation. A Recurrent Equilibrium Network (REN) is trained offline using stored trajectories and nominal-model prediction errors, and is constrained to satisfy a prescribed l2-gain bound, which enables sufficient small-gain conditions for local closed-loop stability and disturbance string stability.
AI.result: Experiments show reduced spacing and velocity errors compared with the nominal controller.
AI.conclusion: The residual learning-based control framework enhances heterogeneous platoon performance while providing stability and string-stability guarantees via the REN's l2-gain constraint.

title: Artificial intelligences and human scientists exhibit complementary strengths in theory building
summary: We investigate the effectiveness of artificial intelligences (AI)-specifically large language models (LLMs)-relative to human scientists at high-level cognitive tasks in social science such as theory formulation, predictions of novel empirical results, and theory revision in response to new evidence. The research domain was academic discourse regarding gender and race inequality. Our findings, comparing 25 LLMs with 13 senior researchers and 60 doctoral scholars, reveal that the AIs outperformed most humans individually on most of the present tasks, while human theories were more diverse and exhibited greater gains in predictive accuracy from aggregation. AI-generated theories were more extensively elaborated, involving additional theoretical paths and latent variables, and were rated as higher quality than human theories by independent raters blinded to source. However, this theoretical complexity was in part ornamental, in that it was not associated with more accurate predictions about empirical patterns in data; in contrast, human scientists achieved greater predictive efficiency with simpler theories. The AIs were significantly more likely than human scientists to revise their theories to incorporate new evidence; human scientists updated their beliefs in a selective way that is sensitive to prior prediction errors. We speculate that the superior processing capacity of artificial intelligences makes them especially well-suited to tasks requiring grappling with complexity, but that the greater diversity of human ideas is essential to wise crowds and collective creativity.

AI.tldr: Comparing 25 LLMs against 73 human scientists on theory formulation, prediction, and revision in gender/race inequality research, AIs outperformed most humans individually and produced higher-rated, more elaborated theories, but this complexity was partly ornamental; human theories were more diverse, aggregated better, and achieved greater predictive efficiency with simpler theories.
AI.motivation: To test whether AI (specifically LLMs) can match or exceed human scientists on high-level cognitive tasks in social science—theory formulation, prediction of novel empirical results, and theory revision—an open question given rapid LLM capability gains.
AI.method: Benchmark comparison in the domain of academic discourse on gender and race inequality: 25 LLMs vs. 13 senior researchers and 60 doctoral scholars, assessed on theory formulation, predictions of novel empirical results, and theory revision in response to new evidence. Theories were rated for quality by independent raters blinded to source; aggregation and predictive accuracy/efficiency were also analyzed.
AI.result: AIs outperformed most humans individually on most tasks. Human theories were more diverse and showed greater gains in predictive accuracy from aggregation. AI theories were more extensively elaborated (more theoretical paths and latent variables) and rated higher quality by blinded raters, but this complexity was partly ornamental—not linked to more accurate predictions. Humans achieved greater predictive efficiency with simpler theories. AIs revised theories to incorporate new evidence significantly more often; humans updated selectively, sensitive to prior prediction errors.
AI.conclusion: AI's superior processing capacity makes it especially suited to complexity-heavy tasks, whereas the greater diversity of human ideas remains essential for wise crowds and collective creativity.

title: ArticulateArena: A Metric for Articulated Kinematics
summary: Modern methods reconstruct or generate simulation-ready articulated objects, predicting not only their geometry but also how their parts are connected and allowed to move. Evaluating the geometry is straightforward, but evaluating the predicted articulation is not, because articulation specifies a motion rather than a shape, and there is no agreed distance between two motions. More specifically, existing protocols score joint type, axis direction, origin, and motion limits separately, although these parameters jointly describe a single physical motion, and the same motion can be written as different parameter values. As a result, a joint can score maximally wrong against an equivalent encoding of itself, and several component errors are ill-conditioned or undefined exactly where predictions become accurate. We propose ArticulateArena, a representation-invariant counterpart of Chamfer distance for articulation that compares the motions one-DOF joints induce rather than the parameters that encode them. It represents each joint by the unordered pair of its Lie-algebra endpoint twists, and we prove that the resulting quotient distance is a metric. It unifies fixed, revolute, prismatic, and helical joints, brings continuous joints into the same score through a compactification, and reads as the RMS motion of the moving part in meters when weighted by its mass distribution. A motion-aware tree edit distance lifts the metric to full kinematic trees, pricing structural errors such as spurious or missing joints in the same motion units as joint errors, and for a fixed inner product it remains a metric on trees up to relabeling. Alongside the metric we release ArticulateArena-20K, a new suite of 19,977 articulated objects with verified kinematics, and we re-evaluate published reconstruction methods on it under the new metric. Project page: https://heyumeng.com/ArticulateArena-web/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ArticulateArena, a representation-invariant metric for evaluating predicted articulation of articulated objects, analogous to Chamfer distance for geometry, defined via Lie-algebra endpoint twists, extended to full kinematic trees with a motion-aware tree edit distance, and accompanied by a new 19,977-object benchmark.
AI.motivation: Evaluating reconstructed or generated articulated objects is difficult for articulation, unlike geometry, because articulation specifies a motion rather than a shape and there is no agreed distance between motions.
