Existing protocols score joint type, axis direction, origin, and motion limits separately, even though these jointly describe one physical motion and equivalent motions can have different parameter encodings. This causes a joint to score maximally wrong against an equivalent encoding of itself, and component errors are ill-conditioned or undefined where predictions become accurate.
AI.method: The authors propose ArticulateArena, a representation-invariant counterpart of Chamfer distance that compares the motions one-DOF joints induce instead of their encoding parameters. Each joint is represented by the unordered pair of its Lie-algebra endpoint twists; the resulting quotient distance is proven to be a metric. It unifies fixed, revolute, prismatic, and helical joints, incorporates continuous joints via compactification, and reads as the RMS motion of the moving part in meters when weighted by mass distribution. A motion-aware tree edit distance lifts the metric to full kinematic trees, pricing structural errors like spurious or missing joints in the same motion units, and remains a metric on trees up to relabeling for a fixed inner product.
AI.result: The method yields a proven metric over joint motions, handles all standard one-DOF joint types uniformly, and extends to kinematic trees. The authors release ArticulateArena-20K, a suite of 19,977 articulated objects with verified kinematics, and re-evaluate published reconstruction methods on it under the new metric.
AI.conclusion: ArticulateArena provides a principled, representation-invariant evaluation for articulation in articulated-object reconstruction and generation, addressing the shortcomings of component-wise parameter scoring, and is supported by a large verified benchmark and re-evaluation of existing methods.

title: ProTTT: Learning to Learn Semantic User Memory with Test-Time Training
summary: Personalization requires language models to capture user-specific knowledge from a growing user history. Existing context-based approaches incur increasing inference costs as user history accumulates and rely on separate retrieval or summarization stages, while parametric-based approaches often require reconstructing user representations when new user data is added. We introduce ProTTT, a profile-supervised meta-learning framework for learning semantic user memory. The memory construction starts from a shared initialization and is updated for each user through test-time training on user history, allowing it to evolve continuously as the history grows. However, since test-time training alone does not explicitly encourage the memory to capture semantic user knowledge necessary for personalization, we learn this shared initialization using textual user profiles as supervision, so that test-time training on user history captures semantic knowledge more effectively. ProTTT consistently outperforms both full history ICL and all parametric baselines across diverse benchmarks, while substantially reducing inference cost by compressing user history into a lightweight parameterized memory. Our analysis also shows that profile supervision is a reliable objective for learning semantic user knowledge and that the resulting memory can track and retain evolving user preferences, while remaining robust across different history sizes. Overall, we demonstrate the effectiveness of test-time training for personalization and establish ProTTT as a baseline for continuously evolving user memory.

AI.tldr: ProTTT is a profile-supervised meta-learning framework that learns a semantic user memory via test-time training on user history, starting from a shared initialization. It outperforms full-history ICL and parametric baselines while cutting inference cost by compressing history into lightweight parameters.
AI.motivation: Personalization requires language models to capture user-specific knowledge from growing user history. Existing context-based approaches scale inference cost with history and rely on separate retrieval/summarization, while parametric approaches need to reconstruct user representations whenever new user data arrives.
AI.method: ProTTT builds a semantic user memory that starts from a shared initialization and is updated per user via test-time training on that user's history, evolving continuously as history grows. To ensure the memory captures semantic user knowledge, the shared initialization is meta-learned using textual user profiles as supervision, so test-time training on history captures semantic knowledge more effectively.
AI.result: ProTTT consistently outperforms full history ICL and all parametric baselines across diverse benchmarks while substantially reducing inference cost by compressing user history into lightweight parameterized memory. Analysis shows profile supervision is a reliable objective for learning semantic user knowledge, and the resulting memory tracks and retains evolving user preferences while remaining robust across different history sizes.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the effectiveness of test-time training for personalization and establishes ProTTT as a baseline for continuously evolving user memory.

title: EpiTransfer: Sparse, Training-Free Long-Range Depth Estimation from Temporal Monocular Aerial Frames
summary: Reliable 3D spatial understanding is essential for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and scene reconstruction. While state-of-the-art learned depth estimation techniques achieve high accuracy in-distribution, they often generalize poorly to novel viewpoints and altitudes. This paper presents a geometrically derived, training-free depth estimation method using epipolar transfer with only two monocular images and camera pose estimates. By leveraging camera motion to synthesize a virtual stereo pair with a freely chosen baseline, our approach transforms temporal correspondence into a stereo triangulation task while mitigating geometric degeneracies inherent to direct two-view triangulation. Validated across outdoor drone flights (to a maximum range of approximately 90\,m) and indoor OptiTrack environments against LiDAR ground truth, the method achieves an indoor AbsRel of 0.092 and $δ< 1.25$ of 0.940, comparable to direct triangulation (AbsRel 0.073) while retaining valid depth over a larger fraction of challenging scenes, and substantially outperforms off-the-shelf learning-based baselines such as ZoeDepth (AbsRel 0.225) and Depth Anything V2 (AbsRel 0.570), which are not trained or fine-tuned for this domain, with no training data required.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training-free depth estimation method based on epipolar transfer that uses two monocular images and camera pose to synthesize a virtual stereo pair, achieving robust generalization across novel viewpoints and altitudes without any training data.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art learned depth estimation methods achieve high in-distribution accuracy but generalize poorly to novel viewpoints and altitudes. Reliable 3D spatial understanding is essential for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and scene reconstruction, creating a need for a method that generalizes beyond training distributions.
AI.method: A geometrically derived, training-free depth estimation approach using epipolar transfer with only two monocular images and camera pose estimates. Camera motion is leveraged to synthesize a virtual stereo pair with a freely chosen baseline, transforming temporal correspondence into a stereo triangulation task while mitigating geometric degeneracies inherent to direct two-view triangulation.
AI.result: Validated on outdoor drone flights (up to ~90 m range) and indoor OptiTrack environments against LiDAR ground truth. Achieves indoor AbsRel of 0.092 and δ<1.25 of 0.940, comparable to direct triangulation (AbsRel 0.073) while retaining valid depth over a larger fraction of challenging scenes. Substantially outperforms learning-based baselines ZoeDepth (AbsRel 0.225) and Depth Anything V2 (AbsRel 0.570), which are not trained or fine-tuned for this domain.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free geometric method delivers depth estimation performance comparable to direct triangulation and far superior to off-the-shelf learning-based baselines, while requiring no training data and generalizing robustly across novel viewpoints and altitudes.

title: CUE-Mem: Benchmarking Long-Term User Memory via Implicit Cues in Multimodal Conversations
comment: 28 pages. Submitted to AAAI 2027. Code: https://github.com/yulinlp/CUE-MEM. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Kkryptonite/CUE-Mem
summary: Long-term memory is essential for multimodal agents that interact with users across sustained conversations. However, user memories are not always explicitly stated: they may also be implied by recurring background objects in images, ambient sounds in audio, or other peripheral multimodal cues. Existing benchmarks largely focus on text-only memory or explicit multimodal evidence, leaving implicit multimodal cues underexplored. We introduce CUE-Mem, a text-image-audio benchmark for evaluating long-term user memory from implicit cues. CUE-Mem contains 2,674 questions across explicit and implicit evidence settings and covers four tasks: Entity Recall, Long Pattern, Personalized Recommendation, and Answer Refusal. Across textualized memory systems, implicit performance remains far below oracle evidence, locating the main bottleneck in preserving and retrieving subtle cues rather than question answerability. Increasing caption detail recovers more of this evidence, but brings uneven gains and rapidly growing token costs, motivating native multimodal access. Yet native access does not uniformly resolve the bottleneck: evidence use depends strongly on the backbone, while multimodal indexing introduces substantial retrieval noise. CUE-Mem provides a testbed for memory systems that selectively retain, retrieve, and use subtle multimodal evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CUE-Mem, a text-image-audio benchmark with 2,674 questions spanning explicit and implicit multimodal evidence across four memory tasks, to evaluate long-term user memory in multimodal agents and reveal the bottleneck in preserving and retrieving subtle implicit cues.
AI.motivation: Long-term memory is essential for multimodal agents in sustained conversations, but user memories are not always explicitly stated—they can be implied by recurring background objects, ambient sounds, or other peripheral cues. Existing benchmarks focus on text-only memory or explicit multimodal evidence, leaving implicit multimodal cues underexplored, so a dedicated benchmark is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct CUE-Mem, a text-image-audio benchmark containing 2,674 questions across explicit and implicit evidence settings, covering four tasks: Entity Recall, Long Pattern, Personalized Recommendation, and Answer Refusal. They evaluate textualized memory systems against oracle evidence and study the effect of caption detail and native multimodal access.
AI.result: For textualized memory systems, implicit performance remains far below oracle evidence, locating the bottleneck in preserving and retrieving subtle cues rather than question answerability. Increasing caption detail recovers more evidence but yields uneven gains and rapidly growing token costs. Native multimodal access does not uniformly resolve the bottleneck: evidence use depends strongly on the backbone, and multimodal indexing introduces substantial retrieval noise.
AI.conclusion: CUE-Mem provides a testbed for memory systems that must selectively retain, retrieve, and use subtle multimodal evidence, highlighting that implicit-cue memory remains an open challenge requiring better backbone-dependent evidence use and reduced multimodal indexing noise.

title: ReSync: Re-Aligning the Two Clocks of Asynchronous World-Action Models
summary: Jointly generating future video and actions has become a standard recipe for world-action models, and the strongest systems denoise the two streams on separate schedules: actions are decoded in few steps so control stays fast, while the video stream runs longer to keep the predicted future sharp. The design is deliberate, but it leaves the two streams on different clocks, and an action can become executable while the future that should justify it is still largely unresolved. We formalize this as a two-clock view of asynchronous inference and introduce the commitment-evidence gap, a quantity read directly from a model's own sampling schedule rather than measured by search. The gap is predictive: as it widens, candidate utility becomes harder to identify and extra candidate sampling buys less, while advancing the world stream buys more, and the two cross. Spending more world computation is therefore not simply better. The useful interval is closed at both ends, and both ends can be read off the schedule before any rollout. ReSync places the computation inside it: hold the action state, advance only the world within the supported window, then resume native denoising. No parameters change and no candidates are compared. On a frozen paired RoboCasa panel this improves success by 4.48 points, while an equal-compute control that waits without advancing the world does not move, and the same rule transfers to a second benchmark and a second backbone without retuning.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes asynchronous joint video-action generation as a "two-clock" inference problem, introduces the "commitment-evidence gap" readable from the sampling schedule, and proposes ReSync, a training-free inference rule that advances only the world stream within a schedule-derived window to improve action success.
AI.motivation: World-action models typically denoise actions and video on separate schedules: actions are decoded in few steps for fast control, while video runs longer for sharpness. This deliberate design puts the two streams on different clocks, so an action can become executable before the future that justifies it is resolved. The authors aim to characterize and exploit this asynchrony rather than ignore it.
AI.method: The authors formalize a two-clock view of asynchronous inference and define the commitment-evidence gap, a quantity read directly from the model's own sampling schedule rather than via search. They show the gap is predictive: wider gaps make candidate utility harder to identify, so extra candidate sampling yields diminishing returns while advancing the world stream yields more, and the two effects cross. This defines a closed useful interval readable before any rollout. ReSync places computation inside this interval: it holds the action state, advances only the world within the supported window, then resumes native denoising, with no parameter changes and no candidate comparison.
AI.result: On a frozen paired RoboCasa panel, ReSync improves success by 4.48 points. An equal-compute control that waits without advancing the world does not move. The same rule transfers to a second benchmark and a second backbone without retuning.
AI.conclusion: Spending more world computation is not simply better: the useful interval is closed at both ends, and both ends are predictable from the schedule before any rollout. ReSync exploits this window to improve success in a training-free, parameter-free, single-sample manner, and generalizes across benchmarks and backbones.

title: EMIR$^2$: Evolution-Aware Memory with Intent-Guided Multi-Round Retrieval
summary: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to leverage historical interactions for future tasks. However, existing memory systems struggle to utilize continuously evolving historical information, as they often rely on static memory representations and single-round retrieval strategies, failing to track factual changes or integrate distributed evidence across long-term interactions. To address these challenges, we propose \textsc{EMIR}$^{2}$, an \textbf{E}volution-Aware \textbf{M}emory framework with \textbf{I}ntent-Guided Multi-\textbf{R}ound \textbf{R}etrieval, enabling LLM agents to maintain evolving historical knowledge and adaptively retrieve relevant evidence. Specifically, \textsc{EMIR}$^{2}$ constructs a State-Evolving Memory Graph (SEMG) that represents long-term memory as evolving knowledge states supported by temporal event trajectories and evidential associations. By maintaining semantic states through evidence-based updates, SEMG preserves historical evolution and enables evidence tracing under complex and conflicting scenarios. Building upon this, we introduce an intent-guided multi-round retrieval mechanism that iteratively identifies missing evidence and expands retrieval based on accumulated information. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemConflict demonstrate that \textsc{EMIR}$^{2}$ improves long-term memory utilization, dynamic and static conflict handling, and complex retrieval performance, achieving relative improvements of more than 12\% in certain categories. These results highlight the effectiveness of jointly modeling memory evolution and adaptive evidence acquisition for long-term agent interactions.

AI.tldr: EMIR² is an evolution-aware memory framework with intent-guided multi-round retrieval that helps LLM agents maintain evolving historical knowledge and adaptively gather evidence, outperforming existing memory systems on long-term interaction benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems struggle to exploit continuously evolving historical information because they rely on static memory representations and single-round retrieval, which fail to track factual changes or integrate distributed evidence across long-term interactions.
AI.method: EMIR² builds a State-Evolving Memory Graph (SEMG) that models long-term memory as evolving knowledge states supported by temporal event trajectories and evidential associations, preserving historical evolution via evidence-based semantic state updates. It adds an intent-guided multi-round retrieval mechanism that iteratively identifies missing evidence and expands retrieval based on accumulated information.
AI.result: Experiments on LoCoMo and MemConflict show EMIR² improves long-term memory utilization, dynamic and static conflict handling, and complex retrieval, with relative gains exceeding 12% in certain categories.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling memory evolution and adaptive evidence acquisition is effective for long-term agent interactions.

title: Integrity Detection and Characterization of Malicious Injections in RAVEN II
summary:
The increasing adoption of robotic systems in surgery, together with the expanding range of procedures they can support and the growing level of autonomy they provide, has substantially increased the complexity of surgical robots. As these systems integrate more sensors, controllers, communication interfaces, and model-driven control components, their attack surface continues to expand. A compromise of the integrity of a surgical robot can therefore cause unintended robot behavior and potentially threaten patient safety.
  In this paper, we characterize the detection boundary of malicious injections on RAVEN II using a public dataset that pairs the platform's telemetry with external high-resolution encoder ground truth. We identify three injection points spanning the command and observation paths and evaluate three injection patterns with increasing temporal dispersion. To capture different detection behaviors, we perform detection at two timescales: the window scale and the session scale. Rather than reporting detection rates at an arbitrarily chosen threshold, we quantify, for each injection point and injection pattern, the smallest end-effector deviation that can be resolved while maintaining an alarm rate acceptable for surgical operation. Our results show that detectability is strongly influenced by how the injected deviation is distributed over time. An abrupt step can be detected at deviations well below the 1 mm clinical tolerance, whereas the same overall deviation spread across a window or a session can remain hidden from single-window statistics. The open source code can be found at http://github.com/RAVENIIROS/RAVENIIIntegrity.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the detection boundary of malicious command/observation injections on the RAVEN II surgical robot, quantifying the smallest end-effector deviation detectable at window and session timescales while keeping alarm rates surgically acceptable.
AI.motivation: Surgical robots are increasingly complex, integrating sensors, controllers, communication interfaces, and model-driven components, which expands their attack surface. Compromising a surgical robot's integrity can cause unintended behavior and threaten patient safety, yet the limits of detecting malicious injections on such platforms are not well understood.
AI.method: Using a public RAVEN II dataset pairing platform telemetry with external high-resolution encoder ground truth, the authors identify three injection points across the command and observation paths and evaluate three injection patterns with increasing temporal dispersion. Detection is performed at two timescales: window scale and session scale. Instead of reporting detection rates at an arbitrary threshold, they quantify, per injection point and pattern, the smallest resolvable end-effector deviation subject to an alarm rate acceptable for surgical operation.
AI.result: Detectability depends strongly on how an injected deviation is distributed over time. An abrupt step is detectable at deviations well below the 1 mm clinical tolerance, whereas the same overall deviation spread across a window or session can evade single-window statistics.
AI.conclusion: The temporal dispersion of an injected deviation, not just its magnitude, governs detectability on RAVEN II. Session-scale analysis is needed to expose slowly distributed injections that window-scale statistics miss, and detection thresholds should be framed in terms of clinically acceptable alarm rates. Open-source code is available at http://github.com/RAVENIIROS/RAVENIIIntegrity.

title: MA-FPPO: Multi-Agent Flow-Pretrained Policy Optimization
summary: Multi-agent flow policies learn cooperative behavior from fixed offline datasets, but often struggle to complete tasks in situations not covered by the offline data. In these situations, agents must both adapt to changes in the environment and coordinate with one another, yet action patterns learned offline are often insufficient for effective adaptation and coordination. To address this problem, we propose Multi-Agent Flow-Pretrained Policy Optimization (MA-FPPO), which uses online fine-tuning to improve the cooperative behavior of models pretrained with flow matching through new interactions with the environment. Building on the behavior learned during pretraining, we construct policies with explicit action likelihoods for discrete and continuous action spaces. We then update the pretrained model using shared team advantages to further improve coordination based on team performance. Our method achieves, on average, relative gains of 52.8% over the strongest listed offline baselines across 30 settings and 29.8% over purely online learning across 38 comparisons with matched online budgets and evaluation protocols.

AI.tldr: MA-FPPO improves pretrained multi-agent flow policies via online fine-tuning, yielding 52.8% gains over offline baselines and 29.8% over online learning.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent flow policies trained from fixed offline datasets struggle in out-of-distribution situations, where agents must simultaneously adapt to environmental changes and coordinate. Offline-learned action patterns are insufficient for this adaptation and coordination.
AI.method: The authors propose Multi-Agent Flow-Pretrained Policy Optimization (MA-FPPO). It uses online fine-tuning of flow-matching-pretrained models through new environment interactions. Policies with explicit action likelihoods are constructed for both discrete and continuous action spaces, and the pretrained model is updated using shared team advantages to improve coordination based on team performance.
AI.result: MA-FPPO achieves an average 52.8% relative gain over the strongest listed offline baselines across 30 settings, and 29.8% over purely online learning across 38 comparisons with matched online budgets and evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: Online fine-tuning of flow-pretrained multi-agent policies with team-level advantages effectively addresses out-of-distribution adaptation and coordination, outperforming both offline baselines and matched-budget online learning.

title: FINGR: Learning Dexterous Hand Control for Real-World Rubik's Cube Solving
summary: Manipulating a Rubik's Cube with a single dexterous hand is a challenging test of sustained, contact-rich control: the hand must execute successive layer turns while keeping the cube secure. Each turn requires some fingers to support the cube while others push a moving layer, release contact, and reset for the next move. To learn this coordination, we introduce FINGR (Future-supervised Interaction Network with Geometric Representations), a policy that combines finger-relative geometry with future interaction prediction. A shared point encoder expresses the cube relative to each fingertip and aggregates its points without depending on cubie indexing. Learned future tokens share the observation encoder and receive supervision for contact-force changes, layer-turn progress, and finger joint displacement at multiple time scales. The resulting representation conditions a flow policy that directly generates finger actions. On a real dexterous hand, our policy achieves 99.0% success over 300 turn attempts, compared with 79.7% for the base flow policy. Integrated with grasping and table-assisted regrasping, the policy solves all ten scrambled $2\times2\times2$ cubes in a mean complete-system time of approximately 137 seconds. The project website is available at https://www.lyt0112.com/projects/FINGR

AI.tldr: FINGR is a flow-matching policy that augments finger-relative geometric representations with future-supervised interaction tokens to achieve reliable single-hand Rubik's Cube manipulation, reaching 99.0% per-turn success and solving all ten scrambled 2×2×2 cubes on real hardware.
AI.motivation: In-hand Rubik's Cube turning is a demanding contact-rich control problem: fingers must alternately support the cube, drive a moving layer, release contact, and reset, demanding sustained and precise coordination. Learning this from real-world experience is hard, and prior flow-based policies lack the structural inductive biases and foresight needed for such sequential, force-sensitive interactions.
AI.method: The paper introduces FINGR (Future-supervised Interaction Network with Geometric Representations), which combines finger-relative geometry with future interaction prediction. A shared point encoder expresses the cube relative to each fingertip and aggregates points without relying on cubie indexing. Learned future tokens share this observation encoder and are supervised at multiple time scales for contact-force changes, layer-turn progress, and finger joint displacement. The resulting representation conditions a flow policy that directly generates finger actions.
AI.result: On a real dexterous hand, FINGR achieves 99.0% success over 300 turn attempts, versus 79.7% for the base flow policy. Combined with grasping and table-assisted regrasping, it solves all ten scrambled 2×2×2 cubes with a mean complete-system time of roughly 137 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Integrating finger-relative geometric encodings with multi-scale future interaction supervision substantially improves contact-rich, single-hand manipulation. FINGR demonstrates that such representations support reliable sequential layer turning and can be embedded in a complete system that repeatedly solves scrambled cubes on real hardware.

title: CUA-SWE: When Computer-Use Agents Meet Visual Software Engineering
summary: Software development requires more than editing code: developers repeatedly run software, interact with its interfaces, visually inspect its behavior, and use these observations to decide what to change next and whether a change works. Existing coding agents and computer-use agents are largely studied in isolation, leaving this integrated development process underexplored. Diagnosing a runtime interaction failure requires agents to connect visual observations with the responsible code, then use the application again to verify the repair. We introduce CUA-SWE, a benchmark, environment, and evaluation pipeline for software engineering with computer use. Beyond studying how GUI feedback supports diagnosis and repair, we ask whether agents can complete software engineering tasks when required specification or operational information is available only through the running application's visual interface. CUA-SWE spans four software engineering domains and requires agents to modify code and configuration, execute commands, interact with running software, and inspect visual feedback within the same task. Each task includes deterministic, task-specific tests that verify whether the resulting software satisfies the requirements and preserves specified behavior. Our evaluation characterizes how frontier agents combine source-level execution with application screenshots and graphical interaction to produce verified software changes. We examine performance across domains and task information requirements, alongside the development behaviors associated with successful repairs. CUA-SWE provides a unified testbed for studying how agents use visual feedback and interaction to guide software engineering, with executable correctness criteria for the resulting software.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CUA-SWE, a benchmark, environment, and evaluation pipeline for software engineering tasks that require agents to combine code editing, command execution, GUI interaction, and visual inspection—unifying coding agents and computer-use agents.
AI.motivation: Software development involves more than editing code: developers run software, interact with interfaces, visually inspect behavior, and use observations to decide changes. Existing coding agents and computer-use agents are largely studied in isolation, leaving the integrated development process underexplored. Diagnosing runtime interaction failures requires connecting visual observations with responsible code and re-running the application to verify repairs.
AI.method: CUA-SWE spans four software engineering domains, requiring agents to modify code and configuration, execute commands, interact with running software, and inspect visual feedback within the same task. Each task includes deterministic, task-specific tests verifying whether the resulting software satisfies requirements and preserves specified behavior. Evaluation characterizes how frontier agents combine source-level execution with screenshots and graphical interaction, across domains and task information requirements.
AI.result: The evaluation reports how frontier agents use visual feedback and graphical interaction to produce verified software changes, examining performance across domains, task information requirements, and development behaviors associated with successful repairs.
AI.conclusion: CUA-SWE provides a unified testbed for studying how agents use visual feedback and interaction to guide software engineering, with executable correctness criteria for resulting software.

title: Test-Time Spatial Reasoning for Robot Manipulation Using Generative Real-to-Sim
summary: Spatial reasoning is fundamental to general robot intelligence, as it enables robots to complete long-horizon tasks involving multi-object interaction. We introduce Simify, a training-free, test-time framework that performs explicit spatial reasoning via massively parallel physics simulation. From a single RGB-D image of a scene, Simify reconstructs simulation-ready assets leveraging 3D generative models and vision-language models. Then given a task specified by a reward function (e.g., build the tallest tower), Simify launches thousands of parallel rollouts in simulation and performs an evolutionary search to optimize object arrangements, typically converging within seconds. We conduct quantitative experiments on real-robot hardware to demonstrate the ability of our framework to execute complex object rearrangement tasks end-to-end with previously unseen objects. Results show that our framework outperforms prior work on foundation models for spatial reasoning by effectively exploiting large-scale parallel simulation during inference, and also highlight the importance of complete and accurate geometry for successful sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: Simify is a training-free, test-time framework for robot spatial reasoning that reconstructs simulation-ready assets from a single RGB-D image and uses massively parallel physics simulation plus evolutionary search to optimize object arrangements within seconds.
AI.motivation: Spatial reasoning is fundamental to general robot intelligence because it enables robots to complete long-horizon tasks involving multi-object interaction.
AI.method: From a single RGB-D image of a scene, Simify reconstructs simulation-ready assets using 3D generative models and vision-language models. Given a task specified by a reward function (e.g., build the tallest tower), it launches thousands of parallel rollouts in simulation and performs an evolutionary search to optimize object arrangements.
AI.result: Quantitative experiments on real-robot hardware show that Simify executes complex object rearrangement tasks end-to-end with previously unseen objects. It outperforms prior work on foundation models for spatial reasoning by leveraging large-scale parallel simulation at inference, and results highlight the importance of complete and accurate geometry for successful sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: Simify enables end-to-end real-robot object rearrangement with unseen objects through test-time parallel simulation and evolutionary search, surpassing prior spatial-reasoning foundation models and emphasizing accurate geometry for sim-to-real transfer.

title: "You're Right, Let Me Fix It": How LLM Agents Damage Correct Work When Falsely Accused
summary: LLM agents increasingly keep working after a task succeeds as they resume after compaction or take over handoffs. Their finished work keeps receiving follow-up input that sometimes falsely accuses it for later failures. We call an agent's acceptance of such a false accusation gaslight sycophancy, and destructive over-correction when acting on it damages previously correct work. We introduce CAVE-Bench, a benchmark of 365 agentic tasks across six domains built around opaque tasks. Every scored run first reaches a verified correct state, whose supporting rationale and history stay in the workspace while the facts that would settle the accusation lie in external or runtime state beyond the agent's reach. The agent cannot confirm or refute the claim with a local check, so the right response should keep the work and ask for the missing evidence. Each task either hands the agent correct work with saved evidence or let it build and verify that work first, and five risk factors set how the accusation enters the workflow. We score accusation acceptance and evidence use from the trajectory and measure harm by deterministic replay of downstream events. Across 14 of the latest models in Claude Code, false accusations damage correct work in up to 60.06% of runs, and stronger models often do so after recovering the supporting evidence. The same model behaves differently across OpenCode, Codex, and Hermes, and a harness gate driven by the benchmark's live signals cuts replayed harm by 74%. These results show that preserving already-correct work under unsupported accusation is a distinct safety challenge for long-lived agents. Our project is in https://henrymao2004.github.io/agent-over-correction/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "gaslight sycophancy" and "destructive over-correction" in long-lived LLM agents, and presents CAVE-Bench, a 365-task benchmark of opaque tasks where agents cannot locally verify follow-up false accusations. Across 14 recent models, false accusations damage correct work in up to 60.06% of runs, while a harness gate using live benchmark signals cuts replayed harm by 74%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly persist across compaction and handoffs, so their finished work keeps receiving follow-up input that sometimes falsely accuses it of causing later failures. Accepting such false accusations (gaslight sycophancy) and acting on them (destructive over-correction) can damage previously correct work, but this failure mode lacks a dedicated benchmark and measurement.
AI.method: The authors build CAVE-Bench, 365 agentic tasks across six domains centered on opaque tasks. Each scored run first reaches a verified correct state, with supporting rationale and history retained in the workspace while decisive facts reside in external or runtime state beyond the agent's reach, preventing local confirmation or refutation; the correct response is to preserve the work and request missing evidence. Tasks either supply correct work plus saved evidence or require the agent to build and verify it, and five risk factors control how the accusation enters the workflow. Acceptance and evidence use are scored from the trajectory, and harm is measured via deterministic replay of downstream events.
AI.result: Across 14 of the latest models in Claude Code, false accusations damage correct work in up to 60.06% of runs, with stronger models often doing so even after recovering the supporting evidence. Behavior varies for the same model across OpenCode, Codex, and Hermes, and a harness gate driven by the benchmark's live signals reduces replayed harm by 74%.
AI.conclusion: Preserving already-correct work under unsupported accusation is a distinct safety challenge for long-lived agents. The findings motivate explicit benchmarks and runtime safeguards targeting gaslight sycophancy and destructive over-correction, rather than assuming stronger models handle accusations reliably.

title: TacGooseBumps (TacGB): Retrofitting Normal-Only Tactile Sensors with Shear Encoding for Learning Contact-Rich Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Wenjie Li and Binyu Yang contributed equally
summary: Contact-rich policies often fail because distinct physical states look alike yet require different actions. Cameras may not reveal whether a connector is aligned or fully seated, while many normal-only tactile sensors can miss the tangential interactions perpendicular to the grasping direction that distinguish these states. We ask whether a learning policy needs calibrated shear measurements, or only a repeatable observation that separates shear-dependent contact states. We introduce TacGooseBumps (TacGB), a passive domed film that mechanically encodes tangential loading as pattern changes in an existing sensor's pressure map. Tangential loading tilts each dome and redistributes pressure across its footprint; an end-to-end policy consumes the resulting maps without added electronics, force reconstruction, or taxel-level dome alignment. Across four imitation-learning tasks and two data-collection pipelines, TacGB improves goal attainment, efficiency, and contact quality: insertion success increases by up to 36 percentage points, and successful insertions are completed faster, while fragile-object placement becomes gentler and drawing becomes more continuous and straight. Signal, stage-wise, failure-mode, and trajectory analyses link these gains to contact regimes in which task-relevant tangential interactions are poorly resolved by vision and normal pressure alone. Together, these results show that shear need not be measured metrically to benefit robot learning; it can instead be mechanically encoded without changing the underlying tactile sensor or the policy's pressure-map input format.

AI.tldr: TacGooseBumps (TacGB) is a passive domed film that mechanically converts tangential (shear) loading into pattern changes in an existing tactile sensor's pressure map, letting an end-to-end imitation-learning policy exploit shear-dependent contact states without calibration, force reconstruction, or added electronics.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation policies fail because physically distinct states can look identical to cameras and to normal-only tactile sensors. In particular, tangential interactions perpendicular to the grasping direction—which distinguish states such as an aligned versus fully seated connector—are poorly captured. The authors ask whether learning actually requires calibrated shear measurements, or merely a repeatable observation that separates shear-dependent contact states.
AI.method: A passive domed film (TacGB) is placed over an existing tactile sensor. Tangential loading tilts each dome and redistributes pressure across its footprint, encoding shear as pattern changes in the sensor's pressure map. An end-to-end policy consumes these maps directly, with no added electronics, no force reconstruction, and no taxel-level dome alignment. Evaluation spans four imitation-learning tasks and two data-collection pipelines.
AI.result: TacGB improves goal attainment, efficiency, and contact quality: insertion success rises by up to 36 percentage points, successful insertions complete faster, fragile-object placement becomes gentler, and drawing becomes more continuous and straighter. Signal, stage-wise, failure-mode, and trajectory analyses attribute these gains to contact regimes where task-relevant tangential interactions are poorly resolved by vision and normal pressure alone.
AI.conclusion: Shear need not be measured metrically to benefit robot learning; it can instead be mechanically encoded without changing the underlying tactile sensor or the policy's pressure-map input format.

title: SWE-MILE: Asynchronous Potential-Induced Milestone Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Software Engineering Agents
summary: Long-horizon software engineering (SWE) agents trained with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically receive only terminal outcome supervision, making it difficult to distinguish productive actions from redundant exploration or functional regressions. We propose SWE-MILE, an asynchronous potential-induced milestone credit assignment framework that derives fine-grained process supervision from workflow runtime, without auxiliary reward models or external evaluators. SWE-MILE quantifies task-relevant file exposure and test-state alignment as navigation and verification potentials, respectively. Differences in these potentials attribute milestone progress and regressions to individual actions, while discounted backward credit propagates supervision to preceding steps. To efficiently acquire intermediate verification states, SWE-MILE further introduces asynchronous shadow probing, which replays repository-changing actions in an isolated sandbox and runs verification in parallel with the agent's primary interaction, largely hiding verification latency. The resulting process credit augments terminal outcome advantages and provides informative learning signals. Experiments on two representative long-horizon SWE tasks demonstrate substantial improvements in agent performance, highlighting workflow runtime signals as a practical source of process supervision for long-horizon SWE agents.

AI.tldr: SWE-MILE is an asynchronous potential-induced milestone credit assignment framework that extracts fine-grained process supervision for long-horizon SWE agents from workflow runtime signals, using file exposure and test-state alignment as navigation and verification potentials, without external reward models.
AI.motivation: RLVR-trained long-horizon SWE agents typically receive only terminal outcome supervision, making it hard to distinguish productive actions from redundant exploration or functional regressions. Fine-grained process supervision is needed but usually requires auxiliary reward models or external evaluators.
AI.method: SWE-MILE quantifies task-relevant file exposure and test-state alignment as navigation and verification potentials. Differences in these potentials attribute milestone progress and regressions to individual actions, and discounted backward credit propagates supervision to preceding steps. Asynchronous shadow probing replays repository-changing actions in an isolated sandbox and runs verification in parallel with the agent's primary interaction to hide verification latency.
AI.result: Experiments on two representative long-horizon SWE tasks demonstrate substantial improvements in agent performance.
AI.conclusion: Workflow runtime signals are a practical source of process supervision for long-horizon SWE agents. The resulting process credit augments terminal outcome advantages and provides informative learning signals.

title: ZeroBot: Learning from Scratch in Minutes with Generative Real2Sim
summary: We present ZeroBot, a real2sim framework for learning a robot manipulation task from scratch in minutes under challenging conditions: zero human demonstrations, zero policy pre-training, and zero known object models. Given only a single view of an object and a goal pose for that object, ZeroBot uses image-to-3D generative models to obtain a complete object mesh, which is used in simulation for large-scale parallel reinforcement learning. To accelerate training, we introduce an action space which leverages the generated geometry and learned value function to sample states involving robot-object contact. When evaluated on real-world tasks including grasping, pushing, articulated object interaction, and multi-stage manipulation, ZeroBot achieves an 87% success rate with an average training time of 119 seconds. These results show the value of using image-to-3D models in a real2sim framework for rapid, autonomous robot learning.

AI.tldr: ZeroBot is a real2sim framework that learns robot manipulation from scratch in minutes with zero human demonstrations, zero policy pre-training, and zero known object models, achieving 87% success on real-world tasks with ~119s training.
AI.motivation: Real-world robot manipulation learning is bottlenecked by the need for human demonstrations, policy pre-training, and known object models. The authors aim to eliminate all three dependencies to enable rapid, autonomous robot learning from minimal input (a single object view and a goal pose).
AI.method: Given a single view of an object and a goal pose, ZeroBot uses image-to-3D generative models to reconstruct a complete object mesh. This mesh is imported into simulation for large-scale parallel reinforcement learning. To accelerate training, the authors introduce an action space that leverages the generated geometry and a learned value function to sample states involving robot-object contact.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world tasks including grasping, pushing, articulated object interaction, and multi-stage manipulation, ZeroBot achieves an 87% success rate with an average training time of 119 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Image-to-3D models within a real2sim framework enable rapid, autonomous robot learning, demonstrating strong real-world performance without human demonstrations, pre-training, or known object models.

title: Can Open-Weight Large Language Models (LLMs) Simulate Human Survey Populations? A Cross-Instrument Calibration Study
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate synthetic survey respondents and digital twins of real people, but whether their output preserves real human statistical structure, rather than surface plausibility, remains unresolved, and most existing evidence comes from proprietary models rather than open-weight ones. We evaluate three open-weight LLM families on a cross-instrument calibration task: conditioning personas on real respondents' verbatim answers to one psychometric instrument and measuring them on a second, construct-distance-controlled instrument, checked against a 2,058-person human panel. Across a 139-pair grid, the simulated cross-instrument correlation tracks the real human correlation at r = 0.70 - 0.73 in every model, driven mainly by correct sign rather than precise magnitude and concentrated in pairs of moderate construct distance. A correlation of this magnitude, obtained from untuned open-weight models conditioned only on individual-level survey data, is a substantively encouraging result for LLM-based behavioral simulation and digital-twin applications: specific model families and releases already reproduce a meaningful share of real human cross-instrument structure without any fine-tuning. This capability does not, however, improve monotonically across model releases: on a matched panel, the newest of three tested Llama releases performs worst on two of three headline metrics, so realizing its promise in practice requires release-specific, distance-aware verification rather than a one-time benchmark.

AI.tldr: Three open-weight LLM families conditioned on real respondents' answers to one psychometric instrument reproduce human cross-instrument correlations on a second instrument at r = 0.70–0.73 across a 139-pair grid; however, capability does not improve monotonically across releases, with the newest Llama performing worst on two of three metrics.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to generate synthetic survey respondents and digital twins, but it is unresolved whether their output preserves real human statistical structure rather than mere surface plausibility. Most existing evidence comes from proprietary models rather than open-weight ones.
AI.method: Cross-instrument calibration task: personas were conditioned on real respondents' verbatim answers to one psychometric instrument and measured on a second, construct-distance-controlled instrument, checked against a 2,058-person human panel. Three open-weight LLM families were evaluated over a 139-pair grid.
AI.result: Simulated cross-instrument correlation tracks real human correlation at r = 0.70–0.73 in every model, driven mainly by correct sign rather than precise magnitude and concentrated in pairs of moderate construct distance. Capability does not improve monotonically across releases: on a matched panel, the newest of three tested Llama releases performs worst on two of three headline metrics.
AI.conclusion: Untuned open-weight models conditioned only on individual-level survey data reproduce a meaningful share of real human cross-instrument structure, encouraging for LLM-based behavioral simulation and digital-twin applications. Realizing this promise requires release-specific, distance-aware verification rather than a one-time benchmark.

title: Estimate, Don't Imitate: Reusing Differentiable State-Based Policies for Visuomotor Control
summary: Simulation-trained manipulation policies can exploit privileged state information to learn effective contact-rich behaviours, but deployment requires acting from partial observations such as noisy camera images. A common solution is teacher-student distillation, in which a visuomotor policy is trained to reproduce the actions of the privileged expert. This requires the student to jointly infer the task-relevant state and relearn the expert's action mapping that is already available. An alternative is to reuse the state-based expert and learn only a perceptual interface that reconstructs its missing state inputs. However, minimising the state estimate error alone does not necessarily minimise the downstream control error induced by these estimates. To bridge this gap, we train a visual state estimator using both direct state supervision and an action-consistency loss backpropagated through the frozen, differentiable expert. A scheduled objective first establishes a physically meaningful state estimate and progressively emphasises errors that affect the expert's actions. Across five goal-conditioned manipulation tasks, retaining the expert consistently outperforms direct pixel-to-action imitation from the same expert demonstration corpus. We further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer on a physical Panda robot, achieving 76% success without retraining the underlying expert.

AI.tldr: The paper trains a visual state estimator using both direct state supervision and an action-consistency loss backpropagated through a frozen differentiable expert, with a scheduled objective that progressively emphasizes control-relevant errors, outperforming direct pixel-to-action imitation and enabling sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Simulation-trained manipulation policies leverage privileged state to learn contact-rich behaviours, but deployment requires partial observations (e.g., noisy camera images). Existing teacher-student distillation forces the student to jointly infer task-relevant state and relearn the expert's action mapping. Reusing the state-based expert and learning only a perceptual interface avoids relearning actions, but minimizing state estimate error alone does not necessarily minimize downstream control error.
AI.method: A visual state estimator is trained with both direct state supervision and an action-consistency loss backpropagated through a frozen, differentiable expert. A scheduled objective first establishes a physically meaningful state estimate and then progressively emphasizes errors that affect the expert's actions.
AI.result: Across five goal-conditioned manipulation tasks, retaining the expert consistently outperforms direct pixel-to-action imitation from the same expert demonstration corpus. Sim-to-real transfer on a physical Panda robot achieves 76% success without retraining the underlying expert.
AI.conclusion: Reusing a frozen state-based expert and learning only a control-aware perceptual interface is more effective than end-to-end visuomotor distillation, and the action-consistency objective bridges the gap between state estimation accuracy and downstream control performance, enabling successful real-robot deployment.

title: Business Compromise Detection with Agentic AI and LLM-driven Knowledge Discovery
comment: Accepted at EMNLP 2026. 13 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables
summary: Detecting compromised business ad accounts is a challenge in digital advertising, as attackers exploit hijacked accounts to launch fraudulent campaigns. Large Language Model (LLM) agents show promise for integrity enforcement, but hallucinated mistakes on hard cases create business friction. In a study we find the autonomous agent is a strong, recall-heavy signal extractor but an unreliable final arbiter, conceding precision on ambiguous decisions. We therefore keep the agent as an investigator that emits a structured, interpretable signal vector, and delegate the verdict to a neuro-symbolic stage: symbolic rules discovered by Inductive Logic Programming (FOIL-IE), a Naïve Bayes calibration layer, and a data-tuned contradiction layer. Evaluating on a compromise-over-sampled population and a realistic low-prevalence sample with subject-matter-expert labels, this arbiter substitution raises MCC from 0.295 to 0.435 (ΔMCC +0.139, 95% CI [+0.026, +0.245], p=0.018, paired bootstrap), lifting precision from 0.250 to 0.446 (1.8x) at a recall cost (0.920 to 0.660). Benchmarked under identical conditions, it also edge tree ensembles (0.386).The rules encode domain w labels while remaininginterpretable and auditable.

AI.tldr: Compromised ad-account detection is reframed as a division of labor: an LLM agent extracts interpretable signals, while a neuro-symbolic arbiter (FOIL-IE rules, Naive Bayes calibration, contradiction layer) issues the verdict.
AI.motivation: Hijacked business ad accounts enable fraudulent campaigns, and LLM agents, though promising for integrity enforcement, hallucinate on hard cases, causing business friction and unreliability as final decision-makers.
AI.method: Keep the LLM agent as an investigator producing a structured, interpretable signal vector, and delegate the verdict to a neuro-symbolic stage: symbolic rules discovered by Inductive Logic Programming (FOIL-IE), a Naive Bayes calibration layer, and a data-tuned contradiction layer. Evaluated on a compromise-over-sampled population and a realistic low-prevalence sample with subject-matter-expert labels.
AI.result: The arbiter substitution raises MCC from 0.295 to 0.435 (delta MCC +0.139, 95% CI [+0.026, +0.245], p=0.018, paired bootstrap), lifting precision from 0.250 to 0.446 (1.8x) at a recall cost (0.920 to 0.660). Under identical conditions it also edges tree ensembles (0.386).
AI.conclusion: Separating signal extraction from adjudication yields a more precise, auditable compromise-detection system; the learned rules encode domain-relevant signals while preserving interpretability and auditability.

title: Quantile Head for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with action heads for robot control. Common action heads have distinct limitations: point regression provides only a point estimate of the action distribution, while standard flow-matching samplers require costly iterative sampling. To address these limitations, we unify regression and flow matching under a shared objective and extend it to derive a quantile objective. This quantile objective guides the design of our Quantile Head, which predicts a median and positive gaps to form ordered marginal action quantiles in one forward pass. These quantiles support multiple sampling strategies without retraining and are jointly supervised to train the default median policy. Our local analysis of this joint supervision shows that, with calibrated nearby quantiles, fixed gaps, and matched correction speed, direct median updates have lower variance than under median-only supervision. Experiments show that this jointly supervised median policy achieves the highest average success rates among the compared methods on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and two real-robot tasks, together with the shortest mean episode time among matched LIBERO baselines; code is available at https://github.com/xwangrs/Quantile-Head-for-VLA.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies regression and flow matching under a shared objective to derive a quantile objective, designing a Quantile Head for VLA models that predicts ordered marginal action quantiles in one forward pass, enabling flexible sampling and a jointly supervised median policy that outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Common action heads in VLA models have distinct limitations: point regression yields only a point estimate of the action distribution, while standard flow-matching samplers require costly iterative sampling. The work aims to overcome both limitations.
AI.method: The authors unify regression and flow matching under a shared objective and extend it to a quantile objective. This guides the design of a Quantile Head that predicts a median and positive gaps to form ordered marginal action quantiles in a single forward pass. These quantiles support multiple sampling strategies without retraining and are jointly supervised to train the default median policy. A local analysis of the joint supervision examines variance under calibrated nearby quantiles, fixed gaps, and matched correction speed.
AI.result: The jointly supervised median policy achieves the highest average success rates among compared methods on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and two real-robot tasks, and attains the shortest mean episode time among matched LIBERO baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantile objective and Quantile Head offer an effective, flexible alternative to point regression and iterative flow-matching sampling. Joint supervision yields a lower-variance median policy that improves success rates and reduces episode time, with code publicly available.

title: From Scene Graphs to Answers: Selective Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous-driving question answering requires reasoning over structured scene information, yet existing vision-language approaches largely delegate heterogeneous reasoning operations to a single neural inference process. We argue that this uniform strategy overlooks a fundamental distinction: some queries admit exact symbolic solutions, while others require semantic interpretation. We introduce a query-adaptive neuro-symbolic reasoning framework that explicitly allocates computation according to the nature of the query. At its core is a hierarchical Spatiotemporal Scene Graph (STSG) that separates persistent object identities from frame-specific states and represents spatial relations and temporal transitions as explicit directed structures. Given a query, a symbolic executor first attempts to resolve it through exact graph operations; only when symbolic execution abstains is an LLM invoked for semantic reasoning. For these unresolved queries, query-conditioned graph retrieval and evidence filtering preserve relation direction, temporal locality, and object semantics, providing the LLM with compact and verified task-relevant evidence. This design shifts the role of the LLM from a universal reasoning engine to a targeted semantic reasoner, while allowing deterministic computation to be handled exactly and efficiently. We evaluate the framework on 5,916 NuScenes-QA questions across all ten scenes of nuScenes v1.0-mini under an oracle-perception setting. The complete system achieves 80.63 percent overall accuracy with GPT-5.4-mini, improving over the corresponding LLM-only configuration by 5.48 percentage points; with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the improvement reaches 6.64 points. The largest gains occur on counting questions, with improvements of 10.20 and 12.61 points, respectively. These results show that selective reasoning improves both accuracy and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: A query-adaptive neuro-symbolic framework for autonomous-driving QA uses a hierarchical Spatiotemporal Scene Graph, where a symbolic executor resolves queries exactly when possible and only invokes an LLM for semantic reasoning when symbolic execution abstains, achieving 80.63% accuracy on NuScenes-QA.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language approaches delegate heterogeneous reasoning operations to a single neural inference process, overlooking the fundamental distinction between queries that admit exact symbolic solutions and those requiring semantic interpretation.
AI.method: The framework builds a hierarchical Spatiotemporal Scene Graph (STSG) separating persistent object identities from frame-specific states, representing spatial relations and temporal transitions as explicit directed structures. A symbolic executor first attempts exact graph operations; only on abstention is an LLM invoked. For unresolved queries, query-conditioned graph retrieval and evidence filtering preserve relation direction, temporal locality, and object semantics, supplying the LLM with compact verified evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5,916 NuScenes-QA questions across all ten scenes of nuScenes v1.0-mini under oracle perception. Full system reaches 80.63% overall accuracy with GPT-5.4-mini (+5.48 points over LLM-only) and +6.64 points with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Largest gains on counting questions (+10.20 and +12.61 points).
AI.conclusion: Selective, query-adaptive reasoning that shifts the LLM from a universal engine to a targeted semantic reasoner improves both accuracy and inference efficiency.

title: AD-E2E-JEPA: A Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture For End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving requires \textit{world models} that can understand the physical world, reason and plan, and operate safely. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate existing action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models, including LeWM, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM for end-to-end autonomous driving (E2EAD). To isolate world-model quality from policy learning, we employ a goal-conditioned zero-shot planning setting that evaluates these models using ground-truth future observations as goals, without training any driving policy. We find that existing JEPA-based world models are either accurate for driving but computationally expensive, or computationally efficient but insufficient for planning. To address this trade-off, we propose \textbf{AD-E2E-JEPA}, which introduces a SIGReg-regularized learnable projector applied to projected patch embeddings. The projector reduces the number of planning patches by $16\times$ and the embedding dimension by $4\times$, achieving a $100\times$ inference speedup while retaining planning performance, with a 0.8-second runtime for an 8-frame rollout over 256 candidate trajectories. \textit{Without} training any driving policy, the world model itself reaches the goals located 20 meters away on average within the displacement of respectively 4.0/2.8 meters, using world-model rollouts over trajectory vocabularies of respectively 256/8,192 candidates. On the NAVSIMv2 benchmark, it achieves 67.3/72.9 EPDMS with multiplicative safety metrics and 84.1/86.5 EPDMS$^{\dagger}$ without them in goal-conditioned zero-shot planning. Experiments further show that the self-supervised pretrained projector improves downstream imitation learning performance from 80.2 to 85.4 EPDMS. The source code is available at https://github.com/HaoranZhuExplorer/AD-E2E-JEPA

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates existing JEPA-based world models for end-to-end autonomous driving and proposes AD-E2E-JEPA, a SIGReg-regularized learnable projector that cuts planning patches 16× and embedding dimension 4×, yielding a 100× inference speedup while retaining planning quality.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving needs world models that understand the physical world, reason, plan, and operate safely. Existing action-conditioned JEPA world models (LeWM, DINO-WM, JEPA-WM) face a trade-off: either accurate for driving but computationally expensive, or efficient but inadequate for planning.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate existing JEPA world models for E2EAD using a goal-conditioned zero-shot planning setup that isolates world-model quality from policy learning by using ground-truth future observations as goals without training a driving policy. They then introduce AD-E2E-JEPA, which adds a SIGReg-regularized learnable projector applied to projected patch embeddings to shrink planning patches and embedding dimensions.
AI.result: AD-E2E-JEPA reduces planning patches by 16× and embedding dimension by 4×, achieving a 100× inference speedup (0.8 s for an 8-frame rollout over 256 candidate trajectories). Without any driving policy, the world model reaches goals ~20 m away within 4.0/2.8 m displacement using 256/8,192 candidate trajectories. On NAVSIMv2 it reaches 67.3/72.9 EPDMS (with multiplicative safety metrics) and 84.1/86.5 EPDMS† (without) in goal-conditioned zero-shot planning. The self-supervised pretrained projector improves downstream imitation learning from 80.2 to 85.4 EPDMS.
AI.conclusion: AD-E2E-JEPA resolves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off of prior JEPA world models, enabling efficient and effective zero-shot planning for end-to-end autonomous driving and improving downstream imitation learning via its self-supervised pretrained projector.

title: Prediction Limits and Koopman Closure of Geometry-Induced Soft State Abstractions
summary: We study when geometry-induced soft state abstractions admit accurate finite-dimensional linear dynamics. Each state is represented by simplex-valued coordinates obtained from class-specific Kernel Affine Hull Machine (KAHM) reconstruction scores, and a matrix is used to predict the next-state coordinates. Our main result is a computable lower confidence bound on the minimum root-mean-square prediction error over all matrices satisfying a prescribed spectral-norm limit. The bound combines within-class variation of successor coordinates with the deviation of soft coordinates from their one-hot reference labels, and can be evaluated from independent state-successor pairs without fitting a prediction matrix. For fixed coordinates and evaluation distribution, the certificate converges almost surely to a population lower bound as the sample size grows; any tolerance below this limit is eventually certified unattainable. Reconstruction-score margins further control the soft-to-hard assignment error. Under deterministic dynamics and exact coordinate closure, eigenvectors of the closure matrix and its reduced transpose induce Koopman and adjoint Koopman eigenfunctions, respectively. A four-state KAHM construction shows that identical soft coordinates can permit exact closure under one dynamics map yet force positive prediction error under another. Experiments on Duffing, Van der Pol, CartPole, MountainCar, and Acrobot compare direct soft-coordinate prediction with state-space DMD/EDMD baselines and report prediction, representation-variation, and spectral diagnostics. The benchmarks assess fitted models but do not numerically evaluate the exclusion certificate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a computable lower confidence bound on the minimum RMS prediction error achievable by any linear predictor (with bounded spectral norm) acting on KAHM-derived soft state coordinates, and shows this certificate converges almost surely to a population lower bound; experiments contrast soft-coordinate prediction with DMD/EDMD baselines.
AI.motivation: Geometry-induced soft state abstractions (state represented by simplex-valued coordinates from class-specific KAHM reconstruction scores) are widely used, but it is unclear when they admit accurate finite-dimensional linear dynamics. The authors seek a pre-fittable, data-driven guarantee that quantifies the intrinsic limit of linear prediction on such coordinates, without requiring a prediction matrix to be fit.
AI.method: States are encoded as simplex-valued coordinates via class-specific Kernel Affine Hull Machine (KAHM) reconstruction scores; a matrix predicts next-state coordinates. The main technical result is a computable lower confidence bound on the minimum root-mean-square prediction error over all matrices respecting a prescribed spectral-norm limit. The bound couples within-class variation of successor coordinates with the deviation of soft coordinates from their one-hot reference labels and is evaluated from independent state-successor pairs without fitting a prediction matrix. The authors also analyze reconstruction-score margins controlling soft-to-hard assignment error, and, under deterministic dynamics with exact coordinate closure, connect eigenvectors of the closure matrix and its reduced transpose to Koopman and adjoint Koopman eigenfunctions.
AI.result: For fixed coordinates and evaluation distribution, the certificate converges almost surely to a population lower bound as sample size grows, so any tolerance below this limit is eventually certified unattainable. A four-state KAHM construction demonstrates that identical soft coordinates can permit exact closure under one dynamics map yet force positive prediction error under another. Experiments on Duffing, Van der Pol, CartPole, MountainCar, and Acrobot compare direct soft-coordinate prediction against state-space DMD/EDMD baselines, reporting prediction, representation-variation, and spectral diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: Soft state abstractions admit accurate finite-dimensional linear dynamics only up to an intrinsic, computable error limit that depends on within-class successor variation and soft-label deviation, not on the choice of prediction matrix. The certificate provides an a priori, fit-free assessment of linear predictability, while benchmarks evaluate fitted models but do not numerically evaluate the exclusion certificate.

title: Beyond Retrieval Relevance: Scene-Grounded Risk Entailment for Vision-Language Driving
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives vision--language driving systems access to external safety knowledge, yet a retrieved risk rule may be relevant without applying to the current scene. A vision--language model (VLM) receiving such knowledge must ground objects, bind entities across time, and verify relations before deciding how to act, leaving the support for risk conclusions implicit. We address this relevance--applicability gap with a Driving-Risk Knowledge Graph (DRKG) and Semantic Web Rule Language (SWRL) reasoning stage before VLM decision-making. Structured perception instantiates scene facts, from which SWRL rules derive events and directed risk relations when their antecedents are jointly satisfied. Recognized events, bound risk relations, and semantic descriptions of activated rules form compact evidence that conditions the VLM and diffusion planner. In matched comparisons on nuReasoning, our method improved the nuReasoning planning score (NPS) by 1.30 points and the non-at-fault collision score (NC) by 2.76 points over the relevance retrieval-based baseline. These gains indicate that scene-applicable risk evidence improves safety-weighted planning relative to semantically retrieved risk knowledge.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Driving-Risk Knowledge Graph (DRKG) with SWRL reasoning to filter retrieved safety knowledge for applicability before VLM decision-making in vision-language driving systems, improving safety-weighted planning over relevance-only retrieval.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides vision-language driving systems with external safety knowledge, but retrieved risk rules may be relevant yet not applicable to the current scene. With a VLM receiving such knowledge, supporting risk conclusions remain implicit, requiring object grounding, cross-time entity binding, and relation verification before action decisions. This creates a relevance-applicability gap.
AI.method: The authors propose a Driving-Risk Knowledge Graph (DRKG) with a Semantic Web Rule Language (SWRL) reasoning stage placed before VLM decision-making. Structured perception instantiates scene facts; SWRL rules derive events and directed risk relations when antecedents are jointly satisfied. Recognized events, bound risk relations, and semantic descriptions of activated rules are compiled into compact evidence that conditions both the VLM and the diffusion planner.
AI.result: On nuReasoning, in matched comparisons, the method improved the nuReasoning planning score (NPS) by 1.30 points and the non-at-fault collision score (NC) by 2.76 points over the relevance retrieval-based baseline.
AI.conclusion: The gains indicate that scene-applicable risk evidence improves safety-weighted planning relative to semantically retrieved risk knowledge, validating the relevance-applicability gap framing and the DRKG + SWRL reasoning approach.

title: MixBench-TS: A Multivariate Time Series Forecasting Benchmark Where Channel Mixing Pays Off
summary: Multivariate Time Series Forecasting (MTSF) models that mix information across channels assume that the past of one channel carries information about the future of another. Yet they are evaluated on a small fixed set of standard datasets whose cross-channel structure is rarely examined. We ask two questions: "How can we reliably measure lagged, non-linear, and joint coupling in MTSF datasets?" and "Do the standard datasets actually have such coupling?" To answer the first, we test four candidate measures on synthetic datasets with planted ground-truth coupling: Granger Causality (GC), Transfer Entropy (TE), lagged Mutual Information (MI), and the CD gain, a model-based measure we introduce that compares a channel-dependent (CD) model to its channel-independent (CI) variant. Only lagged MI and the CD gain recover every planted coupling. For the second question, the answer is a definite no, as the standard datasets have a median of only 23% lagged-coupled channel pairs and a median CD gain of -4.9%, compared to 78% and +4.6% on chaotic ODE systems. We therefore propose MixBench-TS, a benchmark of 10 real-world datasets with a median of 55.5% lagged-coupled pairs and a median CD gain of +1.7%. Across six state-of-the-art models tuned under one protocol, CI models win on 10/10 (MSE) and 8/10 (MAE) standard datasets, but on only 3/10 and 2/10 MixBench-TS datasets. We recommend using our benchmark for evaluating new CD models. Moreover, we propose profiling new datasets with lagged MI and the CD gain before using them to evaluate multivariate models. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/mixbench-ts-B027.

AI.tldr: Standard MTSF datasets largely lack cross-channel coupling, so channel-dependent models appear falsely superior; the authors propose reliable coupling measures (lagged MI, CD gain) and a new benchmark MixBench-TS with genuine cross-channel structure.
AI.motivation: MTSF models that mix information across channels assume one channel's past informs another's future, yet they are evaluated on a small fixed set of standard datasets whose cross-channel structure is rarely examined. The paper questions whether these datasets actually exhibit lagged, non-linear, and joint coupling.
AI.method: The authors first evaluate four candidate coupling measures—Granger Causality (GC), Transfer Entropy (TE), lagged Mutual Information (MI), and a novel model-based CD gain comparing a channel-dependent model to its channel-independent variant—on synthetic datasets with planted ground-truth coupling. They then profile standard datasets and chaotic ODE systems, and construct MixBench-TS, a benchmark of 10 real-world datasets with verified coupling, evaluating six state-of-the-art models under one tuning protocol.
AI.result: Only lagged MI and CD gain recover every planted coupling. Standard datasets show a median of 23% lagged-coupled channel pairs and a median CD gain of -4.9%, versus 78% and +4.6% for chaotic ODE systems. MixBench-TS achieves a median 55.5% lagged-coupled pairs and +1.7% CD gain. CI models win on 10/10 (MSE) and 8/10 (MAE) standard datasets but only 3/10 and 2/10 on MixBench-TS.
AI.conclusion: Standard datasets generally lack meaningful cross-channel coupling, biasing evaluations toward channel-independent models. The authors recommend MixBench-TS for evaluating new CD models and profiling new datasets with lagged MI and CD gain before using them.

title: Reliability-Aware Sparse Route Memory for Round-Trip Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-language navigation (VLN) is typically evaluated as a one-way task, although deployed robots may need to return after reaching a goal. We study continuous round-trip VLN and diagnose failures in directional observability, deviation recovery, and termination stability. We propose a reliability-aware sparse route memory that records the executed Outbound trajectory as ordered geometric anchors and queries them in reverse through a structured hint, action-level arbitration, and terminal verification. On 50 reverse-paired episodes using NaVILA and a simulated Unitree Go2, language-only Return succeeds in 22.0% of episodes, while our online system reaches 55.1%. With exact route information, the same interfaces achieve 86.0%, showing that effective Return requires both accurate information and consistent action on that information. The remaining online gap arises mainly from geometric evidence that is too unreliable to authorise intervention. These results distinguish information quality, behavioural consistency, and online reliability as separate limits in long-horizon navigation.
