AI.tldr: This paper studies continuous round-trip vision-language navigation (VLN), where a robot must return to its start after reaching a goal. It identifies failures in directional observability, deviation recovery, and termination stability, and proposes a reliability-aware sparse route memory that stores the outbound trajectory as ordered geometric anchors and queries them in reverse. On 50 reverse-paired episodes with NaVILA and a simulated Unitree Go2, language-only Return succeeds in 22.0% of episodes, while the online system reaches 55.1%; with exact route information, the same interfaces achieve 86.0%.
AI.motivation: VLN is typically evaluated as a one-way task, yet deployed robots may need to return after reaching a goal. This leaves round-trip navigation understudied, and the specific failure modes that limit a robot's ability to retrace its route (directional observability, deviation recovery, and termination stability) are not well diagnosed.
AI.method: The authors formulate continuous round-trip VLN and introduce a reliability-aware sparse route memory. During the outbound phase, the executed trajectory is recorded as ordered geometric anchors. On the return phase, these anchors are queried in reverse using a structured hint, action-level arbitration, and terminal verification, so that route evidence is only acted upon when it is reliable enough to authorise intervention.
AI.result: Evaluated on 50 reverse-paired episodes using NaVILA and a simulated Unitree Go2, language-only Return succeeds in 22.0% of episodes, whereas the proposed online system reaches 55.1%. When provided with exact route information, the same interfaces achieve 86.0% success, indicating a substantial gap attributable to information quality rather than interface design.
AI.conclusion: Effective Return requires both accurate information and consistent action on that information. The remaining online gap primarily stems from geometric evidence that is too unreliable to authorise intervention. These findings separate information quality, behavioural consistency, and online reliability as distinct limiting factors in long-horizon navigation.

title: World Models with Predictable Long-Horizon Marginals
summary: Accurate one-step predictions do not ensure that a world model's rollouts retain the data distribution. We make the model's decoded stationary law explicit by learning a decoder of a fixed Gaussian reference and constraining the behaviour-averaged transition to preserve that reference. For controlled systems, a joint transition uses a conditional action chart to preserve behaviour occupancy without requiring invariance at each fixed action. Joint state--action rotations and parallel Gaussian noise give an exactly preserving transition with a tractable conditional density. We derive an absolute convergence bound from finite initialization banks and control departure from the reference through conditional action-space divergence. Across $216$ fitted pixel checkpoints on twelve control tasks, the occupancy model with a reference mixture retains every evaluated chain at $10^5$ steps in all $36$ task--seed cells, with a rollout-minus-reference energy-statistic difference of $-0.0002\pm0.0003$ (training-seed standard error). Each of the four nonpreserving comparison arms loses chains, although the Gaussian arm is more accurate at ten steps. An offline DreamerV3 reference also achieves better short-horizon accuracy. These results distinguish three properties of a world model: the distribution it approaches, the rate of approach, and the conditional dynamics it learns.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that accurate one-step predictions do not guarantee that a world model's long-horizon rollouts stay on the data distribution, and proposes an occupancy-preserving transition (via a Gaussian reference decoder, joint state-action rotations, and parallel Gaussian noise) that retains chains at 10^5 steps across 216 pixel checkpoints on twelve control tasks.
AI.motivation: One-step accuracy is a common proxy for world-model quality, but it does not ensure that multi-step rollouts preserve the data distribution; models can drift off the stationary law even while being locally accurate. The authors therefore seek to make the decoded stationary law explicit and to control whether rollouts retain it, separating the distribution a model approaches from its rate of approach and its conditional dynamics.
AI.method: They learn a decoder of a fixed Gaussian reference and constrain the behaviour-averaged transition to preserve that reference. For controlled systems, a joint transition uses a conditional action chart to preserve behaviour occupancy without per-fixed-action invariance. Joint state-action rotations combined with parallel Gaussian noise give an exactly preserving transition with a tractable conditional density. They derive an absolute convergence bound from finite initialization banks and measure departure from the reference via conditional action-space divergence.
AI.result: Across 216 fitted pixel checkpoints on twelve control tasks, the occupancy model with a reference mixture retained every evaluated chain at 10^5 steps in all 36 task-seed cells, with a rollout-minus-reference energy-statistic difference of -0.0002±0.0003 (training-seed standard error). Each of the four nonpreserving comparison arms lost chains, though the Gaussian arm was more accurate at ten steps. An offline DreamerV3 reference also achieved better short-horizon accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Short-horizon accuracy and long-horizon distributional fidelity are distinct properties: the proposed occupancy-preserving model is less accurate at ten steps than some alternatives yet uniquely sustains chains at 10^5 steps. The results distinguish three properties of a world model: the distribution it approaches, the rate of approach, and the conditional dynamics it learns.

title: RAVEL: Asynchronous Rolling Inference for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models are highly effective for generalist robot manipulation, yet their reliance on computationally expensive VLM encoding and multi-step iterative action generation imposes a significant latency bottleneck. The resulting inference latency makes it difficult for robots to respond quickly, especially in dynamic environments. We address this limitation with RAVEL (Rolling Asynchronous VLA Enabling Low-Latency Control), an asynchronous inference framework that addresses the computational bottlenecks of both the VLM backbone and the action expert. To reduce the delay from multi-step action denoising, RAVEL allows near-term actions to be executed after a single denoising step by carrying partially denoised future actions forward in a rolling buffer. To avoid blocking on slow VLM encoding, RAVEL decouples VLM encoding from rolling action generation, allowing the action expert to operate continuously using the latest available VLM context, while a lightweight Fast Observation Pathway (FOP) directly conditions the action expert on current observations. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, RAVEL consistently achieves substantially lower response latency while maintaining the task capability of the underlying VLA, enabling high-frequency and responsive closed-loop control.

AI.tldr: RAVEL is an asynchronous inference framework for flow-based VLA models that cuts latency by rolling partially denoised actions across steps and decoupling slow VLM encoding from continuous action generation, achieving responsive high-frequency control without sacrificing task capability.
AI.motivation: Flow-based VLA models excel at generalist robot manipulation but suffer a latency bottleneck: expensive VLM encoding plus multi-step iterative action generation make inference slow, hindering rapid robot response, especially in dynamic environments.
AI.method: RAVEL targets both bottlenecks. For action generation, near-term actions are executed after a single denoising step by carrying partially denoised future actions forward in a rolling buffer. For encoding, VLM encoding is decoupled from rolling action generation so the action expert runs continuously with the latest available VLM context, while a lightweight Fast Observation Pathway (FOP) directly conditions the action expert on current observations.
AI.result: Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, RAVEL consistently achieves substantially lower response latency while preserving the task capability of the underlying VLA.
AI.conclusion: RAVEL enables high-frequency, responsive closed-loop robot control by removing the latency bottlenecks of flow-based VLA inference without degrading performance.

title: Contract Memory Compiler: Resolve, Then Traverse
summary: External memory lets language-model agents answer questions about histories too long for the answer model's context window. Updates create a harder problem than retrieving a recent fact: changing one relation can redirect a multi-hop question to records about an entity absent from the question. We study this update-dependent evidence selection problem and introduce the Contract Memory Compiler (CMC). Before seeing a question, CMC uses a language model to identify relations in the history and record where each one was stated. It applies later updates to determine the current relations, follows them from entities named in the question, and passes the corresponding original records to the answer model in one call. Thus the current state determines which evidence is read, rather than merely refreshing values in a previously selected context. To the best of our knowledge, CMC achieves state-of-the-art multi-hop accuracy on FactConsolidation, reaching 78.25% overall and 61.0% at 262K. With the extracted relations and answer model held fixed, selecting evidence before resolving updates reduces multi-hop accuracy to 21.50%. We also introduce MQuAKE-MemStream, a derived dataset of ordered memory streams built from MQuAKE-Remastered counterfactual cases.

AI.tldr: The Contract Memory Compiler (CMC) addresses update-dependent evidence selection in external memory for language-model agents, achieving state-of-the-art multi-hop accuracy on FactConsolidation (78.25% overall, 61.0% at 262K).
AI.motivation: External memory allows language-model agents to answer questions about histories that exceed the answer model's context window. However, updates create a harder problem than merely retrieving a recent fact: changing one relation can redirect a multi-hop question to records about an entity not mentioned in the question. This update-dependent evidence selection problem is the core challenge.
AI.method: Before seeing a question, CMC uses a language model to identify relations in the history and record where each was stated. It then applies later updates to determine the current relations, follows them from entities named in the question, and passes the corresponding original records to the answer model in a single call. Thus, the current state determines which evidence is read, rather than merely refreshing values in a previously selected context.
AI.result: CMC achieves state-of-the-art multi-hop accuracy on FactConsolidation: 78.25% overall and 61.0% at 262K. With the extracted relations and answer model held fixed, selecting evidence before resolving updates reduces multi-hop accuracy to 21.50%. Additionally, the authors introduce MQuAKE-MemStream, a derived dataset of ordered memory streams built from MQuAKE-Remastered counterfactual cases.
AI.conclusion: Resolving updates before selecting evidence is crucial for multi-hop accuracy in external memory systems, as demonstrated by CMC's substantial performance advantage over the pre-update evidence selection baseline.

title: FailPatch: Failure Residual Patching for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are typically adapted using successful demonstrations, which provide direct action supervision but rarely cover failure-prone states. Deployment failures expose these states, yet lack the corrective actions needed for conventional supervised learning. We propose FailPatch, a failure-driven residual patching framework that decouples action supervision from execution-reliability supervision. Successful demonstrations ground how the policy should act, while deployment trajectories indicate when its behavior becomes unreliable. We further observe that action hidden representations exhibit clear linear separability between reliable and failure-associated states while directly conditioning action generation. Building on these insights, FailPatch introduces a Null-gated Residual Expert Bank into the action hidden space of a frozen VLA policy. A unified Preserve--Redirect--Trust objective retains the original policy in reliable states, selects residual experts in failure-associated states and redirects representations from failure regions toward success-associated regions under bounded intervention. With only 0.52% trainable parameters, FailPatch improves success rates by 11.0 percentage points on four long-horizon RoboTwin tasks under clean evaluation, 9.5 percentage points under clean-to-random generalization, and 16.7 percentage points over the baseline across three real-world tasks. Project and code: https://github.com/yupeng-2003/FailPatch.

AI.tldr: FailPatch is a failure-driven residual patching framework for VLA policies that decouples action supervision from execution-reliability supervision, adding a Null-gated Residual Expert Bank in the action hidden space to correct failure-prone states with only 0.52% trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: VLA policies are adapted mainly via successful demonstrations, which give direct action supervision but rarely cover failure-prone states. Deployment failures reveal these states but provide no corrective actions for conventional supervised learning.
AI.method: FailPatch decouples action supervision from execution-reliability supervision: demonstrations ground desired behavior, deployment trajectories signal unreliable behavior. Exploiting the linear separability of reliable vs. failure-associated action hidden states, it inserts a Null-gated Residual Expert Bank into the frozen VLA's action hidden space, trained with a unified Preserve-Redirect-Trust objective that preserves the original policy in reliable states, selects residual experts in failure-associated states, and redirects representations toward success regions under bounded intervention.
AI.result: With only 0.52% trainable parameters, FailPatch improves success rates by 11.0 percentage points on four long-horizon RoboTwin tasks under clean evaluation, 9.5 percentage points under clean-to-random generalization, and 16.7 percentage points over baseline across three real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Failure-driven residual patching with a Null-gated Residual Expert Bank offers a parameter-efficient, bounded-intervention way to improve VLA execution reliability, and will be released at the provided project and code repository.

title: Learning from a Thoughtful Teacher: Adaptive On-Policy Self-Distillation for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a question-only student with token-level feedback from a teacher given training-only privileged information (PI). OPSD therefore provides dense, on-policy supervision, and is free of a larger external teacher, but its effectiveness rests on how PI is designed and utilized. Our preliminary diagnostics suggest a significant gap between teacher utility and student learnability, where a small fraction of high-disagreement tokens dominate the distillation signal, and short teacher continuations at these positions further expose more explicit PI leakage than transferable correction cues, indicating a strong intent on injecting PI-conditioned shortcuts. We propose Adaptive On-Policy Self-Distillation (AOPSD), which adapts what information the teacher receives and how strongly its feedback influences learning. AOPSD encodes each solution as a reasoning DAG, orders problems by the student's evolving capability, and reveals only the affordable subgraph and its next frontier as PI. For high-disagreement tokens, AOPSD utilizes short teacher continuations as probes to encourage useful guidance while mitigating PI-conditioned shortcuts among teacher supervisions. On HMMT25, AIME24, AIME25, and BRUMo25, AOPSD achieves 72.5% Pass@8, which is 6.7 percentage points above OPSD and 4.2 above the strongest competing baseline while reducing 15 percentage points of training time at lower cost.

AI.tldr: AOPSD improves on-policy self-distillation by adapting what privileged information (PI) the teacher sees and how strongly its feedback is weighted, avoiding PI-conditioned shortcuts while cutting training cost.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers dense, on-policy supervision without needing a larger external teacher, but its effectiveness depends heavily on how privileged information (PI) is designed and used. Diagnostics reveal a gap between teacher utility and student learnability: a small fraction of high-disagreement tokens dominate the distillation signal, and short teacher continuations at these positions expose more explicit PI leakage than transferable correction cues, suggesting PI-conditioned shortcuts are being injected.
AI.method: AOPSD adapts both the information the teacher receives and the strength of its feedback. It encodes each solution as a reasoning DAG, orders problems by the student's evolving capability, and reveals only the affordable subgraph and its next frontier as PI. For high-disagreement tokens, short teacher continuations are used as probes to encourage useful guidance while mitigating PI-conditioned shortcuts in teacher supervisions.
AI.result: On HMMT25, AIME24, AIME25, and BRUMo25, AOPSD reaches 72.5% Pass@8, 6.7 percentage points above OPSD and 4.2 points above the strongest competing baseline, while reducing training time by 15 percentage points at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Adaptively controlling PI exposure and teacher feedback strength mitigates PI-conditioned shortcuts in on-policy self-distillation, yielding substantial accuracy gains and more efficient training than prior baselines.

title: Unified Visual-Tactile-Action Modeling from Human Demonstrations for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous manipulation requires tactile feedback.However, robot tactile demonstrations are difficult to scale,because dexterous-hand teleoperation provides limited tactile feedback to the operator. In contrast, human demonstrations offer a substantially more scalable source of diverse tactile interactions. Motivated by a simple premise: hands can change, but the underlying physics of interaction does not. We leverage human tactile data to improve dexterous manipulation policies. Specifically, we first build a tactile motion-capture system that synchronously records images, tactile signals, and hand motions. Using this system, we construct the UVTA dataset spanning five contact-rich tasks, with 1,000 human demonstrations covering diverse interaction patterns and 150 robot demonstrations per task. To transfer the underlying physics of human interaction to robot control, we propose a Unified Visual-Tactile-Action Model that maps both embodiments into aligned tactile and action representations and jointly predicts future action and tactile trajectories. The joint objective enables human demonstrations to supervise contact-aware representation learning, while only robot actions are executed during deployment. In real-robot evaluations across five tasks, our method achieves an average success rate of 70%, outperforming the strongest visual-tactile baseline, which achieves 29%, and an architecture ablation, which achieves 42%. Performance improves consistently with additional human demonstrations and exhibits no saturation at 1,000 demonstrations per task, validating the effectiveness of scalable human tactile data for dexterous manipulation. Project page is available at https://uni-vta.github.io/.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using scalable human tactile demonstrations to improve dexterous robot manipulation, introducing the UVTA dataset and a Unified Visual-Tactile-Action Model that aligns human and robot representations through joint action-tactile prediction.
AI.motivation: Robot tactile demonstrations are hard to scale because dexterous-hand teleoperation provides limited tactile feedback to the operator. In contrast, human demonstrations are a far more scalable source of diverse tactile interactions. The work rests on the premise that "hands can change, but the underlying physics of interaction does not," motivating the transfer of human tactile data to robot policies.
AI.method: First, a tactile motion-capture system is built to synchronously record images, tactile signals, and hand motions. Using it, the UVTA dataset is constructed, spanning five contact-rich tasks with 1,000 human demonstrations (diverse interaction patterns) and 150 robot demonstrations per task. Then a Unified Visual-Tactile-Action Model is proposed that maps both embodiments into aligned tactile and action representations and jointly predicts future action and tactile trajectories; the joint objective lets human demonstrations supervise contact-aware representation learning, while only robot actions are executed at deployment.
AI.result: In real-robot evaluations across five tasks, the method achieves an average success rate of 70%, versus 29% for the strongest visual-tactile baseline and 42% for an architecture ablation. Performance improves consistently with more human demonstrations and shows no saturation at 1,000 demonstrations per task.
AI.conclusion: Scalable human tactile data is effective for dexterous manipulation, and aligning human and robot embodiments via joint action-tactile prediction enables contact-aware policy learning that outperforms visual-tactile baselines.

title: Refinement Symmetry in Multimodal Transformers
summary: Attention weights depend on token counts, which change with the representation of a signal. We study refinement symmetry: splitting a representation while preserving content, position, visible context, and total mass should preserve its contribution. Building on proportional and quadrature attention, we show that split invariance forces the local mass factor to be linear for any fixed positive attention kernel, provided that factor is nondecreasing. For changed representations, a physical coupling bounds attention error by separating feature change from weight reallocation. In Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, duplicating half the visual tokens threefold changes 255 of 3,586 MVBench answers under standard attention; measure weighting preserves every answer under matched visibility. Under natural frame resampling, it reduces distributional drift. At twofold merging of a frozen video encoding, a five-seed evaluation shows an all-partition-correct accuracy gain of 1.04 percentage points over global count weighting (average group mass) and 0.93 points over standard attention. The advantage over global count also holds on WorldSense but depends on the compression budget. The result is a representation principle with a measured benefit in robustness across partitions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "refinement symmetry" for attention: splitting a representation while preserving content, position, visible context, and total mass should preserve its contribution. It proves that split invariance forces a linear local mass factor (for any fixed positive attention kernel, with a nondecreasing factor), and proposes "measure weighting" that is invariant to such refinements, demonstrating improved robustness in multimodal models.
AI.motivation: Attention weights depend on token counts, so re-representing a signal (e.g., splitting or duplicating tokens) can change attention outputs even when content, position, visible context, and total mass are preserved. The authors seek a principled invariance—refinement symmetry—so that attention contributions remain stable under such representation changes, improving robustness to token resampling, duplication, and merging in vision-language models.
AI.method: The study formalizes refinement symmetry: splitting a representation while preserving content, position, visible context, and total mass should preserve its contribution. Building on proportional and quadrature attention, it analyzes when split invariance holds, showing it forces the local mass factor to be linear for any fixed positive attention kernel provided the factor is nondecreasing. For changed representations, a physical coupling is introduced to bound attention error by separating feature change from weight reallocation. The resulting measure weighting is evaluated in Qwen2.5-Omni-7B via visual token duplication, natural frame resampling, and frozen video encoding merging, compared against global count weighting and standard attention.
AI.result: In Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, duplicating half the visual tokens threefold changes 255 of 3,586 MVBench answers under standard attention, whereas measure weighting preserves every answer under matched visibility. Under natural frame resampling, it reduces distributional drift. At twofold merging of a frozen video encoding, a five-seed evaluation shows an all-partition-correct accuracy gain of 1.04 percentage points over global count weighting and 0.93 points over standard attention. The advantage over global count also holds on WorldSense but depends on the compression budget.
AI.conclusion: Refinement symmetry yields a representation principle: attention should depend on total mass rather than token count, which is achieved by measure weighting with a linear local mass factor. This principle provides a measured robustness benefit across partitions and representations, improving stability under token duplication, resampling, and merging.

title: WB-WAM: Heterogeneous Body-Hand Pre-training for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation demands coordinated body and hand behavior, while conventional robot pre-training data provide limited coverage of such whole-body motion. We present WB-WAM, a World Action Model that incorporates explicit whole-body action supervision into generative video pre-training. A shared physical action space integrates body, root, and dexterous hand annotations from heterogeneous sources, enabling joint video and action learning from 1880.2 hours of partially annotated video and motion data. The resulting priors are refined through PICO mid-training and adapted to robot tasks with auxiliary forward kinematics supervision. We construct WB-Datasets to support these stages with retargeted egocentric human demonstrations and robot trajectories, allowing task-aligned human motion to supplement limited robot data. Evaluations in simulation demonstrate strong whole-body task performance with 81.9% in HumanoidArena, while real-world experiments further validate WB-WAM with 84.0% mean success across five tasks. Moreover, task-aligned PICO mid-training improves downstream task performance while reducing the need for real-robot demonstrations. These results support heterogeneous whole-body pre-training and human motion transfer as a practical route to data-efficient humanoid loco-manipulation.

AI.tldr: WB-WAM is a World Action Model that injects explicit whole-body action supervision into generative video pre-training, enabling data-efficient humanoid loco-manipulation via heterogeneous pre-training and human motion transfer.
AI.motivation: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body and hand behavior, but conventional robot pre-training data provide limited coverage of whole-body motion. This data gap motivates a pre-training approach that can leverage heterogeneous, partially annotated video and motion sources rather than scarce robot data alone.
AI.method: A shared physical action space integrates body, root, and dexterous hand annotations from heterogeneous sources, allowing joint video and action learning from 1880.2 hours of partially annotated video and motion data. The resulting priors are refined through PICO mid-training and adapted to robot tasks with auxiliary forward kinematics supervision. WB-Datasets supply retargeted egocentric human demonstrations and robot trajectories for each stage, letting task-aligned human motion supplement limited robot data.
AI.result: Simulation evaluation reaches 81.9% in HumanoidArena. Real-world experiments validate WB-WAM with 84.0% mean success across five tasks. Task-aligned PICO mid-training improves downstream task performance while reducing the need for real-robot demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: These results support heterogeneous whole-body pre-training and human motion transfer as a practical route to data-efficient humanoid loco-manipulation.

title: What Would Falsify It? A Variable Specific Evidence Standard for Mechanistic Claims About Self Explanation
summary:
When a language model explains an answer it has already given, does it reuse the computation that produced the answer or reconstruct a story from the answer alone? Attribution, transportability and recoverability are each compatible with causal use without establishing it. We propose an evidence standard: pair each positive statistic with a variable specific null that removes the tested variable's identity while matching relevant nuisance dimensions as far as possible, and audit unmatched dimensions.
  We apply this standard to a known cause. A cue naming a wrong option raises the rate of choosing that option by 64 to 68 percentage points across three models. Explanations mention the cue in 1.8 percent of items or fewer in three of four models tested. Three estimator classes yield favorable statistics, but none establishes causal sensitivity to the cue contrast under its own control in the three-model analysis. In the strongest case, a recovered cue direction reaches $R^2$ of 0.95 and exceeds a geometry matched random direction in all three seeds, while a direction fitted by the same pipeline with cue labels scrambled reproduces 61 to 76 percent of its effect at comparable realized edit magnitude. A fourth model passes one interchange endpoint, but unequal edit magnitudes and a contrast that changes both cue identity and cue-answer agreement limit its interpretation.
  These experiments leave causal access unresolved. They establish an evidentiary requirement: favorable mechanistic statistics must survive controls for variable identity and nuisance structure. Reusable controls separate generic from identity specific transport effects, fit null directions with scrambled labels, and audit realized intervention magnitudes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evidence standard for testing whether a language model's explanation reuses the computation behind its answer: each favorable statistic must be paired with a variable-specific null that removes the tested variable's identity while matching nuisance dimensions. Applying this to a cue-attribution question, favorable statistics from three estimator classes fail to establish causal sensitivity to the cue contrast in a three-model analysis.
AI.motivation: Attribution, transportability, and recoverability are all compatible with genuine causal use without establishing it. Existing mechanistic statistics can appear favorable while reflecting nuisance structure or variable identity rather than the tested causal variable, so a stricter evidentiary standard is needed to distinguish generic from identity-specific effects.
AI.method: The authors define an evidence standard pairing every positive statistic with a variable-specific null that strips the tested variable's identity while matching nuisance dimensions as far as possible, plus an audit of unmatched dimensions. They apply it to a known cause: a cue naming a wrong option that raises selection of that option by 64-68 percentage points across three models. They test explanation mention rates, run three estimator classes, fit a recovered cue direction and compare it to a geometry-matched random direction and to a direction fitted with cue labels scrambled, and check realized edit magnitudes.
AI.result: Explanations mention the cue in 1.8% of items or fewer in three of four models. Three estimator classes yield favorable statistics, but none establishes causal sensitivity to the cue contrast under its own control in the three-model analysis. In the strongest case, the recovered cue direction reaches R^2 of 0.95 and exceeds a geometry-matched random direction in all three seeds, yet a direction fitted with scrambled cue labels reproduces 61-76% of its effect at comparable realized edit magnitude. A fourth model passes one interchange endpoint, but unequal edit magnitudes and a contrast changing both cue identity and cue-answer agreement limit interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The experiments leave causal access unresolved but establish an evidentiary requirement: favorable mechanistic statistics must survive controls for variable identity and nuisance structure. Reusable controls can separate generic from identity-specific transport effects, fit null directions with scrambled labels, and audit realized intervention magnitudes.

title: RLE-Bench: A Qualifying Exam for Coding Agents as Robot Learning Engineers
summary: Coding agents are beginning to move beyond purely digital tasks to tackle physical-world challenges, particularly in robotics. Existing robotics benchmarks, however, primarily focus on the performance of individual artifacts, such as policies or controllers, offering limited coverage of coding agents' broader engineering capabilities. Real-world robotics extends beyond control: agents must build, integrate, diagnose, and improve heterogeneous artifacts under resource constraints and reason from multimodal feedback. To evaluate these broader capabilities, we introduce RLE-Bench, a benchmark of robot-learning tasks spanning four representative robotics development workflows: interactive control, policy learning, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. We use diverse task-specific metrics to evaluate the artifacts submitted by the coding agents, from the success rate the agents achieved to the policy agents trained, the harness agent built, and the mechanical structures the agent designed. We aggregate these metrics into an overall RLE Index and report workflow-specific capability profiles, enabling systematic comparison of coding agents' capabilities across multiple capability dimensions. Beyond performance ranks, we also conduct in-depth case studies examining agent behavior on representative tasks, highlighting both current capabilities and limitations, and pointing to the opportunities robotics tasks have to offer for future agent training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RLE-Bench, a benchmark of robot-learning tasks spanning four robotics development workflows (interactive control, policy learning, perception and estimation, mechanical design) to evaluate coding agents' broader engineering capabilities, aggregating task-specific metrics into an RLE Index and capability profiles.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are moving beyond purely digital tasks into physical-world robotics, but existing robotics benchmarks focus narrowly on individual artifacts like policies or controllers and offer limited coverage of agents' broader engineering capabilities. Real-world robotics requires agents to build, integrate, diagnose, and improve heterogeneous artifacts under resource constraints using multimodal feedback, which current benchmarks fail to assess.
AI.method: The authors design RLE-Bench, comprising robot-learning tasks across four representative robotics development workflows: interactive control, policy learning, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. They employ diverse task-specific metrics to evaluate artifacts submitted by coding agents—such as success rate achieved, policies trained, harnesses built, and mechanical structures designed—and aggregate these into an overall RLE Index, also reporting workflow-specific capability profiles.
AI.result: RLE-Bench enables systematic comparison of coding agents' capabilities across multiple capability dimensions via the RLE Index and workflow-specific capability profiles. In-depth case studies of agent behavior on representative tasks reveal both current capabilities and limitations.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a systematic framework for evaluating coding agents' engineering capabilities in robotics and points to opportunities that robotics tasks offer for future agent training.

title: Expected Reasoning-Step Return Unifies On-Policy Learning from Rewards and Teachers
summary: On-policy reasoning models can learn from task rewards or teacher signals, but these sources differ in form and can favor conflicting updates, leaving unclear which should guide a given reasoning action. We introduce \textbf{Expected Reasoning-Step Return (ERSR)}, which treats semantic reasoning steps as macro-actions and uses Monte Carlo student-policy rollouts to estimate the expected final task reward of student-generated and teacher-proposed actions in a common return space for step-level comparison. ERSR analysis reveals an outcome-dependent asymmetry: student actions are more beneficial than teacher replacements on successful trajectories, whereas teacher replacements become more beneficial on failed trajectories. We further show that student answer-probe gains track student-step ERSR utility and distinguish beneficial from harmful reasoning steps. Based on these findings, we propose \textbf{Return-Referenced On-Policy Learning (R$^2$OPL)}, which reinforces student reasoning on successful trajectories and distills teacher signals on failed ones, while using group success rate for difficulty scaling and student-probe gains for step-level modulation. Experiments across reasoning benchmarks and teacher--student configurations show that R$^2$OPL consistently outperforms strong baselines. ERSR training dynamics further show that R$^2$OPL jointly exploits substantial utility from both reward- and teacher-side signals, whereas existing hybrids often leave substantial residual utility in one branch.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Expected Reasoning-Step Return (ERSR) to compare student vs. teacher reasoning actions in a shared return space, revealing an outcome-dependent asymmetry, and proposes R²OPL, a hybrid method that reinforces student steps on successful trajectories and distills teacher signals on failed ones.
AI.motivation: On-policy reasoning models can learn from task rewards or teacher signals, but these sources differ in form and can favor conflicting updates, leaving unclear which should guide a given reasoning action.
AI.method: ERSR treats semantic reasoning steps as macro-actions and uses Monte Carlo student-policy rollouts to estimate the expected final task reward of student-generated and teacher-proposed actions in a common return space for step-level comparison. Based on the revealed asymmetry, R²OPL reinforces student reasoning on successful trajectories and distills teacher signals on failed ones, using group success rate for difficulty scaling and student-probe gains for step-level modulation.
AI.result: Experiments across reasoning benchmarks and teacher–student configurations show that R²OPL consistently outperforms strong baselines. ERSR training dynamics further show that R²OPL jointly exploits substantial utility from both reward- and teacher-side signals, whereas existing hybrids often leave substantial residual utility in one branch.
AI.conclusion: ERSR provides a principled, unified return space for step-level comparison of reward- and teacher-side signals, exposing an outcome-dependent asymmetry. Leveraging this, R²OPL effectively combines both signal sources and consistently improves reasoning performance over strong baselines.

title: mmHRI: Towards Privacy-Preserving Human-Robot Interaction with Millimeter-Wave Radar
summary: Assistive robots increasingly operate in many human-centered environments and perform various human-robot interaction (HRI) tasks, such as object delivery. However, most existing HRI systems rely on RGB cameras that continuously observe humans to respond to non-verbal commands, such as hand gestures. This raises privacy concerns in privacy- critical environments, such as hospital wards or restaurants, where direct camera observation of humans is restricted. To develop privacy-preserving HRI, we leverage millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar, which can sense human motion through privacy barriers without identifiable imagery. We propose mmHRI, the first multi-modal robot manipulation framework that achieves mmWave radar-guided privacy-preserving HRI. mmHRI introduces two key designs to mitigate the sparsity and temporal inconsistency of radar data in cluttered robot manipulation environments. First, we propose a dual-stream architecture that jointly learns from unfiltered raw radar tensors and radar point clouds to estimate both human actions and 3D poses. To mitigate signal inconsistency, mmHRI further incorporates a memory-based state-space model (MSSM) that retains historical radar features to reduce abrupt changes in pose/action. These estimated human states are then converted into structured textual robot instructions, which control a vision-language-action (VLA) policy for closed-loop robot manipulation and human-aware reactions. Our evaluation covers human action recognition and closed-loop delivery and retrieval. In the privacy-preserving curtain setting, mmHRI achieves 85.09% action-recognition accuracy, outperforming existing radar-based alternatives. Robot trials further demonstrate successful delivery and retrieval under visual occlusion, with stable task performance across unseen subjects, clutter configurations, and environments.

AI.tldr: mmHRI is a multi-modal robot manipulation framework that uses mmWave radar to enable privacy-preserving human-robot interaction, achieving 85.09% action-recognition accuracy and successful closed-loop delivery/retrieval under visual occlusion.
AI.motivation: Most existing HRI systems rely on RGB cameras that continuously observe humans to respond to non-verbal commands such as hand gestures. This raises privacy concerns in privacy-critical environments (e.g., hospital wards, restaurants) where direct camera observation of humans is restricted. The paper aims to develop privacy-preserving HRI without identifiable imagery.
AI.method: The authors leverage millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar, which senses human motion through privacy barriers. mmHRI uses two key designs: (1) a dual-stream architecture that jointly learns from unfiltered raw radar tensors and radar point clouds to estimate human actions and 3D poses; and (2) a memory-based state-space model (MSSM) that retains historical radar features to reduce abrupt changes in pose/action, addressing radar sparsity and temporal inconsistency. Estimated human states are converted into structured textual robot instructions that control a vision-language-action (VLA) policy for closed-loop robot manipulation and human-aware reactions.
AI.result: In the privacy-preserving curtain setting, mmHRI achieves 85.09% action-recognition accuracy, outperforming existing radar-based alternatives. Robot trials demonstrate successful delivery and retrieval under visual occlusion, with stable task performance across unseen subjects, clutter configurations, and environments.
AI.conclusion: mmHRI is the first multi-modal robot manipulation framework achieving mmWave radar-guided privacy-preserving HRI, showing robust and accurate performance for closed-loop delivery and retrieval tasks under visual occlusion.

title: When Better Gets Worse: Improvement Fidelity for Self-Improving Agents in Adaptive Worlds
summary: Self-improving agents increasingly rely on proxy verifiers to choose policy updates, yet deployment can change the world in which those updates are evaluated. An update that looks better to the verifier can therefore become worse after deployment even when the verifier ranks policies well overall. We formalize this gap as Improvement Fidelity, which asks whether proxy improvements preserve the sign and ordering of deployment improvements over the updates an improvement process actually proposes. We show that global policy accuracy need not guarantee update fidelity: operator shift and deployment response can create update-level errors, while candidate margins determine whether those errors change the replacement decision. We introduce PIVOT-KG, a paired, decision-aware validator that allocates scarce high-fidelity evaluation according to the expected reduction in selection regret per unit cost. Across 90 held-out roots in Leduc, Kuhn, and Melting Pot, proxy and deployment optimal sets are disjoint in 51 cases. In an eight-candidate HighwayEnv stress test, PIVOT-KG reduces mean improvement-selection regret from 0.0435 under the exact Uniform validation rule to 0.0055 at the primary budget. Together, these results show why reliable self-improvement should evaluate proposed improvements in the worlds they induce, while providing a practical rule for allocating scarce deployment evidence when it can affect the replacement decision.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Improvement Fidelity—whether proxy-verifier improvements preserve the sign and ordering of deployment improvements across proposed updates—shows global policy accuracy does not guarantee it, and proposes PIVOT-KG, a decision-aware validator that allocates scarce high-fidelity evaluation to reduce selection regret.
AI.motivation: Self-improving agents increasingly rely on proxy verifiers to select policy updates, but deployment alters the world in which those updates are evaluated. An update that appears better to the verifier can become worse after deployment, even when the verifier ranks policies well overall. This mismatch between proxy evaluation and post-deployment outcomes threatens the reliability of self-improvement.
AI.method: The authors formalize the gap as Improvement Fidelity: whether proxy improvements preserve the sign and ordering of deployment improvements over the updates an improvement process actually proposes. They show global policy accuracy does not imply update fidelity, since operator shift and deployment response induce update-level errors, while candidate margins determine whether such errors flip the replacement decision. They then introduce PIVOT-KG, a paired, decision-aware validator that allocates scarce high-fidelity evaluation according to expected reduction in selection regret per unit cost.
AI.result: Across 90 held-out roots in Leduc, Kuhn, and Melting Pot, proxy and deployment optimal sets are disjoint in 51 cases. In an eight-candidate HighwayEnv stress test, PIVOT-KG reduces mean improvement-selection regret from 0.0435 under the exact Uniform validation rule to 0.0055 at the primary budget.
AI.conclusion: Reliable self-improvement should evaluate proposed improvements in the worlds they induce, rather than relying solely on proxy-verifier accuracy. PIVOT-KG provides a practical rule for allocating scarce deployment evidence when that evidence can affect the replacement decision.

title: Proprioceptive Force Estimation for Quadruped Locomotion and Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Payload forces must be accommodated during locomotion, while leash forces can specify desired motion. We investigate whether a shared three-dimensional force estimate in newtons, inferred from proprioceptive history under sustained loading, can support both tasks. An estimator and locomotion policy are jointly trained with supervised force and velocity outputs and learned latent context. The estimated force conditions locomotion and additionally generates planar-velocity and yaw-rate commands for leash guidance through an analytical map. In sustained-force simulation sweeps, temporal means of componentwise force root mean square error range from 1.44 to 2.83\,N. Compared with a domain-randomized baseline, the framework reduces velocity-tracking and base-orientation error scores by 21.6\% and 46.5\%, respectively, and increases mean survival from 68.29\% to 94.60\% in separate sustained-force tests. Unitree Go1 experiments demonstrate stationary vertical and horizontal force estimation, locomotion with an 8.5\,kg payload whose weight exceeds the 70\,N training force limit, and leash guidance using the same force-estimation interface.

AI.tldr: A shared 3D force estimator learned from proprioceptive history supports both payload accommodation and leash-based guidance for quadruped locomotion, validated in simulation and on a Unitree Go1.
AI.motivation: Locomotion controllers must handle two distinct force regimes: sustained payload forces that must be passively accommodated, and leash forces that should actively specify desired motion. Prior approaches typically treat these separately, so the paper asks whether a single 3D force estimate inferred from proprioception can serve both roles.
AI.method: An estimator and a locomotion policy are jointly trained with supervised force and velocity outputs plus a learned latent context, yielding a shared 3D force estimate in newtons from proprioceptive history under sustained loading. The estimated force conditions the locomotion policy and, via an analytical map, is converted into planar-velocity and yaw-rate commands for leash guidance.
AI.result: In sustained-force simulation sweeps, temporal means of componentwise force RMSE range from 1.44 to 2.83 N. Versus a domain-randomized baseline, the framework cuts velocity-tracking and base-orientation error scores by 21.6% and 46.5%, and raises mean survival from 68.29% to 94.60% in separate sustained-force tests. Unitree Go1 experiments show stationary vertical and horizontal force estimation, locomotion with an 8.5 kg payload exceeding the 70 N training force limit, and leash guidance through the same force-estimation interface.
AI.conclusion: A single proprioception-derived 3D force estimate can unify payload accommodation and leash-based motion specification, generalizing beyond the training force range and transferring to real hardware.

title: PINNMorph: Evolving Online Adaptation Policies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a learning-based framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their training behavior can change substantially throughout optimization. Residual distributions, gradient interactions, regional learning difficulty, and model-capacity requirements may evolve over time, while the network architecture and major training mechanisms are typically determined before training. We propose PINNMorph, an online PINN adaptation framework based on large language model (LLM)-guided policy evolution. PINNMorph maintains a population of state-conditioned adaptation policies that map execution diagnostics to controlled interventions over topology modification, additive representation augmentation, objective balancing, gradient handling, adaptive sampling, and optimizer-phase control. At each intervention opportunity, candidate programs are instantiated from the current policy population, selected according to the observed training state, and applied directly to the PINN under training. The resulting model inherits its existing parameters and training state and continues optimization along the same trajectory. Execution outcomes are subsequently used to evaluate interventions and evolve the policy population. Unlike pre-training architecture search or fixed adaptation rules, PINNMorph jointly adapts the current PINN and the policies governing its interventions using feedback from actual training. Experiments on 13 PDE benchmarks show that PINNMorph achieves lower solution errors than SA-PINN, ConFIG, RoPINN, HARMONIC, and PINNsAgent across all evaluated problems. Ablation studies further examine the effects of online adaptation, state-conditioned intervention selection, and execution-feedback-driven policy evolution.

AI.tldr: PINNMorph is an online PINN adaptation framework that uses LLM-guided policy evolution to dynamically modify network topology, representations, objectives, gradients, sampling, and optimizer phases during training, outperforming several PINN baselines across 13 PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: PINN training behavior changes over time: residual distributions, gradient interactions, regional difficulty, and capacity needs evolve, yet architecture and training mechanisms are usually fixed before training. This mismatch between static design and dynamic training dynamics motivates online adaptation.
AI.method: PINNMorph maintains a population of state-conditioned adaptation policies mapping execution diagnostics to controlled interventions over topology modification, additive representation augmentation, objective balancing, gradient handling, adaptive sampling, and optimizer-phase control. At each intervention opportunity, candidate programs are instantiated from the current policy population, selected by observed training state, and applied directly to the PINN under training. The model inherits existing parameters and training state and continues along the same trajectory; execution outcomes evaluate interventions and evolve the policy population. Unlike pre-training architecture search or fixed adaptation rules, it jointly adapts the PINN and its governing policies via LLM-guided evolution using actual training feedback.
AI.result: On 13 PDE benchmarks, PINNMorph achieves lower solution errors than SA-PINN, ConFIG, RoPINN, HARMONIC, and PINNsAgent across all evaluated problems. Ablations examine online adaptation, state-conditioned intervention selection, and execution-feedback-driven policy evolution.
AI.conclusion: Jointly adapting the PINN and the policies that govern its interventions, driven by execution feedback, yields consistently lower solution errors than strong fixed or search-based baselines, and the online, state-conditioned, feedback-driven components each contribute to this gain.

title: GAE: General Action Expert for Real-Time Humanoid Teleoperation
summary: Humanoid avatars extend human physical presence beyond the body, enabling people to participate in social, service, and labor activities through remotely operated robots. This requires teleoperation systems capable of realizing diverse and dynamic whole-body behaviors while maintaining responsive human-robot synchronization. We present General Action Expert(GAE), a unified learning framework for general-purpose, low-latency humanoid whole-body teleoperation. To cover diverse human behaviors, GAE builds a large-scale human motion dataset from heterogeneous sources, including videos, animations, and motion capture, followed by standardization and augmentation. GAE then addresses the noise and embodiment mismatch in human motions with a two-stage training paradigm: a privileged generator policy first tracks human motion references in simulation and rolls out feasible humanoid trajectories; a deployable executor policy then learns to track these generated trajectories under curriculum domain randomization. For responsive human-robot synchronization, GAE introduces a latency-conditioned anticipation mechanism that adaptively compensates for end-to-end delay during real-time teleoperation. Simulation and real-world experiments on Unitree G1 and Westlake O1 robots demonstrate that GAE enables humanoids to smoothly mirror diverse, agile, and expressive human behaviors. Project website: https://wangyf0928.github.io/gae-wlrobotics/

AI.tldr: GAE is a unified learning framework for general-purpose, low-latency humanoid whole-body teleoperation that enables humanoids to mirror diverse human behaviors via large-scale motion data, two-stage policy training, and latency-conditioned anticipation.
AI.motivation: Humanoid avatars extend human presence for social, service, and labor activities via remotely operated robots, requiring teleoperation that achieves diverse, dynamic whole-body behaviors with responsive human-robot synchronization. Existing systems struggle to simultaneously handle diverse human behaviors and low-latency synchronization.
AI.method: GAE builds a large-scale human motion dataset from heterogeneous sources (videos, animations, motion capture), followed by standardization and augmentation. It employs a two-stage training paradigm: a privileged generator policy tracks human motion references in simulation to roll out feasible humanoid trajectories, then a deployable executor policy learns to track these trajectories under curriculum domain randomization. A latency-conditioned anticipation mechanism adaptively compensates for end-to-end delay in real-time teleoperation.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments on Unitree G1 and Westlake O1 robots show that GAE enables humanoids to smoothly mirror diverse, agile, and expressive human behaviors.
AI.conclusion: GAE provides a unified, low-latency framework for general-purpose humanoid whole-body teleoperation, combining large-scale data, two-stage training, and latency anticipation to achieve responsive and expressive humanoid behavior replication.

title: Dude, Where's My State? Execution Information Requirements for Stateful Agents
comment: 35 pages, 12 figures, 15 tables. Supplementary material included
summary: Long-running agents must preserve information that later steps depend on. We introduce the Execution Information Requirement (EIR), a lower bound on the information that must remain accessible for correct completion under specified task and access conditions. We develop LACUNA, a framework that generates tasks with known dependencies and varies information demand, retention, and recovery separately from the difficulty of individual operations. Across four models, restoring a missing result raises accuracy on affected recall steps to 100%, compared with 0% for equal-length irrelevant information. Sufficient storage alone does not ensure success: retention policies can discard required results, errors can propagate through later computations, and agents can stop before recovery is complete. We also introduce VESTIGE, which uses agent execution traces to construct semantic graphs and measure information demand for real tasks. Across 72,562 software-agent trajectories, VESTIGE reveals a steeper distance-related decline in solution-relevant rereading for failed runs (RR 0.951 per distance doubling), while adjusted peak demand alone is not associated with failure. Together, these contributions support evaluating whether agents preserve and recover the information their tasks require.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Execution Information Requirement (EIR) as a lower bound on information that must remain accessible for correct task completion, plus two frameworks: LACUNA, which generates tasks with controlled dependencies to test information demand, retention, and recovery independently of operation difficulty, and VESTIGE, which builds semantic graphs from execution traces to measure information demand in real tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-running agents must preserve information that later steps depend on, yet existing evaluations conflate operational difficulty with information-preservation capacity. The authors aim to isolate whether agents retain, recover, and propagate information their tasks actually require, rather than merely measuring task performance or storage capacity.
AI.method: The authors define the Execution Information Requirement (EIR) as a lower bound on accessible information needed for correct completion under given task and access conditions. They build LACUNA, a synthetic task generator with known dependencies that varies information demand, retention, and recovery separately from individual operation difficulty. They also introduce VESTIGE, which uses agent execution traces to construct semantic graphs and measure information demand for real tasks, analyzed over 72,562 software-agent trajectories.
AI.result: Across four models, restoring a missing result raised accuracy on affected recall steps to 100%, versus 0% for equal-length irrelevant information. Sufficient storage alone did not ensure success due to retention policies discarding required results, error propagation, and premature stopping before recovery. VESTIGE showed a steeper distance-related decline in solution-relevant rereading for failed runs (RR 0.951 per distance doubling), while adjusted peak demand alone was not associated with failure.
AI.conclusion: These contributions provide a basis for evaluating whether agents preserve and recover the information their tasks require, shifting assessment from raw task success or storage capacity toward information-demand-aware metrics.

title: WAM-OPD: Sharpening World Action Models via On-Policy Distillation
summary: Pretrained world action models (WAMs) provide generalist capabilities across diverse robotic manipulation tasks, yet improving target-task performance to an expert level without degrading pretrained skills remains challenging. We explore on-policy distillation (OPD) for WAMs and introduce WAM-OPD. WAM-OPD inherits the advantage of OPD methods that transfer task-specific teacher knowledge under the student's own induced distribution, rather than directly fitting the student to a narrow task-specific data distribution. However, in closed-loop manipulation, the observation histories change as the student policy evolves, requiring fresh environment rollouts to remain on-policy. Applying OPD to WAMs entails repeated data collection, which is costly even in simulation and often impractical on real robots. To avoid repeated environment rollouts during distillation, we introduce prefix-weighted trajectory replay (PWTR). PWTR uses a fixed trajectory pool composed primarily of initial-student rollouts, supplemented with task-specific teacher rollouts to broaden trajectory coverage. For each trajectory replayed from this pool, PWTR conditions the current policy on successive stored histories to generate fresh denoising paths, along which the task-specific teacher provides supervision. Although these denoising paths are refreshed as the policy evolves, the replayed environment trajectories remain fixed. PWTR therefore reweights per-decision distillation losses using proxy importance weights derived from path scores accumulated over the trajectory prefix preceding each decision to mitigate the resulting shift in the history distribution. Simulated and real-world experiments demonstrate task adaptation without additional environment interaction during distillation. In both settings, WAM-OPD improves target-task performance while retaining near-initial performance on tasks excluded from adaptation.

AI.tldr: WAM-OPD applies on-policy distillation to pretrained world action models using prefix-weighted trajectory replay (PWTR), enabling expert-level task adaptation without repeated environment rollouts during distillation.
AI.motivation: Pretrained world action models (WAMs) offer generalist robotic manipulation capabilities, but improving target-task performance to expert level while preserving pretrained skills is hard. On-policy distillation (OPD) is attractive because it transfers task-specific teacher knowledge under the student's own induced distribution, yet applying it to WAMs in closed-loop manipulation would require fresh rollouts as the observation histories evolve—costly in simulation and often impractical on real robots.
AI.method: WAM-OPD adapts OPD to WAMs and introduces prefix-weighted trajectory replay (PWTR). PWTR draws from a fixed trajectory pool composed mainly of initial-student rollouts supplemented with task-specific teacher rollouts for broader coverage. For each replayed trajectory, the current policy is conditioned on successive stored histories to generate fresh denoising paths, along which the task-specific teacher supervises. Because denoising paths are refreshed while environment trajectories stay fixed, PWTR reweights per-decision distillation losses with proxy importance weights derived from path scores accumulated over the trajectory prefix preceding each decision, mitigating the history-distribution shift.
AI.result: In both simulated and real-world experiments, WAM-OPD achieves task adaptation without any additional environment interaction during distillation. It improves target-task performance while retaining near-initial performance on tasks excluded from adaptation.
AI.conclusion: WAM-OPD shows that OPD can be effectively applied to WAMs via PWTR, delivering expert-level target-task performance with preserved generalist skills and no extra rollout cost during distillation.

title: World Agent: Can Language Models Keep a World Running?
summary: World models are moving from generating realistic frames to generating playable worlds, yet whether a delivered world can keep running is not tested anywhere. Existing evaluations stop at generation, at delivery, or at single-step transitions, and each stops at a different point along the way. Correct local state transitions or intermediate outcomes do not guarantee a correctly organized causal event flow. We propose the world agent task, which moves the evaluation point of world generation from the moment of delivery to the continued operation that follows. In this task, a model is not asked to generate a world. It is held responsible for keeping the world running, which requires coordinating events and carrying forward their consequences to constrain subsequent evolution. We instantiate the task in WorldAgent-Benchmark with two complementary tracks. In the maintenance track, the model must ground the events of a continuous narrative into correct transitions of the explicit world state while respecting causal, temporal, and concurrency constraints. In the deduction track, the model must predict how the world will evolve under partial observations and act toward a goal. The maintenance track combines LLM-assisted semantic judgments with programmatic validation and scoring, while the deduction track is evaluated entirely programmatically. Individual judgments are auditable against world states and execution logs, and scores can be recomputed from the saved judgments and execution records. Across 8 models, scores decline steadily as pre-built structure is removed from the world, and causal-relation checking is the weakest component for every model. The benchmark makes the continued operation of a world measurable and distinguishes local completion from failures in event organization. Code and dataset will be released on https://github.com/HCPLab-SYSU/WorldAgent-Benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "world agent" task and WorldAgent-Benchmark to evaluate whether a generated world can keep running (continued operation), not just be delivered. It has a maintenance track (grounding narrative events into correct explicit world-state transitions under causal/temporal/concurrency constraints) and a deduction track (predicting evolution under partial observation toward a goal). Across 8 models, scores drop as pre-built structure is removed, and causal-relation checking is the weakest component.
AI.motivation: World models are shifting from generating realistic frames to generating playable worlds, but there is no test of whether a delivered world can keep running. Existing evaluations stop at generation, delivery, or single-step transitions, and each halts at a different point; correct local transitions or intermediate outcomes do not guarantee a correctly organized causal event flow.
AI.method: Proposes the world agent task, moving the evaluation point from delivery to continued operation, where the model must keep the world running by coordinating events and carrying their consequences forward. Instantiated as WorldAgent-Benchmark with two tracks: (1) maintenance—grounding continuous narrative events into correct explicit world-state transitions respecting causal, temporal, and concurrency constraints; (2) deduction—predicting world evolution under partial observations and acting toward a goal. Maintenance combines LLM-assisted semantic judgments with programmatic validation/scoring; deduction is fully programmatic.
AI.result: Judgments are auditable against world states and execution logs, and scores can be recomputed from saved judgments and execution records. Across 8 models, scores decline steadily as pre-built structure is removed, and causal-relation checking is the weakest component for every model. The benchmark distinguishes local completion from failures in event organization.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark makes the continued operation of a world measurable and separates local completion from event-organization failures. Code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/HCPLab-SYSU/WorldAgent-Benchmark.

title: UMR: Universal Manipulation Representation
comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: General-purpose embodied manipulation hinges on a unified action representation that generalizes across embodiments and scales readily. Yet existing policies rely on embodiment-specific action spaces, making cross-embodiment demonstrations difficult to leverage at scale and limiting transfer to new embodiments and spatial variations. To this end, we introduce Universal Manipulation Representation (UMR), a unified action representation that enables zero-shot skill transfer from human demonstrations to heterogeneous robots. UMR decomposes manipulation into two functionally distinct yet geometrically linked components: embodiment-agnostic World Flow, which describes task-relevant object motion in the world frame, and Ego Trajectory, which represents end-effector motion relative to the current pose. We instantiate UMR as World--Ego Point VLA (WEPVLA), a compact 0.5B-parameter policy that learns in the unified geometric action space through a dual-stream Point Action Adapter and a unified Point Action Expert, with an $SE(3)$ conjugation coupling the two components. To improve data efficiency, we complement UMR with a Data-Efficient Strategy (DES) that diversifies object configurations through stage-aware point-cloud editing while preserving demonstrated contact geometry. In simulation, WEPVLA achieves average success rates of 97.5\% on LIBERO and 85.7\% on the 10-task RLBench benchmark. In real-world experiments, a single policy trained on human demonstrations augmented by DES transfers zero-shot to diverse deployment conditions. With about 10 minutes of collected human demonstrations per task and no robot demonstrations, it achieves 91.7\% average success across six evaluation settings, compared with 60.8\% for HumanEgo. Code and additional materials are available at https://umr-wepvla.github.io/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Universal Manipulation Representation (UMR), a unified action representation that decomposes manipulation into embodiment-agnostic World Flow and Ego Trajectory, instantiated as WEPVLA (a 0.5B-parameter policy) with a Data-Efficient Strategy (DES), enabling zero-shot skill transfer from human demonstrations to heterogeneous robots.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied manipulation policies rely on embodiment-specific action spaces, which makes cross-embodiment demonstrations difficult to leverage at scale and limits transfer to new embodiments and spatial variations. A unified action representation that generalizes across embodiments and scales readily is needed.
AI.method: UMR decomposes manipulation into two functionally distinct yet geometrically linked components: embodiment-agnostic World Flow (task-relevant object motion in the world frame) and Ego Trajectory (end-effector motion relative to the current pose). It is instantiated as WEPVLA, a compact 0.5B-parameter policy learning in a unified geometric action space via a dual-stream Point Action Adapter and a unified Point Action Expert, with an SE(3) conjugation coupling the two components. A Data-Efficient Strategy (DES) diversifies object configurations through stage-aware point-cloud editing while preserving demonstrated contact geometry.
AI.result: In simulation, WEPVLA achieves average success rates of 97.5% on LIBERO and 85.7% on the 10-task RLBench benchmark. In real-world experiments, with about 10 minutes of collected human demonstrations per task and no robot demonstrations, a single policy transfers zero-shot to diverse deployment conditions, achieving 91.7% average success across six evaluation settings, compared with 60.8% for HumanEgo.
AI.conclusion: UMR provides a unified action representation enabling zero-shot skill transfer from human demonstrations to heterogeneous robots. WEPVLA trained with DES demonstrates strong simulation performance and effective real-world zero-shot generalization, substantially outperforming the HumanEgo baseline.

title: IGSD: Environment-Verified Hindsight Self-Distillation for Search Agents
summary: On-policy self-distillation densifies agent training without external teachers: a policy conditioned on privileged hindsight provides step-level guidance for its own unprivileged rollouts. For search agents, however, hindsight can make the teacher prefer a query that does not improve retrieval from the student's state. Existing methods either distill this preference directly or filter it with model-internal scores, but neither strategy verifies the query's executed retrieval consequence. We propose Information-Gain-Gated Self-Distillation (IGSD), which verifies on-policy token proposals with environment feedback before distilling them. Treating each query token as a micro-action, IGSD completes the teacher's token proposal and the student's sampled token into matched queries and executes both from the same failed state with the same retriever. Shared counterfactual controls account for query-conditioned shifts in answer likelihood, so their difference, the executed paired information gain, provides a relative utility contrast for the retrieved documents. IGSD uses this contrast as a positive-only soft weight for candidate-pair distillation, while leaving the GRPO objective unchanged and confining verification to training. Across seven single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks, IGSD reaches macro-average exact-match accuracies of 42.8% and 47.0% with 3B and 7B policies, respectively, without inference-time verification. These results support environment-verified hindsight as an effective approach to reliable action-level supervision for search agents.

AI.tldr: IGSD verifies teacher token proposals with environment feedback (executed retrieval) before distilling them, using executed paired information gain as a positive-only soft weight, achieving 42.8%/47.0% EM on 3B/7B search agents across seven QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation uses privileged hindsight as a teacher for a search agent's own unprivileged rollouts. However, hindsight can lead the teacher to prefer a query that does not actually improve retrieval from the student's state. Existing methods either distill this preference directly or filter it with model-internal scores, but neither verifies the query's executed retrieval consequence.
AI.method: IGSD treats each query token as a micro-action, completes the teacher's token proposal and the student's sampled token into matched queries, and executes both from the same failed state with the same retriever. Shared counterfactual controls account for query-conditioned shifts in answer likelihood, so their difference—the executed paired information gain—provides a relative utility contrast for retrieved documents. This contrast serves as a positive-only soft weight for candidate-pair distillation, while the GRPO objective is left unchanged and verification is confined to training.
AI.result: Across seven single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks, IGSD achieves macro-average exact-match accuracies of 42.8% (3B) and 47.0% (7B) without inference-time verification.
AI.conclusion: Environment-verified hindsight is an effective approach for reliable action-level supervision in search agents.

title: RoboICL: Embodied In-Context Learning with GPT-6 Astra
summary: General-purpose vision-language models offer a promising way to zero-shot robot control: \gptastra{} excels at open-ended and language- or image-conditioned manipulation but remains substantially weaker on high-precision and long-horizon tasks. We introduce \emph{RoboICL}, an in-context robot-control framework that narrows these gaps without robot-specific parameter updates or a learned VLA. RoboICL separates \emph{demonstration context}, which provides recorded examples when available, from \emph{interaction memory}, which accumulates the model's own actions and observed outcomes. Both use a shared observation--action--receipt--observation grammar. To preserve experience across task stages, RoboICL combines sampled demonstration blocks with bounded anchored memory. Fixed anchors keep earlier rollout interactions available for in-context learning, while the latest interaction supports immediate error correction. Across 30 RoboDojo tasks, using zero shot for Open and one demonstration elsewhere, RoboICL improves on official zero-shot \gptastra{} by 20--27 progress-score points in every category. It leads the leaderboard baselines on Memory and Open, achieves comparable performance to the strongest Precision baseline, and remains competitive on Long-Horizon. Its 30-task Overall score is 50.64, versus 33.68 for the strongest baseline. On a separate ten-task subset, RoboICL scores 60.60, within 2.00 points of the $π_{0.5}$ + \gptastra{} hybrid approach. On three real-robot tasks, mean progress rises from 14.45 at zero shot to 63.33 at one shot and 78.89 at three shots. On two development tasks, optional Jev-gated action reuse reduces \gptastra{} calls by 33--48\%. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/Mosi-AI/RoboICL}{https://github.com/Mosi-AI/RoboICL}.

AI.tldr: RoboICL is an in-context robot-control framework built on GPT-based (Astra) vision-language models that improves high-precision and long-horizon manipulation without robot-specific parameter updates or a learned VLA, using a shared demonstration-context and interaction-memory grammar.
AI.motivation: General-purpose vision-language models enable zero-shot robot control but remain substantially weaker on high-precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks. The paper aims to narrow these gaps without costly robot-specific fine-tuning or training a dedicated VLA.
AI.method: RoboICL separates demonstration context (recorded examples when available) from interaction memory (the model's own actions and observed outcomes), both expressed in a shared observation--action--receipt--observation grammar. It combines sampled demonstration blocks with bounded anchored memory: fixed anchors keep earlier rollout interactions available for in-context learning, while the latest interaction supports immediate error correction. An optional Jev-gated action reuse mechanism is also introduced.
AI.result: Across 30 RoboDojo tasks (zero shot for Open, one demonstration elsewhere), RoboICL improves on official zero-shot Astra by 20-27 progress-score points in every category, leads baselines on Memory and Open, matches the strongest Precision baseline, and stays competitive on Long-Horizon (Overall 50.64 vs. 33.68). On a ten-task subset it scores 60.60, within 2.00 points of the pi_0.5 + Astra hybrid.
