On three real-robot tasks, mean progress rises from 14.45 (zero shot) to 63.33 (one shot) and 78.89 (three shots). Jev-gated action reuse cuts Astra calls by 33-48% on two development tasks.
AI.conclusion: RoboICL demonstrates that structured in-context learning (demonstration context plus bounded anchored interaction memory) can substantially boost zero-shot, general-purpose vision-language robot control on precision, memory, open-ended, and long-horizon tasks, with strong real-robot gains and reduced model-call costs, without robot-specific parameter updates.

title: Flat-Consensus Diffusion for Robust Data Reshaping under Noisy Evaluator
summary: Data shape determines how features are structured, how patterns are separated, and how distributions cover the underlying domain. Poor data shape can make models learn noise rather than generalizable structure. This paper studies robust feature-centric data reshaping: generating feature transformations that remain useful, stable, and reproducible under noisy evaluation and imperfect data conditions. We view reshaping operation sequence search as reward-guided diffusion generation, and robust reshaping as searching for regions in the latent reward landscape rather than isolated high-reward transformations. The key challenge is dual instability: noisy evaluators distort local reward guidance, while stochastic generative trajectories can converge to inconsistent solutions. We propose FCDiff, a flat-consensus diffusion framework that addresses both failures through a micro-macro decomposition. The micro layer replaces point-estimate reward guidance with Gaussian-smoothed, Monte Carlo averaged gradients, steering generation toward locally flat reward regions. The macro layer aggregates independently guided trajectories with a weighted Frechet-mean barycenter, selecting consensus-supported basins and filtering stochastic outliers. Across an 8-dataset headline cohort under heavy-tailed evaluator noise, FCDiff attains the best aggregate rank on lower-tail reliability and robustness against both search-based AutoFE and robustness-oriented generative baselines, with statistically significant accuracy gains over every generative baseline. Our results show that robust data reshaping requires searching for flat, consensus-supported regions rather than sharp single-trajectory optima.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FCDiff, a flat-consensus diffusion framework for robust feature-centric data reshaping, which searches for flat, consensus-supported regions in the latent reward landscape to overcome noisy evaluators and stochastic generative instability.
AI.motivation: Data shape governs how features are structured, patterns separated, and distributions cover the domain; poor shape leads models to learn noise instead of generalizable structure. Robust reshaping is challenged by dual instability: noisy evaluators distort local reward guidance, and stochastic generative trajectories converge to inconsistent solutions.
AI.method: The paper formulates reshaping operation sequence search as reward-guided diffusion generation and robust reshaping as searching for regions in the latent reward landscape rather than isolated high-reward transformations. FCDiff uses a micro-macro decomposition: the micro layer replaces point-estimate reward guidance with Gaussian-smoothed, Monte Carlo averaged gradients to steer generation toward locally flat reward regions; the macro layer aggregates independently guided trajectories via a weighted Frechet-mean barycenter, selecting consensus-supported basins and filtering stochastic outliers.
AI.result: Across an 8-dataset headline cohort under heavy-tailed evaluator noise, FCDiff achieves the best aggregate rank on lower-tail reliability and robustness against search-based AutoFE and robustness-oriented generative baselines, with statistically significant accuracy gains over every generative baseline.
AI.conclusion: Robust data reshaping requires searching for flat, consensus-supported regions rather than sharp single-trajectory optima.

title: SAGE: Symbolic Action-Gating and Editing for LLM Task Planners
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, 3 algorithms. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Code and benchmark: https://github.com/mtbui2010/sage_release
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are now the default cognitive core of embodied household agents, yet the plans they emit are rarely checked against a grounded model of the environment before execution, and the task-success they report is often measured on benchmarks so saturated that no method can be separated from another. We present SAGE (Symbolic Action-Gating and Editing), a single-LLM planner built from two lightweight mechanisms: a domain-agnostic symbolic gate (~250 lines of Python, zero tokens, $O(|π|)$) that blocks precondition-violating actions with typed reasons as a runtime safety monitor, and a local edit that regenerates only the failed sub-goal's suffix, keeping completed and untouched work intact; a hybrid seed+live memory store supports cold-start coverage. We evaluate under a leak-free protocol (leave-one-out retrieval) over five open-weight models and a 75-task AI2-THOR benchmark. On the standard benchmark goal-completeness saturates (52% of instances trivially solved) and SAGE ties strong hierarchical baselines. On a harder, method-agnostic multi-goal composition, SAGE's completeness lead re-emerges large (+0.06 to +0.23 across four models). Under injected mid-execution failures, SAGE recovers as reliably as whole-plan replanners at 2.4-3.3x fewer LLM calls. As a verify-before-execute gate, the symbolic monitor blocks unsafe actions before actuation and raises simulator-reported step-success for every planner tested (up to +0.11), a signal the verifier never sees (non-circular). Because the gate calls no model (0.008 ms/plan), it is a safety layer that runs essentially free on the edge: SAGE planning reproduces its quality on a Jetson AGX Orin, where small-model verification helps most. We release the benchmark, the leak-free protocol, the recovery and safety-gate harnesses, and a verifier-portability study (auto-induced on ALFWorld, 0.89 held-out).

AI.tldr: SAGE is a single-LLM embodied household planner combining a zero-token symbolic action gate (runtime precondition verifier, ~250 lines, O(|π|)) with a suffix-local repair mechanism and a hybrid seed+live memory store, evaluated on a leak-free protocol and a 75-task AI2-THOR benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLM planners for embodied household agents emit plans rarely verified against a grounded environment model before execution, and the task-success benchmarks used to compare them are saturated, so reported differences between methods are unreliable and safety/recovery costs are overlooked.
AI.method: Domain-agnostic symbolic gate blocking precondition-violating actions with typed reasons as a runtime safety monitor; local edit regenerating only the failed sub-goal's suffix while preserving completed work; hybrid seed+live memory store for cold-start coverage; evaluation under leave-one-out leak-free retrieval over five open-weight models and 75 AI2-THOR tasks, plus injected mid-execution failure recovery and a verifier-portability study (auto-induced on ALFWorld).
AI.result: Standard benchmark goal-completeness saturates (52% trivially solved) where SAGE ties strong hierarchical baselines; on harder method-agnostic multi-goal composition SAGE leads by +0.06 to +0.23 across four models; under injected failures it recovers as reliably as whole-plan replanners with 2.4-3.3x fewer LLM calls; the gate raises simulator-reported step-success for every planner tested (up to +0.11) with a non-circular signal unseen by the verifier; gate overhead 0.008 ms/plan and quality reproduced on Jetson AGX Orin; verifier portability 0.89 held-out on ALFWorld.
AI.conclusion: A model-free symbolic gate plus suffix-local repair makes embodied LLM planning safer, cheaper, and comparatively stronger than hierarchical baselines on unsaturated composition tasks; planned-saturation on standard benchmarks masks method differences, and the safety layer runs essentially free on edge hardware.

title: CAIRN: Dynamic Fact-Intent DAGs for Multi-Agent Exploration
summary: LLM-powered autonomous systems have demonstrated promising capabilities in mathematical reasoning, engineering, and cybersecurity. Yet how to organize these systems for effective, reliable, and sustained performance remains an open question. In this paper, we present CAIRN, a fact-intent-driven multi-agent paradigm for goal-directed exploration. CAIRN represents observations and planned investigations as a dynamic directed acyclic graph (DAG). A reasoner interprets facts to propose intents, which workers execute to produce new facts. Each intent references its supporting facts and defines a potential exploration branch. The persistent graph preserves goals, dependencies and findings across workers, supporting knowledge reuse and parallel exploration. The graph also makes execution trajectories traceable and auditable, providing a basis for human verification and intervention. We evaluate CAIRN across cybersecurity and mathematical reasoning tasks, examining task success, time to solution, and token consumption. DAG-based coordination can incur higher token costs with no observable performance gains on tasks that require little effort. However, on high-effort tasks (at least 1M tokens), we observe faster solutions in 76.5% of cases, with speedups of up to 3.08x. Moreover, as task effort increases, these time gains become more pronounced while relative token overhead declines, highlighting the potential of DAG-guided parallel exploration.

AI.tldr: CAIRN is a fact-intent-driven multi-agent paradigm that organizes goal-directed exploration as a dynamic DAG, where a reasoner proposes intents from facts and workers execute them to produce new facts. It improves speed on high-effort tasks (faster in 76.5% of cases, up to 3.08x) but adds token overhead without gains on low-effort tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered autonomous systems show promise in math, engineering, and cybersecurity, but how to organize them for effective, reliable, and sustained performance remains unresolved.
AI.method: CAIRN models observations and planned investigations as a dynamic directed acyclic graph. A reasoner interprets facts to propose intents; workers execute intents to yield new facts. Each intent references supporting facts and defines an exploration branch. The persistent graph preserves goals, dependencies, and findings across workers, enabling knowledge reuse, parallel exploration, and traceable/auditable execution for human verification and intervention.
AI.result: Evaluated on cybersecurity and mathematical reasoning tasks (task success, time to solution, token consumption). DAG-based coordination incurs higher token costs with no performance gains on low-effort tasks, but on high-effort tasks (>=1M tokens) yields faster solutions in 76.5% of cases with speedups up to 3.08x. Time gains grow and relative token overhead declines as task effort increases.
AI.conclusion: DAG-guided parallel exploration is a promising coordination structure for high-effort tasks, offering substantial speedups with diminishing relative token overhead, while being less beneficial for low-effort tasks.

title: Bayesian Active Learning for Intent Disambiguation in Interactive Robot Planning
comment: Accepted by CoRL 2026, also presented at IROS 2026 Human-Robot Dialogue workshop
summary: Interactive robot planning requires robots to infer and execute human intentions from natural language instructions that are often ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a powerful interface for clarification, relying on the generative model to drive an multi-turn conversation can introduce systematic failures. We propose a Bayesian framework that treats clarification as an active learning problem over grounded Signal Temporal Logic (STL) task specifications. Our method uses LLMs to initialize candidate formal specifications and translate informative contrasts into natural-language clarification questions, while Bayesian optimization maintains uncertainty estimation over user intent and selects queries that maximize information gain. After convergence, the inferred STL specification is passed to a formal planner to synthesize a verifiable robot trajectory. Across four simulated and real-world task domains, our approach generally achieves higher task satisfaction and requires fewer clarification rounds than LLM baselines, while helping smaller models close the performance gap against larger reasoning models.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian active-learning framework treats multi-turn clarification of ambiguous natural-language robot instructions as uncertainty reduction over grounded STL task specifications, using LLMs to seed candidates and generate questions while Bayesian optimization selects maximally informative queries, then hands the inferred STL spec to a formal planner for verifiable trajectory synthesis.
AI.motivation: Natural language instructions to robots are often ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified, so robots must infer and execute underlying human intentions. LLMs offer a powerful clarification interface, but letting the generative model directly drive multi-turn dialogue can produce systematic failures, such as inconsistent or miscalibrated questions and unreliable uncertainty tracking.
AI.method: Clarification is cast as active learning over grounded STL task specifications. LLMs initialize candidate formal specifications and verbalize informative contrasts as natural-language clarification questions. Bayesian optimization maintains a distribution over user intent, quantifies uncertainty, and selects queries maximizing information gain. Upon convergence, the inferred STL specification is passed to a formal planner to synthesize a verifiable robot trajectory.
AI.result: Across four simulated and real-world task domains, the approach generally achieves higher task satisfaction and requires fewer clarification rounds than LLM baselines, while helping smaller models narrow the performance gap with larger reasoning models.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling clarification from the generative model and grounding it in Bayesian active learning over formal STL specifications yields more reliable, information-efficient human-robot interaction and enables formal verification of the executed plan.

title: Despite Instructions: Frontier Agents Improvise Covert Channels at Test Time
summary: In security-sensitive applications, language-model agents are often required to coordinate without disclosing confidential information. Yet repeated interactions may also let ordinary messages acquire shared private meaning. We study a repeated game with pairs of models in which the sender model observes one of four secret states and selects one of four summaries of the same public report, while the receiver model tries to infer the secret state. We find that model pairs can learn to communicate the secret using only one bit of feedback indicating whether the receiver inferred it correctly. This learning occurs during inference with fixed parameters and no supplied codebook or encoding examples. The effect also persists when agents generate their own free-form updates in a simulated incident-response task. Across ten independent games, pairs of GPT-5.6 Sol agents reach 98.8% final accuracy, compared with 25% chance, despite explicit instructions prohibiting disclosure and a monitor that screens each message without access to the agents' interaction histories. The same interactions that help agents cooperate can therefore allow confidential information to pass through messages intended for legitimate coordination.

AI.tldr: Pairs of language-model agents can covertly encode secret states through ordinary-looking messages via in-context learning from a single correctness bit, achieving 98.8% accuracy while evading an out-of-context monitor.
AI.motivation: Security-sensitive multi-agent settings require coordination without leaking confidential information, but repeated interactions may enable ordinary messages to acquire shared private meaning, creating an underexplored covert-channel risk.
AI.method: A repeated game where a sender observes one of four secret states and picks one of four summaries of the same public report; the receiver infers the state. Pairs receive only one bit of feedback per round (whether the inference was correct) and learn during inference with fixed parameters, no codebook or encoding examples. A free-form, simulated incident-response variant tests generalization; ten independent GPT-5.6 Sol agent pairs are evaluated under explicit non-disclosure instructions and a monitor screening each message without access to interaction histories.
AI.result: Pairs reach 98.8% final accuracy versus 25% chance across ten games, and the effect persists in the free-form incident-response task despite the prohibition and the history-blind monitor.
AI.conclusion: Interactions that enable legitimate cooperation also let confidential information pass through innocuous-coordination messages, exposing a steganographic leakage channel in fixed-parameter LM agents that evades message-level monitoring.

title: NavHarness: Towards Lifelong Embodied Navigation
summary: Frontier models can now perform well on individual embodied navigation tasks through multi-round multimodal reasoning with simple tools. Across successive tasks, however, an agent must also rely on an evolving map and earlier search records, both of which may be incomplete or conflict with new observations. We present NavHarness, a training-free embodied harness towards lifelong navigation that makes memory processing part of the navigation loop. During navigation, its multi-round agentic session draws on maps, task records, and house knowledge, checking them against observations and recording corrections to guide its actions. NavHarness preserves this experience across fresh conversations for new tasks or recovery attempts, while outcome verification and run-end summaries support its later reuse. On GOAT-Bench, NavHarness improves s-SR over context-only independent sessions by 18.6 points with Astra and 22.6 with Opus 5. Using SLAM-estimated poses, NavHarness with GPT-6 Astra achieves state-of-the-art task success of 83.7 s-SR with 36.9 e-SR on GOAT-Bench and 85.9 s-SR on IR2R-CE. To understand these gains, we examine how experience is carried between sessions and find that structured recovery handovers outperform length-matched summaries. In extended deployments across houses, consolidation improves navigation beyond retaining maps and task records, with case studies showing how agents use earlier experience to interpret new goals, investigate unresolved questions, and resume failed searches. We suggest that progress towards lifelong navigation depends on how successive reasoning sessions build on prior experience, alongside improvements in single-task capability.

AI.tldr: NavHarness is a training-free embodied harness that integrates memory processing into the navigation loop, carrying structured experience across sessions to achieve state-of-the-art lifelong navigation performance.
AI.motivation: Frontier models handle individual embodied navigation tasks well via multi-round multimodal reasoning, but across successive tasks agents struggle because the evolving map and earlier search records may be incomplete or conflict with new observations. Existing approaches treat tasks independently, ignoring cross-task experience, which limits progress toward lifelong navigation.
AI.method: NavHarness is a training-free harness that embeds memory processing into the navigation loop. A multi-round agentic session draws on maps, task records, and house knowledge, checks them against observations, and records corrections to guide actions. Experience is preserved across fresh conversations for new tasks or recovery attempts, with outcome verification and run-end summaries enabling later reuse and consolidation.
AI.result: On GOAT-Bench, NavHarness improves s-SR by 18.6 points (Astra) and 22.6 points (Opus 5) over context-only independent sessions. Using SLAM-estimated poses, NavHarness with GPT-6 Astra reaches 83.7 s-SR and 36.9 e-SR on GOAT-Bench and 85.9 s-SR on IR2R-CE. Structured recovery handovers outperform length-matched summaries, and consolidation improves navigation beyond retaining maps and task records alone.
AI.conclusion: Progress toward lifelong navigation depends on how successive reasoning sessions build on prior experience, alongside single-task capability improvements. Case studies show agents using earlier experience to interpret new goals, investigate unresolved questions, and resume failed searches.

title: CoWindow Attention: Full Causal Coverage Is a Collective Property
summary: FullAttn repeatedly exposes the complete causal history to every attention head, creating substantial redundant computation and memory traffic even with IO-efficient dense kernels. We introduce CoWA, a structured attention architecture that distributes access to the causal history across KV heads. All heads share near-diagonal and prefix-sink windows, while complementary long-range windows partition the remaining history. Their union provides full causal coverage although each head attends sparsely to distant tokens. This position-defined attention pattern requires no learned router or indexer, is used consistently during training and inference, and aligns with KV-head tensor parallelism. A window-matched ablation at 8K isolates the effect of complementary long-range allocation: CoWA with 100% collective coverage reaches 89.73% accuracy, compared with 89.97% for FullAttn, while duplicated long-range windows perform substantially worse. Across a broader controlled associative-recall comparison with matched token budgets, CoWA closely tracks FullAttn as the context grows, whereas other sparse patterns lose a substantial fraction of the associations. In an attention-operator benchmark at 128K tokens with tensor parallelism, CoWA reduces forward and backward latency during training by 7.4x and 8.6x and decoding latency during inference by 3.0x over FullAttn. Its per-rank peak operator memory matches FullAttn during training and is 7.6x lower during decoding. Across scaling-law training from 0.6B to 14B parameters, CoWA closely tracks FullAttn in perplexity while reducing total training FLOPs. The resulting 14B models and 32B models from separate continued training achieve comparable knowledge, reasoning, and long-context retrieval scores to FullAttn. These results show that full causal coverage can be a collective property of the head ensemble rather than a duplicated property of every head.

AI.tldr: CoWA replaces per-head full causal attention with a structured pattern where KV heads share local/prefix-sink windows and complementary long-range windows collectively cover the full causal history, preserving accuracy while cutting attention latency and memory.
AI.motivation: FullAttn exposes the entire causal history to every attention head, causing redundant computation and memory traffic even with IO-efficient dense kernels. The paper questions whether full causal coverage must be a property of every individual head or can instead be a collective property of the head ensemble.
AI.method: CoWA distributes access to causal history across KV heads: all heads share near-diagonal and prefix-sink windows, while complementary long-range windows partition the remaining history, so the union yields full causal coverage though each head attends sparsely to distant tokens. The position-defined pattern needs no learned router or indexer, is used identically in training and inference, and aligns with KV-head tensor parallelism.
AI.result: At 8K, a window-matched ablation gives 89.73% accuracy for CoWA with 100% collective coverage vs. 89.97% for FullAttn, while duplicated long-range windows perform substantially worse. In associative-recall comparisons at matched token budgets, CoWA tracks FullAttn as context grows. At 128K with tensor parallelism, CoWA reduces training forward/backward latency by 7.4x/8.6x and inference decoding latency by 3.0x; per-rank peak operator memory matches FullAttn in training and is 7.6x lower in decoding. Scaling-law training from 0.6B to 14B tracks FullAttn perplexity with fewer training FLOPs, and 14B/32B continued-training models match FullAttn on knowledge, reasoning, and long-context retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Full causal coverage can be achieved as a collective property of the head ensemble rather than a duplicated property of every head, yielding large efficiency gains with negligible quality loss.

title: TLC-DiT: Task-Aligned Local Visual Conditioning for Robust Multitask Robot Manipulation
summary: Language-conditioned robot policies have made clear progress in multitask manipulation, but task-relevant local visual evidence usually stays hidden inside a visual backbone or attention layers. This leaves the policy difficult to inspect and fragile under visual change, two symptoms of a missing explicit, task-aligned local visual channel. We present TLC-DiT, a plug-in extension of the Multitask Diffusion Transformer (DiT) policy that adds explicit task-guided local visual feature maps without changing the diffusion objective or the action-generation process. For each camera view, frozen DINOv2 patch features are modulated by the CLIP task embedding through FiLM and refined by a lightweight CoordConv CNN adapter into smooth spatial maps, which are concatenated with the original global image, language, joint-state, and timestep conditions. On LIBERO, TLC-DiT reaches a 93.5% average success rate, compared with 86.5% for Multitask DiT and 79.25% for SmolVLA. On LIBERO-plus, the total success rate improves from 54.07% to 57.24%, with larger gains under camera, background, and sensor-noise changes. In real-world bimanual tasks, TLC-DiT raises Teabag Putting completion from 44% to 89% while maintaining comparable Match Box Opening performance. Feature-map visualizations confirm that the model attends to task-relevant regions across views and perturbations, providing a direct way to inspect the visual evidence.

AI.tldr: TLC-DiT augments a Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy with explicit, task-guided local visual feature maps (FiLM-modulated DINOv2 patches refined by a CoordConv CNN) concatenated onto existing conditions, improving success and robustness without altering the diffusion objective.
AI.motivation: In language-conditioned robot policies, task-relevant local visual evidence remains implicit inside the visual backbone or attention layers, making policies hard to inspect and fragile under visual change—symptoms of a missing explicit, task-aligned local visual channel.
AI.method: For each camera view, frozen DINOv2 patch features are modulated by the CLIP task embedding via FiLM and refined by a lightweight CoordConv CNN adapter into smooth spatial maps. These maps are concatenated with the original global image, language, joint-state, and timestep conditions as a plug-in to Multitask DiT, leaving the diffusion objective and action-generation process unchanged.
AI.result: LIBERO: 93.5% average success vs. 86.5% (Multitask DiT) and 79.25% (SmolVLA). LIBERO-plus: 54.07% to 57.24% total, with larger gains under camera, background, and sensor-noise shifts. Real-world bimanual: Teabag Putting 44% to 89%, with comparable Match Box Opening. Feature-map visualizations confirm attention to task-relevant regions across views and perturbations.
AI.conclusion: An explicit task-guided local visual channel improves performance, robustness, and interpretability of diffusion-based language-conditioned manipulation policies.

title: MassAlloc Attention: Let Attention Allocate Its Own Compute
summary: FullAttn often assigns negligible normalized mass to much of the causal score space, yet dense kernels execute the complete post-score path after forming each QK tile. We introduce MALA, a fused attention primitive that preserves score access to every legal causal interaction and uses normalized contribution to allocate post-score computation. Forward uses its evolving online-softmax normalizer, while backward reuses the finalized normalizer to derive nested retained support using only standard attention state. A common tolerance governs training and inference, allowing for adaptive retention of the work. MALA reduces low-contribution post-score computation. A matched-work study at 8K isolates the benefit of distribution-adaptive allocation: under exactly matched total post-score work, MALA approaches a per-instance reference-mass oracle, with mean omitted mass of 0.0188% versus 0.0182%. Across context lengths from 1K to 32K tokens, the same tolerance maintains low output and gradient errors relative to the reference. Across a broader controlled associative-recall comparison, MALA closely tracks FullAttn as context grows, reaching 89.67% accuracy at 8K compared with 89.97% for FullAttn. In an attention-operator benchmark at 128K tokens with tensor parallelism, MALA reduces forward and backward latency during training by 2.2x and 3.0x and decoding latency during inference by 1.6x relative to FullAttn. Across scaling-law training from 0.6B to 14B parameters, MALA closely tracks FullAttn in perplexity while reducing total training FLOPs. The resulting 14B models and 32B models from separate continued training achieve comparable knowledge, reasoning, and long-context retrieval scores to FullAttn. These results indicate that allocating post-score computation according to normalized attention contributions can retain the evaluated capabilities of FullAttn while reducing attention computation.

AI.tldr: MALA is a fused attention primitive that allocates post-score computation according to normalized attention contribution, retaining the evaluated capabilities of FullAttn while reducing attention computation.
AI.motivation: FullAttn often assigns negligible normalized mass to much of the causal score space, yet dense kernels still execute the complete post-score path after forming each QK tile, wasting computation on low-contribution interactions.
AI.method: MALA preserves score access to every legal causal interaction but uses normalized contribution to allocate post-score computation. Forward passes use the evolving online-softmax normalizer; backward reuses the finalized normalizer to derive nested retained support using only standard attention state. A common tolerance governs both training and inference, enabling adaptive retention of work.
AI.result: In a matched-work study at 8K, MALA approaches a per-instance reference-mass oracle (mean omitted mass 0.0188% vs 0.0182%). From 1K to 32K tokens, the same tolerance maintains low output and gradient errors. On associative recall at 8K, MALA reaches 89.67% vs FullAttn's 89.97%. At 128K tokens with tensor parallelism, MALA reduces training forward/backward latency by 2.2x/3.0x and inference decoding latency by 1.6x. Scaling-law training from 0.6B to 14B tracks FullAttn perplexity while reducing total FLOPs; 14B and 32B continued-training models achieve comparable knowledge, reasoning, and long-context retrieval scores.
AI.conclusion: Allocating post-score computation according to normalized attention contributions can retain the evaluated capabilities of FullAttn while reducing attention computation.

title: When World Models Lie: Adaptive Safety Analysis Under Wrong Imaginations
summary: World models offer a powerful substrate for safety reasoning in high-dimensional robotic systems, but they are also fallible: their predictions can be biased, miscalibrated, or confidently wrong. This creates a central challenge for latent-space safety filters, which often learn Hamilton-Jacobi safety value functions on the dynamics of a world model. If the world model is incorrect, the resulting value function can inherit its errors and produce overconfident safety estimates. Existing latent safety filters often rely on auxiliary signals such as ensemble disagreement or value-target consistency residuals for adaptation, but these signals can remain small even when the world model's predictions deviate from observations. We propose an adaptive latent safety filter that calibrates safety reasoning using directly observed world-model error. Our method uses Adaptive Conformal Inference to construct online uncertainty sets from discrepancies between predicted and observation-inferred latent states, then evaluates safety pessimistically by minimizing the learned value function over these sets. This allows the filter to remain minimally conservative when the world model is accurate, while becoming more cautious when observations reveal model mismatch. We provide a finite-time coverage guarantee for the adaptive uncertainty radius. Through simulation and hardware experiments, we show that our method significantly reduces failures relative to state-of-the-art latent safety filters while preserving task completion.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive latent safety filter for robotic systems that calibrates safety reasoning using directly observed world-model error via Adaptive Conformal Inference, achieving minimal conservatism when accurate and increased caution under model mismatch, with finite-time coverage guarantees.
AI.motivation: World models are fallible—their predictions can be biased, miscalibrated, or confidently wrong—which becomes critical for latent-space safety filters that learn Hamilton-Jacobi safety value functions on world-model dynamics. If the world model is incorrect, the learned value function inherits its errors and yields overconfident safety estimates. Existing latent safety filters rely on auxiliary signals such as ensemble disagreement or value-target consistency residuals for adaptation, but these signals can remain small even when predictions deviate from observations.
AI.method: The authors propose an adaptive latent safety filter that calibrates safety reasoning using directly observed world-model error. It uses Adaptive Conformal Inference to construct online uncertainty sets from discrepancies between predicted and observation-inferred latent states, then evaluates safety pessimistically by minimizing the learned value function over these sets. This enables minimal conservatism when the world model is accurate and greater caution when observations reveal model mismatch. A finite-time coverage guarantee is provided for the adaptive uncertainty radius.
AI.result: Through simulation and hardware experiments, the method significantly reduces failures relative to state-of-the-art latent safety filters while preserving task completion.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating latent safety filters with directly observed world-model error via Adaptive Conformal Inference improves safety without sacrificing task performance, addressing the limitation of auxiliary adaptation signals that fail to detect prediction-observation deviations.

title: SkillVine: Agent Skill Evolution via Branching Exploration
summary: Agent skills encapsulate reusable procedural knowledge that enables LLM agents to perform tasks, and they can be improved automatically using trajectories from interactions with the environment. This is the classic problem of skill evolution. Existing approaches predominately follow a linear evolution paradigm, in which updates are sequentially applied to the latest skill-library version. As a result, they inevitably fall into local optima, leaving many promising evolution paths unexplored. We propose SkillVine, an automatic skill-evolution framework that formulates skill evolution as a graph search problem and employs a branching exploration strategy. Equipped with a trunk-branch collaborative searching mechanism, an intelligent parent-node selector, and an adaptive-granularity update rule, SkillVine achieves a balance between exploration and exploitation. We evaluate SkillVine on 5 benchmarks with two LLMs. Results show that SkillVine discovers better skill-library versions along branches than along the linear trunk and achieves the best test performance in nine of ten benchmark-model combinations.

AI.tldr: SkillVine reformulates automatic agent skill evolution as a graph search problem with branching exploration to escape local optima, outperforming linear evolution baselines on 9/10 benchmark-model combinations.
AI.motivation: Agent skills encapsulate reusable procedural knowledge for LLM agents and can be improved automatically from environment interaction trajectories (skill evolution). Existing approaches follow a linear evolution paradigm where updates are applied sequentially to the latest skill-library version, inevitably converging to local optima and leaving many promising evolution paths unexplored.
AI.method: SkillVine formulates skill evolution as a graph search problem and employs a branching exploration strategy. It comprises three components: a trunk-branch collaborative searching mechanism, an intelligent parent-node selector, and an adaptive-granularity update rule, jointly balancing exploration and exploitation.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5 benchmarks with two LLMs. SkillVine discovers better skill-library versions along branches than along the linear trunk and achieves the best test performance in nine of ten benchmark-model combinations.
AI.conclusion: Branching graph-based skill evolution outperforms the dominant linear paradigm, enabling discovery of superior skill-library versions and stronger test performance across most benchmark-model settings.

title: Predictive Semantic Safety: From Visual Physical Reasoning to Safety-Critical Control
comment: The first two authors contributed equally to this work. Project page: https://www.taekyung.me/pss
summary: Physical interactions can create future hazards that are not apparent from the robot's current geometric surroundings. We present a framework termed Predictive Semantic Safety (PSS), which connects visual physical reasoning to backup-based safety filtering. A vision-language model (VLM) predicts physical events and their timing or directly predicts object displacements. An explicit motion model converts event hypotheses into object trajectories. Split conformal prediction calibrates position errors jointly across specified objects, observation times, and future times; geometric shape bounds convert the resulting position regions into predicted object occupancy. PSS evaluates a prescribed backup maneuver against this occupancy and derives input-affine constraints for minimally modifying the nominal input while preserving backup feasibility under the robot dynamics and input limits. MuJoCo experiments with a Unitree Go1 consider falling fixtures, impact-driven support loss, and contact propagation. PSS achieves a safe episode rate of 99.3%, compared with 43.3% for a Backup Control Barrier Function baseline that only uses current obstacle geometry.

AI.tldr: Predictive Semantic Safety (PSS) combines VLM-based physical event prediction, conformal-calibrated trajectory regions, and backup-based safety filtering to enforce constraints under future physical hazards, achieving 99.3% safe episodes on a Unitree Go1 in MuJoCo.
AI.motivation: Physical interactions can create future hazards not evident from the robot's current geometric surroundings, so safety filtering based only on present obstacle geometry is insufficient.
AI.method: A VLM predicts physical events with timing or object displacements; an explicit motion model converts event hypotheses into trajectories; split conformal prediction calibrates position errors jointly across objects, observation times, and future times; geometric shape bounds turn position regions into predicted object occupancy; PSS evaluates a prescribed backup maneuver against this occupancy and derives input-affine constraints for minimally modifying the nominal input while preserving backup feasibility under robot dynamics and input limits.
AI.result: In MuJoCo experiments with a Unitree Go1 covering falling fixtures, impact-driven support loss, and contact propagation, PSS achieves a 99.3% safe episode rate versus 43.3% for a Backup Control Barrier Function baseline using only current obstacle geometry.
AI.conclusion: Connecting visual physical reasoning to backup-based safety filtering enables substantially safer robot operation against future hazards arising from physical interactions.

title: Retrospective Distillation Attribution via Normalized Response Similarity
summary: Model distillation transfers capabilities through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher responses, often collected from commercial APIs, raising questions of model provenance. Existing distillation attribution methods have been largely evaluated on students immediately after the SFT step. However, a distilled model may undergo further SFT, preference optimization, or reinforcement learning before release, while an auditor may lack access to the pre-distillation checkpoint required by reference-based attribution. To close this gap, we propose SCOUT, an output-only method that aggregates recurring *syntactic patterns* into candidate profiles, filters low-contrast patterns, and calibrates student--candidate distances against inter-candidate distances. SCOUT supports attribution and abstention using only current texts, without model weights, token likelihoods, or historical checkpoints. Auditing publicly released descendants of distilled models spanning diverse post-training objectives, SCOUT consistently identifies the distillation source. Furthermore, tracing teacher-associated *syntactic signatures* along training trajectories reveals that they emerge during distillation and persist through subsequent preference optimization and reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: SCOUT is an output-only model distillation attribution method that aggregates recurring syntactic patterns into candidate profiles, filters low-contrast patterns, and calibrates student-to-candidate distances against inter-candidate distances, enabling source identification and abstention without model weights, token likelihoods, or historical checkpoints.
AI.motivation: Model distillation transfers capabilities via SFT on teacher responses often collected from commercial APIs, raising model provenance concerns. Existing distillation attribution methods are largely evaluated on students immediately after the SFT step, yet real released models may undergo further SFT, preference optimization, or RL, and auditors may lack access to the pre-distillation checkpoint needed by reference-based attribution.
AI.method: SCOUT aggregates recurring syntactic patterns into candidate profiles, filters low-contrast patterns, and calibrates student-candidate distances against inter-candidate distances. It relies only on current texts, requiring no model weights, token likelihoods, or historical checkpoints, and supports both attribution and abstention.
AI.result: When auditing publicly released descendants of distilled models spanning diverse post-training objectives, SCOUT consistently identifies the distillation source. Tracing teacher-associated syntactic signatures along training trajectories shows they emerge during distillation and persist through subsequent preference optimization and reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Output-only syntactic-pattern attribution offers a practical route to provenance auditing of distilled models that have undergone further post-training, with teacher-associated syntactic signatures serving as persistent, checkpoint-free evidence of distillation lineage.

title: FutureDuet: Decoupling Observation Access from Future Supervision in World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) augment robot action generation with future visual supervision. Existing WAMs commonly fuse main and wrist observations into one visual stream and train both with the same future-video objective, despite their different visual dynamics. A stable main camera reveals scene-level task evolution, whereas wrist cameras move with the end effector, mixing local interaction changes with viewpoint shifts and self-occlusion. These contrasting predictive demands suggest that the two views may benefit from different future objectives. We introduce FutureDuet, which retains both views for control, while allowing each visual stream to receive a different future objective. For the main view, future RGB models task evolution, while interaction masks and robot skeletons focus supervision on task objects and robot motion. For the wrist stream, future latent prediction models short-horizon interaction changes without requiring pixel-level reconstruction. ActionDiT jointly reads the resulting Task State and Interaction State, combining scene-level progress with close-range interaction evidence. All auxiliary prediction modules are training-only, adding no inference overhead. FutureDuet achieves 94.2% clean and 94.1% randomized success on RoboTwin50 and 99.2% average success on LIBERO. The improvements are most pronounced on six RoboTwin50 tasks that require precise interaction, averaging gains of 9.2% and 12.8% over Fast-WAM in clean and randomized settings. Controlled studies further show complementary gains from separating the wrist pathway and designing future supervision separately for the two views.

AI.tldr: FutureDuet is a World Action Model that keeps main and wrist camera views for robot control but assigns each a different future-prediction objective—main-view RGB plus interaction masks/skeletons for task evolution, and wrist latent prediction for short-horizon interaction—fed jointly to an ActionDiT, yielding strong RoboTwin50 and LIBERO success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing World Action Models fuse main and wrist observations into a single visual stream and supervise both with the same future-video objective, despite their fundamentally different visual dynamics: the stable main camera captures scene-level task evolution, while the wrist camera moves with the end effector, entangling local interaction changes with viewpoint shifts and self-occlusion. These contrasting predictive demands suggest the two views should be trained with different future objectives.
AI.method: FutureDuet retains both views for control while giving each visual stream a distinct future objective. The main view uses future RGB to model task evolution, with interaction masks and robot skeletons focusing supervision on task objects and robot motion. The wrist stream uses future latent prediction to model short-horizon interaction changes without pixel-level reconstruction. An ActionDiT jointly reads the resulting Task State and Interaction State, combining scene-level progress with close-range interaction evidence. All auxiliary prediction modules are training-only, adding no inference overhead.
AI.result: FutureDuet achieves 94.2% clean and 94.1% randomized success on RoboTwin50 and 99.2% average success on LIBERO. Gains are largest on six RoboTwin50 tasks requiring precise interaction, averaging 9.2% and 12.8% improvements over Fast-WAM in clean and randomized settings. Controlled studies confirm complementary gains from separating the wrist pathway and designing future supervision separately for the two views.
AI.conclusion: Separating the wrist pathway and tailoring future supervision per view provides complementary benefits. FutureDuet validates that view-specific future objectives for main and wrist streams improve precise-interaction robotic manipulation without any inference overhead, since auxiliary prediction modules are training-only.

title: CUA-Sandbox: Efficient Environments for Computer-Use Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning enables computer-use agents to improve through interaction with real software environments, including websites and desktop applications. However, conventional deployments replicate an initialized runtime for each independent rollout, even when trajectories use the same software, incurring repeated memory and initialization costs as the number of parallel environments grows. Does an independent computer-use environment require an independent execution runtime? Our key observation is that trajectories require independent mutable state, while initialized application runtimes can be reused across concurrently evolving environments, making state the natural unit of environment independence. Guided by this observation, we introduce CUA-Sandbox, which separates private state capsules from shared runtimes through state-scoped execution and transactional lifecycle operations, including resets and branches, while retaining the original software interfaces and task evaluators. Experiments show comparable or improved task success relative to Docker, while substantially reducing rollout and resource costs. CUA-Sandbox achieves up to a 6.20x increase in rollout throughput, a 9.2x reduction in per-environment memory, and a 504x reduction in incremental storage.

AI.tldr: CUA-Sandbox decouples mutable state from application runtimes so that computer-use agents can run many parallel rollouts on shared, initialized software runtimes instead of replicating a full runtime per environment, cutting memory, storage, and rollout costs.
AI.motivation: Conventional RL deployments for computer-use agents replicate an initialized runtime for every independent rollout, even when rollouts use the same software. As the number of parallel environments grows, this incurs repeated memory and initialization costs. The paper questions whether an independent computer-use environment truly requires an independent execution runtime.
AI.method: The key observation is that trajectories need independent mutable state, whereas initialized application runtimes can be reused across concurrently evolving environments, making state the natural unit of environment independence. Based on this, CUA-Sandbox separates private state capsules from shared runtimes via state-scoped execution and transactional lifecycle operations, including resets and branches, while preserving the original software interfaces and task evaluators.
AI.result: Experiments show comparable or improved task success relative to Docker, while substantially reducing rollout and resource costs. CUA-Sandbox achieves up to a 6.20x increase in rollout throughput, a 9.2x reduction in per-environment memory, and a 504x reduction in incremental storage.
AI.conclusion: Independent mutable state, not an independent execution runtime, is what computer-use environments require. Sharing initialized runtimes through state-scoped execution and transactional lifecycle management delivers the same or better task success while drastically improving throughput and resource efficiency.

title: RoboIRGBench: Benchmarking Implicit Referential Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks typically assume that task-relevant information is explicitly specified in the instruction. In practice, however, humans frequently refer to objects, quantities, and relations implicitly, requiring robots to recover the intended target from linguistic and perceptual context. We study this capability as Implicit Referential Grounding (IRG) and introduce RoboIRG-Bench, a manipulation benchmark designed to systematically evaluate it. Built upon RoboMME, RoboIRG-Bench contains 40 variants derived from 11 tasks and covers four challenges, including direct, reasoning-mediated, spatial, and contextual referential grounding. As IRG often requires retaining and retrieving previously established context, we evaluate representative VLAs spanning different memory mechanisms. Our evaluation reveals a noticeable referential robustness gap. Models that perform well under explicit instructions can degrade sharply when the same task-relevant information must be recovered from context. Reasoning-mediated and spatial references are particularly challenging, while models using external VLMs show greater robustness but still exhibit significant failures. Moreover, replacing the external VLM with a stronger model does not eliminate these gaps. We further validate these findings on a Franka Research 3 robot arm, where the gap persists under real-world manipulation and manifests as both incorrect referent grounding and downstream execution failures. These results establish IRG as a distinct and underexplored capability for reliable robotic instruction following and highlight the need for VLAs that can robustly integrate language, perception, reasoning, and action.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Implicit Referential Grounding (IRG) and RoboIRG-Bench, a 40-variant manipulation benchmark built on RoboMME, to test whether VLAs can recover intended referents from context rather than explicit instructions. Evaluating VLAs with different memory mechanisms reveals a sharp referential robustness gap, confirmed on a Franka Research 3 arm.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA benchmarks assume task-relevant information is explicitly stated in instructions, whereas real human instructions refer to objects, quantities, and relations implicitly, forcing robots to infer the intended target from linguistic and perceptual context. This underexplored capability is critical for reliable instruction following.
AI.method: The authors formalize IRG and build RoboIRG-Bench on RoboMME, comprising 40 variants from 11 tasks spanning four challenges: direct, reasoning-mediated, spatial, and contextual referential grounding. They evaluate representative VLAs with varying memory mechanisms, ablate external VLM strength, and validate on a Franka Research 3 robot arm.
AI.result: A pronounced referential robustness gap emerges: models strong on explicit instructions degrade sharply when information must be recovered from context. Reasoning-mediated and spatial references are hardest; external-VLM models are more robust but still fail significantly, and stronger VLMs do not close the gap. Real-world experiments show the gap persists, causing incorrect referent grounding and downstream execution failures.
AI.conclusion: IRG is a distinct, underexplored capability for reliable robotic instruction following, motivating VLAs that robustly integrate language, perception, reasoning, and action.

title: Action Shaping: Policies Absorb What They Can Express
summary: Reward shaping has a theorem: a potential-based term can be removed without changing the optimal policy. The same practice on the action channel, an offset added in training and dropped at deployment, has no theorem. Nothing cancels an action offset, so the correction is kept at deployment or removed without a guarantee. We call it action shaping and state its principle. A trainable policy absorbs an offset its own output layer can reproduce exactly, which is what we mean by express; what is absorbed can be removed with the return intact. Its minimal instance is a zero-initialized linear head behind a learnable gate, added to an actor that trains through a learned action-value function, with no penalty or schedule. The gate rises and then falls on its own, for deterministic and stochastic actors alike, and on 20 tasks removing the head costs almost nothing. The condition is exact reproduction, not capacity: a nonlinear head with more parameters is not absorbed, and in a paired control, one linear path added to a nonlinear base head restores absorption. Exact reproduction gives the loss a flat direction that gradient noise drifts along, and the offset's amplitude indicates, before removal, what dropping the head will cost. Action shaping thus gains the counterpart of the shaping theorem, a condition for absorption, together with the mechanism behind it and a diagnostic that reads it. Policies absorb what they can express, and only that.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "action shaping": an offset added to the action channel during training and dropped at deployment. It formalizes an absorption principle—a policy absorbs an offset its output layer can exactly reproduce, and what is absorbed can be removed with the return intact—validated on 20 tasks where removing a zero-initialized gated linear head costs almost nothing.
AI.motivation: Reward shaping has a theorem guaranteeing that a potential-based term can be removed without changing the optimal policy. The analogous practice on the action channel—adding an offset during training and dropping it at deployment—lacks any such guarantee. Nothing formally cancels an action offset, so practitioners must either keep the offset at deployment or remove it without any assurance, creating a gap between a widely-used heuristic and theory.
AI.method: The paper states an "action shaping" principle based on exact reproduction: a trainable policy absorbs an offset its own output layer can reproduce exactly, and what is absorbed can be removed with the return intact. Its minimal instance is a zero-initialized linear head behind a learnable gate, added to an actor trained through a learned action-value function, with no penalty or schedule. The paper analyzes the mechanism (a flat direction in the loss along which gradient noise drifts) and proposes a diagnostic based on the offset's amplitude.
AI.result: The gate rises and then falls on its own for both deterministic and stochastic actors. On 20 tasks, removing the head costs almost nothing. The absorption condition is exact reproduction, not capacity: a nonlinear head with more parameters is not absorbed, while in a paired control, a single linear path added to a nonlinear base head restores absorption. The offset's amplitude indicates, before removal, what dropping the head will cost.
AI.conclusion: Action shaping gains the counterpart of the reward shaping theorem: a condition for absorption, the mechanism behind it, and a diagnostic that reads it. Policies absorb what they can express—and only that.

title: Contact-Aware Impedance Controller for Robot-Assisted Ultrasound Imaging
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA2027)
summary: Safe robot-assisted ultrasound imaging requires a reliable controller able to detect and localize probe--tissue interaction. In this paper, we present a B-mode ultrasound image-based contact perception method and a contact-aware impedance controller for robotic ultrasound imaging. The proposed method detects acoustic contact independently of force measurements, enabling contact-conditioned force/torque taring to reduce residual wrench bias. During contact, the method continuously estimates the effective contact location along the curved probe surface and uses it to update the controller interaction frame, enabling visual servoing of the physical probe--tissue contact point during imaging. Experiments on an agar phantom demonstrated a contact-localization RMSE of $\mathbf{1.46 \pm 0.14}$~mm over probe roll angles from $\mathbf{-15^\circ}$ to $\mathbf{15^\circ}$. During static rolling, the proposed controller maintained task-space tracking accuracy comparable to a conventional fixed-frame impedance controller while reducing the maximum compressive interaction force from $\mathbf{31.56}$~N to $\mathbf{20.09}$~N, corresponding to a $\mathbf{36.3\%}$ reduction. These results demonstrate the potential of ultrasound images as direct contact feedback for safe and accurate robot-assisted ultrasound imaging.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a B-mode ultrasound image-based contact perception method and a contact-aware impedance controller for safe robotic ultrasound imaging, enabling contact detection without force sensors, continuous contact localization, and reduced interaction forces.
AI.motivation: Safe robot-assisted ultrasound imaging requires a reliable controller that can detect and localize probe-tissue interaction. Conventional approaches rely on force measurements, which have limitations such as residual wrench bias, and lack direct contact feedback. There is a need for a method that uses ultrasound images directly as contact feedback to improve safety and accuracy.
AI.method: The authors develop a B-mode ultrasound image-based contact perception method that detects acoustic contact independently of force measurements, enabling contact-conditioned force/torque taring to reduce residual wrench bias. During contact, the method continuously estimates the effective contact location along the curved probe surface and updates the controller interaction frame, allowing visual servoing of the physical probe-tissue contact point during imaging. A contact-aware impedance controller is integrated with this perception method.
AI.result: Experiments on an agar phantom demonstrated a contact-localization RMSE of 1.46 ± 0.14 mm over probe roll angles from -15° to 15°. During static rolling, the controller maintained task-space tracking accuracy comparable to a conventional fixed-frame impedance controller while reducing the maximum compressive interaction force from 31.56 N to 20.09 N, a 36.3% reduction.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the potential of ultrasound images as direct contact feedback for safe and accurate robot-assisted ultrasound imaging.

title: Adaptive Consistency Graph for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Large language model agents can often make reasonable local decisions on short tasks, yet their performance degrades when success requires long sequences of dependent actions and tool calls. During execution, task requirements, historical evidence, and the current execution state may gradually become disconnected, so later decisions can drift from the original objective. We study this problem by introducing the Adaptive Consistency Graph (ACG) for long-horizon execution. ACG incrementally organizes execution evidence and its provenance in a persistent graph, then constructs a temporary requirement-centered view for each decision under a bounded context budget. Rather than replacing the base agent's planner or tool executor, ACG provides a structured and traceable context view for each decision. In the matched evaluation, ACG improves GPT-5.6-luna's average success from 44.5\% with ReAct to 50.2\%, with the largest gain on BrowseComp-Plus (73.5\% versus 62.4\%). We further analyze trajectory structure and inference cost to characterize this improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Adaptive Consistency Graph (ACG), a structured, persistent context-view mechanism that mitigates objective drift in long-horizon LLM agent execution without modifying the base planner or tool executor.
AI.motivation: Large language model agents perform well on short, locally decidable tasks but degrade on long sequences of dependent actions and tool calls. During extended execution, task requirements, historical evidence, and the current execution state can become disconnected, causing later decisions to drift from the original objective. The paper targets this long-horizon consistency problem.
AI.method: ACG incrementally organizes execution evidence and its provenance in a persistent graph. For each decision, it constructs a temporary requirement-centered view under a bounded context budget. It acts as a context-view layer rather than replacing the base agent's planner or tool executor, providing structured and traceable context for each decision.
AI.result: In a matched evaluation, ACG raises GPT-5.6-luna's average success rate from 44.5% with ReAct to 50.2%. The largest gain appears on BrowseComp-Plus (73.5% versus 62.4%). The paper further analyzes trajectory structure and inference cost to characterize the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining a persistent, provenance-aware, requirement-centered context view improves long-horizon agent success at bounded context cost. The approach is modular, complementing existing planners and tool executors.

title: From Language to Task Maps: Compiling Semantic Relations While Preserving Task-Relevant Freedom
summary: Natural-language manipulation instructions specify qualitative relations, whereas continuous controllers require state-evaluable task quantities, differentials, and completion conditions. Because a qualitative relation generally leaves part of the relative configuration unspecified, expanding it into a complete pose can introduce unintended constraints. We present a typed semantic-to-geometric interface in which language specifies entities, relations, and phases, while each relation indexes a registered specification of its task-relevant distinctions and preserved freedoms. A robot-side compiler grounds these specifications, constructs relation-specific task maps and consistent differentials using conformal geometric algebra, and composes the resulting policies through RMPflow. To evaluate the division of responsibility between the language model and the compiler, we compared a Semantic Topology interface with one that additionally requires relation-specific geometric specifications over 60 instructions. Both produced correct shared semantic content in 41/60 cases, but critical errors under their respective interface requirements occurred in 19/60 and 58/60 cases. Across 64 grounded evaluations spanning eight geometric relation forms, the task maps preserved registered null directions and responded to relation-relevant perturbations; analytic directional derivatives agreed with finite differences, and Jacobian ranks matched the registered dimensions. In three closed-loop ablations using a simulated Franka Emika Panda in MuJoCo, fixing a relation-preserved coordinate increased median terminal progress error by 20.24--71.00~mm while the retained relation errors remained within their evaluation bounds. These results support compiling relation-visible geometry and preserved freedom together into composable continuous objectives.

AI.tldr: A typed semantic-to-geometric interface compiles qualitative natural-language relations into relation-specific task maps and consistent differentials (via conformal geometric algebra), composed with RMPflow, so robots get state-evaluable objectives while preserving each relation's intended freedoms.
AI.motivation: Natural-language manipulation instructions are qualitative, while continuous controllers need state-evaluable task quantities, differentials, and completion conditions. Since a qualitative relation leaves part of the relative configuration unspecified, naively expanding it into a full pose injects unintended constraints. The goal is to compile relation-visible geometry together with preserved freedoms into composable continuous objectives.
AI.method: The authors define a typed semantic-to-geometric interface: language specifies entities, relations, and phases; each relation indexes a registered specification of its task-relevant distinctions and preserved freedoms. A robot-side compiler grounds these specifications, builds relation-specific task maps and consistent differentials using conformal geometric algebra, and composes policies through RMPflow. They compare a Semantic Topology interface with one additionally requiring relation-specific geometric specifications over 60 instructions, and validate task maps across 64 grounded evaluations over eight geometric relation forms (checking null-direction preservation, perturbation response, analytic vs. finite-difference derivatives, and Jacobian ranks), plus three closed-loop ablations with a simulated Franka Emika Panda in MuJoCo.
AI.result: Both interfaces produced correct shared semantic content in 41/60 cases, but critical errors under their respective requirements occurred in 19/60 and 58/60 cases. Across 64 grounded evaluations spanning eight geometric relation forms, task maps preserved registered null directions, responded to relation-relevant perturbations, analytic directional derivatives matched finite differences, and Jacobian ranks matched registered dimensions. In three closed-loop ablations, fixing a relation-preserved coordinate increased median terminal progress error by 20.24--71.00 mm, while retained relation errors stayed within evaluation bounds.
AI.conclusion: The findings support compiling relation-visible geometry and preserved freedom together into composable continuous objectives, validating the proposed division of responsibility between the language model and the robot-side compiler.

title: Readout is not Recovery: Dissociating Coordinate Emission from Visual-Corruption Repair in Vision-Language Models
summary: VLM bounding-box localization is both language generation and spatial commitment. Parseable fields such as bbox_2d make localization easy to score, but dimensions that emit coordinate tokens need not repair localization after visual evidence is damaged. We study this readout/recovery separation in Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on single-object COCO grounding. We compare clean coordinate-token readout rankings with corruption-derived repair rankings, using object-mask endpoint replacement for recovery and clean-input flooring for depth localization. In Qwen3-VL, coordinate-token rankings are inert through layer 24, load-bearing from layers 32-35, and peak at layer 34; corruption-derived rankings harm layers 16-24 but become beneficial near layer 35/final. A Kimi-VL-A3B diagnostic shows a matching output-proximal transition despite a different box format. Object-mask recovery separates rank budgets: $k=250$ shows necessity, $k=500$ shows Top-$k$ restoration above random, and $k=d/2$ is largely capacity-driven. Partial-occlusion sweeps reveal that high-overlap coordinate-token sets can hurt at $k=1000$ and help mainly at half-width, while population corruption-derived sets provide no reliable fixed repair set. Edge-attribution patching shows coordinate-token paths are high precision but low recall for detection recovery, and RMSNorm quasi-layer controls do not close the endpoint-repair gap. Endpoint coordinate triage is therefore a useful circuit prior, but occlusion recovery requires a separate benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the separation between coordinate-token readout and corruption-recovery in VLM bounding-box localization, using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on COCO grounding. It finds coordinate-token rankings are inert early, load-bearing late (peaking at layer 34), and that corruption-derived repair rank sets are unreliable, so occlusion recovery needs its own benchmark.
AI.motivation: Bounding-box localization in VLMs is both language generation and spatial commitment. While parseable fields like bbox_2d make localization easy to score, the dimension emitting coordinate tokens may not be able to repair localization once visual evidence is damaged. The authors aim to disentangle this readout/recovery separation to understand whether coordinate-token pathways serve as a genuine circuit prior for localization.
AI.method: They compare clean coordinate-token readout rankings with corruption-derived repair rankings on single-object COCO grounding in Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct. They use object-mask endpoint replacement for recovery and clean-input flooring for depth localization. They also run a Kimi-VL-A3B diagnostic, object-mask recovery across rank budgets (k=250, 500, d/2), partial-occlusion sweeps, edge-attribution patching, and RMSNorm quasi-layer controls.
AI.result: In Qwen3-VL, coordinate-token rankings are inert through layer 24, load-bearing at layers 32-35, and peak at layer 34; corruption-derived rankings harm layers 16-24 but help near layer 35/final. Kimi-VL-A3B shows a matching output-proximal transition despite a different box format. Object-mask recovery separates rank budgets: k=250 shows necessity, k=500 shows Top-k restoration above random, and k=d/2 is largely capacity-driven. Partial-occlusion sweeps show high-overlap coordinate-token sets can hurt at k=1000 and help mainly at half-width, while population corruption-derived sets give no reliable fixed repair set. Edge-attribution patching shows coordinate-token paths are high precision but low recall for detection recovery, and RMSNorm controls do not close the endpoint-repair gap.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint coordinate triage is a useful circuit prior, but occlusion recovery requires a separate benchmark, since coordinate-token pathways do not reliably repair localization after visual evidence is damaged.

title: From World Models to World Action Models: Rethinking Next-State Prediction
summary: Predicting the next state is a core paradigm of World Models for modeling physical dynamics, emphasizing prediction fidelity. As World Models evolve into World-Action Models (WAMs), existing methods still fix the next state before training as RGB, a single latent feature, or a static combination of predefined targets, thereby constraining action learning to the inductive biases preserved by a particular representation. To address this limitation, we propose CF-WAM, a dynamic next-state prediction framework that samples visual, semantic, geometric, and interaction projections of the same future, standardizes them into a common video form, and supervises a unified WAM across these projections. The action-relevant constraints exposed by these projections accumulate across training steps, forcing WAM to capture the underlying state-transition structure that supports multiple projections of the same action-conditioned future. This dynamic mechanism also provides a natural cross-embodiment dynamics reference frame for Human and Robot learning. By jointly learning across different next-state parameterizations, heterogeneous Human and Robot experience can bypass appearance differences and directly contribute to shared state-transition learning, improving cross-embodiment generalization. Experiments show that CF-WAM improves both training efficiency and final control performance, while translating Human experience effectively into policy gains. CF-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa-GR1 with an average success rate of 82.50%, while reaching 82.65% on LIBERO-Plus and up to 84.00% in real-world evaluations.

AI.tldr: CF-WAM is a dynamic next-state prediction framework for World-Action Models that samples multiple projections (visual, semantic, geometric, interaction) of the same future, standardizes them into a common video form, and supervises a unified model across them, achieving SOTA control performance and improved cross-embodiment generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing World-Action Models fix the next-state representation before training as RGB, a single latent feature, or a static combination of predefined targets. This constrains action learning to the inductive biases preserved by a particular representation, limiting flexibility and generalization.
AI.method: CF-WAM samples visual, semantic, geometric, and interaction projections of the same future state, standardizes them into a common video form, and supervises a unified WAM across these projections. Action-relevant constraints from these projections accumulate across training steps, forcing the model to capture the underlying state-transition structure. This dynamic mechanism provides a cross-embodiment dynamics reference frame enabling heterogeneous Human and Robot experience to share state-transition learning by bypassing appearance differences.
AI.result: CF-WAM improves training efficiency and final control performance, translating Human experience into policy gains. It achieves state-of-the-art performance: 82.50% average success on RoboCasa-GR1, 82.65% on LIBERO-Plus, and up to 84.00% in real-world evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically supervising a unified World-Action Model across multiple projections of the next state enhances action learning, cross-embodiment generalization, and control performance over fixed single-representation approaches.

title: Mandela-Bench: Multimodal Models Remember Canonical Images Instead of Seeing Them
summary: Historical photographs and other canonical images can now be edited seamlessly with a single instruction, often leaving no reliable pixel-level trace. In such cases, the only evidence of manipulation may be a fact about what the image depicts. Existing benchmarks instead rely on generator artefacts, image-caption inconsistencies, visual implausibilities, or external references, and therefore do not test whether a model can use its own world knowledge to verify a recognized image. We introduce Mandela-Bench, containing 1,507 edits of canonical images: 1,359 knowledge-only forgeries, each contradicting one verifiable fact, and 148 anchor-free controls that preserve the editing process without introducing a factual contradiction, together with 474 untouched originals. We score not only whether a model detects a forgery, but whether its explanation identifies the inserted entity or the fact being violated. Across 36 multimodal models, from 0.8B parameters to frontier scale, we find a consistent failure mode. When a public figure is removed from a familiar photograph, models still name that person in up to 72.7% of responses. Some models can distinguish the replacement face from the original when shown in isolation, yet still judge the full edited photograph as authentic. Providing the true event and date does not improve knowledge-grounded detection, whereas providing the same information after cropping away the recognizable composition does. Even under explicit verification prompts, only one of the 36 models meets the KGR criterion on at least half of the forged images. These results suggest that the failures cannot be explained by missing knowledge or inadequate perception alone. Instead, they are consistent with recognition biasing verification toward the remembered canonical image rather than the observed edit.

AI.tldr: Mandela-Bench reveals multimodal models fail to detect knowledge-contradicting edits of canonical images because recognition biases verification toward the remembered original rather than the observed edit.
AI.motivation: Canonical images can now be edited seamlessly with no pixel-level trace, so the only evidence of manipulation may be a factual contradiction with world knowledge. Existing benchmarks rely on generator artefacts, caption inconsistencies, implausibility, or external references, and thus never test whether a model can use its own world knowledge to verify a recognized image.
AI.method: Introduce Mandela-Bench: 1,507 edits of canonical images — 1,359 knowledge-only forgeries (each contradicting one verifiable fact), 148 anchor-free controls (same editing process, no factual contradiction), plus 474 untouched originals. Scoring covers both forgery detection and whether explanations identify the inserted entity or violated fact. Evaluated across 36 multimodal models (0.8B to frontier scale), with ablations on providing true event/date information and cropping away recognizable composition.
AI.result: Consistent failure mode: when a public figure is removed from a familiar photograph, models still name that person in up to 72.7% of responses. Some models distinguish the replacement face in isolation yet judge the full edited photo authentic. Providing true event and date does not improve knowledge-grounded detection, but providing the same information after cropping the recognizable composition does. Under explicit verification prompts, only 1 of 36 models meets the KGR criterion on at least half the forged images.
