AI.conclusion: Failures cannot be explained by missing knowledge or inadequate perception alone; they are consistent with recognition biasing verification toward the remembered canonical image rather than the observed edit.

title: ARS: Agentic Reward System for Robot Learning
summary: Progress reward modeling is the problem of estimating how a robot's behavior changes task progress over time. Reliable estimation requires distinguishing meaningful state changes from failed attempts and task-irrelevant actions. We introduce the Agentic Reward System (ARS), an inference framework for progress reward modeling with general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs), without additional reward-model training. Given an offline trajectory and a task instruction, ARS uses adaptive visual inspection for both event proposal and verification. A subagent proposes a task-relevant event timeline, which a primary agent verifies and revises before estimating per-frame progress. ARS can incorporate optional terminal outcome labels and visual references to inform its judgments. It can also audit progress estimates from external reward models. We evaluate ARS with a 27B VLM on a controlled semantic-mismatch benchmark and downstream policy learning in simulation and on a real robot. The benchmark reveals that several evaluated reward baselines assign spurious progress to wrong-object manipulation even in simple pick-and-place scenes. ARS better suppresses these errors and outperforms these baselines in simulation policy learning. We further demonstrate that ARS supports long-horizon policy learning from mixed-quality offline experience on real-robot multi-screw fastening in a full-scale laboratory replica of an industrial washing-machine assembly line. These results suggest that structured inference and verification can improve the usefulness of general-purpose VLMs for robot reward modeling. Code is at https://github.com/midea-ai/ars

AI.tldr: ARS is a training-free inference framework that uses general-purpose VLMs with adaptive visual inspection to model task progress rewards, outperforming baselines on a semantic-mismatch benchmark and downstream policy learning in simulation and real-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Reliable progress reward estimation requires distinguishing meaningful state changes from failed attempts and task-irrelevant actions, a challenge that existing reward baselines fail at—assigning spurious progress to wrong-object manipulation even in simple pick-and-place scenes.
AI.method: ARS is an inference framework for progress reward modeling using general-purpose VLMs without additional reward-model training. Given an offline trajectory and task instruction, it employs adaptive visual inspection for event proposal and verification: a subagent proposes a task-relevant event timeline, and a primary agent verifies and revises it before estimating per-frame progress. It optionally incorporates terminal outcome labels and visual references, and can audit external reward models.
AI.result: Evaluated with a 27B VLM on a controlled semantic-mismatch benchmark and downstream policy learning in simulation and real-robot settings, ARS better suppresses spurious-progress errors than baselines and outperforms them in simulation policy learning. It also supports long-horizon policy learning from mixed-quality offline experience on real-robot multi-screw fastening in a full-scale laboratory replica of an industrial washing-machine assembly line.
AI.conclusion: Structured inference and verification can improve the usefulness of general-purpose VLMs for robot reward modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/midea-ai/ars.

title: Forecasting Intraday USD/CAD Exchange Rate with News-Derived Monetary-Policy Signals
summary: Monetary-policy announcements and central-bank communications play a central role in foreign exchange markets, yet their qualitative, unstructured form makes their forecasting value difficult to quantify. While prior research has largely focused on sentiment extracted from financial news, comparatively little is known about the relative contribution of different dimensions of monetary-policy communication. Existing studies primarily evaluate whether textual information improves overall forecasting performance but provide limited insight into which communication channels drive such improvements. To address this gap, this paper introduces a statistical attribution methodology that decomposes monetary-policy communication into interpretable channels and quantifies their incremental forecasting contribution under false-discovery-rate control. Monetary-policy news is transformed into structured communication signals using large language models (LLMs) and temporal feature engineering. These signals are evaluated using rolling-window experiments with tree-based machine-learning models. The results show that monetary-policy communication contains measurable predictive information. Attribution analysis shows that predictive value is concentrated in a small subset of signals, with communication timing providing the strongest individual feature-level contribution, targeted communication-activity measures also contributing positively, and LLM-derived sentiment providing complementary information at the group level. The findings indicate that communication-based forecasting value extends beyond sentiment alone and that attribution, rather than aggregate accuracy alone, is central to evaluating news-derived signals.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a statistical attribution methodology that decomposes monetary-policy communication into interpretable channels (via LLMs and temporal feature engineering) and quantifies each channel's incremental forecasting value for FX markets under false-discovery-rate control, showing that predictive value is concentrated in a few signals, with communication timing as the strongest contributor and LLM sentiment providing complementary value.
AI.motivation: Monetary-policy announcements and central-bank communications are central to FX markets, but their qualitative, unstructured form makes forecasting value hard to quantify. Prior work mainly extracts sentiment from financial news and evaluates whether text improves overall forecasting performance, leaving unclear which communication channels drive improvements. This paper addresses the lack of insight into the relative contribution of different dimensions of monetary-policy communication.
AI.method: The authors introduce a statistical attribution methodology that decomposes monetary-policy communication into interpretable channels and quantifies their incremental forecasting contribution under false-discovery-rate control. Monetary-policy news is converted into structured communication signals using large language models (LLMs) and temporal feature engineering. These signals are evaluated through rolling-window experiments with tree-based machine-learning models.
AI.result: Monetary-policy communication contains measurable predictive information. Attribution analysis reveals that predictive value is concentrated in a small subset of signals. Communication timing yields the strongest individual feature-level contribution; targeted communication-activity measures also contribute positively; and LLM-derived sentiment provides complementary information at the group level.
AI.conclusion: Communication-based forecasting value extends beyond sentiment alone. Attribution, rather than aggregate accuracy alone, is central to evaluating news-derived signals.

title: Trajectory-Safe Orienteering for Human-Robot Shared Environments
summary: Orienteering problem (OP) has wide real-world applications and also great potential in human-robot collaboration. However, existing approaches struggle to simultaneously ensure safe and feasible trajectories while achieving high-quality task execution in shared workspaces. To this end, this work studies the OP with time windows and variable profits (OPTWVP). A two-stage DEcoupled discrete-Continuous Optimization with Service-time-guided Trajectory (DeCoST) approach is proposed to effectively solve OPTWVP in shared spaces. Meanwhile, the safety-aware time windows of nodes and the discretized workspace are introduced to ensure collision-free trajectories between the end effector and the human. Preliminary results validate the effectiveness of DeCoST in generating collision-free trajectory plans while preserving the quality of orienteering tasks.

AI.tldr: This work addresses the Orienteering Problem with Time Windows and Variable Profits (OPTWVP) in human-robot shared workspaces, proposing a two-stage decoupled discrete-continuous optimization approach with service-time-guided trajectory (DeCoST), which uses safety-aware time windows and a discretized workspace to ensure collision-free trajectories while maintaining task quality.
AI.motivation: Existing orienteering problem approaches struggle to simultaneously guarantee safe, feasible trajectories and high-quality task execution in shared human-robot workspaces, motivating a dedicated formulation and solver for OPTWVP.
AI.method: The paper formulates the OPTWVP and proposes DeCoST, a two-stage DEcoupled discrete-Continuous Optimization with Service-time-guided Trajectory. Safety is enforced via safety-aware time windows of nodes and a discretized workspace to avoid end-effector/human collisions.
AI.result: Preliminary results validate that DeCoST generates collision-free trajectory plans while preserving the quality of orienteering task execution.
AI.conclusion: DeCoST effectively solves OPTWVP in shared spaces, showing promise for safe and productive human-robot collaboration.

title: Agentic Network Traffic Monitoring
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, to appear in IEEE URTC 2026
summary: As the use of agentic artificial intelligence increases in nearly every industry, there exists a widening attack surface. It is necessary to monitor agents to ensure that agents are acting in a way that is aligned with the users intent. Auditing an agent's network traffic provides a clear record of the agent interactions. This work presents a novel approach to monitoring the network traffic of agentic systems using complex valued hypersparse traffic matrices by integrating DBOS (DataBase OS), the OneSparse PostgreSQL database, and the GraphBLAS math library. To develop these concepts an agentic simulator was constructed, allowing a varying numbers of AI agents to collectively survey a virtual environment using different strategies. The resulting network traffic matrices enable easy monitoring of the AI agents.

AI.tldr: This work proposes monitoring agentic AI systems by capturing their network traffic as complex-valued hypersparse traffic matrices, implemented via DBOS, OneSparse PostgreSQL, and GraphBLAS, and validated with an agentic simulator of collaborating AI agents surveying a virtual environment.
AI.motivation: The growing adoption of agentic AI across industries expands the attack surface, creating a need to monitor agents and verify that their actions align with user intent. Auditing network traffic offers a clear record of agent interactions, motivating a scalable monitoring approach.
AI.method: An agentic simulator is built in which a variable number of AI agents collectively survey a virtual environment using different strategies. The resulting network traffic is represented as complex-valued hypersparse traffic matrices, generated by integrating DBOS (DataBase OS), the OneSparse PostgreSQL database, and the GraphBLAS math library.
AI.result: The approach produces network traffic matrices that enable easy monitoring of the AI agents across varying agent counts and survey strategies.
AI.conclusion: Complex-valued hypersparse traffic matrices, enabled by DBOS, OneSparse PostgreSQL, and GraphBLAS, provide a practical and easily interpretable means of monitoring agentic AI systems' network traffic to support alignment auditing.

title: Model-Informed Safe Reinforcement Learning for Bipedal Locomotion via Step-to-Step Prediction
summary: Humanoid robots promise versatile mobility in cluttered, human-centric environments, but real deployment demands principled safety. Classical model-based gait generators yield interpretable motions but often lack the robustness and adaptability of modern reinforcement learning (RL) based approaches. We propose a model-informed reinforcement learning framework anchored to the analytical Angular Momentum Linear Inverted Pendulum (ALIP) template. We provide a step-to-step safety certificate for ALIP stepping via a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF) and use it as (i) a training-time shaping signal and (ii) a runtime action filter that minimally adjusts swing-foot placement to satisfy template-level constraints. Full-order safety is evaluated empirically on the Digit humanoid in MuJoCo with a whole-body controller stack. Compared to an unconstrained baseline, our approach reduces safety-violation events in the reported external-disturbance trial, while larger lateral-velocity transients reveal a safety-tracking tradeoff.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a model-informed RL framework built on the ALIP template, using a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF) as both a training shaping signal and a runtime swing-foot action filter to improve safety of humanoid locomotion, validated on Digit in MuJoCo.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots need versatile mobility in cluttered human-centric environments, but safe real-world deployment requires principled safety guarantees. Classical model-based gait generators are interpretable but lack robustness and adaptability, whereas modern RL approaches are robust and adaptive but lack principled safety. The work aims to combine the strengths of both.
AI.method: The authors anchor a model-informed RL framework to the analytical Angular Momentum Linear Inverted Pendulum (ALIP) template. They derive a step-to-step safety certificate for ALIP stepping via a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF), and use this certificate in two ways: (i) as a training-time shaping signal, and (ii) as a runtime action filter that minimally adjusts swing-foot placement to satisfy template-level constraints. Full-order safety is evaluated empirically on the Digit humanoid in MuJoCo with a whole-body controller stack.
AI.result: Compared to an unconstrained baseline, the approach reduces safety-violation events in the reported external-disturburbance trial. Larger lateral-velocity transients reveal a safety-tracking tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: The DECBF-based ALIP certificate can be effectively integrated into RL as both shaping and a runtime filter to reduce safety violations on a full-order humanoid, though a tradeoff between safety and tracking performance emerges under large lateral-velocity transients.

title: Learning response-aware patient dynamics for respiratory support
summary: Respiratory support can shape the short-term physiological trajectory of critically ill patients, but patients receiving the same intervention may follow different physiological trajectories. Clinical patient dynamics models typically predict future states from recent physiology and recorded interventions, while physiological change is mainly represented through the predicted future state. We propose a response-aware patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during autoregressive state updating. The model decomposes predicted physiological change into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, with room air providing a reference for the decomposition. We provide a formal analysis of this reference-anchored formulation. A response pathway encodes the predicted physiological change and uses it to update the latent patient state across the forecast horizon. Across ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, the proposed model achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to patient dynamics baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a response-aware patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during autoregressive state updating, decomposing predicted change into baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations anchored on room air, and shows more consistent trajectory prediction improvements when physiological states are changing.
AI.motivation: Patients receiving the same respiratory support may follow different physiological trajectories, so representing physiological change only implicitly through the predicted future state is insufficient. The authors aim to explicitly model the physiological change and isolate the effect of respiratory support.
AI.method: The model decomposes predicted physiological change into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, using room air as a reference for the decomposition. The approach includes a formal analysis of this reference-anchored formulation and a response pathway that encodes the predicted physiological change and updates the latent patient state across the forecast horizon.
AI.result: Across ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, the proposed model achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to patient dynamics baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling physiological change and respiratory-support-associated deviations via a reference-anchored, response-aware dynamics model improves trajectory prediction consistency during changing physiological states, while remaining comparable overall to existing baselines.

title: Robot-Assisted Deployment and Maintenance of Inflatable Modules for Lunar Habitation: A Field Demonstration
comment: Author's version of a manuscript accepted at the International Conference on Space Robotics 2026 (iSpaRo 2026). (c) IEEE
summary: Long-term human habitation and in-situ development on the Moon open a new era of space utilization. In this context, robots are a key technology for facilitating the construction of future human outposts. Toward the deployment and establishment of human habitation modules on the lunar surface, we propose a combined system consisting of inflatable modules and a modular, reconfigurable robotic system. This paper presents a report demonstrating various robot-assisted task executions using real hardware, namely the modular and reconfigurable robot MoonBot and the inflatable module HIDAS, to enhance the reliability of their deployment and maintenance. The demonstrated tasks include robotic inspection during inflation, module position alignment, final safety locking, and three-dimensional mapping for post-deployment maintenance. All demonstrations were conducted either in a laboratory environment or at a lunar analogue test site. Finally, lessons learned are discussed to provide essential insights for this robotic application to future lunar habitation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a combined system of inflatable modules and a modular, reconfigurable robot (MoonBot) for lunar habitation; validates robot-assisted deployment and maintenance tasks on real hardware in lab and lunar analogue environments.
AI.motivation: Long-term human habitation and in-situ development on the Moon require constructing future human outposts, for which robots are a key enabling technology. Reliable deployment and maintenance of habitation modules on the lunar surface is an open challenge.
AI.method: A combined system of inflatable modules and a modular, reconfigurable robotic system is proposed. Using real hardware—the modular reconfigurable robot MoonBot and the inflatable module HIDAS—various robot-assisted task executions are demonstrated: robotic inspection during inflation, module position alignment, final safety locking, and three-dimensional mapping for post-deployment maintenance. Demonstrations were conducted in a laboratory environment or at a lunar analogue test site.
AI.result: Multiple robot-assisted tasks were successfully executed with real hardware in laboratory and lunar analogue settings, enhancing confidence in the reliability of deployment and maintenance of the inflatable module system.
AI.conclusion: Lessons learned from the demonstrations are discussed, providing essential insights for applying this robotic approach to future lunar habitation.

title: CLAIRE: A Schema-Grounded Hybrid Workflow for Healthcare Administrative Form Completion
summary: Healthcare administrative staff transfer structured information from electronic health records, referrals, claims systems, provider rosters, and work queues into dynamic forms. We developed and evaluated CLAIRE (Clinical Language and Agentic Intelligence for Reasoning and Entry), a hybrid workflow that separates field-state discovery, source-to-field mapping, deterministic validation, bounded correction, escalation, and audit tracing. We tested five synthetic healthcare administrative schemas, 1,000 source records, four interface variants, two data-quality suites, and six comparators, yielding 24,000 benchmark episodes. A separate strict-output audit evaluated direct mappings from Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B, and a trace-derived operational simulation covered 6,000 episodes. Under the evaluated synthetic benchmark conditions, full CLAIRE achieved 1.000 episode success, field accuracy, required-field completion, and dependency completion in both suites; removing validation reduced stress-suite success to 0.500. In the simulation, 100.0% of clean and validation-stress episodes reached a staff-reviewable draft, compared with 68.6% of escalation challenge episodes, unsupported cases were blocked. Scenario-based savings were 149.7-165.5 seconds per case, not observed staff times. The findings support schema-grounded, validation-first healthcare administrative automation in which language-model components assist mapping but do not authorize unsupported or consequential actions.

AI.tldr: CLAIRE, a hybrid workflow separating field-state discovery, source-to-field mapping, deterministic validation, bounded correction, escalation, and audit tracing, was evaluated on 24,000 synthetic benchmark episodes (plus a 6,000-episode operational simulation), achieving perfect success and field accuracy under its full configuration, with validation identified as decisive.
AI.motivation: Healthcare administrative staff must manually transfer structured information from electronic health records, referrals, claims systems, provider rosters, and work queues into dynamic forms, a labor-intensive and error-prone process that motivates schema-grounded automation without granting language models authority over unsupported or consequential actions.
AI.method: A hybrid workflow (CLAIRE) was designed that decomposes the task into field-state discovery, source-to-field mapping, deterministic validation, bounded correction, escalation, and audit tracing. Evaluation used five synthetic healthcare administrative schemas, 1,000 source records, four interface variants, two data-quality suites, and six comparators, totaling 24,000 benchmark episodes. A separate strict-output audit assessed direct mappings from Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B, and a trace-derived operational simulation covered 6,000 episodes.
AI.result: Under synthetic benchmark conditions, full CLAIRE reached 1.000 episode success, field accuracy, required-field completion, and dependency completion in both data-quality suites; removing validation dropped stress-suite success to 0.500. In simulation, 100.0% of clean and validation-stress episodes produced a staff-reviewable draft versus 68.6% for escalation challenge episodes, with unsupported cases blocked. Scenario-based savings were 149.7-165.5 seconds per case (not observed staff times).
AI.conclusion: The findings support schema-grounded, validation-first automation for healthcare administrative data entry, in which language-model components assist mapping but are not authorized to perform unsupported or consequential actions.

title: MonoEgo: Monocular Metric Egocentric Demonstration Capture with Passive Wrist Constellations and Sparse Workstation Anchors
summary: Image-aligned metric demonstrations often require dedicated tracking hardware and synchronization across devices. We present MonoEgo, a capture system that replaces active wrist instrumentation with offline monocular reconstruction. One 90-FPS global-shutter camera observes calibrated passive wrist constellations, sparse workstation anchors, and the scene on a shared image clock. MonoTag SLAM combines marker corners with ORB geometry and uses visual evidence to reject ambiguous planar-marker poses. Its metric Atlas supports interval scale re-anchoring, verified map merging, and retrospective localization of earlier frames supported by the final map. Camera and wrist-constellation outputs retain validity and map provenance, and unsupported motion is left missing. Experiments show metric tracking beyond continuous anchor visibility, reconnection of supported map components, and recovery of some missing camera poses. Comparisons against a multisensor camera reference and separate stationary-constellation tests characterize trajectory agreement and precision while revealing incomplete coverage and residual geometric uncertainty. The results indicate that passive fixtures and offline reconstruction can reduce capture-side requirements. Dynamic accuracy, deployment, and downstream policy benefits require further study.

AI.tldr: MonoEgo removes active wrist trackers by reconstructing metric hand and camera trajectories offline from a single 90-FPS global-shutter camera observing passive wrist markers, workstation anchors, and the scene.
AI.motivation: Image-aligned metric demonstrations typically need dedicated tracking hardware and cross-device synchronization, which increases capture-side burden and deployment complexity. The paper aims to reduce these requirements.
AI.method: A monocular capture system observes calibrated passive wrist constellations, sparse workstation anchors, and the scene on one shared image clock. MonoTag SLAM fuses marker corners with ORB geometry and rejects ambiguous planar-marker poses using visual evidence. A metric Atlas performs interval scale re-anchoring, verified map merging, and retrospective localization of earlier frames against the final map; unsupported motion is left missing, with validity and map provenance retained.
AI.result: Experiments show metric tracking beyond continuous anchor visibility, reconnection of supported map components, and recovery of some missing camera poses. Comparisons against a multisensor camera reference and separate stationary-constellation tests characterize trajectory agreement and precision, while also revealing incomplete coverage and residual geometric uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Passive fixtures plus offline reconstruction can lower capture-side requirements. Dynamic accuracy, deployment, and downstream policy benefits remain open questions requiring further study.

title: $T^5$: Twin-Critic Training for Token-Level Thoughts in Reinforcement Mid-Training
summary: Reinforcement mid-training lets language models learn internal thoughts from unlabeled text, but efficient token-level credit assignment remains challenging. Existing group-relative methods require costly repeated generation. Learned critics offer single-rollout feedback, but accurate return prediction alone does not ensure reliable policy updates. Our analysis shows how training--inference mismatch and PPO clipping prevent a common offset in advantage estimates from cancelling out, introducing additional update drift. We propose \tfour{}, a twin-critic method that calibrates token-level advantages from a single generated trajectory. After warmup and held-out qualification, the critics provide two advantage estimates, combined using action-dependent weights learned through a conditional-moment saddle-point objective. This objective brings the average advantage at each prefix toward zero, while a signal-retention constraint prevents the correction from erasing the learning signal. Sharing information across text positions avoids repeated sampling of each prefix. Theoretically, we characterize optimal mixing under the signal-retention constraint and establish an upper bound on residual mean-induced drift. Experiments show that, compared with the state-of-the-art critic-free method, \tfour{} improves mean benchmark performance by 7.8\% and reduces mean training-step time by up to 63.4\%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TwinCritic (referred to as \tfour{}), a twin-critic method that calibrates token-level advantages from a single generated trajectory for reinforcement mid-training, eliminating costly repeated generation while correcting advantage bias and reducing update drift.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement mid-training enables language models to learn internal thoughts from unlabeled text, but efficient token-level credit assignment is difficult. Existing group-relative methods need costly repeated generation, while learned critics give single-rollout feedback yet accurate return prediction alone does not guarantee reliable policy updates. The authors identify training–inference mismatch and PPO clipping as causes preventing a common offset in advantage estimates from cancelling, inducing extra update drift.
AI.method: A twin-critic approach: after warmup and held-out qualification, two critics produce two advantage estimates combined via action-dependent weights learned through a conditional-moment saddle-point objective. This objective drives the average advantage at each prefix toward zero, while a signal-retention constraint prevents the correction from erasing the learning signal. Information is shared across text positions to avoid repeated sampling of each prefix. Theoretically, they characterize optimal mixing under the signal-retention constraint and derive an upper bound on residual mean-induced drift.
AI.result: Compared with the state-of-the-art critic-free method, the proposed method improves mean benchmark performance by 7.8% and reduces mean training-step time by up to 63.4%.
AI.conclusion: Twin-critic token-level advantage calibration provides an effective and efficient alternative to repeated generation for reinforcement mid-training, improving both accuracy and training efficiency while theoretically bounding residual drift.

title: Gaze Prompts: Temporally Dense Human Attention for Vision-Language-Action Fine-Tuning
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) fine-tuning pairs images with actions at every step, yet typically provides only a task-level language instruction, leaving moment-to-moment visual relevance implicit. We introduce \emph{eye-tracker-supervised gaze prompting}, which uses gaze recorded during VR teleoperation to provide frame-level visual guidance for VLA fine-tuning. During training, recorded gaze locations are rendered as crosshairs on the robot's head-camera images. At deployment, a lightweight predictor estimates gaze locations from recent images and the instruction, supplying the same type of visual prompt without an eye tracker or changes to the policy architecture. Instantiated with $π_0$, gaze prompting increases mean success from $26.3\%$ to $56.0\%$ across six real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, with gains also observed when a single policy is trained on all six tasks. We release \textsc{GazeMani}, a dataset of $1{,}200$ teleoperated trajectories with synchronized gaze.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces eye-tracker-supervised gaze prompting, which uses gaze recorded during VR teleoperation to provide frame-level visual guidance for VLA fine-tuning, boosting real-world bimanual manipulation success from 26.3% to 56.0%.
AI.motivation: VLA fine-tuning pairs images with actions at every step but only supplies a task-level language instruction, leaving moment-to-moment visual relevance implicit.
AI.method: During training, recorded gaze locations are rendered as crosshairs on the robot's head-camera images. At deployment, a lightweight predictor estimates gaze locations from recent images and the instruction, supplying the same visual prompt without an eye tracker or policy-architecture changes. Instantiated with pi_0.
AI.result: Mean success increases from 26.3% to 56.0% across six real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, with gains also observed when a single policy is trained on all six tasks. The authors release GazeMani, a dataset of 1,200 teleoperated trajectories with synchronized gaze.
AI.conclusion: Gaze prompting supplies frame-level visual guidance that substantially improves VLA fine-tuning, and it transfers to deployment via a learned gaze predictor without requiring an eye tracker.

title: AgentHabit: Characterizing Distinct Behaviors of Agents on Everyday Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents assist users with everyday tasks that can be completed in many reasonable ways. Even when their answers are useful, how agents carry out these tasks may not match users' preferences and needs. For example, agents differ in whether they ask clarifying questions or search the web. We introduce HABIT, a taxonomy of 23 behavioral axes in five categories, which three authors and three LLMs derive bottom-up from 408 agent trajectories across 17 domains. On held-out tasks, HABIT distinguishes models more clearly than existing taxonomies of human values and agent actions while supporting comparably consistent annotation. Building on HABIT, we construct AgentHABIT, a benchmark that profiles each agent's behavioral tendencies from its trajectories on 86 everyday tasks. Profiling 18 models with AgentHABIT reveals a range of distinctive tendencies. For example, most GPT and Claude models state their assumptions and offer alternatives when requirements conflict, whereas Qwen and Google's models more often leave assumptions or changes to requirements unstated. These profiles remain recognizable even when built from entirely different sets of tasks, indicating that they reflect general tendencies rather than task-specific behavior. Prompting agents to adopt specific behaviors shifts some axes readily but barely changes others, while fine-tuning on another model's trajectories changes only part of a model's profile and leaves much of it intact. Overall, HABIT and AgentHABIT provide a systematic framework for characterizing how agents carry out everyday tasks beyond task success, offering insights to guide the development of agents whose behavior better fits users' needs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HABIT, a bottom-up taxonomy of 23 behavioral axes in five categories for characterizing how LLM agents carry out everyday tasks, plus AgentHABIT, a benchmark profiling 18 models' behavioral tendencies across 86 tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can complete everyday tasks in many reasonable ways, but their process (e.g., asking clarifying questions, searching the web) may not match users' preferences and needs. Existing taxonomies of human values and agent actions fail to clearly distinguish models' behavioral styles, so a systematic framework beyond task success is needed.
AI.method: The authors derive HABIT bottom-up from 408 agent trajectories across 17 domains, with three human authors and three LLMs jointly producing 23 behavioral axes grouped into five categories. They then build AgentHABIT, a benchmark that profiles each agent's behavioral tendencies from its trajectories on 86 everyday tasks, and use it to profile 18 models. They test profile robustness across different task sets, sensitivity to prompting, and effects of fine-tuning on another model's trajectories.
AI.result: On held-out tasks, HABIT distinguishes models more clearly than existing taxonomies of human values and agent actions while supporting comparably consistent annotation. Profiling 18 models reveals distinctive tendencies (e.g., most GPT and Claude models state assumptions and offer alternatives under conflicting requirements, whereas Qwen and Google models often leave assumptions or requirement changes unstated). Profiles remain recognizable when built from entirely different task sets, indicating general rather than task-specific tendencies. Prompting shifts some axes readily but barely changes others, and fine-tuning on another model's trajectories alters only part of the profile.
AI.conclusion: HABIT and AgentHABIT provide a systematic framework for characterizing how agents carry out everyday tasks beyond task success, offering insights to guide development of agents whose behavior better fits users' needs.

title: Where Memory Belongs: Ledger, an Object Ledger for Memory-Augmented VLAs
summary: Memory is essential for long-horizon, partially observed robotic manipulation: a robot must remember which object was placed in a drawer, whose cup it moved, or how many action cycles have elapsed. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models embed memory directly inside the policy, but benchmarks show no single in-policy mechanism covers all spatio-temporal dimensions, trailing oracle methods by a wide margin. We argue that memory type dictates where memory should reside: short-term perceptual memory (repetition, timing, retracing) belongs inside the policy, while long-term object memory (persistent spatial state, containment, event history) belongs outside as an explicit, readable record. We present Ledger, a harness that realizes this split over a single fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policy by pairing an in-policy frame-sampling memory with an external spatio-temporal object memory, the ledger, built from a SAM3 tracker and a VLM captioner of the demonstration and read by an LLM planner that decides at step boundaries. On RoboMME, Ledger reaches the highest four-suite average among the evaluated methods, 64.3% (vs. 45.9% for the strongest prior method under identical evaluation), leading object reference (60.7% vs. 40.3%) and object permanence (86.7% vs. 56.2%) using a single set of weights. Choosing the memory source at runtime, from the instruction and the record, removes the need for a task-level router.

AI.tldr: Ledger is a memory harness for robotic manipulation that splits short-term perceptual memory inside a fine-tuned π0.5 VLA policy from long-term object memory kept externally in a readable "ledger," achieving 64.3% four-suite average on RoboMME versus 45.9% for the strongest prior method.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon, partially observed manipulation requires memory of objects, placements, and elapsed actions. Existing VLA models embed memory inside the policy, but benchmarks show no single in-policy mechanism covers all spatio-temporal dimensions, trailing oracle methods by a wide margin.
AI.method: The paper argues memory type dictates memory location: short-term perceptual memory (repetition, timing, retracing) belongs inside the policy, while long-term object memory (persistent spatial state, containment, event history) belongs outside as an explicit readable record. Ledger implements this split over one fine-tuned π0.5 policy, pairing an in-policy frame-sampling memory with an external spatio-temporal ledger built from a SAM3 tracker and a VLM captioner, read by an LLM planner deciding at step boundaries.
AI.result: On RoboMME, Ledger attains the highest four-suite average among evaluated methods at 64.3% (vs. 45.9% for the strongest prior method under identical evaluation), leading on object reference (60.7% vs. 40.3%) and object permanence (86.7% vs. 56.2%) with a single set of weights. Selecting the memory source at runtime from instruction and record eliminates the need for a task-level router.
AI.conclusion: Splitting memory by type—in-policy short-term perceptual memory plus an external long-term object ledger—outperforms unified in-policy memory and removes task-level routing, yielding state-of-the-art RoboMME results.

title: PlanGuard: A Guardrail for Multi-Step Plan Safety in Embodied Agents
summary: Embodied task planners may produce multi-step plans whose subtask dependencies and interactions with the environment create physical risks during execution. Yet existing safeguards overlook such compositional risks, as general-purpose guardrails focus on semantic harm and embodied safety detectors assess subtasks in isolation. To address this gap, we introduce PlanGuard, the first pre-execution detector that evaluates the physical safety of a complete multi-step plan in its current environment. For training and evaluation, we construct a Multi-Step Plan Safety (MSP-Safe) dataset through paired task construction, plan generation using diverse planners, and safety annotation by three judges. Task-oriented SFT on MSP-Safe establishes fundamental plan-safety assessment capabilities, yet a substantial gap remains between compact models suitable for real-time deployment and stronger but costlier large models. Accordingly, we propose Strong-Teacher Adaptive Compensation for On-Policy Distillation (STAC-OPD), which provides compact models with adaptive strong-teacher supervision along their on-policy trajectories. It combines token-level distribution transfer from a fine-tuned strong teacher with probability-routed sequence-level compensation, retaining student-generated targets when the student favors the reference safety decision and using teacher-reconstructed targets otherwise. Across all test subsets, PlanGuard-2B achieves average 87.15% ACC and 87.21% F1, demonstrating effective whole-plan physical-risk detection at compact model scale. Code and dataset will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: PlanGuard is introduced as the first pre-execution detector that assesses the physical safety of an entire multi-step embodied plan in its current environment. Using a newly built MSP-Safe dataset and a distillation method (STAC-OPD), the compact PlanGuard-2B model reaches 87.15% ACC and 87.21% F1 across test subsets.
AI.motivation: Embodied task planners can generate multi-step plans whose subtask dependencies and environmental interactions create compositional physical risks during execution. Existing safeguards fail here: general-purpose guardrails only target semantic harm, and embodied safety detectors evaluate subtasks in isolation. This leaves whole-plan physical safety unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors propose PlanGuard, a pre-execution detector evaluating physical safety of a complete multi-step plan in its current environment. They build the Multi-Step Plan Safety (MSP-Safe) dataset via paired task construction, plan generation with diverse planners, and safety annotation by three judges. Task-oriented SFT on MSP-Safe builds basic plan-safety assessment. To close the gap between compact deployable models and stronger large models, they propose STAC-OPD (Strong-Teacher Adaptive Compensation for On-Policy Distillation), which supplies compact models with adaptive strong-teacher supervision along on-policy trajectories, combining token-level distribution transfer from a fine-tuned strong teacher with probability-routed sequence-level compensation: retaining student-generated targets when the student favors the reference safety decision, otherwise using teacher-reconstructed targets.
AI.result: Across all test subsets, PlanGuard-2B achieves an average of 87.15% accuracy and 87.21% F1, demonstrating effective whole-plan physical-risk detection at compact model scale.
AI.conclusion: PlanGuard enables pre-execution, whole-plan physical safety detection for embodied task planning, a gap left by semantic-focused guardrails and isolated subtask detectors. STAC-OPD allows compact models to approach strong-teacher performance. Code and dataset will be publicly released.

title: Aerial GRIPPER: A Gradient-based Real-time Inverse-game Predictor and Planner
summary: Accurate capture of non-cooperative targets is critical. In an attempt to tackle this intractable challenge, an aerial gripper system integrated with a Gradient-based Real-time Inverse-game Predictor and PlannER (GRIPPER) framework is proposed. The interaction is formulated as a general-sum pursuit-evasion game under incomplete information. Specifically, underlying cost parameters of the target are inferred online, and the open-loop Nash equilibrium (OLNE) strategy is iteratively refined within a receding-horizon loop. To ensure high-frequency execution, a computationally friendly gradient-based inverse-game solver is developed. Without explicit computation of the Hessian inverse, the optimized solution is updated (> 50 Hz) based on implicit differentiation and fast Hessian-vector products. Meanwhile, an anti-disturbance controller is developed to overcome disturbances of uncertain payload and gripper actuation, enabling precise tracking of the planned trajectory and accurate grasping of the target. Simulations and real-world experiments illustrate the superior computational efficiency and task performance of GRIPPER. The task of capturing and delivering a non-cooperative target is accomplished, highlighting the robustness, adaptability, and real-time performance of the framework in highly adversarial scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GRIPPER, an aerial gripper framework that integrates a gradient-based real-time inverse-game predictor and planner to capture non-cooperative targets, achieving >50 Hz planning and successful real-world grasping.
AI.motivation: Accurate capture of non-cooperative targets is critical yet intractable, as such targets behave adversarially and their underlying cost parameters are unknown, requiring online inference and real-time planning under incomplete information.
AI.method: The interaction is formulated as a general-sum pursuit-evasion game under incomplete information. Target cost parameters are inferred online, and the open-loop Nash equilibrium (OLNE) strategy is iteratively refined within a receding-horizon loop. A gradient-based inverse-game solver is developed that avoids explicit Hessian inversion by using implicit differentiation and fast Hessian-vector products. An anti-disturbance controller handles uncertain payload and gripper actuation disturbances.
AI.result: The optimized solution updates at above 50 Hz. Simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate superior computational efficiency and task performance, with the anti-disturbance controller enabling precise trajectory tracking and accurate grasping.
AI.conclusion: GRIPPER accomplishes capturing and delivering a non-cooperative target, highlighting the robustness, adaptability, and real-time performance of the framework in highly adversarial scenarios.

title: Re-derivability Decides What a Staged Agent Pipeline Recovers After an Upstream Fault
comment: 34 pages, 8 figures, 13 tables; preprint under review
summary: One variable sets what an upstream fault costs a staged pipeline of language-model agents: re-derivability, how much of what a stage needs it can rebuild from the original problem. Grounding an inspector agent in that problem is worth +0.608 [+0.517, +0.700] to +0.358 over a blind one on four open-weight backbones served with thinking disabled, and on the two Qwen backbones the blind inspector changes no item at all. That head-to-head is exploratory. One deterministic fault enters the first stage, and we re-expose the original problem to $k = 0,\dots,3$ of the downstream stages with agents, items, fault and topology held fixed, on 120 gsm_hard items per arm at temperature zero. Accuracy under fault rises on four of four backbones, from +0.233 to +0.392, the largest Holm-adjusted $p$ being $2.1\times10^{-6}$. A registered kill test rules out tokens. Blanking every word holds the word slots fixed, and retention tracks the visible fraction on four of four, climbing from 0.221 to 0.692 on the primary. Those two families are confirmatory and everything else here is exploratory. The interaction excludes zero on two of four backbones under the registered pipeline, four of four under a three-stage pipeline, and three of four under full message history, the primary at +0.317. On Llama-3.1-8B the fault carries no detectable cost at any dose, so the other three carry every claim about what a fault costs. Re-derivability also sets what the architecture costs, and no decomposition we measured reliably beats one direct call. With no fault injected the registered pipeline loses to that call by -0.267, -0.125 and -0.317, and on Phi-4 reads +0.058 at $p = 0.118$, which the test fails to separate from zero. The repair that works is cheap and front-loaded: the first re-grounded stage buys +0.394 of matched retention for +59.8 tokens per item on Qwen3-14B, and the stages after it buy nothing.

AI.tldr: Re-derivability (how much of a needed input a downstream stage can rebuild from the original problem) is the single variable governing the cost of an upstream fault in a staged LLM-agent pipeline; re-grounding an inspector in the original problem is the cheap, front-loaded repair, and no staged decomposition reliably beats one direct call when no fault is injected.
AI.motivation: To identify and quantify what determines the cost of an upstream fault in staged, multi-agent language-model pipelines, and to test whether re-exposing the original problem to downstream stages can repair that fault.
AI.method: A staged pipeline with one deterministic fault injected into the first stage; the original problem is re-exposed to k = 0–3 downstream agent stages while agents, items, fault and topology are held fixed. Experiments run on four open-weight backbones with thinking disabled, 120 gsm_hard items per arm at temperature zero. Fault cost is measured as re-derivability (grounded vs. blind inspector); controls include a registered kill test for tokens and a word-blanking manipulation holding word slots fixed; effect sizes with Holm-adjusted p-values and confidence intervals are reported. A comparison against a single direct call is also run with no fault injected.
AI.result: Grounding the inspector in the original problem yields +0.608 [+0.517, +0.700] to +0.358 over a blind inspector on four backbones, with the blind inspector changing no item on either Qwen backbone. Accuracy under fault rises on four of four backbones, from +0.233 to +0.392, largest Holm-adjusted p = 2.1×10⁻⁶. The kill test rules out tokens, and retention tracks visible fraction on four of four (0.221 to 0.692 on the primary). The interaction excludes zero on two of four backbones (registered pipeline), four of four (three-stage), three of four (full message history; primary +0.317). Llama-3.1-8B shows no detectable fault cost at any dose. With no fault, the registered pipeline loses to one direct call by -0.267, -0.125, -0.317, and +0.058 at p = 0.118 on Phi-4. The first re-grounded stage buys +0.394 matched retention for +59.8 tokens/item on Qwen3-14B; later stages buy nothing.
AI.conclusion: Re-derivability is the controlling variable for both fault cost and architecture cost. Fault repair is cheap and front-loaded: re-grounding the first downstream stage in the original problem recovers most retention, while subsequent stages add no benefit. No measured decomposition reliably outperforms a single direct call absent a fault.

title: Efficient World Action Model Inference with Adaptive Intermediate States
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) enable future-aware control by jointly modeling actions and environment dynamics. However, iterative diffusion or flow inference incurs substantial denoising latency. Prior inference state offers a natural opportunity for acceleration, yet changing planning contexts, observations, and intermediate representations can quickly render retained state stale. Preserving useful computation therefore requires adapting inference state rather than reusing it as-is. To this end, we present $\mathrm{WAM}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{ACHINE}}$, a training-free framework that accelerates WAM inference by preserving and adapting inference state for efficient and accurate continuation as the control loop evolves. Across closed-loop replans, Trajectory Remapping remaps replan state from the preceding replan to initialize the next replan, reducing redundant trajectory generation. Across denoising steps, Observation Rebinding performs anticipatory inference during action execution and rebinds retained denoising state to the real observation for continuation when consistency checks pass, reducing latency exposed to the control loop. Across Transformer layers, Residual Rescaling selectively rescales retained layer state and refreshes it through full computation of the middle layers when probe checks fail, reducing repeated Transformer computation. Evaluations of three representative WAM architectures on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 show that $\mathrm{WAM}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{ACHINE}}$ achieves 1.47-3.05$\times$ speedups in observation-to-action latency and 2.23-3.27$\times$ speedups in GPU inference time per replan, while preserving 96.69-99.54% of native WAM task success.

AI.tldr: WAMACHINE is a training-free framework that accelerates World Action Model inference by preserving and adapting inference state across replans, denoising steps, and Transformer layers, achieving up to 3.05x latency speedups while retaining ~97-99.5% of native task success.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) achieve future-aware control by jointly modeling actions and dynamics, but iterative diffusion or flow inference introduces substantial denoising latency. Prior inference state offers a chance to accelerate inference, yet shifting planning contexts, observations, and intermediate representations quickly render retained state stale, so state must be adapted rather than reused as-is.
AI.method: A training-free framework with three complementary mechanisms: (1) Trajectory Remapping, which remaps replan state from the preceding replan to initialize the next replan and cut redundant trajectory generation; (2) Observation Rebinding, which performs anticipatory inference during action execution and rebinds retained denoising state to the real observation upon passing consistency checks; (3) Residual Rescaling, which selectively rescales retained layer state and refreshes it via full computation of middle layers when probe checks fail.
AI.result: Evaluations of three representative WAM architectures on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 show 1.47-3.05x speedups in observation-to-action latency and 2.23-3.27x speedups in GPU inference time per replan, while preserving 96.69-99.54% of native WAM task success.
AI.conclusion: Adapting, rather than statically reusing, inference state is an effective training-free route to accelerating World Action Model inference, delivering substantial latency and GPU-time reductions with minimal loss in task success.

title: Nutri-ATLAS: Embodied Agent for Tabulated Lookup and Assistance for Smarter nutrition
summary: Generative and Agentic IoT systems offer a promising foundation for digital healthcare applications that combine sensing, personalized reasoning, and autonomous interaction in real-world environments. Nutrition assistance is a natural use case, but existing Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems are often limited to passive text interaction and static context, making them unreliable when food descriptions are ambiguous or nutritional evidence is missing. We propose Nutri-ATLAS, an Embodied Agent for Tabulated Lookup and Assistance for smarter nutrition in the real world. It integrates graph-grounded nutrition reasoning, hardware-aware LLM selection, and robot-based evidence acquisition. Nutri-ATLAS builds a unified Food-Nutrient knowledge graph from USDA FoodData Central and FoodKG and learns 64-dimensional GATv2 food and recipe embeddings. A shared hybrid graph-text scoring mechanism supports food nutrition extraction, nutritional gap filling, substitute retrieval, and recipe-level meal composition, while an LLM-guided skill interface navigates landmarks, updates dietary-context and food-accessibility memory, and grounds recommendations in observed food availability. We evaluate Nutri-ATLAS across nutrient estimation, substitution retrieval, recipe recommendation, patient-profile adherence, edge deployment, and real-world embodied execution. On HealthyFoodSubs, the hybrid retriever achieves 37.9% MAP, 80.7% RR@5, and 90.1% RR@10. On NutriBench v2, Dense+GAT retrieval grounds nutrient estimation across nine quantized Qwen3.5-9B configurations. On PFoodReQ, Nutri-ATLAS reaches 78.8% MAP, 83.0% MAR, and 77.5% F1. A patient-profile study shows adherence to allergy and healthy-target constraints for all selected cases.

AI.tldr: Nutri-ATLAS is an embodied, agentic IoT system for real-world nutrition assistance that unifies a Food-Nutrient knowledge graph, GATv2 embeddings, a hybrid graph-text retriever, hardware-aware LLM selection, and robot-based evidence acquisition to deliver grounded nutrient estimation, substitution retrieval, recipe recommendation, and personalized dietary adherence.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based nutrition systems are limited to passive text interaction and static context, making them unreliable when food descriptions are ambiguous or nutritional evidence is missing. There is a need for an embodied, generative-agentic IoT approach that combines sensing, personalized reasoning, and autonomous interaction to ground nutrition assistance in real-world observed availability.
AI.method: Nutri-ATLAS integrates (1) graph-grounded nutrition reasoning via a unified Food-Nutrient knowledge graph built from USDA FoodData Central and FoodKG, with learned 64-dimensional GATv2 food and recipe embeddings; (2) a shared hybrid graph-text scoring mechanism supporting nutrient extraction, nutritional gap filling, substitute retrieval, and recipe-level meal composition; (3) hardware-aware LLM selection for edge deployment; and (4) an LLM-guided skill interface that navigates landmarks, updates dietary-context and food-accessibility memory, and grounds recommendations in observed food availability, enabling robot-based evidence acquisition.
AI.result: Evaluated across nutrient estimation, substitution retrieval, recipe recommendation, patient-profile adherence, edge deployment, and real-world embodied execution. On HealthyFoodSubs, the hybrid retriever achieves 37.9% MAP, 80.7% RR@5, and 90.1% RR@10. On NutriBench v2, Dense+GAT retrieval grounds nutrient estimation across nine quantized Qwen3.5-9B configurations. On PFoodReQ, it reaches 78.8% MAP, 83.0% MAR, and 77.5% F1. A patient-profile study shows adherence to allergy and healthy-target constraints for all selected cases.
AI.conclusion: Nutri-ATLAS demonstrates that combining graph-grounded reasoning, hardware-aware LLM deployment, and embodied robot-based evidence acquisition yields reliable, personalized, and physically grounded nutrition assistance, addressing the ambiguity and missing-evidence limitations of passive LLM systems.

title: On the Numerical Reliability of Differentiable Physics-Based Optimization for Robotic Material Manipulation
comment: Accepted as an oral presentation at the IROS 2026 workshop: Deformable Objects Manipulation: Research Foundations, Reproducibility and Real-World Challenges
summary: Differentiable physics is increasingly used in robotic material manipulation for system identification, trajectory or skill optimization, demonstration generation, and robot or end-effector design. These applications depend on gradients propagated through long, contact-rich simulation rollouts. We study the numerical reliability of those gradients using two Material Point Method (MPM) system-identification benchmarks derived from elastoplastic and granular manipulation. The benchmarks provide controlled cases for three effects that also arise in broader differentiable physics-based optimization. GPU many-to-one sums whose order depends on thread scheduling changed long-horizon gradients and reversed the sign of one parameter gradient relative to a deterministic reference. Finite-difference checks became less reliable for longer rollouts because repeated-run loss variation grew much faster than the loss change produced by the tested parameter perturbations. Observation and loss definitions changed optimization behaviour and the solution preferred by an independent metric. These results motivate reproducible accumulation, finite-difference validation that compares perturbation-induced loss changes with repeated-run variation, and explicit reporting of objective construction when differentiable simulation is used for robotic optimization.

AI.tldr: Differentiable MPM simulators produce numerically unreliable long-horizon gradients: nondeterministic GPU parallel sums alter gradient signs, finite-difference checks degrade over long rollouts, and observation/loss choices shift the optimum.
AI.motivation: Differentiable physics underpins robotic material manipulation tasks such as system identification, skill/trajectory optimization, demonstration generation, and end-effector design, all of which rely on gradients backpropagated through long, contact-rich rollouts. The implicit assumption that these gradients are numerically trustworthy is rarely tested, motivating a study of their reliability.
AI.method: The authors design two MPM (Material Point Method) system-identification benchmarks drawn from elastoplastic and granular manipulation. These controlled benchmarks isolate three effects: (1) GPU many-to-one reduction sums whose order depends on thread scheduling, compared against a deterministic reference; (2) finite-difference gradient checks across rollout lengths, comparing perturbation-induced loss changes against repeated-run loss variation; (3) alternative observation and loss definitions, evaluated via optimization behavior and an independent quality metric.
AI.result: Thread-scheduling-dependent GPU reduction sums perturbed long-horizon gradients and even flipped the sign of one parameter gradient relative to the deterministic reference. Finite-difference checks lost reliability as rollout length grew, because repeated-run loss variance increased much faster than the loss change from tested parameter perturbations. Changing observation and loss definitions altered optimization behavior and the solution favored by an independent metric.
AI.conclusion: Gradients through long contact-rich differentiable simulations are not automatically reliable. The authors recommend reproducible (order-independent) accumulation, finite-difference validation that contrasts perturbation-induced loss changes with repeated-run variation, and explicit reporting of objective construction in differentiable-physics-based robotic optimization.

title: Decision-Sufficient State Representations: Measuring and Reducing Write-Time Regret
comment: 29 pages (10 main, 17 appendix), 12 figures (4 main, 8 appendix), 18 tables (2 main, 16 appendix)
summary: Long tasks produce more history than an LLM agent can hold in its context, and more than it uses reliably even when the history fits. A growing line of work therefore has agents carry a short written state instead: at every step a writer rewrites the state, and a reader acts from the state alone. Steps stay cheap, but anything the writer drops is lost before later decisions reveal that they need it. We quantify this loss and ask whether training can reduce it. Comparing the written state with the best state of the same size written in hindsight, we split the reader's loss into a budget loss, which any state of that size must incur, and a write-time regret, which comes from the writer's choices. In TextWorld cooking games where we control how long a fact must be carried before it is needed, a 128-token state holding the facts wins nearly every game, while prompted language-model writers win at most 17%. Almost all of the loss is write-time regret, and it grows with the delay. We then train the writer from the reader's own loss. DSSR (decision-sufficient state representations) scores candidate states by how well the reader acts after the writer carries them forward, and teaches the writer to prefer the better ones. This forward-rolled score predicts game outcomes ($ρ= 0.48$), whereas scoring a candidate as a fixed context, as hindsight methods usually do, does not ($ρ\leq 0.07$). On a pre-registered test split opened once, training adds +7.0 [+1.9, +12.2] points of success when facts are needed soon, bringing a plain summary writer to the level of belief- and slot-based memory prompts. The gain shrinks as the delay grows and is significant only at the shortest delay. We trace this limit to credit assignment: keeping a fact now pays off only if every later rewrite keeps it too, which a per-step score cannot see.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies information loss in short written-state agent memory, decomposes it into budget loss and write-time regret, and proposes DSSR, which trains the writer by forward-rolling the reader's loss, yielding gains at short delays but limited improvement as delay grows.
AI.motivation: Long tasks exceed an LLM agent's usable context, so agents increasingly carry a short written state rewritten each step. This keeps steps cheap but risks discarding facts that later decisions need. The authors aim to quantify this loss and test whether training the writer can reduce it.
AI.method: Using TextWorld cooking games with controlled fact-carrying delays, they compare the written state against the best same-size hindsight state, decomposing reader loss into budget loss (unavoidable at that size) and write-time regret (writer's fault). They propose DSSR, which scores candidate states by how well the reader acts after the writer carries them forward, training the writer to prefer better candidates.
AI.result: A 128-token oracle state wins nearly every game, while prompted LM writers win at most 17%; almost all loss is write-time regret growing with delay. DSSR's forward-rolled score predicts outcomes (ρ=0.48) whereas fixed-context scoring does not (ρ≤0.07). On a pre-registered test split, training adds +7.0 [+1.9, +12.2] points when facts are needed soon, matching belief- and slot-based memory prompts, but the gain shrinks with delay.
AI.conclusion: Write-time regret dominates the loss in short-state agent memory and grows with delay. Forward-rolled scoring (DSSR) effectively reduces it at short delays, but gains fade as delay increases, a limit traced to credit assignment: retaining a fact pays off only if every later rewrite also keeps it, which per-step scores cannot capture.

title: HOI-Retarget: Contact-Centric Retargeting for Human-Object Interaction
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to ICRA. Website: http://shinben0327.github.io/hoi-retarget
summary: Learning from demonstration (LfD) has enabled humanoid robots to acquire diverse whole-body skills, but extending this paradigm to human-object interaction (HOI) is limited by the availability of robot-compatible interaction references. We present HOI-Retarget, a contact-centric retargeting method that transfers HOI onto a humanoid robot for large-scale motion-data generation. Its windowed trajectory optimization uses every labeled contact as a target in the object frame, balancing body tracking, foot support and smoothness under the robot's kinematic limits. The method can augment a single demonstration across object sizes, absorb contacts reconstructed from monocular video, and extend to several robots manipulating one object. We publicly release the code and the retargeted motion dataset.

AI.tldr: HOI-Retarget is a contact-centric retargeting method that transfers human-object interaction onto humanoid robots via windowed trajectory optimization, enabling large-scale motion-data generation.
AI.motivation: Learning from demonstration has given humanoid robots diverse whole-body skills, but extending it to human-object interaction is bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot-compatible interaction references.
AI.method: A contact-centric retargeting method with windowed trajectory optimization: each labeled contact is treated as a target in the object frame, jointly balancing body tracking, foot support, and smoothness under the robot's kinematic limits.
AI.result: The method augments a single demonstration across object sizes, absorbs contacts reconstructed from monocular video, and extends to multiple robots manipulating a single object. Code and the retargeted motion dataset are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: HOI-Retarget provides a scalable, contact-centric pipeline for generating robot-compatible human-object interaction motion data, broadening LfD applicability to humanoid HOI.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Counterfactual Fragility and Demographic Bias in Clinical Evaluation of LLMs
summary: Clinical LLM evaluation often emphasizes answer accuracy; however, accuracy alone does not test counterfactual consistency or demographic robustness. We evaluated six LLMs on 150 MedQA USMLE questions using two automated perturbation tests to assess their performance. The counterfactual validity (CFV) test asked each model to make a minimal, plausible clinical change that would make a different answer correct. The demographic robustness test added six demographic prefixes to the same vignette and compared the answers and explanations with a no demographic baseline. Of the 900 CFV attempts, 228 (25.3 %) were valid and 672 were invalid. Across 5,400 demographic comparisons, 1,097 answers were changed (20.3%). Automated judging identified 3,128 stereotype evidence flags, including 1,932 in the broad Other category. MedGemma 27B achieved the highest accuracy (87.1%) and CFV (63.3%), lowest answer change rate (16.0%), and low mean Explanation Demographic Dissonance (EDD) score (0.169). However, its accuracy still exceeded its CFV, indicating that correct answers do not guarantee reliable performance on the counterfactual validity task. OpenBioLLM had the highest answer change rate and EDD, whereas GLM had the highest stereotype flag rate. These findings show that accuracy, CFV, answer stability, EDD, and stereotype evidence capture different evaluation aspects. Because all judgments were automated and no clinician validation was available, the results support safety screening but do not establish clinical deployability of the model.

AI.tldr: Six LLMs were evaluated on 150 MedQA USMLE questions using automated counterfactual validity (CFV) and demographic robustness perturbation tests, revealing that accuracy alone fails to capture counterfactual consistency or demographic robustness. MedGemma 27B led on accuracy (87.1%) and CFV (63.3%), yet its accuracy still exceeded its CFV. Findings support safety screening only, not clinical deployability, given the absence of clinician validation.
AI.motivation: Clinical LLM evaluation predominantly emphasizes answer accuracy, but accuracy alone does not test counterfactual consistency or demographic robustness. The authors argue that these additional dimensions are necessary to characterize model behavior, motivating a multi-axis perturbation-based evaluation.
AI.method: Six LLMs were assessed on 150 MedQA USMLE questions via two automated perturbation tests. The counterfactual validity (CFV) test required each model to make a minimal, plausible clinical change rendering a different answer correct. The demographic robustness test appended six demographic prefixes to the same vignette and compared answers and explanations against a no-demographic baseline. Automated judging provided stereotype evidence flags, answer change rates, and Explanation Demographic Dissonance (EDD) scores.
AI.result: Of 900 CFV attempts, 228 (25.3%) were valid and 672 invalid. Across 5,400 demographic comparisons, 1,097 answers changed (20.3%), and automated judging flagged 3,128 stereotype evidence instances, including 1,932 in the broad Other category. MedGemma 27B showed the highest accuracy (87.1%) and CFV (63.3%), lowest answer change rate (16.0%), and low mean EDD (0.169), though its accuracy exceeded its CFV. OpenBioLLM had the highest answer change rate and EDD, while GLM had the highest stereotype flag rate.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy, CFV, answer stability, EDD, and stereotype evidence capture distinct evaluation aspects, so no single metric suffices. Because all judgments were automated with no clinician validation, the results support safety screening but do not establish clinical deployability of the models.

title: Natural State-Prediction Accuracy can Hide Weak Controlled Responsiveness in VLA Readouts
summary: Accurately decoding object states from the internal representations of vision-language-action (VLA) models does not establish that the predictions respond faithfully to changes in the target physical state. In natural observations, object state, robot configuration, occlusion, and task progress vary together, allowing contextual cues to contribute to prediction. In this paper, we introduce an evaluation framework that separates prediction accuracy, target-state responsiveness, and context stability using physically validated observations that cross target coordinates with robot contexts. We demonstrate that high natural-trajectory accuracy can coexist with weak controlled target-state responsiveness in fixed representation-readout pairs. Comparisons and interventions involving representations, readouts, and training data show that the three properties provide distinct diagnostic information. Furthermore, adding responsiveness and context sensitivity to a failure predictor based on initial state error and physical variables reduces policy-failure prediction error on new initializations relative to the specified baseline while same-observation controlled MAE is also informative. These findings motivate evaluating target-state responsiveness and context stability alongside natural prediction accuracy, and examining their relationship to actual policy behavior and task outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an evaluation framework for vision-language-action (VLA) models that disentangles prediction accuracy, target-state responsiveness, and context stability using physically validated observations crossing target coordinates with robot contexts, showing high natural-trajectory accuracy can mask weak controlled target-state responsiveness.
AI.motivation: Accurately decoding object states from VLA internal representations does not guarantee the predictions genuinely respond to changes in the target physical state. In natural observations, object state, robot configuration, occlusion, and task progress co-vary, so contextual cues can drive predictions instead of the actual target state—creating a need to separate genuine responsiveness from contextual shortcuts.
AI.method: The authors propose an evaluation framework that separates three properties—prediction accuracy, target-state responsiveness, and context stability—using physically validated observations that cross target coordinates with robot contexts. They compare and intervene on representations, readouts, and training data, and incorporate responsiveness and context sensitivity into a failure predictor built on initial state error and physical variables.
AI.result: High natural-trajectory accuracy can coexist with weak controlled target-state responsiveness in fixed representation-readout pairs. The three properties yield distinct diagnostic information. Adding responsiveness and context sensitivity to a failure predictor reduces policy-failure prediction error on new initializations relative to the baseline, while same-observation controlled MAE is also informative.
AI.conclusion: Target-state responsiveness and context stability should be evaluated alongside natural prediction accuracy, and their relationship to actual policy behavior and task outcomes should be examined. Natural accuracy alone is an insufficient diagnostic for faithful state decoding in VLA models.

title: Overwhelmed by Choice: Studying LLM Decision Making at Scale
comment: Accepted at TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?, NeurIPS 2026 Workshop. 23 pages
summary: Multiple-choice and candidate-selection evaluations are widely used to assess LLM reasoning and decision-making, yet most benchmarks contain relatively small candidate sets. It remains unclear whether conclusions drawn from these settings remain valid as the candidate space scales. We systematically evaluate LLMs as the number of competing candidates increases and find substantial accuracy degradation across tasks, prompting strategies, and model scales. Controlled analyses show that standard long-context retrieval explanations cannot fully account for this degradation. Instead, we identify two systematic failure patterns. First, gold-margin collapse: the score gap between the correct answer and the strongest distractor progressively shrinks, driven primarily by weakening confidence in the correct answer. Second, earlier candidate preferences become increasingly difficult to overturn, with later candidates exerting progressively weaker influence on the final prediction. Motivated by these findings, we evaluate hierarchical partitioning and permutation-based inference, which improve accuracy by roughly 20 percentage points at $N=160$ on both HotpotQA and MIMIC. Overall, our results identify candidate-set scale as an important evaluation-protocol variable and show that strong small-option performance does not necessarily imply robust large-scale candidate comparison.

AI.tldr: As the number of competing candidates grows, LLM accuracy degrades substantially across tasks, strategies, and model scales—not fully explained by long-context retrieval limits—due to gold-margin collapse and entrenched early-candidate preferences; hierarchical partitioning and permutation-based inference recover ~20 points at N=160.
AI.motivation: Multiple-choice and candidate-selection benchmarks typically use small candidate sets, so it is unclear whether their conclusions hold when the candidate space scales. The paper treats candidate-set size as an evaluation-protocol variable worth systematic study.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of LLMs with increasing numbers of competing candidates across tasks, prompting strategies, and model scales. Controlled analyses test standard long-context retrieval explanations, then identify two failure patterns: gold-margin collapse and hardening earlier-candidate preferences. Two mitigations are evaluated: hierarchical partitioning and permutation-based inference (tested on HotpotQA and MIMIC).
AI.result: Substantial accuracy degradation as candidate count increases. Standard long-context retrieval explanations cannot fully account for it. Gold-margin collapse: correct-vs-strongest-distractor score gap shrinks, driven mainly by weakening confidence in the correct answer. Later candidates exert progressively weaker influence, making earlier preferences hard to overturn. Hierarchical partitioning and permutation-based inference improve accuracy by roughly 20 percentage points at N=160 on both HotpotQA and MIMIC.
AI.conclusion: Candidate-set scale is an important evaluation-protocol variable. Strong performance with small option sets does not imply robust large-scale candidate comparison; mitigation strategies can substantially recover accuracy at large candidate counts.

title: Sufficiency of Zeroth-Order Reward Shaping for Policy Gradient in Stabilization Control
summary: Reward shaping is fundamental to modern robotic control with deep reinforcement learning (RL), yet practitioners still rely heavily on heuristic principles borrowed from classical optimal control and trajectory optimization.
