summary: Robot-aided operations in space stations are essential for reducing the workload of astronauts and improving the efficiency of on-orbit activities. Multi-limbed intra-vehicular robots (MLIVRs) equipped with grappling end-effectors have emerged as a promising solution, as they can securely grasp pre-existing interfaces, such as handrails and seat tracks, thereby enabling stable locomotion and forceful manipulation in microgravity environments. Since graspable locations on these interfaces are spatially limited and discretely distributed, motion planning for MLIVRs must be addressed jointly with foothold planning. This paper presents a simultaneous path and foothold planning framework based on graph theory for MLIVRs. The proposed method efficiently searches for feasible stance sequences for a multi-limbed robot while satisfying manipulability constraints. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated through simulations in a 3D model of the International Space Station (ISS) cabin, demonstrating its capability to generate feasible and efficient locomotion plans in realistic intra-vehicular environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a graph-theoretic framework for simultaneous path and foothold planning of multi-limbed intra-vehicular robots (MLIVRs) in space stations, validated via simulations in a 3D ISS cabin model.
AI.motivation: Robot-aided operations in space stations can reduce astronaut workload and improve on-orbit efficiency. MLIVRs with grappling end-effectors can grasp existing interfaces (handrails, seat tracks) for stable locomotion and forceful manipulation in microgravity. However, graspable locations are spatially limited and discretely distributed, so motion planning must be solved jointly with foothold planning.
AI.method: A simultaneous path and foothold planning framework based on graph theory. It efficiently searches for feasible stance sequences for a multi-limbed robot while satisfying manipulability constraints.
AI.result: Simulations in a 3D model of the International Space Station (ISS) cabin demonstrate the framework's capability to generate feasible and efficient locomotion plans in realistic intra-vehicular environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed graph-theoretic framework enables effective joint path and foothold planning for MLIVRs, yielding feasible and efficient locomotion plans in realistic intra-vehicular space station environments.

title: Planner-as-Router: Joint Plan-Time Model Routing for Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Workflows
comment: Accepted at AIxSET 2026. 8 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Data and Code in github: https://github.com/vsingh45/par-entbench
summary: Running large language model (LLM) agents in production gets expensive fast. A frontier model (the largest, most capable tier) is accurate but can cost 25 times what a small model costs per token, and the gap compounds once a workflow chains several calls together. Planner-as-Router (PaR) attacks this from a different angle. Instead of leaving model-tier selection to some component downstream, it folds the choice into planning itself. As the planner breaks a query into subtasks, it also assigns each one a model size tier (small, mid, or frontier, ordered by capability and price), so the dependencies between subtasks are visible before any specialist runs. Unlike per-call routers such as cascade routing, which look at one node at a time, PaR sees the whole workflow up front and needs no separate router model or training data. We evaluate PaR with EntBench, a benchmark of 54 enterprise agentic tasks across seven classes, graded by actually running the generated Structured Query Language (SQL) and MongoDB queries against live databases. Over 1,157 evaluations spanning eight routers and three seeds, PaR stays on the observed cost-accuracy frontier. It matches a sink-frontier heuristic (frontier model on terminal nodes only) in accuracy at comparable cost and a faithful FrugalGPT cascade at lower cost, and cuts cost 44% against all-frontier routing while giving up 2.9 points of accuracy. Several accuracy gaps fall inside the plus-or-minus six-point confidence interval of a 54-task study, so we frame PaR's advantage as frontier position rather than a clean accuracy win. We also report a preliminary observation, not a validated result: a small pilot hints that cheap routing may carry a hidden compounding penalty on compositional workflows, which we frame as a hypothesis for future measurement. PaR, EntBench, and all evaluation code are open source.

AI.tldr: Planner-as-Router (PaR) folds model-tier selection into the planning step, letting the planner assign each subtask a capability/price tier (small, mid, frontier) while decomposing a query. Evaluated on EntBench (54 enterprise agentic tasks, graded by executing generated SQL/MongoDB against live databases), PaR stays on the observed cost-accuracy frontier, matching a sink-frontier heuristic in accuracy at comparable cost and a faithful FrugalGPT cascade at lower cost, cutting cost 44% versus all-frontier routing for a 2.9-point accuracy drop.
AI.motivation: Running LLM agents in production is expensive: frontier models cost up to 25x more per token than small models, and this gap compounds across chained workflow calls. Existing per-call routers (e.g., cascade routing) decide model tier node-by-node, lacking visibility into the whole workflow and often requiring a separate router model or training data.
AI.method: PaR integrates tier selection into planning rather than delegating it downstream: as the planner decomposes a query into subtasks, it assigns each subtask a model size tier (small, mid, or frontier, ordered by capability and price), exposing subtask dependencies before any specialist runs. This enables workflow-level routing without a dedicated router model or training data. Evaluation uses EntBench, 54 enterprise agentic tasks across seven classes, graded by executing generated SQL and MongoDB queries against live databases, across 1,157 evaluations, eight routers, and three seeds.
AI.result: PaR stays on the observed cost-accuracy frontier: it matches a sink-frontier heuristic (frontier model on terminal nodes only) in accuracy at comparable cost, beats a faithful FrugalGPT cascade in cost, and cuts cost by 44% versus all-frontier routing while sacrificing 2.9 points of accuracy. Some accuracy gaps fall within the ±6-point confidence interval of a 54-task study, so the authors frame PaR's benefit as frontier position rather than a clean accuracy win. A preliminary, non-validated pilot hints at a possible hidden compounding penalty for cheap routing on compositional workflows, framed as a hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: PaR demonstrates that co-designing planning and model-tier routing can keep agentic workflows on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier with no router model or training data. The authors modestly position the contribution as frontier position rather than accuracy dominance, flag a hypothesis about compounding penalties of cheap routing on compositional workflows, and release PaR, EntBench, and all evaluation code as open source.

title: Learning to Act under Visual Interruptions with Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, but they are typically developed and evaluated with all camera streams available throughout task execution. When a camera stops delivering frames during task execution, the policy must continue acting without access to subsequent observations from the missing view. Despite its practical importance, how such interruptions affect closed-loop manipulation remains insufficiently understood. To investigate this problem, we introduce MAIL-Bench, a benchmark that evaluates visual interruptions with VLA models. By interrupting different cameras at multiple stages of each policy's successful reference trajectory, MAIL-Bench measures how well policies retain their capabilities when visual inputs become unavailable. Building on this benchmark, we propose MINT, which first trains VLA policies to remain functional under missing visual inputs. At inference time, MINT selectively supplements missing observations using optical-flow extrapolation or an action-conditioned world model, and withdraws predicted views when they become unreliable. Experiments on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 show that MINT significantly improves task success under camera loss over the original models. Experiments on AgiBot G2 further demonstrate the real-robot deployment under camera loss. The benchmark is available at https://minglejiang.github.io/Mail-Bench/

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MAIL-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating VLA models under camera-stream interruptions during manipulation, and proposes MINT, a method that trains policies to remain functional with missing visual inputs and selectively supplements those inputs at inference via optical-flow extrapolation or an action-conditioned world model.
AI.motivation: VLA models are typically developed and evaluated with all camera streams available throughout task execution, so it remains insufficiently understood how camera interruptions—when a view stops delivering frames—affect closed-loop manipulation, despite the practical importance of this scenario.
AI.method: MAIL-Bench interrupts different cameras at multiple stages of each policy's successful reference trajectory to measure capability retention when visual inputs become unavailable. MINT trains VLA policies to remain functional under missing visual inputs, and at inference time selectively supplements missing observations using optical-flow extrapolation or an action-conditioned world model, withdrawing predicted views when they become unreliable.
AI.result: Experiments on π0.5 and GR00T N1.5 show that MINT significantly improves task success under camera loss over the original models. Experiments on AgiBot G2 further demonstrate real-robot deployment under camera loss.
AI.conclusion: The work provides both a benchmark (MAIL-Bench) for studying visual interruptions in VLA-based manipulation and a method (MINT) that improves robustness to missing camera streams, validated in simulation and on real robots.

title: Precision As You Need: Stochastic Computing Is a Dense Adaptive Quantizer
summary: Matrix multiplications dominate the inference cost of modern transformer-based vision models, yet existing efficiency techniques such as post-training quantization and mixed-precision inference are largely limited to the small set of fixed-width formats (INT4, INT8, BF16, and FP16) supported by conventional accelerators. We revisit stochastic computing (SC) as a way to lift this constraint: viewed as a dense adaptive quantizer, SC controls precision by bit-stream length L rather than a fixed datapath, while each multiplication reduces to a single AND/XNOR gate. We build a GPU library that emulates SC matrix multiplication at scale, exposes stream lengths as first-class kernel arguments, and evaluates SC end-to-end on image classification, object detection and instance segmentation, class-conditional image generation, and visual world-model planning. On top of this substrate, we develop a dynamic per-row mixed-precision policy that assigns stream length per token or group at matched average budget, requires no retraining, and uses the same SC hardware across schedules. Across tasks, SC remains competitive with fixed-format INT quantization at matched bit budgets, while per-row mixed precision helps maintain accuracy at lower average stream lengths. These results provide software-level feasibility evidence that SC can serve as a dense-precision substrate for fine-grained mixed-precision inference on modern vision transformers.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits stochastic computing (SC) as a flexible precision substrate for transformer-based vision models, building a GPU library that emulates SC matrix multiplication and evaluating a dynamic per-row mixed-precision policy across multiple vision tasks.
AI.motivation: Matrix multiplications dominate inference cost in modern transformer-based vision models, but existing efficiency techniques (post-training quantization, mixed-precision inference) are restricted to a small set of fixed-width formats (INT4, INT8, BF16, FP16) supported by conventional accelerators. This limits precision flexibility.
AI.method: The authors treat SC as a dense adaptive quantizer controlling precision via bit-stream length L instead of a fixed datapath, with each multiplication reduced to a single AND/XNOR gate. They build a GPU library that emulates SC matrix multiplication at scale and exposes stream lengths as first-class kernel arguments. On this substrate, they develop a dynamic per-row mixed-precision policy assigning stream length per token or group at a matched average budget, requiring no retraining and using the same SC hardware across schedules.
AI.result: End-to-end evaluation covers image classification, object detection and instance segmentation, class-conditional image generation, and visual world-model planning. Across tasks, SC remains competitive with fixed-format INT quantization at matched bit budgets, while per-row mixed precision helps maintain accuracy at lower average stream lengths.
AI.conclusion: The results provide software-level feasibility evidence that SC can serve as a dense-precision substrate for fine-grained mixed-precision inference on modern vision transformers.

title: Do Not Cut When Uncertain: Rejectable and Calibrated Decision Heads for VLA Policies in Robotic Harvesting
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained with behavior cloning or flow matching are optimized to output an action trajectory, but they cannot express "I don't know" or "I should not act." In robotic harvesting, occlusion makes single-frame decisions fundamentally ambiguous: identical pixels can correspond either to a cuttable stem or to no stem at all. Existing VLAs are forced to commit, leading to high-confidence errors with irreversible consequences. We argue that the failure mode of a VLA is determined not by backbone scale but by its output interface. We propose Rejectable and Calibrated Decision Heads (RCDH), a typed, rejectable, and calibrated output interface that can be attached to a frozen VLA backbone without retraining or new features. RCDH introduces (i) a decision schema with explicit rejection and ordered, conditional decomposition, and (ii) a calibration procedure for risk-aware abstention. We evaluate RCDH on a robotic harvesting platform with controllable leaf occlusion, comparing generative, enumerated, calibrated, and rejectable interfaces. We show that replacing only the output head restores out-of-distribution usability under occlusion while preserving in-distribution performance. We further test whether the ordering of the rejection space is critical. Our results suggest that the right to refuse, rather than a larger model, is the missing interface for reliable manipulation under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: RCDH is a typed, rejectable, calibrated output head attached to a frozen VLA backbone without retraining, enabling risk-aware abstention that restores out-of-distribution usability under occlusion while preserving in-distribution performance in robotic harvesting.
AI.motivation: VLA policies trained with behavior cloning or flow matching output action trajectories but cannot express "I don't know" or "I should not act." In robotic harvesting, occlusion makes single-frame decisions fundamentally ambiguous—identical pixels may correspond to a cuttable stem or to no stem at all. Existing VLAs are forced to commit, causing high-confidence errors with irreversible consequences. The authors argue the failure mode of a VLA is determined not by backbone scale but by its output interface.
AI.method: Propose Rejectable and Calibrated Decision Heads (RCDH), a typed, rejectable, calibrated output interface attachable to a frozen VLA backbone without retraining or new features. RCDH introduces (i) a decision schema with explicit rejection and ordered, conditional decomposition, and (ii) a calibration procedure for risk-aware abstention. Evaluated on a robotic harvesting platform with controllable leaf occlusion, comparing generative, enumerated, calibrated, and rejectable interfaces; also tests whether the ordering of the rejection space is critical.
AI.result: Replacing only the output head restores out-of-distribution usability under occlusion while preserving in-distribution performance. Results suggest the right to refuse, rather than a larger model, is the missing interface for reliable manipulation under uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The failure mode of a VLA is determined by its output interface, not backbone scale. A rejectable, calibrated output head—rather than a larger model—provides the missing interface for reliable manipulation under uncertainty.

title: TRACE: Learning to Self-Calibrate Wireless Digital Twins from ISAC Measurements
summary: Wireless digital twins (DTs) rely on 3D environment models to predict radio propagation and support wireless-network decisions, yet these models are often initialized from imperfect 3D maps. Errors in building position, height, footprint, and orientation can therefore cause a high-fidelity propagation engine to simulate the wrong physical environment. In this paper, we study how a deployed wireless network can repair an existing DT using its own radio frequency (RF) measurements. In particular, we introduce Twin Residual Alignment and Calibration Engine (TRACE), a physics-grounded learning-based self-calibration framework that treats twin maintenance as residual alignment between the physical world and the current DT. Using the same sensing configuration as the physical measurements, TRACE ray-traces the current DT, coherently backprojects the measured and simulated RF onto a common world grid, and extracts the same local region around each building's current DT position. A multi-view corrector then fuses evidence across sensing nodes and neighboring buildings to predict a gated six-parameter correction per building, without relying on absolute layout or sensor ordering, and supports iterative correction through re-rendering. On 5,400 held-out samples from unseen simulated scenes at 28 GHz, TRACE reduces 3D position RMSE from 2.202 m to 0.302 m and yaw RMSE from 4.978° to 0.894°, outperforming ViT and U-Net baselines under changes in layout, building count, sensing-node count, and SNR. On measured 28 GHz RF data from the NIST outdoor courtyard, a model trained only on synthetic RF reduces mean planar wall-position error from 1.00 m to 7.8 cm, without measured-data fine-tuning or geometric labels. These results show that the discrepancy between measured and twin-rendered RF can serve as a learning signal for repairing a wireless DT.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a physics-grounded, learning-based self-calibration framework that repairs imperfect 3D wireless digital twins by aligning measured RF against ray-traced twin renders, predicting per-building 6-parameter corrections.
AI.motivation: Wireless digital twins rely on 3D environment models to predict radio propagation, but these models are often initialized from imperfect 3D maps. Errors in building position, height, footprint, and orientation cause even a high-fidelity propagation engine to simulate the wrong physical environment. The paper asks how a deployed wireless network can repair an existing DT using its own RF measurements.
AI.method: TRACE treats twin maintenance as residual alignment between the physical world and the current DT. Using the same sensing configuration as the physical measurements, it ray-traces the current DT, coherently backprojects measured and simulated RF onto a common world grid, and extracts identical local regions around each building's current DT position. A multi-view corrector fuses evidence across sensing nodes and neighboring buildings to predict a gated six-parameter correction per building, avoiding reliance on absolute layout or sensor ordering, and supports iterative correction via re-rendering.
AI.result: On 5,400 held-out samples from unseen simulated scenes at 28 GHz, TRACE reduces 3D position RMSE from 2.202 m to 0.302 m and yaw RMSE from 4.978° to 0.894°, outperforming ViT and U-Net baselines under changes in layout, building count, sensing-node count, and SNR. On measured 28 GHz RF data from the NIST outdoor courtyard, a model trained only on synthetic RF reduces mean planar wall-position error from 1.00 m to 7.8 cm, without measured-data fine-tuning or geometric labels.
AI.conclusion: The discrepancy between measured and twin-rendered RF can serve as an effective learning signal for repairing a wireless digital twin, enabling accurate self-calibration that generalizes from simulation to real measured data.

title: EMPIRIC: Experiment-Driven Learning of Residual World Models for Robot Planning
comment: The last two authors contributed equally as co-advisors. Website and code: https://yichao-liang.github.io/empiric
summary: A robot should be able to learn through experiments how unfamiliar objects behave and interact, then plan with that knowledge. It need not start from scratch: physics engines supply knowledge of motion and contact, but can omit entire mechanisms, such as glue curing, water heating, or wind. We present EMPIRIC, an agent that learns a residual world model: a physics engine extended with code for the missing mechanisms. The learned programs can introduce new forces, constraints, and hidden state, and Bayesian inference estimates their parameters and states from noisy observations. The resulting model lets the agent predict the outcomes of actions, choose informative experiments, and revise its hypotheses when predictions fail. Across five simulated domains, EMPIRIC learns interpretable, reusable models, and solves more tasks with fewer environment interactions than all three baselines. On a physical robot, it learns wind forces and domino masses to solve a manipulation task. Website and code: https://yichao-liang.github.io/empiric

AI.tldr: EMPIRIC learns a residual world model by extending a physics engine with learned code for missing mechanisms, using Bayesian inference over programs, parameters, and hidden states to predict, experiment, and revise.
AI.motivation: Robots should learn how unfamiliar objects behave through experiments, but starting from scratch is inefficient. Physics engines provide motion and contact knowledge yet often omit entire mechanisms (e.g., glue curing, water heating, wind), leaving gaps the agent must fill.
AI.method: EMPIRIC learns a residual world model: a physics engine augmented with learned code implementing missing mechanisms. The learned programs introduce new forces, constraints, and hidden state, while Bayesian inference estimates their parameters and states from noisy observations.
AI.result: Across five simulated domains, EMPIRIC learns interpretable, reusable models and solves more tasks with fewer environment interactions than all three baselines. On a physical robot, it learns wind forces and domino masses to solve a manipulation task.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting a physics engine with learned residual mechanism programs enables sample-efficient, interpretable, reusable robot learning and transfers to real-world manipulation.

title: Diagnosing Sampled LLM Reasoning in Formal Geometry: Coverage, Realization, and Validity Evidence
summary: Repeated sampling can reveal a correct numerical answer without yielding either a reliable system output or a supported derivation. We present Coverage, Realization, and Validity Evidence (CRV), an evaluation protocol for sampled large language model (LLM) reasoning over formal geometry states. Coverage is answer availability, realization is readout accuracy on the frozen candidate pool, and validity evidence is a label-blinded critic judgment of derivational support rather than a proof certificate. CRV freezes each candidate pool before comparing readouts and analyzes covered failures by correct-answer multiplicity and within-problem discrimination. On HardShift441, a 441-problem set for which a reference solver leaves 406 problems unsolved, a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-7B generator obtains 24.2% average single-sample accuracy and 68.9% pass@16, whereas verifier-weighted self-consistency (WSC) reaches 38.0%. Readout accuracy is particularly low when the correct answer occurs only once or twice in the pool. In a separate constructed audit of 195 covered problems, the critic labels 12 correct-answer representatives as supported, 181 as refuted, and two as uncertain. These results show that coverage, realization, and validity evidence from the critic are distinct quantities and should be reported separately.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CRV (Coverage, Realization, Validity Evidence), a protocol for evaluating sampled LLM reasoning over formal geometry states that separates answer availability, readout accuracy, and derivational support, showing these three quantities are distinct and should be reported separately.
AI.motivation: Repeated sampling can surface a correct numerical answer without a reliable system output or a supported derivation, conflating correctness with genuine reasoning capability. Standard metrics like pass@k and self-consistency obscure this distinction, so there is a need for an evaluation protocol that disentangles answer availability, readout accuracy, and derivational validity.
AI.method: CRV comprises three measures: Coverage (answer availability), Realization (readout accuracy on a frozen candidate pool), and Validity Evidence (a label-blinded critic judgment of derivational support rather than a proof certificate). Each candidate pool is frozen before comparing readouts, and covered failures are analyzed by correct-answer multiplicity and within-problem discrimination. Evaluation uses HardShift441, a 441-problem set where a reference solver leaves 406 problems unsolved, with a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-7B generator and verifier-weighted self-consistency (WSC). A separate constructed audit of 195 covered problems is judged by the critic.
AI.result: On HardShift441, the LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-7B generator achieves 24.2% average single-sample accuracy and 68.9% pass@16, while WSC reaches 38.0%. Readout accuracy is especially low when the correct answer appears only once or twice in the pool. In the audit of 195 covered problems, the critic labels 12 correct-answer representatives as supported, 181 as refuted, and two as uncertain.
AI.conclusion: Coverage, realization, and validity evidence from the critic are distinct quantities and should be reported separately. High pass@k can coexist with low readout accuracy and weak derivational support, so evaluation of sampled LLM reasoning must not conflate these dimensions.

title: QuadHand: A Compact Quadrotor Aerial Manipulator with MRC-SDF-Based Whole-Body Motion Planning
summary: Uncrewed aerial manipulators (UAMs) integrate robotic arms with aerial platforms for three-dimensional physical interaction. However, enlarging the workspace increases arm-induced disturbances, while existing geometric representations face a trade-off between geometric fidelity and computational efficiency in close-proximity interaction. This paper presents QuadHand, a compact quadrotor aerial manipulator with a 3-DoF arm, gripper, and battery-assisted passive CoG compensation module to reduce dominant arm-induced disturbances. We further propose MRC-SDF, a Multi-articulated Robot-Centric Signed Distance Field that preserves fine geometric detail with tractable computation, and a spatiotemporal whole-body trajectory optimization framework that jointly optimizes the quadrotor and manipulator for safe and executable trajectory generation. Simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate safe and executable aerial manipulation in complex environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes QuadHand, a compact quadrotor aerial manipulator with CoG compensation and a novel MRC-SDF representation for safe, efficient whole-body trajectory optimization in complex environments.
AI.motivation: Uncrewed aerial manipulators (UAMs) enable 3D physical interaction, but enlarging the workspace intensifies arm-induced disturbances. Meanwhile, existing geometric representations struggle to balance geometric fidelity and computational efficiency during close-proximity interaction.
AI.method: The authors design QuadHand, a compact quadrotor with a 3-DoF arm, a gripper, and a battery-assisted passive CoG compensation module. They introduce MRC-SDF (Multi-articulated Robot-Centric Signed Distance Field) to preserve fine geometric detail at tractable cost, and develop a spatiotemporal whole-body trajectory optimization framework that jointly optimizes the quadrotor and manipulator.
AI.result: Simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate safe and executable aerial manipulation in complex environments.
AI.conclusion: Integrating passive CoG compensation with an efficient robot-centric SDF and joint whole-body optimization enables safe, executable aerial manipulation, validating the proposed platform and framework.

title: The Commit-Abstain Circuit: Why Language Models Hallucinate Instead of Abstaining
summary: Language models (LMs) often hallucinate by committing to confident answers rather than abstaining, even when they do not have enough information to answer reliably. A large body of existing work mitigates hallucination through detection or abstention mechanisms, but leaves open how models internally arrive at the decision to commit or abstain in the first place. We study this decision through mechanistic analysis, framing hallucination as unsupported commitment: the model commits despite exhibiting signals of unanswerability. Using causal gating, we identify a Commit-Abstain Circuit (CAC), a sparse, causally localised subset of attention heads and MLP sublayers underlying this decision. Across ten LMs (3B-14B) from five families and three benchmarks, the CAC exhibits a recurring accumulate-yet-undercorrect pattern: commitment-promoting components build up commitment in earlier layers, while abstention-promoting components act later as corrective signals that are often insufficient to overturn the accumulated commitment. Building on this finding, a lightweight policy trained on CAC activations improves decision accuracy by 12.2 points over the model's intrinsic commit-abstain margin, reduces false abstentions by 2.5 times, transfers to unseen benchmarks, and extends to larger models (27B-35B). The CAC is both diagnostic, clarifying how models overcommit, and practical, enabling improved abstention decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper mechanistically analyzes how LMs decide to commit or abstain, identifying a sparse Commit-Abstain Circuit (CAC) with an "accumulate-yet-undercorrect" pattern, and uses it to train a lightweight policy that substantially improves abstention decisions.
AI.motivation: LMs often hallucinate by committing to confident answers instead of abstaining despite insufficient information. Existing work addresses hallucination via detection or abstention mechanisms, but how models internally arrive at the commit-or-abstain decision remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors frame hallucination as unsupported commitment and use causal gating to identify the Commit-Abstain Circuit (CAC), a sparse, causally localized subset of attention heads and MLP sublayers. They analyze CAC behavior across ten LMs (3B-14B) from five families and three benchmarks, then train a lightweight policy on CAC activations.
AI.result: The CAC shows a recurring accumulate-yet-undercorrect pattern: commitment-promoting components build commitment in earlier layers, while abstention-promoting components act later as corrective signals that are often insufficient to overturn accumulated commitment. The CAC-based policy improves decision accuracy by 12.2 points over the model's intrinsic commit-abstain margin, reduces false abstentions by 2.5 times, transfers to unseen benchmarks, and extends to larger models (27B-35B).
AI.conclusion: The CAC is both diagnostic, clarifying how models overcommit, and practical, enabling improved abstention decisions. Framing hallucination as unsupported commitment offers a mechanistic account of the commit-abstain decision.

title: ReCAT: Remember, Count, and Time: Structured Recurrent Memory for Robot Manipulation
summary: Memory-dependent manipulation requires robots to make decisions using information that is no longer available to their current sensors, such as recalling an earlier visual cue, tracking task progress, counting repeated events, or estimating elapsed time. We present ReCAT, a language-conditioned policy with structured recurrent memory. An instruction-conditioned encoder forms features from the current observation. A recurrent memory integrates the observation stream through Mamba-2 layers and one causal attention layer. A flow-matching Transformer decoder reads the current and the historical representation through separate cross-attention in every block. ReCAT reaches 95.3\% average success on LIBERO and 62.4\% on RMBench, with the best or tied-best result on six of nine tasks. On three real-robot tasks probing spatial recall, event counting, and interval timing, the best ReCAT variant reaches 66.7\% average success, against 8.3\% for the strongest short-history baseline. Controlled comparisons within ReCAT show that the observation encoder and every-block memory conditioning are needed for this performance. They also show that update rules developed for efficient sequence modeling behave differently as robot memory: additive updates have the highest observed success on counting and timing, and delta-rule updates on spatial recall. Project website is at https://intuitive-robots.github.io/ReCAT

AI.tldr: ReCAT is a language-conditioned robot policy with structured recurrent memory (Mamba-2 layers plus one causal attention layer) whose flow-matching Transformer decoder cross-attends to current and historical representations separately in every block, achieving 95.3% on LIBERO, 62.4% on RMBench, and 66.7% on three real-robot memory-dependent tasks versus 8.3% for the strongest short-history baseline.
AI.motivation: Memory-dependent manipulation requires robots to decide using information unavailable to current sensors, e.g., recalling an earlier visual cue, tracking task progress, counting repeated events, or estimating elapsed time. Existing short-history policies cannot retain such information, so a structured recurrent memory is needed to support these capabilities.
AI.method: ReCAT is a language-conditioned policy with structured recurrent memory. An instruction-conditioned encoder forms features from the current observation. A recurrent memory integrates the observation stream via Mamba-2 layers plus one causal attention layer. A flow-matching Transformer decoder reads current and historical representations through separate cross-attention in every block. Controlled comparisons vary memory update rules (additive vs. delta-rule) and ablate the observation encoder and every-block memory conditioning.
AI.result: ReCAT reaches 95.3% average success on LIBERO and 62.4% on RMBench, with best or tied-best results on six of nine tasks. On three real-robot tasks probing spatial recall, event counting, and interval timing, the best ReCAT variant reaches 66.7% average success versus 8.3% for the strongest short-history baseline. Ablations show the observation encoder and every-block memory conditioning are both required; additive updates perform best on counting and timing, while delta-rule updates perform best on spatial recall.
AI.conclusion: Structured recurrent memory with every-block conditioning and the right update rule substantially improves memory-dependent manipulation over short-history baselines, and update rules borrowed from efficient sequence modeling behave non-uniformly as robot memory, with task-dependent optimal choices.

title: Relic: From Multi-Agent Collaboration to Persistent Organizational Capability
summary: Multiple agents may often conflict in an organization: for example, one coding agent changes an interface in a repository, but another continues to develop on the old version where existing tests become stale. A conversation can resolve the episode, but when the participants change, what makes the lesson continue to govern the team? We introduce Relic, which turns recurring collaboration failures into organization-owned, executable protocols. Members reflect on visible work, propose rules, and govern their adoption. Adopted protocols bind triggers, responsibilities, required evidence, and execution consequences to the runtime, while remaining open to revision and retirement. In one traced case, repeated integration friction produces an interface-review rule that governs later pull requests and is revised as work continues. Across 360 controlled runs over ten software workloads and three models, Relic raises complete-contract delivery from 14.06% to 19.76% (+5.71 percentage points) over a matched structured team without the protocol lifecycle, improving all four verified production endpoints in every model stratum. Under fresh-member transfer, behavioral correctness is 25.4% with no inherited protocol, 34.6% with the same rules provided as readable text, and 41.2% with executable bindings, a +6.5-point advantage over text alone. On the full CooperBench benchmark, after excluding broken benchmark pairs, Relic achieves 367/477 (76.9%), establishing the best reported result among peer-structured systems. On the fixed 48-pair same-model subset, Relic also exceeds Solo (29/48 vs. 26/48), reversing the coordination loss exhibited by the official peer baseline. Together, these results show how collaboration experience can become persistent organizational state that remains useful beyond the members who created it.

AI.tldr: Relic converts recurring multi-agent collaboration failures into organization-owned, executable protocols that persist across membership changes, improving contract delivery and transfer-to-new-members performance.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent organizations, conflicts recur (e.g., one coding agent changes an interface while another develops against the stale version). A conversation may resolve a single episode, but when participants change, the lesson is lost and no durable mechanism keeps the team governed by prior resolutions.
AI.method: Relic has members reflect on visible work, propose rules, and govern their adoption. Adopted protocols bind triggers, responsibilities, required evidence, and execution consequences to the runtime, while remaining open to revision and retirement. Protocols are organization-owned executable artifacts rather than readable text. Evaluated across 360 controlled runs over ten software workloads and three models, with a traced case, a fresh-member transfer study, and results on CooperBench.
AI.result: Complete-contract delivery rises from 14.06% to 19.76% (+5.71 pp) over a matched structured team without the protocol lifecycle, improving all four verified production endpoints in every model stratum. Under fresh-member transfer, behavioral correctness is 25.4% with no inherited protocol, 34.6% with the same rules as readable text, and 41.2% with executable bindings (+6.5 pp over text alone). On the full CooperBench benchmark (excluding broken pairs), Relic achieves 367/477 (76.9%), the best reported result among peer-structured systems; on the fixed 48-pair same-model subset it exceeds Solo (29/48 vs. 26/48), reversing the coordination loss of the official peer baseline.
AI.conclusion: Collaboration experience can be transformed into persistent organizational state that outlives the members who created it, yielding measurable gains in delivery, transfer to new members, and benchmark performance.

title: Zero-Shot Reactive Obstacle Avoidance for Generative Robot Policies
summary: We propose NUDGE (Nudge Update via Differentiable GEometry), a training-free obstacle-avoidance procedure that can be incorporated in any robot policy based on diffusion or flow matching, including diffusion policies and vision-language-action models. Our work injects gradients from a signed distance field, a function returning each point's distance to the nearest obstacle, into the policy at inference time to steer it away from obstacles. It supports any common action parameterization, from absolute or relative joint poses to end-effector poses, through a differentiable joint-trajectory decoder. Experiments show that NUDGE preserves the policy's task distribution and runs reactively in real time.

AI.tldr: NUDGE is a training-free, real-time obstacle-avoidance procedure that injects signed-distance-field gradients into diffusion- or flow-matching robot policies at inference time to steer them away from obstacles.
AI.motivation: Robot policies based on diffusion or flow matching, including diffusion policies and vision-language-action models, lack a general, training-free mechanism for reactive obstacle avoidance that works across policy types and action parameterizations.
AI.method: NUDGE injects gradients from a signed distance field—which returns each point's distance to the nearest obstacle—into the policy at inference time. It supports common action parameterizations (absolute or relative joint poses, end-effector poses) via a differentiable joint-trajectory decoder, and requires no training.
AI.result: Experiments show that NUDGE preserves the policy's task distribution and runs reactively in real time.
AI.conclusion: NUDGE is a broadly applicable, training-free obstacle-avoidance procedure that can be incorporated into any diffusion- or flow-matching robot policy while maintaining task performance and real-time reactivity.

title: Certified Long-Horizon Code Agent Evolution via Validation-Gated Skill Optimization
summary:
Long horizon agent self-evolution without model weight updates is essential for enabling deployed agents to accumulate reusable skills and improve over time. Prior self-evolution work has focused primarily on short-horizon tasks, while repository-level software engineering remains unexplored despite being an ideal testbed for long-horizon adaptation. In this setting, agents are required to solve streams of sequential tasks, navigate complex dependencies with evolving repositories and persistently store and reuse experience. Text-based skill optimization offers an efficient, non-parametric approach for such adaptation. However, existing methods often suffer from unstable updates, performance drawdown, and agent collapse over extended deployments. In this paper, we formalize the concept of in-context self-evolution and introduce VALVE, a validated-gated framework for long-horizon skill optimization. We establish finite convergence, provide theoretical guarantees for future-task gain and drawdown, and derive the validation and evaluation holdout sizes required for a prescribed tolerance, with leading-order scaling
  Empirically, our pipeline, VALVE achieves stable self-improvement over evolution horizon spanning more than 1,000 SWE tasks, with average final and peak gains of $14.9$ and $16.5$ points across three frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude-4.6 and MiniMax-M2.7). The validation gate reduces average drawdown by 75% and produces an 11x more compact skill bank than ungated evolution. We further present extensive ablations identifying the design choices most critical to long-horizon skill evolution.

AI.tldr: VALVE is a validation-gated framework enabling long-horizon, non-parametric self-evolution of agents on repository-level software engineering tasks, achieving stable skill accumulation over 1,000+ SWE tasks with reduced performance drawdown.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agent self-evolution without weight updates is essential for deployed agents to accumulate reusable skills. Prior self-evolution work targets mainly short-horizon tasks; repository-level software engineering—an ideal long-horizon testbed requiring sequential task solving, dependency navigation, and persistent experience reuse—remains unexplored. Existing text-based skill optimization methods suffer from unstable updates, performance drawdown, and agent collapse over extended deployments.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the concept of in-context self-evolution and introduces VALVE, a validated-gated framework for long-horizon skill optimization. It establishes finite convergence, provides theoretical guarantees for future-task gain and drawdown, and derives the validation and evaluation holdout sizes needed for a prescribed tolerance with leading-order scaling.
AI.result: VALVE achieves stable self-improvement over an evolution horizon spanning more than 1,000 SWE tasks, with average final and peak gains of 14.9 and 16.5 points across three frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude-4.6, MiniMax-M2.7). The validation gate reduces average drawdown by 75% and yields an 11x more compact skill bank than ungated evolution. Extensive ablations identify the design choices most critical to long-horizon skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Validation-gated, non-parametric in-context self-evolution enables stable, efficient long-horizon skill optimization in repository-level software engineering, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical gains, avoiding drawdown and skill-bank bloat over extended deployments.

title: Spatial Grafting: Grounding 3D Features for Flow-Matching Robot Policies
summary: Pretrained robot manipulation policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) or world-action models (WAMs) leave interaction-relevant metric geometry implicit. Recent breakthroughs in spatial reconstruction can supply the necessary geometry reliably, but their features describe local shape without stating where it lies with respect to the robot. How best to deliver these features to a pretrained policy remains unresolved. We propose Spatial Grafting, a versatile, lightweight spatial module that binds frozen reconstruction features to metric, robot-relative geometry. Spatial Grafting constructs metric-grounded spatial tokens and injects them into the flow-matching action expert through cross-attention, without modifying the host's perceptual pathway, so the host retains the full benefit of its pretraining. We evaluate it more broadly than any geometry-aware policy we compare against: one graft architecture, with no per-host redesign, on two VLAs and two WAMs, across four simulation benchmarks that span short-horizon manipulation, visual robustness, clutter and long-horizon mobile manipulation, and on three real-robot platforms with single- and dual-arm configurations. On RoboTwin 2.0, a dual-arm manipulation benchmark, the graft improves every host across VLAs and WAMs. Grafted $π_{0.5}$ gains 11.3% and 15.6% on clean and randomized scenes, reaching 94.0% and 92.4%, above the strongest published 3D-conditioned policy, WAM4D (93.8% and 89.9%). The margin widens as the horizon lengthens: on tasks from BEHAVIOR-1K, a dual-arm mobile manipulation challenge scored by average task progress, it surpasses the 2025 challenge winner on five of six tasks,by up to 0.47 Q-score, and exceeds a map-conditioned spatial policy on average across the three tasks both report.

AI.tldr: Spatial Grafting is a lightweight module that binds frozen spatial reconstruction features to metric, robot-relative geometry and injects them into pretrained robot policies via cross-attention, improving one architecture across two VLAs, two WAMs, three real robots, and four simulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Pretrained robot manipulation policies (VLAs and WAMs) leave interaction-relevant metric geometry implicit. Spatial reconstruction features provide geometry but describe local shape without robot-relative placement, and it is unresolved how best to deliver such features to a pretrained policy.
AI.method: Spatial Grafting constructs metric-grounded spatial tokens from frozen reconstruction features and injects them into the flow-matching action expert through cross-attention, without modifying the host's perceptual pathway, preserving pretraining benefits. One graft architecture is used with no per-host redesign.
AI.result: Tested on two VLAs and two WAMs across four simulation benchmarks and three real-robot platforms (single- and dual-arm). On RoboTwin 2.0, the graft improves every host; grafted pi_0.5 gains 11.3% and 15.6% on clean and randomized scenes, reaching 94.0% and 92.4%, above WAM4D (93.8% and 89.9%). On BEHAVIOR-1K it surpasses the 2025 challenge winner on five of six tasks by up to 0.47 Q-score, and exceeds a map-conditioned spatial policy on average across shared tasks.
AI.conclusion: A single lightweight, host-agnostic spatial grafting module reliably grounds frozen reconstruction features in robot-relative metric geometry, yielding consistent and growing improvements across diverse policy hosts, benchmarks, and real-robot settings, with margins widening as task horizon lengthens.

title: X-Tree: Tokenizing Reusable Experience for Efficient Agent Generalization
comment: Project in Progress. Homepage: https://sitaocheng.github.io/xtree/. Code: https://github.com/sitaocheng/X-Tree/
summary: Multi-step agents are trained on flat action streams: SFT and RLVR weight every token uniformly and ignore the sub-procedures that recur across tasks, the hierarchy that lets humans plan top-down from reusable routines. This structure sits unused, and flat training uses each scarce trajectory less fully than its content allows. Recent agents do use that structure, but only as LLM-written skills in context, never in the weights, so their gains do not generalize beyond retrieval. We instead recover this hierarchy from the data itself and train on it, with no LLM calls. Following text tokenizers, which build a vocabulary by counting alone, we score action spans by reusability and merge canonicalized actions into a reusable eXperience tree (X-Tree). Each X-Tree node captures how a frequent and success-bearing skill is composed from sub-skills, guiding efficient generalization. We integrate X-Tree into three training settings: offline RL, with each node as a training instance; online RLVR, with an adaptive skill bonus; and on-policy self-distillation, with X-Tree as the self-teacher's privileged context. Across WebArena, ScienceWorld, and WebShop at three model scales, X-Tree improves over standard recipes at matched data and budget by up to 4.5% SR on WebArena, 5.8% SR on ScienceWorld and 4.1% success on WebShop. Matched analyses attribute the gains to the X-Tree structure and the three integrations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes X-Tree, a method that recovers reusable hierarchical skill structure directly from agent trajectory data (without LLM calls) and integrates it into offline RL, online RLVR, and on-policy self-distillation, improving success rates across WebArena, ScienceWorld, and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Multi-step agents are trained on flat action streams, where SFT and RLVR weight every token uniformly and ignore recurring sub-procedures and hierarchical routines across tasks. This leaves structure unused and underuses scarce trajectories. Prior agents that exploit structure rely on LLM-written in-context skills rather than weights, limiting generalization beyond retrieval.
AI.method: The authors recover hierarchy from data itself without LLM calls. Inspired by text tokenizers that build vocabularies by counting, they score action spans by reusability and merge canonicalized actions into a reusable eXperience tree (X-Tree). Each node represents how a frequent, success-bearing skill is composed from sub-skills. X-Tree is integrated into three settings: offline RL (each node as a training instance), online RLVR (adaptive skill bonus), and on-policy self-distillation (X-Tree as the self-teacher's privileged context).
AI.result: Across WebArena, ScienceWorld, and WebShop at three model scales, X-Tree outperforms standard recipes at matched data and budget: up to +4.5% success rate (SR) on WebArena, +5.8% SR on ScienceWorld, and +4.1% success on WebShop. Matched analyses attribute gains to the X-Tree structure and the three integrations.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly recovering and training on reusable hierarchical skill structure from trajectory data yields consistent and generalizable gains over flat training, without relying on LLM-generated skills.

title: Repair Before You Fuse: Frozen-Host Adaptation for Corrupted-but-Present Sensors
summary: Camera-LiDAR detectors can continue to consume unreliable features even when both sensors remain present, synchronized, and calibrated. We introduce \emph{Boundary Feature Repair} (BFR), a frozen-host adaptation framework that learns task-supervised residual corrections at modality interfaces the detector already consumes. BFR-C repairs each camera feature level read by fusion, whereas BFR-L aligns host-conditioned LiDAR candidates to a selected boundary and routes site-wise innovations relative to the frozen anchor. Their jointly trained composition is BFR-CL. Zero-initialized per-channel scales make every variant an exact detector-level identity before optimization; only the repair modules train, while the encoders, fusion consumer, router, detection head, and host normalization statistics remain fixed. At inference, BFR requires neither clean references, corruption metadata, temporal history, nor online updates. Across the complete 20-corruption, five-severity KITTI-C grid, BFR-C reduces RCE from $14.07$ to $11.92$ on MVX-Net and from $14.29$ to $11.00$ on Focals Conv-F relative to their reproduced frozen baselines. On the latter host, BFR-L raises AP$_{\mathrm{cor}}$ from $73.65$ to $74.48$, while BFR-CL reaches $77.01$ AP$_{\mathrm{cor}}$ and $10.46$ RCE with $86.02$ clean AP. On nuScenes-R, BFR-CL raises the reproduced MoME baseline's mAP robustness ratio from $80.1$ to $81.4$. These results establish boundary repair as a targeted retrofit for corrupted-but-present sensing without retraining the deployed detector.

AI.tldr: BFR is a frozen-host adaptation framework that learns residual corrections at camera-LiDAR fusion interfaces, improving robustness to corruption without retraining the deployed detector.
AI.motivation: Camera-LiDAR detectors can consume unreliable features even when both sensors remain present, synchronized, and calibrated, so corruption-induced feature errors degrade detection. Existing solutions typically require retraining or online adaptation, which is costly and impractical for deployed systems.
AI.method: BFR learns task-supervised residual corrections at modality interfaces the detector already consumes. BFR-C repairs each camera feature level read by fusion; BFR-L aligns host-conditioned LiDAR candidates to a selected boundary and routes site-wise innovations relative to a frozen anchor. BFR-CL is their jointly trained composition. Zero-initialized per-channel scales ensure each variant is an exact detector-level identity before optimization. Only repair modules train; encoders, fusion consumer, router, detection head, and host normalization statistics remain fixed. Inference needs no clean references, corruption metadata, temporal history, or online updates.
AI.result: Across the full 20-corruption, five-severity KITTI-C grid, BFR-C reduces RCE from 14.07 to 11.92 on MVX-Net and from 14.29 to 11.00 on Focals Conv-F versus reproduced frozen baselines. On Focals Conv-F, BFR-L raises AP_cor from 73.65 to 74.48, and BFR-CL reaches 77.01 AP_cor, 10.46 RCE, and 86.02 clean AP. On nuScenes-R, BFR-CL raises MoME's mAP robustness ratio from 80.1 to 81.4.
AI.conclusion: Boundary repair is an effective targeted retrofit for corrupted-but-present multi-modal sensing, improving robustness without retraining the deployed detector.

title: Model-Aware Data Selection from In-and-Out Information Interplay
summary:
LLMs are effective representations that assimilate vast amounts of knowledge during pretraining, but post-training is necessary for models to reliably access this knowledge and "know what they know." We observe an interesting rank equilibrium between knowledge stored in the weights and the data stream passing through the model. Across all model layers, we find that the hidden states (data stream) follow a U-shaped pattern, showing substantial compression in early layers and a steep rise during the late-layer decoding phase. In contrast, the weight rank follows an inverted U-shaped pattern, with very low rank in the early and late layers and high rank in the middle. We interpret this as an in-and-out information interplay: intermediate activations do not need to carry content that the weights can supply later, so they primarily preserve what the weights cannot provide.
  Motivated by this observation, we propose a model-aware data selection method, CAP (Counterfactual Assimilation Profile), which can determine whether a data candidate contains information accessible to the current model by utilizing the divergence gap in early- and late-layer representations between model-generated and reference responses. Across math, code, and science domains, CAP delivers 35.4% greater average improvement over the base model than the strongest baseline under different selection budgets. With only 10% of the data pool, CAP surpasses or matches full-pool training on math and science. We further show that CAP transfers to multimodal data selection and is robust to response horizon and noise.

AI.tldr: The paper observes a "rank equilibrium" between weights and hidden states (U-shaped data stream vs. inverted U-shaped weight rank), interprets it as in-and-out information interplay, and uses it to propose CAP, a counterfactual, model-aware data selection method that outperforms baselines across domains.
AI.motivation: While LLMs absorb vast knowledge during pretraining, post-training is required for models to reliably access this knowledge and to "know what they know." The paper is motivated by the need for effective data selection that targets information the model cannot already supply from its weights.
AI.method: The authors first characterize a rank equilibrium: across layers, hidden states (data stream) follow a U-shaped pattern with substantial early-layer compression and a steep late-layer decoding rise, whereas weight rank follows an inverted U-shape with low rank in early and late layers and high rank in the middle. This suggests intermediate activations need not carry content the weights can supply later. Based on this insight, they propose CAP (Counterfactual Assimilation Profile), a model-aware data selection method that judges whether a candidate contains information accessible to the current model by measuring the divergence gap in early- and late-layer representations between model-generated and reference responses.
AI.result: Across math, code, and science domains, CAP achieves a 35.4% greater average improvement over the base model than the strongest baseline under different selection budgets. Using only 10% of the data pool, CAP surpasses or matches full-pool training on math and science. CAP also transfers to multimodal data selection and is robust to response horizon and noise.
AI.conclusion: The observed weight/activation rank equilibrium provides an interpretable account of in-and-out information interplay, and CAP operationalizes it into an effective, model-aware data selection method that is budget-efficient, cross-domain, transferable to multimodal settings, and robust to horizon and noise.

title: GuardPIBT: Counterfactually Gated Neural Guidance for Ultra-Large-Scale 3D Multi-Agent Path Finding
summary: Large-scale 3D multi-agent path finding becomes increasingly difficult under dense traffic. Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT) scales well, but its one-step goal-directed ordering may become insufficient under dense interactions and large-scale congestion. We present GuardPIBT, which augments rather than replaces the PIBT executor: neural predictions only propose residual reorderings of PIBT's native candidates, while final actions remain determined by PIBT. First, local graph attention models nearby interactions, while global source--goal transport features provide population-level coordination context for candidate reordering. Second, a counterfactual group gate filters reorderings whose closed-loop effects may degrade coordination. Third, for ultra-large populations, population-adaptive grouping preserves decision granularity, asynchronous cached inference amortizes neural computation, and selective repair resolves long-tail agents. PIBT retains validity checking, priority inheritance, and backtracking throughout. Experiments with up to 100,000 agents demonstrate reliable completion across 2D and 3D environments, including all three 100,000-agent warehouse runs with zero audited graph violations. The project website is available at {\color{magenta}\texttt{https://guardpibt.github.io/GuardPIBT/}}.

AI.tldr: GuardPIBT augments the PIBT multi-agent path finding executor with neural residual reordering of candidates, a counterfactual group gate, and population-adaptive grouping/scaled inference, achieving reliable completion with up to 100,000 agents in 2D and 3D.
AI.motivation: Large-scale 3D multi-agent path finding is difficult under dense traffic. PIBT scales well but its one-step goal-directed ordering becomes insufficient under dense interactions and large-scale congestion.
AI.method: GuardPIBT augments rather than replaces PIBT: neural predictions only propose residual reorderings of PIBT's native candidates while final actions remain PIBT-determined. It uses (1) local graph attention over nearby interactions plus global source-goal transport features for population-level coordination context, (2) a counterfactual group gate filtering reorderings whose closed-loop effects may degrade coordination, and (3) for ultra-large populations, population-adaptive grouping, asynchronous cached inference, and selective repair of long-tail agents. PIBT retains validity checking, priority inheritance, and backtracking.
AI.result: Experiments with up to 100,000 agents show reliable completion across 2D and 3D environments, including all three 100,000-agent warehouse runs with zero audited graph violations.
AI.conclusion: Neural residual reordering, counterfactual gating, and scalable grouping/inference mechanisms let PIBT-based planning handle ultra-dense large-scale multi-agent path finding while preserving PIBT's validity guarantees.

title: When Pair Count Is Not the Sample Size: What All-Pairs Agent Comparisons Estimate
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?
summary: When an agent benchmark compares every pair of leaderboard entries, the number of comparisons can look much larger than the independent evidence behind them: A versus B and A versus C both reuse A. Whether this reuse affects inference depends on what the analysis is meant to describe. If the board and its outcomes are fixed, the all-pairs mean is an exact summary of those entries, and any interval must come from another declared source of randomness. If the entries are instead treated as iid draws from a population of future configurations and the pair rule is regular and nondegenerate, the same mean is an order-two U-statistic whose first-order uncertainty depends on the number of configurations, not the number of pairs. We use near ties as the running example, but the distinction extends to other symmetric pair summaries when their regularity conditions hold. We examine both interpretations using a fixed SWE-bench Verified snapshot and an exact binary model with known truth. On SWE-bench, intervals that accounted for shared configurations were more than twice as wide as a pair-iid reference that treated the pairs as independent. In the exact model, pair-iid coverage fell far below the nominal level when edges shared endpoints but remained near nominal for matched independent edges. Results on two other fixed leaderboards show that exact summaries also depend on which pairs are included and how they are weighted. An all-pairs analysis must therefore state what is fixed, what is sampled, and how it handles shared entries and pair aggregation.

AI.tldr: All-pairs leaderboard comparisons reuse entries, so inference is only valid if the analysis declares what is fixed versus sampled; with fixed boards the all-pairs mean is exact, while under an iid configuration model it is an order-two U-statistic whose uncertainty scales with the number of configurations, not pairs.
AI.motivation: Benchmark leaderboards often report all-pairs comparisons, making the comparison count appear to exceed the independent evidence because a single entry (e.g., A in A-vs-B and A-vs-C) is reused. The paper asks whether this reuse inflates or distorts inferential claims, and argues that the answer hinges on the intended target of inference—a fixed board of outcomes versus a population of future configurations.
AI.method: The authors formalize two interpretations: (1) a fixed-board view, where the all-pairs mean is an exact finite-population summary and any interval requires a separately declared randomness source; (2) an iid-configuration view, where, under regular and nondegenerate pair rules, the same mean is an order-two U-statistic with first-order uncertainty governed by the number of configurations rather than pairs. They use near ties as the running example and extend the argument to other symmetric pair summaries meeting regularity conditions, then evaluate both views on a fixed SWE-bench Verified snapshot and on an exact binary model with known ground truth, additionally testing two other fixed leaderboards for sensitivity to pair inclusion and weighting.
AI.result: On SWE-bench, intervals accounting for shared configurations were more than twice as wide as a pair-iid reference treating pairs as independent. In the exact binary model, pair-iid coverage fell far below nominal when edges shared endpoints, but stayed near nominal for matched independent edges. Results on two other fixed leaderboards show exact summaries also depend on which pairs are included and how they are weighted.
AI.conclusion: All-pairs leaderboard analysis must explicitly state what is fixed, what is sampled, and how it handles shared entries and pair aggregation; otherwise interval estimates and coverage claims can be severely misleading, particularly when pairs share configurations.

title: DexAgent: An Agentic Human2Sim2Robot Framework for Dexterous Manipulation with Self-Evolving Tool Library
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Project website: https://dexagent123.github.io/
summary: Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations for dexterous robot manipulation. However, existing human-to-simulation-to-robot (Human2Sim2Robot) pipelines rely on predefined procedures that struggle to accommodate diverse object properties and interactions, particularly those involving articulated and deformable objects. We introduce DexAgent, an agentic Human2Sim2Robot framework that converts a single egocentric human video and a task prompt into physically grounded robot trajectories for policy training. It operates through four stages: semantic understanding of human videos, property-based simulation reconstruction, robot trajectory optimization, and robot data generation. At each stage, DexAgent adapts its approach to the task and object properties by selecting suitable skills from its tool library or developing new ones when needed. Property-specific verifiers assess stage outcomes for physical validity and task-specific requirements and provide feedback for refinement, preventing error propagation through the workflow. This adaptive, verification-guided process allows DexAgent to process diverse objects and long-horizon tasks. In the final stage, DexAgent varies object and robot states in simulation to generate diverse robot trajectories from a single human video, then retextures the rendered observations to facilitate sim-to-real transfer. Newly developed skills and verifiers are retained in its tool library, making it self-evolving to accumulate reusable capabilities. This reduces processing time as DexAgent encounters more human videos. Across eleven real-world tasks, policies trained with DexAgent-generated data achieve a 3.5x higher success rate than competing baselines. Project website: https://dexagent123.github.io/.

AI.tldr: DexAgent is an agentic Human2Sim2Robot framework that turns a single egocentric human video plus a task prompt into physically grounded robot trajectories for dexterous manipulation policy training, achieving 3.5x higher real-world success rates than baselines.
AI.motivation: Human videos are a scalable source of demonstrations for dexterous manipulation, but existing Human2Sim2Robot pipelines rely on predefined procedures that cannot accommodate diverse object properties and interactions, especially for articulated and deformable objects.
AI.method: A four-stage agentic pipeline: (1) semantic understanding of human videos, (2) property-based simulation reconstruction, (3) robot trajectory optimization, and (4) robot data generation. The agent selects or develops skills from a tool library per stage, uses property-specific verifiers to validate physical plausibility and task requirements with refinement feedback to prevent error propagation, varies object/robot states to diversify trajectories, and retextures rendered observations for sim-to-real transfer. New skills and verifiers are retained, making the system self-evolving.
AI.result: Across eleven real-world tasks, policies trained on DexAgent-generated data achieve a 3.5x higher success rate than competing baselines, with reduced processing time as more human videos are encountered.
AI.conclusion: An adaptive, verification-guided agentic framework enables robust handling of diverse and long-horizon manipulation tasks, and its self-evolving tool library accumulates reusable capabilities to improve efficiency over time.

title: The Epistemics of Agent Memory: Measuring, and Governing, the Consolidation Decision in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
comment: 13 pages, 4 tables, no figures. A four-phase research program. Experiments executed and adversarially verified by PRIMA (arXiv:2605.24775); per-phase result files and preregistrations available to reviewers on request; certain mechanism internals held under controlled release (see Section 7)
summary:
Long-horizon LLM agents must convert accumulated experience into durable memory, deciding what to keep, compress, abstract into reusable skills and rules, or forget. We report a four-phase research program on this consolidation problem whose central finding is a shift in what is measured: from how much an agent remembers, to whether its consolidation decisions are any good, to whether those decisions can be trusted.
  Phase 1 learns episodic boundaries from agent traces by downstream utility; an honest near-miss (oracle correlation 0.691 vs a 0.70 bar) whose lasting output is a three-gate anti-leakage protocol. Phase 2 learns when to promote experience and to which abstraction level under a token budget, achieving a verified +22.7% task-success improvement with 7x compression, but exposing a degenerate-forgetting failure and a distribution-shift failure mode we name lambda-prevalence coupling. Phase 3 introduces ConsolidationBench, an oracle-by-construction benchmark that scores consolidation decisions against a known optimum on three non-circular axes; production retrieval systems retain information yet score zero on cross-level transfer. Phase 4 introduces governed consolidation: the decision wrapped in poison-resistance, reversibility, and auditability guarantees with a quality gate. Governance is statistically distinct from the quality score ($r^2 = 0.43$; partial $r = 0.27$; identical-quality policies differ threefold in governance), so the contribution survives independently of the metric's external validity. On that question we report a resolved negative: after a graded-reuse redesign removed a structural ceiling, a two-benchmark study with 2,532 real answer cells finds the quality score does not predict real transfer accuracy (pooled Spearman $ρ= -0.24$, n = 12, CI spanning zero). An adversarial self-critique pass cleared the final claim set with zero surviving overclaims.

AI.tldr: A four-phase research program reframes agent memory consolidation from measuring how much is remembered to whether consolidation decisions are good and trustworthy, culminating in a production benchmark (ConsolidationBench) and a governance layer shown to be statistically distinct from decision quality—while honestly reporting that the quality score fails to predict real transfer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate experience that must be managed: deciding what to keep, compress, abstract into reusable skills/rules, or forget. The paper argues the key measurement question should shift from memory quantity to the quality and trustworthiness of consolidation decisions.
AI.method: A four-phase program: (1) learning episodic boundaries from agent traces via downstream utility, yielding a three-gate anti-leakage protocol; (2) learning when to promote experience and at which abstraction level under a token budget; (3) ConsolidationBench, an oracle-by-construction benchmark scoring consolidation decisions on three non-circular axes; (4) governed consolidation wrapping decisions in poison-resistance, reversibility, and auditability with a quality gate, plus a graded-reuse redesign and a two-benchmark study with adversarial self-critique.
AI.result: Phase 1: near-miss (oracle correlation 0.691 vs 0.70 bar). Phase 2: +22.7% task-success with 7x compression, but reveals degenerate-forgetting and lambda-prevalence coupling failures. Phase 3: retrieval systems retain information yet score zero on cross-level transfer. Phase 4: governance is statistically distinct from quality (r²=0.43; partial r=0.27; threefold governance differences at identical quality). Final study: quality score does not predict real transfer accuracy (pooled Spearman ρ=-0.24, n=12, CI spanning zero).
AI.conclusion: The core contribution—governed consolidation and its independence from the quality metric—survives regardless of the metric's external validity. The authors report a resolved negative on predictive validity and state that an adversarial self-critique pass left zero surviving overclaims.

title: From Pixel to Poses: Object-centric Tool Manipulation Learning from Human Demonstrations
summary: Scaling up robotic manipulation is primarily bottlenecked by the scarcity of real-world robot data. While recent approaches leverage human video demonstrations to mitigate this shortage, they remain computationally expensive and still rely on paired human-robot data for domain alignment. Although current state-of-the-arts excel at long-horizon tasks, they struggle with the delicate and precise control required for complex tool manipulation. To overcome these limitations, we introduce P2P-T, from Pixel to Poses for Tool Manipulation, a data-efficient, object-centric framework that learns tool use directly from human demonstrations. P2P-T bridges the cognitive and physical execution gap through a two-stage approach. First, pretraining an object-centric world model to extract stable pose priors; second, integrating these priors into an efficient, pose-aware low-level policy. By utilizing a robust automated data processing pipeline powered by modern foundation models, P2P-T completely bypasses the need for human-robot aligned data. This reduces overall training overhead drastically. With minimal per-task fine-tuning, our framework achieves a 73% improvement over the previous state of the art in execution performance on complex, real-world tool manipulation tasks that currently remain out of reach for standard large-scale pretrained models.

AI.tldr: P2P-T is a data-efficient, object-centric framework that learns tool manipulation directly from human demonstrations by bridging the gap from pixels to poses via a two-stage world model and pose-aware policy, eliminating the need for paired human-robot data.
AI.motivation: Scaling robotic manipulation is bottlenecked by scarce real-world robot data. Existing human-video-based approaches are computationally expensive, require paired human-robot data for domain alignment, and struggle with the delicate, precise control needed for complex tool manipulation despite excelling at long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: P2P-T uses a two-stage, object-centric approach: (1) pretraining an object-centric world model to extract stable pose priors from human demonstrations, and (2) integrating these priors into an efficient, pose-aware low-level policy. An automated data processing pipeline powered by modern foundation models enables learning without human-robot aligned data.
AI.result: With minimal per-task fine-tuning, P2P-T achieves a 73% improvement over the previous state of the art in execution performance on complex, real-world tool manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: P2P-T enables data-efficient learning of precise tool manipulation from human demonstrations while bypassing human-robot aligned data, drastically reducing training overhead and surpassing prior methods on tasks beyond the reach of standard large-scale pretrained models.

title: Trust and Task Completion in the World of Consumer AI Agents
summary: Action agents do things for people. They send email, spend money, and call businesses while the user is busy with something else, so a mistake can turn into an action before anyone notices. They fail their users in two ways. They break trust when they do something the user never agreed to, or hold back after the user clearly said go. And they fall short on completion when they give up on errands that turn out to be hard. Both depend heavily on the harness around the model, meaning its instructions, tools, context, and guardrails. We built an evaluation that scores trust and completion on the same runs, in a simulated world of businesses with their own websites, inboxes, and phone lines, and of people who write back. A simulated user answers the assistant's questions. Trust means that nothing happens the user did not agree to. No email goes to someone they never approved, no private detail ends up on a group thread, no money is spent past their limit, no stranger's instructions are followed, and nothing is claimed without a source. Every trap has a matched control in which acting is the right call. We use the evaluation to measure Fo, Wajo's personal assistant, against a base model with basic instructions on three foundation models, and against the Fo harness with its guardrails switched off. Fo completes 71% of the errands and keeps the user's trust on 94% of the trap runs. The base models complete 50% to 64% and keep trust on 59% to 75%. On the matched controls, Fo goes ahead slightly less often. OpenClaw, a popular open-source assistant given the same access, completes 42% of the errands it shares with Fo, against 71%, and keeps the user's trust on 74% of the shared trap runs, against 94%. Measuring trust and completion together, on the whole system rather than the model alone, is how we think action agents become safe to hand real work to.
