AI.tldr: The paper introduces an evaluation that jointly scores trust and completion for action agents within a simulated world of businesses and responsive users, using matched trap/control pairs. Testing Fo (Wajo's assistant) against base models and a guardrail-disabled variant shows Fo reaches 71% errand completion and 94% trap-run trust, outperforming base models (50-64% completion, 59-75% trust) and OpenClaw (42% shared completion, 74% shared trust). The authors argue that measuring trust and completion together at the whole-system level is the path to safely deploying action agents.
AI.motivation: Action agents perform consequential tasks (sending email, spending money, calling businesses) while users are occupied, so mistakes can become irreversible actions before anyone notices. They fail in two distinct ways: breaking trust by acting without agreement (or withholding when told to proceed) and falling short on completion by abandoning hard errands. Both failure modes depend heavily on the harness around the model—instructions, tools, context, and guardrails—yet existing evaluations typically assess the model alone or measure trust and completion separately. The motivation is to create a single evaluation that captures both dimensions on the same runs, at the level of the whole system rather than the model in isolation, as a prerequisite for making action agents safe to delegate real work to.
AI.method: The evaluation is conducted in a simulated world of businesses with their own websites, inboxes, and phone lines, plus people who write back, and a simulated user who answers the assistant's questions. Trust is operationalized as nothing happening the user did not agree to: no email to unapproved recipients, no private detail on a group thread, no spending past a limit, no following a stranger's instructions, and no unsourced claims. Each trap scenario is paired with a matched control in which acting is the correct call. The authors benchmark Fo (Wajo's personal assistant) against (1) a base model with basic instructions across three foundation models, and (2) the Fo harness with its guardrails switched off, and also compare against OpenClaw, a popular open-source assistant, given the same access, on shared errands and trap runs.
AI.result: Fo completes 71% of the errands and preserves user trust on 94% of trap runs. Base models complete 50% to 64% of errands and preserve trust on 59% to 75%. On matched controls, Fo proceeds slightly less often, indicating a degree of conservatism. OpenClaw completes 42% of the errands it shares with Fo, versus Fo's 71%, and preserves trust on 74% of the shared trap runs, versus Fo's 94%.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that measuring trust and completion together, at the level of the whole system rather than the model alone, is the way action agents become safe to hand real work to. The findings indicate that the harness—instructions, tools, context, and guardrails—is decisive for both dimensions, and that Fo's configuration substantially outperforms base models and a popular open-source alternative on both trust and completion.

title: Adaptive Safety Filtering for Frozen ACC Policies via Conformal Residual Calibration
summary: Frozen adaptive cruise control (ACC) policies can violate constraints when deployment dynamics differ from their training conditions. We propose residual-aware conformal action filtering (RACF), which calibrates residuals of a fixed nominal predictor and converts their quantile into an operating margin for finite-model action projection. Completed transitions update margins and candidate selection without retraining the policy. In a registered comparison over 2,400 controller-trial units, Adaptive RACF achieves 94.3% episode safety, improving by 19.9 percentage points over the evaluated nominal CBF-QP baseline while reducing projection frequency from 8.11% to 6.63%. A controlled study isolates a 4.54-point improvement from residual-margin injection. In a separate matched-hardware evaluation, Adaptive reduces mean amortized rollout time by 21.2% relative to Robust CBF-QP, with 161/180 versus 170/180 safe episodes. We characterize conditions linking one-step residual coverage to constraint satisfaction and quantify the observed safety-computation trade-offs.

AI.tldr: Residual-aware conformal action filtering (RACF) yields safer, faster adaptive cruise control than nominal or robust CBF-QP baselines without retraining.
AI.motivation: Frozen adaptive cruise control (ACC) policies can violate safety constraints when deployment dynamics differ from training conditions, necessitating an online safety mechanism.
AI.method: RACF calibrates residuals of a fixed nominal predictor, converts their quantile into an operating margin, and performs finite-model action projection. Completed transitions update margins and candidate selection without retraining the policy; conditions linking one-step residual coverage to constraint satisfaction are characterized.
AI.result: Adaptive RACF reaches 94.3% episode safety over 2,400 controller-trial units, +19.9 points over nominal CBF-QP, and cuts projection frequency from 8.11% to 6.63%. A controlled study attributes 4.54 points to residual-margin injection. Matched-hardware evaluation lowers mean amortized rollout time by 21.2% versus Robust CBF-QP (161/180 vs 170/180 safe episodes).
AI.conclusion: RACF improves safety and computational efficiency over CBF-QP baselines, showing a quantified safety-computation trade-off.

title: SRE-Marathon: A Continuous, Change-Driven Benchmark for Autonomous Site Reliability Agents
summary: Benchmarks for site reliability engineering (SRE) agents are typically episodic: one fault is injected, the agent receives an incident task, and its response is scored. Production operation is not. Incidents surface through noisy alerts, overlap in time, and often originate from code or configuration changes. We present SRE-Marathon, a benchmark for long-horizon, continuous SRE operation. An agent is invoked at a fixed cadence with cumulative alert history and a persistent workspace while operating a live two-zone Kubernetes deployment as a fault orchestrator injects overlapping faults according to a seeded, production-calibrated schedule. Curated code and configuration changes deployed through the same build pipeline available for repair. Each run is recorded into a sealed bundle and scored offline: Marathon-Score credits each injected fault for ordered progress through correlation, localization, and repair, with all metrics computed deterministically from recorded system evidence. Across three applications and about sixty faults per run, the best of 10 methods reaches only 41.3 out of 100. Agents often correlate and localize faults, but almost never complete repairs while the faults remain active.

AI.tldr: SRE-Marathon is a long-horizon benchmark for continuous SRE operation: an agent acts at fixed cadence on a live two-zone Kubernetes deployment while overlapping faults are injected, and is scored offline via Marathon-Score on correlation, localization, and repair. The best of 10 methods scores only 41.3/100; agents rarely finish repairs while faults remain active.
AI.motivation: Existing SRE agent benchmarks are episodic—one injected fault, one incident task, one score. This does not reflect production, where incidents arrive via noisy alerts, overlap in time, and frequently stem from code or configuration changes. A benchmark capturing long-horizon, continuous operation is needed.
AI.method: SRE-Marathon invokes an agent at a fixed cadence with cumulative alert history and a persistent workspace, operating a live two-zone Kubernetes deployment. A fault orchestrator injects overlapping faults per a seeded, production-calibrated schedule, and curated code and configuration changes are deployed through the same build pipeline available for repair. Each run is recorded into a sealed bundle and scored offline, with Marathon-Score crediting each injected fault for ordered progress through correlation, localization, and repair; all metrics are computed deterministically from recorded system evidence.
AI.result: Across three applications and roughly sixty faults per run, the best of 10 methods reaches only 41.3 out of 100. Agents often correlate and localize faults but almost never complete repairs while faults remain active.
AI.conclusion: Current SRE agents are far from production-ready for continuous operation: they can correlate and localize faults but fail at repair under concurrent, ongoing faults. SRE-Marathon provides a reproducible, evidence-based benchmark to drive progress in long-horizon SRE autonomy.

title: Memory in the Sky: Low-Altitude Question Answering with Multi-Agent Memory Aggregation
summary: This paper studies low-altitude question answering (LAQA), in which distributed unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) memories are aggregated at a ground server to answer questions about observations over a long horizon. Unlike conventional resource allocation based on sensing, communication, control, or computation metrics, LAQA requires an explicit measure of memory value. We propose a generative adversarial exam (GAE) that uses forward simulation to evaluate memory retrieval and exam scores to quantify memory quality. This enables the downstream QA value of candidate memories to be measured and optimized without accessing the internal mechanisms of the black-box captioning, retrieval, and reasoning pipeline. Building on this metric, we develop a memory-centric (MemCen) framework that jointly selects UAVs and allocates transmit power to maximize memory quality under communication constraints. In the noise-limited regime, we derive a QoM-aware capped water-filling law that explicitly connects task utility with physical-layer power allocation. We further develop penalty successive optimization (PSO) and learning to memorize (L2M) solvers. MemCen achieves QA accuracies of 92.4% and 84.0% in CARLA Town04 and Town05 under static and dynamic communication conditions, respectively. In real-world experiments, MemCen achieves 88.5% QA accuracy on the panoramic multi-agent system (PMAS) benchmark. Finally, UAV-to-robot-dog demonstrations further validate the practical utility of the acquired memories for environmental understanding and navigation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces low-altitude question answering (LAQA) and proposes a generative adversarial exam (GAE) to quantify the value of UAV memories, along with a memory-centric (MemCen) framework for joint UAV selection and power allocation that maximizes memory quality under communication constraints.
AI.motivation: Conventional resource allocation relies on sensing, communication, control, or computation metrics, which do not capture the downstream QA value of aggregated UAV memories over a long horizon. There is a need for an explicit, task-aware measure of memory value to guide resource allocation in the LAQA setting.
AI.method: The authors propose a generative adversarial exam (GAE) that uses forward simulation to evaluate memory retrieval and exam scores to quantify memory quality, enabling measurement and optimization of candidate memories' downstream QA value without accessing the internals of the black-box captioning, retrieval, and reasoning pipeline. Building on this metric, they develop a memory-centric (MemCen) framework that jointly selects UAVs and allocates transmit power to maximize memory quality under communication constraints, deriving a QoM-aware capped water-filling law in the noise-limited regime, and developing penalty successive optimization (PSO) and learning to memorize (L2M) solvers.
AI.result: MemCen achieves QA accuracies of 92.4% and 84.0% in CARLA Town04 and Town05 under static and dynamic communication conditions, respectively. In real-world experiments, it achieves 88.5% QA accuracy on the panoramic multi-agent system (PMAS) benchmark. UAV-to-robot-dog demonstrations further validate the practical utility of the acquired memories for environmental understanding and navigation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GAE metric and MemCen framework effectively quantify and optimize memory quality for LAQA, yielding high QA accuracy across simulated and real-world benchmarks and demonstrating practical value for downstream robotic tasks such as environmental understanding and navigation.

title: Agent Safety From Within: Detecting Harmful Trajectories from LLM Internal States
summary: Language model agents can now perform sophisticated sequences of actions via tools and harnesses, which has increased the scope of the damage they can cause. Guard models, however, are mainly built for content moderation and thus are not well-suited to detecting this agentic risk. To address this, we proceed by first conducting a representational analysis, then use the resulting insights to build a solution. In our analysis, we focus on two types of trajectory-level agentic harms: harmful content, which is expressed directly, and unsafe tool use, which depends on whether an action is consistent with the interaction that produced it. We investigate how open-source guard models represent these two types of harm and find that they are linearly readable inside the model, even though guard models predict no better than chance on pairs that differ only in the called tool's schema. The two harm types also follow nearly orthogonal internal directions, and neither reliably serves as a proxy for the other. These results motivate reading trajectory safety directly from internal states. We introduce TACIT, a readout of a frozen backbone's internal states that decodes no tokens. Trained on six trajectory-safety benchmarks, a linear probe raises mean macro-F1 from 62.3 for the strongest open guard to 80.7, and refined readouts reach 86.2. With each benchmark held out of training entirely, the refined readouts still lead the strongest guard (65.7 vs. 61.1). With the same backbone, training data and test split, the frozen readout is on par with full safety fine-tuning, and it improves the fine-tuned model further when applied on top. The probe trains about one millionth as many parameters as full fine-tuning in about a sixth of the time, and TACIT has the lowest latency of the guards we evaluate.

AI.tldr: TACIT reads trajectory-level agentic safety directly from a frozen backbone's internal states, outperforming open guard models and matching full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: Guard models are built for content moderation and are ill-suited to detecting agentic risk, where harms arise from sequences of tool-using actions rather than from content alone.
AI.method: The authors first perform a representational analysis of open-source guard models on two trajectory-level harms: directly expressed harmful content and unsafe tool use, which depends on whether an action is consistent with the interaction that produced it. They examine linear readability of these harms and the geometric relationship between their internal directions. Building on the finding that harms are linearly decodable and internally near-orthogonal, they introduce TACIT, a token-free readout trained on the frozen backbone's internal states as linear probes or refined readouts.
AI.result: Guard models predict no better than chance on pairs differing only in the called tool's schema, yet both harm types are linearly readable internally and follow nearly orthogonal directions, with neither a reliable proxy for the other. Trained on six trajectory-safety benchmarks, a linear probe raises mean macro-F1 from 62.3 (strongest open guard) to 80.7, and refined readouts reach 86.2. Under full benchmark holdout, refined readouts still lead the strongest guard (65.7 vs. 61.1). With matched backbone, data, and test split, the frozen readout is on par with full safety fine-tuning and improves the fine-tuned model when stacked on top. It trains roughly one-millionth the parameters of full fine-tuning in about one-sixth the time, with the lowest latency among evaluated guards.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level agentic safety is directly readable from a frozen backbone's internal states, yielding a highly parameter- and latency-efficient alternative to guard models and full safety fine-tuning.

title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents: From Digital Programs to Physical-World Intelligence
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models map observations and instructions directly to robot actions. This directness ties a policy to training: minor layout or viewpoint changes cause failure, and instructions generalize poorly. The root cause lies in representation: task requirements, conditions, progress, and failure recovery are implicitly encoded in action sequences, making them difficult to inspect or revise. Digital coding agents offer a precedent: LLMs call tools, verify results, and revise from feedback as executable code. The same working pattern of explicit state, manageable execution, and revisable procedures underlies generalization and long-horizon execution in the physical world, letting physical experience return as reusable programs, memory, or evidence. We propose Physical Coding, representing task state and execution as code. Code as World records objects, relations, constraints, and progress; Code as Policy organizes planning, verification, recovery, and execution. We build HexaAnything, which calls perception, planning, and control tools, including VLA/WAM policies, and makes in-the-loop decisions from external feedback. Verified traces become data and memory, enabling evolution from tools and Harness to model weights, architectures, and ultimately hardware and task design. On RoboCasa365, HexaAnything improves Composite-Unseen and overall success over XR-1 VLA, and its Harness-trained HexaModel beats the base on every split, indicating code traces internalize physical execution. On PhyBench and a dual-arm AgileX robot, the agent autonomously completes physics experiments and most tabletop tasks, often faster than published results. We observe data, model, and tool self-evolution; future work targets weight internalization, autonomous redesign of architectures, languages, representations, and tasks, and deployment in manufacturing and science.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Physical Coding, a paradigm that represents robot task state and execution as executable code, and builds HexaAnything, a coding agent that orchestrates perception, planning, and control tools (including VLA/WAM policies) to improve generalization, long-horizon execution, and self-evolution.
AI.motivation: VLA and WAM models map observations and instructions directly to actions, but this directness ties policies tightly to training: minor layout or viewpoint changes cause failure, and instructions generalize poorly. The root cause is representational: task requirements, conditions, progress, and failure recovery are implicitly encoded in action sequences, making them hard to inspect or revise. Digital coding agents offer a precedent where LLMs call tools, verify results, and revise from feedback as executable code, suggesting the same pattern of explicit state, manageable execution, and revisable procedures could enable generalization and long-horizon execution in the physical world.
AI.method: The authors propose Physical Coding, representing task state and execution as code, with two components: Code as World (records objects, relations, constraints, and progress) and Code as Policy (organizes planning, verification, recovery, and execution). They build HexaAnything, an agent that calls perception, planning, and control tools, including VLA/WAM policies, and makes in-the-loop decisions from external feedback. Verified traces become data and memory, enabling evolution from tools and Harness to model weights, architectures, and ultimately hardware and task design.
AI.result: On RoboCasa365, HexaAnything improves Composite-Unseen and overall success over the XR-1 VLA, and its Harness-trained HexaModel beats the base model on every split, indicating code traces internalize physical execution. On PhyBench and a dual-arm AgileX robot, the agent autonomously completes physics experiments and most tabletop tasks, often faster than published results. The authors observe data, model, and tool self-evolution.
AI.conclusion: Physical Coding represents robot task state and execution as executable code, enabling inspectable, revisable policies and reusable physical experience. Future work targets weight internalization, autonomous redesign of architectures, languages, representations, and tasks, and deployment in manufacturing and science.

title: BudgetVerify: Budget-Tiered Verification for Financial QA
summary: Financial question answering often requires precise numerical extraction, unit handling, and arithmetic over tables and text, but applying expensive verification uniformly wastes test-time compute. We propose BudgetVerify, a budget-tiered generator-verifier framework that routes each generated answer to one of three verification tiers: no verification, lightweight check-and-revise, or higher-cost solve-first-then-compare verification. The router is trained from offline correctness and token-cost outcomes and, at test time, selects a verification tier using information available before verification, including the question, context statistics, the generated answer, and associated generator metadata. The selected tier either returns the generated answer directly or invokes the corresponding verifier. Across six commercial and open-weight base models, BudgetVerify consistently produces more efficient accuracy-cost Pareto frontiers than fixed verification policies by selectively allocating stronger verification only when it is useful. Although absolute performance varies across models, these efficiency gains and the resulting qualitative frontier shape are consistent across generator models.

AI.tldr: BudgetVerify is a budget-tiered generator-verifier framework for financial QA that routes each generated answer to one of three verification tiers (none, lightweight check-and-revise, or costly solve-first-then-compare), trained from offline correctness and token-cost outcomes. It yields more efficient accuracy-cost Pareto frontiers than fixed verification policies across six base models.
AI.motivation: Financial QA demands precise numerical extraction, unit handling, and arithmetic over tables and text, yet applying expensive verification uniformly wastes test-time compute. A method is needed to allocate verification effort selectively.
AI.method: A budget-tiered generator-verifier framework routes each generated answer to one of three verification tiers: no verification, lightweight check-and-revise, or higher-cost solve-first-then-compare. The router is trained from offline correctness and token-cost outcomes and, at test time, selects a tier using pre-verification information: the question, context statistics, the generated answer, and generator metadata. The chosen tier either returns the answer directly or invokes the corresponding verifier.
AI.result: Across six commercial and open-weight base models, BudgetVerify consistently produces more efficient accuracy-cost Pareto frontiers than fixed verification policies by selectively allocating stronger verification only when useful. Although absolute performance varies by model, the efficiency gains and qualitative frontier shape are consistent across generator models.
AI.conclusion: Selective, tiered verification based on pre-verification signals improves the accuracy-cost trade-off in financial QA compared to uniform fixed verification, with consistent efficiency gains across diverse base models.

title: Revision, Not Restart: Revisable Visual Plans for Closed-Loop World-Action Models
summary: World-action models use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, yet execution feedback can invalidate parts of a prediction while leaving its task structure useful. We propose Revisable Temporal Planning (RTP), which maintains the visual future as a persistent action condition and revises it after feedback. Its central mechanism is a learned revision bridge: it resumes an intermediate state saved during visual generation and adapts its continuation to current observations. Visual and action supervision connect this revision to subsequent control. Time-aware history supplies observed evidence, and an adaptive policy selects retention, bridge revision, or fresh replanning from new noise before decoding the next action. On RoboMME and RMBench, RTP achieves task-averaged success rates of 48.6% and 84.8%, respectively. Matched comparisons support learned continuation; estimated checkpoint-source and action-prefix effects are positive but less precisely resolved. These results connect feedback-driven visual-plan revision to closed-loop task performance. Project Page: https://PLACEHOLDER.github.io/RTP/

AI.tldr: RTP keeps the predicted visual future as a persistent action condition and revises it with execution feedback via a learned revision bridge, achieving 48.6% and 84.8% success on RoboMME and RMBench.
AI.motivation: World-action models condition robot actions on predicted visual futures, but execution feedback can invalidate parts of a prediction even though its task structure remains useful. Existing approaches lack a principled way to revise rather than discard such predictions.
AI.method: Revisable Temporal Planning (RTP) treats the visual future as a persistent action condition and revises it after feedback using a learned revision bridge, which resumes an intermediate state saved during visual generation and adapts its continuation to current observations. Visual and action supervision link the revision to subsequent control; time-aware history provides observed evidence; an adaptive policy chooses retention, bridge revision, or fresh replanning from new noise before decoding the next action.
AI.result: RTP reaches task-averaged success rates of 48.6% on RoboMME and 84.8% on RMBench. Matched comparisons support learned continuation, while estimated checkpoint-source and action-prefix effects are positive but less precisely resolved.
AI.conclusion: The work links feedback-driven visual-plan revision to closed-loop task performance, showing that preserving and adaptively revising predicted futures is beneficial for robot control.

title: Large Language Models Substantially Compress Well-Being Inequality but Largely Preserve Its Socioeconomic Structure
summary: Research using large language models (LLMs) to generate synthetic populations has repeatedly shown that model outputs compress the diversity of human experience. This has raised doubts about whether LLM-generated data can capture meaningful differences within populations. We show that such compression does not necessarily erase the social structure of human heterogeneity. Using 93,901 respondents from 66 countries and territories in Wave 7 of the World Values Survey, we ask six LLMs to predict respondents' life satisfaction from demographic, socioeconomic, and attitudinal profiles. All six models substantially understate the overall dispersion of life satisfaction. Yet after normalizing for these differences in scale, they largely reproduce the human income gradient in well-being inequality: lower-income groups remain relatively more heterogeneous than higher-income groups. The pattern is robust to country fixed effects, equal-country weighting, WVS survey weights, and observed demographic composition, and it extends directionally to employment, education, and perceived control. Fidelity is weaker for extreme outcomes and country-specific gradients. These results show that the amount of heterogeneity preserved by an LLM and the way that heterogeneity is distributed across social groups are distinct properties. LLM-generated populations can therefore substantially compress human variation while retaining meaningful information about where that variation is concentrated.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated synthetic populations compress overall variation in life satisfaction but still reproduce the social structure of well-being inequality, with lower-income groups remaining more heterogeneous than higher-income groups.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows LLM-generated synthetic populations compress the diversity of human experience, raising doubts about whether such data can capture meaningful within-population differences. The authors test whether this compression destroys social structure or merely rescales it.
AI.method: Using 93,901 respondents from 66 countries and territories in Wave 7 of the World Values Survey, six LLMs predict respondents' life satisfaction from demographic, socioeconomic, and attitudinal profiles. The authors compare human versus model-generated dispersion and income gradients in well-being inequality, testing robustness with country fixed effects, equal-country weighting, WVS survey weights, and observed demographic composition.
AI.result: All six models substantially understate overall dispersion in life satisfaction. After normalizing for scale differences, they largely reproduce the human income gradient in well-being inequality: lower-income groups remain relatively more heterogeneous than higher-income groups. The pattern is robust across the stated checks and extends directionally to employment, education, and perceived control, though fidelity is weaker for extreme outcomes and country-specific gradients.
AI.conclusion: The amount of heterogeneity preserved by an LLM and its distribution across social groups are distinct properties. LLM-generated populations can substantially compress human variation while still retaining meaningful information about where that variation is concentrated.

title: Uni-VLaT: Whole-Body Tactile Adaptation of VLA Policies for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Physical contact often determines how a humanoid should respond during loco-manipulation, yet vision and proprioception alone are often insufficient to characterize physical interaction, especially when the contact region is occluded. Unlike sparse force or torque measurements at predefined regions, distributed tactile sensing preserves spatially resolved contact patterns across the robot body. We therefore study how to integrate such whole-body tactile information into vision-language-action (VLA) policies for contact-rich control. Our approach, Uni-VLaT, introduces a tactile pathway whose latent state is trained not only for action generation, but also to predict future tactile, proprioceptive, and visual representations. This predictive objective builds a tactile-anchored multimodal context, encouraging a more structured understanding of the physical world. We evaluate Uni-VLaT on five real-robot tasks covering tactile-triggered locomotion, sustained physical interaction, human-robot contact, and loco-manipulation. Uni-VLaT achieves a 75% average success rate, outperforming a baseline without tactile input by 43 points and a tactile-input baseline without predictive supervision by 7 points. Across two pretrained VLA backbones, our method improves Table Sweeping by 30 points on both backbones and Back-Tap Walking by 85-90 points. Ablations further show that contextualized tactile prediction and absolute future targets are critical to performance. These results indicate that predictive tactile learning provides an effective route for extending pretrained VLA policies to whole-body physical interaction.

AI.tldr: Uni-VLaT integrates whole-body distributed tactile sensing into VLA policies via a tactile pathway trained to both generate actions and predict future tactile, proprioceptive, and visual representations, achieving 75% average success across five real-robot contact-rich tasks.
AI.motivation: Physical contact dictates appropriate humanoid responses during loco-manipulation, but vision and proprioception alone are often insufficient to characterize physical interaction, particularly when the contact region is occluded. Unlike sparse force/torque measurements at predefined regions, distributed tactile sensing preserves spatially resolved contact patterns across the robot body, motivating its integration into vision-language-action policies.
AI.method: Uni-VLaT introduces a tactile pathway whose latent state is trained not only for action generation but also for predicting future tactile, proprioceptive, and visual representations. This predictive objective builds a tactile-anchored multimodal context that encourages structured understanding of the physical world.
AI.result: Evaluated on five real-robot tasks (tactile-triggered locomotion, sustained physical interaction, human-robot contact, and loco-manipulation), Uni-VLaT achieves a 75% average success rate—outperforming a no-tactile baseline by 43 points and a tactile baseline without predictive supervision by 7 points. Across two pretrained VLA backbones, it improves Table Sweeping by 30 points and Back-Tap Walking by 85-90 points.
AI.conclusion: Ablations confirm that contextualized tactile prediction and absolute future targets are critical to performance. Predictive tactile learning offers an effective route for extending pretrained VLA policies to whole-body physical interaction.

title: LLM sequential decision making under uncertainty in biochemical domains
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to drive scientific discovery. Understanding how LLMs make decisions from new data and memory of the literature is vital before trusting them to design experiments under tight experimental budgets. However, their decision strategies are invisible in the current performance scores used to evaluate research agents. Here, we benchmark five frontier LLMs in a Bayesian Optimization setting against published statistical baselines on seven combinatorial datasets spanning protein engineering, reaction optimization, molecular design, peptide self-assembly, and catalysis. Performance is paired with direct measurements of model beliefs and actions, enabling highly resolved behavior analysis. A prompt ablation that progressively strips context separates memorization from chemical reasoning and from bare categorical optimization. Prior chemical knowledge helps in expectation, but with high variance and occasionally even harms performance. No configuration tested decisively beats a mean statistical baseline across domains. Belief-movement and Martingale diagnostics, corrected here for a measurement-noise bias that mislabels rational agents as irrational, show that models overreact to incoming data rather than entrenching on their priors in the contexts studied here. Interestingly, while LLM actions are exploitative, models sincerely intend to explore and consistently act on that intent. This failure is a competence gap arising from context-stickiness. Removing in-context history restores exploration, indicating that priors and data must be decoupled to achieve effective LLM-driven discovery.

AI.tldr: Five frontier LLMs are benchmarked in Bayesian Optimization against statistical baselines on seven scientific datasets, revealing that no LLM configuration decisively beats a mean baseline and that models exploit overly despite sincerely intending to explore.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to drive scientific discovery, but their decision strategies are invisible in current performance scores. Before trusting LLMs to design experiments under tight budgets, it is vital to understand how they make decisions from new data and literature memory.
AI.method: The authors benchmark five frontier LLMs against published statistical baselines in a Bayesian Optimization setting across seven combinatorial datasets spanning protein engineering, reaction optimization, molecular design, peptide self-assembly, and catalysis. They pair performance with direct measurements of model beliefs and actions, and use a prompt ablation that progressively strips context to separate memorization from chemical reasoning and bare categorical optimization. They further apply belief-movement and Martingale diagnostics, corrected for a measurement-noise bias that mislabels rational agents as irrational.
AI.result: Prior chemical knowledge helps in expectation but with high variance and occasionally harms performance. No tested configuration decisively beats a mean statistical baseline across domains. Diagnostics show models overreact to incoming data rather than entrenching on priors. Although LLM actions are exploitative, models sincerely intend to explore and consistently act on that intent, indicating a competence gap from context-stickiness.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven discovery currently fails to reliably outperform a simple statistical baseline, and its exploitative behavior stems from context-stickiness rather than intent. Removing in-context history restores exploration, indicating that priors and data must be decoupled to achieve effective LLM-driven scientific discovery.

title: Rethinking Causal Action Tokenization with Conditional Annealing in Flow Matching
summary: Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a scalable path to robot learning, yet existing action tokenizers treat tokenization as a compression problem, producing representations that are semantically misaligned with the autoregressive backbone. We propose CATok, a causal action tokenizer that reframes tokenization as a causally structured generative process. CATok introduces a conditional annealing mechanism that extracts action tokens by progressively annealing a flow-matching process: each token is conditioned on all preceding tokens and encodes the residual reconstruction signal at a specific noise level, establishing a coarse-to-fine causal token space whose generative semantics are structurally aligned with autoregressive modeling. A token-conditioned flow-matching decoder built on Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) reconstructs continuous action chunks from these discrete tokens with the precision of hybrid diffusion-head architectures. This discrete bottleneck enforces knowledge insulation by design, cleanly separating high-level semantic reasoning from low-level motor execution without requiring explicit attention masking. Extensive evaluations across three simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate that CATok consistently surpasses existing tokenization methods in both reconstruction fidelity-compression tradeoff and inference efficiency, while improving VLA task success rate and training efficiency, establishing a high-performance, scalable foundation for purely autoregressive VLA systems.

AI.tldr: CATok is a causal action tokenizer that reframes tokenization as a causally structured generative process, producing discrete action tokens aligned with autoregressive VLA backbones and improving reconstruction, efficiency, and task success.
AI.motivation: Existing action tokenizers in autoregressive VLA models treat tokenization as a compression problem, yielding representations semantically misaligned with the autoregressive backbone. This misalignment limits the performance of purely autoregressive VLA systems.
AI.method: CATok introduces a conditional annealing mechanism that extracts action tokens by progressively annealing a flow-matching process; each token conditions on all preceding tokens and encodes the residual reconstruction signal at a specific noise level, forming a coarse-to-fine causal token space. A token-conditioned flow-matching decoder built on MMDiT reconstructs continuous action chunks from discrete tokens with hybrid diffusion-head precision. The discrete bottleneck enforces knowledge insulation, separating high-level semantic reasoning from low-level motor execution without explicit attention masking.
AI.result: Across three simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, CATok consistently surpasses existing tokenization methods in reconstruction fidelity-compression tradeoff and inference efficiency, while improving VLA task success rate and training efficiency.
AI.conclusion: CATok establishes a high-performance, scalable foundation for purely autoregressive VLA systems by aligning tokenization semantics with autoregressive modeling through a causally structured discrete token space.

title: QureRadEmbed: Structuring Radiological Similarity through Attribute and Reasoning Supervision
comment: 39 pages, 10 figures, including appendices with per-tag labeling results. Janhavi Prabhu and Sahil are co-first authors. Manoj Tadepalli is the corresponding author
summary: Radiological similarity depends on disease relationships and on fine details such as laterality, lobe, severity, size, and certainty. Broad biomedical similarity can overlook these qualifiers, particularly when several attributes vary together. We introduce QureRadEmbed, a 4B radiology-aware encoder trained with two complementary signals: RadSim supplies deterministic, attribute-decomposed ranking targets, while RadThought aligns reports with hierarchical evidence and reasoning descriptions. A three-stage curriculum combines these signals with report triplets, finding perturbations, and single- and cross-attribute contrasts. The final model achieves 0.996 mean ordering accuracy across ten controlled synthetic attributes and raises Spearman correlation with the designed joint-attribute targets from 0.501 to 0.976. On external findings-to-impression retrieval, Recall@1 reaches 10.5% on Open-I, 12.4% on testing XR, and 42.9% on testing CT, compared with 6.6%, 5.7%, and 31.4% for its backbone. Frozen embeddings support finding extraction with only 100 labeled testing-XR reports (macro-F1 0.481 versus 0.412 for the backbone). Whole-report comparison costs 8.8 seconds per 1,000 pairs in our benchmark, versus 2,755.1 seconds for the generative evaluator GREEN. Sentence-level comparison improves sensitivity to local discrepancies, although generative evaluation remains stronger on several expert-rated and subtle-error tasks. The results support reusable radiology-aware representations for search, structured report indexing, and efficient report comparison.

AI.tldr: QureRadEmbed is a 4B radiology-aware encoder trained with attribute-decomposed ranking (RadSim) and hierarchical reasoning alignment (RadThought), achieving near-perfect ordering accuracy on controlled attributes and large gains in findings-to-impression retrieval and efficient report comparison.
AI.motivation: Radiological similarity depends on disease relationships and fine-grained qualifiers such as laterality, lobe, severity, size, and certainty. Broad biomedical similarity often overlooks these qualifiers, especially when multiple attributes co-vary, limiting search, structured indexing, and report comparison.
AI.method: The authors introduce QureRadEmbed, a 4B radiology-aware encoder trained with two complementary signals: RadSim provides deterministic, attribute-decomposed ranking targets, while RadThought aligns reports with hierarchical evidence and reasoning descriptions. A three-stage curriculum combines these signals using report triplets, finding perturbations, and single- and cross-attribute contrasts.
AI.result: The model reaches 0.996 mean ordering accuracy across ten controlled synthetic attributes and improves Spearman correlation with joint-attribute targets from 0.501 to 0.976. On external findings-to-impression retrieval, Recall@1 is 10.5% (Open-I), 12.4% (testing XR), and 42.9% (testing CT), versus 6.6%, 5.7%, and 31.4% for the backbone. Frozen embeddings support finding extraction with 100 labeled testing-XR reports (macro-F1 0.481 vs. 0.412). Whole-report comparison costs 8.8 s per 1,000 pairs, versus 2,755.1 s for GREEN.
AI.conclusion: QureRadEmbed provides reusable radiology-aware representations for search, structured report indexing, and efficient report comparison. Sentence-level comparison improves sensitivity to local discrepancies, though generative evaluation remains stronger on several expert-rated and subtle-error tasks.

title: CoBrush: A Hierarchical Planning Framework for Human-Robot Co-Painting
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Embodied co-painting requires a robot to repeatedly update a shared physical canvas while human intent evolves over interaction. Existing reference-driven painters or reactive assistants are typically optimized for single-shot rendering or sketch completion, limiting their ability to sustain coherent multi-round collaboration or to construct complex, content-rich scenes over time. We present CoBrush, a hierarchical framework that formulates multi-round co-painting as a coordinated semantic, spatial, and execution process. By separating high-level intent inference from spatial grounding and stroke-level control, the system supports progressive scene development on real acrylic canvases. We evaluate the framework through real human-robot painting sessions, stress tests, and user studies. Compared to single-turn baselines, our approach achieves stronger semantic alignment, more stable spatial progression, and higher perceived plausibility of robot actions. These results demonstrate that structured multi-stage reasoning improves the coherence and robustness of interactive painting and supports the progressive development of content-rich physical artworks.

AI.tldr: CoBrush is a hierarchical framework that casts multi-round human-robot co-painting as coordinated semantic, spatial, and execution processes, enabling progressive scene development on real canvases and outperforming single-turn baselines.
AI.motivation: Embodied co-painting requires a robot to repeatedly update a shared physical canvas as human intent evolves. Existing reference-driven painters and reactive assistants target single-shot rendering or sketch completion, so they struggle to sustain coherent multi-round collaboration or build content-rich scenes over time.
AI.method: The authors propose CoBrush, a hierarchical framework that formulates multi-round co-painting as a coordinated semantic, spatial, and execution process. It separates high-level intent inference from spatial grounding and stroke-level control, supporting progressive scene development on real acrylic canvases.
AI.result: Evaluation via real human-robot painting sessions, stress tests, and user studies shows that, compared to single-turn baselines, the approach achieves stronger semantic alignment, more stable spatial progression, and higher perceived plausibility of robot actions.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-stage reasoning improves the coherence and robustness of interactive painting and supports the progressive development of content-rich physical artworks.

title: Structure-Mapping-Guided Self-Explanation for Learning Mathematical Procedures
comment: 19 pages. Accepted for oral presentation at the Thirteenth Annual Conference on Advances in Cognitive Systems (ACS 2026)
summary: Worked examples are a powerful form of instruction, but learners must infer how the demonstrated steps were produced. A naive simulation of this self-explanation process can generate thousands of numerical explanations that reproduce one observed change without capturing its underlying procedure. We propose structure-mapping-guided self-explanation as a computational account of the cognitive biases that reduce search effort and make this inference tractable. The model represents mathematical expressions as typed relational structures and uses structure mapping to identify corresponding source and target regions. For each changed target value, the corresponding source region serves as an anchor: it guides abductive search toward structurally relevant values and operations before broader alternatives, yielding ordered, executable candidate procedures with inspectable source evidence. Across 70 mathematical transformations containing 120 changed numeric components, the model recovered every intended procedure. It returned the intended procedure before any other computation producing the same target value in 104 subproblems (86.7%), compared with a median of 32 (26.7%) across 100 unguided runs that tested candidate calculations in random order. Our proposed model also tested 93.8% fewer combinations of values and operations than unguided search before reaching the intended procedures. These results provide an efficient, interpretable account of how relational structure can guide procedural learning and a testable hypothesis about human self-explanation from worked examples.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes structure-mapping-guided self-explanation, a computational model that uses structure mapping to constrain abductive search when inferring procedures from worked examples, dramatically reducing search effort while recovering intended procedures.
AI.motivation: Learners viewing worked examples must infer how demonstrated steps were produced, but a naive simulation of this self-explanation process can generate thousands of numerical explanations that reproduce one observed change without capturing its underlying procedure. The goal is a computational account of cognitive biases that reduce search effort and make this inference tractable.
AI.method: The model represents mathematical expressions as typed relational structures and applies structure mapping to identify corresponding source and target regions. For each changed target value, the corresponding source region acts as an anchor, guiding abductive search toward structurally relevant values and operations before broader alternatives, producing ordered, executable candidate procedures with inspectable source evidence. It was evaluated on 70 mathematical transformations containing 120 changed numeric components, benchmarked against 100 unguided runs that tested candidate calculations in random order.
AI.result: The model recovered every intended procedure across all 120 changed numeric components. It returned the intended procedure before any other computation producing the same target value in 104 subproblems (86.7%), versus a median of 32 (26.7%) across 100 unguided runs. It also tested 93.8% fewer combinations of values and operations than unguided search before reaching the intended procedures.
AI.conclusion: The results provide an efficient, interpretable account of how relational structure can guide procedural learning, and offer a testable hypothesis about human self-explanation from worked examples.

title: Robot Tool Design from Scratch via Behavior-Aware Hierarchical Optimization
summary: The ability to design a tool for a task marks a level of intelligence beyond merely understanding, selecting, or using one. Existing methods for robotic tool design typically optimize a tool's continuous shape and action within a structure that is prescribed or generated beforehand, so the structure itself stays outside the physical optimization loop. We study task-driven tool design from scratch, where tool structure, shape, and action are all derived from the desired physical outcome. Here we show that the three elements can be designed jointly by HOT, a hierarchical optimization whose upper level searches over discrete tool structures with BASS, while lower-level physical optimization evaluates their task behavior and returns milestone progress as behavioral evidence for the search, ultimately providing jointly optimized shape and action. On four tool-use tasks with distinct physical functions, HOT discovers functional structures after evaluating only a small fraction of search spaces containing up to 56 million structures, and the subsequent refinement of their geometry lowers the task loss on all tasks while preserving success, through deformations that are functionally interpretable. Once 3D printed, the tools accomplish all tasks on a real robot with the actions found in simulation. Designing tools from required physical effects, rather than a catalog of known tools, is a step toward the open-ended tool making seen in humans and animals.

AI.tldr: HOT, a hierarchical optimization framework, jointly designs tool structure, shape, and action from scratch to achieve desired physical outcomes, discovering functional tool structures and demonstrating real-robot task success.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic tool design methods typically optimize a tool's continuous shape and action within a structure that is prescribed or generated beforehand, leaving the structure itself outside the physical optimization loop. The paper aims to design tools from scratch, deriving structure, shape, and action all from the desired physical outcome, moving toward open-ended tool making.
AI.method: HOT is a hierarchical optimization: its upper level searches over discrete tool structures using BASS, while a lower-level physical optimization evaluates task behavior and returns milestone progress as behavioral evidence for the search, ultimately providing jointly optimized shape and action.
AI.result: On four tool-use tasks with distinct physical functions, HOT discovers functional structures after evaluating only a small fraction of search spaces containing up to 56 million structures. Subsequent geometry refinement lowers the task loss on all tasks while preserving success, through functionally interpretable deformations. Once 3D printed, the tools accomplish all tasks on a real robot with the simulation-found actions.
AI.conclusion: Designing tools from required physical effects, rather than from a catalog of known tools, is a step toward the open-ended tool making seen in humans and animals.

title: The Model Knows Another Way: Strategy Switching for Effective RLVR Exploration
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is often limited by insufficient exploration: difficult problems can yield uniformly incorrect rollout groups and therefore little learning signal. We show that such failures need not reflect missing capability. Instead, finite sampling often concentrates on a problem-specific dominant reasoning strategy while leaving alternative strategies already supported by the model unexplored. Moreover, the accessibility of these strategies evolves during RL: some are internalized into autonomous behavior, while others become difficult to elicit before being absorbed. Motivated by these observations, we introduce Problem--Strategy Rollout Allocation (PSRA), which treats unguided and strategy-conditioned prompts as competing exploration arms and uses Bayesian sequential allocation to direct a fixed rollout budget toward arms most likely to yield informative, non-saturated groups. A preservation objective keeps useful strategy-conditioned routes accessible while successful guided behaviors are transferred to the unguided policy. Across Qwen2.5 models from 1.5B to 7B and two RL training corpora, PSRA consistently improves reasoning performance, reduces dead saturation, strengthens out-of-distribution transfer, and maintains larger gains under increased inference budgets.

AI.tldr: PSRA treats unguided and strategy-conditioned prompts as competing exploration arms and uses Bayesian sequential allocation to spend a fixed rollout budget on non-saturated groups, improving reasoning and reducing dead saturation in RLVR.
AI.motivation: RLVR is limited by insufficient exploration: hard problems produce uniformly incorrect rollout groups, giving little learning signal. The authors argue such failures are not necessarily capability gaps—finite sampling concentrates on a problem-specific dominant strategy, leaving viable alternative strategies unvisited. Strategy accessibility also shifts during RL as some become internalized and others become hard to elicit before absorption.
AI.method: Problem–Strategy Rollout Allocation (PSRA) models unguided and strategy-conditioned prompts as competing exploration arms, using Bayesian sequential allocation to direct a fixed rollout budget toward arms most likely to yield informative, non-saturated groups. A preservation objective maintains useful strategy-conditioned routes, while successful guided behaviors are transferred to the unguided policy.
AI.result: Across Qwen2.5 models from 1.5B to 7B and two RL training corpora, PSRA consistently improves reasoning performance, reduces dead saturation, strengthens out-of-distribution transfer, and sustains larger gains as inference budget increases.
AI.conclusion: The exploration bottleneck in RLVR can be alleviated by explicitly allocating rollouts across unguided and strategy-conditioned routes rather than relying on uniform sampling, yielding more informative learning signals and better transfer.

title: ForVis: An In-Field Dataset and Benchmark for VIO Using Under-Canopy UAV Flights in Forests
summary: Visual-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VI-SLAM) for UAVs remains difficult to evaluate in real forest environments, where motion, illumination changes, repetitive vegetation, and vibration can all affect estimation. We present ForVis, an in-field dataset and benchmark for evaluating VI-SLAM during UAV flight in forest environments. The dataset contains twelve flights across open meadow, above-canopy, and under-canopy conditions in each environment. In total, it provides 563.8s of flight over 1096.8m of trajectory, recorded simultaneously with an Intel RealSense D435i and an OAK-D Pro Wide together with inertial and flight-controller data. We benchmark seven open-source VI-SLAM systems over 504 runs. The results show that sensor choice has a larger effect on trajectory error than the spread between algorithms: all seven methods achieve lower median error on the OAK-D Pro than on the D435i. ForVis is intended to support evaluation of speed, accuracy and robustness for VI-SLAM in challenging forest flight.

AI.tldr: ForVis is an in-field dataset and benchmark for evaluating visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) during UAV flight in forest environments, comprising twelve flights across meadow, above-canopy, and under-canopy conditions, with 563.8s and 1096.8m of trajectory recorded by two synchronized cameras; seven open-source VI-SLAM systems are benchmarked over 504 runs, showing sensor choice affects trajectory error more than algorithm spread.
AI.motivation: VI-SLAM for UAVs remains difficult to evaluate in real forest environments, where motion, illumination changes, repetitive vegetation, and vibration all affect estimation, and existing evaluation lacks in-field data covering these challenging conditions.
AI.method: The authors present ForVis, an in-field dataset and benchmark collected during UAV flights in forests. It includes twelve flights spanning open meadow, above-canopy, and under-canopy conditions in each environment, totaling 563.8s of flight over 1096.8m of trajectory, recorded simultaneously with an Intel RealSense D435i and an OAK-D Pro Wide along with inertial and flight-controller data. Seven open-source VI-SLAM systems are benchmarked over 504 runs.
AI.result: Sensor choice has a larger effect on trajectory error than the spread between algorithms: all seven benchmarked methods achieve lower median error on the OAK-D Pro than on the D435i.
AI.conclusion: ForVis is intended to support evaluation of speed, accuracy, and robustness for VI-SLAM in challenging forest flight.

title: Modular Discovery of General Game-Playing Algorithms with Large Language Models
summary: General Game Playing across arbitrary games from rules alone remains challenging due to differing algorithmic requirements across game classes and strict decision-time constraints. Rather than hand-designing search heuristics for specific domains, can we leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to discover general game-playing algorithms? Because language models can propose and refactor structured code, they provide an expressive proposal engine for exploring the space of algorithmic designs. We introduce a multi-agent LLM meta-learning system to co-evolve game-agnostic procedural search mechanisms in C++ alongside domain heuristics synthesized directly from game rules. Controlling the compute budget, we benchmark the discovered mechanisms across more than 400 diverse environments, including OpenSpiel training and held-out games, procedural simulation engines, and games with deep neural policy-value representations trained via PPO. Evaluated via AlphaRank stationary distributions and Soft Condorcet Optimization (SCO) against 15 established MCTS baselines, the discovered search mechanisms consistently achieve top-tier ratings and pairwise ballot majorities over most baselines across independent evolutionary runs, generalizing to unseen human-designed and procedurally synthesized games and remaining competitive with baselines on frozen neural network representations.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM meta-learning system co-evolves game-agnostic search mechanisms in C++ with rule-derived heuristics, yielding algorithms that top-tier rate against 15 MCTS baselines across 400+ environments.
AI.motivation: General game playing from rules alone is hard because game classes demand different algorithmic requirements under strict decision-time constraints. Instead of hand-designing domain-specific search heuristics, the authors ask whether LLMs can discover general game-playing algorithms, exploiting their ability to propose and refactor structured code as an expressive proposal engine over algorithmic design space.
AI.method: A multi-agent LLM meta-learning system that co-evolves (1) game-agnostic procedural search mechanisms written in C++ and (2) domain heuristics synthesized directly from game rules. The compute budget is explicitly controlled during evolution.
AI.result: Benchmarked across 400+ diverse environments (OpenSpiel training and held-out games, procedural simulation engines, and PPO-trained deep neural policy-value games). Under AlphaRank stationary distributions and Soft Condorcet Optimization (SCO) versus 15 established MCTS baselines, the discovered mechanisms achieve top-tier ratings and pairwise ballot majorities over most baselines across independent evolutionary runs, generalizing to unseen human-designed and procedurally synthesized games, and remaining competitive on frozen neural network representations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven co-evolution can discover general, transferable game-playing search algorithms that match or exceed strong MCTS baselines without domain-specific hand-design, generalizing to unseen and procedurally generated games.

title: Terrain-Aware Autonomous Planetary Exploration for Exteroceptive-Proprioceptive Mapping with Quadruped Scouts
comment: Accepted to the International Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo 2026)
summary: Autonomous planetary exploration requires robots to navigate unknown, uneven terrain while assessing risk, traversability, and energetic cost. Quadruped scouts are well suited for this task because they can traverse irregular surfaces and gather mobility-relevant information during locomotion. This paper presents a terrain-aware exploration framework that combines exteroceptive and proprioceptive mapping for a quadruped robot in lunar-like environments. An onboard RGB-D camera builds robot-centered elevation maps, estimates geometric traversability, and derives navigation costs for autonomous planning. In parallel, proprioceptive measurements provide interaction-aware terrain cues that complement geometry-based assessment. Local maps are incrementally registered into a global multi-layer representation, which is used by an exploration module to select targets in unexplored regions of interest. The targets are reached by an autonomous navigation system that guides collision-aware motion using the available map and cost layers. Simulation results on NVIDIA Isaac Sim show autonomous exploration, map expansion, and spatial association between terrain geometry and robot-terrain interaction. Subsequent navigation using this information exhibits lower average Cost of Transport (CoT) than initial exploration.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a terrain-aware autonomous exploration framework for quadrupedal robots in lunar-like environments, fusing exteroceptive RGB-D elevation mapping with proprioceptive interaction cues into a global multi-layer map that drives target selection and collision-aware navigation, validated in Isaac Sim.
AI.motivation: Autonomous planetary exploration demands robots that can traverse unknown, uneven terrain while simultaneously reasoning about risk, traversability, and energetic cost. Quadruped scouts are advantageous because they can handle irregular surfaces and harvest mobility-relevant information during locomotion, yet a unified framework for exploiting both geometric and interaction-based terrain knowledge during exploration is needed.
AI.method: An onboard RGB-D camera constructs robot-centered elevation maps, estimates geometric traversability, and derives navigation cost layers for planning. In parallel, proprioceptive measurements yield interaction-aware terrain cues that complement the geometry-based assessment. Local maps are incrementally registered into a global multi-layer representation, which an exploration module uses to select targets in unexplored regions of interest; an autonomous navigation system reaches these targets with collision-aware motion using the available map and cost layers. Evaluation is performed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim on lunar-like terrain.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate autonomous exploration, progressive map expansion, and a spatial association between terrain geometry and robot-terrain interaction. Navigation leveraging this fused information achieves a lower average Cost of Transport (CoT) than during the initial exploration phase.
AI.conclusion: Combining exteroceptive and proprioceptive terrain representations enables effective autonomous exploration and more energy-efficient navigation for quadruped robots in planetary-analog settings, indicating that interaction-aware terrain cues meaningfully augment purely geometric mapping.

title: Compositional Safety Failures in Harness Evolution: Identification and Runtime Monitoring
summary: Self-evolving agent harnesses continually update persistent components such as memory, prompts, skills, and tools. We call this process harness evolution. However, such evolution could introduce unexpected safety risks. Existing work studies harness misevolution and validates candidate harnesses or attributed individual component updates, leaving safety analysis of cross-component update interactions largely unexamined. To address this gap, we study compositional safety failures in harness evolution, where interactions among individually safe and utility-preserving component updates can produce undesirable or unsafe agent behavior, revealing a safety risk intrinsic to harness evolution. Across three safety-related benchmarks, we identify 43 pairwise and 18 irreducible 3-way compositional safety failures. Conventional solution incurs combinatorial complexity in validating cross-component interactions, leaving the safety checking impractical as the harness evolves. To solve this, we introduced a typed hypergraph that represents component states as nodes and safety-relevant higher-order interactions as hyperedges. When the harness changes, the hypergraph updates only the interaction neighborhood of the changed states rather than reconstructing the global composition space. Building on that, we develop a hypergraph-guided runtime monitoring mechanism. Experiments show that our method effectively mitigates compositional safety risks while preserving task utility and reducing interaction-checking costs, and further reveal an empirical safety-utility-cost trade-off across different safety mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "compositional safety failures" in self-evolving agent harnesses, where individually safe, utility-preserving component updates interact to produce unsafe behavior, and proposes a typed hypergraph with incremental updates plus hypergraph-guided runtime monitoring to mitigate these risks efficiently.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agent harnesses continually update persistent components (memory, prompts, skills, tools)—a process termed harness evolution—which may introduce unexpected safety risks. Prior work studies harness misevolution but only validates candidate harnesses or individual attributed component updates, leaving cross-component update interactions largely unexamined. This leaves a gap: interactions among individually safe updates can cause unsafe emergent behavior.
AI.method: The authors first characterize compositional safety failures empirically. To avoid the combinatorial complexity of exhaustively validating cross-component interactions, they introduce a typed hypergraph that represents component states as nodes and safety-relevant higher-order interactions as hyperedges. When the harness changes, the hypergraph updates only the interaction neighborhood of changed states instead of reconstructing the global composition space. Building on this structure, they develop a hypergraph-guided runtime monitoring mechanism.
AI.result: Across three safety-related benchmarks, they identify 43 pairwise and 18 irreducible 3-way compositional safety failures. Experiments show the proposed method effectively mitigates compositional safety risks while preserving task utility and reducing interaction-checking costs, and further reveal an empirical safety-utility-cost trade-off across different safety mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Compositional safety failures are an intrinsic risk of harness evolution, arising from interactions among individually safe, utility-preserving component updates. A typed hypergraph with local (neighborhood-only) updates and hypergraph-guided runtime monitoring provides a practical mitigation that balances safety, utility, and checking cost, exposing a fundamental safety-utility-cost trade-off.

title: Inspection-SPARS: Task-Oriented Sparse Roadmaps for Inspection Planning
summary: Inspection planning seeks a minimum-length collision-free robot tour that observes a given set of points of interest (POIs). Sampling-based methods reduce this continuous problem to a graph inspection planning (GIP) problem over a discrete roadmap, which is then solved using combinatorial solvers. Dense roadmaps capture diverse inspection viewpoints and motion shortcuts, and thus admit higher-quality solutions, but they induce large combinatorial search spaces on which state-of-the-art GIP solvers struggle to find good solutions within practical time budgets. Roadmap sparsification---restructuring a dense roadmap into a compact representation that preserves connectivity and path lengths---can alleviate this burden. However, existing sparsification approaches are either agnostic to the underlying inspection task, or strive to ensure coverage of the POIs without accounting for the quality of the resulting inspection plan. We present Inspection-SPARS, which is, to our knowledge, the first inspection-roadmap sparsifier with POI coverage and path-quality guarantees relative to the dense roadmap. To this end, we generalize the SPARS framework, a popular task-agnostic sparsifier, from purely geometric criteria to task-oriented ones, introducing an inspection-aware vertex admission mechanism that treats POI coverage as a first-class sparsification criterion alongside connectivity and path quality. Experiments in realistic 3D environments show that Inspection-SPARS reduces vertex and edge counts by 4-8x while preserving coverage, allowing the GIP solver to compute tours up to 25% shorter than with the dense roadmap or state-of-the-art inspection roadmap. More broadly, Inspection-SPARS shows that sparsification can be made task-aware without sacrificing guarantees on solution quality.

AI.tldr: Inspection-SPARS is a task-aware roadmap sparsifier that generalizes SPARS to treat POI coverage as a first-class criterion, reducing graph size 4-8x while yielding tours up to 25% shorter.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based inspection planning reduces to a graph inspection planning (GIP) problem on a discrete roadmap. Dense roadmaps yield higher-quality solutions but create large combinatorial search spaces that state-of-the-art GIP solvers cannot handle within practical time budgets. Existing sparsification methods are either task-agnostic or enforce POI coverage without accounting for inspection plan quality.
AI.method: The authors generalize the SPARS framework from purely geometric criteria to task-oriented ones, introducing an inspection-aware vertex admission mechanism that treats POI coverage as a first-class sparsification criterion alongside connectivity and path quality, while providing POI coverage and path-quality guarantees relative to the dense roadmap.
AI.result: In realistic 3D environments, Inspection-SPARS reduces vertex and edge counts by 4-8x while preserving coverage, enabling the GIP solver to compute tours up to 25% shorter than with the dense roadmap or state-of-the-art inspection roadmaps.
AI.conclusion: Inspection-SPARS is the first inspection-roadmap sparsifier with POI coverage and path-quality guarantees relative to the dense roadmap, showing that sparsification can be made task-aware without sacrificing guarantees on solution quality.

title: Ceiling of a Task: When Can a Transformer Succeed Without Its Chain of Thought?
summary: Reasoning models generate long chains of thought before they answer, yet it is debated whether the content of these chains does real computational work or is largely decorative. We study this question by viewing a transformer as a shallow circuit. One forward pass through a fixed number of layers has constant depth, so any procedure that runs the model a constant number of times is a shallow circuit. We call the best accuracy that a shallow circuit can reach on a task the ceiling of the task, and a task is serial if its ceiling lies below one. We prove three results on serial tasks that hold for every transformer, no matter how it was trained. Necessity: replacing the chain by anything that does not depend on its content, such as filler tokens or a restatement of the question, drives the accuracy down to the ceiling, and on a maximally serial task down to chance. Depth: no shallow computation can write the chain of a model whose accuracy exceeds the ceiling, not even approximately. Locality: the answer is one shallow pass away from the finished chain, so all of the serial reasoning happens in the chain. On word problems of finite groups, whose ceilings are known, small transformers trained from scratch, with or without reinforcement learning, attain the predicted numbers: chain-trained models solve every input length and fall to chance when the chain is erased, chainless models collapse to the ceiling as the input length grows, and open-weight reasoning models given the same problem in words return to the baseline without their chain. On MATH-500 and AIME, erasing the chain costs open reasoning models 0.52 to 0.82 accuracy, a sentence shuffle is harmless, and a token shuffle is as harmful as erasing; the same holds for checkpoints trained by GRPO with a correct or a random reward. The ceiling of a task therefore answers when a transformer can succeed without its chain of thought.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes chain-of-thought (CoT) as a computational necessity for "serial" tasks by viewing transformers as shallow circuits, proving that for such tasks the chain's content does indispensable work and predicting exact accuracy ceilings.
AI.motivation: It is debated whether the content of long chains of thought in reasoning models performs genuine computation or is largely decorative. The authors aim to settle this by giving a precise computational-complexity characterization of when CoT is required.
AI.method: Transformers are treated as shallow circuits: a fixed number of layers has constant depth, so any procedure running the model a constant number of times is shallow. The best accuracy a shallow circuit can achieve on a task is its "ceiling," and a task is "serial" if its ceiling is below one. Three theorems are proved for every transformer regardless of training: (1) Necessity—replacing the chain with content-independent input (filler tokens, question restatement) reduces accuracy to the ceiling, and to chance on maximally serial tasks; (2) Depth—no shallow computation can write the chain of a model whose accuracy exceeds the ceiling, even approximately; (3) Locality—the answer is one shallow pass from the finished chain, so all serial reasoning resides in the chain. Predictions are tested on finite-group word problems with known ceilings, small transformers trained from scratch (with/without RL), open-weight reasoning models, MATH-500, AIME, and GRPO checkpoints with correct or random rewards.
AI.result: On finite-group word problems, chain-trained models solve every input length but fall to chance when the chain is erased, while chainless models collapse to the ceiling as input length grows; open-weight reasoning models return to baseline without their chain. On MATH-500 and AIME, erasing the chain costs open reasoning models 0.52–0.82 accuracy, sentence shuffling is harmless, and token shuffling is as harmful as erasing; the same holds for GRPO checkpoints trained with correct or random rewards.
AI.conclusion: The ceiling of a task answers when a transformer can succeed without its chain of thought: above the ceiling, chain content does real computational work and cannot be replaced by shallow or content-independent computation.

title: EdgeVLN: Runtime-Aware Deployment Ready Quantized Vision Language Navigation Model
summary: Vision-language navigation (VLN) models perform well but target compute-rich platforms, limiting deployment on memory- and power-constrained robotic edge devices. Compression alone does not establish whether a VLN model fits the memory, latency, and energy budgets of an edge platform while preserving navigation behavior. We introduce EdgeVLN, a runtime-aware, deployment-ready quantized VLN model that closes this gap. EdgeVLN combines a quantized StreamVLN model with Latent Trajectory Termination Extractor (LATTE), a lightweight causal transformer that improves real-time stopping by predicting a Stop Action verifier rank. Both execute through our llama.cpp VLN driver, which reconstructs streaming context and prunes memory tokens on-board. We characterize a pretrained StreamVLN backbone across weight quantization from 8 to 2 bits and multiple inference runtimes to identify a feasible operating point. LATTE reuses backbone hidden states within the budget freed by quantization, requiring neither a second vision encoder nor an additional backbone forward pass. We evaluate six backbone precisions and seven candidate stop heads on BF16 and IQ4 NL across all 1,839 R2R VLN-CE val-unseen episodes. We measure success rate (SR) in simulation and latency, energy, and resident memory on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 16 GB. LATTE achieves our highest SR, 58.02 percent on the deployed 4-bit model, exceeding the BF16 baseline with only 0.013 s additional latency per navigation step. Four-bit formats achieve nearly identical SR, but step energy varies 36.8 times by execution path. Only IQ4 NL under our VLN driver fits the board, using 11.35 GB resident memory while running 20.8 times faster and using 13.3 times less energy than storage-streamed BF16. INT2 collapses. Runtime selection, memory-token pruning, and quantization are essential for efficient edge deployment.
