AI.tldr: EdgeVLN is a runtime-aware, quantized VLN system combining a 4-bit StreamVLN backbone with LATTE, a lightweight stop-action verifier, executed via a llama.cpp driver; it fits on a Jetson Orin NX (11.35 GB, 58.02% SR) while being 20.8x faster and using 13.3x less energy than storage-streamed BF16.
AI.motivation: VLN models achieve strong performance but are designed for compute-rich platforms, which hampers deployment on memory- and power-constrained robotic edge devices. Compression alone cannot establish whether a VLN model actually meets a platform's memory, latency, and energy budgets while preserving navigation behavior.
AI.method: EdgeVLN couples a quantized StreamVLN model with LATTE, a lightweight causal transformer that predicts a Stop Action verifier rank for real-time stopping. Both run through a llama.cpp VLN driver that reconstructs streaming context and prunes memory tokens on-board. A pretrained StreamVLN backbone is characterized across 8- to 2-bit weight quantization and multiple runtimes to find a feasible operating point. LATTE reuses backbone hidden states within quantization-freed budget, needing no extra vision encoder or backbone forward pass. Six backbone precisions and seven candidate stop heads are evaluated on BF16 and IQ4 NL over all 1,839 R2R VLN-CE val-unseen episodes, measuring SR, latency, energy, and resident memory on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 16 GB.
AI.result: LATTE attains the highest SR of 58.02% on the deployed 4-bit model, surpassing the BF16 baseline with only 0.013 s extra latency per step. Four-bit formats give nearly identical SR but step energy varies 36.8x by execution path. Only IQ4 NL under the VLN driver fits the board, using 11.35 GB resident memory while running 20.8x faster and consuming 13.3x less energy than storage-streamed BF16. INT2 collapses.
AI.conclusion: Runtime selection, memory-token pruning, and quantization are all essential to efficient edge deployment of VLN models. EdgeVLN demonstrates that a deployment-ready operating point can be identified and that behavior can be preserved, with LATTE improving stopping without significant overhead.

title: On Device Agentic Operation Caches -- Classifier-Centric NL-to-Action Generation
summary:
Agentic AI is increasingly being embedded in software applications to provide natural language interfaces to features and functionality. In most cases these agents are powered by enterprise (100+ billion parameter) or frontier class large language models that require substantial computational resources run and depend on cloud hosted inference to handle the task of transforming natural language inputs into actionable software operations. This reliance on cloud-hosted inference introduces substantial network latency on top of LLM inference times, creates data privacy concerns, and, given the costs of running these models, can rapidly escalate expenses associated with supporting agentic features.
  This paper introduces a novel means of converting the NL-to-Action problem from a generative one into a classification-centric formulation via on-device operation caches. These caches allow an agentic system to handle frequently occurring classes of actions completely on-device -- reducing latency, enhancing privacy, and lowering operational costs. We show that for a classic NL-to-Formula task, generating Excel Formula in response to user requests, this approach reduces total inference cost by 56% when compared to cloud-only model-routing based inference and, on cache hits, reduces the latency to response latency by 5x.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates the NL-to-Action problem from generative to classification via on-device operation caches, achieving 56% lower inference cost and 5x lower cache-hit latency than cloud-only routing for Excel formula generation.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI embedded in software typically relies on enterprise or frontier LLMs with cloud-hosted inference, which introduces network latency, raises data privacy concerns, and rapidly escalates operational costs.
AI.method: Converts the NL-to-Action problem from a generative formulation into a classification-centric one using on-device operation caches, enabling frequent action classes to be handled entirely on-device.
AI.result: On a classic NL-to-Formula task (generating Excel formulas from user requests), the approach reduces total inference cost by 56% versus cloud-only model-routing inference and reduces cache-hit latency to response latency by 5x.
AI.conclusion: On-device operation caches offer a practical way to lower latency, enhance privacy, and cut operational costs for agentic software features while preserving functionality for frequent actions.

title: F4R: Failure-Driven Recognition, Reconstruction, Refinement, and Redeployment for Continual Robot Self-Improvement
summary: The real-world performance of current vision-language-action models is fundamentally constrained by the limited coverage of expert demonstrations and their insufficient understanding of physical interactions. A common remedy is to collect additional real-world demonstrations of newly encountered failures. However, this process is costly, inefficient, potentially unsafe, and difficult to scale. To address this challenge, we propose Failure for Rising (F4R), a failure-driven real-to-sim-to-real closed-loop learning framework that converts real-world failures into targeted policy improvement. F4R first uses an agent to automatically identify and diagnose failures from rollouts. It reconstructs each failure as an interactive, object-centric table-top environment that preserves the task-relevant spatial and physical conditions. The policy is then refined through failure-conditioned sim-real co-training followed by targeted reinforcement learning in the reconstructed environments. The improved policy is subsequently redeployed, while newly observed failures are continuously fed back into the next reconstruction and learning cycle. Real-world evaluations on four manipulation tasks show that F4R achieves 93.75% In-Distribution and 90.0% Out-of-Distribution (OOD) success, outperforming the budget-matched Targeted BC baseline by 18.75 percentage points under OOD conditions without collecting additional real-world corrective demonstrations.

AI.tldr: F4R is a failure-driven real-to-sim-to-real closed-loop framework that reconstructs real-world failures into object-centric simulation environments for targeted policy refinement, improving vision-language-action model robustness without extra real-world corrective demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models are limited by scarce expert demonstrations and poor physical interaction understanding. The usual fix—collecting new real-world demonstrations of failures—is costly, inefficient, unsafe, and hard to scale, so a more scalable way to turn failures into policy improvement is needed.
AI.method: F4R uses an agent to automatically identify and diagnose failures from rollouts, reconstructs each failure as an interactive object-centric table-top environment preserving task-relevant spatial and physical conditions, and refines the policy via failure-conditioned sim-real co-training followed by targeted reinforcement learning in the reconstructed environments. Improved policies are redeployed, with new failures fed back into the next cycle.
AI.result: On four real-world manipulation tasks, F4R achieves 93.75% In-Distribution and 90.0% Out-of-Distribution success, outperforming a budget-matched Targeted BC baseline by 18.75 percentage points under OOD conditions without collecting additional real-world corrective demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Failure-driven real-to-sim-to-real closed-loop learning enables scalable, data-efficient policy improvement by transforming real failures into simulated targeted training signal, substantially boosting OOD generalization.

title: LiteEvo: Automated, Cost-Efficient Harness Evolution for Generalization to Unseen Tasks
summary: An LLM agent is defined by two things: the weights inside its model and the harness of components assembled around it. Harnesses are still handcrafted, and HarnessX, which evolves them automatically, starts each benchmark from a handcrafted harness, reports gains on the tasks it evolved on, and budgets 100 to 175 million meta-agent tokens per benchmark. We propose LiteEvo, a lightweight harness-evolution algorithm whose tool-free meta-agents mine agent trajectories for reusable components, curate them into a versioned library, and compose each round's harness from it, starting every benchmark from the same neutral harness and never naming the benchmark. Evolving on the graded tasks of five agentic benchmarks with a frozen Qwen3.5-9B, LiteEvo lifts pass@2 by 10.5 to 67.7pp and reaches comparable or higher pass@2 than a reproduction of HarnessX (71.0 against 67.3 on average) at 13.0 lower mean API cost. Harnesses evolved on train tasks keep their gains on unseen test tasks of four benchmarks, and LiteEvo also lifts Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 by 1.2 to 71.4pp.

AI.tldr: LiteEvo is a lightweight harness-evolution algorithm in which tool-free meta-agents mine agent trajectories for reusable components, curate them into a versioned library, and compose each round's harness from that library, starting every benchmark from the same neutral harness. Using a frozen Qwen3.5-9B across five agentic benchmarks, it improves pass@2 by 10.5–67.7pp and matches or exceeds a HarnessX reproduction (71.0 vs. 67.3 on average) at 13.0 lower mean API cost, with gains transferring to unseen test tasks and to Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are shaped both by model weights and by the harness of components around them, yet harnesses remain handcrafted. Existing automatic evolution, such as HarnessX, still starts from a handcrafted harness, reports gains only on evolved tasks, and consumes a large meta-agent token budget (100–175M per benchmark). This motivates a lightweight, benchmark-agnostic alternative that evolves harnesses from a neutral starting point and yields transferable improvements at lower cost.
AI.method: LiteEvo evolves harnesses using tool-free meta-agents that mine agent trajectories for reusable components, curate these into a versioned library, and compose each round's harness from it. Every benchmark starts from the same neutral harness and is never named to the method.
AI.result: Evolving on graded tasks of five agentic benchmarks with a frozen Qwen3.5-9B, LiteEvo lifts pass@2 by 10.5 to 67.7pp and reaches comparable or higher pass@2 than a HarnessX reproduction (71.0 vs. 67.3 on average) at 13.0 lower mean API cost. Harnesses evolved on train tasks retain gains on unseen test tasks of four benchmarks, and LiteEvo also lifts Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 by 1.2 to 71.4pp.
AI.conclusion: LiteEvo provides a lightweight, benchmark-agnostic harness-evolution method that rivals a heavier state-of-the-art approach while being substantially cheaper, and its gains generalize to held-out tasks and to a different agent/model setting.

title: CollisionSplatting: Collision-Aware Motion Planning in 3DGS Scenes with Image-Conditioned Objectives and Adjustable Conservatism
summary: Incorporating dense visual information into motion planning remains challenging, as geometric planners rely on abstracted scene representations that discard visual richness, while learned visual models often lack geometric interpretability and computational efficiency. This paper introduces CollisionSplatting, a simple, modular, GPU-accelerated, probability-inspired distance metric with tunable conservatism that operates directly on standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. When combined with learned image-conditioned reward functions, this metric enables joint geometric and visual planning by unifying collision-aware costs with image-space objectives. We integrate the metric into GPU-accelerated Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) and Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree (RRT) planners, and show on-par or better collision-classification performance compared to representative baselines while achieving substantially higher collision-checking throughput and significantly lower VRAM usage. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our metric in real-world vision-guided navigation and manipulation tasks, highlighting 3DGS as a practical bridge between rich perception and real-time motion planning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CollisionSplatting, a GPU-accelerated, probability-inspired distance metric with tunable conservatism that operates directly on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes, enabling joint geometric and visual motion planning.
AI.motivation: Dense visual information is hard to incorporate into motion planning: geometric planners use abstracted scene representations that discard visual richness, while learned visual models often lack geometric interpretability and computational efficiency. A bridge is needed between rich perception and real-time motion planning.
AI.method: The authors propose CollisionSplatting, a simple, modular, GPU-accelerated, probability-inspired distance metric with tunable conservatism that operates directly on standard 3DGS scenes. Combined with learned image-conditioned reward functions, it unifies collision-aware costs with image-space objectives for joint geometric and visual planning. The metric is integrated into GPU-accelerated MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) and RRT (Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree) planners.
AI.result: On-par or better collision-classification performance compared to representative baselines, with substantially higher collision-checking throughput and significantly lower VRAM usage. Effectiveness is further demonstrated in real-world vision-guided navigation and manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The metric positions 3DGS as a practical bridge between rich perception and real-time motion planning, enabling joint visual-geometric planning for real-world robotic tasks.

title: Not Too Hard, Not Too Easy: Learning from Intermediate States for LLM Structured Reasoning
summary: A common principle of effective learning is to practice material that is neither already mastered nor too difficult to permit progress. We ask how to apply this principle to structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. In these tasks, a model can repeatedly revise an incomplete or incorrect candidate solution until it satisfies the problem's constraints. The intermediate candidate solutions along this trajectory provide natural training examples: some are already solved, some cannot yet be repaired by the model, and others lie at its current frontier of achievable progress. We therefore investigate whether pretrained language models can learn to revise such states and whether training on states at this frontier improves reasoning more broadly. To achieve this, we couple a pretrained language-model backbone with a recurrent updater that repeatedly revises an explicit solution state, using the same parameters at every update step. We further introduce Frontier-Oriented Curation Using Self-trajectories (FOCUS), which selects training states from trajectories generated by the current model. FOCUS measures how much the model improves each state within a fixed number of recurrent updates and prioritizes states from which it can make substantial progress. With Qwen3-1.7B, FOCUS achieves 64.4% exact solve accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and 91.1% on Maze-Hard, with similar gains observed across five Qwen and Llama backbones spanning 1.7B to 8B parameters. We further observe zero-shot transfer in the adapted LLM to mathematical reasoning and code execution, even when the recurrent updater is disabled and no downstream fine-tuning is performed.

AI.tldr: The paper studies applying the "desirable difficulty"/frontier-of-learning principle to structured reasoning (Sudoku, mazes) by pairing a pretrained LLM with a recurrent updater and a trajectory-based data curation method (FOCUS) that selects learnable frontier states.
AI.motivation: Effective learning occurs at the frontier: material neither already mastered nor too hard. For structured reasoning tasks where a model iteratively revises a candidate solution, trajectories naturally contain solved states, unreachable states, and states at the model's current frontier of achievable progress. It is unclear whether pretrained LMs can learn to revise such states and whether training on frontier states improves reasoning more broadly.
AI.method: They couple a pretrained LLM backbone with a recurrent updater that repeatedly revises an explicit solution state using shared parameters across update steps. They introduce Frontier-Oriented Curation Using Self-trajectories (FOCUS), which selects training states from trajectories generated by the current model, measuring improvement within a fixed number of recurrent updates and prioritizing states yielding substantial progress.
AI.result: With Qwen3-1.7B, FOCUS achieves 64.4% exact solve accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and 91.1% on Maze-Hard, with comparable gains across five Qwen and Llama backbones (1.7B–8B). Zero-shot transfer to mathematical reasoning and code execution is observed even with the recurrent updater disabled and no downstream fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Curating training states at the model's achievable-progress frontier, via self-generated trajectories, substantially improves structured reasoning and yields zero-shot transfer to other reasoning domains, suggesting frontier-based data selection is a broadly effective training principle for LLM reasoning.

title: Denoising Multi-Robot Trajectories
comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO)
summary: Multi-robot trajectory planning is a fundamental problem in multi-robot coordination but remains computationally challenging due to its nonconvex, multimodal, and high-dimensional nature. This work builds upon D4orm, a dynamics-aware diffusion-denoising framework, and develops a family of planning architectures for diverse operational requirements. Unlike conventional numerical optimization methods, D4orm employs sampling-based optimization to generate solution trajectories through massively parallel sampling, leveraging modern computing architectures such as GPUs. Its diffusion-denoising structure iteratively optimizes \textit{deformations} to candidate control trajectories, providing an efficient and versatile paradigm for generating kinodynamically feasible and conflict-free trajectories. Using D4orm as the building block for advanced planners, we present a decoupled planner for improved scalability, an online receding-horizon planner with feedback control, and a distributed planner for resource-constrained settings. Evaluations with differential-drive and holonomic robots in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that D4orm-based approaches find high-quality solutions faster and more reliably than other sampling-based optimization methods, such as MPPI, as well as a learned diffusion-model-based method. We further demonstrate zero-shot deployment on ten real quadrotors with obstacles, large-scale deconfliction with 100 simulated robots, and fully onboard distributed `lifelong' operation with six ground robots. Overall, these results establish diffusion denoising as a scalable and reliable framework for multi-robot coordination. Code and video: https://github.com/proroklab/d4orm

AI.tldr: This work extends D4orm, a GPU-parallel diffusion-denoising sampler, into a family of multi-robot trajectory planners (decoupled, receding-horizon online, and distributed), which outperform MPPI and a learned diffusion baseline and are validated on real quadrotors and ground robots.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot trajectory planning is nonconvex, multimodal, and high-dimensional, making it computationally hard for conventional numerical optimization and other sampling-based methods.
AI.method: Builds on D4orm, a dynamics-aware diffusion-denoising framework that performs sampling-based optimization via massively parallel GPU sampling; iteratively optimizes deformations to candidate control trajectories to yield kinodynamically feasible, conflict-free plans. It is extended into three planners: a decoupled planner for scalability, an online receding-horizon planner with feedback control, and a distributed planner for resource-constrained settings.
AI.result: D4orm-based planners find high-quality solutions faster and more reliably than MPPI and a learned diffusion-model method. Validated with differential-drive and holonomic robots in 2D/3D, zero-shot deployment on ten real quadrotors with obstacles, large-scale deconfliction with 100 simulated robots, and fully onboard distributed lifelong operation with six ground robots.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion denoising is established as a scalable and reliable framework for multi-robot coordination, supported by strong simulation benchmarks and hardware demonstrations.

title: SeOPD: Self-Evolving LLMs via Online Policy Distillation from Self-Generated Chain-of-Thought
summary: Recent advances in online policy self-distillation (OPSD) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can improve their capabilities by leveraging external privileged information (PI), such as manual annotations or feedback from external environments. However, obtaining accurate annotations and constructing sophisticated environments often require substantial human effort and computation, limiting the scalability of OPSD. While a few recent studies have explored self-improvement without external PI, the resulting gains remain limited. In this work, we explore whether LLMs can achieve comparable self-improvement without external PI. Our key observation is that a single LLM can support multiple reasoning modes, such as deep-thinking and non-thinking modes, with deep thinking generating additional information during reasoning. Based on this observation, we propose Self-Evolving Online Policy Distillation (SeOPD), which enables LLMs to distill and internalize information generated by their own chain of thought (CoT). Specifically, it (1) generates CoT with the deep-thinking mode, (2) produces responses with the non-thinking mode, and (3) uses the generated CoT as PI to provide token-level supervision for the non-thinking response, allowing new information inferred during reasoning to guide the non-thinking mode and be internalized into the shared model parameters, thereby improving both non-thinking and deep-thinking capabilities. Extensive experiments across LLMs and tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of SeOPD.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Self-Evolving Online Policy Distillation (SeOPD), a method enabling LLMs to self-improve without external privileged information by distilling information from their own deep-thinking chain-of-thought into the non-thinking mode within shared parameters.
AI.motivation: Online policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves LLMs using external privileged information (PI) like manual annotations or environment feedback, but acquiring such PI is costly and limits scalability. Existing self-improvement methods without external PI yield only limited gains, motivating the question of whether comparable self-improvement is possible without external PI.
AI.method: SeOPD leverages the observation that a single LLM supports multiple reasoning modes (deep-thinking and non-thinking). It (1) generates a chain of thought using the deep-thinking mode, (2) produces responses using the non-thinking mode, and (3) uses the generated CoT as privileged information to provide token-level supervision for the non-thinking response, so new information inferred during reasoning guides the non-thinking mode and is internalized into the shared model parameters.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various LLMs and tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of SeOPD.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can achieve substantial self-improvement without external privileged information, and the proposed SeOPD improves both non-thinking and deep-thinking capabilities by internalizing self-generated reasoning information.

title: MM-ABC: Towards Generalist Mobile Manipulation via Seeing, Coordinating and Imagining
summary: Mobile manipulation extends robot interaction beyond a fixed kinematic workspace by making the reachable region itself controllable. This flexibility introduces two central challenges: spatially grounded perception under continuous ego-motion and coordinated control of heterogeneous arm and base actions. Existing approaches strengthen geometry through explicit 3D representations or predictive world models, and often decouple mobility and manipulation into separate action streams. We argue that effective mobile manipulation requires not only decoupling, but also representations that support efficient cross-stream collaboration. We present MM-ABC, a foundation model built around Seeing, Coordinating, and Imagining Arm-Base Collaboration. MM-ABC combines sparse multi-level VLM features for spatial perception; a training-only future branch that uses world imagination and geometric intent as extra supervision, strengthening perception and manipulation-intent prediction and improving the overall learning signal; and MM-APT, which coordinates separate manipulation and mobility streams through masked joint attention and clean-action x-prediction. In controlled ablations, replacing clean-action prediction with velocity prediction lowers success on RoboCasa365 composite-seen tasks from 32.8% to 29.2%, and removing future supervision or multilevel conditioning causes larger drops. We pretrain MM-ABC on 5,000+ hours of heterogeneous robot data spanning 400K+ episodes, 12 datasets, and 17 embodiments. Experiments cover EBench, RoboCasa365, ManiSkill-HAB, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world mobile manipulation. MM-ABC achieves 44.71% success on EBench, 61.2% on RoboCasa365, 99.1% on LIBERO, 82.8% on LIBERO-Plus without perturbation training, and 83% mean success on five real-world tasks.

AI.tldr: MM-ABC is a mobile manipulation foundation model using sparse multi-level VLM features for perception, training-only world imagination supervision, and masked joint attention with clean-action x-prediction (MM-APT) to coordinate arm and base streams.
AI.motivation: Mobile manipulation makes the reachable workspace controllable but introduces two challenges: spatially grounded perception under continuous ego-motion and coordinated control of heterogeneous arm and base actions. Prior work strengthens geometry via explicit 3D representations or predictive world models and often decouples mobility from manipulation into separate action streams. The authors argue that effective mobile manipulation needs decoupling plus representations supporting efficient cross-stream collaboration.
AI.method: MM-ABC is a foundation model organized around Seeing, Coordinating, and Imagining Arm-Base Collaboration. It combines (1) sparse multi-level VLM features for spatial perception, (2) a training-only future branch that uses world imagination and geometric intent as extra supervision to strengthen perception and manipulation-intent prediction, and (3) MM-APT, which coordinates separate manipulation and mobility streams via masked joint attention and clean-action x-prediction. Pretraining used 5,000+ hours of heterogeneous robot data across 400K+ episodes, 12 datasets, and 17 embodiments.
AI.result: Controlled ablations show that replacing clean-action prediction with velocity prediction drops success on RoboCasa365 composite-seen tasks from 32.8% to 29.2%, while removing future supervision or multilevel conditioning causes larger drops. MM-ABC reaches 44.71% success on EBench, 61.2% on RoboCasa365, 99.1% on LIBERO, 82.8% on LIBERO-Plus without perturbation training, and 83% mean success on five real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Separate arm and base streams benefit from cross-stream collaboration mechanisms (masked joint attention, clean-action x-prediction), and auxiliary future imagination supervision materially improves learning. MM-ABC generalizes across simulated benchmarks and real-world mobile manipulation tasks.

title: Unlocking Latent Personalization in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to adapt to individual users, yet effective personalization remains challenging when only limited user-specific samples are available. In this work, we take an alternative perspective: pretrained LLMs may already possess latent capacity for personalization, and a few user samples may therefore suffice to guide the model toward user-aligned behavior with minimal user-specific adaptation. From this perspective, we propose LatentPersonal, a framework that formulates personalization as navigation in a shared latent adaptation space. LatentPersonal infers a compact latent representation from a few user samples to guide user-specific model adaptation, regularized with a variational information bottleneck to encourage compact preference representations. We instantiate LatentPersonal with LoRA, leveraging its low-rank parameterization as a natural low-dimensional adaptation space for personalization. By simply inserting a user-specific guidance vector between the shared low-rank factors, the model can navigate toward personalized adaptations through lightweight inference of this compact representation, without updating the shared LoRA parameters. Experiments across multiple personalization datasets demonstrate that LatentPersonal substantially reduces user-specific adaptation overhead while achieving effective personalization from only a few user-specific interactions, with particularly strong performance in the one-shot regime.

AI.tldr: LatentPersonal reformulates LLM personalization as navigation in a shared latent adaptation space, inferring a compact user representation from few samples to steer lightweight LoRA adaptations without updating shared parameters.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly expected to adapt to individual users, but effective personalization is hard when only limited user-specific samples are available. Rather than assuming personalization requires heavy user-specific training, the work posits that pretrained LLMs already possess latent capacity for personalization, so a few samples may suffice to steer user-aligned behavior with minimal adaptation.
AI.method: LatentPersonal formulates personalization as navigation in a shared latent adaptation space. It infers a compact latent representation from a few user samples to guide user-specific adaptation, regularized by a variational information bottleneck to promote compact preference representations. It is instantiated with LoRA, using its low-rank parameterization as a natural low-dimensional adaptation space. A user-specific guidance vector is inserted between the shared low-rank factors, enabling personalized adaptations via lightweight inference of this compact representation without updating shared LoRA parameters.
AI.result: Across multiple personalization datasets, LatentPersonal substantially reduces user-specific adaptation overhead while achieving effective personalization from only a few user interactions, with particularly strong performance in the one-shot regime.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs appear to harbor latent personalization capacity that can be unlocked through a compact, few-sample-derived latent representation, allowing efficient, low-overhead user-specific adaptation via latent-space navigation over shared LoRA factors.

title: Agent Priors-guided Policy Learning
summary: Robots that learn from a few demonstrations often require two forms of generalization. Compositional generalization recombines skills to solve new tasks, and skill generalization lets the learned policy behind each skill work in new situations. The two depend on each other, yet information is lost between composition and the skills it calls. Where a skill works is determined by the structure its policy is trained with, while composition sees the skill only through a separate description, such as a name, an instruction, or a symbolic operator, that omits this structure. Our key idea is to use each policy's structural prior as part of the interface between composition and the skill. A structural prior states what a behavior depends on, for example that a grasp depends only on the gripper's pose relative to the object. Built into training, it shapes where the policy generalizes; stated in language, it tells composition where the policy applies. We instantiate this idea in Agent Priors-guided Policy Learning (APPL). A construction agent segments complete demonstrations into reusable skills, proposes several structural priors for each skill, and trains and verifies one policy per prior. A runtime agent then selects among these prior-specific policies and composes them toward new task goals using their interfaces. Across MetaWorld and long-horizon ManiSkill tasks, APPL improves out-of-distribution skill generalization and enables previously unseen skill compositions; ablating the interface information substantially reduces performance. These results support the use of training-time structural assumptions as a bridge between skill learning and skill composition.

AI.tldr: APPL uses each policy's structural prior as the interface between skill learning and composition, letting a construction agent segment demos and train per-prior policies, and a runtime agent select and compose them for new goals.
AI.motivation: Few-shot robot learning needs two coupled forms of generalization: compositional generalization (recombining skills) and skill generalization (policies working in new situations). Information is lost at the composition-skill boundary: a skill's applicability depends on its policy's training structure, but composition sees the skill only via a description (name, instruction, symbolic operator) that omits that structure.
AI.method: The key idea is to use each policy's structural prior—what a behavior depends on, e.g. a grasp depends only on gripper pose relative to the object—as part of the interface between composition and the skill. A construction agent segments complete demonstrations into reusable skills, proposes several structural priors per skill, and trains and verifies one policy per prior. A runtime agent selects among these prior-specific policies and composes them toward new task goals using their interfaces.
AI.result: Across MetaWorld and long-horizon ManiSkill tasks, APPL improves out-of-distribution skill generalization and enables previously unseen skill compositions; ablating the interface information substantially reduces performance.
AI.conclusion: Training-time structural assumptions can serve as a bridge between skill learning and skill composition.

title: Are Benchmarks Reliable? Toward Structural Diagnosis via Sample-Level Capability Boundaries
comment: Submitted to NeurIPS 2026; Rejected with reviewer scores of 4,4,4
summary: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) relies heavily on benchmark scores, yet aggregate metrics can obscure whether benchmark samples reliably support model comparison. We introduce \textbf{BSDProbe}, a sample-level framework for \emph{benchmark structural diagnosis} that estimates capability boundaries from repeated-response trajectories along ordered model axes. BSDProbe summarizes samples by boundary position, boundary width, boundary-signal validity, and order consistency, then aggregates them into benchmark-level structural profiles. Experiments on six benchmarks show that benchmark reliability is axis-conditioned and heterogeneous: GSM8K and MATH exhibit the most stable measurement structures, MMLU and TriviaQA are relatively stable but heterogeneous, while GPQA and PopQA show stronger axis-conditioned risks. These profiles remain consistent across Qwen3, Qwen2.5, and cross-model axes. BSDProbe further selects compact high-value subsets whose model discriminability reaches up to $8.58\times$ that of the full benchmark. These results suggest that reliable benchmark use requires examining sample-level capability boundaries beyond leaderboard scores.

AI.tldr: BSDProbe diagnoses benchmark reliability at the sample level by estimating capability boundaries from repeated-response trajectories along ordered model axes, revealing that benchmark reliability is axis-conditioned and heterogeneous across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM evaluation relies heavily on aggregate benchmark scores, which can obscure whether individual benchmark samples reliably support model comparison. There is a need to examine sample-level capability boundaries beyond leaderboard scores.
AI.method: BSDProbe, a sample-level framework for benchmark structural diagnosis, estimates capability boundaries from repeated-response trajectories along ordered model axes. It summarizes samples by boundary position, boundary width, boundary-signal validity, and order consistency, then aggregates them into benchmark-level structural profiles, and selects compact high-value subsets.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks, reliability is axis-conditioned and heterogeneous: GSM8K and MATH show the most stable measurement structures; MMLU and TriviaQA are relatively stable but heterogeneous; GPQA and PopQA show stronger axis-conditioned risks. Profiles are consistent across Qwen3, Qwen2.5, and cross-model axes. Selected subsets reach up to 8.58x the model discriminability of the full benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Reliable benchmark use requires examining sample-level capability boundaries rather than relying solely on leaderboard scores, as benchmark reliability varies by model axis and is heterogeneous across benchmarks.

title: LQR-ArUco Fusion: Robust Hierarchical Control for Navigation and Asymmetric Manipulation in Two-Wheeled Robots
comment: 6 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Navigation and Systems (CINS), Dubai, UAE
summary: We propose a hierarchical control framework to address severe dynamic instabilities and navigational drift that arise when a two-wheeled inverted pendulum (TWIP) robot attempts asymmetric object manipulation. While two-wheeled platforms are highly manoeuvrable, their constant balancing adjustments make onboard odometry highly unreliable for precise navigation. Furthermore, the addition of a side-mounted robotic arm introduces unactuated lateral roll moments when a payload is lifted, a challenge heavily compounded on uneven terrain. To solve these coupled problems, our architecture divides the workload. An offboard vision system tracks overhead ArUco markers to provide high-latency global waypoint navigation, bypassing odometry drift. Simultaneously, a low-latency onboard control loop rejects active physical disturbances using inertial and encoder data. In our physical experiments, this dual-loop approach enabled the custom-built robot to navigate accurately, reject transient impacts from speed bumps, adapt to a dynamic seesaw ramp, and carry a payload securely without falling over its narrow wheelbase.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical, dual-loop control framework enables a two-wheeled inverted pendulum (TWIP) robot to perform asymmetric object manipulation by separating high-latency offboard vision-based global navigation from a low-latency onboard disturbance-rejection loop.
AI.motivation: TWIP robots are highly maneuverable, but their constant balancing adjustments render onboard odometry unreliable for precise navigation. Adding a side-mounted robotic arm introduces unactuated lateral roll moments when lifting a payload, a problem exacerbated on uneven terrain. These coupled instabilities and navigational drift must be resolved for asymmetric manipulation.
AI.method: A hierarchical control architecture divides the workload: an offboard vision system tracks overhead ArUco markers to provide high-latency global waypoint navigation, bypassing odometry drift; concurrently, a low-latency onboard control loop rejects active physical disturbances using inertial and encoder data.
AI.result: In physical experiments, the dual-loop approach enabled a custom-built robot to navigate accurately, reject transient impacts from speed bumps, adapt to a dynamic seesaw ramp, and carry a payload securely without falling over its narrow wheelbase.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling slow global vision-based navigation from fast onboard disturbance rejection effectively mitigates the instability and drift inherent to asymmetric manipulation on a TWIP platform, supporting reliable payload transport on challenging terrain.

title: WorldAgent: Verification-Guided Agentic Physical World Construction
summary: Constructing complex physical worlds from language requires coordinating extensive 3D environments, detailed structures and objects at different spatial scales, and interacting physical processes under both stated goals and implicit physical constraints. We present WorldAgent, an agentic framework for verification-guided physical world construction from a single natural-language prompt, without iterative user debugging. A world construction layer expands the prompt into a structured world specification and uses physical knowledge to build scenes and run numerical simulations. After every step, a verification layer inspects scene geometry and simulation states alongside rendered views. Failed checks guide automatic revisions to the specification and re-execution of the affected steps. Accepted worlds pass the required checks and remain editable for further inspection and resimulation. We introduce AgenticSimBench, on which WorldAgent achieves the best scores among the evaluated agent-based methods on five of seven metrics. In a 26-participant user study, it receives the highest mean ratings across all four criteria.

AI.tldr: WorldAgent is an agentic framework that builds complex, simulatable 3D physical worlds from a single natural-language prompt via a construction layer plus a verification layer that inspects geometry, simulation states, and rendered views and triggers automatic revisions. Evaluated on the new AgenticSimBench, it leads evaluated agent-based methods on five of seven metrics and tops all four criteria in a 26-participant user study.
AI.motivation: Constructing complex physical worlds from language is hard: it requires coordinating extensive 3D environments, multi-scale structures and objects, and interacting physical processes that must satisfy both explicitly stated goals and implicit physical constraints. Prior approaches typically need iterative user debugging, which is costly and unscalable.
AI.method: The framework has two components. A world construction layer expands the prompt into a structured world specification and leverages physical knowledge to build scenes and run numerical simulations. A verification layer then inspects scene geometry and simulation states alongside rendered views after every step; failed checks guide automatic revisions to the specification and re-execution of the affected steps. Accepted worlds pass the required checks and remain editable for further inspection and resimulation.
AI.result: On the introduced AgenticSimBench, WorldAgent achieves the best scores among the evaluated agent-based methods on five of seven metrics. In a 26-participant user study, it receives the highest mean ratings across all four evaluation criteria.
AI.conclusion: Verification-guided, agentic construction enables single-prompt generation of complex physical worlds without iterative user debugging, and is both quantitatively and perceptually preferred over evaluated agent-based baselines.

title: Humanoid Loco-Manipulation With Discrete VLA Model
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models using discrete action tokens have proven effective for controling robotic arms on manipulation tasks. For a humanoid, however, the whole-body action space -- legs, torso, arms, and hands -- is far higher-dimensional and heterogeneous, raising tokenization, training, and real-time inference challenges that the previous VLA models do not address. We present Holo-M, to our knowledge the first discrete VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation that intrinsically exploits the language model by extending its vocabulary with action tokens. In this model, we devise a unified action tokenizer that decomposes the humanoid action space into four body-part-specific tokenizers -- end-effector, body, hand, and kinematics -- enabling training across drastically different embodiments and data sources, including humanoid teleoperation, ego-centric human video, and simulation. By extending the language model's vocabulary with these action tokens, we avoid the knowledge-insulation problem inherent to the models that use separate continuous action experts. To meet real-time control requirements, we decode each body part's action tokens through grouped discrete diffusion decoding, rather than using autoregression on the action tokens. We have conducted extensive experiments on the SIMPLE humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark, in which Holo-M achieves the highest success rates in both the generalist and specialist evaluations, leading the second best by significant margins. We will release all the code and model weights.

AI.tldr: Holo-M is the first discrete VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation that extends an LM's vocabulary with action tokens, using a unified four-part action tokenizer and grouped discrete diffusion decoding, achieving top results on the SIMPLE benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete-action-token VLA models work for robotic arms but do not address humanoid whole-body control, whose action space (legs, torso, arms, hands) is far higher-dimensional and heterogeneous, posing tokenization, training, and real-time inference challenges. Continuous action-expert approaches also suffer from knowledge-insulation problems.
AI.method: Extends the language model vocabulary with action tokens (no separate continuous action experts). Uses a unified action tokenizer decomposing the humanoid action space into four body-part-specific tokenizers: end-effector, body, hand, and kinematics, enabling training across different embodiments and data sources (humanoid teleoperation, ego-centric human video, simulation). For real-time control, decodes each body part's action tokens via grouped discrete diffusion decoding instead of autoregression.
AI.result: On the SIMPLE humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark, Holo-M achieves the highest success rates in both generalist and specialist evaluations, leading the second best by significant margins.
AI.conclusion: Holo-M demonstrates that intrinsically exploiting the language model by integrating action tokens into its vocabulary is an effective approach for humanoid loco-manipulation. All code and model weights will be released.

title: CodeSkill: Latent Skill Abstraction for Long-Horizon Code Agents
summary: Code agents require long-horizon decision-making over complex interaction trajectories. However, existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches typically optimize behavior at the token level, creating a mismatch between low-level generation and high-level behavioral reasoning. This limitation leads to inefficient exploration and weak credit assignment under sparse rewards. Moreover, while large-scale agent trajectories often contain recurring multi-step behavioral patterns, their noisy token-level representations hinder effective experience reuse. To address these challenges, we propose CodeSkill, a framework that adapts hierarchical latent skill modeling to the code agent domain. CodeSkill first leverages a teacher model to distill both successful and failed trajectories into multi-level textual abstractions. It then integrates temporal variational inference with reinforcement learning to map these discrete semantics into continuous latent variables, while an adaptive boundary mechanism dynamically gates skill transitions based on execution feedback. The learned skills are injected into a frozen LLM policy as latent semantic prefixes, enabling optimization in a compact semantic space rather than over raw token sequences. By shifting RL from token-level exploration to experience-level reasoning, CodeSkill improves optimization efficiency and long-horizon behavioral coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CodeSkill achieves highly competitive performance against strong open-weight baselines across diverse general and industrial coding benchmarks. Furthermore, the learned skills exhibit strong transferability and robust cross-domain generalization, highlighting the effectiveness of explicit behavioral abstraction for scalable agentic code generation.

AI.tldr: CodeSkill applies hierarchical latent skill modeling to code agents, distilling trajectories into textual abstractions, mapping them to continuous latent skills via temporal variational inference with RL, and injecting them as latent prefixes into a frozen LLM to shift RL from token-level to experience-level reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing RL for code agents optimizes at the token level, causing a mismatch between low-level generation and high-level behavioral reasoning, leading to inefficient exploration and weak credit assignment under sparse rewards. Additionally, recurring multi-step behavioral patterns in large-scale trajectories are hard to reuse due to noisy token-level representations.
AI.method: CodeSkill uses a teacher model to distill successful and failed trajectories into multi-level textual abstractions. It combines temporal variational inference with reinforcement learning to map discrete semantics into continuous latent variables, with an adaptive boundary mechanism that dynamically gates skill transitions based on execution feedback. Learned skills are injected into a frozen LLM policy as latent semantic prefixes, enabling optimization in a compact semantic space.
AI.result: CodeSkill achieves highly competitive performance against strong open-weight baselines across diverse general and industrial coding benchmarks, and its learned skills show strong transferability and robust cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: Shifting RL from token-level exploration to experience-level reasoning improves optimization efficiency and long-horizon behavioral coherence, highlighting the effectiveness of explicit behavioral abstraction for scalable agentic code generation.

title: RoboCompiler: Graph-Native Compilation of Closed-Chain Robots for Consistent Modeling, Control, and Simulation
summary: Robots with kinematic loops, coupled actuators, and changing contacts require consistent models of configuration, motion, force, and dynamics. Yet these interfaces are often reconstructed separately for control and simulation, making closure and actuation consistency difficult to maintain. This paper presents RoboCompiler, a graph-native framework that compiles a canonical mechanism graph into a shared mechanical interface. From bodies, joints, frames, inertias, and actuator ports, it constructs closure paths and analytic residual Jacobians, then assembles feasible configurations through rank-checked continuation and correction. A tangent lift maps independent velocities to full robot and task motion, while paired actuator-port maps preserve virtual work. A constraint-curvature correction extends the reduction to accelerations and projected rigid-body dynamics, including floating-base and support modes. Cycle-local evaluation, generated Jacobians, and dependency-aware reuse enable localized updates when closure inputs change. We evaluate physical loops and task-induced constraints on a Komatsu excavator, Unitree Go2, Franka Panda, Kangaroo, and a six-UPS Stewart platform. High-precision constrained-dynamics and independent Pinocchio checks confirm mechanical consistency; MuJoCo and Isaac Sim/PhysX executions demonstrate task performance and model reuse under native contact. For Kangaroo, compilation reduces residual-and-Jacobian evaluation time by 96.7% and closed-loop rollout wall time by 66.8%, with dynamics and control held fixed.

AI.tldr: RoboCompiler is a graph-native framework that compiles a canonical mechanism graph into a shared mechanical interface, unifying configuration, motion, force, and dynamics for robots with kinematic loops, coupled actuators, and changing contacts. It achieves high-precision consistency and substantial speedups (96.7% faster residual/Jacobian evaluation, 66.8% faster rollout for Kangaroo).
AI.motivation: Robots with kinematic loops, coupled actuators, and changing contacts require consistent models of configuration, motion, force, and dynamics, but these interfaces are often reconstructed separately for control and simulation, making closure and actuation consistency difficult to maintain.
AI.method: RoboCompiler compiles a canonical mechanism graph into a shared mechanical interface: from bodies, joints, frames, inertias, and actuator ports it constructs closure paths and analytic residual Jacobians; assembles feasible configurations via rank-checked continuation and correction; applies a tangent lift mapping independent velocities to full robot/task motion; uses paired actuator-port maps to preserve virtual work; and adds a constraint-curvature correction extending the reduction to accelerations and projected rigid-body dynamics (including floating-base and support modes). Cycle-local evaluation, generated Jacobians, and dependency-aware reuse enable localized updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on physical loops and task-induced constraints across a Komatsu excavator, Unitree Go2, Franka Panda, Kangaroo, and a six-UPS Stewart platform. High-precision constrained-dynamics and independent Pinocchio checks confirm mechanical consistency; MuJoCo and Isaac Sim/PhysX executions demonstrate task performance and model reuse under native contact. For Kangaroo, compilation reduces residual-and-Jacobian evaluation time by 96.7% and closed-loop rollout wall time by 66.8%, with dynamics and control held fixed.
AI.conclusion: RoboCompiler provides a unified, graph-native mechanical interface that maintains closure and actuation consistency across diverse robots, delivering verified mechanical consistency and significant computational speedups while preserving native contact performance in control and simulation.

title: ActiveMem: Dynamic Latent Memory Trees for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-horizon reasoning and decision making. Existing memory systems typically retrieve historical trajectories or summaries as independent context fragments, overlooking the procedural dependencies underlying multi-step execution. As memory scales, such flat retrieval introduces context fragmentation and cross-task interference, leading to structurally inconsistent reasoning trajectories. We propose ActiveMem, a hierarchical memory framework that recursively organizes agent experiences into dependency-aware latent execution trees. ActiveMem abstracts trajectories into reusable subtask nodes while explicitly preserving execution transitions, enabling coherent reasoning-path retrieval conditioned on the current execution state. To support continual adaptation, ActiveMem further learns dynamic memory expansion, retrieval, and pruning policies through reinforcement learning. Experiments across various agent benchmarks demonstrate that ActiveMem consistently improves task completion, reasoning stability, and memory efficiency over existing memory-based agents. Moreover, ActiveMem enables compact open-weight models to achieve competitive performance with substantially larger proprietary systems.

AI.tldr: ActiveMem is a hierarchical memory framework for LLM agents that organizes past experiences into dependency-aware latent execution trees, enabling state-conditioned reasoning-path retrieval and RL-learned memory policies for higher task completion, stability, and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems retrieve historical trajectories or summaries as independent, flat context fragments, ignoring the procedural dependencies inherent in multi-step execution. As memory grows, this flat retrieval causes context fragmentation and cross-task interference, producing structurally inconsistent reasoning trajectories.
AI.method: ActiveMem recursively organizes agent experiences into dependency-aware latent execution trees. It abstracts trajectories into reusable subtask nodes while explicitly preserving execution transitions, allowing coherent reasoning-path retrieval conditioned on the current execution state. It further learns dynamic memory expansion, retrieval, and pruning policies via reinforcement learning to support continual adaptation.
AI.result: Across various agent benchmarks, ActiveMem consistently improves task completion, reasoning stability, and memory efficiency over existing memory-based agents. It also enables compact open-weight models to reach competitive performance with substantially larger proprietary systems.
AI.conclusion: Structuring agent memory hierarchically around procedural dependencies, combined with learned memory management policies, yields more coherent and efficient long-horizon agent reasoning, and helps close the performance gap between small open models and large proprietary ones.

title: DexRoam: Learning Mobile Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Whole-Body Human Demonstrations
summary: Mobile bimanual dexterous manipulation requires continuous coordination of locomotion, whole-body motion, and finger-level dexterity within a single trajectory, creating a severe robot demonstration bottleneck. Egocentric human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but prior approaches ease the transfer by simplifying human motion, discarding exactly the fine-grained, coupled structure such tasks depend on. We present DexRoam, a complete system for learning mobile bimanual dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations, in which whole-body motion remains continuous and coupled throughout the human-to-robot transfer process. To enable scalable collection of whole-body human manipulation demonstrations, we develop a tracker-free capture system using only a consumer VR headset and a head-mounted stereo camera, without external cameras or motion trackers. We then perform three explicit alignment stages---embodiment, action-semantic, and temporal---to map captured motion into the robot action space, preserving fine-grained whole-body motion and allowing human and robot demonstrations to be jointly learned by standard VLA policies. Real-world experiments with different VLA backbones show that human demonstrations consistently improve policy learning across training paradigms, raising average success from 29% to 56% on GR00T N1.7 and from 32% to 57% on pi0.5, while matching robot-only training with half the robot demonstrations. Ablations confirm that each alignment stage is necessary. These results highlight the potential of human demonstrations for scalable whole-body mobile manipulation with preserved fine-grained motion structure.

AI.tldr: DexRoam is a system that learns mobile bimanual dexterous manipulation from tracker-free egocentric human demonstrations by preserving continuous, coupled whole-body motion through a three-stage alignment pipeline, doubling VLA policy success rates and halving robot demonstration needs.
AI.motivation: Mobile bimanual dexterous manipulation demands continuous coordination of locomotion, whole-body motion, and finger-level dexterity within a single trajectory, which creates a severe robot demonstration bottleneck. Egocentric human demonstrations are a scalable alternative, but prior methods ease human-to-robot transfer by simplifying human motion and thereby discarding the fine-grained, coupled structure these tasks rely on.
AI.method: The authors build a tracker-free capture system using only a consumer VR headset and a head-mounted stereo camera (no external cameras or motion trackers) for scalable whole-body human manipulation data collection. They then apply three explicit alignment stages—embodiment, action-semantic, and temporal—to map captured motion into the robot action space while preserving fine-grained whole-body motion, enabling joint learning of human and robot demonstrations with standard VLA policies.
AI.result: Real-world experiments across different VLA backbones show human demonstrations consistently improve policy learning: average success rises from 29% to 56% on GR00T N1.7 and from 32% to 57% on pi0.5, while matching robot-only training using only half the robot demonstrations. Ablations confirm each alignment stage is necessary.
AI.conclusion: Human demonstrations, when transferred without discarding fine-grained whole-body motion structure, enable scalable whole-body mobile manipulation and substantially boost VLA policy learning efficiency and success.

title: CORTEX: A Verified Experience Layer for Generalist Agents
summary: An agent can solve a task today and face the same task under new facts, tools, or governing knowledge tomorrow. Most agent systems can retrieve relevant text or recall prior conversations, but they lack a principled way to decide when a previous solution is still valid, when it must be adapted, and when it should be discarded. We introduce CORTEX (Contextual Orchestration and Reuse of Task EXperience), a general AI systems framework that connects specialized agents through an external layer of verified experience. Each episode records its task conditions, source and tool state, decisive predicates, proof trace, verifier, and outcome. A meta-controller chooses exact replay, checked adaptation, fresh synthesis, or escalation. Accepted episodes can become task patterns and procedural strategies through a challenge-driven development loop. This gives the system an implicit competence layer that can grow without changing model weights. We formalize system contracts for exact replay and source-version separation, and derive when reuse saves computation. A controlled two-domain implementation tests the exact-replay core on 1,000 synthetic cases. Complete-family holdouts test procedural transfer on 1,000 new-family cases across eight clinical and policy splits, with complete fresh-evidence grounding and perfect invariance to irrelevant-field and insertion-order perturbations. The transfer trace exposes the work required for verified strategy execution. These results establish an initial path toward general intelligence through reusable procedures, typed experience, and developmental transfer.

AI.tldr: CORTEX is a framework that lets agents reuse, adapt, or discard prior solutions via an external layer of verified experience, using a meta-controller to choose exact replay, checked adaptation, fresh synthesis, or escalation, and enabling competence growth without changing model weights.
AI.motivation: Agents face recurring tasks under changing facts, tools, or governing knowledge. Existing systems retrieve text or recall conversations but lack a principled basis to decide when a previous solution remains valid, when it must be adapted, or when it should be discarded.
AI.method: CORTEX connects specialized agents through an external layer of verified experience. Each episode records task conditions, source and tool state, decisive predicates, proof trace, verifier, and outcome. A meta-controller selects exact replay, checked adaptation, fresh synthesis, or escalation. Accepted episodes become task patterns and procedural strategies via a challenge-driven development loop. The authors formalize system contracts for exact replay and source-version separation, and derive conditions under which reuse saves computation. Evaluation uses a controlled two-domain implementation: exact-replay core on 1,000 synthetic cases, and complete-family holdouts for procedural transfer on 1,000 new-family cases across eight clinical and policy splits.
AI.result: The exact-replay core and procedural transfer tests show complete fresh-evidence grounding and perfect invariance to irrelevant-field and insertion-order perturbations. The transfer trace exposes the work required for verified strategy execution.
AI.conclusion: The results outline an initial path toward general intelligence through reusable procedures, typed experience, and developmental transfer, providing an implicit competence layer that grows without retraining model weights.

title: LSTMem: Hierarchical Long Short-Term Online Memory for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as long-horizon assistants and agents, where they must both accumulate information across interactions and make the relevant parts available when later requests depend on them. Existing compact online memories typically use a single persistent state both to accumulate history and to serve readout, so what the memory stores cannot be controlled separately from what it exposes to the current computation. We propose LSTMem, an LSTM-inspired online memory that instead equips each layer of a frozen LLM with two matrix-valued states: a cell state that accumulates history and a hidden state whose readouts correct the backbone's attention. Input and forget gates control what the cell stores, while an output gate separately controls what the cell exposes through the hidden state. LSTMem further connects memory across depth through forward hidden-state propagation and block-end feedback, and uses higher-layer reconstruction gradients to refine lower-layer cell states before rebuilding hidden states from shallow to deep layers. Across memory benchmarks on Qwen3-4B-Instruct, LSTMem consistently improves MemoryAgentBench, LoCoMo, and HotpotQA over the plain backbone. Comparisons further show that the LSTM-based memory formulation outperforms an associative-memory counterpart, while removing cross-layer hidden-memory propagation degrades performance. These results demonstrate the benefits of separating memory accumulation from memory expression and organizing memory hierarchically across model depth. The code is available at https://github.com/Longchentong/LSTMem.

AI.tldr: LSTMem is an LSTM-inspired online memory that equips each frozen LLM layer with a cell state for accumulating history and a hidden state whose readouts correct attention, separating storage from expression and propagating memory across depth.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM assistants must accumulate information across interactions and later expose the relevant parts on demand. Existing compact online memories use a single persistent state for both accumulation and readout, so what the memory stores cannot be controlled separately from what it exposes to the current computation.
AI.method: Each layer of a frozen LLM gets two matrix-valued states: a cell state that accumulates history and a hidden state whose readouts correct the backbone's attention. Input and forget gates control what the cell stores, while an output gate controls what the cell exposes via the hidden state. Memory is connected across depth through forward hidden-state propagation and block-end feedback, and higher-layer reconstruction gradients refine lower-layer cell states before hidden states are rebuilt shallow-to-deep.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B-Instruct, LSTMem consistently improves MemoryAgentBench, LoCoMo, and HotpotQA over the plain backbone. The LSTM-based formulation outperforms an associative-memory counterpart, and removing cross-layer hidden-memory propagation degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: Separating memory accumulation from memory expression and organizing memory hierarchically across model depth yield measurable gains, validating the gated dual-state, depth-coupled design of LSTMem. Code is available at https://github.com/Longchentong/LSTMem.

title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
summary: Recurrent models trained from scratch have recently become competitive on ARC-style reasoning tasks, but the usual framing around small recurrent backbones overlooks two important parts of the system: task-conditioned memory and synthetic augmentation data. We study this regime through CHARM, a compact hybrid ARC model that combines recurrent reasoning with structured task memory, synthetic data, and inference-time aggregation. In existing approaches, task-conditioned memory supplies a large hidden source of capacity, reaching more than 30x the size of the recurrent backbone. We introduce a compositional sparse embedding (CoSE) for task conditioning that reduces learned task-memory parameters by over 90% while improving pass@2 in controlled ARC ablations. For the recurrent backbone, recurrent depth helps only when balanced with learning horizon. Combining these ingredients, our system reaches 84% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 46.7% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation. The benefits of structured memory also generalize to unseen puzzles and other domains. Our code, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/water-vapor/charm.

AI.tldr: CHARM is a compact hybrid ARC model combining recurrent reasoning, structured task-conditioned memory, synthetic data, and inference-time aggregation; a new compositional sparse embedding (CoSE) cuts task-memory parameters by >90%, yielding 84% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 46.7% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-2.
AI.motivation: Prior work on recurrent models for ARC-style reasoning focuses narrowly on small recurrent backbones, overlooking two critical system components: task-conditioned memory and synthetic augmentation data. Task-conditioned memory in existing approaches consumes a disproportionately large share of model capacity (over 30x the recurrent backbone), so there is a need to study and optimize this regime rather than only the backbone.
AI.method: The authors study this regime via CHARM, a compact hybrid ARC model integrating recurrent reasoning with structured task memory, synthetic data, and inference-time aggregation. They propose a compositional sparse embedding (CoSE) for task conditioning that reduces learned task-memory parameters by over 90%. They also analyze the recurrent backbone, finding that recurrent depth helps only when balanced with the learning horizon.
AI.result: CoSE improves pass@2 in controlled ARC ablations while removing over 90% of task-memory parameters. CHARM reaches 84% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 46.7% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation. The benefits of structured memory generalize to unseen puzzles and other domains.
AI.conclusion: Task-conditioned memory and synthetic augmentation are essential, underexplored components of recurrent ARC systems. Structured sparse task memory (CoSE) can dramatically reduce parameters while improving accuracy, and recurrent depth must be balanced against learning horizon. Code, dataset, and model checkpoints are released at https://github.com/water-vapor/charm.

title: Next Thoughts Are Distributions: Generative Autoregressive Reasoning in the Latent Space
summary: Reasoning problems often admit multiple valid ways to proceed. Continuous reasoning promises to move computation beyond language tokens into a more compact latent space, but representing several plausible ways to think next remains difficult. We introduce Autoregressive Thought Flow (ATF), which models the next continuous thought as a multimodal distribution. A causal autoregressive model performs the reasoning computation, while a lightweight diffusion head generates a plausible next thought from the resulting condition. The sampled thought is fed back into the model, allowing continuous reasoning to unfold for a variable number of steps while preserving the pretrained backbone. Across mathematical reasoning tasks, ATF improves accuracy with compact latent traces and benefits from reinforcement learning and additional test-time thinking. Multi-sample evaluation shows broader solution coverage, indicating that its multimodal predictions capture useful diversity among reasoning paths. Our results suggest that continuous reasoning is more effective when multiple possible next thoughts remain available rather than being collapsed into a single prediction.

AI.tldr: ATF models the next continuous thought as a multimodal distribution via a diffusion head on a causal autoregressive backbone, enabling diverse latent reasoning paths.
AI.motivation: Reasoning problems admit multiple valid solution paths, but existing continuous reasoning methods collapse the next step into a single prediction, losing useful diversity in the latent space.
AI.method: Autoregressive Thought Flow (ATF): a causal autoregressive model performs the reasoning computation, while a lightweight diffusion head generates a plausible next thought from the resulting condition. The sampled thought is fed back into the model, allowing continuous reasoning to unfold for a variable number of steps while preserving the pretrained backbone.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning tasks, ATF improves accuracy with compact latent traces, benefits from reinforcement learning and additional test-time thinking, and multi-sample evaluation shows broader solution coverage.
AI.conclusion: Continuous reasoning is more effective when multiple possible next thoughts remain available rather than being collapsed into a single prediction, as the multimodal predictions capture useful diversity among reasoning paths.

title: ChronoFlow: Hierarchical Flow Matching for Irregular Time Series Generation
summary: Recent advances in generative modeling have substantially improved time series generation, yet most existing methods either assume a regular temporal grid or focus on feature dynamics under a given sampling structure. This makes them illsuited for generating irregular time series in their native form, where a model must capture not only feature values, but also how many observations occur, when they occur, and which features are observed together. To address this heterogeneous generation problem, we propose ChronoFlow, a unified hierarchical flow matching framework organized by statistical granularity. Following a coarse-to-fine hierarchy, ChronoFlow first generates observation counts and feature-wise frequencies, then jointly generates observation times and feature co-observation patterns, and finally generates values conditioned on the realized pattern. This turns a complex joint generation problem into structurally aligned subproblems while preserving their dependencies. To evaluate complete irregular time series generation, we introduce complementary metrics spanning sample realism, sampling structure, value fidelity, and temporal and cross-feature dependencies, and validate them through controlled corruptions. Across five benchmarks, ChronoFlow achieves strong improvements in generation fidelity over existing baselines, while factorization studies support the proposed hierarchy. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ChronoFlow.

AI.tldr: ChronoFlow is a unified hierarchical flow matching framework for generating irregular time series in their native form, decomposing the heterogeneous generation problem into statistically aligned subproblems across a coarse-to-fine hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Most existing time series generative models assume a regular temporal grid or only model feature dynamics under a fixed sampling structure. They therefore cannot generate irregular time series natively, where a model must jointly capture feature values, the number of observations, their timing, and which features are co-observed.
AI.method: ChronoFlow organizes generation by statistical granularity in a coarse-to-fine hierarchy: it first generates observation counts and feature-wise frequencies, then jointly generates observation times and feature co-observation patterns, and finally generates values conditioned on the realized pattern. This converts the complex joint generation problem into structurally aligned subproblems while preserving their dependencies. Complementary evaluation metrics spanning sample realism, sampling structure, value fidelity, and temporal and cross-feature dependencies are introduced and validated via controlled corruptions.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks, ChronoFlow achieves strong improvements in generation fidelity over existing baselines, and factorization studies support the proposed hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: ChronoFlow provides an effective hierarchical flow matching approach for complete irregular time series generation, with the proposed hierarchy validated by factorization studies and code released publicly.

title: Feedback Makes Perfect: A Closed-Loop Framework for NL-to-STL Translation
summary: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) enables rigorous verification and control of cyber-physical systems, but writing correct specifications requires expertise that most requirement holders lack. Large language models can translate natural-language (NL) requirements into STL, yet stronger translators alone approach an accuracy ceiling. We argue that this ceiling stems from how the task is posed: one-shot, open-loop translation is somewhat ill-defined. Natural language is ambiguous, and, more fundamentally, what a person writes may not always be what they intend, so the target specification is not fully contained in the input text. We therefore reformulate NL-to-STL translation as a closed-loop feedback process. Each generated formula is translated back into natural language for the user to check, and natural-language corrections drive revision until the user accepts the specification. Users never read or write formal syntax. This framework rests on an asymmetry familiar from feedback control theory. The forward path, from ambiguous language to formal logic, is hard and error-prone. The feedback path, from structured STL back to language, can be made highly precise, and a precise feedback path lets an imprecise forward path achieve precise closed-loop behavior. Experiments on 500 expert-authored requirements and seven LLMs support this view. Back-translated explanations agree with expert judgments in 99.5\% of cases. Closed-loop refinement raises strong models from about 89\% open-loop accuracy to 98.0--99.2\%, and yields gains of over 30 percentage points for weaker models (e.g., 17.6\%$\rightarrow$48.0\%). Ablations show these gains come from the semantic content of the feedback rather than from repeated attempts. An expert audit and a 280-session user study further confirm the reliability of the loop. We also identify a capability threshold above which feedback no longer helps.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates NL-to-STL translation as a closed-loop feedback process where generated formulas are back-translated to natural language for user verification, exploiting the asymmetry between hard forward translation and precise feedback to raise accuracy from ~89% to 98.0-99.2% for strong models and over 30 points for weaker ones.
AI.motivation: Writing correct STL specifications requires expertise most requirement holders lack. LLMs can translate NL to STL, but stronger translators alone hit an accuracy ceiling because one-shot, open-loop translation is ill-defined: natural language is ambiguous, and what a person writes may not match their intent, so the target specification is not fully contained in the input text.
AI.method: Reformulate NL-to-STL translation as a closed-loop feedback process. Each generated formula is back-translated into natural language for the user to check, and NL corrections drive revision until acceptance, with users never reading or writing formal syntax.
