AI.method: The authors propose the Multi-task Activation and Contrast Network (MAC-Net), a covariate-aware deep learning framework. It separates tfMRI features into a dedicated neural pathway while restricting participant variables to a terminal late-fusion pathway, preventing dominant covariates from suppressing high-dimensional clinical representations. Baseline data from 6,500 Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study participants were evaluated under family-aware cross-validation and benchmarked against linear models, random forests, and alternative deep architectures. Feature attributions were computed via Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, and Input Gradient.
AI.result: The N-back plus Monetary Incentive Delay configuration achieved R² values of 0.174, 0.238, and 0.277 for fluid, crystallized, and total cognition, outperforming covariate-only baselines (0.178) and alternative deep models (0.217). N-back was the most informative paradigm; adding the Stop Signal Task marginally degraded performance. Attribution methods were highly concordant, localizing working-memory-related frontal, parietal, and cingulate regions.
AI.conclusion: Covariate-aware multi-task modeling yields reproducible cognitive-function estimations, establishing a robust neural engineering framework for clinical translation.

title: What Shared Prefixes Hide: Trajectory Dropout for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own trajectories using dense token-level feedback from a stronger teacher model. Since each update is conditioned on the reasoning prefix already generated by the student, the prefix also shapes how effectively teacher feedback is converted into learning. We find that shared prefixes can lead to weak token-level updates, a phenomenon we call Prefix-Induced Supervision Attenuation (PISA). This attenuation arises in two common cases. (i) High student confidence can weaken corrective gradients even when the teacher disagrees. (ii) Tokens that rely on earlier reasoning can receive learning signals as weak as those for simple local continuations. To solve this problem, we propose Trajectory Dropout, a simple training-time intervention that exposes these weakened signals. The student first performs a standard full-context rollout to generate a complete trajectory. During training, we randomly drop a certain proportion of the student's reasoning trajectory, while the teacher continues to observe the complete trajectory for token-level supervision. This intervention strengthens corrections for overconfident predictions and introduces additional supervision at prefix-sensitive positions. Trajectory Dropout consistently improves average performance across teacher--student model pairs of different scales and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, while also yielding gains on two out-of-domain benchmarks. It can also be flexibly integrated into existing OPD variants with negligible computational overhead, further improving their performance. These results demonstrate that Trajectory Dropout provides a simple mechanism for strengthening token-level supervision across model scales and OPD objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies Prefix-Induced Supervision Attenuation (PISA) in on-policy distillation, where shared reasoning prefixes weaken token-level teacher feedback, and proposes Trajectory Dropout, a simple intervention that randomly drops parts of the student's trajectory during training while the teacher sees the full trajectory, improving performance across scales and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In on-policy distillation (OPD), the student is trained on its own trajectories with dense token-level feedback from a stronger teacher. Because each update is conditioned on the student-generated reasoning prefix, that prefix shapes how effectively teacher feedback translates into learning. The authors find that shared prefixes can cause weak token-level updates, a phenomenon termed Prefix-Induced Supervision Attenuation (PISA), which weakens corrective gradients for high-confidence predictions and provides overly weak signals at prefix-sensitive positions.
AI.method: Trajectory Dropout is a training-time intervention. The student first performs a standard full-context rollout to generate a complete trajectory. During training, a certain proportion of the student's reasoning trajectory is randomly dropped, while the teacher still observes the complete trajectory for token-level supervision. This strengthens corrections for overconfident predictions and introduces additional supervision at prefix-sensitive positions.
AI.result: Trajectory Dropout consistently improves average performance across teacher-student model pairs of different scales and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, and also yields gains on two out-of-domain benchmarks. It integrates flexibly into existing OPD variants with negligible computational overhead, further improving their performance.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory Dropout provides a simple mechanism for strengthening token-level supervision across model scales and OPD objectives, addressing the PISA problem in on-policy distillation.

title: When Does the Concept of "Dog" Emerge in an Audio LLM?
summary: Multimodal large language models answer audio questions, but how they represent auditory semantics and use them in decisions remains unclear, limiting our understanding of response formation. We study dog barking in Qwen2.5-Omni-7B using Jacobian lens (J-lens) readout and directional interventions. We define the dog direction as a J-lens-derived hidden-state vector associated with dog; adding or removing its component modulates dog-related information. We find this information decodable without dog/bark prompt cues or animal-identification requirements. Directional interventions change response tendencies and some final answers, with effects concentrated in late-layer states immediately before generation across species classification, vocalization classification, and sound description. The dog direction shows no comparable advantage over controls in animal/other classification. These results provide causal-intervention evidence that the dog direction affects output scores in a task-dependent manner, most consistently at L22 and L24 immediately before generation.

AI.tldr: Using Jacobian-lens readout and directional interventions on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, dog-barking representations are decodable without prompt cues and causally shift audio answers mainly in late layers (L22/L24) just before generation.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs can answer audio questions, but how they internally represent auditory semantics and use that information in decision-making is unclear, limiting understanding of how responses are formed. The paper aims to reveal and causally test the internal representation of a specific sound concept (dog barking).
AI.method: The authors study dog barking in Qwen2.5-Omni-7B using a Jacobian-lens (J-lens) readout and directional interventions. They define a "dog direction" as a J-lens-derived hidden-state vector associated with dog, and add or remove its component to modulate dog-related information. They test decodability without dog/bark prompt cues or animal-identification requirements, and apply interventions across species classification, vocalization classification, and sound description tasks.
AI.result: Dog-related information is decodable without dog/bark prompt cues or animal-identification requirements. Directional interventions alter response tendencies and some final answers, with effects concentrated in late-layer states immediately before generation. The dog direction shows no comparable advantage over controls in animal/other classification. Effects are most consistent at layers L22 and L24.
AI.conclusion: The dog direction causally affects output scores in a task-dependent manner, most consistently at L22 and L24 immediately before generation. This provides causal-intervention evidence that auditory semantic representations in multimodal LLMs are used selectively depending on the task.

title: LiveOption: Evaluating LLM Agents in Structured Option Trading with Nonlinear Payoffs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems (MAS) have shown promise in financial decision-making, yet existing evaluations focus on equity trading and primarily assess directional prediction, overlooking the structural complexity of derivative markets. Option trading introduces fundamentally different challenges, including nonlinear payoffs and multi-leg strategy construction, requiring structured decisions rather than simple directional bets. We introduce LiveOption, an evaluation framework for LLM-based agents in option trading. LiveOption formulates the problem as structured sequential decision-making under realistic execution and capital constraints, and provides a reproducible environment with standardized interaction protocols. The framework includes three task suites covering portfolio overlays, event-driven earnings trading, and 0DTE intraday trading. We further propose a hierarchical metric suite that evaluates action validity, decision quality, risk characteristics, and outcome-level performance. Experiments show that current agents often fail to achieve competitive returns in most scenarios. LiveOption offers a principled testbed for evaluating structured decision-making beyond outcome-based metrics.

AI.tldr: LiveOption is a reproducible evaluation framework for LLM-based agents in option trading, framing the problem as structured sequential decision-making under realistic execution and capital constraints, spanning portfolio overlays, event-driven earnings trading, and 0DTE intraday trading, with a hierarchical metric suite covering action validity, decision quality, risk, and outcomes, revealing that current agents often fail to achieve competitive returns.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs and multi-agent systems in finance focus on equity trading and primarily assess directional prediction, overlooking the structural complexity of derivative markets. Option trading poses fundamentally different challenges, such as nonlinear payoffs and multi-leg strategy construction, which demand structured decisions rather than simple directional bets, so a dedicated testbed is needed.
AI.method: The paper introduces LiveOption, which formulates option trading as structured sequential decision-making under realistic execution and capital constraints and provides a reproducible environment with standardized interaction protocols. It includes three task suites (portfolio overlays, event-driven earnings trading, and 0DTE intraday trading) and a hierarchical metric suite evaluating action validity, decision quality, risk characteristics, and outcome-level performance.
AI.result: Experiments show that current agents often fail to achieve competitive returns in most scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LiveOption offers a principled testbed for evaluating structured decision-making beyond outcome-based metrics.

title: Just Let Linear States Forget the Distant Past: Prefix Caching via Suffix Replay for Hybrid LLMs
summary:
Hybrid LLMs interleave full-attention layers with linear-attention layers to reduce long-context inference cost, but this structure complicates prefix caching. Full-attention KV caches are token-addressable, whereas linear-attention layers maintain recurrent states that cannot be rolled back to arbitrary prefix boundaries. Existing systems materialize recurrent-state checkpoints, restricting prefix reuse to checkpoint-aligned positions.
  We present SuffixReplay, the first prefix caching system that lets hybrid LLMs reuse cached prefixes at every cache-supported page boundary without materializing recurrent-state checkpoints. Our key insight is to just let linear states forget the distant past. Modern linear-attention mechanisms use recurrent decay and gating to attenuate the influence of old inputs. Therefore, instead of checkpointing every prefix boundary, SuffixReplay approximates the state at a matched boundary by replaying only a recent suffix of the layer's input hidden states, which we retain as anchors. At the algorithmic level, SuffixReplay combines layer-wise and token-wise anchor sparsity with a bounded replay budget to control storage, computation, and quality. At the system level, it uses an independently managed anchor sidecar and a pipelined replay path to overlap anchor movement and state reconstruction with the native serving pipeline. We evaluate SuffixReplay on three hybrid LLMs: OLMo-Hybrid-7B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.6-27B-FP8. Across these models, SuffixReplay retains 91.4-100% of full-prefill quality on average across LongBench and RULER, while using only 0.36-0.51x the amortized per-token storage of SGLang's default 8192-token checkpoint cache. Integrated into SGLang, SuffixReplay reduces median TTFT by 15-70% on branching workloads, sustains 2.3-4.3x SGLang's throughput when the working set exceeds HBM, and matches SGLang on high-hit continuation traffic.

AI.tldr: SuffixReplay is a prefix caching system for hybrid LLMs that enables prefix reuse at every page boundary without storing recurrent-state checkpoints, by replaying only a recent suffix of hidden states that are retained as anchors.
AI.motivation: Hybrid LLMs interleave full-attention and linear-attention layers to lower long-context inference cost, but this breaks prefix caching: full-attention KV caches are token-addressable, while linear-attention recurrent states cannot be rolled back to arbitrary prefix boundaries. Existing systems therefore materialize recurrent-state checkpoints, which restricts prefix reuse to checkpoint-aligned positions and incurs high storage.
AI.method: SuffixReplay exploits the recurrent decay and gating of modern linear attention, which attenuate old inputs, so the state at a matched boundary can be approximated by replaying only a recent suffix of the layer's input hidden states retained as anchors, instead of checkpointing every boundary. It combines layer-wise and token-wise anchor sparsity with a bounded replay budget to control storage, computation, and quality. System-level components include an independently managed anchor sidecar and a pipelined replay path that overlaps anchor movement and state reconstruction with the native serving pipeline.
AI.result: Evaluated on OLMo-Hybrid-7B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.6-27B-FP8, SuffixReplay retains 91.4-100% of full-prefill quality on average across LongBench and RULER while using only 0.36-0.51x the amortized per-token storage of SGLang's default 8192-token checkpoint cache. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces median TTFT by 15-70% on branching workloads, sustains 2.3-4.3x SGLang's throughput when the working set exceeds HBM, and matches SGLang on high-hit continuation traffic.
AI.conclusion: SuffixReplay removes the checkpoint-alignment constraint on prefix reuse in hybrid LLMs by approximating recurrent states via bounded suffix replay, achieving near-full-prefill quality with substantially lower storage and improved TTFT and throughput in a production serving stack.

title: Federated Multi-Modal Human Activity Recognition using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) from heterogeneous wearable sensors is fundamental to the Internet of Health Things (IoHT), supporting rehabilitation, elderly care, and smart healthcare. Existing multimodal fusion methods often assign fixed equal weights to sensor streams, overlooking differences in modality importance, acquisition cost, and sensor quality, which can vary due to movement, incorrect placement, or temporary blockage. We propose an adaptive and cost-aware multimodal HAR framework based on multi-agent reinforcement learning for centralized HAR and extend it to federated learning as FedMHAR. In the centralized setting, multimodal fusion is formulated as a cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) problem, where each sensing modality is assigned a PPO-based agent that learns per-sample fusion weights, enabling the model to emphasize informative modalities while down-weighting costly sensors when cheaper alternatives provide sufficient information. In the federated setting, we introduce BiFL-PPO, a bidirectional federated optimization strategy in which a server-side PPO policy learns client-specific trust weights and feeds them back to adapt local learning rates and proximal regularization. Unlike round-level optimization, BiFL-PPO uses dense batch-level rewards for more frequent feedback and stable training under heterogeneous client data. Evaluation on the MEx Rehabilitation and UTD Multimodal Human Action datasets shows that the centralized framework achieves 87.30% and 94.98% accuracy, respectively, outperforming conventional fusion methods and state-of-the-art HAR models. FedMHAR achieves 79.74% and 77.49% in the federated setting, consistently surpassing FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, FedNova, and AdaFedProx, while providing more stable performance and reducing sensor acquisition cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive, cost-aware multimodal HAR framework using multi-agent RL (PPO agents per modality for per-sample fusion weights), extended to federated learning as FedMHAR with a bidirectional optimization strategy BiFL-PPO that learns client trust weights.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal fusion methods assign fixed equal weights to sensor streams, overlooking differences in modality importance, acquisition cost, and sensor quality that vary due to movement, incorrect placement, or temporary blockage.
AI.method: Centralized: multimodal fusion formulated as cooperative MARL, each sensing modality assigned a PPO-based agent learning per-sample fusion weights. Federated: FedMHAR with BiFL-PPO, a bidirectional federated optimization where a server-side PPO policy learns client-specific trust weights fed back to adapt local learning rates and proximal regularization, using dense batch-level rewards instead of round-level optimization.
AI.result: Centralized: 87.30% (MEx Rehabilitation) and 94.98% (UTD Multimodal Human Action) accuracy, outperforming conventional fusion and SOTA HAR models. Federated FedMHAR: 79.74% and 77.49%, surpassing FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, FedNova, and AdaFedProx, with more stable performance and reduced sensor acquisition cost.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, cost-aware multimodal fusion via MARL and its federated extension enable emphasis on informative modalities and down-weighting of costly sensors, improving accuracy and stability while reducing acquisition cost.

title: RelaxKV: Recomputation Guided by the Query with Sparse Context Attention for Efficient KV Cache Reuse
summary: Cross-request KV caching reduces the prefill cost of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), but conventional prefix caching severely limits cache reuse across requests. Position-Independent Caching (PIC) removes this constraint by reusing independent chunks, but their KV states miss cross-chunk interactions. Existing methods selectively recompute token states to recover these missing interactions, but primarily allocate the recomputation budget to selecting which states to recompute, while fixing the recomputation context to the full causal prefix. We introduce RelaxKV, which formulates selective cache repair as a joint allocation problem over repair targets and recomputation context. Guided by the user query, RelaxKV identifies layer-specific repair targets and restricts their recomputation to a query-relevant context, reducing attention computation. Across four decoder models, RelaxKV at a 15% anchor ratio improves aggregate LongBench performance over ProphetKV on all models. On Qwen3-14B, RelaxKV provides a stronger quality-TTFT trade-off than ProphetKV across a 5%-30% anchor-ratio sweep, and achieves the best selective results on RULER-MV and LV-Eval at 16K and 32K context lengths. Controlled ablations further demonstrate the importance of recomputation context selection.

AI.tldr: RelaxKV reformulates selective KV cache repair for RAG as a joint allocation problem over both repair targets and recomputation context, restricting recomputation to query-relevant context to cut attention computation while improving quality.
AI.motivation: Cross-request KV caching cuts RAG prefill cost, but prefix caching restricts reuse, and Position-Independent Caching (PIC) loses cross-chunk interactions. Existing selective recomputation methods recover these interactions but allocate budget only to choosing which states to recompute, fixing the recomputation context to the full causal prefix—an unexplored inefficiency.
AI.method: RelaxKV formulates selective cache repair as a joint allocation problem over repair targets and recomputation context. Guided by the user query, it identifies layer-specific repair targets and restricts their recomputation to a query-relevant context, thereby reducing attention computation.
AI.result: Across four decoder models at a 15% anchor ratio, RelaxKV improves aggregate LongBench performance over ProphetKV on all models. On Qwen3-14B it yields a stronger quality-TTFT trade-off than ProphetKV over a 5%–30% anchor-ratio sweep, and achieves the best selective results on RULER-MV and LV-Eval at 16K and 32K context lengths. Controlled ablations confirm the importance of recomputation context selection.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing recomputation context alongside repair targets—rather than fixing the context to the full causal prefix—is key to efficient and effective selective KV cache repair in RAG.

title: When Evidence Changes the Subject: Subject-Typed Claim Licensing for Learned Routing
summary: Modern learned systems increasingly combine learned components with search, repair, or external solvers. Benchmarks often measure the resulting end-to-end system, while scientific claims may concern only one component, creating an attribution problem: evidence can fail to support the requested component-level claim while still supporting a positive conclusion about the larger system. Existing evidence-to-claim methods primarily calibrate claim strength. We argue that composite systems require a second dimension: scientific subject. We address this problem with subject-typed claim licensing, which separates weaker conclusions about the requested subject from positive but non-substitutive credit about another subject. We instantiate this idea in SCOPE-Routing for preference-conditioned multigraph routing. Non-authors reproducibly apply the declared semantics; held-out review yields fewer reference-relative upward deviations than unstructured review, while the difference from a strong evidence checklist remains unresolved; and a controlled routing study shows that score-optimal and claim-eligible methods can differ while valid hybrid-system credit is preserved. These results motivate treating claim strength and scientific subject as distinct dimensions of evidence-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "subject-typed claim licensing," a framework that treats claim strength and scientific subject as distinct dimensions for evaluating evidence in composite learned systems, instantiated as SCOPE-Routing.
AI.motivation: Learned systems increasingly combine learned components with search, repair, or external solvers, so benchmarks measure the end-to-end system while scientific claims may concern only one component. This creates an attribution problem where evidence supports a positive conclusion about the larger system but fails to support the requested component-level claim. Existing evidence-to-claim methods only calibrate claim strength, leaving subject attribution unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors propose subject-typed claim licensing, which separates weaker conclusions about the requested subject from positive but non-substitutive credit about another subject. They instantiate this as SCOPE-Routing for preference-conditioned multigraph routing, using non-author reproducibility to apply the declared semantics, a held-out review comparison against unstructured review and a strong evidence checklist, and a controlled routing study.
AI.result: Non-authors reproducibly apply the declared semantics. Held-out review yields fewer reference-relative upward deviations than unstructured review, though the difference from a strong evidence checklist remains unresolved. The controlled routing study shows that score-optimal and claim-eligible methods can differ while valid hybrid-system credit is preserved.
AI.conclusion: These results motivate treating claim strength and scientific subject as distinct dimensions of evidence-based evaluation for composite learned systems.

title: What Happens During Autonomous Deep Research After the User Steps Away?
summary: In autonomous deep research, a user provides a task and relevant background, then leaves the agent to conduct an extended investigation without further human intervention. We study how this initial user information is reflected in intermediate actions and how these actions relate to final recommendations. We introduce DRaligned, a counterfactual behavioral evaluation framework built on PDR-Bench. By varying one task-relevant user factor while keeping the remaining context fixed, we compare acquisition requests, working drafts, and final reports. Source-grounded extraction, blinded local judgments, and deterministic aggregation yield coarse directional measurements while leaving ambiguous cases unresolved. Our experiments show that strong user-specific delivery can emerge from a largely shared research process: agents investigate similar broad questions but allocate requests differently, and final recommendations distinguish user conditions more clearly than explicit requests do. Reports can also integrate user factors that were not jointly visible during acquisition. In readable draft-to-report comparisons, recommendations often retain their coarse user-specific direction despite substantial rewriting. Final directional differences recur across tested agent models, execution harnesses, and evaluator models, even as execution paths vary. These findings describe how initial user information shapes autonomous research and clarify the relationship between the process an agent follows and the recommendations it delivers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DRaligned, a counterfactual behavioral evaluation framework built on PDR-Bench, to examine how a user's initial task information propagates through an autonomous deep research agent's intermediate actions and shapes its final recommendations.
AI.motivation: In autonomous deep research, the user supplies a task and background and then withdraws, leaving the agent to investigate independently. It remains unclear how the initial user information is reflected in the agent's intermediate actions and how those actions relate to the final recommendations it delivers.
AI.method: DRaligned performs counterfactual evaluation on PDR-Bench: it varies one task-relevant user factor while holding the rest of the context fixed, then compares acquisition requests, working drafts, and final reports. The analysis uses source-grounded extraction, blinded local judgments, and deterministic aggregation to produce coarse directional measurements, leaving ambiguous cases unresolved.
AI.result: Strong user-specific delivery can emerge from a largely shared research process: agents investigate similar broad questions but allocate requests differently, and final recommendations separate user conditions more clearly than explicit requests do. Reports can also integrate user factors not jointly visible during acquisition. In draft-to-report comparisons, recommendations usually retain their coarse user-specific direction despite substantial rewriting. Final directional differences recur across agent models, execution harnesses, and evaluator models, even as execution paths vary.
AI.conclusion: The findings characterize how initial user information shapes autonomous research and clarify the relationship between the process an agent follows and the recommendations it ultimately delivers.

title: PPG-LM: A Photoplethysmography-Language Model with Multi-Level Clinical Alignment
summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is widely recorded by clinical monitors and consumer wearables, providing a scalable source of continuous physiological information. These recordings offer an opportunity for physiological assessment at scale, but realizing this potential requires models to learn from both signal-derived physiological supervision and broader clinical context captured in electronic health records (EHRs). This involves aligning information spanning local observations, care events, and entire visits with PPG representations at corresponding temporal scales. However, existing PPG foundation models primarily rely on task-specific prediction heads, while the medical knowledge of large language models does not necessarily translate into waveform understanding. To bridge this gap, we introduce PPG-LM, the first PPG-language model family to learn physiological representations from both signal-derived supervision and broader clinical context captured in EHRs. To construct clinically grounded captions, we develop an automatic captioning pipeline that generates segment-, event-, and visit-level descriptions from signal measurements and structured EHR records. We then learn from these pairs through a two-stage framework that first establishes segment-language correspondence through contrastive learning and waveform-conditioned captioning, then extends alignment to events and visits through time-aware aggregation and temporal statement matching. Pretrained on approximately 73k hours of PPG, PPG-LM supports language-based recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and segment captioning. Experiments on MC-MED, MIMIC-III, and VitalDB show improved retrieval and caption factuality over language-model baselines and gains over PPG and time-series foundation models on multiple clinical prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: PPG-LM is the first PPG-language model family that aligns PPG waveforms with clinically grounded, multi-level natural language captions derived from signals and EHRs, enabling retrieval, captioning, and improved clinical prediction.
AI.motivation: PPG is widely recorded yet underused for scalable physiological assessment. Realizing this potential requires models to learn from both signal-derived physiological supervision and broader clinical context in EHRs across multiple temporal scales (segments, care events, visits). Existing PPG foundation models rely on task-specific heads, and LLM medical knowledge does not transfer to waveform understanding.
AI.method: The authors build an automatic captioning pipeline generating segment-, event-, and visit-level descriptions from signal measurements and structured EHR records. They train PPG-LM with a two-stage framework: (1) contrastive learning plus waveform-conditioned captioning for segment-language correspondence; (2) time-aware aggregation and temporal statement matching to extend alignment to events and visits. Pretrained on ~73k hours of PPG.
AI.result: PPG-LM supports language-based recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and segment captioning. On MC-MED, MIMIC-III, and VitalDB, it improves retrieval and caption factuality over language-model baselines and outperforms PPG and time-series foundation models on multiple clinical prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Aligning PPG representations with multi-scale clinical language provides a scalable, generalizable route to physiological assessment, bridging waveform understanding with clinical context and improving downstream performance.

title: EverMine: Dissecting the Self-Evolution of Research Capabilities in Long-Horizon Alpha Research
summary: Self-evolving agents aim to turn research feedback into reusable skills, tools, and research rules. Whether these accumulated capabilities continue to improve later research requires controlled evaluation. Long-horizon alpha discovery provides a state-dependent setting: once a new factor enters the portfolio, the predictive information already covered changes, so the value of the same candidate or experience may change over time. We introduce EverMine, an empirical framework for studying self-evolving research capabilities in long-horizon alpha discovery. EverMine decomposes the research state into history (Hist), the current factor portfolio (Frontier), and reusable capabilities (Cap). Under matched resource limits, we compare complete runs with fixed or evolving Cap, and replace Cap while holding Hist and Frontier fixed to estimate the conditional value of accumulated capabilities. We also combine full trajectories with historical-state replay to examine how experience-based decisions affect candidate selection and portfolio outcomes. Across 18 long-horizon trajectories, end-to-end comparisons show no consistent gain from Cap evolution. Across 48 continuation branches from shared Hist and Frontier states, accumulated Cap also does not consistently outperform the initial Cap. Parameter tuning of existing factor structures can still improve the portfolio. In an exploratory replay of two screening batches from one Evolving trajectory, some screened-out candidates have positive marginal value at the original state, yet submitting all screened-out candidates sequentially slightly lowers final portfolio IC in both batches. These results show that candidate value depends on the evolving portfolio and submission order, and motivate evaluating self-evolving research capabilities through end-to-end outcomes, conditional capability value, and the consequences of experience-based decisions.

AI.tldr: EverMine evaluates self-evolving research capabilities in long-horizon alpha discovery, finding no consistent advantage from accumulated capabilities over fixed ones.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents aim to convert research feedback into reusable skills, tools, and rules, but whether these accumulated capabilities improve later research requires controlled evaluation. Long-horizon alpha discovery provides a state-dependent setting where a factor's value depends on the current portfolio.
AI.method: The framework decomposes the research state into history (Hist), current factor portfolio (Frontier), and reusable capabilities (Cap). Under matched resource limits, complete runs with fixed or evolving Cap are compared, and Cap is replaced while holding Hist and Frontier fixed to estimate conditional capability value. Full trajectories are combined with historical-state replay to study how experience-based decisions affect candidate selection and portfolio outcomes.
AI.result: Across 18 long-horizon trajectories, end-to-end comparisons show no consistent gain from Cap evolution. Across 48 continuation branches from shared Hist and Frontier states, accumulated Cap does not consistently outperform initial Cap. Parameter tuning of existing factor structures can still improve the portfolio. In an exploratory replay of two screening batches, some screened-out candidates have positive marginal value at the original state, yet submitting all screened-out candidates sequentially slightly lowers final portfolio IC in both batches.
AI.conclusion: Candidate value depends on the evolving portfolio and submission order. This motivates evaluating self-evolving research capabilities through end-to-end outcomes, conditional capability value, and the consequences of experience-based decisions.

title: Reasoning on the Simplex: Geometric Fixed-Point Models
summary: Looped reasoners spend test-time compute by iterating a weight-tied map, but a small residual does not mean the state is a fixed point when that map lives in unconstrained latent space. We propose Geometric Fixed-Point Reasoning (GFPR), in which the iterated state is the prediction itself: a field of categorical beliefs on a product of simplices, whose argmax is the answer at every step. Because the state is a belief, task structure can be imposed through compact convex relaxations, either as structured readouts or directly in the recurrent state; in the latter case the update remains a continuous self-map, so a fixed point exists for any parameters. At about 7M parameters, GFPR reaches 95.1% exact match on Sudoku-Extreme, 92.0% on Maze-Hard, and 100% sequence accuracy on S_5 length 128, above the published FPRM numbers at the same scale. The same update also trains a 201M language model on FineWeb-Edu in which each site is a distribution over the vocabulary; with 24 Picard steps it is above GPT-2 small on four zero-shot multiple-choice tasks and above GPT-2 medium on ARC-Easy.

AI.tldr: GFPR makes the iterated state a field of categorical beliefs on a product of simplices (a continuous self-map), guaranteeing a fixed point exists for any parameters, and achieves strong results on reasoning and language tasks.
AI.motivation: In looped reasoners, a small residual does not imply the state is a fixed point when the iterated map lives in unconstrained latent space; the state may drift without converging to a true solution. This motivates placing the iterated state in a structured, constrained space where convergence is meaningful.
AI.method: Geometric Fixed-Point Reasoning (GFPR) makes the iterated state the prediction itself: a field of categorical beliefs on a product of simplices, whose argmax is the answer at each step. Task structure is imposed via compact convex relaxations, either as structured readouts or directly in the recurrent state; the latter keeps the update a continuous self-map, so a fixed point exists for any parameters.
AI.result: At ~7M parameters, GFPR achieves 95.1% exact match on Sudoku-Extreme, 92.0% on Maze-Hard, and 100% sequence accuracy on S_5 length 128, surpassing published FPRM at the same scale. The same update also trains a 201M language model on FineWeb-Edu with per-site distributions over the vocabulary; using 24 Picard steps it exceeds GPT-2 small on four zero-shot multiple-choice tasks and GPT-2 medium on ARC-Easy.
AI.conclusion: By iterating over a belief-state (product of simplices) that is a continuous self-map, GFPR guarantees fixed-point existence and generalizes from small-scale structured reasoning to large-scale language modeling, outperforming comparable baselines.

title: OSCC: Certified Observation-Safe Coupling Optimization for Gradient-Noise Control in Imperfect-Information Learning
summary: Coupled rollouts can reduce the noise of counterfactual action comparisons, but two issues prevent standard common-random-number constructions from serving as a general learning primitive in imperfect-information environments. First, an invalid coupling may expose hidden state, synchronize endogenous policy randomness, or misalign chance events after counterfactual histories diverge. Second, in multi-action policy optimization, lower return-contrast variance is not by itself the relevant objective: the optimizer depends on the return covariance matrix after projection through the local policy-gradient geometry. We introduce observation-safe counterfactual coupling (OSCC), a framework that defines an admissible class through marginal preservation, information-state safety, branch-local policy randomness, semantic event alignment, and trace-before-oracle replay. We derive a gradient-aware coupling criterion showing that, for marginal-preserving couplings, policy-gradient noise changes are determined by policy-Jacobian-weighted off-diagonal return covariance. This motivates OSCC-Select, a calibration-only selector that chooses among independent, root-only, continuation-only, and fully coupled rollouts using separate safety and gain certificates. Its gain target combines projected gradient noise with measured physical sampling cost and falls back to independent sampling whenever a simultaneous lower confidence bound does not certify improvement. On 100,000 fixed-root Leduc comparisons, the fully coupled CP-GRPO instantiation reduces return-contrast variance from 41.1158 to 18.1441, a 55.87% reduction, while preserving the declared branch marginals. With three actions, OSCC-Select chooses continuation coupling and attains gradient-noise trace 0.0783 versus 0.0917 for return-variance selection. Increasing calibration from 64 to 2,048 groups raises certification from 0.327 to 0.995.

AI.tldr: OSCC is a framework for safe, gradient-aware counterfactual rollout coupling in imperfect-information games, with a calibration-only selector (OSCC-Select) that provably targets policy-gradient noise rather than return-variance alone.
AI.motivation: Coupled rollouts reduce noise in counterfactual action comparisons, but standard common-random-number constructions cannot be used as a general learning primitive in imperfect-information settings: invalid couplings may leak hidden state, synchronize endogenous policy randomness, or misalign chance events after histories diverge. Moreover, in multi-action policy optimization, minimizing return-contrast variance is not the correct objective, since the optimizer depends on the return covariance matrix projected through local policy-gradient geometry.
AI.method: The paper introduces observation-safe counterfactual coupling (OSCC), defining an admissible coupling class via marginal preservation, information-state safety, branch-local policy randomness, semantic event alignment, and trace-before-oracle replay. It derives a gradient-aware coupling criterion showing that for marginal-preserving couplings, policy-gradient noise changes are governed by policy-Jacobian-weighted off-diagonal return covariance. This motivates OSCC-Select, a calibration-only selector that picks among independent, root-only, continuation-only, and fully coupled rollouts using separate safety and gain certificates; its gain target combines projected gradient noise with measured physical sampling cost and reverts to independent sampling unless a simultaneous lower confidence bound certifies improvement.
AI.result: On 100,000 fixed-root Leduc comparisons, the fully coupled CP-GRPO instantiation cuts return-contrast variance from 41.1158 to 18.1441 (55.87% reduction) while preserving declared branch marginals. With three actions, OSCC-Select selects continuation coupling, attaining gradient-noise trace 0.0783 versus 0.0917 for return-variance-based selection. Raising calibration from 64 to 2,048 groups increases certification from 0.327 to 0.995.
AI.conclusion: Safe counterfactual coupling must be validated along safety and gradient-relevant gain axes rather than return variance alone. OSCC supplies this admissibility framework and OSCC-Select operationalizes it, yielding certified variance reduction, better projected gradient-noise behavior, and calibration-driven reliability.

title: Dr. Free: You Don't Need Difficulty Rewards for Self-Evolving Search Agents
summary: A central limitation of current data-free self-evolution methods for training search agents is their reliance on difficulty-based proposer rewards. These methods reward a proposer for generating questions that challenge a co-evolving solver, using solver difficulty as a proxy for question quality. Yet difficulty alone is insufficient to distinguish questions that require cross-passage evidence from those that are answerable via simpler shortcuts. In addition, measuring difficulty demands repeated solver rollouts for every candidate question, leading to substantial computational costs. In this paper, we introduce \methodname, the first self-evolving search framework that eliminates difficulty-based proposer rewards and directly optimizes for evidence necessity relative to shortcut contexts. Dr. Free samples relational chains from a knowledge graph and pairs them with aligned passages, giving question generation an explicit multi-hop structure. A generated question receives a positive information-gain reward only when the likelihood of the target answer under the complete evidence passages exceeds the maximum likelihood under all evaluated shortcut contexts. Because this signal is computed from teacher-forced likelihoods, it removes the need for pass-rate estimation and reduces proposer training time by over $7\times$. Experiments on seven open-domain QA benchmarks show that Dr. Free outperforms prior data-free search agents and the supervised baseline, with large improvements on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Dr. Free is a self-evolving search-agent training framework that replaces difficulty-based proposer rewards with an evidence-necessity reward computed via teacher-forced likelihoods, improving multi-hop QA while cutting proposer training time by over 7x.
AI.motivation: Current data-free self-evolution methods for search agents rely on difficulty-based proposer rewards, using solver difficulty as a proxy for question quality. This is problematic for two reasons: (1) difficulty alone cannot distinguish questions requiring cross-passage evidence from those solvable via simpler shortcuts; (2) measuring difficulty requires repeated solver rollouts per candidate question, incurring substantial computational cost.
AI.method: Dr. Free eliminates difficulty-based proposer rewards and directly optimizes for evidence necessity relative to shortcut contexts. It samples relational chains from a knowledge graph and pairs them with aligned passages, giving question generation an explicit multi-hop structure. A generated question receives a positive information-gain reward only when the likelihood of the target answer under the complete evidence passages exceeds the maximum likelihood under all evaluated shortcut contexts. Since this signal is computed from teacher-forced likelihoods, pass-rate estimation is unnecessary.
AI.result: Proposer training time is reduced by over 7x. On seven open-domain QA benchmarks, Dr. Free outperforms prior data-free search agents and a supervised baseline, with large improvements on multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing directly for evidence necessity, rather than solver difficulty, yields a more effective and computationally efficient self-evolving search-agent training signal, particularly benefiting multi-hop question answering.

title: OpenFC: Learning Verification Policies towards Open-Search Fact Checking
summary: Open-search fact checking is not merely retrieval followed by classification, but a sequential decision problem in which every query, source visit, and stopping decision reshapes the evidence available for verification. Yet existing systems often distribute these decisions across predefined pipelines or separately prompted modules rather than learning them as a unified task-specific policy. We introduce \textbf{OpenFC}, a unified verification-policy training framework that post-trains Qwen3-8B as a compact next-action controller over reasoning, evidence acquisition, and stopping. OpenFC learns this policy in two stages. \textbf{Stepwise-Calibrated Cold Start (SCCS)} uses a strong training-time supervisor to review post-initial reasoning, tool-use, and stopping proposals before execution, producing reliable trajectories for supervised fine-tuning without access to gold verdicts. \textbf{Verification-Aware Reinforcement Learning (VA-RL)} then improves the cold-start policy on unresolved claims through budget-aware tool rewards, label-aware advantage reweighting, and localized response masking. Across six fact-checking benchmarks, OpenFC achieves 70.39\% average accuracy and 63.30\% macro-F1, the highest overall averages among the evaluated methods. Stage-wise ablations further show that SCCS and VA-RL provide complementary gains, supporting the design of the two-stage training framework. These results position OpenFC as a strong and effective framework for open-search fact-checking. We will open-source our code and release the model checkpoints to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: OpenFC post-trains Qwen3-8B as a compact next-action controller for open-search fact checking via a two-stage policy training framework, achieving state-of-the-art averages across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Open-search fact checking is a sequential decision problem where queries, source visits, and stopping decisions reshape available evidence, yet existing systems distribute these decisions across predefined pipelines or separately prompted modules rather than learning them as a unified task-specific policy.
AI.method: OpenFC learns a verification policy in two stages: Stepwise-Calibrated Cold Start (SCCS), which uses a strong training-time supervisor to review post-initial reasoning, tool-use, and stopping proposals before execution to produce reliable trajectories for SFT without gold verdicts; and Verification-Aware Reinforcement Learning (VA-RL), which improves the cold-start policy on unresolved claims via budget-aware tool rewards, label-aware advantage reweighting, and localized response masking.
AI.result: Across six fact-checking benchmarks, OpenFC achieves 70.39% average accuracy and 63.30% macro-F1, the highest overall averages among evaluated methods. Stage-wise ablations show SCCS and VA-RL provide complementary gains.
AI.conclusion: OpenFC constitutes a strong and effective framework for open-search fact checking, with code and model checkpoints to be open-sourced for reproducibility.

title: JustQuant: You Don't Need Smoothing, SVD, or Rotation for 4-Bit Activation Quantization
summary: Recent generative models have become increasingly powerful, but their inference cost continues to grow. Model quantization offers a promising way to compress these models and accelerate inference. However, at 4 bits, activation quantization is substantially more challenging than weight quantization. Recent post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) methods have made progress in 4-bit activation quantization by introducing smoothing, SVD branches, rotations, mixed precision, or advanced formats such as NVFP4. These additional operators and data types impose demanding requirements on inference engines and hardware, limiting the broad adoption of low-precision models. Can quantization be achieved using only plain low-bit operators? To answer this question, we propose JustQuant, a simple yet effective framework that moves the complexity of low-bit quantization from deployment-time operators into the training process. We first revisit model quantization from the perspective of knowledge distillation and show that a key reason existing PTQ and QAT methods fail is that they typically exploit supervision at only a single level. We then introduce Theseus QAD, a quantization-aware distillation method that progressively applies multi-level supervision, analogous to the gradual replacement process in the Ship of Theseus. Extensive experiments on DiT and diffusion large language models show two distinct regimes. For smaller models, Theseus QAD can serve as a lightweight warm-up stage that substantially improves subsequent QAT with plain operators, while naive QAD may collapse in the same setting. For larger models, Theseus QAD provides a stronger distillation training path than ordinary QAD. Across both regimes, JustQuant improves low-bit quantization quality while avoiding the complex operators required by many existing PTQ methods.

AI.tldr: JustQuant is a framework that shifts the complexity of 4-bit activation quantization from deployment-time operators into training, using a quantization-aware distillation method called Theseus QAD that applies multi-level supervision. It improves low-bit quantization quality on DiT and diffusion LLMs without complex operators.
AI.motivation: Generative models are increasingly powerful but costly to run. Quantization compresses and accelerates them, yet 4-bit activation quantization remains much harder than weight quantization. Existing PTQ/QAT methods achieve progress via smoothing, SVD branches, rotations, mixed precision, or formats like NVFP4, but these operators and data types burden inference engines and hardware, limiting adoption. The authors ask whether quantization can be done with only plain low-bit operators.
AI.method: JustQuant moves low-bit quantization complexity from deployment-time operators into training. It revisits quantization through knowledge distillation, arguing existing PTQ/QAT methods fail because they use supervision at only a single level. It introduces Theseus QAD, a quantization-aware distillation method that progressively applies multi-level supervision, analogous to the gradual replacement in the Ship of Theseus.
AI.result: Experiments on DiT and diffusion large language models reveal two regimes. For smaller models, Theseus QAD acts as a lightweight warm-up that substantially improves subsequent QAT with plain operators, whereas naive QAD may collapse. For larger models, Theseus QAD provides a stronger distillation training path than ordinary QAD. Across both regimes, JustQuant improves low-bit quantization quality while avoiding complex operators used by many existing PTQ methods.
AI.conclusion: Quantization can be achieved with only plain low-bit operators by relocating complexity into training. JustQuant with Theseus QAD improves 4-bit activation quantization quality for DiT and diffusion LLMs and avoids the complex operators and formats required by many existing PTQ methods.

title: Supervision Recovery for Time Series Anomaly Detection via Context-Anchored Pairing
summary: Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) remains challenging not only because anomaly labels are scarce, but also because temporal anomalies are highly context-dependent. Existing methods often rely on unsupervised objectives or surrogate abnormal patterns, providing limited supervision for context-dependent normal--anomalous distinctions. We propose Context-Anchored Pair Supervision (CAPS), a supervision-recovery framework for TSAD. CAPS views ideal anomaly supervision as a matched comparison between normal and anomalous outcomes under the same temporal context, and seeks to recover such supervision without target-domain anomaly labels. Using simulated normal--anomalous pairs, CAPS learns structure and anomaly-semantic representations through reconstruction, background consistency, and within-pair counterfactual recombination. The resulting anomaly representations form a continuous semantic space with coarse modes and induce a sampleable multimodal prior. CAPS conditionally realizes sampled semantics as residual-form effects on target reference trajectories. The resulting context-anchored normal--anomalous counterparts provide temporal supervision for discriminative detector learning. Experiments on nine datasets show that CAPS achieves the strongest aggregate performance across all four evaluation metrics among the compared methods, while complementary ablations and transfer analyses support the roles of context anchoring, semantic disentanglement, and conditional realization.

AI.tldr: CAPS is a supervision-recovery framework for time series anomaly detection that reconstructs context-matched normal-anomalous pairs without target-domain labels, enabling strong discriminative detector learning.
AI.motivation: Time series anomaly detection faces two core obstacles: scarce anomaly labels and the highly context-dependent nature of temporal anomalies. Existing methods rely on unsupervised objectives or surrogate abnormal patterns, which provide limited supervision for distinguishing normal from anomalous behavior under specific temporal contexts.
AI.method: CAPS treats ideal anomaly supervision as a matched comparison between normal and anomalous outcomes within the same temporal context. Using simulated normal-anomalous pairs, it learns structure and anomaly-semantic representations via reconstruction, background consistency, and within-pair counterfactual recombination. These anomaly representations form a continuous semantic space with coarse modes, inducing a sampleable multimodal prior. Sampled semantics are conditionally realized as residual-form effects on target reference trajectories, yielding context-anchored normal-anomalous counterparts that provide temporal supervision for discriminative detector learning.
AI.result: Across nine datasets, CAPS achieves the strongest aggregate performance on all four evaluation metrics compared with competing methods. Ablations and transfer analyses confirm the contributions of context anchoring, semantic disentanglement, and conditional realization.
AI.conclusion: CAPS demonstrates that recovering context-anchored normal-anomalous supervision without target-domain labels is an effective strategy for time series anomaly detection, with its key components validated through ablation and transfer studies.

title: EAT: Expert Account Tracker for Efficient MoE Inference
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as a revolutionary method to scale Transformer models. However, traditional MoE architecture still suffers from inefficiency since a large number of experts are unnecessarily activated. Existing approaches for reducing the number of activated experts often overlook the historical performance of each expert. In this paper, we propose EAT, a novel method called Expert Account Tracker (EAT), which utilizes history-awareness metrics and adaptive thresholding to dynamically select the most important experts, thereby reducing the activated expert number while effectively maintaining the model performance. Experiments show that EAT outperforms the existing baseline Top-P method across multiple models and datasets, achieving over 25% an average reduction compared to the vanilla method in the number of activated experts and performing better token generation speed compared to the baseline. Furthermore, the performance of pruned models can be efficiently recovered via OPD using only 9K data. Additionally, through ablation studies, we find that excessively reducing the number of activated experts can significantly harm model performance, and the importance of experts varies across layers, with higher-level experts being generally more critical.

AI.tldr: EAT (Expert Account Tracker) dynamically selects important experts in MoE Transformers using history-awareness metrics and adaptive thresholding, cutting activated experts by >25% while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional MoE architectures are inefficient because many experts are unnecessarily activated. Existing methods for reducing activated experts ignore the historical performance of each expert.
AI.method: EAT leverages history-awareness metrics combined with adaptive thresholding to dynamically select the most important experts, reducing the number of activated experts while maintaining model performance.
AI.result: EAT outperforms the Top-P baseline across multiple models and datasets, achieving over 25% average reduction in activated experts versus the vanilla method and better token generation speed. Pruned models recover performance via OPD with only 9K data. Ablations show excessive expert reduction harms performance, and expert importance varies by layer with higher-level experts being more critical.
AI.conclusion: EAT provides an efficient, history-aware approach to expert selection in MoE models, enabling substantial reduction in activated experts without performance loss.

title: ParaAgent: Reinforcing Parallel Acting in Open-World Tool Environments
summary: Language model agents are increasingly deployed in open-world tool environments, which require balancing exploring unknown capabilities and exploiting known ones. Existing methods face a performance-efficiency tradeoff: they either rigidly decouple exploration and execution or interleave them without coordination. We argue that the key lies not in whether to decouple or interleave them, but in how to coordinate them across granularities. We introduce ParaAct, a structured parallel-action loop that combines phase-level Exploration $\rightleftharpoons$ Execution with action-level parallelism. To learn this loop, ParaAgent combines multi-agent cold-start demonstrations with reinforcement learning under multi-level advantage decoupling, making planning structure explicit and supervising it with step-, phase-, and trajectory-level rewards. Learning is supported by our ToolEnv, a scalable simulator grounded in 50,011 realistic tool interfaces. On two open-world tool benchmarks, ParaAgent-4B achieves the best average success among all baselines, including GPT-4.1 systems, with the largest gains on multi-tool tasks. Behavioral analyses show that these gains stem from this action organization, highlighting its importance for capable and efficient open-world agents.

AI.tldr: ParaAct is a structured parallel-action loop coordinating phase-level exploration⇌execution with action-level parallelism; ParaAgent learns it via multi-agent cold-start plus RL with multi-level advantage decoupling, and a ToolEnv simulator grounded in 50,011 tool interfaces. ParaAgent-4B tops open-world tool benchmarks, beating GPT-4.1 systems.
AI.motivation: Language model agents in open-world tool environments must balance exploring unknown capabilities and exploiting known ones. Existing methods face a performance-efficiency tradeoff: they either rigidly decouple exploration and execution or interleave them without coordination. The paper argues the crux is not decoupling vs. interleaving, but how to coordinate them across granularities.
AI.method: ParaAct: a structured parallel-action loop combining phase-level Exploration⇌Execution with action-level parallelism. ParaAgent learns this loop by combining multi-agent cold-start demonstrations with reinforcement learning under multi-level advantage decoupling, making planning structure explicit and supervising it with step-, phase-, and trajectory-level rewards. Learning is supported by ToolEnv, a scalable simulator grounded in 50,011 realistic tool interfaces.
AI.result: On two open-world tool benchmarks, ParaAgent-4B achieves the best average success among all baselines, including GPT-4.1 systems, with the largest gains on multi-tool tasks.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral analyses show the gains stem from this action organization, highlighting its importance for capable and efficient open-world agents.

title: Trajectory Unlearning on LLM-based Agents
summary: Existing large language model (LLM) unlearning has focused primarily on removing specific knowledge, such as harmful facts, private data, or copyrighted content. However, as LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, a fundamental yet overlooked problem emerges: beyond suppressing what an agent knows, an agent should not reproduce undesired behaviors through its action trajectories. In this work, we introduce trajectory-level unlearning, a new problem formulation that targets the removal of specific action trajectories in long-horizon agentic tasks, rather than factual knowledge. We identify two fundamental challenges that distinguish trajectory unlearning from knowledge unlearning: (1) our unlearning target is what the agent \emph{does}, not what it \emph{says}; and (2) trajectories are sequentially dependent action sequences that cannot be decomposed into isolated prompt-response pairs without losing inter-step structure. To address these challenges, we propose Group-injected Relative Policy Optimization (GiRPO), which injects forget trajectories into the policy rollout group with penalized rewards and isolates the normalization statistics, yielding a stable and bounded unlearning signal that does not corrupt gradient updates for normal task trajectories. We construct trajectory unlearning benchmarks from two application scenarios, household tasks (ALFWorld) and online shopping (WebShop), and design three complementary metrics for evaluating forgetting quality and model utility. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that GiRPO effectively unlearns target trajectories while preserving task success rates, outperforming existing knowledge-unlearning baselines on both forgetting quality and task utility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces trajectory-level unlearning for LLM agents, targeting removal of specific action trajectories in long-horizon tasks, and proposes GiRPO to achieve it without harming normal task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning focuses on removing factual knowledge (harmful facts, private data, copyrighted content). As LLMs become autonomous agents, a new gap appears: an agent should not reproduce undesired behaviors through its action trajectories. This is a fundamental overlooked problem that knowledge unlearning does not address.
AI.method: The authors formulate trajectory-level unlearning as a new problem. They identify two challenges: (1) the target is what the agent does, not what it says; (2) trajectories are sequentially dependent action sequences that cannot be decomposed into isolated prompt-response pairs without losing inter-step structure. They propose Group-injected Relative Policy Optimization (GiRPO), which injects forget trajectories into the policy rollout group with penalized rewards, isolates normalization statistics, and yields a stable bounded unlearning signal that does not corrupt gradient updates for normal task trajectories.
AI.result: The authors construct trajectory unlearning benchmarks from ALFWorld (household tasks) and WebShop (online shopping) with three complementary metrics for forgetting quality and model utility. Experiments show GiRPO effectively unlearns target trajectories while preserving task success rates, outperforming existing knowledge-unlearning baselines on both forgetting quality and task utility.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level unlearning is a distinct and necessary problem for agentic LLMs. GiRPO provides an effective, stable solution that removes undesired action trajectories while maintaining model utility, establishing a strong baseline for future work.

title: Scalable and Data-Driven Decision Support in the Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul Process
comment: Published in: 2022 IEEE International Conference on Industrial Engineering and Engineering Management (IEEM)
summary:
Several businesses apply maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) principles to the life-cycle of their existing products. In cases like casted gas turbine component Product Lifecycle Management (PLM), repairing components in frequent intervals can extend the lifetime expectation of the product, provide higher cost efficiency compared to newly produced components, and even improve the part design during the repair cycle. Another aspect of repair concerns sustainability, as products often contain rare materials. The emissions produced by the repair process are usually smaller than mining materials and casting new components.
  To optimize the repair process further, we propose the Smart Expert System (SES), which assists engineering experts with machine learning-based decision support throughout the repair process. We elaborate on its IT architecture and present machine learning models employed for representative MRO use cases. The SES is evaluated using actual industry data from a leading gas turbine company and demonstrably fulfills formulated requirements concerning the suitability of the overall decision support and the stability of the enclosing IT architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Smart Expert System (SES) that provides machine learning-based decision support to engineering experts across the MRO lifecycle of casted gas turbine components, validated on real industry data.
AI.motivation: Businesses increasingly apply MRO principles to product lifecycles. Repairing casted gas turbine components at frequent intervals extends product lifetime, is more cost-efficient than producing new components, and can improve part design during the repair cycle. Repair also supports sustainability, since products often contain rare materials and repair emissions are typically lower than those from mining and casting new components. To further optimize this process, engineering experts need better decision support.
AI.method: The authors propose the Smart Expert System (SES) to assist engineering experts with machine learning-based decision support throughout the repair process. They detail the SES's IT architecture and present machine learning models developed for representative MRO use cases.
AI.result: The SES is evaluated using actual industry data from a leading gas turbine company. It demonstrably fulfills the formulated requirements regarding the suitability of the overall decision support and the stability of the enclosing IT architecture.
AI.conclusion: The SES effectively supports MRO decision-making for gas turbine components, meeting requirements for decision support suitability and IT architecture stability based on real-world industry evaluation.

title: Probe to Act: Elevating Browser-Use Agent via Active Visual Probing
summary: Browser-use agents require seamless alignment between structured web metadata and visual information, while preserving relevant context across long interactions. Existing interfaces often rely on either screenshot-level action prediction or static Set-of-Marks overlays, leaving the model to resolve dense DOM-pixel alignment before every operation. We introduce Probe to Act (P2A), an active probing framework for the browser-agent loop that moves this alignment into decision time. P2A addresses an asymmetric bridge between symbolic DOM hypotheses and screenshot layout by rendering on-demand symbolic DOM structure back into pixels. Before committing a state-changing browser operation, the agent can issue lightweight probes to translate DOM handles into pixel evidence, map screen regions back to DOM candidates, register visual-only targets, and commit verified notes. These interleaved processes naturally produce evidence-based memory: only probed, acted-on, or explicitly committed observations are kept across steps, preserving only decision-critical evidence in long-horizon contexts. P2A can be used as a prompting strategy for proprietary models under the standard DOM+SoM interface, and can be distilled into open-weight models through cold-start synthesis and self-bootstrapped SFT. Across three browser-use benchmarks, P2A shows clear gains on task success rate for both proprietary and fine-tuned models; on VisualWebArena, for example, it improves Gemini-3-Pro from 54.1% to 61.2% and Qwen3-VL-8B from 24.6% to 32.9%, while matching the costly full-observation history ($\sim$3$\times$) at only $\sim$1.2$\times$ the peak retained input context of action-only history.

AI.tldr: P2A is an active probing framework that lets browser agents resolve DOM-pixel alignment on demand at decision time, yielding evidence-based memory and consistent task-success gains.
AI.motivation: Browser-use agents need to align structured web metadata (DOM) with visual/screenshot information while retaining relevant context over long interactions. Existing interfaces rely on screenshot-level action prediction or static Set-of-Marks overlays, forcing the model to resolve dense DOM-pixel alignment before every action, which is costly and error-prone.
AI.method: P2A moves alignment to decision time as an asymmetric bridge between symbolic DOM hypotheses and screenshot layout: it renders on-demand symbolic DOM structure back into pixels. Before a state-changing operation, the agent issues lightweight probes to translate DOM handles into pixel evidence, map screen regions back to DOM candidates, register visual-only targets, and commit verified notes. Interleaving probes yields evidence-based memory, keeping only probed/acted-on/committed observations. Usable as a prompting strategy for proprietary models under DOM+SoM, or distilled into open-weight models via cold-start synthesis and self-bootstrapped SFT.
AI.result: On three browser-use benchmarks, P2A improves task success rates for both proprietary and fine-tuned models. On VisualWebArena, Gemini-3-Pro rises from 54.1% to 61.2%, and Qwen3-VL-8B from 24.6% to 32.9%, matching the performance of costly full-observation history (~3x) while using only ~1.2x the peak retained input context of action-only history.
AI.conclusion: Active, on-demand DOM-pixel probing with evidence-based memory enables more accurate and context-efficient browser-use agents, generalizing across proprietary and distilled open-weight models.

title: AgentBoundary: Counterfactual Evaluation of Safety in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) in conversational settings is largely framed around whether to answer or refuse a request. In agentic settings, however, the same models must decide whether to act as permission-critical evidence emerges during execution. This creates a distinct challenge: apparent risk, action permissibility, and task competence are easily confounded, making agentic over-refusal difficult to distinguish from ordinary task failure. To address this, we introduce AgentBound, the first four-way counterfactual generation-and-evaluation framework for tool-using agent safety. AgentBound transforms the same executable workflow by independently varying apparent risk and action permissibility, enabling controlled comparisons of risky-looking but authorized tasks and routine-looking but unauthorized tasks. These comparisons jointly diagnose over-refusal and unsafe compliance while controlling for task competence. We instantiate AgentBound as a human-validated 4,000-task evaluation suite with trajectory-based and post-state-based judgments. Across 17 model and harness configurations, high safety frequently coexists with poor authorized-task completion: GPT-5.5 blocks 99.5\% of routine-looking unauthorized actions yet completes only 28.7\% of risky-looking authorized tasks. We further train a lightweight runtime calibration module that improves authorized-task completion by 18.2\% on average across 10 evaluated configurations, while improving unsafe-action blocking by 5.4\% on average. These show that effective agentic alignment requires action decisions to track permission-relevant execution evidence, rather than refusal strength alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentBound, a four-way counterfactual generation-and-evaluation framework (and 4,000-task suite) that disentangles apparent risk, action permissibility, and task competence in tool-using agents, revealing that high safety often coexists with poor authorized-task completion.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment for LLMs in conversational settings is framed as answer-vs-refuse, but in agentic settings models must decide whether to act as permission-critical evidence emerges during execution. This creates a challenge where apparent risk, action permissibility, and task competence are confounded, making agentic over-refusal hard to distinguish from ordinary task failure.
AI.method: AgentBound is a four-way counterfactual generation-and-evaluation framework that transforms the same executable workflow by independently varying apparent risk and action permissibility, enabling controlled comparisons of risky-looking but authorized vs. routine-looking but unauthorized tasks. It is instantiated as a human-validated 4,000-task suite with trajectory-based and post-state-based judgments, and a lightweight runtime calibration module is trained.
AI.result: Across 17 model/harness configurations, high safety frequently coexists with poor authorized-task completion; GPT-5.5 blocks 99.5% of routine-looking unauthorized actions but completes only 28.7% of risky-looking authorized tasks. The calibration module improves authorized-task completion by 18.2% on average across 10 configurations while improving unsafe-action blocking by 5.4% on average.
AI.conclusion: Effective agentic alignment requires action decisions to track permission-relevant execution evidence, rather than refusal strength alone.

title: Audit-First VAPO: Risk-Certified Selective Updates under Imperfect Verification
summary: Imperfect verifiers can assign a harmful update direction even when clipping and regularization bound its magnitude. We introduce Audit-First VAPO, which separates discrete directional admission from continuous magnitude control. An observation-only accept-appeal-abstain policy uses a finite secondary-verification budget; its action trace is frozen before clean labels are joined. Simultaneous finite-sample bounds then certify selected harmful risk, coverage, and verifier-call rate over a predeclared policy family. Conditional Hoeffding-Azuma bounds account for the dependence induced by shared budgets, and rollout or verifier changes initiate a new certification stage. After admission, a bounded trust-clip-KL actuator controls magnitude. We evaluate two models on two reasoning benchmarks against static RLVR, matched-random selection, confidence thresholding, noise correction, and verifier augmentation. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and GSM8K at target risk $ρ=0.08$, RC-VAPO achieves 74.1% accuracy, selected harmful risk 0.0697, coverage 0.4125, and relative verifier cost $1.16\times$. At matched coverage and update magnitude, its selected-risk difference from matched random is -0.0260 with paired 95% interval $[-0.0364,-0.0157]$. Across asymmetric, confidence-dependent, and correlated-verifier noise, the certificate is satisfied on 57 of 60 independent runs. These comparisons isolate informative directional selection from proposal suppression, update shrinkage, and additional verifier computation.

AI.tldr: Audit-First VAPO separates directional admission (an accept-appeal-abstain policy certified by finite-sample bounds) from magnitude control (bounded trust-clip-KL), yielding certified harmful-risk, coverage, and verifier-call guarantees for verifier-guided policy updates.
AI.motivation: Imperfect verifiers can assign harmful update directions even when clipping and regularization bound the update magnitude, so magnitude control alone is insufficient.
AI.method: An observation-only accept-appeal-abstain policy with a finite secondary-verification budget; its action trace is frozen before clean labels are joined. Simultaneous finite-sample bounds certify selected harmful risk, coverage, and verifier-call rate over a predeclared policy family, with conditional Hoeffding-Azuma bounds handling dependence from shared budgets and new certification stages on rollout/verifier change. A bounded trust-clip-KL actuator then controls magnitude.
AI.result: Two models on two reasoning benchmarks versus static RLVR, matched-random selection, confidence thresholding, noise correction, and verifier augmentation. On Qwen3.5-0.8B/GSM8K at target risk 0.08, RC-VAPO reaches 74.1% accuracy, selected harmful risk 0.0697, coverage 0.4125, relative verifier cost 1.16x; at matched coverage and magnitude, selected-risk difference vs matched random is -0.0260 with paired 95% interval [-0.0364, -0.0157]. Certificate satisfied on 57/60 runs across asymmetric, confidence-dependent, and correlated-verifier noise.
AI.conclusion: The comparisons isolate informative directional selection from proposal suppression, update shrinkage, and extra verifier computation.

title: CompoWorld: Compositional Environment Scaling for General Agents
summary: Automatically generated environments provide a scalable source of interaction data for training general agents. However, existing approaches mainly generate tasks within a single environment, while real-world workflows require agents to connect information and actions across multiple services.
