We introduce Compositional Environment Scaling (\textbf{CompoWorld}), which expands the task space by composing a finite library of reusable services. Coding agents turn tool specifications into verified services with typed states and shared interfaces, while a world model handles tools that cannot be reliably implemented. A random-walk procedure connects services through dependency graphs, enabling the generation and verification of tasks that require information to flow across services. Verified trajectories support supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while our Completion-Focused Rubric Reward guides reinforcement learning (RL) toward full task completion by emphasizing criteria with lower pass rates within each rollout group. We construct 448 services exposing 10,130 tools and use 3K SFT trajectories and 1K RL tasks to train Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Experimental results show that CompoWorld improves on its backbone by 9.17 points on average across eight benchmarks. On AutomationBench, it surpasses frontier models such as Claude Opus 4.6 and leads all compared agent-specialized 35B-A3B models.

AI.tldr: CompoWorld scales agent training by composing reusable services into multi-service, cross-dependency tasks, using verified trajectories for SFT and a Completion-Focused Rubric Reward for RL, improving a 35B-A3B backbone by 9.17 points on average across eight benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing auto-generated environment approaches mainly produce tasks within a single environment, whereas real-world workflows require agents to connect information and actions across multiple services. This gap limits the transferability and complexity of trained agents.
AI.method: CompoWorld expands the task space by composing a finite library of reusable services. Coding agents convert tool specifications into verified services with typed states and shared interfaces, while a world model handles tools that cannot be reliably implemented. A random-walk procedure links services via dependency graphs, generating and verifying tasks that require information flow across services. Verified trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a Completion-Focused Rubric Reward drives reinforcement learning (RL) toward full task completion by emphasizing criteria with lower pass rates within each rollout group.
AI.result: The authors build 448 services exposing 10,130 tools and train Qwen3.6-35B-A3B using 3K SFT trajectories and 1K RL tasks. CompoWorld improves on its backbone by 9.17 points on average across eight benchmarks. On AutomationBench, it surpasses frontier models such as Claude Opus 4.6 and leads all compared agent-specialized 35B-A3B models.
AI.conclusion: Compositional scaling of reusable services offers an effective, scalable path to generate multi-service, cross-dependency agent tasks. Combining verified trajectories for SFT with a completion-focused rubric reward for RL yields substantial gains, enabling a 35B-A3B model to outperform much larger frontier models on cross-service automation benchmarks.

title: RSD-Poker: Structure-Adaptive and Shift-Robust Risk-Utility Certification for Residual Policies in Imperfect-Information Games
summary: Residual policy adaptation provides a lightweight way to modify a strong reference policy, but a shared scale and a fixed subgroup partition can hide heterogeneous degradation and become fragile when the deployment mixture of information states changes. We introduce RSD-Poker, a structure-adaptive and shift-robust certification framework that freezes a bank of residual families and scales, learns a policy-visible partition on an independent structure split, and freezes that partition before calibration labels are joined. Each candidate-group pair receives a weighted simultaneous upper certificate for anchor-relative risk and a lower certificate for weak-response utility. A robust group-to-candidate map is then selected over a predeclared uncertainty set of deployment group proportions. Under independent calibration units drawn from each frozen group's law, a candidate bank and partition fixed before calibration, and invariant within-group conditionals, the selected map satisfies its declared mixture-robust risk budget and utility certificate with probability at least $1-ζ_{risk}-ζ_{util}$. The information contract supports both a teacher-backed transform and a teacher-free observation-only student. The retained deterministic 24-state audit remains an exact replay diagnostic: empirical-zero selects $α=0.08$, raising the weak-response proxy from 4.2082 to 4.2889 with $0/12$ held-out threshold crossings. On stratified held-out states, the learned-partition dual selector raises weak utility from 4.4074 under global dual certification to 4.4936 and lowers held-out violation from 0.0215 to 0.0078; its mixture-robust variant reaches violation 0.0059. Across five observation-only checkpoints, risk-calibrated residuals attain weak utility $4.3659\pm0.0177$ and violation rate $0.0178\pm0.0057$.

AI.tldr: RSD-Poker is a structure-adaptive, shift-robust certification framework for residual policy adaptation that learns a policy-visible subgroup partition, certifies each candidate-group pair, and selects a group-to-candidate map robust to shifts in deployment group proportions.
AI.motivation: Residual policy adaptation is lightweight, but a shared scale and fixed subgroup partition can hide heterogeneous degradation and become fragile when the deployment mixture of information states shifts. This motivates a structure-adaptive and shift-robust certification approach.
AI.method: Freeze a bank of residual families and scales; learn a policy-visible partition on an independent structure split and freeze it before calibration labels are joined. For each candidate-group pair, compute a weighted simultaneous upper certificate for anchor-relative risk and a lower certificate for weak-response utility; select a robust group-to-candidate map over a predeclared uncertainty set of deployment group proportions. Guarantees rely on independent calibration units, a pre-calibration frozen candidate bank and partition, and invariant within-group conditionals. Supports a teacher-backed transform and a teacher-free observation-only student.
AI.result: Deterministic 24-state audit: empirical-zero selects alpha=0.08, raising weak-response proxy from 4.2082 to 4.2889 with 0/12 held-out threshold crossings. On stratified held-out states, the learned-partition dual selector raises weak utility from 4.4074 (global dual certification) to 4.4936 and lowers held-out violation from 0.0215 to 0.0078; mixture-robust variant reaches 0.0059. Across five observation-only checkpoints, risk-calibrated residuals attain weak utility 4.3659+/-0.0177 and violation rate 0.0178+/-0.0057.
AI.conclusion: The selected map satisfies its declared mixture-robust risk budget and utility certificate with probability at least 1-zeta_risk-zeta_util, and empirical results show improved utility and reduced violation under both teacher-backed and observation-only settings.

title: Auditing Agent Actions through Query-Conditioned Attribution
summary: LLM agents increasingly take consequential actions through interactions with users, policies, and external tools. Auditing these agents requires automated attribution of realized actions to their historical basis. However, existing attribution formulations do not provide question-specific traces for diverse auditing objectives. Additionally, when access to the acting model is limited (e.g., in API-only deployments), applicable methods commonly rely on costly input perturbations or external LLM analysis of complete trajectories. We therefore formulate $\textit{query-conditioned agent action attribution}, a new task that takes a natural-language auditing query as input and recovers the source and ordered intermediate evidence for the query-specified aspect of an action. We instantiate this task with $A^3Bench$, a benchmark comprising 1,396 auditing queries across policy basis, parameter provenance, failure propagation, and unsafe-behavior tracing. To enable efficient, query-specific attribution, we use small open-weight models as attribution proposers that combine query-conditioned gradient saliency with query-semantic relevance to rank history units. Our proposer consistently achieves stronger source and evidence rankings at lower inference cost than open-weight baselines, improving source MRR by up to 40.9\% and evidence MAP by 42.1\% with only two forward passes and one backward pass. Controlled evaluations confirm that our proposer improves attribution specificity by adapting its rankings to fine-grained changes in the auditing query. Building on a proposer ensemble, our end-to-end system surpasses the strongest frontier-model baseline in source accuracy (64.5\% vs.\ 60.4\%) while reducing empirical deployment latency by 29.9\% relative to the fastest frontier API baseline. Code and data will be released after the initial review period following final validation and cleanup.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces query-conditioned agent action attribution, a new task for tracing an action's source and ordered intermediate evidence given a natural-language auditing query, instantiated via the A3Bench benchmark (1,396 queries). A small open-weight proposer combining query-conditioned gradient saliency with query-semantic relevance achieves stronger, more query-specific attribution at lower cost than baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly take consequential actions through interactions with users, policies, and external tools, making automated auditing that attributes realized actions to their historical basis necessary. Existing attribution formulations fail to provide question-specific traces for diverse auditing objectives, and under limited model access (e.g., API-only deployments) applicable methods rely on costly input perturbations or external LLM analysis of full trajectories.
AI.method: The authors formulate query-conditioned agent action attribution: given a natural-language auditing query, recover the source and ordered intermediate evidence for the query-specified aspect of an action. They build A3Bench, a benchmark of 1,396 auditing queries spanning policy basis, parameter provenance, failure propagation, and unsafe-behavior tracing. Small open-weight models serve as attribution proposers, combining query-conditioned gradient saliency with query-semantic relevance to rank history units. An ensemble of proposers forms the end-to-end system.
AI.result: The proposer achieves stronger source and evidence rankings than open-weight baselines at lower inference cost, improving source MRR by up to 40.9% and evidence MAP by 42.1% using only two forward passes and one backward pass. Controlled evaluations show improved attribution specificity via adaptation to fine-grained query changes. The ensemble system surpasses the strongest frontier-model baseline in source accuracy (64.5% vs. 60.4%) while reducing empirical deployment latency by 29.9% versus the fastest frontier API baseline.
AI.conclusion: Query-conditioned attribution with a lightweight saliency-plus-relevance proposer enables efficient, query-specific auditing of LLM agent actions, outperforming both open-weight and frontier API baselines in ranking quality, accuracy, and latency. Code and data will be released after the initial review period following final validation and cleanup.

title: SWE-Game: Can Coding Agents Build the Games We Want?
summary: We introduce SWE-Game, a benchmark of 247 tasks grounded in 41 executable reference Godot games spanning 13 gameplay categories in 2D and 3D. Five task types cover development from a brief, implementation from a game design document, skeleton completion, repair of 83 injected-fault cases, and Godot-to-Unity porting. Reference materials specify the intended gameplay, while a shared instrumentation interface lets evaluator-owned drivers and probes execute actions and observe independently implemented games. Evaluation combines engine-state checks, certified reference-input replay, and agent-authored feature demonstrations to assess mechanic correctness, demonstrated playability, and behavioral restoration and preservation after repairs. Game-specific vision-language rubrics separately assess presentation. Across six models, Opus5 achieves the highest overall score in all five task types. Best overall scores remain below 60 out of 100 across the three construction tasks, with Brief-to-Game reaching 50.38. Analysis of reviewed submissions identifies requirement omissions and gameplay logic errors as predominant implementation problems. On human-labeled behaviors from 100 agent-built games, executable checks achieve 92.59% balanced accuracy, compared with 78.41% for a video-based VLM judge. Rubric-based visual scores reach a Spearman correlation of 0.829 with human ratings of 200 gameplay clips. Together, these results characterize current agent capabilities across game-development activities and support combining runtime evidence with visual assessment.

AI.tldr: SWE-Game is a benchmark of 247 game-development tasks built on 41 executable Godot reference games across 13 gameplay categories. It spans five task types, from briefs and design docs to repair and engine porting, and evaluates agents via engine-state checks, certified input replay, and rubric-based visual scoring. Best models still fall below 60/100 on construction tasks, and executable checks outperform a video-based VLM judge (92.59% vs. 78.41% balanced accuracy).
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks rarely evaluate end-to-end game development, where correctness depends on executable gameplay, engine state, and subjective presentation rather than text or static artifacts. The authors aim to characterize agent capabilities across the full range of game-development activities using verifiable, independently implemented reference games rather than single-model or video-only judging.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 247 tasks over 41 executable reference Godot games covering 13 gameplay categories in 2D and 3D, with five task types: development from a brief, implementation from a game design document, skeleton completion, repair of 83 injected-fault cases, and Godot-to-Unity porting. Reference materials specify intended gameplay, while a shared instrumentation interface allows evaluator-owned drivers and probes to execute actions and observe independently implemented games. Evaluation combines engine-state checks, certified reference-input replay, and agent-authored feature demonstrations to assess mechanic correctness, demonstrated playability, and behavioral restoration/preservation after repairs. Game-specific vision-language rubrics separately assess presentation. Six models were tested.
AI.result: Opus5 achieved the highest overall score in all five task types among six models, yet best overall scores remained below 60/100 on the three construction tasks, with Brief-to-Game reaching 50.38. Reviewed submissions most often failed due to requirement omissions and gameplay logic errors. On human-labeled behaviors from 100 agent-built games, executable checks reached 92.59% balanced accuracy versus 78.41% for a video-based VLM judge. Rubric-based visual scores showed a Spearman correlation of 0.829 with human ratings on 200 gameplay clips.
AI.conclusion: The results characterize current agent capabilities across game-development activities and support combining runtime evidence with visual assessment, rather than relying on video-based judging alone.

title: TopoMamba: A Load-Support Relation-Guided Multi-Directional State-Space Model for Topology Optimization
summary: Deep learning has emerged as an efficient alternative for predicting high-performance material distributions in topology optimization. Existing methods struggle to accurately capture load-transfer information, limiting out-of-distribution generalization, while their model architectures often incur high computational costs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes TopoMamba, a topology prediction framework incorporating a load-support relation-guided multi-directional state-space model. Coupling physical fields with load-support relations enables more effective modeling of mechanical dependencies. A load-support relation-guided spatially adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically adjusts multi-directional scan features according to spatial conditions. Mamba is coupled with the solid isotropic material with penalty method to enhance structural mechanical performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Results on two-dimensional topology optimization benchmarks demonstrate that TopoMamba achieves superior topology prediction accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and computational efficiency over state-of-the-art models. The proposed load-support physics-guided framework enables efficient optimization of more complex structural systems.

AI.tldr: TopoMamba is a load-support relation-guided multi-directional state-space framework for topology optimization that improves prediction accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and computational efficiency over state-of-the-art models.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods for predicting high-performance material distributions in topology optimization struggle to accurately capture load-transfer information, which limits out-of-distribution generalization. Additionally, their model architectures often incur high computational costs.
AI.method: The paper proposes TopoMamba, a topology prediction framework based on a load-support relation-guided multi-directional state-space model. It couples physical fields with load-support relations to better model mechanical dependencies. A load-support relation-guided spatially adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically adjusts multi-directional scan features according to spatial conditions. Mamba is coupled with the solid isotropic material with penalty (SIMP) method to enhance structural mechanical performance while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.result: On two-dimensional topology optimization benchmarks, TopoMamba achieves superior topology prediction accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed load-support physics-guided framework enables efficient optimization of more complex structural systems.

title: One Latent, Many Tokens: Jointly Learning Compressed Embeddings for Efficient Language Diffusion
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, and 8 tables. Includes appendices
summary: Most continuous diffusion language models process one latent position per token at each sampling step, making generation expensive. Two-stage methods lower the cost by reducing the latent length, but they fix the compressed embedding space before training the diffusion model. Embeddings from the fixed space can be difficult to model with diffusion and decode reliably into tokens, which limits generation quality after compression. To address this problem, we introduce JPEG-DLM (Joint-embedding Prediction for Efficient Generation with Diffusion Language Model), which jointly trains a compressor, a flow matching model and a decoding module. With joint-embedding prediction, JPEG-DLM learns compressed embeddings that are more structured, easier to model with diffusion and reliably decodable into tokens. JPEG-DLM achieves the lowest mean Gen-PPL and highest throughput among recent diffusion and flow models on LM1B and OWT. At a compression rate of 0.5 on OWT, it reaches a Gen-PPL of 34.52 and approximately 2.3 times ELF's throughput. These results suggest that jointly learning compressed embeddings offers a promising path toward efficient diffusion language modeling. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: JPEG-DLM jointly trains a compressor, a flow matching model, and a decoding module to learn compressed embeddings that are structured, easy to model with diffusion, and reliably decodable, achieving the lowest Gen-PPL and highest throughput among recent diffusion and flow models on LM1B and OWT.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion language models process one latent position per token per sampling step, making generation expensive. Two-stage methods reduce cost by shortening the latent length, but they fix the compressed embedding space before training the diffusion model. Such fixed embeddings can be hard to model with diffusion and to decode reliably into tokens, limiting generation quality after compression.
AI.method: JPEG-DLM (Joint-embedding Prediction for Efficient Generation with Diffusion Language Model) jointly trains a compressor, a flow matching model, and a decoding module. Through joint-embedding prediction, it learns compressed embeddings that are more structured, easier to model with diffusion, and reliably decodable into tokens.
AI.result: JPEG-DLM achieves the lowest mean Gen-PPL and highest throughput among recent diffusion and flow models on LM1B and OWT. At a compression rate of 0.5 on OWT, it reaches a Gen-PPL of 34.52 and approximately 2.3 times ELF's throughput.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning compressed embeddings offers a promising path toward efficient diffusion language modeling. Code will be released soon.

title: SpecRead: A Benchmark for Measuring Whether Language Models Understand Hardware Specifications
comment: 13 pages. Benchmark data and code at https://github.com/EDGAhab/specread
summary: Existing benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) in hardware design evaluate downstream artifacts such as generated RTL, assertions, or testbenches. When a model fails such a benchmark, the failure is ambiguous: it may have misread the specification, or it may have understood the specification and failed to write the code. We present SpecRead, a benchmark that isolates specification comprehension from generation ability. SpecRead v2.1 contains 385 questions over 10 open-source OpenTitan IP blocks: exact retrieval, cross-section reasoning, contradiction detection in mutated specifications, and spec-RTL consistency checking, plus 82 controls (41 distractor, 41 consistent-RTL). Type-4 items are built from real RTL mutations; we retain only mutations that Icarus Verilog simulation shows to change observable behavior. A with-spec vs. without-spec ablation suggests the questions require the excerpt, not training recall alone (without-spec accuracy 3/20 on the t1/t2 subset), though memorization of the source text may still help spot mutations. As an initial characterization with a small model, Ministral-3B scores 33.2% overall (128/385; macro average 39.0%): 55.2% on retrieval, 51.7% on cross-section reasoning. On the two contradiction-focused types, the verdict-plus-location measure gives 48.0% (t3) and 63.3% (t4), with a 51.2% false-positive rate on distractors and 100% on consistent-RTL controls. Layered scoring shows the model locates contradictions well (78.9-81.6% location accuracy) but scores lower on their category (43.9-49.7%). A structured "rule-table" prompting intervention lowers accuracy on every question type except t2 (tied). SpecRead is automatically scorable by deterministic checks, with gray-zone cases counted wrong under the conservative main scoring. The benchmark is regenerable for type-3 items via mutation injection, and built exclusively from public sources.

AI.tldr: SpecRead is a new benchmark that isolates specification comprehension from code generation in LLM-based hardware design, containing 385 questions over 10 OpenTitan IP blocks, and reveals that a small model locates contradictions well but struggles with categorization and is hurt by structured prompting.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks for hardware design evaluate downstream artifacts (generated RTL, assertions, testbenches), so failures are ambiguous: a model may have misread the specification or understood it but failed to write correct code. A benchmark is needed to disentangle specification comprehension from generation ability.
AI.method: SpecRead v2.1 comprises 385 questions over 10 open-source OpenTitan IP blocks covering four types: exact retrieval, cross-section reasoning, contradiction detection in mutated specifications, and spec-RTL consistency checking, plus 82 controls (41 distractor, 41 consistent-RTL). Type-4 items derive from real RTL mutations retained only if Icarus Verilog simulation confirms changed observable behavior. Scoring is deterministic with gray-zone cases counted wrong under a conservative main score; a with-spec vs. without-spec ablation tests reliance on the excerpt, and a structured "rule-table" prompting intervention is evaluated.
AI.result: Without-spec accuracy is 3/20 on the t1/t2 subset, indicating questions require the excerpt rather than training recall alone, though memorization may aid mutation spotting. Ministral-3B scores 33.2% overall (128/385; macro average 39.0%): 55.2% retrieval, 51.7% cross-section reasoning. Contradiction-focused types yield 48.0% (t3) and 63.3% (t4) on verdict-plus-location, with a 51.2% false-positive rate on distractors and 100% on consistent-RTL controls. Layered scoring shows strong location accuracy (78.9-81.6%) but lower category accuracy (43.9-49.7%). The rule-table intervention lowers accuracy on all types except t2 (tied).
AI.conclusion: SpecRead isolates specification comprehension from generation, is deterministically scorable, regenerable for type-3 items via mutation injection, and built exclusively from public sources. Under conservative scoring, current small-model performance highlights gaps in contradiction categorization and false-positive control.

title: BIRD: Distilling Decision Boundaries into Rationales for MLLM Adaptation
summary: Adapting general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to specialized domains requires learning domain-specific decision criteria, which often hinge on subtle visual distinctions between otherwise plausible answers. Rationale augmentation aims to expose such evidence through additional observations or inter-sample comparisons, yet a visually valid cue is not necessarily decision-relevant: it may describe how samples differ without changing the model's relative preference between competing answers. We therefore introduce BIRD, a self-improving Boundary-Informed Rationale Distillation framework that uses model-specific confusions to locate unresolved local decision boundaries and distills the evidence that resolves these confusions into rationales. For each sample, BIRD retrieves candidate neighbors from the target MLLM's own representation space and selects the most confusable one according to its answer preferences. It then generates answer-blind candidate evidence from their visual differences and functionally verifies which evidence most effectively strengthens the model's preference for the correct answer while avoiding inappropriate transfer across the pair. The verified evidence is then distilled into a single-sample rationale for standard supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on medical and chart VQA show that BIRD outperforms competing rationale-augmentation methods across two target MLLMs, while further analyses demonstrate clearer separation of confusable answers and stronger gains from model-matched supervision.

AI.tldr: BIRD is a self-improving Boundary-Informed Rationale Distillation framework that locates model-specific confusable decision boundaries via neighbor retrieval and distills functionally-verified evidence into single-sample rationales for supervised fine-tuning, outperforming competing rationale-augmentation methods on medical and chart VQA.
AI.motivation: Adapting general-purpose MLLMs to specialized domains requires learning domain-specific decision criteria often based on subtle visual distinctions. Existing rationale augmentation exposes visually valid cues, but a visually valid cue is not necessarily decision-relevant—it may describe how samples differ without changing the model's relative preference between competing answers. This gap motivates locating actually unresolved local decision boundaries and distilling only evidence that resolves them.
AI.method: BIRD uses model-specific confusions to locate unresolved local decision boundaries. For each sample, it retrieves candidate neighbors from the target MLLM's own representation space and selects the most confusable one according to the model's answer preferences. It then generates answer-blind candidate evidence from their visual differences and functionally verifies which evidence most effectively strengthens the model's preference for the correct answer while avoiding inappropriate transfer across the pair. The verified evidence is distilled into a single-sample rationale for standard supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: On medical and chart VQA, BIRD outperforms competing rationale-augmentation methods across two target MLLMs. Further analyses show clearer separation of confusable answers and stronger gains from model-matched supervision.
AI.conclusion: Decision-relevant rationales grounded in model-specific confusions and functionally verified evidence provide more effective domain adaptation than merely visually valid cues, yielding better discrimination of confusable answers and benefiting from model-matched supervision.

title: Self-Designed Evaluators and Warm Memory for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: A tool-using language-model agent deployed over a long stream of tasks receives no reward, so it cannot tell whether it succeeded, cannot safely retry, and cannot label the experience it needs to improve. We present SelfSuite, in which the agent's own base model, given only the world's public materials, designs a small evaluation suite of weighted judges and grounded per-task briefs, freezes it, and uses it to gate a keep-best retry and to label a typed, outcome-tracked memory. On matched five-repeat benchmarks over tau2-bench and AppWorld, SelfSuite scores above the plain agent without any labels, matches methods given ten expert labels on tau2-bench, and trails Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) on AppWorld, where code execution gives a direct success signal. In an ablation campaign run on the same tasks, it is above label-free ACE in every repeat, and the gated second attempt is the only component whose removal hurts in every repeat. We also simulate a subject-matter expert who grades ten onboarding tasks per world. Using those labels to calibrate SelfSuite's evaluator gives a small, consistent gain, and using them to warm up ACE's memory lifts ACE to tie calibrated SelfSuite. A single-run study on a second model family shows the same ordering.

AI.tldr: SelfSuite lets a reward-less tool-using LLM agent self-build a frozen evaluation suite from public materials to gate retries and label a typed memory, matching expert-label methods on tau2-bench without labels.
AI.motivation: An agent running over a long task stream receives no reward signal, so it cannot detect success, retry safely, or label experiences for improvement. Existing approaches either rely on expert labels or on direct success signals (e.g., code execution), which are unavailable in many open-ended deployments.
AI.method: The agent's own base model, given only the world's public materials, designs a small evaluation suite of weighted judges and grounded per-task briefs, then freezes it. This frozen suite gates a keep-best retry mechanism and labels a typed, outcome-tracked memory, providing self-supervision without external labels or reward.
AI.result: On matched five-repeat benchmarks over tau2-bench and AppWorld, SelfSuite outperforms the plain agent with no labels, matches methods given ten expert labels on tau2-bench, and trails ACE on AppWorld (where code execution supplies a direct success signal). In ablations, it beats label-free ACE in every repeat, and the gated second attempt is the only component whose removal hurts in every repeat. Expert labels on ten onboarding tasks per world yield a small consistent gain when calibrating SelfSuite's evaluator, and warm-starting ACE's memory with them lifts ACE to tie calibrated SelfSuite. A single-run study on a second model family shows the same ordering.
AI.conclusion: Self-generated, frozen evaluation suites can substitute for external labels in reward-free agent deployments, enabling reliable retry gating and memory labeling that rival expert-supervised and signal-supervised baselines, with the gated retry being the most consistently essential component.

title: Robust Biomolecular Complex Design Across Protein Conformational Landscapes
summary: Proteins populate conformational ensembles, yet structure-based biomolecular design typically optimizes candidates against a single target conformation. Consequently, a candidate that fits one state can lose favorable interactions or develop steric clashes when the target adopts another. We introduce FlexEvo, a model-agnostic evolutionary framework that adapts candidates once at inference time from a single target conformation to improve compatibility with alternative natural conformations unseen during adaptation, without retraining the source model or requiring a conformational ensemble. FlexEvo casts cross-state adaptation as geometry-constrained bi-objective optimization, balancing preservation of input-state interactions against robustness to plausible conformational perturbations. To limit the search space and reduce invalid structural edits, geometry-derived FlexBoxes define protected anchor regions, adaptable regions for local exploration, and forbidden regions for clash avoidance. A unified all-atom representation supports topology-preserving adaptation across diverse binder categories, while Pareto selection preserves nondominated candidates across the two objectives. We evaluate FlexEvo across multiple generation baselines and nine representative binder categories spanning diverse molecular sizes and structural topologies. FlexEvo reduces the category-balanced mean relative performance degradation from 47.8% to 4.4%, while adding only 1.4--3.1 minutes of adaptation per sample. These results establish single-state inference-time adaptation as a practical route toward robust biomolecular complex design across protein conformational landscapes.

AI.tldr: FlexEvo is a model-agnostic, inference-time evolutionary framework that adapts binder candidates, generated from a single target conformation, to remain compatible with unseen alternative target conformations without retraining or requiring an ensemble.
AI.motivation: Structure-based biomolecular design typically optimizes candidates against one target conformation, but proteins exist as conformational ensembles. A candidate fitting one state can lose favorable interactions or develop steric clashes in another state, motivating adaptation across conformational landscapes.
AI.method: FlexEvo casts cross-state adaptation as geometry-constrained bi-objective optimization, balancing preservation of input-state interactions against robustness to plausible conformational perturbations. Geometry-derived FlexBoxes define protected anchor regions, adaptable regions for local exploration, and forbidden regions for clash avoidance. A unified all-atom representation enables topology-preserving adaptation across binder categories, and Pareto selection retains nondominated candidates across both objectives.
AI.result: Across multiple generation baselines and nine representative binder categories with diverse molecular sizes and topologies, FlexEvo reduces category-balanced mean relative performance degradation from 47.8% to 4.4%, adding only 1.4--3.1 minutes of adaptation per sample.
AI.conclusion: Single-state inference-time adaptation is a practical route toward robust biomolecular complex design across protein conformational landscapes.

title: HTN Planning as a Coordination Layer for Multi-Server MCP Tool Orchestration
comment: 5 pages. Camera-ready version of a paper accepted at the ICAPS 2026 Workshop on Hierarchical Planning (HPlan 2026), Dublin. Non-archival. Code: https://github.com/PCfVW/hplan26-artifact
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) isolates servers by design: only the host can orchestrate cross-server workflows. When the host is a large language model, the resulting orchestrations are non-deterministic, non-reproducible, and pay one inference round-trip per tool call. We present a coordination architecture in which a Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planner generates a verifiable cross-server plan once, and a runtime middleware executes it deterministically across multiple MCP servers, binding cross-action data dependencies via a template mechanism (\verb|${context.X}|) substituted at execution time. The architecture mirrors MCP's isolation constraint: each compound task decomposes into server-local primitive actions, and inter-server data flow is bound at execution time via JSON-path output extractors. We instantiate the architecture on five HTN domains spanning laboratory robotics, bioinformatics and multiscale modelling, and demonstrate end-to-end execution from a browser-based plan controller against eight live third-party MCP servers querying real biological databases.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an HTN-based coordination architecture that plans cross-server MCP workflows once and executes them deterministically via runtime middleware, replacing non-deterministic LLM-orchestrated tool calls, and demonstrates it on five HTN domains with eight live third-party MCP servers.
AI.motivation: MCP isolates servers by design, so only the host can orchestrate cross-server workflows. When that host is an LLM, the resulting orchestrations are non-deterministic, non-reproducible, and incur one inference round-trip per tool call—an inefficiency and reliability problem for cross-server workflows.
AI.method: A coordination architecture coupling a Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planner, which generates a verifiable cross-server plan once, with runtime middleware that executes the plan deterministically across multiple MCP servers. The architecture mirrors MCP's isolation constraint: each compound task decomposes into server-local primitive actions, and inter-server data flow is bound at execution time using JSON-path output extractors via a template mechanism (${context.X}) substituted at execution time.
AI.result: The architecture is instantiated on five HTN domains spanning laboratory robotics, bioinformatics, and multiscale modelling, and demonstrates end-to-end execution from a browser-based plan controller against eight live third-party MCP servers querying real biological databases.
AI.conclusion: HTN planning combined with deterministic runtime middleware enables verifiable, reproducible cross-server MCP orchestration without per-call LLM inference, while respecting MCP's server-isolation design, as validated across multiple scientific domains and live third-party servers.

title: Skill2Env: Capability-Oriented Environment Synthesis from Skills for General Agents
summary: Executable environments are critical for post-training agents on tasks that require tool use and multi-step interaction, but constructing executable tasks together with their environments remains difficult to scale. Skills provide reusable domain knowledge, operational procedures, and tool-use instructions, but a substantial gap remains between the information contained in a skill and a concrete, challenging task with a complete executable environment. To address this gap, we introduce Skill2Env, a capability-oriented framework that starts from a skill and uses agent capability demands to guide task and environment synthesis. Skill2Env represents these demands through reusable difficulty patterns and instantiates them into task blueprints that specify objectives, challenges, environment facts, information boundaries, and acceptance criteria. These blueprints guide the joint construction of task instructions, execution substrates, workspaces, and rubric-based evaluators around source skills. We further propose Iterative Task Hardening, which uses solver execution evidence to identify insufficiently challenging task designs, strengthen or extend their difficulty-pattern instantiations, and revise the corresponding blueprints and environments. Using 1.5K high-scoring trajectories generated from Skill2Env environments for supervised fine-tuning, we observe consistent improvements across a broad range of agent benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of capability-oriented environment synthesis for agent post-training.

AI.tldr: Skill2Env is a capability-oriented framework that synthesizes executable agent tasks and environments starting from reusable skills, guided by difficulty patterns, and further improved via Iterative Task Hardening. Training on 1.5K trajectories from these environments yields consistent gains across agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Executable environments are essential for post-training agents on tool-use and multi-step tasks, but building them at scale is hard. Skills contain reusable domain knowledge, procedures, and tool-use instructions, yet there is a large gap between a skill and a concrete, challenging task with a fully executable environment. This work aims to close that gap.
AI.method: Skill2Env starts from a skill and uses agent capability demands to drive synthesis. It encodes demands as reusable difficulty patterns, instantiates them into task blueprints specifying objectives, challenges, environment facts, information boundaries, and acceptance criteria. These blueprints guide joint construction of task instructions, execution substrates, workspaces, and rubric-based evaluators around source skills. Iterative Task Hardening then uses solver execution evidence to detect insufficiently challenging designs, strengthen or extend difficulty-pattern instantiations, and revise blueprints and environments.
AI.result: Supervised fine-tuning on 1.5K high-scoring trajectories generated from Skill2Env environments produces consistent improvements across a broad range of agent benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Capability-oriented environment synthesis is effective for agent post-training, enabling scalable construction of executable tasks from skills and yielding transferable agent improvements.

title: Learning Strategies to Break Judges
summary: As AI agents surpass human performance, it becomes exceedingly hard for system designers to evaluate them directly and understand their failure modes. Consequently, agents themselves are being deployed extensively to evaluate, judge, and provide feedback on model traces. But this raises an important question: how can we trust the judge? In this work, we propose an agent-guided method to find weaknesses of agentic judges that expose interpretable failure mechanisms. Our method focuses on mathematical reasoning and proceeds in two stages: first, we deploy adversarial agents to mutate a set of sound proofs by introducing errors, attempting to misguide judges---in other words, injecting errors that judges are unable to catch. Then, we distill these attempts into a small set of mutation strategies which allow us to analyze the failure modes of the judges. To ensure that these strategies are not overfit to the initial set of proofs, we evaluate them by applying the mutation strategies to a held-out set of proofs and querying the same judge. We deploy our method on GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Opus 5, paired with their agent orchestrators, Codex and Claude Code, respectively. These are used both as mutators to introduce errors and as judges to evaluate correctness of mathematical reasoning. We find that across all the agentic judges, we are able to distill mutation strategies that consistently bypass their evaluations, thereby enabling us to ascertain actionable failure modes. Our analysis also reveals that judge reliability degrades at the frontier: errors in Olympiad-level proofs or graduate-level mathematical texts are detected more consistently, whereas flaws in research-level manuscripts are more likely to escape detection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an agent-guided adversarial method to uncover and interpret the failure modes of agentic judges that evaluate mathematical reasoning, distilling reusable mutation strategies that reliably bypass frontier judges.
AI.motivation: As AI agents exceed human performance, direct human evaluation becomes infeasible, so agents are increasingly deployed as judges of model traces. This raises the trust problem of how to verify the reliability of these judges and understand their failure modes.
AI.method: A two-stage adversarial pipeline: (1) adversarial agents mutate a set of sound proofs by injecting errors intended to evade detection, and (2) these attempts are distilled into a small set of mutation strategies capturing interpretable failure modes. Strategies are validated on a held-out proof set via re-querying the same judge to avoid overfitting. Applied to GPT-5.6-sol with Codex and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code, used both as mutators and as judges.
AI.result: Across all agentic judges, distilled mutation strategies consistently bypass their evaluations, yielding actionable failure modes. Judge reliability degrades at the frontier: errors in Olympiad-level proofs and graduate-level mathematical texts are detected more consistently, while flaws in research-level manuscripts more often escape detection.
AI.conclusion: Agentic judges exhibit systematic, analyzable vulnerabilities rather than random failures. The proposed framework provides a transferable, non-overfit means of auditing judge reliability, and its findings warn against trusting agentic judges on the most advanced mathematics.

title: Evidence-Inference Reconstruction: When The Evidence Is Recalled But The Reasoning Goes Wrong
summary: Modern multi-hop LLM agents are equipped with built-in mechanisms to detect errors in intermediate reasoning steps. Such errors trigger corrective actions from these agents, which mostly follow the paradigm of retrying the steps or the reasoning trajectories. Not only are these retries expensive, we present in this paper that they are also potentially unnecessary. To this end, we introduce Evidence-Inference Reconstruction (EIR), which uses structured state to guide one retrieval trajectory, accumulating source evidence in the process. We show that as long as the relevant evidence has been collected, EIR is capable of generating the correct answer in a single final model call even if erroneous evidence has been mixed in due to incorrect intermediate reasoning steps. In one evaluation, using Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4.1 Mini, we evaluate EIR on matched 1,000-question subsets of HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, showing that EIR improves Answer F1, the overlap between the model's and the correct answer, over the baseline by 8.3--32.8 points, Agentic SSR by 10.6--29.1 points, and Reflexion by 1.1--15.9 points. Additionally, we show that EIR averages 4.85 total model calls per question, compared with 35.29 for Agentic SSR and 12.41 for Reflexion. Together, these results corroborate EIR's central premise: separating evidence retrieval from the final answer model call can improve answer accuracy while utilizing substantially less computation.

AI.tldr: EIR uses structured state to accumulate source evidence in one retrieval trajectory, enabling correct final answers in a single call even with mixed-in erroneous evidence, improving accuracy while cutting model calls.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop LLM agents detect intermediate reasoning errors but correct them by retrying steps or entire trajectories, which is expensive and potentially unnecessary. The paper argues retries can be avoided if relevant evidence is collected.
AI.method: Evidence-Inference Reconstruction (EIR): a structured state guides a single retrieval trajectory that accumulates source evidence, separating evidence retrieval from the final answer model call.
AI.result: On matched 1,000-question subsets of HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4.1 Mini, EIR improves Answer F1 over baseline by 8.3-32.8 points, Agentic SSR by 10.6-29.1, and Reflexion by 1.1-15.9. EIR averages 4.85 model calls/question vs. 35.29 (Agentic SSR) and 12.41 (Reflexion).
AI.conclusion: Separating evidence retrieval from the final answer model call improves answer accuracy while using substantially less computation.

title: Is your uncertainty map wrong, or is its target? Exact diagnostics for the Tweedie diagonal, and a gradient-free alternative
summary:
A diffusion model can predict a follow-up medical scan from a baseline, but a clinician needs a per-voxel map of where that prediction can be trusted. Many such maps approximate the diagonal of the Tweedie posterior covariance, and are evaluated against another approximation of it, so whether the estimator or the target limits them is unclear. We compute the exact diagonal on six checkpoints across fourteen model-corpus conditions. Hutchinson at M=200 tracks it at rank agreement of at least 0.92 everywhere, yet in four of the fourteen the exact diagonal is anti-correlated with the denoising error, reaching -0.13, so a faithful estimator reproduces that reversal. All four are real-image conditions; on the models' own samples the reversal does not appear, so evaluating on generated samples flatters this family. What limits these maps is the target, not the estimator.
  We then introduce Tweedie Probe-Tangent (T-PT), a gradient-free residual probe that corrupts one model-supported prediction repeatedly and measures the voxel-wise variance of the denoiser's response. T-PT reads a different functional of the same Jacobian, and its exact second-order form ranks with the diagonal wherever the diagonal reverses; at thirty probes it returns a map too unstable to reproduce that ranking, while Hutchinson at M=5 already reproduces it, so T-PT there is not evidence against the reversal. We offer it as an instrument, not a better approximation. On brain MRI at full resolution, where every Jacobian-based estimator we test runs out of memory, T-PT leads a twenty-chain Monte-Carlo ensemble on five of eight endpoints inside tissue and trails it on none, at 16x fewer network evaluations; over the whole volume the ensemble leads, and fifty chains close the tissue gap. On lung CT the ensemble is ahead throughout. Both lose most of their discrimination where the change is, which remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that limitations of Tweedie-posterior-diagonal uncertainty maps for diffusion-based follow-up scan prediction stem from the estimation target, not the estimator, and introduces T-PT, a gradient-free residual probe, as a scalable instrument for Jacobian-based voxel-wise uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Clinicians need per-voxel trust maps for diffusion-model predictions of follow-up medical scans. Existing maps approximate the Tweedie posterior covariance diagonal and are evaluated against another approximation, leaving unclear whether the estimator or the target is the limiting factor.
AI.method: Exact diagonal of the Tweedie posterior covariance is computed on six checkpoints across fourteen model-corpus conditions, compared against Hutchinson (M=200) and correlated with denoising error. T-PT (Tweedie Probe-Tangent) is a gradient-free residual probe that repeatedly corrupts one model-supported prediction and measures voxel-wise variance of the denoiser response; it reads a different functional of the same Jacobian. Evaluated on brain MRI at full resolution and lung CT, with comparison to a twenty-chain Monte-Carlo ensemble.
AI.result: Hutchinson at M=200 tracks the exact diagonal with rank agreement at least 0.92 everywhere, yet in four of fourteen conditions the exact diagonal is anti-correlated with denoising error (down to -0.13); all four are real-image conditions and the reversal does not appear on generated samples. T-PT's exact second-order form ranks with the diagonal where the diagonal reverses, but at thirty probes it is too unstable; Hutchinson at M=5 already reproduces the ranking. On brain MRI, T-PT leads a twenty-chain Monte-Carlo ensemble on five of eight tissue endpoints, trails on none, at 16x fewer network evaluations; over the whole volume the ensemble leads, and fifty chains close the tissue gap. On lung CT the ensemble leads throughout. Both lose discrimination where the change is.
AI.conclusion: What limits these uncertainty maps is the target, not the estimator. T-PT is offered as an instrument rather than a better approximation, and it scales where Jacobian-based estimators run out of memory. Loss of discrimination in change regions remains an open problem.

title: Dual-Vocabulary Language Model for Cross-Tokenizer Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) bridges teacher supervision and student behavior, but different teacher-student tokenizers introduce misalignment in both input tokenization (#1) and output logits (#2). Existing approaches address the former by matching same-text spans or converting tokens to bytes, often losing fine-grained token information or disrupting the native-token paradigm, while for the latter, strategies such as ranking, padding, or key-token selection retain only shared logit dimensions, resulting in much distribution loss. In this paper, we propose Dual-Vocabulary Language Model (DVLM), which replaces the teacher's LM head with a new student-vocabulary projection head and obtains full-dimensional student logits (for #2). To support student tokens (for #1), it takes a Parallel-Tokenized Sequence (PTS) as input, which concatenates the original teacher-tokenized sequence and a re-tokenized sequence formed by independently converting each student token into a teacher-token group. To avoid inference inconsistency with the original teacher tokens, the Hybrid-Prefix Attention (HPA) further restricts re-tokenized groups to their corresponding teacher prefix and uses its last state as the aggregation of the original student-token representation for projection into the student vocabulary space. Similarly, via the combined use of PTS and HPA, the DVLM teacher can provide distribution-aligned supervision with the student's input-tokenization and output-logit during OPD. Experimental results demonstrate that our DVLM teacher has a similar converged loss as the original teacher model and enables student models to improve performance across six reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: DVLM addresses tokenizer misalignment in on-policy distillation by using a student-vocabulary projection head for full-dimensional student logits and a Parallel-Tokenized Sequence with Hybrid-Prefix Attention for student-token input, yielding distribution-aligned teacher supervision and improved student performance on six reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation bridges teacher supervision and student behavior, but differing teacher-student tokenizers cause misalignment in both input tokenization and output logits. Prior fixes for input either match same-text spans or convert tokens to bytes, losing fine-grained token information or breaking the native-token paradigm; fixes for logits (ranking, padding, key-token selection) keep only shared logit dimensions, causing substantial distribution loss.
AI.method: The paper proposes Dual-Vocabulary Language Model (DVLM). It replaces the teacher's LM head with a new student-vocabulary projection head to obtain full-dimensional student logits. For student tokens, it takes a Parallel-Tokenized Sequence (PTS) as input, concatenating the original teacher-tokenized sequence with a re-tokenized sequence independently formed by converting each student token into a teacher-token group. Hybrid-Prefix Attention (HPA) restricts re-tokenized groups to their corresponding teacher prefix and uses its last state as the aggregation of the original student-token representation for projection into the student vocabulary space, avoiding inference inconsistency. Combined PTS and HPA let the DVLM teacher provide distribution-aligned supervision matching the student's input-tokenization and output-logit during OPD.
AI.result: Experimental results show that the DVLM teacher achieves a converged loss similar to the original teacher model and enables student models to improve performance across six reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: DVLM resolves both input-tokenization and output-logit misalignment in on-policy distillation via full-dimensional student logits, PTS, and HPA, delivering distribution-aligned teacher supervision that preserves the native-token paradigm while improving student performance on reasoning tasks.

title: Vestrum: Improving Agent Harnesses by Adapting Their Verification, Structure and Memory
summary: An agent harness controls how a language model accesses information, uses tools, preserves memory, and checks its work. Improving this software is costly when each evaluation requires a long interaction with an environment. We introduce Vestrum, a framework that turns failures in execution traces into scoped harness changes without training the task model. Its organizing overhypothesis is that tasks of a shared kind may exhibit recurring failures whose remedies transfer within that kind. Vestrum expresses failures as recognizable classes, proposes changes across verification, retrieval, decomposition, and knowledge synthesis, and screens their scope before evaluating them as a bundle. A persistent lessons file informs subsequent proposals. Across five settings and two baseline harnesses, the frozen harnesses improve held-out performance: UltraHorizon rises from 47.6 to 59.8 over GAM, Terminal-Bench 4 Hard from 63.7% to 70.3% of checks passed over Claude Code on eight held-out tasks at 1.03x test cost, and cell-type annotation agreement from 67.5% to 77.8% on held-out sections of one slide, alongside gains on LoCoMo and AMA-Bench. Across our searches, verification grounded in evidence helped both intermediate steps and final answers, at lower cost at intermediate steps, while critics asked to rebuild finished answers broke more than they repaired. On the three memory benchmarks, Vestrum also scores above the evaluated GEPA configurations in every paired evaluation.

AI.tldr: Vestrum is a framework that converts failures observed in execution traces into scoped, transferable changes to an agent harness (verification, retrieval, decomposition, knowledge synthesis) without training the task model, improving frozen harnesses across five settings and outperforming evaluated GEPA configurations on three memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Improving agent harness software—which governs how a language model accesses information, uses tools, preserves memory, and checks its work—is costly because each evaluation requires long environment interactions. The authors hypothesize that tasks of a shared kind exhibit recurring failures whose remedies transfer within that kind, motivating a cheaper, scope-aware way to evolve harnesses.
AI.method: Vestrum expresses execution failures as recognizable classes, proposes harness changes across verification, retrieval, decomposition, and knowledge synthesis, screens their scope before evaluating them as a bundle, and maintains a persistent lessons file to inform subsequent proposals. It performs this harness modification without training the task model.
AI.result: Across five settings and two baseline harnesses, frozen harnesses improved held-out performance: UltraHorizon rose from 47.6 to 59.8 over GAM; Terminal-Bench 4 Hard rose from 63.7% to 70.3% of checks passed over Claude Code on eight held-out tasks at 1.03x test cost; cell-type annotation agreement rose from 67.5% to 77.8% on held-out sections of one slide, with additional gains on LoCoMo and AMA-Bench. Verification grounded in evidence helped intermediate steps and final answers, at lower cost at intermediate steps, whereas critics asked to rebuild finished answers broke more than they repaired. On the three memory benchmarks, Vestrum scored above the evaluated GEPA configurations in every paired evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Turning execution failures into scoped, transferable harness changes is an effective and cost-efficient alternative to training the task model and to full re-evaluation per change, yielding consistent held-out gains across diverse settings and surpassing evaluated GEPA configurations on memory benchmarks.

title: Laya as a Typed Probabilistic Assessor: An Independent Reproduction and a Preregistered Study of Calibration and Selective Escalation
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures. Ancillary files include the frozen preregistration, all run manifests, per-decision prediction records, and the metric code
summary: The shipped Laya Typed-Decisions checkpoint, a 421M-parameter ModernBERT-large assessor that answers typed choice/noul/score questions over workflow state, is uniformly under-confident. The signed confidence-accuracy gap is $-0.214$, every occupied reliability bin's accuracy exceeds its confidence, and that sign uniformity collapses every binned ECE variant to the same value, $0.214$. The card frames the risk as over-confidence; the measured direction is the opposite, and the direction decides which way a confidence-gated cascade fails. A single disjointly fitted temperature ($T=0.469$, sharpening) removes most of the miscalibration (held-out ECE $0.204$ to $0.037$) and outperforms the shipped per-option-count table. The frozen selection rule instead chose isotonic regression, which overfit and failed its held-out NLL contrast on both tracks, so hypothesis H2 is not supported. Re-running the released checkpoint on its full official test split reproduces the card's headline accuracy ($0.767$ vs. $0.766$). The retrospective E1 reproduction preceded the analysis freeze; E2-E8 were prospectively preregistered, and 20 of 22 executed confirmatory tests reject under Benjamini-Hochberg FDR at $q=0.05$ (two descoped). The frozen gate beats random escalation but misses its 10% accepted-set error target on both tracks, an exploratory out-of-distribution probe finds no zero-shot transfer (accuracy $0.617$), and every score measures agreement with a synthetic teacher whose self-agreement ceiling ($0.735$) the specialist exceeds. Per-decision predictions, run manifests, and the frozen preregistration are in the ancillary files. The author has no affiliation with the model's publisher, the dataset's publisher, or TypeSafe.

AI.tldr: The shipped Laya Typed-Decisions 421M ModernBERT assessor is uniformly under-confident (signed gap −0.214) rather than over-confident as its card claims; a single temperature T=0.469 fixes most miscalibration (ECE 0.204→0.037), beating the shipped mapping, while the frozen isotonic selection overfit, refuting H2.
AI.motivation: Assess whether the released Laya Typed-Decisions checkpoint's calibration matches its model card, which frames the risk as over-confidence. The direction of miscalibration is consequential: it determines whether a confidence-gated cascade escalates too rarely or too often. The work also tests a preregistered confidence-mapping hypothesis (H2) and evaluates the frozen confidence gate against a stated error target.
AI.method: Post-hoc calibration study on a 421M-parameter ModernBERT-large assessor answering typed choice/noun/score questions. Reliability-bin analysis of the signed confidence-accuracy gap; comparison of a single disjointly fitted temperature (T=0.469, sharpening) against the shipped per-option-count table and isotonic regression selected by the frozen rule; reproduction of headline accuracy on the full official test split; retrospective E1 reproduction followed by prospectively preregistered confirmatory tests E2–E8 with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q=0.05); evaluation of the frozen gate against random escalation and a 10% accepted-set error target; exploratory out-of-distribution probe; synthetic-teacher agreement scoring.
AI.result: Signed confidence-accuracy gap is −0.214; every occupied reliability bin's accuracy exceeds its confidence, making all binned ECE variants collapse to 0.214. Temperature scaling reduces held-out ECE from 0.204 to 0.037 and outperforms the shipped per-option-count table. Isotonic regression overfit and failed its held-out NLL contrast on both tracks, so H2 is unsupported. Official test split reproduces the card's headline accuracy (0.767 vs. 0.766). 20 of 22 executed confirmatory tests reject under BH FDR at q=0.05 (two descoped). The frozen gate beats random escalation but misses its 10% accepted-set error target on both tracks. The OOD probe shows no zero-shot transfer (accuracy 0.617). All scores measure agreement with a synthetic teacher whose self-agreement ceiling is 0.735, which the specialist exceeds.
AI.conclusion: The checkpoint is systematically under-confident, contradicting the model card's over-confidence framing, and this sign uniformity has direct cascade-design implications. A single fitted temperature is a stronger and simpler correction than the frozen isotonic mapping, which overfit; H2 is therefore rejected. The released checkpoint's accuracy reproduces on the official split, the confirmatory battery largely rejects, and the gate improves on random escalation without meeting its 10% error target. Reported quality is bounded by the synthetic teacher's 0.735 self-agreement ceiling, which the specialist surpasses. Ancillary files provide per-decision predictions, run manifests, and the frozen preregistration; the author is unaffiliated with the model, dataset, and TypeSafe publishers.

title: How code helps different tasks? A decompositional lens on LLM post-training
summary: Evaluating code data as a single corpus can obscure which types of code data benefit which models and downstream tasks. Effective data selection requires understanding both the benefits of individual categories and whether these benefits persist when categories are combined. We introduce a decompositional lens for studying these effects in LLM post-training. We first decompose an execution-verified code corpus into interpretable categories based on the computational patterns of its solutions. Through controlled fine-tuning experiments, we compare individual categories with a balanced mixture across instruction-tuned models on question answering, mathematics, and code generation. The resulting response maps reveal recurring gains in average question-answering performance, while the same category can improve one model or task and degrade another. The best-performing category also varies with the starting model and target task. We then compose compact mixtures guided by these results and examine whether benefits observed in individual categories persist under joint training. On selected model--task pairs, mixtures whose constituents each improve the target task outperform both their best constituent and full-corpus training while using roughly 10--15\% of the full corpus. These exploratory findings illustrate a \emph{less is more} pattern and highlight how the value of code data in post training depends on which categories are combined for which model and task.

AI.tldr: This paper applies a "decompositional lens" to code-data post-training: it splits an execution-verified code corpus into interpretable computational-pattern categories, maps which categories help which models/tasks, and shows that small purpose-built mixtures (≈10–15% of the corpus) can beat both their best constituent and full-corpus training.
AI.motivation: Treating code data as a single undifferentiated corpus hides which categories of code benefit which models and downstream tasks, and whether those benefits survive when categories are combined. Effective data selection needs category-level attribution and composition evidence, which prior coarse-corpus studies do not provide.
AI.method: The authors take an execution-verified code corpus and decompose it into interpretable categories based on the computational patterns of the solutions. They run controlled fine-tuning experiments comparing individual categories against a balanced mixture, across instruction-tuned models, on question answering, mathematics, and code generation. The outcomes are summarized as "response maps" of category × model × task effects. They then compose compact mixtures guided by these maps and test whether per-category gains persist under joint training, comparing mixtures against their best constituent and against full-corpus training.
AI.result: Response maps show recurring gains in average question-answering performance, but the same category can help one model or task while hurting another, and the best category varies by starting model and target task. In the composition stage, on selected model–task pairs, mixtures whose constituents each individually improve the target task outperform both their best constituent and full-corpus training while using only about 10–15% of the full corpus.
AI.conclusion: Code data value in LLM post-training is not a property of the corpus as a whole but depends on which categories are combined, for which model and which task. Category-level decomposition plus guided composition yields a "less is more" pattern, where small, well-chosen mixtures can exceed full-corpus training, making data selection a combinatorial rather than purely volumetric problem.

title: R$^2$ Flow: Recursive Self-Improvement via Recursive Skill Evolution
summary: LLM-based agents can improve themselves across tasks by reusing and revising the skills they orchestrate into executable procedures. Flow-based training fits this loop: it samples procedures in proportion to reward, and the flow through each skill credits it for the next library revision. Three obstacles stand in the way of making this self-improvement reliable: flow training suffers strategy collapse over tree-structured histories; nonnegative flow-based credit rewards frequent use as if it were benefit; and library edits rest on the task reward the policy optimizes. We introduce R$^2$ Flow, a recursive self-improvement framework that alternates policy learning, independent verification, and versioned skill-library updates on a shared-state orchestration graph. The graph merges histories that differ only in the order of independent steps, allowing flow training to pool evidence across equivalent executions. A flow-share readout of the trained flow, invariant to the backward policy, and a separate signed utility rank which skills to change, verifier evidence decides whether an edit is warranted, and a residual-variance plateau sets when to update. Committed edits reshape the graph the next policy learns on, realizing recursive skill evolution. Across question answering, mathematical reasoning, interactive decision making, and code generation, R$^2$ Flow improves task accuracy and library-edit precision over heuristic orchestration, reinforcement learning, and skill-evolution baselines, and transfers across executors. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/r2flow.

AI.tldr: R$^2$ Flow is a recursive self-improvement framework for LLM agents that alternates policy learning, independent verification, and versioned skill-library updates on a shared-state orchestration graph, addressing strategy collapse, misattributed credit, and reward-driven edits.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents can self-improve by reusing and revising orchestrated skills, and flow-based training matches this loop by sampling procedures in proportion to reward and crediting skills via flow. However, three obstacles undermine reliable self-improvement: (1) flow training suffers strategy collapse over tree-structured histories; (2) nonnegative flow-based credit conflates frequent use with benefit; and (3) library edits rely on the same task reward the policy optimizes, lacking independent evidence.
AI.method: R$^2$ Flow alternates policy learning, independent verification, and versioned skill-library updates on a shared-state orchestration graph. The graph merges histories differing only in the order of independent steps, letting flow training pool evidence across equivalent executions. A flow-share readout of the trained flow, invariant to the backward policy, together with a separate signed utility, ranks which skills to change; verifier evidence decides whether an edit is warranted; and a residual-variance plateau sets when to update. Committed edits reshape the graph for the next policy, enabling recursive skill evolution.
AI.result: Across question answering, mathematical reasoning, interactive decision making, and code generation, R$^2$ Flow improves task accuracy and library-edit precision over heuristic orchestration, reinforcement learning, and skill-evolution baselines, and transfers across executors.
AI.conclusion: R$^2$ Flow provides a reliable recursive self-improvement loop for LLM agents by jointly addressing strategy collapse, credit misattribution, and unverified library edits through shared-state graph-based flow training and verifier-gated, versioned skill-library updates.

title: When Successful Strategies Fail: Adaptation to Environmental Novelty in Terminal Agents
comment: 53 pages, including references and appendices; 10-page main text with 5 figures
summary: LLM agents increasingly solve long-horizon tasks by autonomously interacting with their environment. In doing so, their strategies rely on assumptions about that environment: which resources and tools exist, where they are located, and how they behave. When these assumptions no longer hold, reliable agents must detect the change and adapt while pursuing the same goal. We study this adaptation capability through environmental novelty: a change that keeps the task objective fixed while invalidating an assumption underlying an otherwise successful trajectory. We introduce AGNI, an automated pipeline that extracts trajectory-relevant assumptions, injects targeted environmental changes, and validates that the resulting novel tasks remain solvable. Across three terminal benchmarks, AGNI produces diverse novelties spanning resources, interfaces, constraints, and execution semantics. Evaluating multiple LLM agents reveals a substantial adaptation gap between base and novel tasks. Trajectory analysis suggests that agents often encounter evidence of the change but fail to diagnose its cause and revise their strategy. Finally, post-training for environmental novelty improves adaptation to held-out novel tasks while also improving performance on base tasks. Our results highlight a gap between task competence and adaptive capability and motivate environmental variation as a core dimension of agent training and evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies LLM agents' ability to adapt to "environmental novelty"—changes that keep the task objective fixed but invalidate assumptions behind a previously successful trajectory. It introduces AGNI, an automated pipeline that extracts trajectory-relevant assumptions, injects targeted environmental changes, and validates solvability, and finds a substantial adaptation gap that post-training can reduce.
AI.motivation: LLM agents solve long-horizon tasks by interacting with environments and relying on assumptions about resources, tools, locations, and behavior. When these assumptions break, reliable agents must detect and adapt. The work is motivated by the gap between task competence and adaptive capability, and the lack of systematic methods to evaluate adaptation.
AI.method: AGNI, an automated pipeline that (1) extracts trajectory-relevant assumptions, (2) injects targeted environmental changes creating "environmental novelty" while keeping the goal fixed, and (3) validates that the resulting novel tasks remain solvable. Evaluated across three terminal benchmarks with diverse novelties spanning resources, interfaces, constraints, and execution semantics.
AI.result: Across three terminal benchmarks, AGNI produces diverse novelties. Evaluating multiple LLM agents reveals a substantial adaptation gap between base and novel tasks; trajectory analysis shows agents often encounter evidence of the change but fail to diagnose its cause and revise strategy. Post-training for environmental novelty improves adaptation to held-out novel tasks and also improves base-task performance.
AI.conclusion: There is a gap between task competence and adaptive capability in LLM agents. Environmental variation should be treated as a core dimension of agent training and evaluation, and post-training on novelty can simultaneously improve adaptation and base performance.

title: Curating Merchant-Matching Training Data with Two Confidence-Gated Local LLM Judges
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables, Accepted for publication in 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW), SENTIRE 2026 Workshop
summary: Merchant matching resolves a noisy payment descriptor to a retrieved merchant entity or returns no match. A key challenge in curating training labels is distinguishing teacher abstention from evidence that no acceptable entity exists: false no-match labels contaminate pseudo-labeled data, while conservative labeling reduces coverage. We investigate whether agreement between two local large language model judges improves pseudo-label reliability. A label is retained only when the judges agree, with separate ordered thresholds for selections and abstentions that guarantee disjoint positive and negative label sets. Retrospective replay on 2,000 expert-annotated queries shows that higher selection thresholds can improve positive-label purity, whereas higher abstention thresholds increase false no-match labels. At thresholds (0.86, 0.80), Muse Glimmer 30B and Gemma 4 31B jointly label 1,633 queries (81.7% coverage) at 96.88% purity; positive and negative purities are 99.47% and 93.38%. This exceeds either constituent model at the same thresholds by more than two percentage points, with lower coverage. A split-half check finds only 0.14 percentage points of threshold-selection optimism. A symmetric threshold of 0.86 adds 40 erroneous no-match labels, while 46 false abstentions persist even with no confidence threshold. Across five matched within-model comparisons, higher reasoning effort yields no clear F0.5 gain and increases median latency by 1.8-5.0 times. These results motivate separate thresholding and auditing for positive and negative pseudo-labels. The study establishes label purity, not student utility; fresh-data curation and student fine-tuning remain necessary to demonstrate downstream value.

AI.tldr: Two local LLM judges with separate ordered thresholds for selections and abstentions yield reliable merchant-matching pseudo-labels, but positive and negative labels require separate thresholding and auditing.
AI.motivation: Curating training labels for merchant matching is hard because teacher abstention must be distinguished from genuine evidence that no acceptable entity exists. False no-match labels contaminate pseudo-labeled data, while conservative labeling reduces coverage. The paper investigates whether agreement between two local large language model judges can improve pseudo-label reliability.
AI.method: A label is retained only when two local LLM judges agree, using separate ordered thresholds for selections and abstentions that guarantee disjoint positive and negative label sets. The approach is evaluated via retrospective replay on 2,000 expert-annotated queries, with a split-half check for threshold-selection optimism, a symmetric-threshold comparison, and five matched within-model comparisons of reasoning effort on F0.5 and latency.
