By intervening at intermediate reasoning states across two model families and multiple scales, we find that self-refinement largely consolidates probability mass onto solutions already reachable from the current state, rather than making new ones reachable. These interventions reveal two failure regimes: execution bottlenecks, where the correct path is reachable and reflection can recover it, and knowledge bottlenecks, where relevant external information makes it reachable. Motivated by this distinction, we introduce FlyBy, a selective querying framework, and train 4B and 8B variants to reason first, diagnose what remains unresolved, and, at a knowledge bottleneck, query stronger models whose parametric knowledge extends beyond its own. Supervised fine-tuning bootstraps a multi-depth query action, and cost-aware reinforcement learning calibrates whether to query, what to ask, and how much to spend. On 1,158 hard problems across six benchmarks, FlyBy-4B achieves 45.96% pass@8, surpassing Qwen3-14B (41.64%) at 2.7 times lower serving cost, while also exceeding Qwen3-8B in pass@1 (16.85% vs. 15.31%). Scaling to FlyBy-8B further improves pass@8 to 51.81%.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that extra "thinking" in small reasoning models mainly consolidates existing solutions rather than discovering new ones, distinguishing execution bottlenecks (recoverable by reflection) from knowledge bottlenecks (requiring external info). It proposes FlyBy, a selective querying framework where models reason, diagnose unresolved issues, and query stronger models at knowledge bottlenecks, trained via SFT and cost-aware RL.
AI.motivation: Scaling test-time computation improves reasoning and is attractive for cheap small reasoning models. However, the authors question whether additional thinking is always the right operation, since self-refinement may not make new solutions reachable.
AI.method: Interventions at intermediate reasoning states across two model families and multiple scales reveal two failure regimes: execution bottlenecks and knowledge bottlenecks. Based on this, FlyBy is introduced: a selective querying framework with 4B and 8B variants that reason first, diagnose unresolved issues, and query stronger models at knowledge bottlenecks. Training uses SFT to bootstrap a multi-depth query action, plus cost-aware RL to calibrate whether to query, what to ask, and spending.
AI.result: On 1,158 hard problems across six benchmarks, FlyBy-4B reaches 45.96% pass@8, surpassing Qwen3-14B (41.64%) at 2.7x lower serving cost, and also beats Qwen3-8B in pass@1 (16.85% vs 15.31%). FlyBy-8B improves pass@8 to 51.81%.
AI.conclusion: Self-refinement has inherent limits, mainly consolidating reachable solutions rather than generating new ones. Distinguishing execution from knowledge bottlenecks and selectively querying stronger models enables small reasoning models to achieve strong performance at lower cost.

title: SAGE: Structured Strategic Reasoning for Efficient LLM Game Playing
summary: A strong LLM strategic agent should reason prospectively over uncertain futures, adapt its strategy to opponents' behavioral tendencies, and continuously recalibrate its decision process from interaction experience. However, incorporating these sources in free-form reasoning could lead to unsupported strategic assumptions, inconsistent opponent estimates, and harmful interference from irrelevant historical interactions. To address these issues, we propose SAGE, a training-free inference-time framework that structures LLM strategic reasoning around three coordinated operations: anchor, adapt, and recalibrate. SAGE first anchors reasoning to an equilibrium policy that provides a strategically valid prior. It then conditions deviations from this anchor on a soft belief over opponent behavioral tendencies, enabling opponent-specific exploitation. Finally, SAGE distills strategically related interactions into counterfactual hypotheses about previously missing considerations, allowing past experience to recalibrate the model's reasoning. We evaluate SAGE on three repeated imperfect-information games: Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, and Goofspiel, against various opponent types in each game. Compared with reasoning-intensive LLM agents, including Suspicion-Agent, ReTA, Agent-Pro, EMO, and Hypothetical Minds, SAGE achieves up to a 127.6% payoff improvement in Liar's Dice while reducing input and output token usage by up to 80% and 90%, respectively. In direct match-up play, it attains non-negative mean payoff against 5/10, 8/10, and 8/10 evaluated opponents in Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, and Goofspiel, respectively, while using relatively fewer tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/chenzhwsysu57/SAGE.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a training-free inference-time framework that structures LLM strategic reasoning into three operations—anchor, adapt, and recalibrate—to improve decision-making in repeated imperfect-information games while using fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Strong LLM strategic agents should reason prospectively over uncertain futures, adapt to opponents' behavioral tendencies, and recalibrate from interaction experience. However, free-form reasoning risks unsupported strategic assumptions, inconsistent opponent estimates, and harmful interference from irrelevant historical interactions.
AI.method: SAGE coordinates three operations: (1) anchor reasoning to an equilibrium policy as a strategically valid prior; (2) condition deviations from this anchor on a soft belief over opponent behavioral tendencies for opponent-specific exploitation; (3) distill strategically relevant interactions into counterfactual hypotheses about previously missing considerations to recalibrate reasoning.
AI.result: On Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, and Goofspiel, SAGE achieves up to a 127.6% payoff improvement in Liar's Dice versus reasoning-intensive LLM agents (Suspicion-Agent, ReTA, Agent-Pro, EMO, Hypothetical Minds), while cutting input and output token usage by up to 80% and 90%. In direct match-ups, it attains non-negative mean payoff against 5/10, 8/10, and 8/10 opponents respectively, using relatively fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: Structuring LLM strategic reasoning through equilibrium anchoring, belief-conditioned adaptation, and counterfactual recalibration yields stronger and more token-efficient play in repeated imperfect-information games than reasoning-intensive LLM agents.

title: Fuzzy Distribution Modeling for Synthetic Tabular Data Generation with Causality Preservation
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Published in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Fuzzy Systems (FUZZ-IEEE), Maastricht, the Netherlands
summary: Synthetic tabular data generation provides an effective alternative for the training of machine learning models when real-world data is limited or inaccessible. However, the heterogeneous, non-smooth, and incomplete nature of tabular data poses fundamental challenges to conventional probabilistic and deep generative models, where their interpretability remains limited. This paper proposes a novel fuzzy distribution modeling methodology for synthetic tabular data generation based on fuzzy sets theory. Feature distributions are represented using fuzzy sets and feature dependencies are modeled through Fuzzy Cognitive Maps, resulting in a low-parameter, and an interpretable data representation. Synthetic samples are generated by sampling fuzzy concepts rather than raw values, enabling native support for mixed data types, missing values, and domain constraints. The methodology further supports linguistic queries and IF-THEN reasoning, facilitating transparent simulation of decision-making processes. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive performance with respect to utility, fidelity and privacy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while offering substantially improved interpretability. These results establish fuzzy distribution modeling as a principled and effective approach for synthetic tabular data generation in fuzzy systems and decision support applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a fuzzy distribution modeling methodology for synthetic tabular data generation, using fuzzy sets to represent feature distributions and Fuzzy Cognitive Maps to model dependencies, achieving competitive utility, fidelity, and privacy with improved interpretability.
AI.motivation: Real-world data is often limited or inaccessible, making synthetic tabular data a useful alternative for training ML models. However, tabular data is heterogeneous, non-smooth, and incomplete, which challenges conventional probabilistic and deep generative models that also lack interpretability.
AI.method: Feature distributions are represented using fuzzy sets, and feature dependencies are modeled through Fuzzy Cognitive Maps, yielding a low-parameter, interpretable representation. Synthetic samples are generated by sampling fuzzy concepts rather than raw values, providing native support for mixed data types, missing values, and domain constraints. The approach also supports linguistic queries and IF-THEN reasoning.
AI.result: On benchmark datasets, the method achieves competitive performance in utility, fidelity, and privacy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while substantially improving interpretability. It also enables transparent simulation of decision-making via linguistic queries and IF-THEN reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Fuzzy distribution modeling is established as a principled and effective approach for synthetic tabular data generation, particularly suited to fuzzy systems and decision support applications.

title: SemRD-V2X: Closure-Guided Communication with Bounded Inference for Cooperative Perception
summary: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) cooperative perception improves 3-D detection by sharing intermediate features, but dense remote features may repeat context that the ego agent can infer locally. Most communication-efficient designs optimize masks or codes empirically, leaving a more basic question open: which remote evidence is indispensable given the receiver's own observation? We introduce a closure-fidelity perspective on ego conditioned remote perception. Under a finite deductive abstraction and explicit conditions, its rate--distortion function decomposes over an irredundant core, and the exact zero-distortion rate becomes $P_A H(π_A)$. This analysis suggests a concrete design principle: transmit compact evidence and recover derivable context with bounded receiver-side inference. Guided by this principle, SemRD-V2X is an operational neural proxy that combines exact-budget BEV support selection, pointwise channel compression, and masked shared-weight reconstruction before standard fusion. Experiments on simulated V2XSet and real-world DAIR-V2X validate the resulting design. In a controlled five-run V2XSet comparison against a locally reproduced V2X-ViT-v1 baseline on one Tesla V100, SemRD-V2X reduces the analytical feature payload by $26.6\times$ while improving AP@0.5/AP@0.7 by 4.13/8.57 points, with 3.81\% additional mean compute latency. These results position closure fidelity as both an analytical lens and an actionable design principle for communication-efficient cooperative perception.

AI.tldr: SemRD-V2X frames ego-conditioned cooperative perception via a "closure-fidelity" rate–distortion view: only irredundant remote evidence is indispensable, yielding an exact zero-distortion rate of P_A H(π_A). Guided by this, it selects compact BEV evidence, compresses channels, and reconstructs masked features, cutting payload 26.6× while improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Dense remote features in V2X cooperative perception repeat context the ego agent can infer locally, so much transmitted data is redundant. Existing communication-efficient designs optimize masks or codes empirically without answering the fundamental question of which remote evidence is truly indispensable given the receiver's own observation.
AI.method: The authors introduce a closure-fidelity perspective on ego-conditioned remote perception. Under a finite deductive abstraction and explicit conditions, the rate–distortion function decomposes over an irredundant core, with exact zero-distortion rate P_A H(π_A). This yields a design principle: transmit compact evidence and recover derivable context via bounded receiver-side inference. They implement this as SemRD-V2X, a neural proxy combining exact-budget BEV support selection, pointwise channel compression, and masked shared-weight reconstruction before standard fusion.
AI.result: On simulated V2XSet and real-world DAIR-V2X, the design is validated. In a controlled five-run V2XSet comparison against a locally reproduced V2X-ViT-v1 baseline on one Tesla V100, SemRD-V2X reduces analytical feature payload by 26.6× while improving AP@0.5/AP@0.7 by 4.13/8.57 points, with only 3.81% additional mean compute latency.
AI.conclusion: Closure fidelity serves as both an analytical lens and an actionable design principle for communication-efficient cooperative perception, showing that compact evidence plus bounded receiver-side inference can outperform denser feature sharing.

title: Improving Large Language Models for Code through Runtime Program-State Reasoning
summary: Large language models receive limited explicit training in reasoning about runtime program states. We study whether training models to reason about runtime program states improves downstream software-engineering capabilities. We introduce two complementary program-state reasoning tasks. Buggy input-output reasoning requires a model to generate a concrete input that exposes a behavioral difference between a buggy program and a hidden correct implementation and to predict the resulting execution behavior. Precondition-postcondition reasoning requires an agent to symbolically characterize a bug-triggering precondition, predict the expected postcondition, explain their causal connection, and instantiate this reasoning as an executable regression test. By incorporating these two tasks into a staged post-training pipeline, we develop Comet-9B, a 9B language model based on Qwen3.5-9B Base. We evaluate the resulting checkpoints on repository-level patch generation, regression-test generation, and security PoC generation. Adding both program-state reasoning tasks to supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on issue resolution improves success rates by 7.25 percentage points on SWE-bench Pro and 9.70 points on SWT-Bench Verified. Sequential reinforcement learning on the two tasks yields further gains of 7.25, 26.79, and 4.67 percentage points on SWE-bench Pro, SWT-Bench Verified, and CyberGym, respectively. Despite having only 9B parameters, Comet-9B achieves a score comparable to the reported GPT-5.2 result on SWE-bench Pro and matches the reported success rate of a GPT-4o-based agent on SWT-Bench Verified.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two runtime program-state reasoning tasks—buggy input-output reasoning and precondition-postcondition reasoning—and integrates them into a staged post-training pipeline to build Comet-9B, a 9B model that substantially improves repository-level patch generation, regression-test generation, and security PoC generation.
AI.motivation: Large language models receive only limited explicit training in reasoning about runtime program states, which may constrain their downstream software-engineering capabilities. The authors investigate whether training models explicitly to reason about runtime program states improves these capabilities.
AI.method: The authors design two complementary program-state reasoning tasks. Buggy input-output reasoning requires generating a concrete input that exposes a behavioral difference between a buggy program and a hidden correct implementation and predicting the resulting execution behavior. Precondition-postcondition reasoning requires symbolically characterizing a bug-triggering precondition, predicting the expected postcondition, explaining their causal connection, and instantiating the reasoning as an executable regression test. These tasks are incorporated into a staged post-training pipeline (SFT on issue resolution plus sequential reinforcement learning) to develop Comet-9B, a 9B model based on Qwen3.5-9B Base.
AI.result: Adding both program-state reasoning tasks to SFT on issue resolution improves success rates by 7.25 percentage points on SWE-bench Pro and 9.70 points on SWT-Bench Verified. Sequential reinforcement learning on the two tasks yields further gains of 7.25, 26.79, and 4.67 percentage points on SWE-bench Pro, SWT-Bench Verified, and CyberGym, respectively. Despite having only 9B parameters, Comet-9B achieves a score comparable to the reported GPT-5.2 result on SWE-bench Pro and matches the reported success rate of a GPT-4o-based agent on SWT-Bench Verified.
AI.conclusion: Explicit training in reasoning about runtime program states is an effective way to improve downstream software-engineering capabilities, enabling a compact 9B model to reach performance comparable to much larger or agent-based systems on benchmark tasks.

title: CoeF-SFL: Preserving Collaborative Server-Client Learning with Enhanced Communication Efficiency
summary: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables resource-constrained clients to participate in collaborative training, but vanilla SFL exchanges smashed data and gradients at every batch, which incurs significant communication overhead. Recent methods reduce this overhead with an auxiliary network at the client-side cut layer. However, we identify that this approach makes the client optimize a local objective that differs from the end-to-end objective, which fundamentally limits the collaborative training between the client and the server. We propose Compensated Feedback based SFL (CoeF-SFL), a communication-efficient framework that retains the end-to-end objective without any auxiliary network. In CoeF-SFL, the client and the server exchange the smashed data and the gradients once per round and reuse them during local training. Since this reuse makes the gradients stale on the client side, we compensate them with a curvature-based correction in the activation space and develop two variants. CoeF-D approximates the Hessian with a diagonal gradient outer product, while CoeF-J exploits the tractable Jacobian-based Hessian of a surrogate loss that upper-bounds the true loss. We provide the theoretical background of each method, characterizing its compensation. Across vision and language tasks, model capacities, cut layers, and data distributions, CoeF-SFL significantly outperforms auxiliary-network-based methods under the same communication frequency, and the improvement is most substantial on vision tasks. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CoeF-SFL-2686/README.md

AI.tldr: CoeF-SFL is a communication-efficient Split Federated Learning framework that removes the auxiliary network and keeps the end-to-end objective, exchanging smashed data and gradients once per round and compensating the resulting stale gradients with curvature-based corrections (CoeF-D and CoeF-J).
AI.motivation: Vanilla SFL exchanges smashed data and gradients at every batch, causing heavy communication overhead. Existing remedies add an auxiliary network at the client-side cut layer, but this makes the client optimize a local objective that diverges from the end-to-end objective, fundamentally limiting client-server collaborative training.
AI.method: CoeF-SFL exchanges smashed data and gradients once per round and reuses them during local training, avoiding any auxiliary network while retaining the end-to-end objective. The resulting staleness of client-side gradients is compensated by a curvature-based correction in activation space. Two variants: CoeF-D approximates the Hessian with a diagonal gradient outer product; CoeF-J uses a tractable Jacobian-based Hessian of a surrogate loss that upper-bounds the true loss. Theoretical characterization of each compensation is provided.
AI.result: Across vision and language tasks, model capacities, cut layers, and data distributions, CoeF-SFL significantly outperforms auxiliary-network-based methods under the same communication frequency, with the largest gains on vision tasks.
AI.conclusion: Retaining the end-to-end objective without an auxiliary network and correcting stale gradients via curvature-based compensation yields a superior communication-efficiency/accuracy trade-off in SFL.

title: PersMem: Internalizing Personality into Dual-Pathway Memory for LLM Agents
summary: The profile of a role-playing agent usually depends on the pre-defined personality in a system prompt, whereas its memory processing pipeline, including prioritisation of stored memories and subsequent retrieval, remains independent of this personality. This separation causes the agent's memory processing to be inconsistent with the pre-defined personality, and makes it difficult to validate whether agent behaviours follow this personality. In this paper, we propose Personality-Integrated Memory (PersMem), which integrates personality into the agent's memory processing pipeline, making it consistently personality-dependent. PersMem processes memory using four steps, where the personality is mapped to operation-specific parameters controlling: (i) affective appraisal annotating emotion states of the user input; (ii) retention of previously stored memories along with the current input; (iii) passive affect-driven memory retrieval exploring memories similar to user input in semantics and personality-guided emotions; and (iv) active goal-driven memory retrieval that refines and selects passively retrieved memories for the reply. Consequently, consistency with the pre-defined personality can be examined by inspecting memory-processing traces during human-agent interactions. We evaluate these personality-dependent differences in attachment and Big Five settings. PersMem exceeds the chance baseline for four-way attachment classification by 23.1 percentage points. In Big Five dialogue comparisons, PersMem achieves 67.5% accuracy, 6.7 percentage points above a baseline using uniformly sampled memories. On CoSER, PersMem achieves an average score of 66.13, with scores of 69.33 for Character Fidelity and 84.33 for Storyline Quality. Together, these results show that PersMem produces distinguishable personality-related memory-processing patterns.

AI.tldr: PersMem integrates personality into a role-playing agent's memory pipeline via four personality-mapped steps, yielding distinguishable, inspectable personality-dependent memory-processing patterns.
AI.motivation: In role-playing agents, personality is typically set only via the system prompt, while memory prioritisation and retrieval run independently of personality. This separation makes memory processing inconsistent with the predefined personality and makes it hard to verify whether agent behaviour conforms to that personality.
AI.method: PersMem maps personality to operation-specific parameters controlling four memory steps: (i) affective appraisal annotating emotion states of user input; (ii) retention of prior memories plus current input; (iii) passive affect-driven retrieval of memories similar to user input in semantics and personality-guided emotions; and (iv) active goal-driven retrieval that refines and selects passively retrieved memories for the reply. Consistency is then inspectable via memory-processing traces.
AI.result: Evaluated on attachment and Big Five settings. PersMem exceeds the chance baseline by 23.1 percentage points on four-way attachment classification; reaches 67.5% accuracy in Big Five dialogue comparisons (6.7 points above a uniform-sampling baseline); and on CoSER attains an average of 66.13, with 69.33 Character Fidelity and 84.33 Storyline Quality.
AI.conclusion: PersMem produces distinguishable personality-related memory-processing patterns, and its traces enable inspection of personality consistency during human-agent interaction.

title: Org-Agent: Beyond Personal Assistants Towards Organizational Agents
summary: Language model agents serving organizations must coordinate requests from multiple users while using knowledge distributed across their interactions. We identify two complementary capabilities for this setting, namely cross-user interaction and decision-making, as well as cross-user memory and knowledge use. Both capabilities are governed by organizational constraints across three aspects: user identity, authority, and access permissions; the attribution and temporal validity of information; and rules for resolving conflicting requirements across users and completion requirements for joint decisions. These constraints shape what information or decisions must be obtained before an action can proceed and what conditions must be satisfied during its execution. Motivated by this, we introduce Org-Agent, a unified constraint-centric reasoning framework that organizes task execution in three stages. Specifically, Org-Agent decomposes a task into atomic subtasks and constructs a task dependency graph whose edges encode the dependencies among them. Building on this graph, it schedules the subtasks in dependency order through topological sorting. It then executes each subtask while accounting for the task's constraints, supported by evidence-acquisition and memory-management tools. Experiments on MUSES-Bench and GroupMemBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Org-Agent on both capabilities, and ablations further support the contributions of dependency modeling and tool use.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Org-Agent, a constraint-centric reasoning framework for language model agents in organizational settings, organized into three stages (task decomposition with dependency graphs, topological scheduling, and constraint-aware execution), validated on MUSES-Bench and GroupMemBench.
AI.motivation: Language model agents serving organizations must coordinate multi-user requests while leveraging knowledge distributed across interactions. Two complementary capabilities are needed: cross-user interaction and decision-making, and cross-user memory and knowledge use. Both are governed by organizational constraints spanning user identity, authority, and access permissions; information attribution and temporal validity; and conflict resolution across users plus joint-decision completion requirements. These constraints determine what information or decisions must precede an action and what conditions must hold during execution.
AI.method: Org-Agent is a unified constraint-centric reasoning framework with three stages: (1) decomposing a task into atomic subtasks and constructing a task dependency graph whose edges encode inter-subtask dependencies; (2) scheduling subtasks in dependency order via topological sorting; (3) executing each subtask while accounting for the task's constraints, supported by evidence-acquisition and memory-management tools.
AI.result: Experiments on MUSES-Bench and GroupMemBench demonstrate Org-Agent's effectiveness on both capabilities (cross-user interaction/decision-making and cross-user memory/knowledge use). Ablations further support the contributions of dependency modeling and tool use.
AI.conclusion: Org-Agent effectively addresses organizational constraint-governed multi-user coordination for language model agents, with dependency modeling and constraint-aware tool use as key contributors to performance.

title: SkillFocus: Evolving Agent Skills via Capability Decomposition
summary: Agent skill evolution seeks to improve reusable procedural guidance for large language model (LLM) agents through iterative revision. Existing methods base each revision mainly on execution trajectories or feedback, leaving recurring behavioral requirements across tasks implicit and tying revision to the behavior of the current skill. We introduce SkillFocus, which decomposes recurring task requirements into a capability space that remains fixed as the skill evolves, separating what tasks require from how the current skill behaves. SkillFocus maps current task outcomes to this space to identify the capability that leaves the most tasks unresolved, then uses that capability to determine what to revise and which evidence to use. Across four benchmarks spanning heterogeneous tasks, SkillFocus achieves the best held-out accuracy on all four, outperforming the strongest competing result by 5.7 points on average while using 24\% fewer evolution tokens on average than the closest iterative baseline. Controlled studies further show that capabilities derived from recurring task requirements outperform task-semantic and execution-derived alternatives, while randomizing task--capability assignments reduces final accuracy by up to 20.2 points. Matching evidence to the selected capability increases candidate gain by 4.4 points under prioritized revision.

AI.tldr: SkillFocus evolves LLM agent skills by decomposing recurring task requirements into a fixed capability space, revising the capability that leaves the most tasks unresolved, yielding best held-out accuracy on four benchmarks (+5.7 points average) with 24% fewer evolution tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing agent skill evolution methods revise skills mainly from execution trajectories or feedback, which leaves recurring behavioral requirements across tasks implicit and ties revision to the behavior of the current skill rather than to what tasks actually require.
AI.method: SkillFocus decomposes recurring task requirements into a capability space that stays fixed as the skill evolves, separating what tasks require from how the current skill behaves. It maps current task outcomes to this space to identify the capability that leaves the most tasks unresolved, then uses that capability to determine what to revise and which evidence to use, matching evidence to the selected capability under prioritized revision.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks spanning heterogeneous tasks, SkillFocus achieves the best held-out accuracy on all four, outperforming the strongest competing result by 5.7 points on average while using 24% fewer evolution tokens than the closest iterative baseline. Controlled studies show capabilities derived from recurring task requirements outperform task-semantic and execution-derived alternatives, randomizing task-to-capability assignments reduces final accuracy by up to 20.2 points, and matching evidence to the selected capability increases candidate gain by 4.4 points under prioritized revision.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly grounding skill revision in a fixed capability space derived from recurring task requirements improves both effectiveness and efficiency of agent skill evolution, and the capability space and evidence-matching design are each causally important to performance.

title: Mathematics for and by human cognition: A resource-rational search for bottlenecks in problem-solving
summary: Human cognitive constraints are generally viewed as limiting factors in problem-solving. We argue that these constraints can instead play a critical role in driving advances in mathematics and beyond. We propose a theory of mathematical abstraction as a resource-rational search for bottlenecks in problem-solving. Bottlenecks arising from cognitive constraints create pressure to restructure existing knowledge, potentially giving rise to novel formalisms with applications beyond the problems that originally motivated them. Drawing on episodes from the history of mathematics, we illustrate how such bottlenecks can drive the development of novel abstractions and examine how cognitive constraints and affective responses shape this process. Finally, we discuss the implications of this account for machine mathematical discovery and argue that incorporating human-like constraints may facilitate the discovery of useful mathematical abstractions.

AI.tldr: Cognitive constraints, typically seen as limiting, can actually drive mathematical advances; the authors propose a resource-rational theory of abstraction as a search for problem-solving bottlenecks, illustrate it with historical cases, and suggest that human-like constraints may aid machine mathematical discovery.
AI.motivation: To overturn the prevailing view that human cognitive constraints merely limit problem-solving, arguing instead that they are critical drivers of mathematical abstraction, and to understand how such constraints (plus affective responses) shape the development of novel formalisms.
AI.method: A theoretical framework: mathematical abstraction is modeled as a resource-rational search for bottlenecks in problem-solving, where constraints generate pressure to restructure existing knowledge. The framework is illustrated and supported via episodes from the history of mathematics and analysis of how cognitive and affective factors influence the process.
AI.result: Bottlenecks arising from cognitive constraints create pressure to restructure knowledge, potentially yielding novel formalisms whose applications extend beyond the problems that originally motivated them; historical episodes demonstrate such constraint-driven abstraction.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive constraints can be productive rather than purely limiting in mathematical discovery; accordingly, incorporating human-like constraints into AI may facilitate the discovery of useful mathematical abstractions, with implications for machine mathematical discovery.

title: OSPD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Persona-Consistent Dialogue
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 22 pages, including references and appendices
summary: Maintaining persona consistency across multi-turn dialogues remains a core challenge for role-playing language models. Off-policy distillation from external teachers incurs distribution mismatch that compounds across dialogue turns, while reinforcement learning struggles with reward ambiguity inherent in subjective persona fidelity. We propose OSPD, an on-policy self-distillation framework where the same model serves as both teacher and student under asymmetric information: the teacher receives a complete character profile while the student sees only a brief summary, and the student generates trajectories from its own policy. We find that teacher confidence in role-playing dialogue exhibits a bimodal structure---sharply peaked at character-critical tokens yet diffuse at generic utterances---and introduce role-aware divergence switching to match this structure. A progressive trait masking curriculum further forces staged internalization of character knowledge along semantic dimensions. Experiments on CharacterBench, CharacterEval, and SocialBench show that OSPD substantially improves persona consistency over supervised fine-tuning and multi-turn RL baselines, without requiring any external teacher or reward model.

AI.tldr: OSP D is an on-policy self-distillation framework where one model acts as both teacher and student under asymmetric information, improving persona consistency in multi-turn role-playing dialogues without external teachers or reward models.
AI.motivation: Maintaining persona consistency across multi-turn dialogues is a core challenge for role-playing language models. Off-policy distillation from external teachers suffers from distribution mismatch that compounds over turns, while reinforcement learning struggles with reward ambiguity in subjective persona fidelity.
AI.method: OSP D uses the same model as teacher and student under asymmetric information: the teacher sees a complete character profile while the student sees only a brief summary and generates trajectories from its own policy. It introduces role-aware divergence switching, motivated by the observed bimodal teacher confidence (sharply peaked at character-critical tokens, diffuse at generic utterances), and a progressive trait masking curriculum that forces staged internalization of character knowledge along semantic dimensions.
AI.result: Experiments on CharacterBench, CharacterEval, and SocialBench show that OSP D substantially improves persona consistency over supervised fine-tuning and multi-turn RL baselines, without requiring any external teacher or reward model.
AI.conclusion: OSP D offers an effective on-policy self-distillation approach for persona-consistent role-playing, avoiding the distribution mismatch of off-policy distillation and the reward ambiguity of RL, and eliminating reliance on external teachers or reward models.

title: Beyond End-to-End Black Box Mapping: An Intentional Agent Framework for Cognitive-driven Facial Reaction Generation
summary: Automatic human-like facial reaction generation (FRG) is essential for building intelligent systems that can engage in human-computer interaction (HCI). While diverse and context-appropriate facial reactions can reflect latent appraisal and affective processes in human interaction, most existing FRG methods rely on end-to-end architectures that directly map speaker behaviours to listener expressions without an explicit intermediate internal state. We reformulate FRG as generation mediated by a structured internal-state process and propose the \textbf{Intentional Agent}, which shifts FRG from direct stimulus-response mapping to stimulus-grounded generation through explicit intermediate states. To represent temporal internal-state evolution, we propose an internal dynamics model that integrates emotional drives with an iterative Inner Thought Flow (ITF) within a structured intermediate state used for subsequent generation. This state can continue to update during conversational silences. Furthermore, to bridge abstract internal states with physiological actions, we formulate FRG as a downstream affective mapping from this latent thought flow to facial expressions. Experiments on the REACT 2025 dataset show an FRDist of 72.39 and an FRDiv of 0.5057; perceptual plausibility is evaluated separately through blinded human ratings. A blinded human evaluation of 96 reactions found no significant difference in mean score between Full and ground truth ($5.527$ vs.\ $5.195$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=.076$), while Full significantly outperformed Event-Triggered and Heuristic-Only (both $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<.001$). The Reaction Quality Scorer (RQS) correlated strongly with human judgements (Pearson $r=.855$; Spearman $ρ=.821$, both $p<.05$), supporting its use as an automatic metric. These results underscore the immense potential of endogenous dynamics in building highly autonomous, human-like agents.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates facial reaction generation (FRG) as generation mediated by an explicit internal-state process, proposing the Intentional Agent, which uses an internal dynamics model (emotional drives plus iterative Inner Thought Flow) and a downstream affective mapping to produce listener facial expressions, validated on REACT 2025 with competitive FRDist/FRDiv and human-rated plausibility on par with ground truth.
AI.motivation: Automatic human-like FRG is important for building intelligent HCI systems, and diverse, context-appropriate reactions can reflect latent appraisal and affective processes. However, most existing FRG methods rely on end-to-end architectures that map speaker behaviours directly to listener expressions without an explicit intermediate internal state, lacking the structured internal-state process that characterizes human interaction.
AI.method: The authors reformulate FRG as stimulus-grounded generation through explicit intermediate states and propose the Intentional Agent. An internal dynamics model represents temporal internal-state evolution by integrating emotional drives with an iterative Inner Thought Flow (ITF) within a structured intermediate state used for subsequent generation; this state can continue updating during conversational silences. FRG is further formulated as a downstream affective mapping from the latent thought flow to facial expressions, bridging abstract internal states with physiological actions.
AI.result: On the REACT 2025 dataset, the method achieves an FRDist of 72.39 and an FRDiv of 0.5057. In a blinded human evaluation of 96 reactions, no significant difference in mean score was found between Full and ground truth (5.527 vs. 5.195, pHolm=.076), while Full significantly outperformed Event-Triggered and Heuristic-Only baselines (both pHolm<.001). The Reaction Quality Scorer (RQS) correlated strongly with human judgements (Pearson r=.855; Spearman ρ=.821, both p<.05), supporting its use as an automatic metric.
AI.conclusion: These results underscore the immense potential of endogenous dynamics in building highly autonomous, human-like agents, showing that explicit intermediate internal states can support plausible and diverse facial reaction generation comparable to real human reactions.

title: Social Circuits behind Multi-agent Echo Chambers
summary: Language-model agents exchange messages to combine evidence, but their communication can also create echo chambers that reinforce shared errors. However, overall task performance does not explain how a message changes the receiving agent's internal activations and affects its decision. In this work, we introduce Social Circuits, a framework for tracing message effects through receiver activations. We compare the receiver's answers before and after changing a message. Then, we restore selected activations recorded under the original message to determine how much of the message effect these activations reproduce. Based on Social Circuits, we propose Circuit-Guided Deliberation (CGD), which learns to select useful messages using receiver activation changes. We establish when activation replacement preserves receiver decisions and bound the gap between CGD's task performance and the best achievable through message selection. Experiments show that receiver activation changes explain the message effects and guide message selection that improves the task performance. Across three models and four datasets, CGD achieves the highest or joint-highest average accuracy in our main comparisons while generating fewer tokens than multi-agent baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Social Circuits, a framework that traces how messages between language-model agents alter the receiver's internal activations and decisions, and uses these activation changes to build Circuit-Guided Deliberation (CGD), a message-selection method that improves accuracy with fewer tokens than multi-agent baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent language-model communication can produce echo chambers that reinforce shared errors, yet aggregate task performance alone does not reveal how a received message modifies the receiving agent's internal activations or drives its decision. The work aims to open this black box by causally linking messages to receiver internals.
AI.method: Social Circuits compares a receiver's answers before and after perturbing a transmitted message, then restores activations recorded under the original message to measure how much of the message effect those activations reproduce. Building on this, Circuit-Guided Deliberation (CGD) learns to select useful messages from receiver activation changes. The authors establish conditions under which activation replacement preserves receiver decisions and derive a bound on the gap between CGD's task performance and the best achievable via message selection.
AI.result: Experiments show that receiver activation changes causally explain message effects and can guide message selection that improves task performance. Across three models and four datasets, CGD attains the highest or joint-highest average accuracy in the main comparisons, while emitting fewer tokens than multi-agent baselines.
AI.conclusion: Tracing message effects through receiver activations offers an interpretable and effective mechanism for message selection in multi-agent language-model deliberation, yielding better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than existing multi-agent approaches.

title: CORTEX: Learning to Share and Specialize in Dense Language Models
summary: Large language models are trained on heterogeneous data mixtures, where different knowledge domains require both shared knowledge and specialization. Existing modular approaches typically impose explicit components or discover modules through interpretability analysis after training. In this work, we propose CORTEX, a learning dynamics-inspired framework that learns internal modularization within dense language models. CORTEX partitions trainable matrices into parameter groups and learns module assignments from domain-conditioned gradient and cross-domain gradient similarity. We introduce the selective lesion score and module-domain mutual information to characterize the target-domain lesion effects and alignment, and analyze how module assignment affects the trade-off between assignment bias and update magnitude. Experiments with 160M, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-32B backbone models show that CORTEX achieves the highest synthetic-domain exact match and largest average perplexity reduction, while remaining competitive on real-domain evaluations and forming identifiable modules.

AI.tldr: CORTEX is a learning-dynamics-inspired framework that learns internal modularization within dense LLMs by partitioning weight matrices into parameter groups and assigning modules via domain-conditioned gradient and cross-domain gradient similarity, achieving strong synthetic-domain performance and identifiable modules.
AI.motivation: LLMs are trained on heterogeneous data mixtures where different knowledge domains need both shared knowledge and specialization. Existing modular approaches either impose explicit components or discover modules through post-hoc interpretability analysis; there is a need for a method that learns internal modularization during training in dense models.
AI.method: CORTEX partitions trainable matrices into parameter groups and learns module assignments from domain-conditioned gradient and cross-domain gradient similarity. It introduces the selective lesion score and module-domain mutual information to characterize target-domain lesion effects and alignment, and analyzes the trade-off between assignment bias and update magnitude.
AI.result: With 160M, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-32B backbones, CORTEX achieves the highest synthetic-domain exact match and the largest average perplexity reduction, remains competitive on real-domain evaluations, and forms identifiable modules.
AI.conclusion: CORTEX enables learning-dynamics-driven internal modularization in dense LLMs, yielding improved synthetic-domain performance, competitive real-domain results, and interpretable module structure.

title: Escaping Local Views: Discovering Latent Concepts for Interpretable Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Efficient cooperation is challenging due to the usual partial observability of each agent in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Recurrent networks encode local interaction histories, but their hidden representations provide limited insight into the information underlying individual decisions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel interpretable framework, called escaping local views (ELV), which introduces semantically structured latent concepts to render policy decisions transparent. Specifically, each agent extracts low-dimensional semantic concepts from its local observation and action-observation trajectory. These concepts are jointly encoded into a contextual latent variable via a variational autoencoder (VAE), which builds a bridge between local views and global semantics. To explicitly model the decision of each agent, we employ a dual-path attention mechanism in which one module estimates the salience of individual concepts relative to the global context, while the other captures higher-order cooperative patterns with pairwise concept interactions. Furthermore, we incorporate a concept prediction module that derives an intrinsic reward from next-concept prediction errors, which incentivizes agents to explore regions of semantic novelty. Experiments in multiple environments verify that ELV not only achieves competitive performance but also explicitly provides how agents reason about their decisions.

AI.tldr: ELV is an interpretable multi-agent RL framework that introduces semantically structured latent concepts, encoded via a VAE into contextual latent variables and processed by a dual-path attention mechanism with a concept-prediction intrinsic reward to make policy decisions transparent while maintaining competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning is difficult due to partial observability. Recurrent networks encode local interaction histories, but their hidden representations offer limited insight into the information underlying individual decisions, harming interpretability.
AI.method: The proposed escaping local views (ELV) framework extracts low-dimensional semantic concepts from each agent's local observation and action-observation trajectory. A VAE jointly encodes these concepts into a contextual latent variable, bridging local views and global semantics. A dual-path attention mechanism models decisions: one module estimates the salience of individual concepts relative to the global context, the other captures higher-order cooperative patterns via pairwise concept interactions. A concept prediction module derives an intrinsic reward from next-concept prediction errors, encouraging exploration of semantic novelty.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple environments show that ELV achieves competitive performance and explicitly reveals how agents reason about their decisions.
AI.conclusion: ELV offers an interpretable approach to multi-agent cooperation by combining semantically structured latent concepts, dual-path attention, and concept-prediction intrinsic rewards, making policy decisions transparent without sacrificing competitive performance.

title: When Does Structured Knowledge Help Neural Theorem Proving?
summary: Does structured mathematical knowledge help LLMs prove theorems in Lean 4? If so, for which models, and does the answer vary by problem? Formal libraries such as Mathlib encode 285,000+ verified theorems with syntactic dependencies, but the semantic layer mathematicians rely on for discovery (analogies, generalizations, cross-domain bridges) remains implicit. We introduce MathAgent, which builds this layer as a knowledge graph, MathKG, and uses it to augment LLM theorem provers. MathKG connects 364 Mathlib theorems and definitions by 9,434 typed semantic edges inferred via LLM-based relation extraction anchored to verified Mathlib declarations. We run a controlled ablation across four augmentation modes (no context, knowledge-graph context, Mathlib retrieval, both) and five models: Qwen3-8B/32B, their Lean-specialized derivatives Goedel-Prover-V2-8B/32B, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, on miniF2F, plus PutnamBench and MathOlympiadBench for Sonnet. Three findings emerge. (i) Specialization dominates augmentation: Lean fine-tuning adds 33-38 percentage points of solve rate in every mode, and a specialized 8B model beats a $4\times$ larger general one by 29-35 points, while no augmentation mode improves solve rate by more than 3 points. (ii) Augmentation is capability-conditioned: knowledge-graph context helps small models but hurts large ones, with the specialized model gaining more relative to its general base at every scale. (iii) Yet the augmentation modes solve different problems: an oracle selecting the best mode per problem solves 6% to 58% more than the unaugmented prover, a complementarity effect that strengthens on harder problems (32% more on PutnamBench). These results motivate adaptive strategies that select augmentation by model capability and problem. Code, data, and artifacts are available at https://github.com/sarehnabi/mathagent

AI.tldr: MathAgent builds a semantic knowledge graph (MathKG) from Mathlib to augment LLM theorem provers in Lean 4, finding that Lean fine-tuning dominates augmentation while the modes exhibit strong per-problem complementarity.
AI.motivation: Formal libraries like Mathlib encode over 285,000 verified theorems with syntactic dependencies, but the semantic layer mathematicians rely on (analogies, generalizations, cross-domain bridges) remains implicit. The paper asks whether injecting structured mathematical knowledge helps LLMs prove theorems in Lean 4, for which models, and whether the benefit varies by problem.
AI.method: They introduce MathAgent, which constructs MathKG, a knowledge graph connecting 364 Mathlib theorems and definitions via 9,434 typed semantic edges extracted by LLM-based relation extraction anchored to verified Mathlib declarations. It augments LLM provers under four modes (no context, knowledge-graph context, Mathlib retrieval, both). A controlled ablation is run across five models (Qwen3-8B/32B, Goedel-Prover-V2-8B/32B, Claude Sonnet 4.6) on miniF2F, with Sonnet also evaluated on PutnamBench and MathOlympiadBench.
AI.result: (i) Specialization dominates augmentation: Lean fine-tuning adds 33-38 percentage points in every mode, and a specialized 8B model beats a 4x larger general model by 29-35 points, while no augmentation mode improves solve rate by more than 3 points. (ii) Augmentation is capability-conditioned: knowledge-graph context helps small models but hurts large ones, with specialized models gaining more relative to their general base at every scale. (iii) Augmentation modes solve different problems: an oracle selecting the best mode per problem solves 6% to 58% more than the unaugmented prover, rising to 32% more on PutnamBench.
AI.conclusion: Structured semantic knowledge augments LLM theorem provers only marginally and conditional on model capability, but the per-problem complementarity of augmentation modes is substantial and grows on harder problems. This motivates adaptive strategies that select augmentation by model capability and problem. Code, data, and artifacts are released on GitHub.

title: PowerBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Retrieval and Reasoning in Power Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents offer new opportunities for automated analysis in industry. However, rigorous evaluation of such agents-for example, within power system scenarios-remains hindered: real operational data are confidential, and existing public resources fail to fully capture the chained dependencies and heterogeneous evidence. To address this gap, we propose PowerBench, comprising (1) a generation framework that derives interconnected heterogeneous operational data through a common dependency chain, and (2) a synthetic dataset generated by this framework. The dataset covers 761 devices across 100 device types, with 13.35 million hourly telemetry records spanning two years and 24,939 operational documents. Building on this dataset, we construct 300 questions across three task families that evaluate frontier LLMs' ability to complete analysis tasks that require autonomous evidence retrieval and reasoning across interconnected and heterogeneous data under restricted tool calls and time budgets. Results demonstrate that the evaluated frontier LLMs remain challenged on these tasks: the best model reaches only 74.2% joint accuracy. Our trace analysis further reveals that model performance varies across evidence discovery, content retrieval, tool use, reasoning over evidence, and answer submission. These findings provide detailed insights for evaluating LLM agents and guiding their reliable deployment in industry. The framework, dataset, and benchmark tasks are available at https://github.com/open-compass/PowerBench.

AI.tldr: PowerBench introduces a generation framework and synthetic dataset (761 devices, 100 types, 13.35M hourly telemetry records, 24,939 documents) plus 300 benchmark questions across three task families to rigorously evaluate LLM agents on power system analysis; the best frontier model achieves only 74.2% joint accuracy.
AI.motivation: Rigorous evaluation of LLM agents in power system scenarios is hindered because real operational data are confidential and existing public resources fail to capture chained dependencies and heterogeneous evidence.
AI.method: A generation framework derives interconnected heterogeneous operational data through a common dependency chain, producing a synthetic dataset covering 761 devices across 100 device types, 13.35 million hourly telemetry records spanning two years, and 24,939 operational documents. From this, 300 questions across three task families are constructed to test autonomous evidence retrieval and reasoning across interconnected heterogeneous data under restricted tool calls and time budgets.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs remain challenged: the best model reaches only 74.2% joint accuracy. Trace analysis reveals performance varies across evidence discovery, content retrieval, tool use, reasoning over evidence, and answer submission.
AI.conclusion: PowerBench provides detailed insights for evaluating LLM agents and guiding their reliable industrial deployment; the framework, dataset, and benchmark tasks are publicly released.

title: Does Model Uncertainty Track Human Ambiguity? Evidence from Multi-Annotator Vision Benchmarks
summary: Human-model alignment is critical for trustworthy AI-assisted decision-making systems. Yet, most work evaluates model predictions against single ground-truth labels, overlooking that humans themselves often disagree on labels, a signal of genuine ambiguity. We investigate whether models struggle on the same instances that humans find difficult. We measure this on two vision datasets (FER+ and CIFAR-10H) where multiple human annotations per image capture human disagreement patterns. We evaluate eight pretrained models across three architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNetV3) in two parts: first, whether model uncertainty (softmax confidence, entropy) correlates with human disagreement, and second, whether predictive multiplicity measures (inter-model disagreement, Jensen-Shannon divergence) do. We find that it does not: alignment is weak in both dimensions. At the discrete label level, 50.4% of CIFAR-10H images and 33.5% of FER+ images receive multiple valid classifications from humans, while the models converge on only one. These instances represent a critical failure case where humans perceive ambiguity and would request expert review, yet models decide confidently. At the continuous score level, single-model uncertainty correlates weakly with human disagreement ($ρ= 0.24--0.55$), and predictive multiplicity provides only modest improvement. Widely-used uncertainty quantification methods do not reliably identify instances humans find ambiguous. Model uncertainty should not be treated as a trustworthy signal by default for decision-making in high-stakes scenarios.

AI.tldr: Models do not struggle on the same instances humans find ambiguous: both single-model uncertainty and predictive multiplicity align only weakly with human disagreement, so model uncertainty is not a trustworthy default signal in high-stakes decisions.
AI.motivation: Human-model alignment is essential for trustworthy AI-assisted decision-making, yet most evaluations rely on single ground-truth labels and ignore the fact that humans frequently disagree, which signals genuine ambiguity. The paper asks whether models fail exactly where humans find instances difficult.
AI.method: Using FER+ and CIFAR-10H, which provide multiple human annotations per image, the authors evaluate eight pretrained models spanning ResNet, EfficientNet, and MobileNetV3. They test two dimensions: (1) whether model uncertainty (softmax confidence, entropy) correlates with human disagreement, and (2) whether predictive multiplicity measures (inter-model disagreement, Jensen-Shannon divergence) do.
AI.result: Alignment is weak in both dimensions. At the discrete label level, 50.4% of CIFAR-10H images and 33.5% of FER+ images receive multiple valid human classifications, while models converge on a single label. At the continuous score level, single-model uncertainty correlates weakly with human disagreement (ρ = 0.24–0.55), and predictive multiplicity yields only modest improvement.
AI.conclusion: Widely-used uncertainty quantification methods do not reliably identify instances humans find ambiguous. These form a critical failure case where humans would request expert review but models decide confidently, so model uncertainty should not be treated as a trustworthy signal by default in high-stakes decision-making.

title: Can AI Make Money in Crypto? Measuring the Gap from Backtests to Real Markets
summary: AI-based trading methods have rapidly evolved from machine learning and reinforcement learning to large language models (LLMs) and trading agents, yet their performance is still predominantly assessed through historical backtesting. Such evaluations provide limited evidence of whether a method can generalize to unseen future markets or whether its backtested performance can be sustained in realistic trading frictions (e.g., latency, slippage, liquidity constraints, and market impact). We present a unified benchmark that evaluates representative machine learning, reinforcement learning, LLM-based, and agent-based trading methods in cryptocurrency markets through three progressively more realistic stages: historical backtesting, prospective exchange-based paper trading, and real-money live trading. These stages jointly increase temporal realism by moving from historical to unseen future markets, and execution realism by moving from offline simulation toward live trading. This protocol enables us to quantify the backtest-to-realization gap, identify when performance begins to deteriorate, and compare how this gap differs across major classes of AI trading methods. We further provide a unified open-source system supporting all three evaluation stages, together with a public platform that continuously updates benchmark results. Code is available at https://github.com/Starlien95/Awesome-TradingAI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unified three-stage benchmark (historical backtesting, prospective paper trading, and real-money live trading) to evaluate ML, RL, LLM-based, and agent-based trading methods in cryptocurrency markets, quantifying the backtest-to-realization gap.
AI.motivation: AI trading methods have advanced from ML and RL to LLMs and trading agents, but their evaluation relies almost entirely on historical backtesting. Backtests give limited evidence of generalization to unseen future markets or robustness under realistic frictions such as latency, slippage, liquidity constraints, and market impact. A standardized, increasingly realistic evaluation is needed.
AI.method: A unified benchmark evaluates representative ML, RL, LLM-based, and agent-based trading methods in cryptocurrency markets through three progressively realistic stages: (1) historical backtesting, (2) prospective exchange-based paper trading, and (3) real-money live trading. These stages jointly raise temporal realism (historical to unseen future markets) and execution realism (offline simulation to live trading). A unified open-source system supports all three stages, plus a public platform that continuously updates benchmark results.
AI.result: The protocol quantifies the backtest-to-realization gap, identifies when performance begins to deteriorate across evaluation stages, and compares how this gap differs across the major classes of AI trading methods.
AI.conclusion: Historical backtesting alone is insufficient for assessing AI trading methods. Progressive evaluation from backtesting to paper trading to live trading, enabled by the proposed open-source benchmark and continuously updated public platform, provides more reliable evidence of generalization and real-world viability.

title: EOPSA: Efficient On-Policy Self-Distilled Safety Alignment
comment: 32 pages, 9 figures. Code and models are available at the project repositories
summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for safety alignment, delivering dense, token-level supervision by distilling from a teacher conditioned on refusal-oriented privileged prompts. However, we reveal that this paradigm suffers from critical inefficiencies that degrade both training efficiency and general reasoning capabilities. Specifically, we diagnose two fundamental bottlenecks: (1) supervisory collapse over extended rollouts, where the teacher's corrective efficacy degrades precipitously as the student's generation prefix lengthens, injecting noisy gradients into late-stage tokens; and (2) gradient dilution from stylistic shifts, where the distillation objective is dominated by safety-irrelevant stylistic discrepancies induced by privileged prompting, washing out genuine safety signals and impairing base reasoning. To resolve these issues, we propose Efficient On-Policy Self-Distilled Safety Alignment (EOPSA), which concentrates computational and gradient budgets exclusively on reliably supervised, safety-critical tokens. EOPSA incorporates two coordinated mechanisms: (i) Adaptive Rollout Scheduling, which dynamically bounds the generation horizon guided by a novel Teacher Rescue Rate (TRR) metric to operate strictly within reliable supervision regimes; and (ii) Selective Distillation, which filters out safety-neutral tokens to restrict gradient updates exclusively to safety-pivotal transitions. Extensive evaluations across reasoning models up to 32B parameters demonstrate that EOPSA slashes rollout computation by $\sim$50% and backpropagates through merely $\sim$2% of tokens, consistently outperforming full-token distillation baselines in both safety compliance and reasoning retention.

AI.tldr: EOPSA improves on-policy self-distillation for safety alignment by restricting supervision to reliable, safety-critical tokens, cutting rollout computation ~50% and backpropagating through ~2% of tokens while outperforming full-token distillation on safety and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Prior On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) safety alignment is inefficient and harms reasoning due to two bottlenecks: (1) supervisory collapse over extended rollouts, where teacher corrective efficacy degrades as the student prefix lengthens, injecting noisy gradients into late-stage tokens; and (2) gradient dilution from stylistic shifts caused by privileged prompting, which dominates the objective with safety-irrelevant stylistic discrepancies and washes out genuine safety signals.
AI.method: EOPSA concentrates compute and gradient budgets on reliably supervised, safety-critical tokens via two mechanisms: (i) Adaptive Rollout Scheduling, which bounds the generation horizon using a Teacher Rescue Rate (TRR) metric to stay within reliable supervision regimes; and (ii) Selective Distillation, which filters out safety-neutral tokens so updates occur only on safety-pivotal transitions.
AI.result: Across reasoning models up to 32B parameters, EOPSA reduces rollout computation by ~50% and backpropagates through only ~2% of tokens, consistently surpassing full-token distillation baselines in both safety compliance and reasoning retention.
AI.conclusion: Targeting the two identified bottlenecks—supervisory collapse and gradient dilution—through adaptive rollout scheduling and selective distillation yields a substantially more efficient and effective safety alignment method than full-token OPSD.

title: PairPref: When Should Memory Guide the Answer? A Benchmark for Contextual Preference Use
summary: Memory-augmented assistants use retrieved preferences to guide their responses. A small change in the situation can change whether a preference is appropriate while barely affecting its retrieval similarity. Memory benchmarks typically test whether systems store and retrieve preferences, with less attention to when those preferences should apply. We introduce PairPref, a benchmark of contextual preference use. Each pair changes only the situation, keeping the preference, request, and four candidate replies fixed. The preference remains valid in both situations. In the selection track, models must choose the reply that applies the preference only where appropriate. In the free-generation track, they must decide when to apply it without seeing candidate replies. Both tracks use the same 1,227 pairs across 45 preferences and eight situation categories. We evaluate eight models, most of which achieve selection scores ($Δ$) of 51 to 65 points. In free generation, however, both responses are appropriate for their respective situations in only 3.6\% to 18.3\% of pairs. Models continue to apply the preference in both situations even with fewer retrieved memories, alternative presentation formats, and a stricter prompt. These results show that models still struggle to judge when user preferences apply and respond accordingly.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PairPref, a benchmark for contextual preference use in memory-augmented assistants, showing that models can select appropriate replies but fail to judge when preferences apply during free generation.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented assistants use retrieved preferences to guide responses, but a small situational change can make a preference inappropriate while its retrieval similarity barely changes. Existing memory benchmarks focus on whether systems store and retrieve preferences, paying less attention to when those preferences should actually apply.
AI.method: PairPref is a benchmark of contextual preference use. Each pair changes only the situation while keeping the preference, request, and four candidate replies fixed, and the preference remains valid in both situations. It includes two tracks: a selection track, where models choose the reply applying the preference only where appropriate, and a free-generation track, where models must decide when to apply it without seeing candidate replies. Both tracks use the same 1,227 pairs across 45 preferences and eight situation categories, and eight models are evaluated.
AI.result: Most models achieve selection scores (Δ) of 51 to 65 points. In free generation, however, both responses are appropriate for their respective situations in only 3.6% to 18.3% of pairs. Models continue to apply the preference in both situations even with fewer retrieved memories, alternative presentation formats, and a stricter prompt.
AI.conclusion: Models still struggle to judge when user preferences apply and to respond accordingly, despite performing well on preference selection.

title: The Marathon of Scientific Reasoning: Robustness of Scientific Agents to Perturbations in Multi-Turn Interactions
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents are increasingly used for scientific problem solving, yet their robustness to imperfections arising during multi-turn interactions remains poorly understood. We introduce \textsc{SciARP} (\textbf{Sci}entific \textbf{A}gent \textbf{R}obustness to \textbf{P}erturbations), a benchmark for evaluating scientific agents under scientifically plausible perturbations throughout multi-turn problem solving. \textsc{SciARP} transforms 620 scientific problems into interdependent tasks of 3--13 turns and defines 13 perturbation types spanning problem understanding, evidence processing, reasoning, and conclusion formation. Clean and perturbed versions of each task are independently executed under matched settings, producing paired live trajectories for evaluating both task success and process reliability. Experiments across eight LLMs from four model families reveal three key robustness characteristics. First, different classes of scientific perturbations exhibit distinct robustness profiles and can decouple task progression from scientific reliability: agents may continue advancing through the task even after their information or reasoning has become unreliable. Second, stronger clean-task performance does not necessarily translate into stronger robustness, as models with higher clean-task accuracy can exhibit larger degradation under perturbation. Third, perturbation effects exhibit strong temporal dynamics: they may remain latent for multiple turns before emerging and subsequently propagate through downstream dependencies. Together, these findings show that current scientific agents remain insufficiently robust to scientifically plausible perturbations, with failures often remaining undetected, propagating, and resisting recovery.

AI.tldr: SciARP is a benchmark evaluating the robustness of LLM-based scientific agents to scientifically plausible perturbations during multi-turn problem solving, revealing that agents decouple task progression from scientific reliability, that clean-task strength does not imply robustness, and that perturbation effects are temporally dynamic.
AI.motivation: LLM-based scientific agents are increasingly used for scientific problem solving, but their robustness to imperfections arising during multi-turn interactions remains poorly understood. Existing evaluation lacks a systematic way to test how such agents behave under realistic, scientifically plausible perturbations across an entire multi-turn workflow.
AI.method: The authors introduce SciARP, a benchmark that transforms 620 scientific problems into interdependent tasks of 3--13 turns and defines 13 perturbation types spanning problem understanding, evidence processing, reasoning, and conclusion formation. Clean and perturbed versions of each task are executed independently under matched settings, producing paired live trajectories that allow evaluation of both task success and process reliability. Experiments cover eight LLMs from four model families.
AI.result: Experiments reveal three key robustness characteristics. First, different classes of scientific perturbations exhibit distinct robustness profiles and can decouple task progression from scientific reliability, with agents advancing even after their information or reasoning becomes unreliable. Second, stronger clean-task performance does not necessarily translate into stronger robustness, as models with higher clean-task accuracy can show larger degradation under perturbation. Third, perturbation effects exhibit strong temporal dynamics, remaining latent for multiple turns before emerging and subsequently propagating through downstream dependencies.
AI.conclusion: Current scientific agents remain insufficiently robust to scientifically plausible perturbations, with failures often going undetected, propagating, and resisting recovery. SciARP exposes these gaps and motivates robustness-aware evaluation and design of scientific agents.

title: APOLO: Automatic Prompt Optimization for Ontology Learning
comment: Accepted at the Posters and Demos Track of the International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2026)
summary: Ontology Learning (OL) from text has advanced with the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs), but it remains challenging due to the limited availability of annotated training data and the difficulty of adapting LLMs to perform OL effectively. We address this via APOLO - Automatic Prompt Optimization for Ontology Learning, by casting OL as an explicit prompt optimization problem over LLM modules. To obtain training data, we employ a multi-agent system that generates text-ontology pairs from existing expert-curated ontologies. We then propose two ontology learner architectures: a greedy and an autoregressive learner, and optimize both using GEPA, a greedy evolutionary prompt optimizer built on DSPy. Experiments on two ontologies - a biomedical (DOID) and a plant ontology (PO) show consistent improvements after optimization across nearly all model and mode combinations, with autoregressive learners achieving the largest gains. Our results demonstrate that prompt optimization is a viable and lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for OL, and that the autoregressive formulation better captures ontological structure than the greedy approach.

AI.tldr: APOLO casts ontology learning (OL) from text as an explicit prompt optimization problem over LLM modules, generates synthetic text-ontology training pairs via a multi-agent system, and optimizes greedy and autoregressive learner architectures using GEPA (a DSPy-based evolutionary prompt optimizer). It improves nearly all model/mode combinations on DOID and PO, with autoregressive learners gaining most.
AI.motivation: OL from text with LLMs is hindered by scarce annotated training data and the difficulty of adapting LLMs to perform OL effectively, calling for a lightweight adaptation strategy.
AI.method: The authors introduce APOLO, framing OL as prompt optimization over LLM modules. Training data comes from a multi-agent system synthesizing text-ontology pairs from expert-curated ontologies. Two ontology learner architectures—greedy and autoregressive—are optimized with GEPA, a greedy evolutionary prompt optimizer built on DSPy.
AI.result: Experiments on a biomedical ontology (DOID) and a plant ontology (PO) show consistent post-optimization improvements across nearly all model and mode combinations, with autoregressive learners achieving the largest gains.
AI.conclusion: Prompt optimization is a viable, lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for OL, and the autoregressive formulation better captures ontological structure than the greedy approach.

title: Remember Before You're Asked: MemDream for Self-Probing Memory Evolution
summary: Memory is essential for enabling LLM-based agents to maintain coherent, personalized behavior over long-horizon interactions. However, existing memory systems share a fundamental limitation: they never proactively test their own memory, repairing it only after real queries expose weaknesses. This reactive paradigm means every retrieval failure corresponds to a real interaction in which the cost has already been paid. We propose MemDream, a framework that enables self-probing memory evolution for LLM agents. Our framework periodically enters offline dream cycles where three specialized agents (Dreamer, Analyst, Consolidator) collaboratively probe, diagnose, and repair the memory graph before failures occur. A policy trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization learns which repair operations produce durable retrieval improvements, while a soft decay mechanism provides reversible forgetting driven by the same anticipatory signal. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemoryAgentBench demonstrate that MemDream improves answer F1 by 4.5 points on LoCoMo and achieves a 9.1-point higher overall score on MAB over the strongest reactive-evolution baselines.

AI.tldr: MemDream enables LLM agents to proactively self-probe and repair their memory before retrieval failures occur, using offline "dream cycles" with three specialized agents and RL-trained repair policies.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems are fundamentally reactive—they repair memory only after real queries expose weaknesses, so every retrieval failure corresponds to a real interaction where the cost has already been paid and cannot be recovered.
AI.method: MemDream enters offline dream cycles in which three specialized agents (Dreamer, Analyst, Consolidator) collaboratively probe, diagnose, and repair the memory graph. A policy trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization learns which repair operations yield durable retrieval improvements, and a soft decay mechanism provides reversible forgetting driven by the same anticipatory signal.
AI.result: On LoCoMo, MemDream improves answer F1 by 4.5 points; on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), it achieves a 9.1-point higher overall score compared to the strongest reactive-evolution baselines.
