AI.conclusion: MemDream shifts memory maintenance from a reactive to a proactive paradigm, showing that anticipatory self-probing and offline repair yield substantial retrieval and answer-quality gains over reactive-evolution approaches.

title: SGG-ReflAct: Sub-Goal Guided ReflAct with Structured Planning for Reliable Long-Horizon Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in reasoning backbones have empowered large language model (LLM)agentstotackle complex, multi-step tasks. However, as reasoning horizons grow, inconsistent internal beliefs induce intermediate errors that cause agents to drift from their goals. This limitation also persists in REFLACT, which reflects only on the end-goal at each step without explicitly considering intermediate sub goals. To address this problem, we propose SGG-ReflAct (Sub-Goal Guided Re flAct), a reasoning backbone that integrates sub-goals generated through a single path LLM planner into the reflection process. We further extend this framework to BeamSGG-ReflAct, which replaces the single-path planner with a beam search based LLM planner for structured plan exploration. We run experiments on ALF World, ScienceWorld, and Jericho with multiple LLM models. SGG-ReflAct out performs REFLACT in nearly all settings, achieving best success rate gains of 14.9 percentage points on ALFWorld and 8.0 percentage points on ScienceWorld with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Our experimental analysis shows that SGG-ReflAct re duces hallucinated actions and achieves its largest gains on procedurally ordered tasks. Furthermore, experimental results with BeamSGG-ReflAct show that the backbone's effectiveness depends on plan quality: explicitly specifying the re quired operations recovers gains that plan searching alone cannot achieve. These results demonstrate that SGG-ReflAct offers a practical and highly effective rea soning backbone, enabling LLM agents to achieve reliable performance in com plex, long-horizon tasks through easy integration.

AI.tldr: SGG-ReflAct integrates sub-goals from an LLM planner into the reflection process of LLM agents, improving long-horizon task success over REFLACT, with a beam-search variant (BeamSGG-ReflAct) showing that explicit operation specification matters more than plan search alone.
AI.motivation: As reasoning horizons grow, inconsistent internal beliefs produce intermediate errors that cause LLM agents to drift from their goals. REFLACT only reflects on the end-goal at each step and neglects intermediate sub-goals, limiting performance on complex, multi-step tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose SGG-ReflAct (Sub-Goal Guided ReflAct), a reasoning backbone that incorporates sub-goals generated by a single-path LLM planner into the reflection process. They extend it to BeamSGG-ReflAct by replacing the single-path planner with a beam-search-based LLM planner for structured plan exploration. Experiments are run on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and Jericho with multiple LLM models.
AI.result: SGG-ReflAct outperforms REFLACT in nearly all settings, with best success-rate gains of 14.9 percentage points on ALFWorld and 8.0 percentage points on ScienceWorld using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Analysis shows it reduces hallucinated actions and yields the largest gains on procedurally ordered tasks. BeamSGG-ReflAct results indicate effectiveness depends on plan quality: explicitly specifying required operations recovers gains that plan searching alone cannot achieve.
AI.conclusion: SGG-ReflAct is a practical, highly effective reasoning backbone that enables LLM agents to achieve reliable performance on complex, long-horizon tasks through easy integration.

title: SkillRubric: Co-Evolving Actor Guidance and Evaluator Rubrics for Multimodal Agents
summary: Recent work incorporates reusable skills distilled from past interactions into multimodal agent training, providing procedural guidance for long-horizon planning and tool use. However, policy optimization in these methods remains driven primarily by sparse outcome rewards, providing little supervision for intermediate decisions. Rubric-based rewards address this limitation through explicit intermediate criteria, but reliable rubrics are difficult to construct at scale and often disconnected from the procedure followed by the actor. We observe that a well-structured skill naturally specifies both how to act and what successful execution should achieve. Based on this insight, we introduce SkillRubric, which represents each skill through aligned actor-facing guidance and an evaluator-facing rubric. A multimodal verifier evaluates skill-defined goals using screenshots and tool outputs, assigning completion and progress rewards to the responsible turns. We further introduce an alternating co-evolution scheme that validates guidance revisions through paired rollouts under a frozen policy and rubric revisions offline under fixed guidance. Experiments across diverse multimodal agent benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance gains, while controlled paired rollouts further show that evolved skills provide more effective guidance for planning and tool use than their preceding versions.

AI.tldr: SkillRubric represents each reusable skill as aligned actor-facing guidance plus an evaluator-facing rubric, enabling dense intermediate rewards for multimodal agent training while co-evolving guidance and rubrics.
AI.motivation: Multimodal agents trained with distilled reusable skills still rely on sparse outcome rewards, offering little supervision for intermediate decisions. Rubric-based rewards provide intermediate criteria but are hard to construct reliably at scale and are often disconnected from the actor's actual procedure.
AI.method: The authors exploit the observation that a well-structured skill specifies both how to act and what success means. SkillRubric pairs actor-facing guidance with an evaluator-facing rubric per skill. A multimodal verifier checks skill-defined goals using screenshots and tool outputs, assigning completion and progress rewards to responsible turns. An alternating co-evolution scheme validates guidance revisions via paired rollouts under a frozen policy, and rubric revisions offline under fixed guidance.
AI.result: Consistent performance gains across diverse multimodal agent benchmarks; controlled paired rollouts show evolved skills give more effective guidance for planning and tool use than prior versions.
AI.conclusion: Aligning skill guidance with rubric-based evaluation yields dense, procedure-consistent rewards, and co-evolving guidance and rubrics improves long-horizon multimodal agent performance.

title: FlowState: Execution State as Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon tasks require LLM agents to continually draw on information from earlier interactions. However, retaining the full history increases context costs, while compressing it risks losing details needed later, and the relevance of historical information often becomes apparent as the task progresses. To address these challenges, we propose FlowState, which treats execution state as memory that can be retained and revisited across requests, unifying current decision-making with the reuse of historical information. FlowState preserves semantically typed state nodes, their relations, and references to raw tool observations, separating persistent retention from on-demand access. Within a single execution loop, Incremental State Update (ISU) maintains the current state based on new inputs and feedback, while Progressive State Access (PSA) progressively reveals historical states and supporting evidence as needed during reasoning. Together, these mechanisms enable agents to reassess prior decisions in light of new information and guide subsequent actions. Compared with a full-context baseline using the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash model, FlowState improves the average success rate on MemoryArena and the average pass rate on $τ^3$-Bench by 4.55 and 13.95 percentage points, respectively, while reducing total token consumption by 43.2% and 40.6%. These results demonstrate the performance and efficiency advantages of FlowState on long-horizon tasks.

AI.tldr: FlowState treats execution state as reusable memory across requests, using incremental state updates and progressive state access to improve success rates (up to +13.95 pp) while cutting token consumption ~40-43% on long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tasks require LLM agents to continually reuse earlier interaction information, but retaining full history raises context costs while compressing it risks losing later-needed details. Moreover, the relevance of historical information often only becomes apparent as the task progresses, so fixed compression or full retention are both suboptimal.
AI.method: FlowState treats execution state as memory retained and revisited across requests, unifying decision-making with historical information reuse. It preserves semantically typed state nodes, their relations, and references to raw tool observations, separating persistent retention from on-demand access. Within a single execution loop, Incremental State Update (ISU) maintains current state from new inputs and feedback, while Progressive State Access (PSA) progressively reveals historical states and supporting evidence as needed during reasoning, enabling reassessment of prior decisions.
AI.result: Against a full-context baseline with the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash model, FlowState improves average success rate on MemoryArena by 4.55 pp and average pass rate on $τ^3$-Bench by 13.95 pp, while reducing total token consumption by 43.2% and 40.6%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: FlowState demonstrates both performance and efficiency advantages on long-horizon tasks, validating state-as-memory with incremental updates and progressive access as an effective alternative to full-context retention.

title: PersonaManifold: Revealing and Exploiting Curved Geometry in LLM Persona Representations
summary: Controlling persona in large language models (LLMs) at inference time is important for role-playing, personalized dialogue, and social simulation. Recent methods extract persona vectors from the model's activation space and apply Euclidean operations---addition, scaling, and linear interpolation---under the linear representation hypothesis. However, these methods themselves report systematic failures: non-orthogonal trait dimensions, asymmetric ceiling and resistance effects, and significant deviations in multi-trait composition, suggesting that the linear isotropic assumption does not hold. We propose PersonaManifold, a framework that models persona representations as points on a curved, low-dimensional Riemannian submanifold in activation space. We estimate the manifold's intrinsic geometry---local metric tensors, geodesic distances, and Ollivier-Ricci curvature---and introduce geodesic steering, which interpolates between personas along manifold geodesics rather than Euclidean straight lines. We also propose the Behavioral Similarity Triplet (BST) benchmark, which automatically generates situational questions grounded in six established psychological constructs and defines persona similarity through behavioral responses rather than self-report questionnaires. Experiments on three open-source LLMs show that persona activations form a manifold with heterogeneous curvature, geodesic distance predicts behavioral similarity more accurately than Euclidean alternatives with independent contributions from anisotropy and curvature, and geodesic steering produces more coherent intermediate personas on both our BST benchmark and external evaluations, with the advantage concentrated in high-deviation regions where the manifold deviates most from flatness.

AI.tldr: PersonaManifold models persona representations as points on a curved low-dimensional Riemannian submanifold in LLM activation space and steers personas along geodesics rather than Euclidean lines, outperforming linear methods especially where the manifold is most non-flat.
AI.motivation: Inference-time persona control in LLMs matters for role-playing, personalized dialogue, and social simulation. Existing persona-vector methods assume a linear representation hypothesis and use Euclidean addition, scaling, and interpolation, but report systematic failures—non-orthogonal trait dimensions, asymmetric ceiling and resistance effects, and large multi-trait composition deviations—indicating the linear isotropic assumption is invalid.
AI.method: The authors propose PersonaManifold, which treats persona representations as points on a curved, low-dimensional Riemannian submanifold of activation space. They estimate intrinsic geometry (local metric tensors, geodesic distances, Ollivier-Ricci curvature) and introduce geodesic steering, interpolating between personas along manifold geodesics instead of Euclidean straight lines. They also introduce the Behavioral Similarity Triplet (BST) benchmark, auto-generating situational questions from six psychological constructs and defining persona similarity via behavioral responses rather than self-report questionnaires.
AI.result: Across three open-source LLMs, persona activations form a manifold with heterogeneous curvature; geodesic distance predicts behavioral similarity more accurately than Euclidean alternatives, with independent contributions from anisotropy and curvature; geodesic steering yields more coherent intermediate personas on BST and external evaluations, with the advantage concentrated in high-deviation regions where the manifold deviates most from flatness.
AI.conclusion: Persona representation geometry is non-Euclidean, and curvature-aware, geodesic-based steering offers a principled and empirically superior approach to inference-time persona control, particularly in strongly non-flat regions.

title: Nudgeability: Reasoning Models Follow Confidence Signals Without Tracking Their Own Competence
summary:
Reasoning language models that can call tools must decide during inference whether to answer unaided or delegate. Any self-reflection mechanism for this must answer three questions: where the reflective signal comes from (verbal reports, output distributions, hidden states, a separate predictor), how it is presented to the model (numerical prediction, confidence token, prompt injection), and whether it changes the model's subsequent action. We isolate the third question. At a fixed point in otherwise identical reasoning trajectories, we insert a single first-person sentence expressing either confidence or doubt; the model then continues reasoning and chooses whether to answer directly or call a tool. Comparing these counterfactual continuations measures the causal effect of the reflective signal on delegation. We call this behavioral response Nudgeability and measure it along two dimensions: sensitivity, how strongly confidence and doubt change delegation rates, and targeting, whether delegation increases for problems the model cannot solve unaided and decreases for those it can.
  Across nine small-to-medium open-weight reasoning models from three families (Qwen, Gemma, and GLM) and two tasks, models are consistently sensitive: doubt increases delegation and confidence decreases it, with a median confidence-to-doubt swing of 20.6 percentage points, and 53 to 70 points for the larger provider-served models. This responsiveness is poorly targeted: a median 42% of induced flips are well-targeted, only a +2 percentage-point lift over a random-selection baseline. Confidence language is thus a strong control surface for delegation, but current models use it only weakly in accordance with their actual competence. Nudgeability offers a simple, post-training-free way to evaluate both sensitivity and targeting as endogenous self-reflection mechanisms mature.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Nudgeability," a post-training-free behavioral probe that measures the causal effect of a single first-person confidence or doubt sentence on whether a reasoning model delegates to a tool, decomposed into sensitivity and targeting.
AI.motivation: Tool-calling reasoning models must decide during inference whether to answer unaided or delegate, and any self-reflection mechanism for this involves three design questions: the source of the reflective signal, its presentation format, and whether it actually changes subsequent action. Prior work conflates these, leaving the causal action-changing question unisolated.
AI.method: At a fixed point in otherwise identical reasoning trajectories, the authors insert a single first-person sentence expressing confidence or doubt, then let the model continue reasoning and choose whether to answer directly or call a tool. Comparing these counterfactual continuations yields the causal effect of the reflective signal on delegation, measured along two dimensions: sensitivity (how strongly confidence vs. doubt shifts delegation rates) and targeting (whether delegation rises for problems the model cannot solve unaided and falls for those it can).
AI.result: Across nine small-to-medium open-weight reasoning models from three families (Qwen, Gemma, GLM) and two tasks, models are consistently sensitive: doubt increases delegation and confidence decreases it, with a median confidence-to-doubt swing of 20.6 percentage points, rising to 53–70 points for larger provider-served models. However, responsiveness is poorly targeted: a median 42% of induced flips are well-targeted, only a +2 percentage-point lift over a random-selection baseline.
AI.conclusion: Confidence language acts as a strong control surface for delegation, but current models use it only weakly in accordance with their actual competence. Nudgeability provides a simple, post-training-free way to evaluate both sensitivity and targeting as endogenous self-reflection mechanisms mature.

title: Diffusion Subgoal Planning for Long-Horizon Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) learns goal-directed policies from reward-free data, but in long-horizon tasks, goal-conditioned value functions often provide unstable guidance due to sparse rewards and discounting. Hierarchical methods partially mitigate this issue via subgoal decomposition; however, high-level decision-making still relies on noise-sensitive value estimates, leading to unstable behavior in complex environments. We address this limitation by proposing \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{S}ubgoal \textbf{P}lanning (\textbf{DSP}), a diffusion-based framework for high-level subgoal generation. DSP casts high-level planning as guided generative inference over goal-conditioned subgoals and learns both conditional and unconditional flows, enabling classifier-free guidance to introduce a goal-directed bias at inference time. By removing explicit value-based guidance from high-level planning, DSP generates reachable and goal-directed subgoals through a generative model while retaining hierarchical execution. Experiments on offline GCRL benchmarks demonstrate that DSP outperforms prior methods on a range of navigation and manipulation tasks, with particularly strong performance in maze environments that require multi-step subgoal planning.

AI.tldr: DSP is a diffusion-based high-level subgoal planning framework for offline goal-conditioned RL that replaces noise-sensitive value guidance with guided generative inference using classifier-free guidance, achieving strong performance on long-horizon navigation and manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon offline GCRL, goal-conditioned value functions give unstable guidance due to sparse rewards and discounting. Hierarchical methods mitigate this via subgoal decomposition, but their high-level decisions still depend on noise-sensitive value estimates, causing unstable behavior in complex environments.
AI.method: DSP casts high-level planning as guided generative inference over goal-conditioned subgoals. It learns both conditional and unconditional flows, enabling classifier-free guidance to inject a goal-directed bias at inference time. This removes explicit value-based guidance from high-level planning while retaining hierarchical execution.
AI.result: On offline GCRL benchmarks, DSP outperforms prior methods across navigation and manipulation tasks, with notably strong results in maze environments requiring multi-step subgoal planning.
AI.conclusion: Replacing value-based high-level guidance with diffusion-based generative subgoal planning yields reachable, goal-directed subgoals and improves long-horizon offline GCRL performance.

title: Calibrated Uncertainty for Informative Path Planning in Aquatic Environmental Monitoring
summary: Informative Path Planning for scalar field reconstruction uses predictive uncertainty to direct sensing vehicles toward maximally informative locations. Gaussian Processes provide this signal but their stationary isotropic kernels are misspecified for non-homogeneous phenomena such as oil spills, producing miscalibrated estimates that degrade planning. We investigate whether replacing the Gaussian Process with a well-calibrated Deep Ensemble improves path planning outcomes, and whether uncertainty quality interacts with the choice of planning algorithm. Five strategies ($ε$-Greedy, Value Greedy, Uncertainty Greedy, Monte Carlo Tree Search, and Receding Horizon Orienteering) share a common Deep Ensemble backbone trained on physics-based oil spill simulations. On held-out stochastic spill scenarios, the Deep Ensemble reduces normalised reconstruction error by $83\%$ relative to the Gaussian Process baseline. Crucially, well-calibrated uncertainty amplifies the importance of the planning strategy: the performance gap between algorithms is negligible under miscalibrated models but becomes substantial under the ensemble, where multi-step lookahead planners outperform greedy selection by up to $32\%$ in reconstruction error and achieve IoU above $0.85$. Monte Carlo Tree Search is the recommended planner, matching Orienteering in reconstruction quality at an order-of-magnitude lower computational cost.

AI.tldr: Replacing a Gaussian Process with a well-calibrated Deep Ensemble drastically improves informative path planning for oil spill reconstruction, and reveals that planning algorithm choice only matters when uncertainty is well-calibrated.
AI.motivation: Informative path planning for scalar field reconstruction relies on predictive uncertainty to guide sensing. Gaussian Processes are commonly used but their stationary isotropic kernels are misspecified for non-homogeneous phenomena like oil spills, yielding miscalibrated uncertainty and degraded planning. The paper asks whether a well-calibrated Deep Ensemble improves planning outcomes and whether uncertainty quality interacts with the choice of planning algorithm.
AI.method: Five planning strategies (ε-Greedy, Value Greedy, Uncertainty Greedy, Monte Carlo Tree Search, Receding Horizon Orienteering) share a common Deep Ensemble backbone trained on physics-based oil spill simulations, and are evaluated on held-out stochastic spill scenarios against a Gaussian Process baseline.
AI.result: The Deep Ensemble reduces normalised reconstruction error by 83% versus the Gaussian Process. Under miscalibrated models the gap between planners is negligible, but with well-calibrated ensemble uncertainty multi-step lookahead planners outperform greedy selection by up to 32% in reconstruction error, achieving IoU above 0.85. Monte Carlo Tree Search matches Orienteering in reconstruction quality at an order-of-magnitude lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Well-calibrated uncertainty is not merely a better estimator but a precondition for planning algorithm choice to matter. Deep Ensembles are recommended over Gaussian Processes for non-homogeneous scalar field reconstruction, and Monte Carlo Tree Search is the recommended planner for its favorable quality-to-cost trade-off.

title: SpeechCritic: Learning a Diagnostic Speech Judge from Limited Human Preferences
summary: Human speech conveys rich perceptual information, such as emotion and speaker identity, yet most automatic speech quality judges reduce it to a single naturalness score. We study diagnostic speech judges: given two candidates, a diagnostic judge decides which is better, along which perceptual dimensions (e.g., timbre, emotion, timing) they differ, and which audible cues support its decision. Learning such judges is challenging: expert annotation is costly, and simply prompting a frontier audio-language model to produce labels is unreliable: our probing reveals substantial errors and unstable instruction following. We introduce SpeechCritic, which learns a diagnostic judge in a reference-conditioned cross-lingual setting from only about 300 human-labeled comparisons. Rather than replacing the frontier model, SpeechCritic calibrates it with these labels: for each dimension, it selects the acoustic measurements that agree with human judgments, maps them to A/Tie/B probabilities, and passes these to the model as non-binding hints alongside the audio. Compared with the same model labeling without hints, this raises dimension-level agreement with humans by 6.3 points and cuts the mismatch with human Tie rates by 10.4 points. We then train a 7B judge on this supervision and find that different training signals shape different judge behaviors: SFT establishes the task, OPD transfers the teacher's dimension-level strengths and weaknesses, and RL helps most on clear-cut comparisons where human raters agree. Notably, human listeners also find that RL makes rationales cite more specific, localized acoustic cues, although it never directly rewards rationale text. Finally, we show that the pipeline is language-pair agnostic by instantiating it on both English-Japanese and English-Spanish. Together, these results demonstrate a path from limited human preferences to a diagnostic speech judge.

AI.tldr: SpeechCritic learns a diagnostic speech judge from only ~300 human-labeled comparisons in a reference-conditioned cross-lingual setting, calibrating a frontier audio-language model with dimension-specific acoustic measurements as non-binding hints, then training a 7B judge via SFT, OPD, and RL.
AI.motivation: Human speech carries rich perceptual information (emotion, speaker identity, timbre, timing), but most automatic speech quality judges collapse it into a single naturalness score. Diagnostic judges that decide which of two candidates is better, along which perceptual dimensions, and with which audible cues, are desirable but hard to learn: expert annotation is costly, and directly prompting a frontier audio-language model to produce labels is unreliable, as probing reveals substantial errors and unstable instruction following.
AI.method: SpeechCritic operates in a reference-conditioned cross-lingual setting and requires only about 300 human-labeled comparisons. Instead of replacing the frontier model, it calibrates it: for each perceptual dimension, it selects acoustic measurements that agree with human judgments, maps them to A/Tie/B probabilities, and supplies these to the model as non-binding hints alongside the audio. A 7B judge is then trained on this supervision using SFT, OPD (transferring the teacher's dimension-level strengths and weaknesses), and RL.
AI.result: Compared with the same model labeling without hints, the calibration raises dimension-level agreement with humans by 6.3 points and reduces the mismatch with human Tie rates by 10.4 points. The three training signals shape different judge behaviors: SFT establishes the task, OPD transfers the teacher's dimension-level strengths and weaknesses, and RL helps most on clear-cut comparisons where human raters agree. Human listeners also find that RL makes rationales cite more specific, localized acoustic cues, even though rationale text is never directly rewarded. The pipeline is shown to be language-pair agnostic, instantiated on both English-Japanese and English-Spanish.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a viable path from limited human preference data to a diagnostic speech judge that identifies which candidate is better, along which perceptual dimensions they differ, and which acoustic cues support the decision, generalizing across language pairs.

title: TULIP: Targeted LLM Unlearning at Layers Identified Per-Input
summary: Representation-level unlearning intervenes on the intermediate hidden states of LLMs. Although knowledge is distributed across layers, existing methods operate at a single fixed layer for the entire forget set. We ask whether such a fixed layer is sufficient. To answer this, we design a hijacking experiment that grafts hidden states of the target model into an oracle trained only on the retain set. The oracle cannot produce the forget answer on its own, yet it produces the answer from the grafted state. Thus, the answer is formed at an intermediate layer and merely read out afterward, so unlearning should focus on formation, not readout. Moreover, the layer where formation ends varies widely across inputs. Motivated by these findings, we propose Targeted Unlearning at Layers Identified Per-input (TULIP). For each input, TULIP uses the logit lens to locate the formation-readout boundary and removes the hidden state's alignment with the forget answer's unembedding vector there. TULIP consistently outperforms output- and representation-level baselines on TOFU, PISTOL, and WMDP across Llama, Qwen, and Zephyr models. It also remains robust to paraphrase and quantization attacks. Beyond standalone use, its per-input layer selection serves as a plug-and-play component that further improves existing methods.

AI.tldr: TULIP performs representation-level LLM unlearning at a per-input layer (the formation-readout boundary located via the logit lens) rather than a single fixed layer, outperforming output- and representation-level baselines and resisting paraphrase and quantization attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing representation-level unlearning intervenes at a single fixed layer across the entire forget set, even though knowledge is distributed across layers. The authors question whether a fixed layer suffices and investigate where the forget answer is actually formed in the network.
AI.method: A hijacking experiment grafts the target model's hidden states into an oracle trained only on the retain set; the oracle cannot produce the forget answer alone but does so from the grafted state, showing the answer is formed at an intermediate layer and merely read out afterward. The authors then propose TULIP, which for each input uses the logit lens to locate the formation-readout boundary and removes the hidden state's alignment with the forget answer's unembedding vector at that layer.
AI.result: TULIP consistently outperforms output- and representation-level baselines on TOFU, PISTOL, and WMDP across Llama, Qwen, and Zephyr models, and remains robust to paraphrase and quantization attacks. Its per-input layer selection also acts as a plug-and-play component that improves existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Because the layer where forget-answer formation ends varies widely across inputs, unlearning should target formation rather than readout at a per-input layer. TULIP operationalizes this insight, demonstrating superior and more robust unlearning and offering a reusable per-input layer-selection module.

title: After the Fix: How Corrected Agent Histories Transfer to Related Tasks
summary: Does repairing an episode make its experience a better memory for the next task? We transfer the same failed source before and after accepted repair to a fixed target, alongside independent execution. Our 3,300 runs cover 100 ThinkingBox pairs and the same 100 APEX pairs with and without source-state inheritance, under eleven conditions. ThinkingBox's Full/Skill/Hybrid correction gains are 44/29/32 percentage points, with corrected performance 25/22/18 points above independence; inference weakens at the task-family level. Yet 12 of Full's 15-point larger correction gap over Skill come from worse uncorrected performance, not better corrected memory. Moreover, 22 of Full's 46 upward transitions restore observed baseline success. Neither APEX regime establishes comparable aggregate correction benefits. Action evidence connects workflow gains with reusable obligations and convention conflicts with source-local choices. Text APEX's accepted execution reaches 52% versus its summary's 40%, without robust global/group-level superiority or an estab- lished advantage over independence. Smaller handoffs reduce input but increase calls. The value of repairing experience is therefore distinct from the value of reusing it: memory updates require both a previous-version reference and a fresh-start reference.

AI.tldr: Repairing a failed episode and reusing its memory are distinct benefits: gains from corrected memory require both a previous-version and a fresh-start reference, and many apparent "repair" gains come from worse uncorrected baselines rather than better corrected memory.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether repairing a failed source episode makes its experience a better memory for a subsequent target task, and whether the value of repairing experience is separable from the value of reusing it.
AI.method: The same failed source is transferred to a fixed target before and after accepted repair, alongside independent execution. 3,300 runs cover 100 ThinkingBox pairs and the same 100 APEX pairs, with and without source-state inheritance, under eleven conditions.
AI.result: ThinkingBox Full/Skill/Hybrid correction gains are 44/29/32 percentage points, with corrected performance 25/22/18 points above independence; inference weakens at the task-family level. However, 12 of Full's 15-point larger correction gap over Skill come from worse uncorrected performance, not better corrected memory, and 22 of Full's 46 upward transitions merely restore observed baseline success. APEX shows no comparable aggregate correction benefits. Text APEX accepted execution reaches 52% versus its summary's 40%, without robust global/group-level superiority or established advantage over independence. Smaller handoffs reduce input but increase calls.
AI.conclusion: The value of repairing experience is distinct from the value of reusing it: memory updates require both a previous-version reference and a fresh-start reference.

title: LLMs for Executable Multi-Agent System Specification Generation
summary: MAS specifications express the effects of the actions of the agents and their environment, as well as other temporal phenomena, such as the intervals during which an agent may perform an action. The specification of a MAS should also be executable in order to allow for run-time monitoring. Constructing the specification of a MAS requires formal language expertise, while machine learning techniques depend on labelled data which are rarely available. To address these issues, we propose `genRTEC', a method that leverages pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate executable MAS specifications, in the language of the `Run-Time Event Calculus' (RTEC), from natural language descriptions. genRTEC constructs MAS specifications with complex hierarchical and cyclic dependencies based only on short natural language descriptions of the concepts involved. We present an extensive empirical evaluation of genRTEC, spanning various MAS specifications, including both a qualitative and a quantitative assessment. Our results demonstrate that genRTEC constructs executable MAS specifications of high predictive accuracy without compromising reasoning efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes genRTEC, a method that uses pre-trained LLMs to generate executable Multi-Agent System (MAS) specifications in the Run-Time Event Calculus (RTEC) language from short natural language descriptions, achieving high predictive accuracy without sacrificing reasoning efficiency.
AI.motivation: MAS specifications must express action effects and temporal phenomena (e.g., action intervals) and be executable for run-time monitoring. However, writing such specifications demands formal language expertise, whereas machine learning approaches rely on labelled data that is rarely available.
AI.method: genRTEC leverages pre-trained Large Language Models to generate executable MAS specifications in RTEC from natural language. It constructs specifications with complex hierarchical and cyclic dependencies based solely on short natural language descriptions of the involved concepts.
AI.result: An extensive empirical evaluation across various MAS specifications, including qualitative and quantitative assessments, shows that genRTEC produces executable MAS specifications with high predictive accuracy while preserving reasoning efficiency.
AI.conclusion: genRTEC addresses the expertise and labelled-data barriers of MAS specification by enabling LLM-based generation of executable RTEC specifications from natural language, yielding accurate and efficient results.

title: A Persistent State for Auditable Mixture-of-Experts Routing
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models repeatedly route tokens to sparse subsets of experts, but conventional routers expose no routing-specific record of how cross-layer influences accumulate. We introduce Scratchpad-Augmented Mixture-of-Experts (SA-MoE), which gives each router access to a low-dimensional persistent state that is not provided to the experts. Learned layerwise writes update this state, and their realized post-update changes exactly decompose the state-mediated contribution to any later routing margin, forming a routing ledger. Across sparsely upcycled SmolLM2- and Gemma-based models and three independent training seeds per architecture, this pathway adds less than 1% analytical forward compute and is strongly used by trained routers: local removal of its router contribution changes the selected Top-2 expert set in 87.6% and 69.9% of decisions, respectively. Relative to a matched latest-write-only control, persistent accumulation increases long-horizon future-routing accessibility by 19.4 and 12.2 percentage points, with positive effects in every seed. More than 90% of absolute ledger contribution comes from non-recent writes in both families, and full-forward suppression of ledger-selected writes changes later routing and output distributions. The ledger is an exact provenance object for the persistent-state pathway, not a complete causal explanation of routing. Sensitivity-aware scores better predict full-forward intervention effects, and post-hoc methods recover related cross-layer attribution without architectural modification. SA-MoE instead makes one routing-specific computational history explicit and directly inspectable within the model's natural forward computation.

AI.tldr: SA-MoE augments MoE routers with a persistent low-dimensional state not shared with experts, whose learnable layerwise writes form an exact "routing ledger" decomposing state-mediated contributions to later routing margins, adding <1% compute while heavily influencing expert selection.
AI.motivation: Conventional MoE routers expose no routing-specific record of how cross-layer influences accumulate, leaving the routing process opaque and hard to inspect.
AI.method: Each router receives a low-dimensional persistent state; learned layerwise writes update it, and the realized post-update changes exactly decompose the state-mediated contribution to any later routing margin. Evaluated on sparsely upcycled SmolLM2- and Gemma-based models across three seeds, with matched latest-write-only controls, sensitivity-aware scoring, and full-forward interventions.
AI.result: Adds <1% analytical forward compute; local removal of router contribution changes Top-2 expert sets in 87.6% and 69.9% of decisions. Persistent accumulation increases long-horizon future-routing accessibility by 19.4 and 12.2 pp over latest-write-only, positive in every seed. Over 90% of absolute ledger contribution comes from non-recent writes; full-forward suppression of ledger-selected writes alters later routing and output distributions. Sensitivity-aware scores better predict intervention effects, and post-hoc methods recover related attribution.
AI.conclusion: The ledger is an exact provenance object for the persistent-state pathway, not a complete causal explanation of routing. SA-MoE makes a routing-specific computational history explicit and directly inspectable within the model's natural forward computation.

title: MechReasoner: A Simulator and Benchmark for Mechanistic Reasoning in Qualitative Physics
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables, and 2 algorithms; includes supplementary material. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/idiap/mech-reasoner
summary: This work introduces MechReasoner, a mechanistic qualitative simulator grounded in confluence-based qualitative physics, together with a benchmark for mechanistic inference. Current large language models (LLMs) generate fluent mechanistic descriptions that do not reliably follow from underlying structural and causal constraints. The benchmark tests whether answers preserve simulator-licensed ambiguity, quantified claims, episode-graph transition evidence, repairs, and trace-support judgments. Its 1,120 items are generated deterministically from admissible interpretation sets, component states, scenario restrictions, confluence constraints, and derivation steps across 18 catalog mechanisms and six task families. Each mechanism undergoes converter checks of structure and topology and behavioral checks against quantitative simulations. GPT-5.5 accuracy decreases as family-specific mechanistic complexity increases, from 76.1% in the lowest-complexity bucket (B1) to 38.0% in the highest-complexity bucket (B4). The negative association remains after controls for rendered-prompt and expected-answer length. These results show that qualitative simulators can support auditable NLP benchmarks for mechanistic inference.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MechReasoner, a confluence-based qualitative simulator, and a 1,120-item deterministic benchmark for mechanistic inference, showing that GPT-5.5 accuracy drops from 76.1% to 38.0% as mechanistic complexity increases.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce fluent mechanistic descriptions that do not reliably follow underlying structural and causal constraints, and there is a lack of auditable benchmarks that test whether answers respect simulator-licensed ambiguity, quantified claims, transition evidence, repairs, and trace-support judgments.
AI.method: MechReasoner is a mechanistic qualitative simulator grounded in confluence-based qualitative physics. The benchmark items are generated deterministically from admissible interpretation sets, component states, scenario restrictions, confluence constraints, and derivation steps, spanning 18 catalog mechanisms and six task families. Each mechanism is validated via converter checks of structure and topology and behavioral checks against quantitative simulations.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 accuracy declines with family-specific mechanistic complexity, from 76.1% in the lowest-complexity bucket (B1) to 38.0% in the highest-complexity bucket (B4). The negative association persists after controlling for rendered-prompt and expected-answer length.
AI.conclusion: Qualitative simulators can support auditable NLP benchmarks for mechanistic inference.

title: Beyond Skill Evolution: Self-Evolving Context Management Policies for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses
summary: Harness evolution improves LLM agents by learning from execution trajectories, but existing experience- and skill-based methods are less effective on long-horizon tasks. As interactions grow, useful evidence can be buried by redundant or outdated context, making context management itself a key bottleneck. We introduce ContextEvo, a framework that learns a context policy from long-horizon trajectories. ContextEvo reconstructs the model-visible context at key decision points, identifies context-related failures, and applies targeted policy updates. Starting from the open-source Pi-agent harness, ContextEvo improves performance across three long-horizon task benchmarks, achieving results comparable to or better than several prominent agent harnesses, including Codex, OpenCode, and OpenClaw. Additional analyses show that fixed or locally evolved context strategies can fall short under long-horizon information pressure, while our methods adapt to the information demands of each environment.

AI.tldr: ContextEvo learns a context policy from long-horizon trajectories to manage the growing context bottleneck in LLM agents, outperforming harnesses like Codex and OpenCode on three long-horizon benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing experience- and skill-based harness evolution methods are less effective on long-horizon tasks. As interactions grow, useful evidence gets buried by redundant or outdated context, making context management itself a key bottleneck.
AI.method: ContextEvo reconstructs the model-visible context at key decision points, identifies context-related failures, and applies targeted policy updates to learn a context policy. It starts from the open-source Pi-agent harness.
AI.result: ContextEvo improves performance across three long-horizon task benchmarks, achieving results comparable to or better than prominent harnesses including Codex, OpenCode, and OpenClaw.
AI.conclusion: Fixed or locally evolved context strategies can fall short under long-horizon information pressure, whereas ContextEvo adapts to the information demands of each environment.

title: OmniTide: Co-Designing Algorithms and Systems for Efficient On-Device Omni-LLM Streaming
summary: On-device streaming omni-modal inference safeguards user privacy and eliminates prohibitive per-token API costs, but faces a critical bottleneck: the continuous influx of multimodal data rapidly exhausts constrained memory and compute budgets via monotonic KV cache growth. Existing sparse attention methods fall short, either incurring prohibitive online estimation latency or destroying interleaved cross-modal context, while failing to resolve physical memory fragmentation. We present OmniTide, the first algorithm-system co-design tailored for efficient on-device streaming omni-modal inference. Driven by the observation of modality-aware structural sparsity, OmniTide adopts a unit-based abstraction with two components: (1) At the algorithm level, OmniPick logically retains critical multimodal context based on unit boundaries and modality importance to preserve task accuracy; (2) At the system level, OmniPage physically partitions the cache by retention likelihood and dynamically compacts surviving sparse tokens, minimizing both memory fragmentation and data-movement overhead. Extensive evaluations across three streaming benchmarks and two consumer-device architectures show that OmniTide achieves up to $12.72\times$ kernel speedups and $2.40\times$ lower stream-loop latency. On StreamingBench, it improves accuracy by up to 18.0 percentage points over sliding-window baselines at comparable session cost. OmniPage further reduces the physical KV span by up to 26.7% relative to native logical eviction, unlocking real-time, infinite-context streaming on edge devices.

AI.tldr: OmniTide is an algorithm-system co-design for on-device streaming omni-modal inference that combines unit-based logical retention (OmniPick) with physical cache partitioning and compaction (OmniPage) to combat KV cache growth, achieving up to 12.72x kernel speedups and 26.7% KV span reduction.
AI.motivation: On-device streaming omni-modal inference protects privacy and avoids per-token API costs, but continuous multimodal input causes monotonic KV cache growth that exhausts memory and compute. Existing sparse attention methods suffer from high online estimation latency, destroy interleaved cross-modal context, and fail to address physical memory fragmentation.
AI.method: Unit-based abstraction exploiting modality-aware structural sparsity, with two components: OmniPick at the algorithm level logically retains critical multimodal context based on unit boundaries and modality importance; OmniPage at the system level physically partitions the cache by retention likelihood and dynamically compacts surviving sparse tokens to minimize memory fragmentation and data movement.
AI.result: Across three streaming benchmarks and two consumer-device architectures: up to 12.72x kernel speedups and 2.40x lower stream-loop latency; on StreamingBench, up to 18.0 percentage point accuracy improvement over sliding-window baselines at comparable session cost; OmniPage reduces physical KV span by up to 26.7% relative to native logical eviction.
AI.conclusion: The algorithm-system co-design enables real-time, infinite-context streaming on edge devices by jointly preserving cross-modal task accuracy and minimizing physical memory overhead.

title: A General Harness for Protein Foundation Model Fitness Prediction
summary: Accurate fitness prediction is central to protein engineering and understanding sequence-function relationships. With advances in deep learning, protein foundation models (PFMs) have become widely used for this task. Recent analyses, however, show that these models share preferences reflecting their training corpora, while unreliable inputs can further distort fitness predictions. Family-specific evolutionary evidence and structural context can help address these limitations by providing complementary constraints on model scores, motivating VenusREM-Harness (VRH), a general, model-agnostic, training-free Retrieval-Enhanced Mutation harness. It fuses frozen model scores with multiple sequence alignment (MSA) evidence according to model uncertainty, then applies gated background correction and score shrinkage based on structural confidence and solvent exposure. Across 1,211 assays and 3.1 million measured variants from ProteinGym, VenusMutHub, and the newly curated viral benchmark VenusViroHub, all 71 configurations improve Spearman correlation on all 3 benchmarks by 0.073 on average, with broad gains across 5 metrics. Extended analyses relate retrieval gains to model-MSA preference differences, assess domain-level gains and immune-escape cases, and quantify computational speedups. Built with VRH, VenusREM2 is the first to rank highest in all function, taxon, MSA-depth, and mutation-depth categories, with a ProteinGym Average Spearman of 0.556, 0.038 above the prior best.

AI.tldr: VenusREM-Harness (VRH) is a training-free, model-agnostic retrieval-enhanced mutation harness that fuses frozen protein foundation model scores with MSA evidence and structural context, improving fitness prediction across 1,211 assays and 3.1M variants.
AI.motivation: Protein foundation models (PFMs) are widely used for fitness prediction, but they inherit biases from their training corpora and are sensitive to unreliable inputs, which distorts predictions. Family-specific evolutionary evidence and structural context can supply complementary constraints to correct these limitations, motivating a general, model-agnostic enhancement approach.
AI.method: VRH fuses frozen model scores with multiple sequence alignment (MSA) evidence according to model uncertainty, then applies gated background correction and score shrinkage based on structural confidence and solvent exposure. It is training-free and model-agnostic. The resulting model, VenusREM2, is built with VRH.
AI.result: Across 1,211 assays and 3.1 million measured variants from ProteinGym, VenusMutHub, and the newly curated viral benchmark VenusViroHub, all 71 configurations improve Spearman correlation on all 3 benchmarks by 0.073 on average, with broad gains across 5 metrics. VenusREM2 ranks highest in all function, taxon, MSA-depth, and mutation-depth categories, with a ProteinGym Average Spearman of 0.556, 0.038 above the prior best.
AI.conclusion: VRH provides consistent, generalizable fitness-prediction gains by combining retrieval-based evolutionary evidence and structural context with frozen PFM scores. Extended analyses relate retrieval gains to model-MSA preference differences, assess domain-level gains and immune-escape cases, and quantify computational speedups.

title: Jailbreak Context Lingers: Divergent Safety Routing and Its Cross-Task Predictability in Tool Agents
comment: 28 pages, 9 figures, 17 tabels, ICLR 2027 Under Review
summary: As large language models increasingly operate as tool-using agents, post-jailbreak safety feedback is often assumed to serve as a reliable safeguard; however, how lingering jailbreak context shapes subsequent agent behavior remains largely unexplored. To systematically examine this dynamic, we introduce a paired continuation framework across 192 parent tasks spanning 42 domains, evaluating 12,148 analyzed continuation pairs (curated from a 12,288-pair initially design) across eight diverse agents. We find that identical safety feedback induces sharply model-dependent behavioral routing rather than uniform protection: redirecting unsafe trajectories toward legitimate completion (\emph{rescue}), sustaining unauthorized execution (\emph{persistent unsafe}), or triggering over-refusal on benign tasks (\emph{collateral loss}). Through layer-wise activation patching, we discover a shared \emph{late-commit pattern} where causal intervention effects surge sharply near the final layers (relative depths of 0.958--0.984) despite an over 30-fold variation in peak magnitude across architectures. Crucially, critical-layer representations correlate with macroscopic routing outcomes, and intervening at these layers causally alters concrete next-step tool actions. Building on this causal foundation, we test whether localized intervention-derived features can serve as predictive proxies for full-trajectory routing outcomes on unseen parent tasks under leave-one-parent-task-out evaluation, finding that they provide viable predictive signals in responsive agents with peak ROC AUCs reaching 0.675 for \emph{rescue}, 0.777 for \emph{collateral loss}, and 0.702 for \emph{persistent unsafe}. These findings establish a mechanistic lens and a predictive baseline for anticipating the safety and utility trade-offs of post-jailbreak feedback in autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how lingering jailbreak context shapes the subsequent behavior of tool-using LLM agents receiving post-jailbreak safety feedback. It introduces a paired continuation framework across 192 parent tasks and 42 domains, revealing three model-dependent behavioral routings (rescue, persistent unsafe, collateral loss) and identifying a shared "late-commit" pattern in the final layers that causally links to these outcomes and offers predictive signal.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents increasingly use tools, post-jailbreak safety feedback is assumed to be a reliable safeguard, yet how residual jailbreak context affects later agent behavior is largely unexplored. The authors aim to systematically characterize this dynamic and the safety-utility trade-offs it entails.
AI.method: A paired continuation framework spanning 192 parent tasks across 42 domains, with 12,148 analyzed continuation pairs (curated from an initial 12,288-pair design) and eight diverse agents. Layer-wise activation patching is used to probe causal mechanisms, followed by leave-one-parent-task-out evaluation testing whether intervention-derived localized features predict full-trajectory routing on unseen tasks.
AI.result: Identical safety feedback yields model-dependent routing into three outcomes: rescue, persistent unsafe, and collateral loss. Activation patching reveals a shared late-commit pattern with causal effects surging near the final layers (relative depths 0.958–0.984), despite over 30-fold variation in peak magnitude across architectures. Critical-layer representations correlate with routing outcomes and causally alter next-step tool actions. Predictive features achieve peak ROC AUCs of 0.675 (rescue), 0.777 (collateral loss), and 0.702 (persistent unsafe) in responsive agents.
AI.conclusion: Post-jailbreak safety feedback is not a uniform safeguard; its effect is routed by model-specific internal dynamics concentrated in late layers. The late-commit pattern provides a mechanistic lens, and intervention-derived features offer a predictive baseline for anticipating safety-utility trade-offs in autonomous agents.

title: VCN-Bench: A Video-Contextualized Navigation Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning over Prior Visual Experience
summary: Spatial reasoning is fundamental to embodied agents, yet it remains unclear whether spatial understanding can be carried forward to guide sequential interactions. Existing spatial-reasoning benchmarks typically terminate at offline predictions, while navigation benchmarks evaluate spatial reasoning as part of instruction following and exploration. We introduce VCN-Bench, a \textbf{V}ideo-\textbf{C}ontextualized \textbf{N}avigation benchmark for probing closed-loop spatial reasoning over prior visual experience in MLLMs. Given a prior video covering both the initial location and destination, the agent is tasked with reasoning out the instruction-specified target and navigating toward it with the inferred spatial context. Built on Matterport3D, VCN-Bench contains five instruction types, 100k training episodes, and 1,250 evaluation episodes. Navigation serves as the primary evaluation, while diagnostic goal identification helps distinguish destination-resolution errors from subsequent navigation failures. We further propose MV-DualVLN, a planning-oriented baseline that jointly leverages prior video and in-episode observations. Experiments reveal limited navigation performance, a substantial destination-resolution-to-navigation gap, and frequent navigation failures even after correct destination identification.

AI.tldr: VCN-Bench is a new video-contextualized navigation benchmark (built on Matterport3D; 5 instruction types, 100k training and 1,250 evaluation episodes) that probes closed-loop spatial reasoning from prior visual experience in MLLMs, together with MV-DualVLN, a planning-oriented baseline. Experiments show weak navigation, a large destination-resolution-to-navigation gap, and frequent failures even after correct destination identification.
AI.motivation: Spatial reasoning is fundamental to embodied agents, but it is unclear whether spatial understanding transfers to guiding sequential interactions. Existing spatial-reasoning benchmarks stop at offline predictions, while navigation benchmarks treat spatial reasoning merely as part of instruction following and exploration, leaving closed-loop spatial reasoning over prior visual experience unprobed.
AI.method: The authors introduce VCN-Bench, a Video-Contextualized Navigation benchmark built on Matterport3D. Given a prior video covering both the initial location and destination, the agent must infer the instruction-specified target and navigate to it using the inferred spatial context. It comprises five instruction types, 100k training episodes, and 1,250 evaluation episodes. Navigation is the primary evaluation, with diagnostic goal identification separating destination-resolution errors from downstream navigation failures. They also propose MV-DualVLN, a planning-oriented baseline that jointly leverages prior video and in-episode observations.
AI.result: Experiments reveal limited navigation performance, a substantial gap between destination resolution and navigation, and frequent navigation failures even when the destination is correctly identified.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop spatial reasoning over prior visual experience remains challenging for current MLLMs; VCN-Bench and MV-DualVLN expose this gap and provide a testbed and baseline for future work on video-contextualized navigation.

title: ResonAct: Streaming Metrics for Runtime Diagnosis and Self-Healing in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly used to automate enterprise workflows involving multiple specialized agents, external tools, and long-running task execution. Failures may arise from tool degradation, context propagation errors, coordination breakdowns, or repeated agent interactions that prevent task completion. While existing observability frameworks provide traces and logs, diagnosis and remediation are largely performed after execution completes, limiting opportunities for recovery during runtime. We present ResonAct, a runtime self-healing framework that enables continuous monitoring, diagnosis, and remediation of multi-agent systems through streaming operational metrics. ResonAct ingests execution traces, agent interactions, and tool invocations into a streaming analytics layer that continuously derives task progress, context health, and tool reliability metrics. These metrics serve as runtime control signals for detecting anomalous execution patterns and localizing root causes using a structured failure model. Based on the diagnosed failure, ResonAct dynamically selects remediation policies and performs actions. The framework operates as an external control plane, enabling intervention without modifying application agents or orchestration logic. We evaluate ResonAct across enterprise workflow scenarios and AppWorld benchmarks. The results show that the streaming metric-based analysis identifies execution degradations and localizes faults. Furthermore, policy-driven remediation improves task completion rates by up to 10.00 percentage points, with detection precision ranging from 70.59% to 82.91%, recall from 63.09% to 100%, recovery rates from 10.48% to 46.67%, and runtime overhead ranging from $-0.25%$ to 14.12% across the evaluated configurations.

AI.tldr: ResonAct is a runtime self-healing framework for multi-agent systems that uses streaming operational metrics to continuously monitor, diagnose, and remediate failures as an external control plane, improving task completion rates by up to 10.00 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems increasingly automate enterprise workflows involving specialized agents, external tools, and long-running execution, but failures arise from tool degradation, context propagation errors, coordination breakdowns, or repeated agent interactions. Existing observability frameworks provide traces and logs, yet diagnosis and remediation are largely performed post-execution, limiting runtime recovery opportunities.
AI.method: ResonAct ingests execution traces, agent interactions, and tool invocations into a streaming analytics layer that continuously derives task progress, context health, and tool reliability metrics. These metrics act as runtime control signals to detect anomalous execution patterns and localize root causes via a structured failure model. Based on the diagnosed failure, it dynamically selects remediation policies and executes actions, operating as an external control plane without modifying application agents or orchestration logic.
AI.result: Across enterprise workflow scenarios and AppWorld benchmarks, streaming metric-based analysis identifies execution degradations and localizes faults. Policy-driven remediation improves task completion rates by up to 10.00 percentage points, with detection precision of 70.59%-82.91%, recall of 63.09%-100%, recovery rates of 10.48%-46.67%, and runtime overhead of -0.25% to 14.12% across evaluated configurations.
AI.conclusion: Streaming metric-based runtime analysis combined with policy-driven remediation enables effective self-healing of multi-agent systems, improving task completion with modest runtime overhead while requiring no modification to existing agents or orchestration logic.

title: FromPitch2Board: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Long-Horizon Football Management
summary: Long-horizon agent benchmarks typically report how far an agent progresses, but do not identify whether its performance comes from the foundation model, scaffold, responsibility scope, match-control granularity, or horizon. We introduce FromPitch2Board, a deterministic football-management benchmark that studies five configurable factors through controlled comparisons on a single simulator, using paired seeds and a frozen calibration. We evaluate four foundation models and four agent scaffolds. In the Model Track, Coach points Z-scores span 0.19, while Manager points Z-scores span 0.68, with GPT-5.6 showing a sharp rise in passivity under responsibility expansion. Its responsibility ladder rises from 46.1 to 58.1 points with recruitment, then falls to 46.8 under full management, localizing the regression to the final responsibility boundary. Across that boundary, its skipped-decision rate rises from 1.1% to 57.9%. Within the Flash-Pro pair crossed across every scaffold, scaffold choice changes Manager points Z-scores by up to 0.48 relative to the fixed stateless scaffold. The 3Y cohort shows a directional reversal in mean ranking between years one and three, while a selected Claude Code+Pro configuration peaks in year three and remains below that peak, showing that responsibility scope and horizon expose behavior changes that a single headline score conceals.

AI.tldr: FromPitch2Board is a deterministic football-management benchmark that decomposes long-horizon agent performance into five configurable factors (foundation model, scaffold, responsibility scope, match-control granularity, horizon) via paired-seed, frozen-calibration controlled comparisons, revealing that headline scores mask responsibility- and horizon-induced behavior shifts.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agent benchmarks report how far an agent progresses but fail to attribute performance to its underlying causes—foundation model, scaffold, responsibility scope, match-control granularity, or horizon. This confounds interpretation of aggregate scores and hides behavior changes that emerge under expanded responsibility or longer horizons.
AI.method: The authors build FromPitch2Board, a deterministic football-management simulator benchmark, and run controlled comparisons along five configurable factors using paired seeds and a frozen calibration, evaluating four foundation models and four agent scaffolds. Performance is reported as Coach points Z-scores and Manager points Z-scores, alongside diagnostics such as skipped-decision rates and a responsibility ladder spanning partial to full management.
AI.result: Coach points Z-scores span 0.19 versus 0.68 for Manager points, indicating greater model sensitivity under broader responsibility. GPT-5.6 becomes sharply passive as responsibility expands: its ladder rises from 46.1 to 58.1 points with recruitment, then drops to 46.8 under full management, with skipped-decision rate jumping from 1.1% to 57.9% across the final responsibility boundary. In the Flash-Pro pair crossed across all scaffolds, scaffold choice shifts Manager points Z-scores by up to 0.48 relative to a fixed stateless scaffold. The 3Y cohort shows a directional reversal in mean ranking between years one and three; a selected Claude Code+Pro configuration peaks in year three and stays below that peak.
AI.conclusion: Responsibility scope and horizon expose behavior changes that a single headline score conceals, and long-horizon agent performance must be attributed across model, scaffold, responsibility scope, granularity, and horizon rather than summarized by one aggregate metric.

title: RSI-Router: Evolving Subtask-Level LLM Routing and Skills for Cost-Efficient Agents
summary: Practical deployment of large language model (LLM) agents requires strong task performance at affordable inference cost. For long-horizon agentic tasks, this performance-cost trade-off can be improved through within-task large-small model collaboration, as smaller models can handle some stages even when they cannot solve the full task. In this paper, we introduce RSI-router, a routing framework that constructs subtask-level model assignments and model-specific skills through recursive self-improvement over accumulated experience. Each iteration consists of four stages: Subtask Mining derives subtask definitions and identification rules from training trajectories; Routing Strategy Evolution proposes and evaluates diverse model assignments; Model-Specific Skill Evolution compares routed and large-model-only trajectories to diagnose failures and develop reusable execution skills; and Pareto-Optimal Router Selection updates the Pareto population using historical and newly generated routers while retaining dominated routers as experience for subsequent evolution. Routing between DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.5-9B, RSI-router consistently surpasses the DeepSeek-only baseline at roughly half the inference cost (48.3%) across five agentic benchmarks. In particular, on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, it cuts inference cost by 74.7-82.2% while simultaneously improving performance; on Terminal-Bench 2.0, it achieves a 16.7% relative performance gain at 18.0% lower cost. Moreover, RSI-router establishes a stronger performance--cost Pareto frontier than 9 routing methods.

AI.tldr: RSI-router is a recursive self-improvement routing framework for within-task large-small LLM collaboration, achieving frontier performance-cost trade-offs on agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLM agents demands strong task performance at affordable inference cost. On long-horizon agentic tasks, a large-only model is costly, but small models can still handle some stages even if they cannot solve the whole task, motivating subtask-level collaboration.
AI.method: The framework iterates four stages over accumulated experience: (1) Subtask Mining derives subtask definitions and identification rules from training trajectories; (2) Routing Strategy Evolution proposes and evaluates diverse model assignments; (3) Model-Specific Skill Evolution contrasts routed vs. large-model-only trajectories to diagnose failures and build reusable skills; (4) Pareto-Optimal Router Selection updates the Pareto population using historical and new routers, keeping dominated routers as experience. Routing is instantiated between DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.result: Across five agentic benchmarks, RSI-router consistently beats the DeepSeek-only baseline at roughly half the inference cost (48.3%). On ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop it cuts cost by 74.7-82.2% while improving performance; on Terminal-Bench 2.0 it gains 16.7% relative performance at 18.0% lower cost. It also achieves a stronger performance-cost Pareto frontier than 9 routing methods.
AI.conclusion: Subtask-level, recursively self-improved large-small collaboration yields a superior performance-cost Pareto frontier for long-horizon agentic tasks, validating routing with model-specific skills as a practical deployment strategy.

title: PDE-JEPA: Predictive Representation Learning of Latent Dynamics Modeling for Parametric PDEs
summary: Physical trajectories contain more than snapshots of a system: they also reveal how its states evolve under governing conditions. However, representation learning for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) has largely relied on reconstruction-based objectives that emphasize recovering observed physical fields. In this paper, we investigate predictive representation pretraining as an alternative to reconstruction-based learning. We find that predictive representations preserve rich physical information, yet this advantage alone does not ensure accurate field evolution. Based on these observations, we introduce PDE-JEPA for parametric PDE dynamics. Specifically, we first train an encoder using a masked-latent prediction to capture the underlying regularities of PDE dynamics. To explicitly adapt the pretrained representation toward a more dynamics-aligned state space, we then introduce a geometry projector that aligns latent trajectory geometry with the evolution geometry of physical fields. Finally, building on this geometry-aligned latent space, we further develop a physics-structured latent predictor that decomposes the dynamics into parameter-independent evolution and parameter-dependent response components. Extensive experiments on nine widely used PDE benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by an average of 33.4\% in-distribution, while achieving an average improvement of 51.4\% when extrapolating to unseen governing parameters. The project page is available \href{https://tanpig-x.github.io/PDE-JEPA/}{here}.

AI.tldr: PDE-JEPA is a predictive representation pretraining framework for parametric PDEs that combines masked-latent prediction, a geometry projector aligning latent trajectory geometry with physical evolution geometry, and a physics-structured latent predictor, outperforming SOTA by 33.4% in-distribution and 51.4% on extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Representation learning for parametric PDEs has largely relied on reconstruction-based objectives that emphasize recovering observed physical fields. However, physical trajectories contain more than snapshots of a system: they also reveal how states evolve under governing conditions. The authors investigate predictive representation pretraining as an alternative, finding that while predictive representations preserve rich physical information, this advantage alone does not ensure accurate field evolution.
AI.method: The proposed PDE-JEPA framework for parametric PDE dynamics consists of three components: (1) an encoder trained with masked-latent prediction to capture underlying regularities of PDE dynamics; (2) a geometry projector that aligns latent trajectory geometry with the evolution geometry of physical fields, adapting the pretrained representation toward a more dynamics-aligned state space; and (3) a physics-structured latent predictor that decomposes the dynamics into parameter-independent evolution and parameter-dependent response components, built on the geometry-aligned latent space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on nine widely used PDE benchmarks demonstrate that the framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by an average of 33.4% in-distribution, while achieving an average improvement of 51.4% when extrapolating to unseen governing parameters.
AI.conclusion: Predictive representation pretraining is an effective alternative to reconstruction-based learning for parametric PDEs, but requires explicit geometric alignment and physics-structured prediction to translate preserved physical information into accurate field evolution.

title: From Human Narrative to Harmonic Structure: A Human-Centered Investigation of Algorithmic Music Generation through the Chord Wheel Diagram
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, link to GIT
summary: Contemporary AI-based music generation can produce compositions that satisfy formal requirements of tonality and musical coherence. However, whether musical expression can be described by mathematical properties alone remains a fundamental question. Human composers operate within personal and cultural contexts that influence harmonic decisions and deliberate departures from established patterns. This study investigates six narrative-driven popular songs by Bob Dylan, Johnny Cash, and Ritchie Valens. Original human harmonies are compared with outputs of an explainable computational harmonizer operating on the same melodies without access to the original chord progressions. We examine harmonic vocabulary, functional persistence, repetition, non-diatonic events, and tension-resolution patterns using Chord Wheel Diagrams and BPMN-based representations. Results show that high melody-chord compatibility does not necessarily imply preservation of the original human harmonic decision pattern. Some generated harmonizations retain the economical structure of the reference, while others alter harmonic diversity or suppress distinctive events while remaining compatible with the melody. Rather than quantifying artistic quality, the study introduces narrative-conditioned harmonic structure as a complementary perspective for computational music analysis. The findings suggest that generative systems may benefit from modeling not only harmonic correctness, but also structural identity, context, and human compositional intention.

AI.tldr: This study compares human chord progressions in six narrative-driven popular songs by Bob Dylan, Johnny Cash, and Ritchie Valens with harmonizations generated by an explainable computational harmonizer using the same melodies, showing that high melody-chord compatibility does not guarantee preservation of the original human harmonic decision patterns.
AI.motivation: AI music generation can satisfy formal requirements of tonality and musical coherence, but whether musical expression is fully describable by mathematical properties remains open. Human composers work within personal and cultural contexts that shape harmonic decisions and intentional departures from established patterns, so correctness-based evaluation may miss what is artistically distinctive.
AI.method: Six narrative-driven popular songs by Bob Dylan, Johnny Cash, and Ritchie Valens were analyzed. Original human harmonies were compared with outputs of an explainable computational harmonizer run on the same melodies without access to the original chord progressions. The analysis covered harmonic vocabulary, functional persistence, repetition, non-diatonic events, and tension-resolution patterns, using Chord Wheel Diagrams and BPMN-based representations.
AI.result: High melody-chord compatibility does not necessarily imply preservation of the original human harmonic decision pattern. Some generated harmonizations retain the economical structure of the reference, while others alter harmonic diversity or suppress distinctive events while remaining compatible with the melody.
AI.conclusion: Rather than quantifying artistic quality, the study introduces narrative-conditioned harmonic structure as a complementary perspective for computational music analysis. Generative systems may benefit from modeling not only harmonic correctness, but also structural identity, context, and human compositional intention.

title: SeLMRoute: Probabilistic Semantic Evidence for Large Language Model Routing
summary: Large language model (LLM) routing aims to select the most suitable model for each incoming query. Most existing routers learn this decision directly from query embeddings, model representations, preference data, or clusters of similar examples. Such approaches can be effective, yet the representation used for routing rarely states what a query actually requires. We introduce SeLMRoute, a routing framework that separates the extraction of candidate-independent semantic evidence from the learning of candidate performance and the application of deployment objectives. A decision model first evaluates a set of interpretable questions about the query, such as its reasoning requirements and use of external knowledge, with each judgment retained as a probability distribution. The resulting probabilistic semantic state is used by a lightweight supervised router to estimate candidate model performance. Routing objectives are applied after performance estimation, which allows the same semantic state to support performance-oriented and cost-aware decisions. On the LLMRouterBench (15 datasets, 20 candidate models, 11,481 queries), SeLMRoute achieves an average accuracy of $72.08\% \pm 0.45$, while grouped five-fold out-of-fold evaluation reaches $72.64\%$, compared with $69.23\%$ for the strongest fixed candidate.
