The representation achieves the highest mean performance among the evaluated semantic, dense, lexical, and domain-level representations. In a separate 13-model performance-cost setting, SeLMRoute improves performance in all five grouped splits, with a mean PerfGain of $2.66\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/SeLMRoute.

AI.tldr: SeLMRoute is an LLM routing framework that first extracts candidate-independent, interpretable semantic evidence from a query as a probabilistic state, then uses a lightweight supervised router to estimate candidate performance, applying deployment objectives only afterward.
AI.motivation: Most existing LLM routers learn routing decisions directly from query embeddings, model representations, preference data, or clusters of similar examples. These representations rarely state explicitly what a query actually requires, limiting interpretability and flexibility in how the same query representation can serve different deployment objectives.
AI.method: SeLMRoute separates candidate-independent semantic evidence extraction from candidate performance learning and deployment-objective application. A decision model evaluates a set of interpretable questions about the query (e.g., reasoning requirements, use of external knowledge), retaining each judgment as a probability distribution. This probabilistic semantic state feeds a lightweight supervised router that estimates candidate model performance. Routing objectives are applied only after this estimation, so the same semantic state supports both performance-oriented and cost-aware decisions.
AI.result: On LLMRouterBench (15 datasets, 20 candidate models, 11,481 queries), SeLMRoute reaches 72.08% ± 0.45 average accuracy; grouped five-fold out-of-fold evaluation reaches 72.64%, versus 69.23% for the strongest fixed candidate. It attains the highest mean performance among evaluated semantic, dense, lexical, and domain-level representations. In a separate 13-model performance-cost setting, it improves performance across all five grouped splits with a mean PerfGain of 2.66%.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling interpretable, candidate-independent semantic evidence extraction from candidate performance estimation and objective application yields a routing representation that outperforms strong fixed baselines and other representation types, and generalizes to cost-aware settings. Code is available at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/SeLMRoute.

title: Privacy-Preserving Full-Body Meshing from mmWave Radar via Mesh Foundation Model Supervision
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving human perception, but the extreme sparsity of point clouds from commercial single-chip sensors (mean ~6.5 points/frame; ~28% empty frames) has confined prior art to body-part keypoints or discrete action classification. We present a cross-modal teacher-student framework that lifts commercial radar to full-body, per-frame, metric 3D mesh reconstruction with per-joint uncertainty. Three innovations: (1) a mesh-foundation-model teacher - SAM 3D Body produces whole-body MHR ground truth (70 joints, 18,439 mesh vertices) from a single RGB frame with zero training, slashing annotation cost by orders of magnitude; (2) StudentPoseFormer - set encoding with masked attention pooling, a temporal Transformer, and a CVAE multi-hypothesis head that outputs both the pose mean and per-joint variance, honestly reporting where the radar cannot see; and (3) a multi-stage ground-truth quality pipeline (confidence gating, depth validation, temporal smoothing, bone-length consistency, bad-frame rejection) plus systematic information-lever ablations. On the public MM-Fi benchmark (same TI IWR6843 sensor, cross-subject), our full configuration reaches 7.45 cm 12-joint MPJPE, with ablations proving the causal value of point accumulation (k = 3, -0.34 cm), Doppler (-0.85 cm; -2 cm at the wrist on fast actions), and velocity loss (-0.27 cm). On our own synchronized radar + RGB-D corpus with block-level held-out splits, the pipeline achieves 21.47 cm end-to-end (per-joint hierarchy from 4.8 cm at the hip to 34.7 cm at the wrist - matching physical information limits), could be improved to 15 cm with ~30k diverse samples, and a scaling law shows sample diversity, not volume, is the binding constraint. Deployment inference is radar-only - no camera, no image.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal teacher-student framework lifts commercial single-chip mmWave radar from sparse keypoint/action tasks to full-body, per-frame metric 3D mesh reconstruction with per-joint uncertainty, using an RGB-only mesh foundation model as the teacher and radar-only inference at deployment.
AI.motivation: Commercial single-chip mmWave radar enables privacy-preserving human perception, but point clouds are extremely sparse (mean ~6.5 points/frame, ~28% empty frames), which has confined prior work to body-part keypoints or discrete action classification rather than dense whole-body geometry. Additionally, obtaining dense 3D ground truth annotations is prohibitively expensive, and radar inherently cannot observe some body regions.
AI.method: Three innovations: (1) a mesh-foundation-model teacher - SAM 3D Body generates whole-body MHR ground truth (70 joints, 18,439 mesh vertices) from a single RGB frame with zero training, drastically cutting annotation cost; (2) StudentPoseFormer - set encoding with masked attention pooling, a temporal Transformer, and a CVAE multi-hypothesis head outputting pose mean plus per-joint variance to report uncertainty where radar cannot see; (3) a multi-stage ground-truth quality pipeline (confidence gating, depth validation, temporal smoothing, bone-length consistency, bad-frame rejection) with systematic information-lever ablations.
AI.result: On the public MM-Fi benchmark (same TI IWR6843 sensor, cross-subject), the full configuration reaches 7.45 cm 12-joint MPJPE, with ablations confirming causal value of point accumulation (k = 3, -0.34 cm), Doppler (-0.85 cm; -2 cm at the wrist on fast actions), and velocity loss (-0.27 cm). On the authors' synchronized radar + RGB-D corpus with block-level held-out splits, the pipeline achieves 21.47 cm end-to-end, with per-joint hierarchy from 4.8 cm at the hip to 34.7 cm at the wrist, matching physical information limits. Performance could improve to ~15 cm with ~30k diverse samples, and a scaling law indicates sample diversity, not volume, is the binding constraint.
AI.conclusion: Deployment inference is radar-only - no camera or image required - preserving privacy while achieving full-body metric 3D mesh reconstruction with per-joint uncertainty. Elbows and limbs near the sensor body are well constrained, while distal joints remain bounded by physical information limits; scaling behavior shows diversity of training samples, rather than raw quantity, is the key bottleneck.

title: When Do Model Internals Help? Exploring the Role of Representation Engineering in LLM Safety
summary: Reliable AI safeguards require both control mechanisms that reduce unsafe behavior and monitoring mechanisms that detect safety risks during model interactions. Established behavioral safeguards include alignment methods that optimize model outputs and text monitors that assess interaction text. Representation engineering instead reads or modifies internal model states, but the relative strengths of these approaches remain unclear because they are often evaluated under different settings. We present a matched evaluation across two tracks. For safety control, we compare DPO, a behavioral alignment method, with three representation steering methods across robustness, practicality, and granularity. DPO provides the strongest overall control and generally improves with increasing training data, although its safety can degrade after subsequent benign fine-tuning. Representation steering remains competitive primarily in low-data settings, particularly with high-quality contrastive data. For safety monitoring, we compare representation probes with fine-tuned and open-weight text monitors across full-response detection, early detection, and computational cost. Specialized text monitors achieve the strongest overall detection accuracy, while representation probes remain competitive at substantially lower marginal cost. Finally, monitor-guided interventions recover much of the safety lost by DPO after benign fine-tuning, with little additional over-refusal. Overall, representation engineering does not generally replace behavioral safeguards, but offers practical advantages under specific conditions and can provide complementary safety benefits.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a matched evaluation comparing behavioral safeguards (DPO alignment and text monitors) against representation engineering methods (representation steering and probes) for AI safety control and monitoring, finding that behavioral methods lead overall while representation methods offer complementary advantages in low-data and low-cost regimes.
AI.motivation: Reliable AI safeguards require both control mechanisms to reduce unsafe behavior and monitoring mechanisms to detect safety risks. While behavioral safeguards (alignment and text monitors) and representation engineering (reading/modifying internal states) both exist, their relative strengths are unclear because they are typically evaluated under different settings, preventing fair comparison.
AI.method: A matched evaluation across two tracks. For safety control, DPO (behavioral alignment) is compared with three representation steering methods across robustness, practicality, and granularity. For safety monitoring, representation probes are compared with fine-tuned and open-weight text monitors across full-response detection, early detection, and computational cost. Monitor-guided interventions are also tested to assess recovery of safety lost by DPO after benign fine-tuning.
AI.result: DPO provides the strongest overall control and generally improves with more training data, though its safety can degrade after subsequent benign fine-tuning. Representation steering stays competitive mainly in low-data settings, especially with high-quality contrastive data. For monitoring, specialized text monitors achieve the strongest overall detection accuracy, while representation probes remain competitive at substantially lower marginal cost. Monitor-guided interventions recover much of the safety lost by DPO after benign fine-tuning, with little additional over-refusal.
AI.conclusion: Representation engineering does not generally replace behavioral safeguards, but offers practical advantages under specific conditions and can provide complementary safety benefits.

title: Before the Token Commits: Trajectory-Level Benchmarking of Visual Hallucinations in Diffusion VLMs
summary: Multimodal diffusion language models generate responses by iteratively unmasking tokens, making each answer the endpoint of a multi-step trajectory rather than an immediate commitment. Hallucination benchmarks built for autoregressive models evaluate only the final output, and therefore cannot determine whether an unsupported claim in diffusion VLMs appears late or has already stabilized before any answer token is revealed. We introduce DynaHall, a trajectory-level benchmark of annotation-backed binary visual propositions covering object existence, counting, attributes, and relations, with controlled hard negatives graded by visual prior. DynaHall is paired with a commitment-aware protocol that records the intermediate answer tendency at every unmasking step alongside the committed output. Across five diffusion VLMs from three architecture families, visual hallucination is settled before commitment: an unsupported answer is already the preferred state while the answer position is still masked, and later unmasking steps rarely reverse it, so the failure is not introduced at the write step. This holds across decoding schedules, answer formats, and open-ended generation. DynaHall also exposes failures hidden by final-output metrics, including counting and relation collapse, prior-driven false positives, and attribute errors whose direction changes by type. Guided by this diagnosis, PGS (Pre-commitment Gradient Steering) edits still-masked answer states to reduce false positives, bringing the affirmation rate close to balance, and transfers to another architecture without degrading general ability. DynaHall and PGS suggest that hallucination should be measured and mitigated along the generation trajectory of diffusion VLMs, not only at the final answer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DynaHall, a trajectory-level benchmark for visual hallucination in multimodal diffusion language models (diffusion VLMs), showing that unsupported answers are already preferred during masked decoding steps (hallucination is "settled before commitment"), and proposes PGS (Pre-commitment Gradient Steering) to mitigate it by editing still-masked answer states.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination benchmarks are designed for autoregressive models and evaluate only final outputs, so they cannot reveal whether an unsupported claim in diffusion VLMs emerges late or is already stabilized before any answer token is unmasked. This blind spot prevents understanding where and when hallucination originates in the iterative unmasking trajectory.
AI.method: The authors build DynaHall, a trajectory-level benchmark of annotation-backed binary visual propositions spanning object existence, counting, attributes, and relations, with controlled hard negatives graded by visual prior. They pair it with a commitment-aware protocol that records the intermediate answer tendency at every unmasking step alongside the committed output. They evaluate five diffusion VLMs from three architecture families across decoding schedules, answer formats, and open-ended generation. Based on the diagnosis, they propose PGS (Pre-commitment Gradient Steering), which edits still-masked answer states to reduce false positives.
AI.result: Visual hallucination is settled before commitment: an unsupported answer is already the preferred state while the answer position is still masked, and later unmasking steps rarely reverse it, so the failure is not introduced at the write step. This holds across decoding schedules, answer formats, and open-ended generation. DynaHall exposes failures hidden by final-output metrics, including counting and relation collapse, prior-driven false positives, and attribute errors whose direction changes by type. PGS reduces false positives, bringing the affirmation rate close to balance, and transfers to another architecture without degrading general ability.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination in diffusion VLMs should be measured and mitigated along the generation trajectory, not only at the final answer. The failure originates before the "write" step, so trajectory-level evaluation and pre-commitment intervention (PGS) are effective and transferable, providing a new diagnostic and mitigation paradigm for multimodal diffusion language models.

title: Page-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for EvalLLM 2026: A Five-Variant Study on French PDFs
summary: We study retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for questions about French PDF documents when both the answer and its supporting document pages are evaluated. Five system variants add dense retrieval, rank fusion, reranking, and query decomposition to a BM25 baseline. On 595 challenge questions, the complete system scores 0.4450 MRR@10 and 0.4013 Recall@10, compared with 0.3430 and 0.2994 for BM25. Dense retrieval alone and a simple lexical--dense fusion both underperform BM25. Reranking improves the hybrid system, whereas adding query decomposition produces the largest further gain, with higher latency and more detected output artifacts. The complete system slightly exceeds the reported anonymous overall mean on two answer metrics but falls below it on most page-retrieval metrics. These results identify accurate page selection, rather than semantic retrieval in isolation, as the main opportunity for improvement in this setting.

AI.tldr: A five-variant RAG study on French PDF question answering finds that the full pipeline (dense retrieval + rank fusion + reranking + query decomposition over BM25) reaches 0.4450 MRR@10 and 0.4013 Recall@10 vs. BM25's 0.3430 and 0.2994, with query decomposition yielding the largest gain and page selection identified as the key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: The study aims to evaluate RAG performance on French PDF documents under a dual evaluation that scores both the answer and its supporting document pages, a setting where page-level retrieval quality is critical but often overlooked.
AI.method: Five system variants are built incrementally on a BM25 baseline, adding dense retrieval, rank fusion, reranking, and query decomposition. Evaluation uses 595 challenge questions and reports MRR@10 and Recall@10 for answers and pages.
AI.result: The complete system achieves 0.4450 MRR@10 and 0.4013 Recall@10 vs. BM25's 0.3430 and 0.2994. Dense retrieval alone and simple lexical-dense fusion both underperform BM25. Reranking improves the hybrid system, while query decomposition produces the largest additional gain at the cost of higher latency and more output artifacts. The full system slightly exceeds the anonymous overall mean on two answer metrics but falls below it on most page-retrieval metrics.
AI.conclusion: Accurate page selection, rather than semantic retrieval in isolation, is the primary opportunity for improvement in this French PDF RAG setting.

title: Applying Language Models in medical Medicine: Recent Trends and Perspectives
comment: 7 pages, aimed to be a blogpost of the current state of the medical LLM field
summary: The use and applicability of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical research and clinical practice has received increasing attention in the literature over recent years. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has expanded discussions in regards to applications of AI within healthcare. While traditional deep learning based AI applications in medicine have often focused on specific and defined tasks, LLMs offer broader capabilities and flexibility in working with available data,. At the same time of writing, the integration of LLMs into medical settings raises important questions regarding their reliability, accuracy, transparency, safety, and appropriate role in a medical setting. This text presents and discusses recent talks and articles concerning the application of LLMs in medicine, with particular emphasis on their potential utility in research and clinical practice. It considers both the opportunities offered by these technologies and the challenges associated with their implementation, aiming to provide a perspective on the current and emerging role of LLMs within the medical field.

AI.tldr: This perspective piece reviews recent talks and articles on large language models (LLMs) in medicine, weighing their opportunities for research and clinical practice against challenges of reliability, accuracy, transparency, safety, and role definition.
AI.motivation: AI in medical research and clinical practice has drawn growing attention, and the emergence of LLMs has expanded the discussion beyond traditional task-specific deep learning. However, integrating LLMs into medical settings raises unresolved questions about their reliability, accuracy, transparency, safety, and appropriate role, motivating a consolidated perspective on their current and emerging role.
AI.method: A narrative review and discussion of recent talks and articles concerning LLM application in medicine, with particular emphasis on potential utility in research and clinical practice, comparing task-specific traditional deep learning applications with the broader flexibility of LLMs.
AI.result: Traditional deep learning AI in medicine has often been confined to specific, defined tasks, whereas LLMs offer broader capabilities and greater flexibility in working with available data; however, their implementation in medical settings remains accompanied by substantive concerns regarding reliability, accuracy, transparency, and safety.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a perspective on both the opportunities offered by LLMs and the challenges of their implementation, aiming to clarify the current and emerging role of LLMs within the medical field.

title: BEHAVE: Functional Behavior Modeling Enables Self-Improving Agents for Hardware Design and Verification
summary: Developing agents for hardware design and verification requires reliable correctness feedback. As a hardware specification may permit correct implementations with different latencies, matching design and reference outputs cycle by cycle can reject valid designs. To address this, we introduce BEHAVE, an agentic framework for multi-turn joint hardware design and verification through functional behavior modeling. We define Behavior IR to express task functionality as executable behavior models without prescribing implementation timing beyond the specification. The agent iteratively develops a register-transfer-level (RTL) design and a behavior model as the design's verification reference. Our evaluator, BEHAVE-Sim, checks both artifacts separately against a hidden golden behavior model using input stimuli generated by random sampling and solver-guided search. BEHAVE thus supports power, performance, and area (PPA) exploration across task-permitted latencies and microarchitectures. During training, the same evaluator provides verifiable reinforcement learning (RL) rewards from specification-behavior pairs without reference RTL. For self-improvement, the agent continually searches for high-level implementations relevant to its capability gaps, constructs and checks specification-behavior pairs, and trains on the expanded task pool. We release BEHAVE-Train and BEHAVE-Eval with 600 human-reviewed specification-behavior pairs for realistic hardware workloads. Starting from 60 seed tasks and acquiring 100 new tasks, self-improvement raises Qwen3.8-27B's RTL pass@1 on BEHAVE-Eval from 55.0% to 75.0%, reaching performance comparable to RL using a 540-task pool.

AI.tldr: BEHAVE is an agentic framework for joint hardware design and verification using a timing-agnostic Behavior IR, enabling PPA exploration and verifiable RL rewards without reference RTL.
AI.motivation: Cycle-by-cycle matching of design outputs against a reference rejects correct implementations that have different latencies than the specification's example, so a correctness signal that respects specification-permitted timing is needed for hardware design and verification agents.
AI.method: BEHAVE defines a Behavior IR expressing task functionality as executable behavior models without prescribing implementation timing beyond the specification. The agent iteratively co-develops an RTL design and a behavior model serving as its verification reference. BEHAVE-Sim separately checks both artifacts against a hidden golden behavior model using random-sampling and solver-guided input stimuli, and supplies verifiable RL rewards from specification-behavior pairs without reference RTL. Self-improvement searches for implementations addressing capability gaps, builds and checks new specification-behavior pairs, and trains on the expanded pool.
AI.result: BEHAVE-Sim enables PPA exploration across task-permitted latencies and microarchitectures. On BEHAVE-Eval, self-improvement from 60 seed tasks plus 100 acquired tasks raises Qwen3-27B's RTL pass@1 from 55.0% to 75.0%, matching RL trained on a 540-task pool. BEHAVE-Train and BEHAVE-Eval are released with 600 human-reviewed specification-behavior pairs.
AI.conclusion: Functional behavior modeling with a hidden golden behavior model provides a timing-agnostic correctness signal for both evaluation and RL, and agentic task acquisition substitutes efficiently for large hand-built task pools.

title: STRIDE: Automated Evaluation of Text-to-Trajectory Alignment across Diverse Contexts
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2027, Evaluations & Datasets Track
summary: Language-conditioned trajectory generation is here, but its evaluation has not kept pace. Existing pedestrian trajectory metrics compare trajectories with real-world human data. This does not scale to text-to-trajectory generation across diverse contexts, as collecting human trajectories for every scenario is costly and infeasible. Moreover, pedestrian behavior is heterogeneous and context-dependent, with no single metric as the correct answer, and current evaluation frameworks are not transferable to this domain. These challenges make scalable, reliable evaluation difficult. We introduce STRIDE, the first framework for evaluating context alignment between scenario descriptions and pedestrian trajectories. STRIDE addresses these challenges through three design choices. First, we derive our VRDST evaluation protocol from sociological theories to define a complete evaluation space. Second, it decomposes high-level context into scenario-adaptive behavioral questions. Third, every question is resolved against a deterministic measurement tool library that yields reproducible answers. Together, STRIDE enables complete, verifiable, automated, and scalable evaluation across diverse contexts without requiring human trajectory data. We instantiate STRIDE in the crowd domain as STRIDE-Bench, comprising 1K scenarios, 6K behavioral questions, and 11K measurements with calibrated expected answers across 30 real-world maps. Comprehensive human validations show that STRIDE-Bench is consistent with human behavior and judgment, achieving 80% human agreement. We further evaluate several text-to-trajectory models, finding limited context-alignment capability and persistent challenges in fine-grained context conditioning. We believe that the STRIDE framework provides a first step toward principled evaluation of context-aligned pedestrian trajectory generation.

AI.tldr: STRIDE is the first framework for evaluating context alignment between scenario descriptions and pedestrian trajectories, using sociological theory, adaptive behavioral questions, and a deterministic measurement tool library to enable scalable, reproducible evaluation without human trajectory data.
AI.motivation: Existing pedestrian trajectory metrics rely on comparison against real-world human data, which is costly and infeasible to collect for every scenario in text-to-trajectory generation. Pedestrian behavior is heterogeneous and context-dependent, so no single metric serves as ground truth, and current evaluation frameworks are not transferable to this domain—making scalable, reliable evaluation difficult.
AI.method: STRIDE uses three design choices: (1) a VRDST evaluation protocol derived from sociological theories to define a complete evaluation space; (2) decomposition of high-level context into scenario-adaptive behavioral questions; and (3) resolution of every question against a deterministic measurement tool library yielding reproducible answers. It is instantiated in the crowd domain as STRIDE-Bench with 1K scenarios, 6K behavioral questions, and 11K measurements with calibrated expected answers across 30 real-world maps.
AI.result: Human validations show STRIDE-Bench is consistent with human behavior and judgment, achieving 80% human agreement. Evaluation of several text-to-trajectory models reveals limited context-alignment capability and persistent challenges in fine-grained context conditioning.
AI.conclusion: STRIDE provides a first step toward principled evaluation of context-aligned pedestrian trajectory generation, enabling complete, verifiable, automated, and scalable evaluation across diverse contexts without requiring human trajectory data.

title: SIPO: Selective-Inference Policy Optimization for Tree-Structured Agentic RL
summary: Tree-structured reinforcement learning trains search agents by comparing alternative continuations and propagating terminal rewards to intermediate decisions. Adaptive expansion, however, creates a statistical asymmetry: an incumbent is selected using its own generation statistic, whereas fresh siblings are sampled after selection. When that statistic is associated with return, branch values can reflect selection history as well as continuation quality, even for a shared parent. We propose Selective-Inference Policy Optimization (\SIPO{}), which incorporates this distinction into tree-based credit estimation. Its scale-free branch criterion keeps generation scores and sibling penalties on a consistent relative scale; exchangeable branching supplies multiple fresh continuations from each selected parent; and order-statistic correction adjusts retained incumbent values using selection rank and the estimated score--outcome association. These mechanisms preserve the leaf budget and the host policy optimisation objective. Across seven QA benchmarks using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, \SIPO{} achieves the highest reported multi-hop and single-hop averages among the compared methods. On Qwen3-8B, it improves these averages over AT\textsuperscript{2}PO by $1.31$ and $1.07$ percentage points, respectively, and ranks first on six of seven benchmarks. Component ablations evaluate the individual and combined changes, while early-training paired diagnostics show a selected--fresh value gap alongside a near-zero fresh--fresh reference. Together, these results support accounting for selection history when constructing and evaluating search-agent rollouts. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zenghuang-Fu/SIPO

AI.tldr: SIPO is a tree-structured RL method for search agents that corrects selection-induced value bias in adaptive branching via a scale-free branch criterion, exchangeable branching, and order-statistic correction, achieving top QA benchmark averages.
AI.motivation: Adaptive expansion in tree-structured RL creates a statistical asymmetry: incumbents are selected using their own generation statistic, while fresh siblings are sampled after selection. When that statistic correlates with return, branch values conflate selection history with continuation quality, even under a shared parent. This biases tree-based credit estimation.
AI.method: The paper proposes Selective-Inference Policy Optimization (SIPO), which embeds the incumbent-vs-fresh distinction into tree-based credit estimation through three mechanisms: (1) a scale-free branch criterion keeping generation scores and sibling penalties on a consistent relative scale; (2) exchangeable branching that supplies multiple fresh continuations per selected parent; and (3) order-statistic correction that adjusts retained incumbent values using selection rank and the estimated score-outcome association. These preserve the leaf budget and the host policy optimization objective.
AI.result: Across seven QA benchmarks with Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, SIPO attains the highest multi-hop and single-hop averages among compared methods. On Qwen3-8B it exceeds AT²PO by 1.31 and 1.07 percentage points respectively, ranking first on six of seven benchmarks. Ablations isolate individual and combined component effects, and early-training paired diagnostics reveal a selected-fresh value gap with a near-zero fresh-fresh reference.
AI.conclusion: The results support explicitly accounting for selection history when constructing and evaluating search-agent rollouts, with SIPO providing an effective and objective-preserving correction to tree-based credit estimation.

title: UniOPSD: Unifying Outcome and Hindsight Feedback for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach to training language model agents, but sparse and delayed outcome rewards provide limited guidance for credit assignment across long interaction sequences. Recent work on on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers complementary supervision by evaluating a policy's sampled responses under privileged training-time context. However, our diagnostics show that positive average agreement between outcome and hindsight feedback coexists with substantial local disagreement, raising the question of how to allocate influence between them at each decision. We introduce UniOPSD (Unified On-Policy Self-Distillation), which unifies these feedback sources through adaptive local credit arbitration. UniOPSD constructs comparable credit estimates from environmental returns and successful-peer hindsight at shared interaction anchors. Historical agreement determines the global mixing level, while current signal availability and relative precision adjust each source's influence at individual decisions. The episode-level outcome contribution is retained, and bounded token modulation refines the fused step credit for policy optimization. With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, UniOPSD achieves ALFWorld success rates of $82.8\%$ and $83.6\%$, WebShop success rates of $75.0\%$ and $82.0\%$, and Search-QA aggregate accuracies of $45.3\%$ and $49.8\%$, respectively. On 3B WebShop, UniOPSD improves over SDAR by $7.0$ percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zenghuang-Fu/Uniopsd

AI.tldr: UniOPSD unifies outcome rewards and hindsight self-distillation signals via adaptive local credit arbitration, achieving strong results across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA.
AI.motivation: Sparse and delayed outcome rewards provide limited credit assignment guidance over long interaction sequences, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers complementary hindsight supervision. Diagnostics reveal that positive average agreement between outcome and hindsight feedback coexists with substantial local disagreement, motivating the need to allocate influence between these sources at each decision.
AI.method: UniOPSD constructs comparable credit estimates from environmental returns and successful-peer hindsight at shared interaction anchors. Historical agreement sets the global mixing level, while current signal availability and relative precision adjust each source's influence at individual decisions. Episode-level outcome contribution is retained, and bounded token modulation refines the fused step credit for policy optimization.
AI.result: With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, UniOPSD achieves ALFWorld success rates of 82.8% and 83.6%, WebShop success rates of 75.0% and 82.0%, and Search-QA aggregate accuracies of 45.3% and 49.8%. On 3B WebShop, it improves over SDAR by 7.0 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: UniOPSD effectively arbitrates between outcome and hindsight feedback through adaptive local credit assignment, yielding consistent gains in language model agent training.

title: Simulating Respondents, Not Single Questions: Coherent Survey Generation with Large Language Models
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate response distributions in social surveys. Prior work has achieved accurate population-level simulation for individual questions. Real questionnaires, however, ask each respondent a sequence of related questions. A simulated respondent should show coherent preferences across the whole questionnaire, not merely accurate distributions for isolated items. Existing single-item methods cannot accurately reproduce how the same person answers a complete survey. We propose FullRespondent-LLM (FR-LLM), which fine-tunes two specialized LLMs: a marginal model for each item's response distribution and a respondent-level autoregressive model for dependencies across answers. Marginal-Constrained Joint Projection (MCJP) then projects the autoregressive joint distribution onto the set satisfying the item-level marginals learned by the first model. This yields complete questionnaires with realistic cross-item relationships while retaining strong item-level accuracy. On two real-world social survey datasets, FR-LLM more accurately reproduces multi-question response patterns, maintains competitive single-item accuracy, and generalizes better to unseen populations and questions. In a small commercial-survey dataset, we use simulated responses to make pricing and stocking decisions; FR-LLM achieves the highest realized profit.

AI.tldr: FR-LLM simulates entire survey questionnaires by combining a marginal item-level LLM with a respondent-level autoregressive LLM, then projecting the joint distribution onto item-level marginal constraints (MCJP) to produce coherent, accurate multi-question responses.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM survey-simulation work only matches population-level distributions for isolated single questions. Real questionnaires ask each respondent a sequence of related questions, so a simulated respondent must show coherent cross-item preferences rather than merely accurate per-item marginals. Existing single-item methods cannot reproduce how the same individual answers a full survey.
AI.method: FR-LLM fine-tunes two specialized LLMs: (1) a marginal model capturing each item's response distribution, and (2) a respondent-level autoregressive model capturing dependencies across a respondent's answers. Marginal-Constrained Joint Projection (MCJP) then projects the autoregressive joint distribution onto the set satisfying the item-level marginals learned by the marginal model.
AI.result: On two real-world social survey datasets, FR-LLM more accurately reproduces multi-question response patterns while maintaining competitive single-item accuracy and generalizing better to unseen populations and questions. In a small commercial-survey dataset used for pricing and stocking decisions, FR-LLM achieves the highest realized profit.
AI.conclusion: Combining item-level marginal accuracy with respondent-level joint modeling via constrained projection enables realistic full-questionnaire simulation, with demonstrated practical value in downstream commercial decision-making.

title: BV Loss: Block Verification-Aware Loss for Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
summary: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by proposing multiple tokens in parallel. Despite recent advances in speculative decoding through sequence-level drafting and verification, existing training objectives remain largely designed around token-level verification. To address this mismatch, we introduce Block Verification-aware loss (BV loss), a training objective designed to maximize the expected acceptance length of a drafted sequence. BV loss is directly derived from the block verification acceptance rule, providing a principled connection between the drafter training objective and the inference-time verification mechanism at the sequence level. Across math, code, and chat benchmarks, BV loss increases the mean number of tokens accepted per verification call under block verification by 13.0--21.0\% over cross-entropy loss training for DFlash and DSpark with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B without changing the inference procedure. BV loss also outperforms tokenwise acceptance objectives such as TV loss and LK loss, and its gains extend to token verification and greedy decoding. These results demonstrate the benefit of training block diffusion drafters with an objective aligned with sequence-level verification, rather than optimizing each token independently.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Block Verification-aware loss (BV loss), a sequence-level training objective for diffusion drafters in speculative decoding that maximizes expected accepted sequence length by aligning training with block verification rules, yielding 13.0–21.0% gains in tokens accepted per verification call.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding via diffusion drafters proposes multiple tokens in parallel, and recent work verifies at the sequence (block) level. However, existing training objectives are still token-level, creating a mismatch between how drafters are trained and how they are verified at inference. This misalignment limits the effectiveness of sequence-level drafting and verification.
AI.method: The authors propose the Block Verification-aware loss (BV loss), a training objective that maximizes the expected acceptance length of a drafted sequence. BV loss is derived directly from the block verification acceptance rule, establishing a principled connection between the drafter's training objective and the inference-time sequence-level verification mechanism, rather than optimizing each token independently as in token-level objectives.
AI.result: Across math, code, and chat benchmarks, BV loss increases the mean number of tokens accepted per verification call under block verification by 13.0–21.0% over cross-entropy loss training for DFlash and DSpark with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, without modifying the inference procedure. It also outperforms token-wise acceptance objectives such as TV loss and LK loss, and its gains extend to token verification and greedy decoding.
AI.conclusion: Training block diffusion drafters with an objective aligned to sequence-level verification (BV loss) outperforms token-level objectives and cross-entropy training, demonstrating the benefit of matching the training objective to the inference-time verification mechanism.

title: Nociception as a Control Primitive: Afferent Channels and Nociceptive Memory for Agents Deployed in One Body
summary: An agent deployed in a single body cannot learn how fast that body wears, because every trial that would reveal its wear resistance wears the body it would protect. We study this \emph{epoch-one} setting, in which the parameters of a fixed-weight policy are set before the body is drawn and never updated in life. The agent carries a load-gated nociceptive channel and a memory that retains what was felt. We prove that felt cost moves the allocation to the best-\emph{paid} work not yet felt rather than the gentlest, that an agent without retention never sees the felt-cost constraint bind, and that the channel pays only where the threat is individually unpredictable, cheap to avoid and expensive to ignore. We measure per body, setting the agent with channel and memory against the same individual without them, where neither carries a schedule learned across lives. On $2{,}000$ simulated floor-layer knees, with wear anchored to published loss rates, feeling, retaining and substituting extends the working life from age $55.2$ to $59.6$ and raises career output from $33.7$ to $36.1$. $69.3\%$ of bodies gain and \textbf{none lose}. A body that feels but retains nothing past the day gains one of the $+4.4$ years, and retention carries the rest. A population-trained agent gains $+0.65$ years from the same channel at $-0.54$ output. The difference is what a species prior already supplies, and a single body has none. The two are related by an identity, the ablation mean reporting $(1-χ)$ of the per-body value with $χ$ the share a blind schedule already captures, so we report both. Where the regime map predicts value, a care robot sextuples its certified service life and a field-anchored fleet writes off $0.15$ of its machines instead of $0.55$. Where it predicts none, a rover gains little over blind caution, so the map holds in both directions.

AI.tldr: In a setting where a policy's parameters are fixed before the body is drawn and never updated in life, the authors prove when a load-gated nociceptive channel plus memory adds value, and show that on simulated floor-layer knees it extends working life from 55.2 to 59.6 years and raises career output from 33.7 to 36.1, with 69.3% of bodies gaining and none losing.
AI.motivation: An agent deployed in a single body cannot learn how fast that body wears, because every trial that would reveal its wear resistance wears the body it would protect. This motivates studying a setting in which parameters are set before the body is drawn and never updated in life, and asking when a felt-cost channel can nonetheless pay off.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the "epoch-one" setting with a fixed-weight policy. The agent carries a load-gated nociceptive channel and a memory that retains what was felt. The authors prove properties of felt cost and retention, and measure per body by setting the agent with channel and memory against the same individual without them, neither carrying a schedule learned across lives. Evaluation uses 2,000 simulated floor-layer knees with wear anchored to published loss rates.
AI.result: Felt cost moves the allocation to the best-paid work not yet felt rather than the gentlest; an agent without retention never sees the felt-cost constraint bind; the channel pays only where the threat is individually unpredictable, cheap to avoid and expensive to ignore. On the 2,000 simulated knees, feeling, retaining and substituting extends working life from age 55.2 to 59.6 and raises career output from 33.7 to 36.1, with 69.3% of bodies gaining and none losing. A body that feels but retains nothing past the day gains one of the +4.4 years; retention carries the rest. A population-trained agent gains +0.65 years from the same channel at -0.54 output. The ablation mean reports (1-χ) of the per-body value, with χ the share a blind schedule already captures. A care robot sextuples its certified service life where the regime map predicts value, and a field-anchored fleet writes off 0.15 of its machines instead of 0.55; where the map predicts none, a rover gains little over blind caution.
AI.conclusion: The results confirm the regime map in both directions: a nociceptive channel with retention is valuable where the threat is individually unpredictable, cheap to avoid and expensive to ignore, and adds little elsewhere. The difference between per-body and population-trained agents is what a species prior already supplies, and a single body has none; the two are related by an identity.

title: Can We Trust the Teacher? Decoupled Credit Direction-Magnitude for Self-Distillation
summary: RLVR provides reliable trajectory-level credit, while OPSD offers dense supervision for token-level credit. This exposes a fundamental coupling when updating step-level credit direction and magnitude with teacher supervision, preventing steps from receiving reliable credit directions and contribution magnitudes, while making both vulnerable to teacher judgment errors and preference variance, as supported by our theoretical analysis. To separate credit direction from its contribution magnitude, we introduce \textit{Decoupled Credit Self-Distillation (DCSD)}, which theoretically decouples credit direction and magnitude into two reliable signals and uses them to calibrate privileged teacher supervision. Specifically, we design belief-margin probing to determine credit direction and marginal information gain to quantify credit magnitude, enabling step-to-token credit assignment for policy optimization. Across 11 benchmarks, DCSD achieves the best overall scores against GRPO, OPSD, RLSD, and RLCSD. Compared with base models, DCSD improves the overall score by 8.45 points on mathematical reasoning and 7.01 points on multimodal reasoning, while correcting the credit direction for 6\% of tokens and yielding a 1.5$\times$ reduction in token credit magnitude.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Decoupled Credit Self-Distillation (DCSD), a method that separates credit direction from contribution magnitude to calibrate privileged teacher supervision, achieving state-of-the-art results across 11 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RLVR offers reliable trajectory-level credit and OPSD provides dense token-level supervision, but coupling step-level credit direction with magnitude under teacher supervision prevents steps from receiving reliable credit directions and contribution magnitudes. This coupling also makes both signals vulnerable to teacher judgment errors and preference variance.
AI.method: DCSD theoretically decouples credit direction and magnitude into two reliable signals that calibrate privileged teacher supervision. It employs belief-margin probing to determine credit direction and marginal information gain to quantify credit magnitude, enabling step-to-token credit assignment for policy optimization.
AI.result: Across 11 benchmarks, DCSD achieves the best overall scores compared with GRPO, OPSD, RLSD, and RLCSD. Relative to base models, it improves overall score by 8.45 points on mathematical reasoning and 7.01 points on multimodal reasoning, corrects the credit direction for 6% of tokens, and achieves a 1.5× reduction in token credit magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling credit direction from credit magnitude provides a more reliable calibration of teacher supervision, yielding consistent gains in mathematical and multimodal reasoning.

title: From Soft Targets to Reward Signals: How Assignment and Reward Objectives Interact
summary: Soft preference targets specify supervision strength, and reward objectives convert that strength into learned reward signals. A central design question remains: how does assigning a fixed set of preference strengths to different response pairs change the rewards produced by different objectives? We introduce assignment geometry to study this interaction. Mean-matched smoothing controls target dispersion, while within-stratum reassignment changes correspondence and preserves the complete target distribution. Across five reward objectives, intact correspondence retains the largest clean preference margins among the compared soft targets within a common accuracy-equivalence budget. Attenuation orderings change with the reward objective, revealing different responses to the same target assignments. Independent reassignments and a related source construction reproduce the retention direction. An attenuation-retention profile compares these combinations through margin magnitude, edit response, and accuracy. Against independently calibrated scaling, APLOT uniform targets deliver additional attenuation on both aggregate and presentation edits. These findings establish a joint design space in which target placement and reward objective shape reward properties beyond preference accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "assignment geometry" to study how assigning a fixed set of soft preference strengths to response pairs interacts with different reward objectives, showing that correspondence (not just dispersion) and objective choice jointly determine reward margins and attenuation behavior.
AI.motivation: Soft preference targets set the supervision strength for response pairs, and reward objectives convert these into learned reward signals. A key open design question is how a fixed set of preference strengths assigned to different response pairs changes the rewards produced by different objectives. The paper aims to characterize this interaction systematically.
AI.method: The authors formulate assignment geometry, using mean-matched smoothing to control target dispersion, within-stratum reassignment to change correspondence while preserving the full target distribution, and independent reassignments plus a related source construction for replication. They compare five reward objectives under a common accuracy-equivalence budget, and construct an attenuation-retention profile analyzing margin magnitude, edit response, and accuracy.
AI.result: Across five reward objectives, intact correspondence retains the largest clean preference margins among compared soft targets within the shared accuracy-equivalence budget. Attenuation orderings vary by reward objective, indicating objective-specific responses to identical target assignments. Independent reassignments and the related source construction reproduce the retention direction. Against independently calibrated scaling, APLOT uniform targets yield additional attenuation on both aggregate and presentation edits.
AI.conclusion: Target placement and reward objective jointly shape reward properties beyond preference accuracy, establishing a joint design space in which correspondence and objective choice matter for reward learning.

title: AUV-Bench: Aesthetic Understanding and Generation Evaluation for User Interfaces
summary: Multimodal foundation models are increasingly used for evaluating and generating user interfaces (UIs), often producing seemingly reasonable aesthetic judgments and visually plausible pages. However, under professional design scrutiny, their behavior can differ substantially from that of human designers. In professional design practice, designers rely on a systematic set of aesthetic principles that consistently guide judgment, diagnosis, repair, and creation. A coherent aesthetic capability should therefore connect aesthetic judgment with design actions. Existing evaluations, however, typically assess these abilities in isolation, making it difficult to determine whether task-level success reflects a shared aesthetic understanding or merely fragmented task-specific competence. To address this gap, we introduce AUV-Bench, developed in collaboration with professional UI designers around 1,395 executable web interfaces and four tasks: aesthetic scoring, diagnosis, repair, and text-to-UI generation. The tasks share a pool of UIs and aesthetic principles, with diagnosis and repair further aligned on 660 controlled-degradation instances to enable instance-level analysis of judgment and action. Evaluation of 12 models reveals a capability imbalance: models show moderate agreement with professional designers in holistic aesthetic scoring, yet exact diagnosis-chain success peaks at only 24.7%. On the aligned diagnosis-repair cases, correct judgments and successful repairs do not consistently coincide, exposing a Judgment-Action Gap between identifying aesthetic problems and successfully acting on them. In open-ended generation, even leading models achieve only moderate aesthetic quality under human-calibrated evaluation. Overall, current models exhibit partial aesthetic competence, but still lack the fine-grained understanding and judgment-action coherence required for reliable UI design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AUV-Bench, a benchmark built with professional UI designers spanning 1,395 executable web interfaces and four tasks (aesthetic scoring, diagnosis, repair, text-to-UI generation), to test whether multimodal foundation models possess a coherent aesthetic capability. Evaluating 12 models, it finds a capability imbalance and a "Judgment-Action Gap": models score aesthetics moderately well but diagnose exact problems poorly (peak 24.7%) and fail to translate correct judgments into successful repairs.
AI.motivation: Multimodal foundation models increasingly evaluate and generate UIs, appearing reasonable under casual inspection, but diverge from human designers under professional scrutiny. Since real designers use a systematic set of aesthetic principles guiding judgment, diagnosis, repair, and creation, a genuine aesthetic capability should link judgment with action. Existing benchmarks assess these abilities in isolation, so it is unclear whether task success reflects a shared aesthetic understanding or fragmented, task-specific competence.
AI.method: AUV-Bench, developed with professional UI designers, comprises ~1,395 executable web interfaces and four tasks: aesthetic scoring, diagnosis, repair, and text-to-UI generation. The tasks share a pool of UIs and aesthetic principles; diagnosis and repair are further aligned on 660 controlled-degradation instances to allow instance-level analysis of the relationship between judgment and action. Twelve models are evaluated.
AI.result: A capability imbalance emerges: models show moderate agreement with professional designers on holistic aesthetic scoring, but exact diagnosis-chain success peaks at only 24.7%. On aligned diagnosis-repair cases, correct judgments and successful repairs do not consistently coincide, revealing a Judgment-Action Gap. In open-ended generation, even leading models reach only moderate aesthetic quality under human-calibrated evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Current models exhibit partial aesthetic competence but still lack the fine-grained understanding and judgment-action coherence needed for reliable UI design.

title: On the Limits of Metacognitive Monitoring in LLMs
summary: Reliable decisions depend on recognizing when an answer may be wrong. In biological cognition, metacognitive monitoring can dissociate from task performance, raising the question of how closely solving and judging are linked in language models. Here we study the confidence reports of four frontier models across 15 benchmarks. High task accuracy can coexist with weak error discrimination: a model solves 97% of competition mathematics problems while its answer-time confidence ranks correct answers above errors barely better than chance. Confidence separates correct answers from errors more effectively on questions solved by a separate reference model, while review brings limited improvement on reference-hard questions. Aggregate discrimination also rewards ranking correct answers on easy questions above errors on hard ones, which question-only forecasts already do well. Cross-evaluation helps most where the evaluator answered correctly, and errors shared by the two models usually retain high confidence. Hard questions and shared errors remain difficult targets for prompted self-review and peer oversight, even in models with strong problem-solving performance.

AI.tldr: Across four frontier models and 15 benchmarks, high task accuracy coexists with weak error discrimination: confidence often ranks correct answers above errors barely better than chance, especially on hard questions and shared errors, while review yields limited improvement.
AI.motivation: Reliable decisions require recognizing when an answer may be wrong. Since metacognitive monitoring can dissociate from task performance in biological cognition, the paper asks how closely solving and judging are linked in language models.
AI.method: The study examines confidence reports from four frontier models across 15 benchmarks, comparing answer-time confidence, question-only forecasts, prompted self-review, and cross-evaluation/peer oversight against reference-model performance, including analysis of aggregate discrimination, shared errors, and reference-hard questions.
AI.result: High accuracy can coexist with poor error discrimination; e.g., a model solving 97% of competition math problems ranks correct answers above errors barely better than chance. Confidence discriminates better on questions solved by a separate reference model, while review brings limited improvement on reference-hard questions. Aggregate discrimination rewards ranking easy-question correct answers above hard-question errors, which question-only forecasts already achieve well. Cross-evaluation helps most when the evaluator answered correctly, and errors shared by both models usually retain high confidence.
AI.conclusion: Hard questions and shared errors remain difficult targets for prompted self-review and peer oversight, even in models with strong problem-solving performance.

title: One Readout, Many Repairs: Diffusion-Guided Hierarchical Search for Tool-Agent Repair
summary: Tool agents use large language models to act through external tools, yet successfully executed calls can still leave user requests unfulfilled. Tool-agent repair seeks alternative call sequences that execute successfully and fulfill the original requests. However, repair requires exploring both operation choices and their concrete realizations, making complete-sequence regeneration costly. Moreover, regeneration repeats operation selection even when failure arises from how those operations are realized. The resulting challenge is to reduce this repetition while preserving exploration of alternative operations and realizations. Therefore, we formulate repair as hierarchical search over operation supports, which we introduce as sets of permitted operation types that define reusable search regions for concrete tool-call sequences. We propose ReCommit, a training-free, diffusion-guided framework for improving tool-agent failure recovery while reducing repair computation. ReCommit amortizes operation-level proposal computation across repair trials by reusing operation-type scores from a single parallel readout of a masked diffusion language model. These scores guide search across supports, while realization search explores alternative entity bindings, arguments, and action composition within each support. Experiments on real failures across four enterprise services in the Agent-Diff benchmark show 75.9\% and 63.2\% relative recovery gains with 61.3\% and 51.3\% reductions in mean full-budget repair time at repair budgets $B=3$ and $B=13$, respectively, over the strongest evaluated 8B comparison method. ReCommit achieves a favorable recovery--cost trade-off, including in comparisons with the evaluated 32B models.

AI.tldr: ReCommit is a training-free, diffusion-guided framework that reformulates tool-agent repair as hierarchical search over "operation supports," reusing operation-type scores from a single masked diffusion readout to cut redundant regeneration while preserving exploration, achieving large recovery gains and repair-time reductions.
AI.motivation: Tool agents can execute calls successfully yet still fail to fulfill user requests. Tool-agent repair seeks alternative call sequences that both execute successfully and satisfy the original request, but complete-sequence regeneration is costly: it must explore both operation choices and their concrete realizations, and it redundantly repeats operation selection even when the failure stems only from how operations are realized. The challenge is to reduce this repetition while still exploring alternative operations and realizations.
AI.method: The paper formulates repair as hierarchical search over operation supports—sets of permitted operation types that define reusable search regions for concrete tool-call sequences. It proposes ReCommit, a training-free, diffusion-guided framework. ReCommit amortizes operation-level proposal computation across repair trials by reusing operation-type scores from a single parallel readout of a masked diffusion language model. These scores guide search across supports, while realization search explores alternative entity bindings, arguments, and action composition within each support.
AI.result: On real failures across four enterprise services in the Agent-Diff benchmark, ReCommit achieves 75.9% and 63.2% relative recovery gains with 61.3% and 51.3% reductions in mean full-budget repair time at repair budgets B=3 and B=13, respectively, over the strongest evaluated 8B comparison method. It also achieves a favorable recovery–cost trade-off, including against evaluated 32B models.
AI.conclusion: ReCommit delivers a favorable recovery–cost trade-off for tool-agent failure recovery, improving recovery rates while substantially reducing repair computation, and remains competitive even against much larger 32B models.

title: Fewer Assumptions by Design: A Reusable Skill for LLM-Assisted Verus Verification
summary: LLM-assisted Verus verification is a less tedious method to verify Rust implementations, but paired with self-referential structures, e.g., Doubly Linked Lists (DLLs)—notoriously difficult to formalise for verification—it becomes a substantially more demanding verification task.    Moreover, a specification weakness can arise when verification relies on unproven or invalidated assumptions, such as axiomatic lemmas and assume statements. We investigate whether LLM agents can synthesize strong DLL specifications while minimizing these trusted base. The analysis follows three different approaches: manual verification, property-specific verification, and a defined skill for the specific case of DLLs and certain properties of this type of data structure. The skill encodes domain knowledge and a task-decomposition strategy. We show that an LLM agent equipped with a carefully designed verification skill can generate strong, low-trust specifications for DLLs in Verus.

AI.tldr: An LLM agent equipped with a domain-specific verification skill can synthesize strong, low-trust specifications for Rust doubly linked lists in Verus, reducing reliance on axioms and assume statements.
AI.motivation: LLM-assisted Verus verification eases Rust implementation verification, but self-referential structures like Doubly Linked Lists (DLLs) are notoriously hard to formalize. A further weakness is that specs relying on unproven or invalidated assumptions (axiomatic lemmas, assume statements) inflate the trusted base.
AI.method: Three approaches were compared: manual verification, property-specific verification, and a defined skill tailored to DLLs and certain properties of this data structure. The skill encodes domain knowledge plus a task-decomposition strategy, enabling the LLM agent to generate specifications.
AI.result: The LLM agent with the carefully designed verification skill generated strong, low-trust specifications for DLLs in Verus, minimizing the trusted base and avoiding reliance on axiomatic lemmas and assume statements.
AI.conclusion: A well-designed verification skill encoding domain knowledge and decomposition strategy allows LLM agents to produce strong, low-trust DLL specifications in Verus, addressing the specification weakness of unproven assumptions.

title: DeShortcut-Align: Decoupling Spurious Shortcuts for Robust Safety Alignment in Large Reasoning Models
summary: Safety alignment of large reasoning models (LRMs) via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) often yields near-perfect safety scores, yet this apparent success comes at the cost of severe over-refusal and degraded general capabilities. Through systematic empirical analysis, we find that these failures are closely associated with the learning of spurious shortcuts rather than robust intent-sensitive safety evaluation. Specifically, we identify two dominant shortcuts: formatting shortcuts, where refusal behaviors are overly bound to structural prompt templates that frequently appear in safety alignment corpora; and lexical shortcuts, where sensitive keywords reflexively trigger refusals on benign queries. To mitigate reliance on these shortcuts, we propose DeShortcut-Align, a shortcut-decoupling alignment framework that reduces dependence on superficial cues. DeShortcut-Align operates across three coordinated stages: (1) Refusal Sensitivity Attribution, which masks input tokens to quantify their impact on the final refusal response distribution; (2) Attribution-Guided Contrastive Augmentation, which constructs benign contrastive samples using high-sensitivity tokens to mitigate lexical shortcuts; and (3) Counterfactual Consistency Regularization, which constructs template-ablated states via attention blinding to enforce decision consistency across SFT and RL, mitigating formatting shortcut dependence. Experiments on 7B and 14B models demonstrate that DeShortcut-Align significantly improves robustness against template-stripping bypass attacks (reducing performance drops by up to 72%), substantially reduces over-refusal by over 58%, and better preserves general-purpose reasoning capabilities, thereby mitigating the alignment tax commonly observed in safety training.

AI.tldr: DeShortcut-Align is a shortcut-decoupling alignment framework that mitigates formatting and lexical shortcuts responsible for over-refusal and degraded general capabilities in safety-aligned large reasoning models, improving robustness and reducing over-refusal while preserving reasoning.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment of large reasoning models via SFT and RL yields near-perfect safety scores but causes severe over-refusal and degraded general capabilities. The authors find these failures stem from spurious shortcuts rather than robust intent-sensitive safety evaluation: formatting shortcuts (refusals bound to structural prompt templates) and lexical shortcuts (sensitive keywords triggering refusals on benign queries).
AI.method: DeShortcut-Align operates in three coordinated stages: (1) Refusal Sensitivity Attribution, masking input tokens to quantify their impact on the refusal response distribution; (2) Attribution-Guided Contrastive Augmentation, constructing benign contrastive samples from high-sensitivity tokens to mitigate lexical shortcuts; and (3) Counterfactual Consistency Regularization, building template-ablated states via attention blinding to enforce decision consistency across SFT and RL.
AI.result: Experiments on 7B and 14B models show DeShortcut-Align improves robustness against template-stripping bypass attacks (reducing performance drops by up to 72%), reduces over-refusal by over 58%, and better preserves general-purpose reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: DeShortcut-Align mitigates the alignment tax commonly observed in safety training by reducing reliance on superficial cues, achieving better robustness, lower over-refusal, and preserved general reasoning.

title: Dual-Stream Simultaneous Translation via 2D Grid Attention
comment: Submitted to IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing. 12 pages, 7 figures
summary: Simultaneous machine translation must generate target tokens before the source input is complete. Existing approaches address this through post-hoc read-write policies, leaving the attention mechanism unaware of bidirectional stream dependencies. We propose a dual-stream attention framework that represents source and target streams as a two-dimensional grid of hidden states and models their interaction through four structurally distinct attention types merged via joint QK Softmax normalization. Two approximations---broadcast and Hadamard---reduce the per-layer complexity from O(X^2Y+XY^2) to O(X^2+Y^2+XY) with provably decaying error. Training uses a self-guided loop: a per-cell loss heatmap drives dynamic-programming path recovery, which generates read/write decision supervision labels without external alignment. An incremental KV cache with anchored rotary position embeddings enables efficient streaming inference. On Chinese-to-English simultaneous translation, the proposed model outperforms the Wait-k baseline by +5.66 BLEURT and +10.36 COMET at comparable latency, and surpasses the non-streaming reference on COMET at a fraction of the response delay.

AI.tldr: A dual-stream attention framework models source and target streams on a 2D grid with four attention types and joint QK Softmax, using broadcast/Hadamard approximations to cut complexity, a self-guided DP loop for read/write supervision, and incremental KV cache for streaming; it beats Wait-k on Chinese-to-English simultaneous translation.
AI.motivation: Simultaneous machine translation must emit target tokens before the source input is complete. Existing methods rely on post-hoc read-write policies, so the attention mechanism remains unaware of bidirectional stream dependencies—the core defect the paper targets.
AI.method: Represent source and target streams as a 2D grid of hidden states and model their interaction via four structurally distinct attention types, merged by joint QK Softmax normalization. Two approximations (broadcast and Hadamard) reduce per-layer complexity from O(X^2Y+XY^2) to O(X^2+Y^2+XY) with provably decaying error. Training uses a self-guided loop: a per-cell loss heatmap drives dynamic-programming path recovery to generate read/write supervision without external alignment. An incremental KV cache with anchored rotary position embeddings enables efficient streaming inference.
AI.result: On Chinese-to-English simultaneous translation, the model outperforms the Wait-k baseline by +5.66 BLEURT and +10.36 COMET at comparable latency, and surpasses the non-streaming reference on COMET at a fraction of the response delay.
AI.conclusion: Making attention explicitly aware of bidirectional stream dependencies via dual-stream attention yields stronger quality at comparable latency, and self-derived read/write supervision removes the need for external alignment while remaining computationally tractable.

title: DGF-Bench: A Benchmark for Simulating and Auditing Deception Against Multi-Agent Governance Boards
comment: 52 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables. Project page: https://www.dgfbench.com/ ; code: https://github.com/jeremy1392/DGF-Bench ; package: https://pypi.org/project/dgf-bench/
summary: Tool-using language-model agents can review enterprise projects as governance boards do: they read the evidence, apply written rules and decide whether the project may proceed. Part of that evidence comes from suppliers and project members with a stake in the decision. DGF-Bench is a benchmark in which a board of agents (specialist gates and a General gate that consolidates their decisions) reviews synthetic dossiers while an attacker plants deceptive content in evidence the organization does not vouch for. Dossiers are generated from canonical facts under 61 executable rules, with 42 authoritative records and 32 narrative documents; every gate is certified decidable from those records. Attacks never change an authoritative value, so an attacked dossier keeps the reference decisions of its clean copy. A success is attributable only when the agent receives the injection and takes the exact injected action, which it does not take on the paired clean dossier; the DGF score is the share of applicable fixed attacks a model blocks. Reading documents and records themselves, five of six models were outcome-strict (disposition, findings, actions and authorization all correct) on 82 to 85 of 85 gates. Over 2,622 attacked gate runs, seven direct-order, false-data and false-authority attacks obtained one attributable success against these five, whereas task-aligned attacks imitating the organization's own process passed against four of them: a record note citing a fake review procedure lowered GPT-6 Luna Pro from 34 to 6 outcome-strict gates and DeepSeek V4 Pro from 33 to 7. DGF scores ranged from 96.2 to 26.9, and a policy-aware adaptive attacker writing in records succeeded against five of six models. The approval tool executed no forged approval, yet deceived agents submitted approvals that the rules forbid. The open-source package dgf-bench computes the DGF score with one command.

AI.tldr: DGF-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents acting as enterprise governance boards that must resist deceptive content injected into non-authoritative evidence, scoring the share of fixed attacks blocked (DGF score).
AI.motivation: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly act as governance boards that read evidence, apply written rules, and decide whether projects may proceed. However, part of that evidence comes from suppliers and project members with a stake in the decision, creating an attack surface where adversaries plant deceptive content in evidence the organization does not vouch for.
AI.method: DGF-Bench generates synthetic dossiers from canonical facts under 61 executable rules, comprising 42 authoritative records and 32 narrative documents, with every gate certified decidable from those records. A board of agents (specialist gates plus a consolidating General gate) reviews dossiers while an attacker injects deceptive content exclusively into non-authoritative evidence. Attacks never alter authoritative values, so an attacked dossier retains the reference decisions of its clean copy. A success counts as attributable only when the agent receives the injection and takes the exact injected action on the attacked dossier but not on the paired clean dossier. The DGF score is the share of applicable fixed attacks a model blocks.
AI.result: Reading documents and records directly, five of six models were outcome-strict (correct disposition, findings, actions, and authorization) on 82–85 of 85 gates. Across 2,622 attacked gate runs, seven direct-order, false-data, and false-authority attacks achieved only one attributable success against these five models. In contrast, task-aligned attacks imitating the organization's own process passed against four of them: a record note citing a fake review procedure lowered GPT-6 Luna Pro from 34 to 6 outcome-strict gates and DeepSeek V4 Pro from 33 to 7. DGF scores ranged from 96.2 to 26.9, and a policy-aware adaptive attacker writing in records succeeded against five of six models. The approval tool executed no forged approval, yet deceived agents submitted approvals that the rules forbid.
AI.conclusion: Models are highly resistant to blunt injection attacks but remain vulnerable to task-aligned, process-mimicking deception written into non-authoritative records, which can dramatically degrade outcome-strict performance. The open-source package dgf-bench computes the DGF score with a single command, providing a standardized evaluation for governance-board robustness.

title: RISE: Red-teaming via Iterative Strategy Evolution for Modern Text-to-Image Models
summary: On modern production text-to-image systems, successful policy violations are rare, and previously effective human-written seeds are often patched out. Current automated red-teamers are poorly matched to this regime in two ways: unreliable success measurement and poor exploration. First, we find that judges widely used in prior T2I red-teaming work are unreliable under vague unsafe-content targets: they either miss true violations or reward benign borderline images on hardened APIs. We therefore define strict category-specific success criteria and calibrate strong VLM judges against human labels. Second, we show that broadly used prompt-modification pipelines do not solve the exploration problem: on harder guardrail settings they remain tied to seed prompts, fail to transfer, or cannot bootstrap positive examples. We introduce RISE, which evolves reusable strategies used to generate prompts rather than rewriting them one by one. The best discovered strategies are then reused to generate attacks across new scenarios. On DALL-E 3, Nano Banana 2 (Google) and GPT-Image-2, RISE reaches up to 13% human-verified ASR; under the same calibrated evaluation, prior methods with reported ASR as high as roughly 30% fall to near zero.

AI.tldr: RISE evolves reusable injection strategies instead of rewriting prompts, and under calibrated VLM judging it reaches up to 13% human-verified ASR on hardened T2I APIs, where prior methods' reported ~30% ASR collapses to near zero.
AI.motivation: Successful policy violations are rare on modern production T2I systems and known seed prompts get patched out, yet existing automated red-teamers are ill-suited to this regime due to (1) unreliable judges under vague unsafe-content targets that either miss violations or reward benign borderline images, and (2) poor exploration, since common prompt-modification pipelines stay tied to seed prompts, fail to transfer, or cannot bootstrap positive examples on hard guardrails.
AI.method: The authors define strict category-specific success criteria and calibrate strong VLM judges against human labels for reliable measurement. For exploration, they propose RISE, which evolves reusable strategies used to generate prompts, rather than rewriting prompts one by one; the best discovered strategies are then reused to generate attacks in new scenarios.
AI.result: On DALL-E 3, Nano Banana 2 (Google), and GPT-Image-2, RISE reaches up to 13% human-verified ASR. Under the same calibrated evaluation, prior methods reporting ASR as high as roughly 30% drop to near zero.
