AI.conclusion: Accurate, category-specific and human-calibrated evaluation is necessary for valid red-teaming claims on hardened T2I systems, and strategy-level evolution that yields reusable, transferable prompt-generation strategies markedly outperforms prompt-level rewriting.

title: PDEU-Bench: Benchmarking the Personalized Planning Lifecycle of Tool-Calling LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from tool-calling systems that execute isolated instructions into task-oriented agents that pursue user goals through sustained, multi-step interactions. However, existing benchmarks for personalized tool use largely assess isolated calls or reactive execution, leaving unclear whether agents can formulate, execute, and revise an explicit plan while preserving user preferences throughout long-term interaction. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{PDEU-Bench} (\textbf{P}ersonalized plan \textbf{D}efinition, plan \textbf{E}xecution, and plan \textbf{U}pdate \textbf{Bench}mark), a benchmark for evaluating the complete planning lifecycle of personalized tool-using agents. PDEU-Bench comprises 214 long-horizon interaction tasks spanning 12 everyday domains and 94 tools, with stage-specific assessments of preference adherence and plan quality. Extensive evaluations of 15 representative open-source and closed-source LLMs reveal a pronounced gap between local tool execution and dynamic planning: LLMs can often instantiate preferences in individual calls, yet struggle to construct coherent plan definition and plan update. We further evaluate mainstream personalization and memory-augmentation methods. Although these methods improve particular stages, none of the evaluated methods reliably propagates user preferences throughout the complete lifecycle, and their gains frequently fail to transfer to subsequent execution. Fine-grained error analysis further reveals that preference omissions and conflicts persist throughout the planning lifecycle, highlighting the need for future research to parameterize LLMs with preference-aware information retrieval and memory capabilities. We provide the relevant code and data in the appendix to support future research.

AI.tldr: PDEU-Bench is introduced to evaluate the full planning lifecycle (definition, execution, update) of personalized tool-using LLM agents across 214 long-horizon tasks, 12 domains, and 94 tools, revealing that current LLMs and personalization/memory methods fail to propagate user preferences across the complete lifecycle.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are shifting from isolated tool-calling to sustained, goal-oriented multi-step interaction, but existing personalized tool-use benchmarks only assess isolated calls or reactive execution. It remains unclear whether agents can formulate, execute, and revise an explicit plan while preserving user preferences over long-term interaction.
AI.method: PDEU-Bench (Personalized plan Definition, Execution, and Update Benchmark) with 214 long-horizon interaction tasks spanning 12 everyday domains and 94 tools, featuring stage-specific assessments of preference adherence and plan quality. Evaluations of 15 representative open-source and closed-source LLMs plus mainstream personalization and memory-augmentation methods, with fine-grained error analysis.
AI.result: A pronounced gap between local tool execution and dynamic planning: LLMs can instantiate preferences in individual calls but struggle to construct coherent plan definition and plan update. Personalization and memory-augmentation methods improve particular stages, yet none reliably propagates user preferences across the full lifecycle, and their gains often fail to transfer to subsequent execution. Preference omissions and conflicts persist throughout the planning lifecycle.
AI.conclusion: Current methods do not reliably maintain preference adherence across the complete planning lifecycle, underscoring the need for LLMs parameterized with preference-aware information retrieval and memory capabilities. Code and data are provided to support future research.

title: Proactive Dialogue Policy Optimization via Cognitive-State Transition
summary: Proactive dialogue requires agents to continually adapt their policies to user feedback while progressing toward task objectives over multiple turns. To move beyond imitation learning on static datasets, recent approaches use user simulators to collect interactive data for policy optimization. However, many simulators do not explicitly model the evolution of user cognition, limiting the consistency and state dependence of feedback across turns. Moreover, representing each action only by a high-level strategy label overlooks the large utterance space and cannot distinguish alternative realizations of the same strategy. To this end, we jointly design a $\textbf{Cog}$nitive User $\textbf{Sim}$ulator $\textbf{(Cog-Sim)}$ and $\textbf{C}$ognitive-$\textbf{S}$tate $\textbf{T}$ransition--Driven $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{O}$ptimization $\textbf{(CSTPO)}$. Cog-Sim maintains the user's cognitive and affective states and generates responses through constrained state transitions across turns, so feedback depends on both the realized utterance and the user's current state. CSTPO organizes each action as a hierarchical strategy--utterance representation: a high-level strategy label constrains utterance sampling, and utterances are optimized within each label. Sparse complete-branch sampling reuses shared dialogue prefixes and estimates separate strategy-level and utterance-level advantages, enabling fine-grained optimization at both levels. Across three tasks, Cog-Sim exhibits monotonic dose--response relationships and is preferred over prompt-based simulators for naturalness. CSTPO improves Qwen3-14B's performance to a level comparable to that of GPT-5.5-based planning methods.

AI.tldr: The paper jointly designs a Cognitive User Simulator (Cog-Sim) that models evolving user cognitive/affective states, and a Cognitive-State Transition-Driven Policy Optimization (CSTPO) method that treats actions hierarchically as strategy-label plus utterance and optimizes both levels via sparse complete-branch sampling.
AI.motivation: Proactive dialogue agents must adapt policies to user feedback across turns. Existing user simulators often fail to explicitly model the evolution of user cognition, limiting consistency and state-dependence of feedback. Additionally, representing actions only by high-level strategy labels ignores the large utterance space and cannot distinguish alternative realizations of the same strategy.
AI.method: Cog-Sim maintains the user's cognitive and affective states and generates responses through constrained state transitions across turns, so feedback depends on both the realized utterance and the user's current state. CSTPO organizes each action as a hierarchical strategy-utterance representation, where a high-level strategy label constrains utterance sampling and utterances are optimized within each label. Sparse complete-branch sampling reuses shared dialogue prefixes and estimates separate strategy-level and utterance-level advantages for fine-grained two-level optimization.
AI.result: Across three tasks, Cog-Sim shows monotonic dose-response relationships and is preferred over prompt-based simulators for naturalness. CSTPO improves Qwen3-14B's performance to a level comparable to GPT-5.5-based planning methods.
AI.conclusion: Modeling user cognitive state evolution and adopting hierarchical strategy-utterance action representations with two-level advantage estimation jointly enhance proactive dialogue policy optimization, yielding more natural simulated feedback and stronger agent performance.

title: VD-DeepStack: Bridging Visual Comparison and Language Reasoning for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
summary: Few-shot visual anomaly detection is fundamentally a visual comparison task, requiring fine-grained inspection of a query against normal references. Many recent methods based on large vision-language models (LVLMs) emphasize comparative reasoning through language chain-of-thought. Yet discrete, abstract descriptions may underrepresent dense, fine-grained visual differences, leaving a gap between visual comparison and its expression in language. To address this gap, we propose Visual Difference DeepStack (VD-DeepStack), which explicitly conditions language reasoning on query-reference visual differences. Specifically, we fuse DINO features with the LVLM visual hierarchy to strengthen fine-grained representations, then construct dense difference evidence from residuals between query features and softly matched reference features. The difference-evidence path injects spatially weighted difference vectors into query-image states at multiple decoder depths, while an auxiliary visual-context path provides fine-grained appearance information to support their interpretation. Experiments on 4 industrial and 2 medical anomaly benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements in few-shot anomaly detection over baselines relying on textual comparative reasoning. These results support mitigating the visual comparison-reasoning gap through the joint design of comparison representations and their integration into the decoder. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: VD-DeepStack conditions LVLM language reasoning on explicit query-reference visual difference evidence, fusing DINO features into the visual hierarchy and injecting matched residual difference vectors at multiple decoder depths, yielding substantial few-shot anomaly detection gains across industrial and medical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Few-shot visual anomaly detection is fundamentally a fine-grained visual comparison task. Recent LVLM methods rely on language chain-of-thought for comparative reasoning, but discrete abstract descriptions underrepresent dense, fine-grained visual differences, creating a gap between visual comparison and its linguistic expression.
AI.method: VD-DeepStack explicitly conditions language reasoning on query-reference visual differences. It fuses DINO features with the LVLM visual hierarchy to strengthen fine-grained representations, then builds dense difference evidence from residuals between query features and softly matched reference features. A difference-evidence path injects spatially weighted difference vectors into query-image states at multiple decoder depths, while an auxiliary visual-context path supplies fine-grained appearance information.
AI.result: Experiments on 4 industrial and 2 medical anomaly benchmarks show substantial improvements in few-shot anomaly detection over baselines relying on textual comparative reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Mitigating the visual comparison-reasoning gap via joint design of comparison representations and their decoder integration is effective. Code to be released upon acceptance.

title: AX is the New AEO
summary: In 2023, AI models answered from training data and hallucinated when it ran out, and businesses were told to seed that knowledge. Models' training knowledge has since given way to live web search, and the advice followed it there: answer-engine optimization, or AEO, now tells businesses to scatter breadcrumbs across forum threads, listicles, and off-site citations, so AI engines are likelier to surface and recommend them. But being surfaced is no longer enough: an agent opens the results and reads them before deciding, and one buyer question sends it through several rounds of search and fetch. What decides the outcome at this drill-down step is whether the agent can fetch and read the business's own site: agent experience (AX). We argue that AX is the new AEO. We run 37,927 agent journeys, each a buyer question about a business, across four independent harnesses over 1,056 real businesses, matched on fame, prior model knowledge, and two AEO proxies, then split based on their AX level. Only 7-10% of the finished answer comes from the model's training knowledge, whether or not the site is readable. Agent-ready businesses have answers built from their own pages 78% of the time against 56% and are clearly recommended 1.9x more often, while every grounded answer about a not-agent-ready business costs the agent 64% more. Holding business, harness, and question fixed, answers built from the site are 41% more accurate. The dominant failure is not fabrication but omission: web-built answers are 3.7x more likely to contain none of the facts the buyer asked for. Baselines differ sharply across the four harnesses, with clear-recommendation rates varying sevenfold from stack to stack, yet the effect holds in every one. In the agentic web era, being readable beats being talked about, and improving a site's AX is the strongest lever a business has.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that "agent experience" (AX)—whether an AI agent can fetch and read a business's own site—has become the decisive factor in the agentic web era, replacing answer-engine optimization (AEO). Across 37,927 agent journeys on 1,056 businesses, agent-ready sites yield answers built from their own pages 78% of the time (vs. 56%), are clearly recommended 1.9x more often, and produce 41% more accurate answers, with omission rather than fabrication as the dominant failure mode.
AI.motivation: AI models once answered from training data and were advised to "seed" knowledge, then shifted to live web search, which spawned AEO advice to scatter breadcrumbs across forums, listicles, and off-site citations. But being surfaced is no longer sufficient: an agent now opens results, reads them, and runs multiple rounds of search and fetch per buyer question. The paper's motivation is that the drill-down step—where the agent must fetch and read the business's own site—is what actually decides the outcome, and this AX dimension has been neglected in favor of AEO visibility tactics.
AI.method: The authors run 37,927 agent journeys, each a buyer question about a business, across four independent harnesses over 1,056 real businesses. Businesses are matched on fame, prior model knowledge, and two AEO proxies, then split by their AX level (agent-readability of their own site). The study measures how much of the finished answer derives from training knowledge vs. the site, clear-recommendation rates, accuracy, and failure-mode composition, holding business, harness, and question fixed.
AI.result: Only 7-10% of the finished answer comes from the model's training knowledge, whether or not the site is readable. Agent-ready businesses have answers built from their own pages 78% of the time versus 56%, and are clearly recommended 1.9x more often. Every grounded answer about a not-agent-ready business costs the agent 64% more. Holding business, harness, and question fixed, answers built from the site are 41% more accurate. The dominant failure is omission, not fabrication: web-built answers are 3.7x more likely to contain none of the facts the buyer asked for. Baseline clear-recommendation rates vary sevenfold across the four harnesses, yet the effect holds in every one.
AI.conclusion: In the agentic web era, being readable beats being talked about. Improving a site's AX is the strongest lever a business has, and AX is framed as the new AEO—shifting strategic priority from off-site visibility tactics toward ensuring agents can actually fetch and read the business's own site.

title: ProofLoom: Proof-Obligation-Driven Theory Construction for Autoformalizing Research-Level Stochastic Optimization
comment: 38 pages, 5 figures. Code and supplementary materials: https://github.com/Trace231/ProofLoom
summary: Formalizing research-level stochastic optimization in Lean requires both an algorithm model and domain theory connecting foundational libraries to convergence proofs. Revising a model to restore provability can change the mathematical claim. We introduce ProofLoom, a fully automated LLM-agent system for Proof-Obligation-Driven Theory Construction. Given a published algorithm, target theorem, and source proof, ProofLoom autonomously constructs the Lean model and supporting theory. Open proof obligations drive the development of definitions, interfaces, lemmas, and proof plans. Signature contracts record evidence and obligations for model revisions; an independent Judge rejects unsupported assumptions and weakened conclusions. Planner expands the published argument into intermediate claims, and Audit checks whether the Lean proof follows it. Across tasks, SOptLib accumulates verified mathematics and construction experience: reusable results are extracted, generalized, and verified, while modeling decisions and failed proof routes are recorded. Later tasks retrieve these results and records and contribute new developments, forming a cycle of construction, accumulation, and reuse. On fifteen textbook and research-paper tasks, ProofLoom obtains mean human ratings of 6.3/7 and 6.4/7, compared with 4.9/7 and 5.0/7 for the strongest of six baselines. Across 33 developments, it produces 490,693 lines of algorithm-local Lean code with no sorry. The formalizations also expose 28 incorrect formulas, proof gaps, and algorithm-analysis mismatches in published sources across 22 developments, each with checked evidence.

AI.tldr: ProofLoom is a fully automated LLM-agent system that constructs Lean formalizations of stochastic optimization algorithms from published sources, using proof obligations to drive theory development and an accumulating verified library (SOptLib) for reuse.
AI.motivation: Formalizing research-level stochastic optimization in Lean requires both an algorithm model and domain theory linking foundational libraries to convergence proofs. When a model must be revised to restore provability, the underlying mathematical claim can change, so automated support is needed to manage this tension between model fidelity and provability.
AI.method: ProofLoom takes a published algorithm, target theorem, and source proof and autonomously builds the Lean model and supporting theory. Open proof obligations drive development of definitions, interfaces, lemmas, and proof plans. Signature contracts record evidence and obligations for model revisions; an independent Judge rejects unsupported assumptions and weakened conclusions; a Planner expands the published argument into intermediate claims; and an Audit checks whether the Lean proof follows it. Results accumulate in SOptLib, where reusable results are extracted, generalized, and verified, and modeling decisions and failed routes are recorded for retrieval in later tasks.
AI.result: On fifteen textbook and research-paper tasks, ProofLoom achieves mean human ratings of 6.3/7 and 6.4/7 versus 4.9/7 and 5.0/7 for the strongest of six baselines. Across 33 developments it produces 490,693 lines of algorithm-local Lean code with no sorry, and exposes 28 incorrect formulas, proof gaps, and algorithm-analysis mismatches in published sources across 22 developments, each with checked evidence.
AI.conclusion: ProofLoom demonstrates that obligation-driven LLM-agent construction can automate research-level Lean formalization while accumulating reusable verified mathematics, forming a cycle of construction, accumulation, and reuse that also surfaces errors in published sources.

title: Safe Greenhouse Climate Control Using Lagrangian-Constrained PPO with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary: Greenhouse climate control balances economic return with maintaining temperature, humidity and CO2 within crop-adapted growth ranges. Conventional reinforcement learning (RL) greenhouse controllers use fixed reward penalties to limit climate constraint violations, yet such heuristic penalties cannot explicitly constrain long-term cumulative violations. Poorly tuned weights either lead to overly conservative policies and lower yields, or fail to suppress persistent climate deviations that harm photosynthesis and induce crop diseases. To address this issue, we formulate greenhouse climate regulation as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and use a Lagrangian safe RL framework RCPO-PPO to separate economic optimization and cumulative safety constraints, enabling adaptive penalty adjustment without manual tuning. To handle strong nonlinear, time-varying coupling between greenhouse microclimate and crop growth, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) as policy and value approximators for improved nonlinear representation. Sinusoidal cyclic time features are embedded in observations to capture diurnal environmental periodicity. Simulations use a classic winter lettuce greenhouse model driven by 40-day real weather disturbances. Compared with vanilla penalty-based PPO, our method cuts cumulative climate violations by 18.65% and raises lettuce economic profit by 2.91%, keeping violations stable near the safety threshold. This decoupled CMDP optimization with KAN-based policy representation mitigates long-term climate risks and boosts planting profits, offering a constraint-aware control strategy for precision greenhouse cultivation.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates greenhouse climate control as a Constrained Markov Decision Process and applies the RCPO-PPO safe RL framework with KAN-based policy/value networks and sinusoidal time features, cutting cumulative climate violations by 18.65% and increasing lettuce profit by 2.91% versus penalty-based PPO.
AI.motivation: Conventional RL greenhouse controllers rely on fixed heuristic reward penalties that cannot explicitly constrain long-term cumulative climate violations. Poorly tuned weights cause either overly conservative policies with lower yields or persistent climate deviations harming photosynthesis and inducing crop diseases, and manual tuning is required.
AI.method: Greenhouse climate regulation is cast as a CMDP, solved with the Lagrangian safe RL framework RCPO-PPO to decouple economic optimization from cumulative safety constraints and enable adaptive penalty adjustment. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks replace MLPs as policy and value approximators for stronger nonlinear representation of the microclimate-crop coupling, and sinusoidal cyclic time features are embedded in observations to capture diurnal periodicity.
AI.result: In simulations using a classic winter lettuce greenhouse model driven by 40-day real weather disturbances, the method reduces cumulative climate violations by 18.65% and raises lettuce economic profit by 2.91% compared with vanilla penalty-based PPO, while keeping violations stable near the safety threshold.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled CMDP optimization with KAN-based policy representation mitigates long-term climate risks and boosts planting profits, providing a constraint-aware control strategy for precision greenhouse cultivation.

title: Action-Space Shaping for LLM Agents: Measuring and Mitigating Tool-Schema Bias
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on tool-use agentic tasks when given a fixed tool schema. Yet a tool schema is not the action space of an agent; it is merely one interface representation of it. The same executable action can be exposed through many different, functionally equivalent tool definitions, and an agent that has truly learned a task should behave consistently across them. We show that current agents often do not, a phenomenon we term schema bias. To study this systematically, we introduce an executable transformation framework that rewrites a native tool schema using nine operators, including merging and splitting tools, altering how a single tool is expressed, and distributing one action across several dependent calls. The tasks, executable actions, and reachable states remain fixed, so any change in success is attributable to the interface alone. Evaluating eleven LLMs, including two closed models, on up to 32 schema variants, we ask how large schema bias is, how it manifests, whether the difficulty of a schema variant can be predicted without a full evaluation, and whether training removes it. We find that schema bias is substantial even for the newest models: success rates range from complete failure to 97% depending solely on the schema. To reliably estimate schema difficulty, it requires running a small sample of the target queries. Training repairs a schema variant only when that variant appears in the training data.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "schema bias": LLM tool-use agents' success varies drastically (from total failure to 97%) across functionally equivalent tool schema variants with identical actions and states, and training only fixes variants seen in training.
AI.motivation: LLM tool-use agents are typically evaluated with a fixed tool schema, but a schema is only one interface representation of the underlying action space. The same executable action can be exposed through many functionally equivalent definitions, and a truly task-capable agent should perform consistently across them. The authors aim to test this consistency and expose a previously unstudied failure mode.
AI.method: An executable transformation framework that rewrites a native tool schema using nine operators: merging/splitting tools, altering a single tool's expression, and distributing one action across several dependent calls. Tasks, executable actions, and reachable states are held fixed so any success change is due to interface alone. Eleven LLMs (including two closed models) are evaluated on up to 32 schema variants, addressing four questions: magnitude of schema bias, its manifestations, predictability of variant difficulty without full evaluation, and whether training removes it.
AI.result: Schema bias is substantial even for the newest models: success rates range from complete failure to 97% depending solely on the schema. Predicting schema difficulty reliably requires running a small sample of target queries. Training repairs a schema variant only when that variant appears in the training data.
AI.conclusion: Agentic tool-use capability is not schema-invariant; current LLM agents overfit to specific interface representations rather than the underlying action space. Robust evaluation must account for schema variation, and generalization to unseen schema variants does not emerge from training.

title: APEX-Voice: Can Voice Agents Complete Professional Workflows Through Full-Duplex Interaction
summary: Full-duplex voice agents can now listen, speak, use tools, and act during spoken interactions, but fluent dialogue does not guarantee correct completion of delegated professional workflows. We introduce APEX-Voice, a benchmark of 120 interactive professional workflows spanning ten work archetypes such as form completion, corporate negotiation, coordination, consulting, and interviewing. Each workflow executes in a stateful Voice Workbench environment with task-specific knowledge, typed tools, gold-annotated final work artifact, authorization constraints, and a user simulation policy backed by validated, pre-compiled speech realizations. We evaluate both artifact field accuracy and end-to-end workflow success, which requires the correct terminal state, valid process, completed actions, and a valid final artifact. Across five frontier real-time voice agents-GPT-Live-1, Gemini-3.8-Live, Grok-Voice-Think-2.0, Step-Audio3, and GPT-realtime-2.1, none exceeds 25% Pass@1, and the best Reliable@3 is only 10.8%. Moreover, stateful coordination is the dominant failure point across systems, while success decreases further on workflows requiring greater knowledge retrieval and mid-speech corrections. Overall, APEX-Voice is the first benchmark for evaluating whether voice agents can translate conversational competence into dependable professional work.

AI.tldr: APEX-Voice is a new benchmark of 120 interactive professional voice workflows across ten work archetypes, evaluated in a stateful Voice Workbench environment. Testing five frontier real-time voice agents on artifact accuracy and end-to-end success, none exceed 25% Pass@1 and the best Reliable@3 is only 10.8%, with stateful coordination the dominant failure mode.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex voice agents can converse fluently, but fluent dialogue does not guarantee correct completion of delegated professional workflows. Existing evaluation gaps leave unclear whether voice agents can translate conversational competence into dependable professional work, motivating a dedicated benchmark.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark of 120 interactive professional workflows spanning ten work archetypes (form completion, corporate negotiation, coordination, consulting, interviewing, etc.). Each workflow runs in a stateful Voice Workbench with task-specific knowledge, typed tools, a gold-annotated final work artifact, authorization constraints, and a user simulation policy backed by validated, pre-compiled speech realizations. Evaluation covers both artifact field accuracy and end-to-end workflow success, requiring correct terminal state, valid process, completed actions, and a valid final artifact.
AI.result: Across five frontier real-time voice agents (GPT-Live-1, Gemini-3.8-Live, Grok-Voice-Think-2.0, Step-Audio3, GPT-realtime-2.1), none exceeds 25% Pass@1, and the best Reliable@3 is only 10.8%. Stateful coordination is the dominant failure point across systems, and success drops further on workflows needing greater knowledge retrieval and mid-speech corrections.
AI.conclusion: APEX-Voice is positioned as the first benchmark for evaluating whether voice agents can translate conversational competence into dependable professional work, revealing substantial headroom for stateful, workflow-grounded voice agent performance.

title: Before Acting, Change the State: Prospective State Intervention for Web Agents under Deceptive Interfaces
summary: LLM-based Web agents can autonomously complete user tasks, yet deceptive interfaces can steer them toward outcomes that conflict with users' interests. Existing defenses primarily intervene on agent behavior through blocking, guidance, or replanning. We identify a distinct failure mode: a task-valid action can still realize an unauthorized consequence because of the current Web state. This motivates treating task-relevant Web state itself as a runtime control target. We introduce Veer, an agent-side runtime defense that leaves task planning to the base agent and intervenes on Web state when a proposed action would produce an unauthorized consequence. Before modifying the live environment, Veer constructs a prospective intervention trajectory toward a safe task-relevant state and executes it with runtime grounding and verification. Across TrickyArena and WebDecept, Veer achieves the highest safe task completion in all three evaluation settings, exceeding the next-best defense by 15.9 and 25.0 percentage points on TrickyArena-Single and TrickyArena-Multi, respectively, while reducing dark-pattern success on WebDecept to 0.3%. These gains persist across dark-pattern types and all 12 agent, model, and benchmark configurations. Ablations show that active state intervention provides the largest gain, while prospective rollout and temporal evidence contribute additional improvements. These results establish task-relevant Web state as an effective runtime control target for protecting Web agents from deceptive outcomes.

AI.tldr: Veer is an agent-side runtime defense that treats task-relevant Web state as a control target, intervening on the environment when an action would cause an unauthorized consequence; it achieves top safe task completion and near-zero dark-pattern success across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Web agents can autonomously complete user tasks, but deceptive interfaces can steer them toward outcomes conflicting with users' interests. Existing defenses intervene on agent behavior via blocking, guidance, or replanning. The authors identify a distinct failure mode: a task-valid action can still realize an unauthorized consequence due to the current Web state, motivating treatment of task-relevant Web state itself as a runtime control target.
AI.method: Veer is an agent-side runtime defense that leaves task planning to the base agent and intervenes on Web state when a proposed action would produce an unauthorized consequence. Before modifying the live environment, it constructs a prospective intervention trajectory toward a safe task-relevant state and executes it with runtime grounding and verification.
AI.result: Across TrickyArena and WebDecept, Veer achieves the highest safe task completion in all three evaluation settings, exceeding the next-best defense by 15.9 and 25.0 percentage points on TrickyArena-Single and TrickyArena-Multi, respectively, while reducing dark-pattern success on WebDecept to 0.3%. Gains persist across dark-pattern types and all 12 agent, model, and benchmark configurations. Ablations show active state intervention provides the largest gain, while prospective rollout and temporal evidence contribute additional improvements.
AI.conclusion: These results establish task-relevant Web state as an effective runtime control target for protecting Web agents from deceptive outcomes.

title: From One-Shot Generation to Incremental Music Composition: Adapting a General-Purpose Instruction LLM for Persistent Symbolic Editing
summary: Most music-generation systems are still framed and evaluated primarily as producers of complete outputs, whereas composition often proceeds through successive revisions to a shared musical artifact. This paper studies a different use of a general-purpose instruction-following large language model: not as a one-shot music generator, but as a reusable operator over an evolving symbolic score. We formulate incremental composition as a sequence of operation-aware state transitions over persistent ABC notation, with explicit requirements on what each operation may change and what it must preserve. The interaction includes two artifact-initialization variants and three editing operations -- chord addition, inpainting, and transposition. We instantiate the formulation by adapting Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on 496,038 operation-aware dialogue records derived from Irish traditional music. The comparison with the unadapted model is used to test the feasibility of learning this interaction contract, not to claim novelty for fine-tuning itself. Across 500 dialogues per model (1,750 attempted output states), checker admission rises from 29.37% to 99.37%, while compliance conditional on admission rises from 0.7205 to 0.9798. Strict eligibility for reference-relative musical-feature analysis increases from 14 to 1,548 outputs, and Longest Common Subsequence analysis does not show a systematic increase in high-overlap sequences relative to held-out baselines under the specified protocol. The results support the technical feasibility of persistent, operation-aware symbolic editing with a general-purpose instruction LLM. They do not establish superior musical quality or human-AI co-creativity, which remain questions for musician-centered evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes symbolic music generation as incremental, operation-aware editing of a persistent ABC score using a general-purpose instruction LLM (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct + LoRA), rather than one-shot generation.
AI.motivation: Most music-generation systems are framed and evaluated as producers of complete outputs, yet real composition proceeds through successive revisions to a shared musical artifact. The authors aim to study a different LLM use case: a reusable operator over an evolving symbolic score, treating incremental composition as operation-aware state transitions with explicit change/preservation contracts.
AI.method: Incremental composition is formulated as a sequence of operation-aware state transitions over persistent ABC notation, with requirements on what each operation may change and must preserve. The interaction includes two artifact-initialization variants and three editing operations: chord addition, inpainting, and transposition. The formulation is instantiated by adapting Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on 496,038 operation-aware dialogue records derived from Irish traditional music. Comparison with the unadapted model tests feasibility of learning the interaction contract, not novelty of fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across 500 dialogues per model (1,750 attempted output states), checker admission rises from 29.37% to 99.37%, and compliance conditional on admission rises from 0.7205 to 0.9798. Strict eligibility for reference-relative musical-feature analysis increases from 14 to 1,548 outputs. Longest Common Subsequence analysis shows no systematic increase in high-overlap sequences relative to held-out baselines under the specified protocol.
AI.conclusion: The results support the technical feasibility of persistent, operation-aware symbolic editing with a general-purpose instruction LLM. They do not establish superior musical quality or human-AI co-creativity, which remain open questions for musician-centered evaluation.

title: Automated feature engineering, AutoML, and decision-focused learning for improved energy consumption forecasting
comment: PhD thesis, School of Computer Science, University of Nottingha, United Kingdom
summary: The rising cost and demand for energy, together with environmental sustainability goals, create major challenges for energy management. Energy Consumption Forecasting (ECF) supports planning by predicting future consumption, but Machine Learning (ML) models for ECF often depend on expert-driven Feature Engineering (FE). This thesis addresses that dependence through three contributions. First, it establishes and evaluates a comprehensive FE pipeline for ECF and investigates domain-specific features. Second, it introduces AutoEnergy, a domain-tailored automated FE algorithm that generates interpretable features from timestamps and lagged consumption and integrates with AutoML for end-to-end ECF modelling. Across eighteen real-world energy datasets spanning residential, commercial, industrial, renewable, and grid domains, AutoEnergy reduces forecasting error by 19.52%-84.72% relative to baseline AutoML and established automated FE methods, while running 1.31-4.41 times faster, with gains varying by dataset. Third, AutoEnergy is integrated with Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) for a Battery Energy Storage System problem, jointly forecasting electricity prices and demand while optimising charging and discharging decisions. On a real-world UK property dataset, this approach reduces operating costs by 22.9%-56.5% compared with the same DFL models without automated FE. Overall, the results show that domain-specific automated FE can reduce reliance on manual feature design, improve forecasting accuracy, and translate predictive gains into measurable operational benefits in energy management.

AI.tldr: This thesis develops a domain-tailored automated feature engineering method (AutoEnergy) for energy consumption forecasting and decision-focused battery storage optimization, reducing forecasting error by 19.52%–84.72% and operating costs by 22.9%–56.5%.
AI.motivation: Rising energy costs, demand, and sustainability goals pose major energy management challenges. Energy Consumption Forecasting (ECF) supports planning, but ML models for ECF typically rely on expert-driven Feature Engineering (FE), which is labor-intensive and a barrier to scalable, accurate forecasting.
AI.method: The thesis makes three contributions: (1) establishing and evaluating a comprehensive FE pipeline for ECF and investigating domain-specific features; (2) introducing AutoEnergy, a domain-tailored automated FE algorithm that generates interpretable features from timestamps and lagged consumption and integrates with AutoML for end-to-end ECF modelling; and (3) integrating AutoEnergy with Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) for a Battery Energy Storage System problem, jointly forecasting electricity prices and demand while optimizing charging and discharging decisions.
AI.result: Across eighteen real-world energy datasets spanning residential, commercial, industrial, renewable, and grid domains, AutoEnergy reduces forecasting error by 19.52%–84.72% relative to baseline AutoML and established automated FE methods, while running 1.31–4.41 times faster, with gains varying by dataset. On a real-world UK property dataset, the DFL-integrated approach reduces operating costs by 22.9%–56.5% compared with the same DFL models without automated FE.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific automated FE can reduce reliance on manual feature design, improve forecasting accuracy, and translate predictive gains into measurable operational benefits in energy management.

title: TermJudge: A Document-Level Metric Judging, Not Counting, Terminology in Machine Translation Evaluation
summary: Existing automatic metrics for evaluating terminological use in machine translation (MT) penalise any divergence from a fixed reference, conflating translation errors with the valid terminological variation that human translators routinely produce. We introduce TermJudge, a document-level terminology metric that assigns an interpretable verdict to every term occurrence: glossary-conforming occurrences are settled deterministically, while divergences are assessed under a two-step LLM-as-judge procedure using the full document context: the first detects and labels terminology errors; the second sorts valid document-level variations from inconsistencies. Validated against expert error annotations and document-level human MQM scores, TermJudge ranks first in both system- and segment-level meta-evaluation, ahead of glossary-conformity and quality-estimation baselines. When applied to eight systems translating academic documents, under two prompting conditions, we observe that glossary injection improves terminology translation in all paired comparisons, by removing genuine errors rather than valid variation. TermJudge is released as open-source code.

AI.tldr: TermJudge is a document-level LLM-as-judge terminology metric that distinguishes genuine terminology errors from valid terminological variation, outperforming glossary-conformity and quality-estimation baselines and revealing that glossary injection reduces errors without suppressing valid variation.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic metrics for terminological use in MT penalize any divergence from a fixed reference, conflating actual translation errors with legitimate terminological variation that human translators routinely produce. This limits their validity as evaluation tools.
AI.method: TermJudge assigns an interpretable verdict per term occurrence. Glossary-conforming occurrences are settled deterministically, while divergences are assessed via a two-step LLM-as-judge procedure using full document context: first detecting and labeling terminology errors, then separating valid document-level variations from inconsistencies.
AI.result: Validated against expert error annotations and document-level human MQM scores, TermJudge ranks first in both system- and segment-level meta-evaluation, ahead of glossary-conformity and quality-estimation baselines. Applied to eight systems translating academic documents under two prompting conditions, glossary injection improves terminology translation in all paired comparisons by removing genuine errors rather than valid variation.
AI.conclusion: TermJudge provides a context-aware, interpretable terminology metric that separates errors from valid variation and demonstrates that glossary injection improves terminology accuracy without penalizing legitimate variation. It is released as open-source code.

title: Environmental requirements for the use of social information by artificial life agents using evolved plastic artificial neural networks
summary: Evolved Plastic Artificial Neural Networks (EPANNs) consist of two principal processes, the first, evolution, and the second, development and in-life learning. In the context of the origins of social = learning, very few studies have been carried out using ALIFE models based on EPANN requirements. Studies in this field have usually involved an imitative teacher/pupil relationship. This, however, ignores the possibility that the observed behaviour is a consequence of social information cues rather than direct imitation or teaching. Starting with the first of the EPANN processes (evolution), a series of experiments was undertaken using artificial neural network (ANN) based agents in a variety of foraging environments to examine under what minimal environmental conditions the use of social information might have evolved, as measured by the number of generations taken to meet a specified fitness criterion. NEAT (Neuroevolution of Augmenting Topologies) was the ANN used as its evolutionary algorithm would evolve a network's topology as well its weights. Unintentionally, in the experiment there was a simple network topology based on the location of the nearest food item which enabled agents to swiftly meet the fitness criterion. With this topology, additional information, social or otherwise, was not required and could have proved to be a hindrance. However, this does indicate that for the use of social information to have evolved, it would require a greater degree of complexity in the environment to do so.

AI.tldr: Evolved Plastic Artificial Neural Networks (EPANNs) comprise evolution plus development/in-life learning. Prior social-learning studies using ALIFE/EPANN models typically assume imitative teacher–pupil relationships, overlooking social information cues. Using NEAT-based ANN agents in foraging environments, the author tested minimal conditions under which social information use could evolve (measured by generations to reach a fitness criterion). A simple topology based on nearest-food location sufficed, so extra social information was unnecessary and potentially detrimental, implying social information use would require greater environmental complexity to evolve.
AI.motivation: Studies on the origins of social learning in ALIFE models based on EPANN requirements are scarce, and existing ones usually rely on an imitative teacher/pupil relationship. This overlooks the possibility that observed behavior stems from social information cues rather than direct imitation or teaching.
AI.method: Focusing on the first EPANN process (evolution), a series of experiments used ANN-based agents in various foraging environments to examine under what minimal environmental conditions social information use might have evolved. NEAT (Neuroevolution of Augmenting Topologies) was employed because its evolutionary algorithm evolves network topology as well as weights. Fitness was measured by the number of generations needed to meet a specified criterion.
AI.result: Unintentionally, a simple network topology based on the location of the nearest food item allowed agents to meet the fitness criterion swiftly. With this topology, additional information, social or otherwise, was not required and could even have been a hindrance.
AI.conclusion: For the use of social information to have evolved, a greater degree of complexity in the environment would be required.

title: AutoDataBench: Can Agents Write the Data That Feeds the Self-Improvement Loop?
summary: Recent gains in language model capability have come more from data than from architecture. Frontier labs and data companies produce verifiable agentic tasks, which supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning then turn into capability.This production line still rests on human labour and on human-in-the-loop collaboration. Automating task creation would let data production scale with compute rather than with expert headcount, would extend to more domains, and would enable a key step in recursive self-improvement (RSI). Current evaluations of an agent's ability to write such tasks measure how a model performs after training on what the agent produced. That does not match common practice in the data industry, where data is delivered sample by sample and each sample is accepted against a set of criteria rather than put straight into training. No existing evaluation asks whether an individual task meets the acceptance criteria of a data pipeline. We therefore introduce AutoDataBench. Given an original benchmark task and a record of the target model attempting it, an agent must write a new task for the same suite that meets practical acceptance standards on validity, novelty, difficulty and behavioural coverage. Across three benchmarks of executable agent tasks, no agent we evaluate scores above 20 out of 100 at the default time budget of 45 minutes. Giving the strongest agent four times as long improves its score substantially, while the cost of one usable task stays almost unchanged. Current agents can write training tasks of the required quality, but not efficiently. AutoDataBench provides a direct measure of an agent's capacity for autonomous data synthesis: one artifact at a time, judged against the criteria a production pipeline would apply, and without a training run. Code and data are available at https://github.com/StarDewXXX/AutoDataBench.

AI.tldr: AutoDataBench is introduced as an evaluation that asks whether an agent can synthesize individual agentic training tasks that meet production data-pipeline acceptance criteria (validity, novelty, difficulty, behavioural coverage), rather than whether training on an agent's output improves downstream performance. Across three executable agent-task benchmarks, no evaluated agent exceeds 20/100 at a 45-minute budget; quadrupling the strongest agent's time markedly improves its score while cost per usable task stays roughly constant, indicating agents can produce required-quality data but not efficiently.
AI.motivation: Recent language-model progress derives more from data than architecture: frontier labs and data companies generate verifiable agentic tasks, which SFT and RL convert into capability. This pipeline still depends on human labour and human-in-the-loop collaboration. Automating task creation would let data production scale with compute rather than expert headcount, extend to more domains, and enable a step toward recursive self-improvement. However, existing evaluations of an agent's ability to write such tasks measure downstream performance after training on agent-produced data. That mismatches industry practice, where data is delivered sample by sample and each sample is accepted against criteria rather than fed directly into training. No existing evaluation asks whether an individual task satisfies a data pipeline's acceptance criteria.
AI.method: AutoDataBench is a benchmark for autonomous data synthesis that evaluates task-writing ability at the level of individual artifacts. Given an original benchmark task and a record of a target model attempting it, an agent must write a new task for the same suite that meets practical acceptance standards on four axes: validity, novelty, difficulty, and behavioural coverage. Evaluation is performed per sample against production-style acceptance criteria, without any training run.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks of executable agent tasks, no evaluated agent scores above 20 out of 100 at the default 45-minute time budget. Granting the strongest agent four times as long substantially improves its score, while the cost of one usable task remains almost unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Current agents can write training tasks of the required quality, but not efficiently. AutoDataBench directly measures an agent's capacity for autonomous data synthesis—one artifact at a time, judged against production-pipeline criteria, and without a training run. Code and data are available at https://github.com/StarDewXXX/AutoDataBench.

title: WebPageBench: Event-Level Verification and Controlled UI-Variant Generation for Web Agents
summary: We present WebPageBench, an open framework for evaluating web agents in which every task is verified from the interface's own event log. Six instrumented mock sites with brand identifiers removed (a marketplace, a bookstore, a grocery service, rail ticketing, hotel search and a document cabinet) emit typed events with parameters as a user or an agent acts. A task declares the events it requires, and success is decided by matching them, with no judge model and no scraping of rendered pages. The same instrumentation supports controlled UI variation: one configuration switch re-renders a task through a different implementation of a single control while the prompt and the success conditions stay completely identical, so sensitivity to interface form can be measured under a fixed task specification. The WebPageBench release consists of three components: 152 tasks, divided into 65 canonical scenarios and 87 control variants across light/dark UI-modes; a common runner evaluated with six browser/DOM harness configurations and five screenshot-only GUI-agent families; and a public leaderboard of 24 model-harness pairs. On the public 152-task leaderboard the gap between what agents declare finished and what the log confirms reaches 41 points (one configuration declares every task finished and satisfies the conditions on 59%).

title: Persona Following Is Not Selective Control: The Neutrality Gap in LLM User Simulation
summary: Persona prompting is widely used to construct user simulations with large language models (LLMs), yet it relies on a largely untested assumption: specifying one user attribute should change that attribute alone. We test this assumption and identify a systematic failure of selective control: across all eight black-box LLMs we audit, changing a target attribute also shifts responses on unspecified, non-target attributes. For example, describing a user as more risk-seeking shifts color choices, even though the prompt never mentions color; we term this cross-attribute influence. Semantic, contextual, and internal analyses collectively suggest that models treat a persona prompt as evidence about the user and extend the inferred profile to unspecified preferences, a process we call trait-conditioned completion. We next ask whether explicitly specifying non-target attributes restores selective control. When a non-target attribute is assigned a clear direction, models generally follow the declaration and suppress the target attribute's influence. However, when the same attribute is declared neutral, the target continues to affect choices across all five open-weight checkpoints, even when the model correctly reports the declared state. This disparity, the neutrality gap, demonstrates that successful persona following does not imply selective persona control, which additionally requires keeping non-target attributes stable. We operationalize this distinction with a three-state diagnostic that leaves the non-target attribute unspecified or declares it directional or neutral; because directional tests can be passed by simply following the stated persona, the neutral state reveals failures they miss. In a post hoc analysis of independent items, neutral declarations leave 51-81% of items target-sensitive, against at most 1 of 320 item-pole comparisons under directional ones.

AI.tldr: Persona prompting in LLMs fails to provide selective control: changing a target attribute also shifts responses on unspecified non-target attributes ("cross-attribute influence"), and neutral declarations of non-target attributes fail to suppress this influence ("neutrality gap"), requiring a three-state diagnostic to detect.
AI.motivation: Persona prompting is widely used for LLM-based user simulation under an untested assumption: that specifying one user attribute changes only that attribute. The paper tests whether this assumption of selective control actually holds.
AI.method: The authors audit eight black-box LLMs by varying a target persona attribute and measuring responses on unspecified non-target attributes, supported by semantic, contextual, and internal analyses. They then test whether explicitly specifying non-target attributes restores selective control, comparing directional versus neutral declarations across five open-weight checkpoints. They introduce a three-state diagnostic (unspecified / directional / neutral) and conduct a post hoc analysis of independent items.
AI.result: All eight audited LLMs exhibit cross-attribute influence: changing a target attribute (e.g., risk-seeking) shifts choice behavior on unrelated attributes (e.g., color), suggesting models treat persona prompts as evidence and extend inferred profiles via "trait-conditioned completion." Directional declarations of non-target attributes largely restore control, but neutral declarations do not: the target still affects choices in all five open-weight checkpoints even when the model correctly reports the declared neutral state (the "neutrality gap"). In post hoc analysis, neutral declarations left 51-81% of items target-sensitive versus at most 1 of 320 item-pole comparisons under directional ones.
AI.conclusion: Successful persona following does not imply selective persona control, which additionally requires keeping non-target attributes stable. Directional tests can be passed merely by following the stated persona, so a neutral state is needed to expose failures. The three-state diagnostic operationalizes this distinction and reveals systematic limitations of persona prompting for controlled user simulation.

title: What Drives Citations in Production Large Language Models? An Observational Multi-Method Study of Two Million AI Citations Across Ten Thousand Web Pages
summary: Production large language models retrieve and cite web pages alongside generated answers, yet the page-level features that predict citation frequency remain poorly characterised. We present an observational study of approximately 2 million LLM citations from four commercial engines (ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI, Gemini) over six months, joined to 10,000 crawled pages from nineteen B2B SaaS workspaces. Sixty-plus features are tested using a nine-method consensus framework combining mixed-effects regression with domain fixed effects, FDR correction, stability-selection Lasso, double machine learning, generalised additive models, and temporal hold-out replication. Four findings survive all checks. First, prompt-content alignment (Jaccard overlap between page tokens and the full workspace prompt corpus, including non-citing prompts) is the dominant page-level predictor (beta = +0.37, 95% CI [+0.33, +0.41], q ~ 10^-73). Second, the standard AEO checklist (FAQ blocks, structured data, Core Web Vitals) shows positive effects in pooled data that reverse or collapse to zero once domain fixed effects are applied: Simpson's paradox with practical consequences for the AEO literature. Third, domain-level AI authority exceeds the strongest non-alignment page-level feature by a factor of six in mean absolute SHAP value. We release the analytic pipeline as a methodological contribution.

AI.tldr: An observational study of ~2M LLM citations across four commercial engines finds that prompt-content alignment is the dominant page-level predictor of citation frequency, while the standard AEO checklist reverses or vanishes under domain fixed effects (Simpson's paradox), and domain-level AI authority dominates all page-level features.
AI.motivation: Production LLMs cite web pages alongside generated answers, but the page-level features that predict citation frequency are poorly characterised, leaving practitioners and the AEO (answer engine optimisation) literature without validated guidance.
AI.method: ~2M LLM citations from four commercial engines (ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI, Gemini) over six months, joined to 10,000 crawled pages from nineteen B2B SaaS workspaces. Sixty-plus features tested via a nine-method consensus framework: mixed-effects regression with domain fixed effects, FDR correction, stability-selection Lasso, double machine learning, generalised additive models, and temporal hold-out replication. SHAP used for feature-importance comparison.
AI.result: Four findings survive all checks. (1) Prompt-content alignment (Jaccard overlap between page tokens and the full workspace prompt corpus, including non-citing prompts) is the dominant page-level predictor (beta = +0.37, 95% CI [+0.33, +0.41], q ~ 10^-73). (2) The standard AEO checklist (FAQ blocks, structured data, Core Web Vitals) shows positive pooled effects that reverse or collapse to zero under domain fixed effects — a Simpson's paradox. (3) Domain-level AI authority exceeds the strongest non-alignment page-level feature by a factor of six in mean absolute SHAP value.
AI.conclusion: Page-level AEO tactics are largely confounded by domain effects, and prompt-content alignment plus domain-level AI authority are the robust drivers of LLM citation. The authors release the analytic pipeline as a methodological contribution.

title: When Valid Tool Calls Change Meaning: Formation-Consistent Dispatch for LLM Agents
summary: Tool-enabled agents form calls from model-visible interfaces, while hosts later select their implementation. Standard dispatch omits the descriptor-handler relation. An unchanged and schema-valid call can therefore acquire a different security effect during rollout, reconnect, or delayed approval. We call this failure schema-epoch drift. We present formation-consistent dispatch (FCD), which connects implementation analysis to execution authority. Reviewed profiles produce provenance-bound over-approximations of declared in-scope effects from official source. Under a closed-target approval policy, a verifier applies each formed call to a summary and captures a successor only when its effects fit the call's security contract. Atomic admission and a final-hop fence preserve this decision to the effect. The exact source retains priority, and the captured successor becomes eligible only after source retirement. Stock releases and deployment changes reproduced the failure. Four profiles covered 32 official releases: 29 required no release-specific change and three escalated. A frozen 16-release expansion matched a separate source oracle. In a preregistered stock comparison, FCD completed all three pending calls whose effect remained private and blocked all three whose omission became public. Exact pinning and release-wide denial stopped all six calls, while release-wide approval completed all six but produced three public effects. A separate lifecycle experiment carried a formation-captured certificate across source retirement. The same safe certificate installed later governed new formations without expanding the pending call's authority.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "schema-epoch drift," a security failure where unchanged, schema-valid tool calls acquire different security effects because standard dispatch omits the descriptor-to-implementation relation. It proposes formation-consistent dispatch (FCD), which binds implementation analysis to execution authority via provenance-bound profiles, a summary-based verifier under closed-target approval, and atomic admission with a final-hop fence. FCD resolved all pending calls correctly in a preregistered stock comparison, whereas pinning, release-wide denial, and release-wide approval all failed.
AI.motivation: Tool-enabled agents form calls from model-visible interfaces, but hosts select the implementation later. Standard dispatch decouples the descriptor from its handler, so an unchanged, schema-valid call can acquire a different security effect during rollout, reconnect, or delayed approval. This gap between declared interface and actual effect is unaddressed by existing dispatch mechanisms, motivating a dispatch scheme that keeps security analysis consistent with the implementation ultimately executed.
AI.method: Formation-consistent dispatch (FCD) links implementation analysis to execution authority. Reviewed profiles generate provenance-bound over-approximations of declared in-scope effects from official source. Under a closed-target approval policy, a verifier applies each formed call to a summary and captures a successor only when its effects fit the call's security contract. Atomic admission and a final-hop fence preserve this decision through to the effect. The exact source retains priority, and the captured successor becomes eligible only after source retirement.
AI.result: Stock releases and deployment changes reproduced the failure. Four profiles covered 32 official releases: 29 required no release-specific change and three escalated. A frozen 16-release expansion matched a separate source oracle. In a preregistered stock comparison, FCD completed all three pending calls whose effect remained private and blocked all three whose omission became public. Exact pinning and release-wide denial stopped all six calls, while release-wide approval completed all six but produced three public effects. A separate lifecycle experiment carried a formation-captured certificate across source retirement, and the same safe certificate installed later governed new formations without expanding the pending call's authority.
AI.conclusion: FCD closes the descriptor-handler gap that enables schema-epoch drift, delivering correct, effect-preserving decisions where pinning, blanket denial, and blanket approval fail. Its decision is durable across source retirement and preserves existing authority boundaries, indicating that binding implementation analysis to execution authority is necessary for safe dispatch of tool-enabled agents.

title: Can Generative AI Automate Data Extraction for Meta-Analysis? A Case Study on Intercropping Research
summary: Meta-analysis is the synthesis of information from multiple sources to arrive at an overarching conclusion. There is a large need for meta-analysis in agricultural research to synthesize what is known and analyze overarching patterns. Extracting data from published literature is, however, labor-intensive, time-consuming, and tedious, and is impeded by a lack of standardization in research design, units of measurement, and terminology. These challenges are particularly evident in the domain of crop species mixtures, also called intercropping. With the growing capabilities of LLMs, many recent attempts have focused on building systems and tools to automate data collection, yet rigorous assessment against human-labeled ground truth is often missing. In this research, we evaluate three LLM-based approaches---direct zero-shot prompting, a staged workflow, and a multi-agent system---with six open-weight models to extract data from the intercropping literature. The results are evaluated against the manually curated ground truth and through a downstream statistical analysis. Overall, direct zero-shot prompting is the strongest and most consistent approach, achieving the highest mean similarity-adjusted F1 of 0.577, although none of the approaches is close to fully accurate. In the downstream analysis, most model--approach combinations recover the direction of the relationship between the predictor and outcome variables, but do not estimate its magnitude accurately.

AI.tldr: This work compares three LLM-based approaches (direct zero-shot prompting, a staged workflow, and a multi-agent system) across six open-weight models for extracting data from intercropping literature, validating against human-curated ground truth and downstream statistics. Direct zero-shot prompting performed best with a mean similarity-adjusted F1 of 0.577, though no approach was fully accurate; downstream, most combinations recovered the direction but not the magnitude of predictor-outcome relationships.
AI.motivation: Meta-analysis is valuable in agricultural research for synthesizing knowledge and identifying overarching patterns, but extracting data from published literature is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and impeded by non-standardized research design, measurement units, and terminology—challenges especially acute in crop species mixtures (intercropping). Despite growing LLM-based efforts to automate data collection, rigorous evaluation against human-labeled ground truth is often absent.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three LLM-based approaches—direct zero-shot prompting, a staged workflow, and a multi-agent system—using six open-weight models to extract data from the intercropping literature. Performance is assessed against a manually curated ground truth and through a downstream statistical analysis.
AI.result: Direct zero-shot prompting proved the strongest and most consistent approach, achieving the highest mean similarity-adjusted F1 of 0.577, though none of the approaches approached full accuracy. In downstream analysis, most model–approach combinations recovered the direction of the predictor–outcome relationship but failed to estimate its magnitude accurately.
AI.conclusion: Direct zero-shot prompting outperforms more complex staged and multi-agent pipelines for intercropping data extraction, and current LLM approaches remain insufficient for fully accurate meta-analytic data extraction, particularly for quantitative magnitude estimation, underscoring the need for continued methodological improvement.

title: DoAtlas-2: A Foundation for Self-Evolving Causal Biomedical Discovery
comment: Technical report. 185 pages, 5 figures. Yulong Li, Rong Xia and Yuxuan Zhang contributed equally. Corresponding authors: Eran Segal, Imran Razzak
summary: We introduce DoAtlas-2, a foundation for self-evolving causal biomedical discovery that organizes knowledge around causal mechanisms and advances through external evidence from human populations. DoAtlas-2 integrates 771 research resources covering more than 720,000 participants in 48 countries, from longitudinal clinical phenotypes, medical imaging, and continuous physiological signals to eight molecular layers, together with an evidence network of approximately 4.7 million literature-derived records over 93,566 concepts and 149,383 candidate causal relations. DoAtlas-2 autonomously formulates research questions from evidence gaps and unresolved mechanisms, prespecifies their causal designs, and generates validated analyses. Supporting, challenging, and unresolved results continuously revise mechanistic interpretations, the causal evidence state, and the discovery frontier, so that DoAtlas-2 self-evolves within a closed loop of hypothesis generation, empirical testing, and renewed discovery. DoAtlas-2 has systematically evaluated 2,031 research questions. In the Human Phenotype Project (HPP), it formulated 4,014 candidate pathway questions across vascular, early-glycemic, and hepatic-metabolic systems, and screening of the first 1,079 yielded statistical support for 756. Representative studies identify blood pressure as a convergence node linking adiposity, hepatic, and lipid phenotypes to vascular outcomes, and show that an adiposity-inflammation-blood-pressure pathway is largely attenuated by joint adjustment for body mass index (BMI) and smoking. The discovered vascular network constitutes a completely interpretable predictive foundation, admitting exact attribution of every prediction and closed-form mediation effects. DoAtlas-2 thereby unifies causal mechanism discovery, population-evidence testing, and interpretable prediction within one continuously evolving foundation.

AI.tldr: DoAtlas-2 is a self-evolving biomedical discovery foundation organizing knowledge around causal mechanisms and advancing via human population evidence, integrating 771 resources (>720,000 participants, 48 countries) with a ~4.7M-record literature evidence network; it autonomously formulates and tests causal research questions in a closed loop, evaluating 2,031 questions and supporting 756 of the first 1,079 HPP pathway questions, while enabling fully interpretable prediction.
AI.motivation: Biomedical discovery is fragmented across siloed data resources and literature, and causal mechanisms are rarely tested at scale in human populations. There is a need for a foundation that unifies causal mechanism discovery, population-level evidence testing, and interpretable prediction, and that can self-evolve by closing the loop between hypothesis generation, empirical testing, and renewed discovery.
AI.method: DoAtlas-2 integrates 771 research resources covering >720,000 participants in 48 countries, spanning longitudinal clinical phenotypes, medical imaging, continuous physiological signals, and eight molecular layers, plus an evidence network of ~4.7M literature-derived records over 93,566 concepts and 149,383 candidate causal relations. It autonomously formulates research questions from evidence gaps and unresolved mechanisms, prespecifies causal designs, and generates validated analyses; supporting, challenging, and unresolved results continuously revise mechanistic interpretations, the causal evidence state, and the discovery frontier within a closed loop of hypothesis generation, empirical testing, and renewed discovery. Validation is conducted on 2,031 research questions and, in the Human Phenotype Project (HPP), on 4,014 candidate pathway questions across vascular, early-glycemic, and hepatic-metabolic systems.
AI.result: DoAtlas-2 systematically evaluated 2,031 research questions. In HPP, it formulated 4,014 candidate pathway questions and screening of the first 1,079 yielded statistical support for 756. Representative studies identify blood pressure as a convergence node linking adiposity, hepatic, and lipid phenotypes to vascular outcomes, and show that an adiposity-inflammation-blood-pressure pathway is largely attenuated by joint adjustment for BMI and smoking. The discovered vascular network forms a completely interpretable predictive foundation, admitting exact attribution of every prediction and closed-form mediation effects.
AI.conclusion: DoAtlas-2 unifies causal mechanism discovery, population-evidence testing, and interpretable prediction within one continuously evolving foundation, demonstrating that closed-loop, evidence-driven self-evolution can scale causal biomedical discovery across integrated multi-omic, phenotypic, and literature resources.

title: Using Context Is Not Enough: Test-Time Training for Personalized Reward Modeling
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models (LLMs) with human preferences, yet most pipelines learn a single reward model that overlooks individual differences in preferences. Personalized reward models (PRMs) address this by conditioning rewards on user-specific feedback, most commonly through in-context learning (ICL), where a user's historical comparisons are supplied as contextual preference pairs. However, we identify a key limitation of ICL-based PRMs: they fail to capture the preference relations conveyed by contextual pairs. To address this, we propose Preference-Aligned Test-Time Training (P-TTT), which explicitly encodes these relations into user-specific fast weights for personalized reward prediction. P-TTT introduces sequence-level update and apply operations to match the response-level granularity of preference feedback, together with a preference-aligned objective that directly uses pairwise preference relations to guide fast-weight adaptation. Notably, P-TTT is simple to implement and computationally efficient, updating fast weights within a single forward pass without inference-time backpropagation. Extensive experiments show that P-TTT more effectively captures historical preference relations and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that in-context learning (ICL) based personalized reward models (PRMs) fail to capture preference relations conveyed by contextual pairs, and proposes Preference-Aligned Test-Time Training (P-TTT), which encodes these relations into user-specific fast weights for personalized reward prediction.
AI.motivation: RLHF aligns LLMs with human preferences, but most pipelines learn a single reward model that overlooks individual differences. Personalized reward models (PRMs) address this by conditioning rewards on user-specific feedback, commonly via ICL where a user's historical comparisons are provided as contextual preference pairs. However, the authors identify a key limitation: ICL-based PRMs fail to capture the preference relations conveyed by contextual pairs.
AI.method: P-TTT explicitly encodes contextual preference relations into user-specific fast weights. It introduces sequence-level update and apply operations to match the response-level granularity of preference feedback, together with a preference-aligned objective that directly uses pairwise preference relations to guide fast-weight adaptation. The method is simple to implement and computationally efficient, updating fast weights within a single forward pass without inference-time backpropagation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that P-TTT more effectively captures historical preference relations and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.
AI.conclusion: P-TTT offers an effective and efficient solution for personalized reward modeling by encoding preference relations into fast weights at test time, overcoming the limitations of ICL-based PRMs.

title: Sol-H3: Recursive Self-Improvement for MiniMax-H3 Inference Acceleration on Sol-Engine across Cloud and Edge
summary: Video diffusion models are rapidly scaling and exhibiting enhanced generation capabilities. Among these recent advancements, MiniMax-H3 stands out as a highly capable, production-level open-source model. However, its 33-billion parameters and multi-step iterative denoising process introduce substantial computational overhead. Consequently, their practical production is hindered by generation latency in the cloud deployment like NVIDIA-GB200, alongside strict memory limits that pose further challenges at the edge device like DGX-Spark. To address these diverse hardware bottlenecks from cloud to edge device, we present a full-stack inference pipeline that integrates efficient algorithmic design with optimized operator implementations. Algorithmically, we introduce a cross-resolution two-stage generation scheduler that exploits the step-wise nature of diffusion: early low-resolution steps rapidly establish the global layout, while later high-resolution steps focus refinements of local and perceptual details. These stages are connected by a learned latent-to-latent mapping module, completely eliminating the computationally expensive VAE decode-reencode cycle for resolution transferring cross different resolutions. For operator implementation, we deploy a Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) loop that searches kernel fusions and memory layouts, evaluating latency together with numerical agreement. Together, these optimizations deliver up to 30x end-to-end speedup and 20% lower memory: a 5-second 1344x768 video with audio is generated 3.5x faster than real time on an 8xGB200 node, and in under a minute fully memory-resident on a single DGX Spark.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a full-stack inference pipeline for MiniMax-H3 video diffusion (33B params), combining a cross-resolution two-stage generation scheduler with a learned latent-to-latent mapping (avoiding VAE decode-reencode) and a Recursive Self-Improvement kernel search loop, achieving up to 30x end-to-end speedup and 20% lower memory across cloud (8xGB200) and edge (DGX Spark) deployments.
AI.motivation: MiniMax-H3 is a capable production-level open-source video diffusion model, but its 33B parameters and multi-step iterative denoising cause substantial computational overhead.
