Practical production is limited by generation latency in cloud deployment (e.g., NVIDIA GB200) and strict memory constraints at the edge (e.g., DGX Spark), creating diverse hardware bottlenecks from cloud to edge that need a unified solution.
AI.method: A full-stack inference pipeline integrating efficient algorithmic design with optimized operator implementations. Algorithmically, a cross-resolution two-stage generation scheduler exploits the step-wise nature of diffusion: early low-resolution steps establish global layout, while later high-resolution steps refine local and perceptual details; these stages are connected by a learned latent-to-latent mapping module that eliminates the expensive VAE decode-reencode cycle for resolution transfer. For operators, a Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) loop searches kernel fusions and memory layouts, evaluating latency alongside numerical agreement.
AI.result: Up to 30x end-to-end speedup and 20% lower memory. A 5-second 1344x768 video with audio is generated 3.5x faster than real time on an 8xGB200 node, and in under a minute fully memory-resident on a single DGX Spark.
AI.conclusion: The proposed full-stack inference pipeline effectively addresses diverse hardware bottlenecks from cloud to edge for the MiniMax-H3 video diffusion model, delivering substantial latency and memory improvements across both data-center and edge deployment scenarios.

title: DuplexCadence: Exact State and Execution from a Speech Model's Declared Timelines
summary: Full-duplex speech models support streaming interaction that listens and speaks at the same time. Serving them is governed by a strict, repeating deadline: conversation advances on a one-second cadence, and every second of input must be turned into a second of speech before the next second arrives. Because stages within a session run in strict sequence, per-invocation overhead cannot be batched away. Profiling reveals that the autoregressive stages of a duplex second already fit within the period, whereas the token-to-audio synthesis tail is what causes overruns. This tail stage suffers from orchestration slack where the GPU is left waiting as thousands of tiny, regular operations are issued one by one, while also wasting substantial memory by over-provisioning state at static implementation constants. Existing remedies, such as graph recording and demand-sized allocation, fail because streaming state dynamics violate their prerequisites. The root cause is that the runtime lacks the model's native clocks: the per-region counters that govern advancement rates and retention policies. We propose DuplexCadence, which explicitly declares native clocks to the runtime and derives two mutually enabling rules: demand-sized state allocation at a stable address, and exact-shape graph replay without padding. The former eliminates idle memory and stabilizes tensor pointers, while the latter removes orchestration slack without padding overhead. Evaluated on four released models across three decoder architectures with bit-for-bit identical output, DuplexCadence reaches $2.85\times$ the stock runtime's speed at $38.8\%$ lower peak memory. On the live duplex path, mean SPEAK time falls from $14\%$ over the one-second cadence to $2\%$ under it, enabling models to reliably keep up with interactive speech while markedly expanding multi-

AI.tldr: DuplexCadence exposes a model's native clocks to the runtime, enabling demand-sized state allocation at stable addresses and exact-shape graph replay without padding, achieving 2.85x speedup and 38.8% lower peak memory while cutting duplex SPEAK time from 14% over the one-second cadence to 2% under it.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex speech models must meet a strict one-second cadence: each second of input must become a second of speech before the next arrives. Stages run in strict sequence, so per-invocation overhead cannot be batched away. Profiling shows the autoregressive stages fit within the period, but the token-to-audio synthesis tail overruns due to orchestration slack (GPU idle while thousands of tiny operations are issued serially) and wasted memory from over-provisioned static state. Existing fixes (graph recording, demand-sized allocation) fail because streaming state dynamics violate their prerequisites, since the runtime lacks the model's native clocks governing advancement rates and retention.
AI.method: DuplexCadence explicitly declares native clocks (per-region counters governing advancement rates and retention policies) to the runtime and derives two mutually enabling rules: (1) demand-sized state allocation at a stable address, eliminating idle memory and stabilizing tensor pointers; and (2) exact-shape graph replay without padding, removing orchestration slack without padding overhead.
AI.result: Evaluated on four released models across three decoder architectures with bit-for-bit identical output: 2.85x the stock runtime's speed at 38.8% lower peak memory. On the live duplex path, mean SPEAK time drops from 14% over the one-second cadence to 2% under it.
AI.conclusion: Declaring native clocks to the runtime via DuplexCadence overcomes the prerequisites that defeat prior remedies, letting duplex speech models reliably keep up with interactive speech while markedly expanding multi-session serving capacity.

title: Tool Mediation Alters Refusal Mechanisms in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed with access to external tools, yet harmful tool-mediated interactions are less likely to be refused when compared to regular conversational ones. As this change in refusal behavior remains underexplored, we investigate its underlying mechanisms across a diverse set of open-weight language models. We find that information about the harmfulness of a request remains strongly encoded in the model's representations and transfers across conversational and tool-mediated inputs. Evidence from representation geometry and neuron-level analysis further indicates that the two interaction modes systematically distribute harm-related computation differently. Crucially, while conversational inputs can be refused at relatively low levels of perceived harmfulness, tool-mediated inputs remain permissive until harmfulness crosses a substantially higher effective refusal threshold. Moreover, tool-mediated refusal is also more brittle: progressively weakening the refusal computation disrupts tool-mediated refusal at lower intervention strengths than conversational refusal, even when benign capabilities remain intact. Together, our findings indicate that tool mediation does not simply reduce the internal perception of harm, but instead impacts its conversion into refusal. Overall, this suggests tool-mediated environments may intrinsically reduce robustness of models to harmful requests, and that conventional safety evaluations may not fully transfer to LLM agents.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why LLMs refuse harmful tool-mediated interactions less often than conversational ones, finding that harmfulness is still internally encoded but the threshold and computation for converting it into refusal differ between the two modes.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly operate with external tools, yet tool-mediated harmful requests are less likely to be refused than equivalent conversational ones. This gap in refusal behavior is underexplored, and conventional safety evaluations may not capture risks specific to LLM agents.
AI.method: The authors analyze refusal mechanisms across a diverse set of open-weight language models, comparing conversational and tool-mediated inputs. They use representation-level probes (showing harmfulness encoding transfers across modes), representation geometry, and neuron-level analysis, and they vary perceived harmfulness levels and intervention strengths to map effective refusal thresholds and brittleness.
AI.result: Harmfulness information remains strongly encoded and transfers across conversational and tool-mediated inputs, but the two modes distribute harm-related computation differently. Tool-mediated inputs remain permissive until harmfulness crosses a much higher effective refusal threshold, and tool-mediated refusal is more brittle—disrupted at lower intervention strengths than conversational refusal even while benign capabilities remain intact.
AI.conclusion: Tool mediation does not merely reduce internal perception of harm; it impairs the conversion of that perception into refusal. Tool-mediated environments may intrinsically reduce model robustness to harmful requests, implying conventional safety evaluations may not transfer to LLM agents.

title: From Migration to Calibration: Preserving Agent Capabilities across Models, Jurisdictions, and Scale
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures. Methodological proposal: three-layer agent calibration framework; no empirical results reported
summary: Agents need calibration when deployment conditions change: replacing a driving model, including a foundation-to-post-trained transition; crossing jurisdictions; or scaling across heterogeneous markets and sources. Interface compatibility alone does not establish capability retention or target-contract satisfaction. We formulate agent calibration as constrained behavioral adaptation across three interacting layers: information preservation, harness adaptation, and user acceptance; the layers apply to every scenario, not one-to-one to the three. The basic objective is non-degradation on prespecified capability measures while satisfying target requirements; aggregate improvement is stronger. Information calibration preserves independently validated source content still applicable to the target task. Harness calibration aligns observable artifacts at semantic checkpoints and repairs them through iteration, tool substitution, or local replanning within explicit budgets. User calibration enforces recipient-specific output contracts: templates, schemas, and section-level preferences. A global e-commerce example shows how shared standards coexist with site- and market-specific adapters and validation. We distinguish trainable policies from frozen-backbone configuration or controller optimization, and evidence verification from relative judgment and DPO/GRPO optimization. Recent harness-transfer and judge-validity studies motivate target-native execution records, separate audits of task validity and near-tie ranking, and matched target-native optimization controls. We propose held-out evaluations for model changes, cross-border adaptation, and scale, including a factorial test of source evidence and checkpoint repair and group-level reporting to prevent aggregate gains from masking local failures. This is a methodological proposal; implementation and empirical validation remain future work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes agent calibration as constrained behavioral adaptation across three interacting layers—information preservation, harness adaptation, and user acceptance—to ensure capability retention and target-contract satisfaction when deployment conditions change.
AI.motivation: Deployment conditions change through driving-model replacement (including instruction-tuned transitions), crossing jurisdictions, and scaling across heterogeneous markets and sources. Interface compatibility alone cannot establish capability retention or target-contract satisfaction, creating a need for a principled calibration framework.
AI.method: The paper formulates calibration with a non-degradation objective on prespecified capability measures while satisfying target requirements (with aggregate improvement as a stronger goal). Three layers are specified: information calibration preserves independently validated source content still applicable to the target task; harness calibration aligns observable artifacts at semantic checkpoints and repairs them via iteration, tool substitution, or local replanning within explicit budgets; user calibration enforces recipient-specific output contracts such as templates, schemas, and section-level preferences. It distinguishes trainable policies from frozen-backbone configuration or controller optimization, and evidence verification from relative judgment and preference-optimization methods, and recommends target-native execution records, separate audits of task validity and near-tie ranking, and matched target-native optimization controls.
AI.result: A global e-commerce example illustrates how shared standards can coexist with site- and market-specific adapters and validation. Proposed held-out evaluations cover model changes, cross-border adaptation, and scale, including a factorial test of source evidence and checkpoint repair plus group-level reporting to prevent aggregate gains from masking local failures.
AI.conclusion: The work is a methodological proposal; implementation and empirical validation remain future work.

title: PEARL: Adaptive Prefill-Decode Execution with Elasticity for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Multi-turn rollout dominates the cost of agentic reinforcement learning (RL). Asynchronous execution and elastic GPU resources can accelerate this stage, but adding rollout replicas yields diminishing returns while training GPUs remain idle between updates. We observe that effective resource use also depends on the prefill--decode (PD) configuration. Both the choice between colocation and disaggregation and the optimal PD ratio vary with the workload, making resource scaling and PD configuration interdependent. Exploiting this opportunity requires selecting effective configurations and realizing their benefits within transient resource-availability windows despite reconfiguration costs.
  We present PEARL, an asynchronous agentic RL system that coordinates external resource elasticity, temporary reuse of idle training GPUs, and adaptive PD execution. PEARL maintains a unified GPU--worker--role state and uses runtime profiles to predict rollout batch completion time, accounting for environment-induced reductions in decode concurrency. It selects the PD mode and ratio under the current GPU budget and translates each decision into an incremental transition plan that minimizes worker and role changes. Cost-aware switching and borrowing policies suppress transitions with insufficient expected benefit while ensuring timely return of training GPUs. Our evaluation show that PEARL achieves $2.17$--$2.79\times$ the throughput of fixed-resource ROLL across different LLMs. Compared with RLBoost+, throughput improves by up to approximately 26.9\% for Qwen3-8B and 36.3\% for Qwen3-30B-A3B.

AI.tldr: PEARL is an asynchronous agentic RL system that jointly manages resource elasticity, temporary reuse of idle training GPUs, and adaptive prefill-decode (PD) execution, achieving 2.17–2.79x the throughput of fixed-resource ROLL and up to 26.9–36.3% improvement over RLBoost+.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn rollout dominates the cost of agentic RL. Asynchronous execution and elastic GPU resources help, but adding rollout replicas yields diminishing returns while training GPUs sit idle between updates. Effective resource use also depends on the PD configuration—both the choice between colocation and disaggregation and the optimal PD ratio vary with workload—making resource scaling and PD configuration interdependent. Exploiting this requires selecting effective configurations and realizing their benefits within transient resource-availability windows despite reconfiguration costs.
AI.method: PEARL coordinates external resource elasticity, temporary reuse of idle training GPUs, and adaptive PD execution. It maintains a unified GPU–worker–role state and uses runtime profiles to predict rollout batch completion time, accounting for environment-induced reductions in decode concurrency. It selects the PD mode and ratio under the current GPU budget and translates each decision into an incremental transition plan minimizing worker and role changes. Cost-aware switching and borrowing policies suppress transitions with insufficient expected benefit while ensuring timely return of training GPUs.
AI.result: PEARL achieves 2.17–2.79x the throughput of fixed-resource ROLL across different LLMs. Compared with RLBoost+, throughput improves by up to approximately 26.9% for Qwen3-8B and 36.3% for Qwen3-30B-A3B.
AI.conclusion: Jointly coordinating resource elasticity, idle-GPU reuse, and adaptive PD configuration enables substantial agentic RL rollout throughput gains over fixed-resource and prior elastic baselines.

title: FONDANT: Strong and Best-Effort Planning via Antichains
summary: A classical solution concept in fully observable nondeterministic (FOND) planning, is the strong policy (aka winning strategy in the closely related area of reactive synthesis), i.e., such a policy ensures that the goal is reached in an adversarial environment. When strong policies are not available or there is no evidence that the environment is adversarial, one can resort to best-effort policies, which always exist, and which follow the classic decision-theoretic principle that an agent should not use a dominated strategy. A typical positional best-effort policy works as follows: from every state, it follows a strong policy if one exists from that state (such states are called ``strong-winning''), else a weak policy if one exists from that state (``weak-winning''), and else is unconstrained (``losing''). In this work, we introduce a sound and complete planner for both best-effort planning and strong planning. The algorithm that underpins the planner is quite simple: it represents certain sets of states, such as the winning regions, by their $\subseteq$-minimal elements. The algorithm returns uniform policies, i.e., it returns a policy $π_t$ that is a strong solution starting in every strong-winning state, and it returns a policy $π_w$ that is a weak solution starting in every weak-winning state, and it provides a certificate for the set of losing states. We implemented the algorithm with some simple optimizations (calling it FONDANT), and evaluated it on a benchmark set consisting of the instances that were used in the evaluation of leading strong planners PR2 and FOND-SAT, and the best-effort planner BeSyftP. On coverage, our implementation is at least as good on all domains, and outperforms on some domains; and on wall time, it is slower on small and medium-sized instances, and outperforms on larger instances.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FONDANT, a sound and complete planner for strong and best-effort planning in FOND, representing winning regions by their ⊆-minimal elements to return uniform policies plus certificates for losing states.
AI.motivation: Strong policies may not exist or the environment may not be adversarial, motivating best-effort policies that follow the decision-theoretic principle of avoiding dominated strategies. Existing planners lack a unified sound and complete approach covering strong planning, best-effort planning, and certificates for losing states.
AI.method: The planner represents certain state sets, such as winning regions, by their ⊆-minimal elements. The algorithm returns uniform policies: a policy π_t that is a strong solution from every strong-winning state, a policy π_w that is a weak solution from every weak-winning state, and a certificate for the set of losing states. The implementation, FONDANT, adds simple optimizations.
AI.result: Evaluated on benchmarks used by leading strong planners PR2 and FOND-SAT and the best-effort planner BeSyftP. On coverage, FONDANT is at least as good on all domains and outperforms on some; on wall time, it is slower on small and medium instances but outperforms on larger instances.
AI.conclusion: FONDANT provides a sound and complete planner for both best-effort and strong planning, yielding uniform policies and losing-state certificates, with competitive coverage and superior scalability on larger instances.

title: 5W1H+Which: Context-Valid Semantic Indexing with Progressive Ontology Binding
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of a proposed indexing method with falsifiable hypotheses; not empirically validated
summary: Transforming raw data into queryable knowledge requires both early extraction of reusable information and explicit types, relations, and applicability conditions for particular tasks. If indexing selects content too early around a single business schema, later tasks may be unable to use information that was omitted. If the index retains only open-ended text, however, rule-based reasoning lacks checkable premises. We propose 5W1H+Which, a semantic indexing design that separates content extraction from ontology binding. The 5W1H questions organize source-grounded content units; Which points to versioned ontology elements and records mapping relations, scope, and validation status. Time, location, system environment, and participant roles are not merely retrieval labels: together, they constrain the contexts in which facts, bindings, and rules apply. Unbound content remains searchable, while bound content enters a formal reasoning path only after premise checks. The method further distinguishes business valid time, system knowledge time, and operational traces, and uses dependency records to support binding revalidation and the maintenance of derived conclusions. A worked example of migration from an on-premises server to a cloud environment illustrates the different treatment of world-state changes, ontology-version changes, and changes in rule applicability. We formulate three groups of falsifiable hypotheses concerning cross-task evidence coverage, control of contextual misuse, and incremental update cost. The planned evaluation includes a strong typed fact-graph baseline with the same evidence, temporal information, and budget, to test whether benefits arise from 5W1H organization, deferred binding, or additional information and engineering effort. The contribution is a testable indexing mechanism, not a claim to a new universal ontology or a demonstrated performance advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes 5W1H+Which, a semantic indexing design that separates source-grounded content extraction (via 5W1H questions) from versioned ontology binding (via "Which"), constraining applicability by time, location, system environment, and participant roles, and formulating falsifiable hypotheses for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Raw data must be transformed into queryable knowledge, requiring both early extraction of reusable information and explicit types, relations, and applicability conditions. Indexing solely around a single business schema risks omitting later-useful content, while retaining only open-ended text leaves rule-based reasoning without checkable premises. The authors seek a design that avoids premature commitment yet retains formal reasonability.
AI.method: 5W1H+Which is a semantic indexing design separating content extraction from ontology binding. The 5W1H questions organize source-grounded content units, while "Which" points to versioned ontology elements and records mapping relations, scope, and validation status. Time, location, system environment, and participant roles act as applicability constraints rather than mere labels. Unbound content stays searchable; bound content enters a formal reasoning path only after premise checks. The method distinguishes business valid time, system knowledge time, and operational traces, using dependency records to support binding revalidation and maintenance of derived conclusions.
AI.result: A worked example of migration from on-premises server to cloud illustrates differentiated treatment of world-state changes, ontology-version changes, and changes in rule applicability. Three groups of falsifiable hypotheses are formulated concerning cross-task evidence coverage, control of contextual misuse, and incremental update cost.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a testable indexing mechanism, not a universal ontology claim or a demonstrated performance advantage. Planned evaluation includes a strong typed fact-graph baseline with identical evidence, temporal information, and budget, to isolate whether benefits stem from 5W1H organization, deferred binding, or additional engineering effort.

title: Beneath the Tokens: A Performance Engineering Study of Multi-Token Prediction in GPU-Accelerated LLM Inference
summary: Autoregressive large language model inference repeatedly invokes the target model to generate one token at a time, making generation sensitive to GPU memory movement and sequential execution. This study evaluates two-token multi-token prediction (MTP) against autoregressive decoding in a controlled single-request deployment on an NVIDIA A10G GPU. A 360-request benchmark covered plain-text, reasoning-intensive, and tool-calling workloads, while runtime telemetry, Nsight Systems, PyTorch Profiler, and selected Nsight Compute measurements were used to explain the observed performance. MTP increased output throughput by \(1.91\times\) to \(2.19\times\) across all prompts and reduced time to first output by 10.0--14.2\%. Median mean acceptance length ranged from 2.370 to 2.595 tokens per verification iteration. Profiling showed that MTP introduced a longer and more complex execution path, including proposal, sampling, attention, gathering, and reduction operations. However, it required 56.4--78.1\% fewer executions of the selected repeating CUDA Graph per generated token. The dominant MTP GEMM kernel was not faster than the dominant autoregressive GEMV kernel, and selected instances of both approached the A10G memory-bandwidth limit. These results show that MTP improved inference through amortization: greater token progress reduced repeated GPU execution sufficiently to outweigh the additional speculative-execution cost.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks two-token multi-token prediction (MTP) against standard autoregressive decoding for a single-request LLM deployment on an NVIDIA A10G GPU, finding that MTP improves throughput and latency through amortization of repeated GPU execution rather than through faster individual kernels.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLM inference generates one token per invocation, making generation highly sensitive to GPU memory movement and sequential execution, which limits throughput and increases latency. The authors seek to determine whether multi-token prediction can mitigate these bottlenecks and to mechanistically explain any observed gains using detailed profiling.
AI.method: Controlled single-request deployment of two-token MTP versus autoregressive decoding on an NVIDIA A10G GPU. A 360-request benchmark spanning plain-text, reasoning-intensive, and tool-calling workloads. Runtime telemetry, Nsight Systems, PyTorch Profiler, and selected Nsight Compute measurements were used to attribute performance differences.
AI.result: MTP raised output throughput by 1.91x-2.19x across all prompts and reduced time to first output by 10.0-14.2%. Median mean acceptance length was 2.370-2.595 tokens per verification iteration. MTP imposed a longer, more complex execution path (proposal, sampling, attention, gathering, reduction) yet required 56.4-78.1% fewer executions of the selected repeating CUDA Graph per generated token. The dominant MTP GEMM kernel was not faster than the dominant autoregressive GEMV kernel, and selected instances of both approached the A10G memory-bandwidth limit.
AI.conclusion: MTP improves inference performance through amortization: greater token progress per verification iteration reduces repeated GPU execution enough to outweigh the added speculative-execution overhead, even though the underlying dominant kernels are not individually faster.

title: ASCT: Attentive Search over Counterfactual Trees for Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Terminal utility evaluates a complete agentic workflow, but learning requires credit for the decisions within it. We introduce Attentive Search over Counterfactual Trees (ASCT), a framework that turns training-time multi-step search into local action credit. At actor-visited states, an auxiliary tree evaluates alternative legal actions from the same recoverable prefix. Its action-value table is centered by the frozen actor's probabilities and supplies credit for PPO on actor-sampled trajectories. This protocol connects counterfactual evaluation to policy learning while deploying the actor alone. Uniform, UCT, and cost-aware AgentUCT instantiate the framework. On HotpotQA agentic retrieval-augmented generation, all three improve mean held-out utility over trajectory-return PPO and workflow-adapted VinePPO. Across three seeds, ASCT-AgentUCT reaches 0.6187 utility versus 0.5939 for VinePPO, with gains in answer F1 and execution cost, and uses 50.3% fewer recorded auxiliary Qwen tokens. Transfer and component-description studies examine the learned policies beyond the training setting.

AI.tldr: ASCT turns training-time multi-step search over counterfactual action trees into local credit signals for PPO, enabling improved agentic workflows (e.g., HotpotQA RAG) while deploying only the actor.
AI.motivation: Terminal utility can evaluate a complete agentic workflow, but assigning credit to the individual decisions within it is difficult. Standard trajectory-return credit is coarse, so a method is needed that provides local, per-action credit for multi-step agentic decisions.
AI.method: Attentive Search over Counterfactual Trees (ASCT): at actor-visited states, an auxiliary search tree evaluates alternative legal actions from the same recoverable prefix. The resulting action-value table is centered by the frozen actor's probabilities and supplies local credit for PPO on actor-sampled trajectories. Three instantiations are given: Uniform, UCT, and cost-aware AgentUCT.
AI.result: On HotpotQA agentic retrieval-augmented generation, all three ASCT variants outperform trajectory-return PPO and workflow-adapted VinePPO in mean held-out utility. Across three seeds, ASCT-AgentUCT reaches 0.6187 utility vs. 0.5939 for VinePPO, with gains in answer F1 and execution cost, and 50.3% fewer recorded auxiliary Qwen tokens.
AI.conclusion: ASCT connects counterfactual evaluation to policy learning while deploying the actor alone. Transfer and component-description studies further examine the learned policies beyond the training setting.

title: EP-Mem: Elastic Privacy Memory for Social Relationship-Aware LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents face critical privacy risks when acting as delegates in human-agent-human communication. To prevent such breaches, agents must understand users' social relationships and adhere to context-dependent social information disclosure boundaries. Current studies on agent memory privacy focus on instantaneous interactions, leaving the long-term relational disclosure problem unexplored. In this paper, we propose EP-Mem, an Elastic Privacy Memory architecture that reframes privacy as user-owned boundary control across social roles. EP-Mem introduces (1) token-level memory driven by user-configurable a privacy policy that stratifies persons and events, combining domain-level default circulation rules with fact-level whitelist/blacklist exceptions; and (2) a pluggable sidecar with a privacy engine that aligns disclosure controls with memory across summary, detail, and boundary granularities, enforced throughout generation, storage, and retrieval. We construct EP-Bench, to our knowledge the first long-term multi-party benchmark with cross-session correlated events for policy-conditioned relational disclosure. Experiments show that EP-Mem achieves 94.0% privacy classification accuracy, improves disclosure-permission judgment from 22% to 68%, and reduces privacy leakage by 75.6%, while maintaining retrieval performance and cross-benchmark generalization.

AI.tldr: EP-Mem is an elastic privacy memory architecture that reframes privacy as user-owned boundary control across social roles, enabling long-term relational disclosure control in LLM agents. It combines policy-driven token-level memory with a pluggable privacy engine sidecar, and is evaluated on EP-Bench, the first long-term multi-party benchmark for policy-conditioned relational disclosure.
AI.motivation: LLM agents acting as delegates in human-agent-human communication face critical privacy risks. Preventing such breaches requires agents to understand users' social relationships and respect context-dependent disclosure boundaries. Existing agent memory privacy studies focus only on instantaneous interactions, leaving the long-term relational disclosure problem unexplored.
AI.method: EP-Mem comprises: (1) token-level memory driven by a user-configurable privacy policy that stratifies persons and events, combining domain-level default circulation rules with fact-level whitelist/blacklist exceptions; and (2) a pluggable sidecar with a privacy engine that aligns disclosure controls with memory across summary, detail, and boundary granularities, enforced throughout generation, storage, and retrieval. The paper also constructs EP-Bench, a long-term multi-party benchmark with cross-session correlated events for policy-conditioned relational disclosure.
AI.result: EP-Mem achieves 94.0% privacy classification accuracy, improves disclosure-permission judgment from 22% to 68%, and reduces privacy leakage by 75.6%, while maintaining retrieval performance and cross-benchmark generalization.
AI.conclusion: EP-Mem effectively addresses the previously unexplored long-term relational disclosure problem by reframing privacy as user-owned boundary control, demonstrating strong gains in privacy classification, disclosure judgment, and leakage reduction without sacrificing retrieval performance or generalization.

title: Towards Reliable AI Data Scientists: Data Agents with Workflow Harnesses
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for data-intensive work, yet reliable data analysis requires more than general-purpose reasoning and ad hoc tool augmentation. Data Agents, equipped with workflow harnesses, offer a promising paradigm for automating the end-to-end data science lifecycle. This paper examines Data Agents from a harness-centric perspective. First, we introduce a taxonomy of Data Agents and associated data environments, organizing the literature around five functional stages: perception, planning, execution, verification, and repair. Second, we analyze the key technical routes within each stage, identifying 15 distinct approaches ranging from data structure probing to data state reconstruction. Third, we identify four open reliability problems: inactive semantic calibration, missing clarification, missing experience transfer, and the missing verification-repair repository. These problems explain why silent failures can persist even when individual components function correctly, highlighting the need for rigorous workflow harnesses and shared reliability resources. Finally, we summarize the horizontal task families of Data Agents, examine their vertical application settings, and benchmarks for evaluation, while maintaining a companion repository at https://github.com/DEEP-PolyU/Awesome-Data-Agents.

AI.tldr: This survey examines Data Agents from a harness-centric perspective, offering a taxonomy across five functional stages, 15 technical routes, four open reliability problems, and an overview of task families, applications, and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for data-intensive work, but reliable data analysis demands more than general-purpose reasoning and ad hoc tool augmentation. Workflow-equipped Data Agents offer a promising paradigm for automating the end-to-end data science lifecycle, motivating a systematic, harness-centric review.
AI.method: The paper adopts a harness-centric perspective: it constructs a taxonomy of Data Agents and data environments organized around five functional stages (perception, planning, execution, verification, repair), then analyzes key technical routes within each stage, covering 15 distinct approaches from data structure probing to data state reconstruction. It also surveys horizontal task families, vertical application settings, and evaluation benchmarks.
AI.result: The analysis identifies 15 distinct technical approaches across the five stages and four open reliability problems: inactive semantic calibration, missing clarification, missing experience transfer, and the missing verification-repair repository. These explain why silent failures persist even when individual components function correctly.
AI.conclusion: Reliable Data Agents require rigorous workflow harnesses and shared reliability resources. The paper highlights the need for a verification-repair repository and provides a companion repository for ongoing tracking.

title: Imprint Reader: From Weight-Update Readout to Behavioral Intervention
summary: As language models take a growing role in AI development, a natural aspiration is for them to reflect on their own learning process, as humans do, and use that reflection to improve themselves. At the same time, these models have an advantage that human learners lack, since training leaves parameter-level traces that can, in principle, be inspected directly. However, current models cannot decode these traces into an explicit account of what they have learned. To this end, we introduce the \textit{Imprint Reader}, a model trained with \textit{Semantic Mount-and-Read Tuning} (SaRT) to describe frozen weight updates. SMaRT mounts each update onto the Reader and uses an anchor-free meta-query to elicit a natural-language description, while no-change and random-perturbation controls discourage unsupported claims. On held-out updates, the joint Reader reaches judge-based Pass@100 of $2\%$ for knowledge and $16\%$ for behavior. These results demonstrate the feasibility of natural-language readout while pointing to reliability across updates as the next step. Beyond free-form generation, the Reader provides a differentiable proxy for the gap between a specified target behavior and a candidate weight update. Its coordinate-aligned gradients support intervention through MetaEdit. At a $0.5\%$ pruning rate, Reader-guided selection raises measured harmful-prompt refusal from $57.9\%$ to $64.1\%$ under a safety-maintenance target. Using behavior descriptions without target-task training data, MetaEdit increases the frequency of backtracking and sub-goal expressions in mathematical reasoning traces and raises BFCL Overall from $41.69\%$ to $44.60\%$.

AI.tldr: The Imprint Reader, trained via Semantic Mount-and-Read Tuning (SaRT), decodes frozen weight updates into natural-language descriptions and serves as a differentiable proxy enabling Reader-guided pruning and MetaEdit interventions that improve refusal and reasoning behavior.
AI.motivation: Language models should be able to reflect on their own learning as humans do, and unlike humans, their training leaves parameter-level traces that can in principle be inspected. However, current models cannot decode these weight-update traces into an explicit account of what they have learned.
AI.method: SaRT mounts each frozen weight update onto the Reader and uses an anchor-free meta-query to elicit a natural-language description, with no-change and random-perturbation controls to discourage unsupported claims. The Reader's coordinate-aligned gradients support intervention via MetaEdit.
AI.result: On held-out updates, the joint Reader achieves judge-based Pass@100 of 2% for knowledge and 16% for behavior. At 0.5% pruning, Reader-guided selection raises harmful-prompt refusal from 57.9% to 64.1% under a safety-maintenance target. Using behavior descriptions without target-task training data, MetaEdit increases backtracking and sub-goal expressions in math traces and raises BFCL Overall from 41.69% to 44.60%.
AI.conclusion: Natural-language readout of weight updates is feasible, though reliability across updates remains the next step. Beyond free-form generation, the Reader provides a differentiable proxy for the gap between target behavior and a candidate update, enabling effective selective pruning and behavior-targeted editing.

title: Textual User Taste: Natural-Language User Context for Foundation-Model Recommender System at Scale
summary: Foundation model recommender systems require user context that can be consumed by large language models, reasoned over, and refined through natural-language interaction. Traditional behavioral embedding vectors remain highly effective for retrieval and ranking, but they are opaque to users and not natively expressed for language model workflows. We present Textual User Taste, a system that generates structured natural-language taste profiles from listening behavior, interaction signals, content metadata, and optional user feedback, and deploys them to millions of Spotify users. We describe the end-to-end production lifecycle required to generate, evaluate, optimize, and maintain these representations at industrial scale, including prompt development and compression, user steering, and integration with downstream personalization systems. Because no unique ground-truth taste profile exists, we introduce a multi-faceted evaluation framework to evaluate taste profiles as a production representation: they carry user-specific predictive signal independently, and when integrated with behavioral embeddings, improve MRR by 0.6% for future-track prediction and NDCG@7 by 2.2% for search ranking. Our evaluation also reveals that taste profiles support positive natural-language steering, while exposing important limitations, including challenges with negation and short-term temporal adaptation. These findings position taste profiles not as replacements for behavioral embeddings, but as an interpretable and steerable interface between evolving user context and foundation-model recommender systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents "Textual User Taste," a production system that generates structured natural-language taste profiles from Spotify listening behavior and deploys them to millions of users. Since no ground-truth taste profile exists, the authors propose a multi-faceted evaluation framework showing that taste profiles independently carry predictive signal and improve ranking metrics when combined with behavioral embeddings.
AI.motivation: Foundation-model recommender systems require user context that large language models can consume, reason over, and refine through natural-language interaction. Traditional behavioral embedding vectors are effective for retrieval and ranking but are opaque to users and not natively expressed for language-model workflows. This creates a gap between the interpretable, steerable user context that foundation models need and the opaque representations that current systems rely on.
AI.method: The system generates structured natural-language taste profiles from listening behavior, interaction signals, content metadata, and optional user feedback, and deploys them to millions of Spotify users. The authors describe the end-to-end production lifecycle required to generate, evaluate, optimize, and maintain these representations at industrial scale, including prompt development and compression, user steering, and integration with downstream personalization systems. Because no unique ground-truth taste profile exists, they introduce a multi-faceted evaluation framework to assess taste profiles as a production representation.
AI.result: Taste profiles carry user-specific predictive signal independently. When integrated with behavioral embeddings, they improve MRR by 0.6% for future-track prediction and NDCG@7 by 2.2% for search ranking. The evaluation also reveals that taste profiles support positive natural-language steering, while exposing limitations including challenges with negation and short-term temporal adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Taste profiles should not be viewed as replacements for behavioral embeddings but as an interpretable and steerable interface between evolving user context and foundation-model recommender systems.

title: The Argument and the Letterhead: Source-Position Coherence in AI Evaluation
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Preregistrations, materials and code available on GitHub. Preprint; not yet peer reviewed
summary: An argument can be surprising coming from a particular speaker without being a bad argument. Do AI evaluators keep these judgments apart? Two preregistered descriptive studies and a later Jev supplement collected 2,976 usable evaluations of six fixed texts about US AI policy, Germany's debt brake and Swiss nuclear energy. Each text was presented under several source attributions. The key comparison asks whether the gap between two sources changes when the argument changes. On Sol, for example, a national-security argument received mean ratings of 0.359 under CODEPINK and 0.639 under College Republicans; a civil-rights argument received 0.742 and 0.721. A constant preference for one source cannot explain that pattern. Related interactions appeared across topics and recent model configurations, including those with reasoning enabled, while several comparisons yielded small effects. The later European Jev supplement yielded five interactions below the adopted absolute reference of 0.05; its distinct rubric and interrupted collection limit comparison with the chat systems. Some written evaluations explicitly invoked a mismatch between a source and its attributed position. Taken together, the numerical and verbal evidence supports source-position coherence as a plausible explanation, alongside competing accounts involving credibility, authenticity and interpretation of the task. The paper develops this inference through controlled comparisons, reports conditional post hoc p-values in an appendix, and documents the human decisions and delegated checks behind an AI-conducted study.

AI.tldr: Across 2,976 AI evaluations of fixed argument texts shown under varied source attributions, the gap between two sources shifts when the argument changes, indicating evaluators track source-position coherence rather than applying a constant source preference.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses whether AI evaluators conflate two distinct judgments: whether an argument is surprising given its speaker, and whether it is a good argument. It asks whether evaluators apply a constant preference for a source regardless of the argument's content, or whether their assessments depend on the fit between the source and the position being argued.
AI.method: Two preregistered descriptive studies plus a later Jev supplement collected 2,976 usable evaluations of six fixed texts concerning US AI policy, Germany's debt brake, and Swiss nuclear energy. Each text was presented under several source attributions, and the key comparison tested whether the gap between two sources changes when the argument changes. Conditional post hoc p-values are reported in an appendix, and the paper documents the human decisions and delegated checks behind the AI-conducted study.
AI.result: On Sol, a national-security argument received mean ratings of 0.359 under CODEPINK and 0.639 under College Republicans, whereas a civil-rights argument received 0.742 and 0.721 respectively, a pattern a constant source preference cannot explain. Related interactions appeared across topics and recent model configurations, including those with reasoning enabled, while several comparisons yielded small effects. The European Jev supplement yielded five interactions below the adopted absolute reference of 0.05, though its distinct rubric and interrupted collection limit comparison with the chat systems. Some written evaluations explicitly invoked a mismatch between a source and its attributed position.
AI.conclusion: The numerical and verbal evidence supports source-position coherence as a plausible explanation, alongside competing accounts involving credibility, authenticity, and interpretation of the task. The paper develops this inference through controlled comparisons, reports conditional post hoc p-values in an appendix, and documents the human decisions and delegated checks behind an AI-conducted study.

title: EvoIn: Bridging Evolution and Internalization for Agent Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent work has explored improving agents by jointly evolving their harnesses and models, but often takes a ''potpourri'' approach that bundles together new tools, new decision-making procedures, and model adaptation to the evolved harness under a single notion of agent improvement. In this paper, we instead investigate how agents can improve their decision-making procedures. In particular, we propose EvoIn, an agent fine-tuning framework that bridges evolution and internalization. EvoIn first analyzes agent execution traces to evolve and validate new decision-making procedures by temporarily instantiating them in the harness. The validated procedures guide the agent to generate improved reasoning traces. These traces are then rewritten into self-contained reasoning traces, removing explicit references to harness instructions while expressing the induced decision logic as the model's own reasoning. Finally, EvoIn fine-tunes the model on the rewritten traces, internalizing these procedures so that the improved decision-making persists without the evolved harness at inference time. We evaluate EvoIn on diverse benchmarks and find that it consistently enables agents to learn stronger decision-making procedures, raising the pass rate by 10.9 points in-domain and by 9.2 points out-of-domain. Results further show that the internalized decision procedures generalize to unseen tasks. Case studies show that agents can learn to decide how to solve a task before solving it, for example by checking a document's length to choose between reading it in full and searching it. EvoIn is also broadly applicable, showing consistent improvements on another model family.

AI.tldr: EvoIn is a fine-tuning framework that evolves new decision-making procedures in an agent's harness, validates them, rewrites the resulting traces into self-contained reasoning, and fine-tunes the model to internalize these procedures so gains persist without the evolved harness.
AI.motivation: Prior work on jointly evolving agent harnesses and models uses a "potpourri" approach that conflates new tools, new decision-making procedures, and model adaptation under one notion of improvement, making it unclear how agents can specifically improve their decision-making procedures.
AI.method: EvoIn analyzes agent execution traces to evolve and validate new decision-making procedures by temporarily instantiating them in the harness. Validated procedures guide the agent to produce improved reasoning traces, which are rewritten into self-contained traces that remove explicit harness-instruction references and express the induced decision logic as the model's own reasoning. The model is then fine-tuned on these rewritten traces to internalize the procedures.
AI.result: EvoIn consistently enables agents to learn stronger decision-making procedures, raising pass rate by 10.9 points in-domain and 9.2 points out-of-domain. Internalized procedures generalize to unseen tasks, and consistent improvements are observed on another model family.
AI.conclusion: The internalized decision procedures persist without the evolved harness at inference time and generalize to unseen tasks, e.g., deciding whether to read a document in full or search it based on length, showing broad applicability across model families.

title: AbGaze: Attentive Geometric Representation Learning for End-to-End Antibody Design
summary: Computational antibody design requires representations that capture the geometric patterns underlying antigen--antibody interactions, yet existing approaches often rely on scalar distances or surface-intrinsic features, leaving cross-molecular geometry largely implicit. We present AbGaze, an end-to-end antibody design framework based on attentive geometric representation learning, which encodes distance, spatial direction, and surface-normal orientation of antigen surfaces relative to antibody-residue local frames, and adaptively aggregates these geometric interactions according to their interfacial context. The learned interaction representation is shared across multi-CDR co-design, complex structure prediction, and affinity optimization, with local-frame geometric supervision further constraining the representation. AbGaze outperforms prior methods across all three tasks: relative to the second-best method, it improves amino-acid recovery by 7.1% and reduces structural error by 14.9% on average over the six CDRs, improves interface docking quality (DockQ) by 6.6%, and raises the affinity improvement rate (IMP) by 32.5%.

AI.tldr: AbGaze is an end-to-end antibody design framework that learns attentive geometric representations of antigen-antibody interactions, encoding distance, direction, and surface-normal orientation relative to antibody-residue local frames, and sharing this representation across multi-CDR co-design, complex structure prediction, and affinity optimization.
AI.motivation: Computational antibody design requires representations capturing the geometric patterns underlying antigen-antibody interactions. Existing approaches typically rely on scalar distances or surface-intrinsic features, leaving cross-molecular geometry largely implicit and thus limiting design performance.
AI.method: AbGaze uses attentive geometric representation learning that encodes distance, spatial direction, and surface-normal orientation of antigen surfaces relative to antibody-residue local frames, then adaptively aggregates these geometric interactions based on interfacial context. The learned interaction representation is shared across multi-CDR co-design, complex structure prediction, and affinity optimization, with local-frame geometric supervision further constraining it.
AI.result: AbGaze outperforms prior methods on all three tasks. Versus the second-best method, it improves amino-acid recovery by 7.1% and reduces structural error by 14.9% on average over six CDRs, improves interface docking quality (DockQ) by 6.6%, and raises the affinity improvement rate (IMP) by 32.5%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, adaptive encoding of cross-molecular geometry within antibody local frames, coupled with shared use across design and optimization tasks and local-frame supervision, yields consistent gains in antibody design, structure prediction, and affinity optimization.

title: Training-Free Clinical Reasoning through Medical Ontologies and Cognitive Mapping: A Symbolic-Probabilistic Knowledge Graph Framework
summary: Most clinical prediction systems learn patient-variable-outcome associations; we investigate a training-free diagnostic paradigm mapping patient observations to explicit medical knowledge. CKG Reasoner integrates candidate-specific Evidence Feature Nodes, patient-reference matching, a bounded Information Gate, knowledge-weighted evidence accumulation, disease similarity, and decisive clinical rules. Missing-aware normalization and coverage auditing distinguish absent from unavailable evidence. Candidate ranking is separate from outcome-label-independent K-means clustering, which uses four derived evidence coordinates (evidence strength, relative magnitude, directional similarity, and evidence completeness), not raw predictors or targets, to derive cohort-level assignments. Across six retrospective cohorts - four dengue (N = 1000, 1523, 989, 1018), malaria (N = 2190), and influenza (N = 4569) - a uniform, label-free, cohort-fitted K = 2 protocol yielded positive-class F1 scores of 0.996, 0.634, 0.936, 0.917, 0.695, and 0.842, and all-record accuracies of 0.996, 0.558, 0.914, 0.893, 0.707, and 0.906, respectively, with full partition-decision coverage using the frozen package and disease-specific knowledge representations. Neither scoring nor clustering uses outcome labels. Logistic regression provides a supervised baseline. Influenza incorporates confirmatory molecular PCR and is not independent pre-test prediction. Results characterize knowledge-grounded evidence separation, auditability, and sensitivity, not prospective clinical validity or comparative superiority. FOL/LLM-based clinical explanation remains unevaluated.

AI.tldr: CKG Reasoner is a training-free diagnostic paradigm that maps patient observations to explicit medical knowledge via evidence feature nodes, gating, and knowledge-weighted accumulation, then derives cohort-level assignments through label-free K-means on four evidence coordinates. Evaluated on six retrospective cohorts (dengue, malaria, influenza), it achieved variable positive-class F1 (0.634–0.996) with full partition-decision coverage.
AI.motivation: Most clinical prediction systems learn patient-variable-outcome associations, which are opaque and rely on outcome labels. The authors seek a training-free diagnostic paradigm that instead maps patient observations to explicit medical knowledge, aiming for transparency, auditability, and label independence.
AI.method: CKG Reasoner integrates candidate-specific Evidence Feature Nodes, patient-reference matching, a bounded Information Gate, knowledge-weighted evidence accumulation, disease similarity, and decisive clinical rules. Missing-aware normalization and coverage auditing distinguish absent from unavailable evidence. Candidate ranking is separated from an outcome-label-independent K-means clustering that uses four derived evidence coordinates (evidence strength, relative magnitude, directional similarity, evidence completeness) rather than raw predictors or targets to derive cohort-level assignments. A uniform, label-free, cohort-fitted K = 2 protocol is applied; logistic regression serves as a supervised baseline.
AI.result: Across six retrospective cohorts—four dengue (N = 1000, 1523, 989, 1018), malaria (N = 2190), and influenza (N = 4569)—positive-class F1 was 0.996, 0.634, 0.936, 0.917, 0.695, 0.842, and all-record accuracy was 0.996, 0.558, 0.914, 0.893, 0.707, 0.906, respectively, with full partition-decision coverage using the frozen package and disease-specific knowledge representations. Neither scoring nor clustering uses outcome labels. Influenza incorporates confirmatory molecular PCR and is not independent pre-test prediction.
AI.conclusion: Results characterize knowledge-grounded evidence separation, auditability, and sensitivity, not prospective clinical validity or comparative superiority. FOL/LLM-based clinical explanation remains unevaluated.

title: Narrowing the Horizon: Quantifying Topic Saliency Shifts in Generative Monoculture
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become central to how we access and share information, they play an increasingly powerful role in shaping global knowledge. However, as these models evolve, their outputs risk converging into a \textit{generative monoculture}, where the diversity of perspectives they represent narrows over time. Studies at the model level often fail to pinpoint which specific topics or viewpoints are being marginalised or amplified in this process. In this paper, we introduce a method to measure shifts in topic saliency across model families, tracking what gains or loses prominence during post-training. Applying this approach to a case study of climate change discourse, we demonstrate how homogenisation affects the representation of diverse solutions across different models. We also test interventions to counter this trend, showing that specialised models can help preserve a broader range of perspectives. This underscores the importance of monitoring topic saliency to diagnose the risks of monoculture and to ensure AI systems reflect a pluralism of ideas. Data and Code are accessible \href{https://github.com/oriane/topic_saliency_shift}{here}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a method to measure shifts in topic saliency across LLM families to detect "generative monoculture"—the narrowing of represented perspectives—and tests interventions to preserve pluralism.
AI.motivation: As LLMs mediate access to and sharing of information, their outputs risk converging into a generative monoculture that narrows the diversity of perspectives. Model-level studies often fail to identify which specific topics or viewpoints are marginalized or amplified during this convergence.
AI.method: The authors propose a method to measure shifts in topic saliency across model families, tracking what gains or loses prominence during post-training. They apply it to a case study of climate change discourse and test interventions—including specialized models—to counter homogenisation.
AI.result: Applying the approach to climate change discourse shows how homogenisation affects the representation of diverse solutions across different models. Interventions reveal that specialised models can help preserve a broader range of perspectives.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring topic saliency is important for diagnosing the risks of monoculture and ensuring AI systems reflect a pluralism of ideas. Data and code are publicly available.

title: Reliability Engineering for AI Systems: Challenges, Methods, and Directions
summary: AI reliability concerns whether an AI system performs its intended function dependably over a stated period and under stated operating conditions, with stated evidence. As these systems become more autonomous, that function includes more than a correct output. Retrieval, memory, tool use, permissions, human oversight, and interactions among systems must operate consistently and safely, and, for generative systems, so must the reasoning process that produces the output. Average benchmark accuracy measures capability; it does not quantify this broader reliability claim. This paper adapts established reliability engineering methods, from failure definitions and operational envelopes to FMEA, accelerated testing, field monitoring, and reliability growth, to AI systems. A four-level diagnostic framework classifies failures as component, operational-loop, agentic-conduct, or network and governance failures. Test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV), sequential monitoring, and FRACAS create and refresh evidence. SMART provides statistical guidance for measurement, analysis, assessment, and test planning; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides organizational guidance for governance, evaluation, monitoring, and mitigation. Three cases illustrate the program: adversarial testing of a convolutional neural network, perception-error propagation, and autonomous-vehicle disengagements. Established reliability engineering provides a usable foundation; new measurements and safety guardrails are still needed as these systems are self-evolving.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes AI reliability as a measurable engineering property, adapting classical reliability engineering methods (failure definitions, operational envelopes, FMEA, accelerated testing, field monitoring, reliability growth) to AI systems. It proposes a four-level failure diagnostic framework and integrates TEVV, sequential monitoring, FRACAS, SMART statistical guidance, and the NIST AI RMF, illustrated through three cases.
AI.motivation: As AI systems become more autonomous, their intended function extends beyond producing a correct output to encompass retrieval, memory, tool use, permissions, human oversight, and inter-system interactions, as well as the reasoning process in generative systems. Average benchmark accuracy measures capability, not this broader reliability claim, so a more rigorous, evidence-based framework is needed to define, quantify, and monitor dependability over a stated period and operating conditions.
AI.method: The paper adapts established reliability engineering methods to AI, including failure definitions, operational envelopes, FMEA, accelerated testing, field monitoring, and reliability growth. It introduces a four-level diagnostic framework classifying failures as component, operational-loop, agentic-conduct, or network and governance failures. Evidence is created and refreshed through TEVV, sequential monitoring, and FRACAS; SMART provides statistical guidance for measurement, analysis, assessment, and test planning, while the NIST AI RMF provides organizational guidance for governance, evaluation, monitoring, and mitigation.
AI.result: Three cases illustrate the proposed program: adversarial testing of a convolutional neural network, perception-error propagation, and autonomous-vehicle disengagements, demonstrating how the framework and methods apply across different failure levels and system types.
AI.conclusion: Established reliability engineering provides a usable foundation for AI reliability, but new measurements and safety guardrails remain necessary because these systems are self-evolving.

title: Hyper Algorithm Design Agent: Evolving Learnable Optimizer from Zero
summary: Meta-Black-Box Optimization (MetaBBO) is one of the highlights in the recent AI for Optimization trend. This paradigm's bi-level workflow leverages the learnable algorithm design policy at meta level to ensure the performance and generalization improvement on the low-level optimization task. While MetaBBO helps advance the performance lower bound of the resulted optimization system, it is currently handcrafted and customized case by case to adapt different optimization problems, which inevitably introduces inherent subjectivity and hence restricts the performance upper bound and usability in practice. In this paper, we address this issue by regarding MetaBBO's design loop as coding task, where we could introduce openendedness into MetaBBO with recursive self-improvement capability of advanced coding agents. Specifically, we propose a dual-agent framework: i) a task agent continuously refines the codebase of a target MetaBBO approach through code evolution; ii) a hyper agent progressively modifies the task agent and itself to provide open-ended design behavior; iii) the evolved MetaBBO codebase is evaluated and all in-execution information is fed back to the agents for recursive self-referential improvement. As a result, given a naive MetaBBO template, our framework automates a design evolution and finds novel variants superior to up-to-date human-made MetaBBO baselines. Surprisingly, the experimental results also demonstrate that our framework supports fast adaption across different optimization domains. Solid interpretation analysis further reveals interesting design principles emerge in such open-ended process. This work serves as the first exploration on automating design of complex learning-assisted optimization algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dual-agent, code-evolution framework that automates the design of Meta-Black-Box Optimization (MetaBBO) algorithms, replacing handcrafted, case-by-case design with open-ended, recursively self-improving coding agents that discover novel MetaBBO variants outperforming human-made baselines and adapting across optimization domains.
AI.motivation: MetaBBO uses a bi-level workflow with a learnable algorithm design policy at the meta level to improve performance and generalization on low-level optimization tasks. However, MetaBBO's design loop is currently handcrafted and customized case by case for different optimization problems, which introduces inherent subjectivity and thereby restricts both the performance upper bound and practical usability.
AI.method: The authors treat MetaBBO's design loop as a coding task and inject open-endedness via recursive self-improvement of coding agents. They propose a dual-agent framework: (i) a task agent continuously refines a target MetaBBO approach's codebase through code evolution; (ii) a hyper agent progressively modifies the task agent and itself to sustain open-ended design behavior; (iii) the evolved MetaBBO codebase is evaluated, and all in-execution information is fed back to the agents for recursive self-referential improvement. Starting from a naive MetaBBO template, the framework automates design evolution.
AI.result: Given a naive MetaBBO template, the framework automates design evolution and finds novel variants superior to up-to-date human-made MetaBBO baselines. It also supports fast adaptation across different optimization domains. Interpretation analysis reveals that interesting design principles emerge during the open-ended process.
AI.conclusion: The work serves as the first exploration of automating the design of complex learning-assisted optimization algorithms, demonstrating that treating MetaBBO design as a coding task with recursive self-improving agents can surpass human-crafted baselines and generalize across domains.

title: TMCS: Tool-Grounded Multi-Agent Reasoning for Compositional Chemical Problem Solving
summary: Despite the promise of Large Language Models (LLMs) in computational chemistry, rigorous combinatorial chemistry problems remain difficult because they require quantitatively constrained molecular modification, candidate validation, and systematic revision after failed attempts. Existing tool-augmented chemical agents demonstrate useful planning and tool use, but they rarely provide a unified loop for property-driven molecular optimization and workflow-level composition. To bridge this gap, we propose Tool-Grounded Multi-Agent Reasoning for Compositional Chemical Problem Solving (TMCS), a step-by-step multi-agent framework that formalizes chemical problem solving as an interpretable, tool-augmented workflow. At the task level, specialized agents leverage external tools, few-shot trajectory memory, and structured reflection to iteratively refine solutions. At the workflow level, TMCS chains generation, understanding, editing, description, and optimization into a closed-loop pipeline. Evaluations across multiple chemical tasks demonstrate that TMCS consistently enhances chemical reasoning across both open- and closed-source base models, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: TMCS is a tool-grounded multi-agent framework that formalizes compositional chemical problem solving as an interpretable, tool-augmented workflow with task-level refinement and workflow-level closed-loop chaining, achieving state-of-the-art chemical reasoning across open- and closed-source LLMs.
AI.motivation: Rigorous combinatorial chemistry problems remain challenging for LLMs because they demand quantitatively constrained molecular modification, candidate validation, and systematic revision after failed attempts. Existing tool-augmented chemical agents support planning and tool use but rarely offer a unified loop for property-driven molecular optimization and workflow-level composition.
AI.method: TMCS is a step-by-step multi-agent framework (Tool-Grounded Multi-Agent Reasoning for Compositional Chemical Problem Solving). At the task level, specialized agents use external tools, few-shot trajectory memory, and structured reflection to iteratively refine solutions. At the workflow level, TMCS chains generation, understanding, editing, description, and optimization into a closed-loop pipeline.
AI.result: Evaluations across multiple chemical tasks show that TMCS consistently enhances chemical reasoning for both open- and closed-source base models, attaining state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: TMCS bridges the gap in unified, tool-grounded, property-driven molecular optimization and workflow-level composition, establishing an interpretable closed-loop framework that improves chemical reasoning across diverse tasks and model types.

title: Jev thinks "I don't know'', but doesn't say it: Introducing Sys1Cal-v1 Dataset for Probability Calibration
summary:
The appearance of Jev marked the era of System One Models, foundation models that return structured decisions with probability distributions rather than text. Aside from low cost and great speed, Jev's central promise is that these probabilities are calibrated: such claim is not backed by any public test and available external benchmarks evaluate confidence calibration, not whether every returned option probability has the right numerical meaning. To tackle this issue, we introduce Sys1Cal-v1, a dataset of True/False questions about a proposition $A$ for which the exact probability $P(A)$ is known by construction. Each item is queried through the three Jev primitives - Noul, Choice and Score - and evaluated by total variation distance from the ground-truth distribution, which can be used to estimate a soft accuracy of System One Models.
  We showcase the utility of Sys1Cal-v1 as a benchmark dataset by evaluating Jev and SemIf, an open-source Choice-style baseline. In this work, however, we focus even more deeply on Jev, by studying the calibration of its Score and Choice answers. In particular, we discover a peculiar behaviour that can be explained by assuming that Jev suppresses a third truth value, going beyond True and False. In other words, in 	exttt{Choice} answers, $P(A)$ and $P(
eg A)$ are presented as if $P(A)+P(
eg A)=1$, while a term $P(U)
eq0$ is missing in the sum. Recovering $P(U)$ leads to an improvement of median soft accuracy in 	exttt{Choice} answers from $0.771$ to $0.978$, suggesting that, even in binary decisions, Jev wants to answer with a third option:``I don't know''.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Sys1Cal-v1, a new dataset of True/False questions with known ground-truth probabilities, to benchmark the calibration of System One Models like Jev. It reveals that Jev appears to suppress a third truth value ("I don't know"), and recovering this missing probability improves median soft accuracy from 0.771 to 0.978.
AI.motivation: System One Models like Jev promise calibrated probabilities for structured decisions, but this claim lacks public testing. Existing external benchmarks evaluate confidence calibration generally, not whether each returned option probability has correct numerical meaning. There is a need for a benchmark that verifies the exact numerical validity of returned probabilities.
AI.method: The authors introduce Sys1Cal-v1, a dataset of True/False questions about a proposition A where the exact probability P(A) is known by construction. Each item is queried through Jev's three primitives—Noul, Choice, and Score—and evaluated using total variation distance from the ground-truth distribution to estimate soft accuracy. They evaluate Jev and the open-source Choice-style baseline SemIf, focusing deeply on Jev's Score and Choice calibration.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals a peculiar behavior in Jev that can be explained by assuming it suppresses a third truth value beyond True and False. In Choice answers, P(A) and P(¬A) are presented as if P(A)+P(¬A)=1, while a missing term P(U)≠0 is omitted. Recovering P(U) improves median soft accuracy in Choice answers from 0.771 to 0.978.
AI.conclusion: Even in binary decisions, Jev appears to want to answer with a third option: "I don't know." The Sys1Cal-v1 benchmark proves useful for testing System One Model calibration, and accounting for the suppressed third truth value substantially improves calibration accuracy.

title: Jailbreaks for Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification in Large Reasoning Models
summary: While Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) excel at complex reasoning, alignment through reinforcement learning often induces systemic overconfidence. In production environments, where logits may be unavailable, robust black-box uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for trustworthiness and safety. Focusing on question-answering for LRMs, we show that existing black-box methods, such as paraphrase-based self-consistency and confidence verbalization, offer little to no improvement over simple repeated sampling, suggesting that alignment suppresses useful output variability. We introduce prompt-level relaxation operators that broaden the model's effective output distribution by approximating the effect of an optimal policy obtained with a stronger KL-regularization parameter, hence closer to the reference model. Theoretically, we demonstrate that relaxation improves calibration. We propose Jailbreak for Uncertainty (J4U), a jailbreak-derived technique for UQ that empirically reproduces the behavioral signatures predicted by our relaxation theory. Across 3 datasets and 4 LRMs, including a closed-source production model, J4U's improvement over repeated sampling achieves statistical significance in up to 6 times more LRM-dataset-metric settings than the strongest black-box UQ state-of-the-art baseline we evaluate, with average ECE reductions up to 5 times larger. These results provide a practical tool for UQ in black-box LRM deployment.

AI.tldr: LRM alignment causes overconfidence; the authors propose prompt-level relaxation theory and introduce J4U, a jailbreak-derived black-box uncertainty quantification method that reliably outperforms repeated sampling and existing black-box UQ baselines.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are well-aligned via reinforcement learning but become systematically overconfident. In production, logits are often unavailable, so robust black-box uncertainty quantification (UQ) is needed for trustworthiness and safety. Existing black-box methods (paraphrase-based self-consistency, confidence verbalization) give little or no gain over simple repeated sampling, indicating alignment suppresses useful output variability.
AI.method: The authors introduce prompt-level relaxation operators that broaden the model's effective output distribution by approximating an optimal policy under stronger KL-regularization (closer to the reference model). They theoretically prove relaxation improves calibration, and propose Jailbreak for Uncertainty (J4U), a jailbreak-derived black-box UQ technique that empirically reproduces the predicted behavioral signatures of the relaxation theory.
AI.result: Across 3 datasets and 4 LRMs (including a closed-source production model), J4U's improvement over repeated sampling reaches statistical significance in up to 6× more LRM-dataset-metric settings than the strongest black-box UQ baseline evaluated, with average ECE reductions up to 5× larger.
AI.conclusion: J4U provides a practical, effective tool for uncertainty quantification in black-box LRM deployment, addressing overconfidence induced by RL alignment without requiring access to logits.

title: Don't Inoculate Everything: Stratified Inoculation Prompting Narrows Backdoor Triggers and Preserves Desired Traits
summary: Supervised fine-tuning can teach language models undesired behaviours alongside desired ones. Inoculation prompting (IP) aims to limit unwanted generalisation by requesting the undesired behaviour during training and removing the request at inference. However, undesired behaviour can still appear under unrelated prompts. IP can also hinder learning of the desired behaviour. We address these limitations in settings where both behaviours co-occur in most training examples, so filtering out examples with undesired behaviour leaves only a small clean subset. We introduce stratified inoculation prompting (SIP). SIP leverages a small clean subset to demonstrate that desired behaviour should persist without the undesired one across different contexts. SIP oversamples these clean examples under diverse non-eliciting prompts while inoculating the rest. SIP substantially reduces expression of undesired behaviour while preserving more of the desired behaviour than IP.
