The paper aims to separate the hard problem from the mapping problem, setting aside deep metaphysical disagreements by granting that experience supervenes on a system's organisation and focusing on the tractable question of the grain of description at which that supervenience base sits.
AI.method: The authors extend Marr's three levels of analysis into a five-level hierarchy of functional descriptions (behavioural, computational, intrinsic causal-structural, organismic, and organism-environment) grounded in supervenience, coarse-graining, and multiple realisability. They position major consciousness theories within this hierarchy according to which level each takes as critical, develop operationalisable indicators for each level, assess current AI systems against them, and combine theoretical credences with indicator evidence via a Bayesian model.
AI.result: In illustrative assessments of current LLMs, the verdict depends as much on where theoretical credence is placed as on how evidence is read, ranging from below 0.01 to roughly 0.8 under different stipulated readings and credence distributions, demonstrating sensitivity to assumptions. The consciousness indicators at each level closely overlap with the architectural features needed for general intelligence.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports a structured agnosticism: theoretical commitments are made explicit, credences update as evidence accumulates, and assessments take the form of aggregated probabilities rather than verdicts. The overlap between consciousness indicators and general-intelligence architecture suggests increasingly capable AI may become a stronger candidate for consciousness.

title: RIDE: Reference-Anchored Inference-Time Diffusion Editing for Scaffold Hopping
summary: Scaffold hopping is a critical task in drug discovery, which seeks to discover new, structurally distinct molecules that share key functional groups and similar 3D shape with a reference binding ligand. Existing diffusion-based scaffold hopping methods formulate the problem as conditional generation of scaffolds given the functional groups. However, they lack a principled mechanism to jointly enforce 2D structural novelty and preserve the 3D shape of the reference ligand. Here, we introduce RIDE, a Reference-anchored Inference-time Diffusion Editing framework for scaffold hopping. RIDE recovers the reference diffusion noise trajectory conditioned on the binding pocket and functional groups, selects an optimal trajectory segment for editing via noise perturbation, and conducts a value-guided scaffold sampling to generate new scaffolds. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that, compared to baselines, RIDE consistently generates scaffolds with lower 2D similarity and higher 3D similarity to the reference, with an average improvements of 11.7% and 7.3%, respectively. Further analysis reveals that RIDE can accommodate various reward functions, and can preserve 3D similarity even when this is not explicitly included in the reward. Two case studies illustrate RIDE's ability to generate distinct scaffolds with different structures and properties, and its ability to introduce substantial 2D variation while maintaining very high 3D similarity. RIDE is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RIDE-C8A0.

AI.tldr: RIDE is a reference-anchored inference-time diffusion editing framework for scaffold hopping that jointly enforces 2D structural novelty and preserves 3D shape similarity to a reference ligand.
AI.motivation: Scaffold hopping aims to discover structurally distinct molecules sharing key functional groups and similar 3D shape with a reference binding ligand. Existing diffusion-based methods formulate this as conditional scaffold generation given functional groups, but lack a principled mechanism to jointly enforce 2D structural novelty and preserve the 3D shape of the reference ligand.
AI.method: RIDE recovers the reference diffusion noise trajectory conditioned on the binding pocket and functional groups, selects an optimal trajectory segment for editing via noise perturbation, and performs value-guided scaffold sampling to generate new scaffolds.
AI.result: RIDE consistently generates scaffolds with lower 2D similarity and higher 3D similarity to the reference than baselines, with average improvements of 11.7% and 7.3%, respectively. It accommodates various reward functions and can preserve 3D similarity even when this is not explicitly included in the reward. Two case studies show its ability to generate distinct scaffolds with different structures and properties while introducing substantial 2D variation with very high 3D similarity.
AI.conclusion: RIDE provides an effective inference-time diffusion editing approach for scaffold hopping, achieving a better trade-off between 2D novelty and 3D shape preservation, and is publicly available.

title: Verifiable Visual Rewards Transfer from Synthetic Scenes to Natural Prompts
summary: Precise instruction following in image generation, such as satisfying object counts and spatial relations, remains an open challenge at least in part because it is learned using unreliable reward models such as object detectors and vision-language models. We introduce Verifiable Visual Rewards (VVR), the first framework for programmatically verifiable image rewards, and show that training on it generalizes to natural prompts. Each VVR task is a scene of geometric objects and relations among them, from which we derive both the prompt and a deterministic verifier, so tasks can be generated in any number and at any chosen complexity. We release VVRBench, with 10,000 tasks over 32 constraint types, and VVRBench-Challenge, with 720 more complex tasks; the strongest model we evaluate---GPT-Image-2.5---solves 21.4% of VVRBench-Challenge. Using VVR scores as rewards for reinforcement learning (RLVVR) raises the accuracy of Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium on VVRBench from 2.8% to 28.3% and demonstrates consistent easy-to-hard generalization. These gains extend to out-of-domain benchmarks, and mixing VVR into existing objectives further improves overall performance and human preference, motivating the adoption of VVR into standard image generation post-training recipes.

AI.tldr: VVR is the first framework for programmatically verifiable image rewards, enabling training image generation models to follow precise instructions by generalizing from synthetic geometrically verified tasks to natural prompts and out-of-domain benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Precise instruction following in image generation (e.g., object counts and spatial relations) remains challenging, largely because it is learned using unreliable reward models such as object detectors and vision-language models.
AI.method: The authors introduce Verifiable Visual Rewards (VVR), where each task is a scene of geometric objects and relations from which both a prompt and a deterministic verifier are derived, allowing tasks to be generated in any number and at any chosen complexity. They release VVRBench (10,000 tasks, 32 constraint types) and VVRBench-Challenge (720 more complex tasks), and use VVR scores as rewards for reinforcement learning (RLVVR).
AI.result: The strongest evaluated model, GPT-Image-2.5, solves 21.4% of VVRBench-Challenge. Using VVR scores as RL rewards raises Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium's accuracy on VVRBench from 2.8% to 28.3%, with consistent easy-to-hard generalization. Gains extend to out-of-domain benchmarks, and mixing VVR into existing objectives further improves overall performance and human preference.
AI.conclusion: VVR provides reliable, verifiable rewards that improve precise instruction following and generalize broadly, motivating its adoption into standard image generation post-training recipes.

title: Not All Thinking is Created Equal: Latent Reasoning Discovers a Recurrent Search Algorithm for Depth Generalization
summary: Large Language Models can perform multi-step reasoning and improve task performance through different forms of intermediate computation, from token-based traces to computation carried out in latent space. However, a question remains open: do these different forms of thinking rely on the same underlying mechanism? To address this, we train and compare five variants of the same GPTNeoX backbone from scratch on an extended multi-hop reasoning task (ProsQA-Ext): a vanilla model, a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) model, a Pause Token model, and two latent-reasoning models that are optimized end-to-end without intermediate reasoning traces. We find that, strong in-distribution (ID) performance does not guarantee depth generalization. Vanilla, CoT, and Pause Token models solve ID problems well, but rely largely on local graph features and generalize poorly to out-of-distribution (OOD) problems with longer hops. In contrast, latent variants generalize better and show internal dynamics consistent with forward reachability propagation on the graph. Causal interventions and circuit analysis localize this computation to a sparse recurrent search circuit in the bottleneck latent model: an attention head retrieves graph relations, an MLP and the residual stream update the reachability state across recurrent steps, while multiple attention heads together then do the candidate matching. Together, these results show that different thinking mechanisms can learn distinct computational solutions, even at similar ID performance. In this setting, latent recurrence supports a reusable forward-search algorithm that generalizes beyond the training depth.

AI.tldr: Comparing five variants of the same GPTNeoX backbone (vanilla, CoT, Pause Token, and two latent-reasoning models) on an extended multi-hop reasoning task, the paper shows that strong in-distribution performance does not guarantee depth generalization: token-based models rely on local graph features and fail on longer-hop OOD problems, whereas latent-recurrence models generalize better by learning a forward reachability search algorithm localized to a sparse recurrent circuit.
AI.motivation: Different forms of intermediate computation in LLMs—from token-based traces (CoT, Pause Tokens) to latent-space computation—improve multi-step reasoning, but it is unclear whether they rely on the same underlying mechanism. This work asks whether these "thinking" forms learn shared or distinct computational solutions, and why some generalize in reasoning depth while others do not.
AI.method: Five variants of the same GPTNeoX backbone are trained from scratch on an extended multi-hop reasoning task (ProsQA-Ext): a vanilla model, a Chain-of-Thought model, a Pause Token model, and two latent-reasoning models optimized end-to-end without intermediate reasoning traces. The authors evaluate in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance on longer-hop problems, then apply causal interventions and circuit analysis; internal dynamics are probed for signatures of forward reachability propagation on the graph.
AI.result: Vanilla, CoT, and Pause Token models solve ID problems well but rely largely on local graph features and generalize poorly to OOD problems with longer hops. Latent variants generalize better and exhibit internal dynamics consistent with forward reachability propagation on the graph. Causal interventions and circuit analysis localize this computation to a sparse recurrent search circuit in the bottleneck latent model: an attention head retrieves graph relations, an MLP and the residual stream update the reachability state across recurrent steps, and multiple attention heads together perform candidate matching.
AI.conclusion: Different thinking mechanisms can learn distinct computational solutions even when ID performance is similar, since ID accuracy is not a reliable indicator of depth generalization. In this setting, latent recurrence supports a reusable forward-search algorithm that generalizes beyond the training depth, while token-based reasoning tends to exploit local features. The findings suggest that architectural/mechanistic choices—not just intermediate-trace format—determine whether a model learns depth-generalizable reasoning.

title: PhoneCLI: From App Interfaces to Callable Commands for Mobile Agents
summary: Mobile GUI agents operate through a perception--action loop: at each step they screenshot the device, invoke a vision--language model (VLM), and emit an action. It is slow, costly, and brittle, yet most of what it does is navigation---and everyday navigation is static, ordered, and endlessly repeated. We present PhoneCLI, which compiles an app's GUI navigation into callable commands, without any app-internal API, runtime instrumentation, or model training. Offline, PhoneCLI explores a target app from the outside and distills its screens, interactive elements, and navigation edges into a semantically annotated map; each screen yields one deterministic command: a replay sequence that reaches it. Online, the agent selects a command, verifies it before execution, and then executes it deterministically in sub-second time at zero VLM cost; open-ended interaction and every failure of the compiled path fall back to the embedded VLM interpreter, exactly the pure VLM agent, so compilation can only help. On AndroidLab, PhoneCLI improves the task success rate while reducing steps and token consumption, and it transfers to AndroidWorld's official M3A agent with consistent efficiency gains. What PhoneCLI compiles is the app's navigation rather than one run, so it serves new tasks, not only repeated ones.

AI.tldr: PhoneCLI compiles an app's GUI navigation into deterministic, reusable commands offline (via an annotated screen/navigation map), enabling sub-second, zero-VLM-cost execution that falls back to the VLM interpreter on failures, improving success rate while cutting steps and tokens.
AI.motivation: Mobile GUI agents rely on a slow, costly, and brittle perception-action loop (screenshot + VLM + action per step), even though most of their work is static, ordered, and repeated navigation.
AI.method: PhoneCLI compiles GUI navigation into callable commands without app-internal API, runtime instrumentation, or model training. Offline it explores an app externally and distills screens, interactive elements, and navigation edges into a semantically annotated map, yielding one deterministic replay-sequence command per screen. Online it selects, verifies, then executes commands deterministically, falling back to the embedded VLM interpreter on open-ended interaction or path failure.
AI.result: On AndroidLab, PhoneCLI improves task success rate while reducing steps and token consumption; it transfers to AndroidWorld's official M3A agent with consistent efficiency gains.
AI.conclusion: PhoneCLI compiles the app's navigation rather than a single run, so it serves new tasks, not only repeated ones. Since compilation can only help (fallback equals the pure VLM agent), it is a strict efficiency improvement.

title: Verifier Errors in RLVR: Reward Hacking, Limits of Feedback, and Selective Control
summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), imperfect verifiers can reward incorrect responses, creating opportunities for reward hacking. Using gradient flow with a fixed verifier, we characterize the conditions under which reward rises while correctness falls. We then show that the observations available during RLVR are, in general, insufficient to detect or identify accepted errors, or to guarantee their reduction without sacrificing correct responses. To address this limit, we construct a correction using additional feedback about correctness from audits. This correction achieves \emph{selective control}: at the current policy, it lowers the probability of accepted errors and raises that of correct responses, provided it outweighs the pressure toward errors from verifier reward. Experiments with log linear and neural contextual bandits and with a language model support the analysis and show that selective control under partial auditing reduces accepted errors while increasing correctness.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes reward hacking in RLVR with imperfect verifiers, proves that standard RLVR observations cannot detect or reduce accepted errors without hurting correct responses, and proposes an audit-based correction that achieves selective control over both error and correctness probabilities.
AI.motivation: In RLVR, imperfect verifiers can mistakenly reward incorrect responses, enabling reward hacking where reward increases while true correctness declines. The paper aims to characterize when this happens and whether it can be mitigated using only the information available during RLVR.
AI.method: The authors use gradient flow with a fixed verifier to derive conditions under which reward rises while correctness falls. They then show that RLVR observations are generally insufficient to detect accepted errors or reduce them without sacrificing correct responses. To overcome this, they construct a correction based on additional correctness feedback from audits, which yields selective control: at the current policy it lowers accepted-error probability and raises correct-response probability, provided the audit signal outweighs the verifier's error pressure. They validate with log-linear and neural contextual bandits and a language model.
AI.result: The analysis establishes that reward hacking conditions exist and that standard RLVR observations are inadequate for detection/reduction of accepted errors. The audit-based correction achieves selective control, and experiments across bandits and a language model show that partial auditing reduces accepted errors while increasing correctness.
AI.conclusion: Selective control via partial auditing can counteract reward hacking in RLVR, reducing accepted errors and improving correctness, thereby addressing a fundamental limitation of verifier-based reinforcement learning.

title: Report: Progressive Disclosure of Agent Skills
summary: Users of Workday's deployed LLM-based agents often request features which can be addressed by defining named procedures, also known as skills, in the LLM context, effectively augmenting agents' capabilities. However, as an agent's skills library grows in size, so does the agent's operational cost. Progressive disclosure (lazy-loading) of skills as needed may reduce operational costs, but its impact on overall latency and skill-retrieval quality remains unclear. In this report, we investigate the impact empirically and find that progressive disclosure improves skill-retrieval quality but marginally degrades overall latency.

AI.tldr: This report empirically studies progressive disclosure (lazy-loading) of skills in Workday's deployed LLM-based agents, finding that it improves skill-retrieval quality while only marginally degrading overall latency.
AI.motivation: As an agent's skills library (named procedures defined in the LLM context) grows, so does its operational cost. Progressive disclosure of skills may reduce operational costs, but its impact on overall latency and skill-retrieval quality remains unclear.
AI.method: An empirical investigation of progressive disclosure (lazy-loading) of skills as needed in Workday's deployed LLM-based agents.
AI.result: Progressive disclosure improves skill-retrieval quality but marginally degrades overall latency.
AI.conclusion: Progressive disclosure is a favorable trade-off for scaling agents' skills libraries, delivering higher skill-retrieval quality at only a marginal latency cost.

title: Reasoning with Continuous Latent Diffusion
summary: Continuous diffusion generates complete reasoning solutions through iterative refinement in latent space. We introduce Latent Flow Reasoning Models (LFRMs), an ELF-based training and inference recipe. Our experiments show that accurate decoding alone does not ensure strong reasoning performance. We therefore learn compact representations from multiple layers of a strong autoregressive teacher. Their decomposition also enables asynchronous denoising at different rates. We show that prompt encodings need only preserve the information required for the correct text-conditional score, rather than exactly match teacher features, and use a staged curriculum to learn a compact prompt encoder that replaces the teacher Transformer at inference. We adapt DiffusionNFT to learned self-conditioning guidance and incorporate gold-solution endpoints to supplement sparse rewards. Our supervised models outperform reported results from recent continuous-diffusion baselines at comparable backbone scales on mathematical reasoning and HumanEval code generation. With a 638M-parameter denoising backbone and learned prompt conditioning, post-NFT LFRM-L achieves 63.74% pass@1 on GSM8K and 24.6% on MATH500 at 64 denoising steps, and 32.85% on HumanEval and 30.18% on HumanEval+ at 128 denoising steps. Code will be available at: https://github.com/chengxiang/LFRM

AI.tldr: LFRMs are ELF-based latent flow reasoning models that learn compact multi-layer representations from an autoregressive teacher, use a staged curriculum for a compact prompt encoder, and adapt DiffusionNFT with learned self-conditioning and gold endpoints, achieving strong math and code results at 638M scale.
AI.motivation: Accurate decoding in continuous diffusion does not guarantee strong reasoning; the paper aims to build continuous-diffusion reasoning models that match or surpass autoregressive-style reasoning quality at comparable backbone scales.
AI.method: ELF-based training and inference recipe. Learn compact representations from multiple layers of a strong autoregressive teacher, with decomposition enabling asynchronous denoising at different rates. Prompt encodings only need to preserve information for the correct text-conditional score rather than exactly match teacher features. A staged curriculum learns a compact prompt encoder that replaces the teacher Transformer at inference. Adapt DiffusionNFT to learned self-conditioning guidance and incorporate gold-solution endpoints to supplement sparse rewards.
AI.result: Supervised models outperform recent continuous-diffusion baselines at comparable backbone scales on mathematical reasoning and HumanEval code generation. With a 638M denoising backbone and learned prompt conditioning, post-NFT LFRM-L achieves 63.74% pass@1 on GSM8K and 24.6% on MATH500 at 64 denoising steps, and 32.85% on HumanEval and 30.18% on HumanEval+ at 128 denoising steps.
AI.conclusion: Continuous latent flow reasoning with compact teacher-derived representations, curriculum-learned prompt encoding, and adapted NFT guidance yields competitive reasoning and code generation performance, with code to be released.

title: Reinforcing Agentic Creativity in Scientific Ideation with Night Science
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at structured, verifiable tasks, but their low-entropy bias can produce homogeneous and predictable outputs, limiting their utility for open-ended scientific ideation. Effective discovery, however, spans a broader creative spectrum: from structured day science to loosely structured, serendipitous night science that reaches ideas beyond those typically considered. We introduce AI Night-Scientist, an agentic framework that uses reinforcement learning to teach models when and how to depart from predictable reasoning. Grounded in cognitive science, we model creativity along three axes: action (what to do and how creatively), process (when to explore versus exploit), and outcome (the novelty and usefulness of the resulting idea). We use these axes to train models with GRPO, exposing them to varying degrees and forms of creativity throughout training. This produces substantially more diverse scientific proposals, expanding the range of research directions by 27.8% and contribution types by 14.9% over the base model. It also improves predicted citation impact by up to 32.0 percentage points and originality by 66.2 points. These gains cannot be reproduced by simply increasing decoding temperature; instead, we find that semantic guidance specifying what kind of creativity to pursue is critical. Overall, our results suggest that creativity is a learnable, multi-level ability that can be shaped to help researchers reach ideas beyond those typically explored by LLMs.

AI.tldr: AI Night-Scientist is an RL-based agentic framework that trains LLMs to flexibly depart from predictable reasoning, producing more diverse, novel, and higher-impact scientific ideas.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at structured, verifiable tasks but their low-entropy bias yields homogeneous, predictable outputs, limiting open-ended scientific ideation. Effective discovery requires a broader creative spectrum, from structured "day science" to loosely structured, serendipitous "night science" that reaches unconventional ideas.
AI.method: Grounded in cognitive science, creativity is modeled along three axes—action (what to do and how creatively), process (when to explore vs. exploit), and outcome (novelty and usefulness). Models are trained with GRPO, exposing them to varying degrees and forms of creativity, with semantic guidance specifying what kind of creativity to pursue.
AI.result: The framework yields substantially more diverse scientific proposals: research directions expand by 27.8% and contribution types by 14.9% over the base model. Predicted citation impact improves by up to 32.0 percentage points and originality by 66.2 points. These gains cannot be reproduced by simply increasing decoding temperature; semantic guidance about the type of creativity is critical.
AI.conclusion: Creativity is a learnable, multi-level ability that can be shaped via reinforcement learning to help researchers reach ideas beyond those typically explored by LLMs.

title: Failure-Transparent Agents: Benchmarking Post-Failure Reporting in Tool-Using Language Models
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP 2027)
summary: Tool-using agents can fail twice: a required tool can fail, and the agent can then report success without the evidence needed to justify it. Existing benchmarks often entangle this reporting failure with tool selection, recovery, and environment dynamics. We introduce Failure-Transparent Agents (FTA), a controlled benchmark that fixes the failed observation and required evidence state before generation, making post-failure claims directly auditable. FTA contains 100 tasks with deterministic failure traces spanning five failure families, a neutral control, and four user-pressure conditions, and evaluates unsupported claims alongside useful recovery. Across six models, three response policies, and 3,600 human-annotated responses, false-success rates are 22.8% under the baseline policy, 9.3% with a transparency instruction, and 0.8% with a structured evidence contract. Fabricated-detail rates decrease from 28.3% to 14.3% and 0.8%, while useful responses increase from 74.9% to 89.2% and 98.8%, respectively. The tested evidence-contract policy is associated with substantially lower post-failure reporting errors while useful-response rates remain high within this blocked-task benchmark.

AI.tldr: FTA is a controlled benchmark of 100 tasks with deterministic tool-failure traces that isolates and audits post-failure reporting errors, showing that a structured evidence contract cuts false-success and fabricated-detail rates to under 1% while raising useful responses to 98.8%.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents face a dual failure mode: a required tool fails, and the agent then claims success without supporting evidence. Prior benchmarks confound this reporting failure with tool selection, recovery, and environment dynamics, so the honesty of post-failure claims cannot be cleanly measured.
AI.method: FTA fixes the failed observation and required evidence state before generation, making post-failure claims directly auditable. It comprises 100 tasks with deterministic failure traces across five failure families, a neutral control, and four user-pressure conditions, and jointly evaluates unsupported claims and useful recovery. Six models are tested under three response policies, yielding 3,600 human-annotated responses.
AI.result: False-success rates are 22.8% under the baseline policy, 9.3% with a transparency instruction, and 0.8% with a structured evidence contract. Fabricated-detail rates fall from 28.3% to 14.3% and 0.8%, while useful-response rates rise from 74.9% to 89.2% and 98.8%.
AI.conclusion: The evidence-contract policy is associated with substantially fewer post-failure reporting errors while keeping useful-response rates high within this blocked-task benchmark.

title: Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL
summary: People learn not only by repeating successful actions, but also by recounting and explaining their experiences, revising their understanding to guide future behavior. Can a language-model agent improve its future actions by training only on explanations of its own experience? We investigate this question by studying Retrospection-Only Fine-Tuning (ROFT), a minimal online procedure designed to isolate the effect of explanation-only training on subsequent behavior. The agent attempts a task, observes available feedback, generates a retrospective explanation, and is fine-tuned with a next-token prediction loss on the explanation tokens alone. The procedure uses neither an external teacher nor a reward-based policy update. In software-engineering experiments with Qwen3.5-4B, ROFT is trained on problems with mixed successful and unsuccessful base-model attempts. On held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro, it reaches 49.2% and 26.8% solve rates after 20 updates without using a verifier, compared with GRPO's 48.0% and 25.3% after 40 updates in the evaluated runs, and makes faster early progress in training time and sampled attempts. It also learns to solve individual tasks on which all 64 sampled base-model attempts failed, showing that learning can begin without any initially successful trajectories. Behavioral analyses find that ROFT indirectly assigns credit to actions, encouraging good actions and discouraging incorrect ones. Moreover, prompting retrospections to emphasize more direct solutions yields shorter subsequent attempts even without an explicit length penalty. Together, these findings show that learning to explain can also improve learning to do, establishing self-generated retrospections as useful training targets and motivating further study of explanation-to-action transfer.

AI.tldr: ROFT fine-tunes a language-model agent only on self-generated retrospective explanations of its own task attempts, with no verifier or reward-based policy update, and it improves future task performance in software-engineering benchmarks, even matching or exceeding GRPO with fewer updates.
AI.motivation: People improve not only by repeating successful actions but also by explaining experiences and revising their understanding. The paper asks whether a language-model agent can improve its future actions by training only on explanations of its own experience, isolating the effect of explanation-only learning on subsequent behavior.
AI.method: Retrospection-Only Fine-Tuning (ROFT): a minimal online procedure. The agent attempts a task, observes available feedback, generates a retrospective explanation, and is fine-tuned with a next-token prediction loss on the explanation tokens alone. It uses neither an external teacher nor a reward-based policy update. Tested with Qwen3.5-4B on software-engineering problems containing mixed successful and unsuccessful base-model attempts.
AI.result: On held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro, ROFT reaches 49.2% and 26.8% solve rates after 20 updates without a verifier, versus GRPO's 48.0% and 25.3% after 40 updates, with faster early progress in training time and sampled attempts. It also solves individual tasks on which all 64 sampled base-model attempts failed. Behavioral analyses show ROFT indirectly assigns credit to actions, encouraging good actions and discouraging incorrect ones, and prompting retrospections toward more direct solutions yields shorter attempts without an explicit length penalty.
AI.conclusion: Learning to explain can also improve learning to do, establishing self-generated retrospections as useful training targets and motivating further study of explanation-to-action transfer.

title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
summary: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics that reflect expert standards and fix the values correct as of an information cutoff. Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. This expert guidance governs every agent, as prompts and as rules that code enforces, and a Task Bank of reusable criteria carries it across tasks. In long-horizon loops that follow the expert guidance, a writer agent researches every expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, and failures escalate to a human. On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, its rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria, their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark, built from in-house analysts' key questions across 78 tasks and eight asset classes, shows that rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.

AI.tldr: FinAutoRubric replaces costly fixed per-item expert rubrics with a system where experts write reusable guidance that agents and code use to automatically generate, review, and validate query-specific rubrics for finance research agents.
AI.motivation: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics reflecting expert standards with values correct at an information cutoff. Existing expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics that are costly to extend and cannot encode individual institutions' own standards.
AI.method: Experts specify reusable evaluation guidance; agents and code then perform query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. Expert guidance governs every agent both as prompts and as code-enforced rules, with a Task Bank of reusable criteria carrying it across tasks. In long-horizon loops, a writer agent researches each expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, with failures escalating to a human.
AI.result: On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, FinAutoRubric rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria; their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark spans 78 tasks and eight asset classes and shows rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.
AI.conclusion: Reusable expert guidance combined with agent- and code-driven rubric generation yields scalable, institution-adaptable finance evaluation rubrics that match expert scoring, agree with human grading, and are preferred by analysts, while the new benchmark exposes remaining headroom for future models.
